%===========================================================================
\phantomsection\section*{The point}
\label{sec:point}
%===========================================================================

Here's the whole thing before any of the careful parts. I'm going to start with one small picture,
take it apart, and keep asking what each piece means, as far down as I can get before I hit
something that holds or something I can't get under. I'll tell you which. Then I'll put it back
together at the end and you can check whether it still stands.

One warning about how this went, because it explains the shape of everything after it. Most of the
time I had the hunch first and found the names later. Over and over, somebody had been here before
me. Sometimes that made my day. Sometimes it pissed me off. You'll see both.

\subsection*{Two computers that end up the same}

Put two computers on a table. Hand each of them the same list of a thousand numbers.

The first one sorts it. It compares, swaps, walks the list again and again until nothing is out of
order. Then it does one more thing: it walks the whole list front to back and checks that every
number is no bigger than the one after it. That check could have failed. It passes. Then it tidies
up after itself, wipes its scratch work, and leaves the sorted list in memory. (That check compares
neighbours, so what it settles is that the output is in order. That the output holds your
thousand numbers and no others is a second claim, and it would take a second check comparing the
output with the input. When I say sorted below, I mean in order.)

The second one never looks at your list. Somebody typed the sorted version into it earlier, same
thousand numbers, same order, and it puts them in memory.

Now wait until both are done and look inside. Same bits in memory. Same bits on the screen. Set it
up right, which you can, and it's the same everything, down to the last bit. One of them found
something out about your list and stood behind it. The other one is holding identical bits and found
out nothing. Wheel them out on a cart, swap them, wheel them back, and ask me which is which. I
can't tell you. You can't tell me. And the part that bugs me most: built the ordinary way, neither
machine can tell you either.

Sure, while they ran they were different. One did thousands of comparisons, the other did a copy.
But the runs are over and the runs are gone, and nobody was being sloppy. Ordinary computers are
built to forget how their bits got there, on purpose. Later in this chapter there's the sentence
where a physicist said so in 1961, and why he said it costs heat.

Who cares? Anybody who's been handed a sheet that says ``all tests passed.'' Anybody who's looked at
an inspection sticker on a windshield: the sticker looks the same whether somebody checked the
brakes or somebody sold the sticker. An audit, a proof, a ledger, an AI that sounds very sure of
itself: every one of them is a pile of bits that could have come out of either computer, and the
question that matters is the one the bits can't answer. Did something establish this, or did it just
print it? I'll come back to every one of those at the end of this chapter and say which of them this
book actually helps with. Fair warning: fewer than you'd hope.

I'm going to call the difference \emph{established}. The first machine established that your list is
sorted. The second has the same answer and established nothing. The rest of this chapter is me
taking that one word apart.

\subsection*{Look harder}

The obvious answer is: just look harder. Don't look at the end, look at everything. So make the
computers as lookable as computers get. Scale them up to the size of a warehouse, every wire a
lamp that's lit or dark, every switch something you can walk up to and touch. Nothing hidden in a
chip too small to see. Put both of them side by side and walk the floor.

While they run, sure, you'd see the difference. One has a whole wing lighting up, comparing and
swapping, and the other just copies. But they finish. The comparing wing goes dark. Now walk the
floor and look at every single lamp. The sorted list is spelled out in lit and dark lamps in both,
the same pattern, and everything else is dark in both, because both cleaned up.

There is no lamp anywhere that says ``a check ran here and passed.'' Not hidden. Not encrypted. Just
not there. You can see everything there is, and the thing I'm after isn't one of the things there
is. Looking harder doesn't help, because the problem isn't that you can't see enough. It's that
nothing was kept.

That's the shape I want you to carry through the rest: the problem was never visibility. It's keeping.

\subsection*{So keep the trace}

Then the fix is obvious, isn't it? Don't let the run go. Keep the trace: every comparison, every
swap, the check and its answer, written down as it happens. Wheel the computers out on the cart and
back, read the traces, and you'll know which one sorted. Problem solved?

It's the right instinct, and it gets most of the way to this book. But take it apart, because
``just keep the trace'' has three things wrong with it, and each one is a piece of
what comes later.

First, a trace is bits, and bits can be typed in. Whoever typed the sorted list into the second
machine can type a trace in too: ``compared, swapped, checked, passed,'' a few thousand lines of
it, every one of them plausible. A trace written by a program is something the program produced,
and the machine running the program doesn't care whether it's true. So keeping the trace doesn't
answer the question. It moves it. Did something establish this trace, or did it just print it?

Second, the way out of that is to take the pen away from the program. Don't let the program write
its own trace. Have something underneath it write the trace, one step at a time, as the steps
actually happen, so nothing a program does can add a line that didn't happen or erase one that
did. Airplanes do a version of this. Flight recorders go back to a prototype David Warren built in
Melbourne in the 1950s. He was an Australian scientist at the Aeronautical Research Laboratories,
working on jet fuel, and after a string of unexplained airliner crashes he wanted a box that would
hold the instrument readings and the voices in the cockpit for whoever came looking afterwards; I
know his story from museum and encyclopedia accounts, and I haven't read his own report. The
recorders that came out of that idea are fed by the aircraft's own instruments. Nobody's account of
events goes into them. And they're built to survive the crash, so the investigators don't have to
depend on anyone's memory of what happened. That's the right shape, and it isn't mine. Later in
this chapter it gets its name from computer security, a reference monitor, and I'll say outright
that a machine built that way would be doing what this book describes. What the book adds is
narrower than a rulebook for everything underneath. It's about the records that go up and never
come back down: what that something has to keep for good, and what keeping it costs.

Third, you can't keep all of it. A full trace grows with every step and never stops growing, and a
machine with finite memory runs out. Even the flight recorder doesn't keep everything. The cockpit
voice recorder is a loop. I went looking for how long the loop is, and it has kept growing: for
decades it held the last thirty minutes, an American rule in 2008 raised that to at least two
hours, and big airliners built since 2021 carry twenty-five hours. Whatever the length, everything older
gets recorded over. Every real machine that keeps a trace keeps a
window of it, or a fingerprint of it, and forgets the content.

The fingerprint is the sharpest reply, so take it seriously. Fold every new line of the trace
into a fixed-size scramble of everything before it, and you've got a hash chain. The timestamps of
Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, two cryptographers at Bellcore whose story comes later in this
chapter, work that way; so do the audit logs the cryptographers Bruce Schneier
and John Kelsey designed in 1999; and so do the measurement registers in the security chip a lot
of computers carry, the TPM. A running program can only extend those registers, folding a new
measurement in. It can't write a value of its own into them, and the ones that matter here start over only at the next
reboot. That really does keep something about the whole trace in a few dozen bytes. But look at
what it keeps. It keeps a binding. The content isn't in it: to read the history you still need the trace
stored somewhere, and the fingerprint only tells you whether a copy somebody hands you is the one
that went in. The binding holds only because nobody knows how to find two traces with the same
fingerprint, which is a bet on how hard a search is. No law of nature backs it. That part isn't only my opinion.
The computer scientists Moni Naor and Guy Rothblum proved a sharp version of it in 2005, and they even call the thing a
fingerprint: keep a small private fingerprint of a big file somebody else stores, check the file
by reading only a little of it, and against an opponent with unlimited computing the size of the
fingerprint times the amount you read has to be on the order of the whole file. Do even slightly
better than that against an opponent with limited computing, and you've shown that one-way
functions exist, which is the hardness bet in its barest form. Their setting is a stored file. A
growing trace is a different setting, but it's the same bet, with its terms written down. And squeezing traces that keep
growing into a fixed number of bits has to land many traces on one fingerprint. That's a merge, hidden behind how hard it is to find which traces share a seat. It's the
same merge as the people and chairs further down, where four people have to sit in three chairs. Fingerprints are great. They're not a way out of forgetting. They're a very clever way of
forgetting.

So the real question was never ``save everything.'' It's this:
what's the smallest thing worth keeping for good, and what does keeping it cost? The answer this
book ends up with is the commitment, in the database's sense, a question closed, and the trace
drops away. (The cryptographer's sealed envelope also goes by the name commitment. It's a different
thing, and both come up later.) Not every comparison the sort made. Just the
one fact that a check of this very claim passed and the question got closed. And here's the part
that matters most: on a finite machine, keeping even that one fact for good forces the machine to
forget something somewhere else. That's the chairs, further down. And keeping things for good
fills up, which Part II turns into a count.

So the premise was never that computers can't keep records. They keep records all day. It's that
nothing in the rules of an ordinary computer makes the record paid for, permanent, or earned, and
those three come in at different places, so here's where. Paid for is the model's one rule: in the
Thiele Machine, the step that raises the record has to cost something. Permanent is a premise, the
one the chairs need, and one of the conditions Part III puts on a record. Earned, meaning a check
of this very claim passed first, isn't in the model's core at all. It's what the step of the small
machine in Part IV enforces, proved for that machine and every program on it run from a clean start. One more word rides
along with permanent, and it'll come up when I line my record up against other people's: dated. A
record that goes up and stays up went up at some particular step. The first raising occurs at a
definite step in the execution history. The latch itself does not store that step number. So
dated, in this book, means dated in the execution history, and carrying a timestamp is a
different property that the record doesn't have. A machine that charges one mark for every step it takes meets the first rule, and the charging does
nothing toward
the others, and I'll keep pointing that out.

\subsection*{Computed, stored, established}

Three words that get used like they're one.

\emph{Computed} is about the steps. The first machine computed the sorted list. The second didn't.

\emph{Stored} is about the bits. Both machines stored it.

\emph{Established} is neither, and that's the whole problem. It isn't the steps, because they're gone. It
isn't the bits, because they're identical. It's something like this: the first machine has a right
to lean on ``this list is sorted,'' because it ran a test that could have failed, the test passed, the
test was about this very list, and then the question got closed. The second machine has the same
sentence and no right to it. That's a true fact about the two of them, and it's written down
nowhere, in either one. (Whose right, strictly? A machine doesn't lean on anything, any more than a
filing cabinet does. It's the right of whoever reads the first machine to lean on what it says, and
the machine is where the grounds for that right would have to be kept. ``The machine has a right''
is shorter, so I'll keep saying it, and now you know what it's short for.)

Four words I'll hold still from here on. A \emph{check} is the test, the thing that could say no. A
\emph{commit} is the closing, the question shut for good, about that edition of that thing. The
\emph{record} is whatever stays behind to say so. And \emph{established} is all three, about one thing.
That's the working sense. The book cashes it at three depths: a paid closing in the bare model; an
object with a checked relation and a paid event, in Part III; and the whole chain on the small
machine, in Part IV. Each place says which one it means.

Which raises a fair question. What if the second machine, handed the typed-in list, runs the check
on it? Then it has established that the list is sorted. Full stop. It didn't do the sorting and it
doesn't need to. The line I'm drawing is between checked and unchecked. Whether the list was
computed or copied doesn't enter into it, and ``found out nothing'' up there was about the copier that never looked. So whatever this
book ends up counting, it isn't how hard anybody worked.

People say ``a right to lean on it'' about a lot of things that turn out to be vibes, so I had to find
out whether this one was anything. So I went looking. Here's what I ran into.

\subsection*{The clerk who forgets everything}

The picture of a computer I started with is a person with a pencil, a strip of paper and a short
list of rules. So I went back to the source, Alan Turing's 1936 paper, to see how far he actually
takes it.

He takes it a long way. Back then a ``computer'' was a job, a human doing sums by hand, and Turing
modelled that person. He's careful with the person's mind: whatever the clerk knows, beyond a
handful of states, has to go down on the paper. Then he goes all the way. He imagines the clerk
getting up, walking off, forgetting everything, and coming back later. To pick up where he left
off, the clerk leaves himself ``a note of instructions,'' and Turing says that note \emph{is} the clerk's
state of mind, as far as the computation is concerned. Marks on paper and a note. That's the whole
state.

My two computers are sitting right inside that. Suppose the clerk didn't write the note. Somebody
slipped it under the door, in the right form, with the right instructions. He comes back, reads it,
carries on, and every mark he makes from then on is exactly what he'd have made if he'd written it
himself. Turing's model can't tell the clerk who did the work from the clerk who was handed a note
saying he did. It was never asked to. Turing wanted something you could check without crawling into
anybody's head, and a note on a desk is about as checkable as it gets. That's why the paper still
works ninety years later. It's also why there's no place in it for the thing I'm after.

So the founding picture of computing is a man who leaves his desk, forgets everything he was doing,
and trusts a sticky note. I relate to him deeply.

And now the question nobody needs answered to follow the argument, which is exactly the kind I
can't leave alone: who were those clerks? Real people. In the late 1800s the Harvard Observatory hired rooms full of women to
do the arithmetic of the sky, cataloguing stars by hand for a fraction of a man's wage, and some of
them made discoveries of their own, Henrietta Leavitt's way of telling how far away a star is among
them. (I took the wages and the discoveries from Dava Sobel's history of those women, and from the
historians at the American Institute of Physics, who put the men's hourly pay at nearly five times
the women's.) Rooms like that ran artillery tables in both world wars; that part I took from David Alan Grier's history of human computers. So when Turing modelled ``the computer,'' he was modelling somebody's actual
afternoon. Does that change the argument? Not a bit. But it changes the picture, for me anyway: the
sticky note was always a person trusting another person's work, and the question of whether the
work behind it was really done is older than any machine.

\subsection*{Information doesn't have it either}

My next guess was information: one machine got some, the other didn't. That one died fast. Claude
Shannon, who turned information into a number in 1948, says on his first page that the meaning of a
message is ``irrelevant to the engineering problem.'' His number measures how many messages you
\emph{could} have sent. What the one you sent did is outside it, which is exactly right for building telephone
lines and exactly no help to me. Same message out of the same set, same number, for both computers.
He'd give them the same number if one of them got hit by lightning and came out right by luck.

Fine, forget the set and look at the one message. In the 1960s three people, separately, worked
out how to measure the information in one string: Ray Solomonoff, an American who was after a theory
of guessing what comes next from what came before; Andrei Kolmogorov, the great Soviet mathematician; and Gregory Chaitin, an Argentine-American mathematician who later worked at IBM. Their measure is
the length of the shortest program that prints the string. Same two computers, same string, same number. And
then there's the thing in that theory I keep going back to and standing on, to see if it creaks.
Running a program can't add this kind of information. What comes out can't hold more than what went
in plus the program, give or take a little. Leonid Levin, who studied under Kolmogorov in Moscow and
later left the Soviet Union to teach at Boston University, proved a general version of this, and he has
a one-liner for it that's too good not to repeat: you can torture an uninformed witness all you
want, you won't get information about the crime.

Which means, as far as information goes, sorting your list told you nothing. The sorted list holds
nothing that ``your list, plus the word \emph{sort}'' didn't already hold.

Logic says the same thing in a different coat. The standard logic of knowing, the
one the Finnish philosopher Jaakko Hintikka worked out in 1962, has a property people call logical omniscience: if you know
some facts, you automatically know everything that follows from them. So by that logic, once you
knew every number on your list, you already knew whether it was sorted. Hintikka flagged the problem
himself, in the same book, and people have been trying to fix it since. The fixes read like a pile
until I asked each one the same thing: when it lets you write \emph{known} next to ``sorted,'' what
does it make you write in the margin? Hintikka's margin is empty. Each fix writes one thing there.

The fix that comes closest to me is from 1995, by Sergei Artemov, a logician now at the City University of New York
who studied under that same Kolmogorov (the 1995 report came out of Cornell). He wanted a logic that could
name the proof itself. What I think he's saying: you only get to know a thing if you've built an actual
justification for it, and the justification rides along with the claim. That's a reason traveling
with the claim, which is almost a record. Only almost, because it's a way of writing things down and reasoning about
them, and nothing in his margin says the reason was ever run, or when.
People have taught it to count, too: Ho Ngoc Duc, a logician at Leipzig, in 1997, made knowing
take reasoning steps, and Artemov and Roman Kuznets, a logician then at Bern, in 2014, asked how big a justification can get before knowing by it
stops being feasible. I took those for rivals at first. As I read them now, Duc counts the
steps the knower takes and Artemov and Kuznets weigh what you'd hand somebody to check it, one
distance from two ends. It has a computational side, too: Francisco Bavera and Eduardo Bonelli, two Argentine computer
scientists who work on what programming languages mean, in 2018 turned justification logic into a lambda calculus whose terms carry, and can inspect, the
history of the computation that made them, and Samuel Bucheli, Meghdad Ghari and Thomas Studer, three logicians, Studer the head of the logic group at Bern, put justifications on a time line in 2017, where they persist and change.

Line that up against the margin this book wants: earned, paid for, permanent, dated. Artemov's
reason is nearly earned, the steps and the sizes are prices, the time line is a date. Their
time line keeps its dates. Mine is dated only in the execution history: the raise happened at a
definite step, and the latch doesn't keep the step number. What none of it has
is the closing of a question as a step with a price. Their prices are on reasoning, and the Bern
justifications change, the one thing a closed question doesn't do. Push on mine, though, and it gives twice. Artemov's margin holds the reason itself, and mine only
says a check passed. And their prices grow with how hard the thing was to know. This book charges the
step that raises the record, and how long the checking took never enters it, so for a measure of
effort, read theirs.

So the two most careful accounts I could find, one about bits and one about knowing, say the same
thing: the sort added nothing.

And yet you know something after the sort that you didn't before. You can read the smallest number
off the first slot. You can stop worrying. Something happened. That's the clue, and it's the first
solid thing I've got: whatever
\emph{established} is, it isn't new bits. It's the same bits, \emph{settled}.

\subsection*{The guy who got closest}

Somebody had that clue before me, and on that clue he's the closest neighbour I've found, so he gets the most room
and the hardest push.

Charles Bennett, a physicist at IBM, wrote a paper in 1988 that starts where I just ended up:
information isn't the same as value. His example is an almanac of where the moon and planets will
be every day for a hundred years. It has no more information than the equations it was calculated
from, but it saves you doing the calculating. So the value is the work. He called the amount of
work a thing carries its \emph{depth}.

Was this my idea, already done, by a guy at IBM? The only way to find out was to find where it
parts from mine, because if I couldn't find that place I'd just be renaming his idea. And it's one
word: \emph{plausibly}. Depth is the amount of work a thing was \emph{plausibly} made with. Bennett says
straight out that you can't know how a message actually came to be; for all you know it came from
flipping coins. Depth is read off the finished thing, the way a fossil's age is read off the
fossil.

Bring the two computers back. The sorted list in the first one has some depth. The identical list in
the second has exactly the same depth, because depth looks at the list and nothing else. A
photocopy of a deep thing is just as deep. Depth tells you \emph{some} work was done, somewhere, by
someone. It's not a record that \emph{this} machine did it, and it's not a receipt for what doing it
cost.

So Bennett's standing right next to the line, on the other side of it, and as far as I can tell he
got his own question right. He asked how much work a thing embodies. I'm asking who has the right to
lean on it and what they paid to get there. His answer lives in the object. Mine, if I've got one,
has to live in the machine.

\subsection*{Statues that walk off}

If it isn't in the information, maybe it's in the knowing, so I went and read the philosophers.
And there it was again: people had been arguing about the difference between having the right
answer and knowing it for a couple thousand years.

Plato's version is a joke about statues. There was a story that the sculptor Daedalus made statues
so lifelike they'd walk off if you didn't tie them down. Plato says true opinions are like that:
they wander off, and they're not worth much until you tie them down with the reason why. Once
they're tied down, they're knowledge, and they stay put. Knowledge tied to a reason, and knowledge
that stays. Of everybody I'd have bet on to hand me that shape, Plato wasn't on the list.

Then in 1963 a philosopher named Edmund Gettier broke the tidy version in three pages. Smith and Jones are up for the same job. Smith has good reason to think
Jones will get it, and he's counted the coins in Jones's pocket: ten. So Smith figures, with good reason, that
the man who'll get the job has ten coins in his pocket. Then Smith gets the job, and, unknown to
him, Smith also has ten coins in his pocket. True, believed, backed by a reason. Not knowledge. He
was right by luck, because his reason was about the wrong pocket.

That's the push that matters for a machine. Checking one pocket and committing to a claim about
another is right by luck. So whatever a machine commits to, the check underneath has to be about
\emph{this very claim}, and I'd better say exactly what that means, because it carries a lot of weight
later.

A check is about this very claim when four things hold. It tests the same property the commit names.
A cousin of that property won't do. It tests that property on the same thing the commit names, and
the thing next to it won't do either. Nothing has written to that thing between the check and the commit, so it's still the same
edition the check looked at. And the check is honest: it says yes when the property is true and no
when it isn't, on every value it could ever be handed, this one and all the others. Break the first three and
you're Smith with his ten coins. Break the fourth and the check is just a rubber stamp. Later in the
book I build a machine whose step won't let a commit through unless the first three hold, and whose
checks come with a proof of the fourth.

Two notes on those four, because they matter later. The fourth asks for more than it needs. To rule
out luck, a check only has to never say yes when the property is false; saying yes every time it's
true is a bonus. And the third is a very old bug in computing wearing Gettier's coat. Security people
call it time-of-check-to-time-of-use: check a file, use it, and something swaps the file in between
(Matt Bishop and Michael Dilger, two computer security researchers at the University of California,
Davis, wrote up how to hunt for it in 1996). Databases guard against the
same thing by making sure, just before a commit, that nothing they read has been written since;
H. T. Kung and John Robinson, two computer scientists at Carnegie-Mellon, called that optimistic concurrency control in 1981. A philosopher's
pocket and a sysadmin's race condition, same bug. One limit, said now: a machine can only promise
``nothing has written to that thing'' about its own memory; for brake pads or a voter roll the
third condition becomes a premise about whoever measured (Section~\ref{sec:models}).

And here's where I went further than this chapter needs, because the obvious next question is:
does anything fix Gettier? People tried for years. The first patch is ``no false steps in the
reasoning'': Smith's mistake was believing Jones would get the job, so rule that out. Then a
philosopher named Alvin Goldman came back with barns, and he credits the barns to Carl Ginet,
another philosopher working on what it takes to know something. You're driving
through a county that, unknown to you, is full of fake barns, just painted fronts propped up to look
like the real thing. You look at the one real barn in the county and think ``that's a barn.'' True. Believed. Good
reason, your own eyes, and no false step anywhere. And still you were lucky: if you'd glanced at
the next one over you'd have believed the same thing and been wrong. Every patch gets a new barn,
and as far as I can tell the arguing hasn't stopped. Which tells me something I'll keep: whether a
check was good isn't only about this one case. It's about what the check would have done on the
cases next door. Hold on to that, because it's the next section.

\subsection*{What ``could have failed'' means}

I keep saying the first machine's test \emph{could have failed}. Take that apart, because it's the
piece everything else hangs off.

The machine is deterministic. Given your list, the check was always going to pass. So in what sense
could it have failed? By ``could have failed'' I mean this: hand the checking stage an out-of-order
candidate output and it says no. I do not mean hand the whole sorter an unsorted input; putting
that input in order is its job. The relevant counterfactual is a defective candidate reaching the
checker. An ordinary unsorted input reaching the sorter isn't it. Chance has nothing to do with
it. The copier that never checks has no corresponding rejection.

Here's the shape. A check is a question asked of every possible input, and it splits them into two
piles: the ones it says yes to and the ones it says no to. ``Could have failed'' just means the no
pile isn't empty. A check that says yes to everything has an empty no pile, and it distinguishes no
inputs, however long it runs and however official it looks. It can still be sound, when its
property holds of everything, and then it's sound and tells you nothing you didn't have. A philosopher, Robert Nozick, made a
version of this a condition for knowing, in 1981: you know a thing only if, had it been false, you
wouldn't believe it.

Push on it once more, because this is where it really gives. ``Could have failed'' is a fact about the
\emph{procedure}, about what the check would have done on other lists. It isn't a fact about the end
state at all. Look at the first machine's memory when it's done: a sorted list. Nothing in those
bits says ``and whatever made me would have caught a mistake.'' That's the warehouse again, every
lamp visible and none of them saying it. The one thing that makes the first machine's answer
worth more is exactly the kind of thing those bits can't hold: the copier ends with the same
bits, and neither machine kept anything else. An end state can hold more than the answer, and the
only way a machine can own this
is to write something down at the moment the check passes, and to have that something mean what it
says. More than anything else in this chapter, that's why I ended up needing a record. A better
answer wouldn't have done it. Even then the record only carries half of it. It can say a check ran on an
edition and passed. That the check would have said no on a bad list is a fact about the checker,
and that half rides on a proof about the checker, which somebody outside the machine has to read
and accept. Where that kind of chain of reasons stops is the swamp of the philosopher Karl Popper, a little further down.

One more thing that tripped me up and then didn't. Rig a check to pass only on your one list. Is
that cheating? No. It's a perfectly honest check of a different claim, ``this is that exact list,''
and it has a big no pile: every other list. It establishes exactly that and nothing more. What a
check establishes is whatever it's honest about.

Put that next to the empty no pile and the two fit together: a check establishes what it's honest
about. An empty no-pile means the check distinguishes no inputs. It can still be sound for a
property that holds on every input; soundness and nontriviality are different requirements. One
thing I'll say plainly now, so it doesn't ambush you in Part IV: the small machine I build there
doesn't police this. Its step makes sure a commit was checked first, about the same thing, by a
checker proved honest. It doesn't stop you asking a question that can't come out no, like ``is this
number at least zero.'' Ask one and the whole chain runs, three marks paid, and nothing is
established but the chain. The certificate I show off there asks one that can fail.

\subsection*{Settled, whether it's true or not}

Then I ran into Charles Sanders Peirce, an American scientist and philosopher, in an 1877 essay called ``The Fixation of Belief.'' He was asking what inquiry is for, and his answer named the thing I'd been running together without noticing. The point of inquiry, he says, is to get out of doubt and settle on a
belief. And when someone objects that surely what people want is a \emph{true} belief, he answers like a
guy who's watched a lot of arguments end: ``as soon as a firm belief is reached we are entirely
satisfied, whether the belief be true or false.''

That's funny, and then it isn't, because he's right. Settling and being right are two different
events. A question can be closed on a wrong answer, and once it's closed it acts closed. Peirce cares
a lot about which ways of settling hold up (science wins, for him, because it has to answer to
something outside any one person), but the settling itself, the question snapping shut, is there
every time, and it never comes with a guarantee.

Karl Popper came at it from the other side. He was a philosopher from Vienna asking what separates
science from everything else, and in his 1934 book, the one that came into English as \emph{The Logic
of Scientific Discovery}, he says every test has to stop somewhere, at some
statement somebody decides to accept, and nothing in the evidence forces you to stop there instead
of one step further. You stop when you're satisfied. His picture is a jury: the verdict is a
decision about what happened, and the jury deciding it doesn't make it true. Science, for him, is a
building on piles driven into a swamp, and the piles stop where somebody's satisfied they'll hold.
They never reach firm ground.

A real jury has a problem Popper doesn't mention, because a real jury is twelve people.
Lewis Kornhauser and Lawrence Sager, two law professors writing in the Yale Law Journal, noticed in 1986 that a court that votes by majority on
each premise of a case and also on the verdict can end up contradicting itself: every judge
is consistent, and the court isn't. Christian List and Philip Pettit, two philosophers writing
in Economics and Philosophy, turned that in 2002
into a theorem. No way of combining people's yes-or-no judgments on connected questions
meets a short list of conditions that each look harmless on their own and always hands back a consistent,
complete group judgment. A group's settling is a rule's settling, and which rule you pick
decides which of the honest settlings sticks. I haven't tried to put a group on the
machine, and that's where I'd expect the first wall to be.

Popper's swamp sent me further down, because it's the oldest problem in the book and it doesn't have a
bottom. Ask why you believe something and you get a reason. Ask why you believe the reason and you
get another one. Sextus Empiricus, a skeptic and doctor who lived probably in the second or third century and
whose whole method was holding off judgment, wrote down the ancient version, credited to someone called
Agrippa, and in 1968 the German philosopher Hans Albert, who with Popper led the school called critical rationalism, gave it a name with a joke in it: the
Münchhausen trilemma, after the baron who claimed he pulled himself out of a swamp by his own hair.
Every chain of reasons does one of three things. It goes on forever. It loops back on itself. Or it
stops somewhere, because somebody decided it stops. People have argued for a very long time about
which of the three to live with. So ``when do I actually know, and when am I done checking?'' doesn't get a clean answer
from anybody. What you can do is be honest about where you stopped and why. That's a lot of what
the rest of this book is: every place it stops is written down, with its name on it, so you can
decide whether you'd have stopped there too.

Lay Peirce and Popper on top of each other and here's what shows through. The check is one act. The stopping
is another. The check can run as long as you like and it never \emph{makes} you stop; at some point
something decides, and the deciding is its own event. That's the second machine's whole trick: it
skipped the check and kept the answer.

And a logician said the part I didn't expect a logician to say. Per Martin-Löf, a Swedish logician whose type theory sits underneath the kind of proof checker that
checks this book, says a proof is an act, and once it's done it's done. His
words, from lectures he gave in Siena in 1983: ``a proof is, not an object, but an act \ldots{} Only
secondarily, and irrevocably, does it become the act that has been performed.'' That took me a few
reads, and the tenses unlocked it: first the act being done, then, for good, the act that has been
done. You could say that's true of everything that ever
happened. Fine. But it's the two computers again: the first machine's check happened, irrevocably,
and the machine right now carries no trace of it. The past can't be undone. The \emph{record} of it can
be lost, unless something keeps one. That gap is where this book lives.

Then the intuitionists got there first, which by now I should've expected. The Dutch mathematician L.~E.~J. Brouwer, who held that a mathematical truth is something a mind
makes evident, argued from 1948 on about an idealised mathematician working in stages, the creating
subject. The people after him only came clear to me once I sorted them by three words: the act, the
object, and the trace the act leaves behind, which Martin-Löf's sentence has no room for. The logician Georg Kreisel (1967), Austrian-born and then at Stanford, wrote it down as a formula: the subject has evidence for
$A$ at stage $n$. That's a trace, something you can come back and ask about after the act is over. Anne Troelstra (1969), a Dutch logician who studied under Brouwer's student
Arend Heyting and became one of the leading authorities on intuitionism, added that the
subject never forgets what it has made evident, so the trace never fades. That's how Mark van Atten (2018), a philosopher in Paris who has spent years on Brouwer, credits it; the
Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on intuitionism lists the never-forgets axiom among Kreisel's own, and I
haven't settled which is right. Van Atten, going through the whole history, reads the formula as ``by stage $n$ the Creating Subject has made $A$ evident.'' Look at the
tense. \emph{Has made} is Martin-Löf's ``the act that has been performed,'' reached from the other
end. And look at
what that carries. It's tied to a stage; at any stage you can ask whether it's happened yet; it
never goes away; and it's never wrong. Van Atten even says the subject can't just accept a proof
handed to it from outside: it has to go through the steps and rebuild the evidence itself. That's
the copier who runs the check. And then there's G\"oran Sundholm, a philosopher of logic at Leiden. He has long kept a proof as an act
apart from a proof as an object (1998), and, as I understand his work, apart from its trace as well.
In a 2014 paper he worked through how Brouwer's theory of the creating subject sits beside the thesis
that every effective procedure is a program, which is the side this book's machines live on. I
know that second paper only by what it sets out to do, so I lean on it lightly.

Set their trace beside my record and the columns nearly all fill: their stage is my dated, their never
forgetting my permanent, their never wrong my earned. Their stage is written into the trace,
though, and my dated is only a step in the run that the latch doesn't keep. The empty one is the price, and I think
I see why. For a mind with unlimited memory, never forgetting costs nothing. A finite machine pays to
keep anything for good, and that's the chairs, still to come.
So it's the closest thing to my \emph{established} that I've found. The formula is around sixty
years old, and the idea under it, Brouwer's creating subject, is older than that. Push on my side
from theirs, though, and it gives twice. Van Atten's subject won't take a proof from outside,
and my machine takes exactly one: its checker is trusted on a proof about the checker that somebody
did outside every run. And their evidence is never wrong because, for Brouwer, made evident is what
true means. Mine is right only as far as that checker is honest. Where they differ, the difference is honest: their subject is an idealised mind with
unlimited time and memory, and mine is a machine with a finite table that establishes only the
claims its program checks.

\subsection*{Not a switch}

So far I've been talking about \emph{established} as if it were a light switch: on or off, the first
computer on and the second one off. That bothered me the whole time I was writing it, and for a
while I couldn't say why. It felt too small, the way a word can be technically right and still not
cover what you're pointing at. I don't trust that feeling on its own, because I've had it plenty of
times about things that turned out to be nothing. So I went looking for something outside my own head
that would either give the feeling something to stand on or show me I was imagining it.

I didn't know what I was looking for, at first, beyond a rough shape: two things that look exactly the
same and differ in how far something about them has been settled. So I started collecting anything
that seemed to have that shape, and most of what I collected fell apart as soon as I looked at it
closely. How each one fell apart taught me more than the thing itself did, so I'll go through them
in the order it happened. Every story below is the version I could piece together from the records I
could reach, and where I couldn't reach a record I'll say so. Check me.

The first batch was all hidden things. A pea under one of three cups. A tree, whose age you can't see
from the outside. A forged painting that looks right until somebody tests the paint. A glass of gas,
where the thermometer shows one temperature and underneath there are uncountably many arrangements of
molecules that would all show the same reading. Plato's prisoners in the cave, who see shadows on a
wall. The things casting them stay behind their backs (Section~\ref{sec:windows} tells their story). Every one of these looked promising for about a minute. Then I noticed they
all fail the same way: look harder and the hidden thing shows up. Lift the cup. Cut the trunk and count
the rings. Run the paint test. Look at the molecules, at least in principle. Turn around in the cave.
In each case the hidden part is a fact about the object that better eyes could find. That isn't what
the two computers have. You can see every lamp in the warehouse and not find the check.

That failure gave me the first real tool I had, and it's a crude one. Give an observer perfect vision of
the visible thing, as much detail as they want, and ask whether they could read the difference off it.
If they could, it's something hidden, and that's not what I'm after. If they couldn't, it might be. I
want to be honest about how much weight that test can hold. It's a judgment, and I'm the one making it,
with whatever blind spots I have. Somebody careful can look straight at the evidence and still read it
wrong, because of what they expected to see. So I treat the test as a way of sorting my own examples.
It isn't a verdict, and if you find a case where it sorts wrongly, that tells me something about the test
and about me.

The second batch got past that test and failed a different way. A clock face reads three o'clock and
doesn't show how many days have gone by; no amount of staring at the face tells you. And a computer can
keep a complete history of what it did. That one has a story behind it. In 1961 Rolf Landauer, a
physicist at IBM, argued that a computer has to give off heat whenever it throws information away, and
that real computers throw information away all the time. Twelve years later a younger colleague of his,
Charles Bennett, asked whether they had to. His answer, in a 1973 paper, was no. A machine can write down
every step it takes, copy out its answer, and then run itself backward, retracing its steps and wiping
the history as it goes, until it holds only the input and the answer and has never thrown anything
away. It costs about twice the steps and a lot of scratch paper, and that's all it costs. Bennett thanks
Landauer at the end for raising the question in the first place, which I like: the man whose principle
says forgetting costs is the one who asked whether you could get out of it. The history it keeps along the
way is real extra information, sitting out where anyone could read it, so it isn't a hidden fact
of the first batch's kind. And keeping it and unwinding it throws nothing away, so by Landauer's own reckoning it owes no heat;
the steps and the scratch paper are the whole bill. It can also be run back down. Neither of those
two, the keeping that owes no heat and the running back down, fits what happened to the first
computer, which did something that can't be undone and paid for it in work.
If the standing I'm after could be added for free and taken back for free, it would just be
bookkeeping. So that batch taught me what else I needed: something that only moves one way, and costs
something to move.

The third batch came closer and still didn't quite fit. In 1782 James Six, a Canterbury man from a
family of silk weavers who had taken up watching the weather, described a thermometer for the Royal
Society. He wanted the coldest moment of every night, and he'd found that with an ordinary thermometer
you had to be looking at it when it happened, because, in his words, ``if it be not immediately
noticed, it can never after be known.'' His fix was two little steel markers in the tube that the column
pushes up and that stay where they're left. That's a record that only moves one way. Then he spoils it,
for my purposes, in the same paper: every evening he wrote the numbers down and slid the markers back
with a magnet, ``without a touch.'' A record anybody can reset with a magnet is not the thing I'm after,
and Six would have been the first to say he wasn't the first to build one; his paper lists the
thermometers that came before his.

Since 1996, starting with oral polio vaccine, vials of vaccine bought through UNICEF have carried
a small sticker, a square inside a circle. The square darkens as the vial takes on heat, and the darkening doesn't undo when the vial cools.
When the square matches the circle, the vaccine shouldn't be used. One way, and it can't be reset. But
it's chemistry. The reaction in the square is chosen to run about as fast as the vaccine itself spoils,
so the sticker is really reading the vaccine's own condition by a proxy. Nobody ran a check; the heat
did.

Closer still: the International Vocabulary of Metrology, the reference book that measurement
laboratories work from, says a result is traceable only if it ``can be
related to a reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing to the
measurement uncertainty.'' That's a lot like what I want, a standing earned by checks, step by step. The
same document adds that traceability ``does not ensure \ldots that there is an absence of mistakes,''
which is the true-versus-established split written into an international standard. And the top of the
chain wasn't fixed either. When the official copies of the kilogram were compared with the prototype in
1889, 1946 and around 1991, they had drifted apart by tens of micrograms over the century, and nobody
can say which one moved, because the prototype was the kilogram. In 2019 the kilogram was redefined by
fixing a constant of nature, Planck's constant, instead. A chain like that can also lapse: if the calibrations stop, new
results stop being traceable. The standing has to be kept up, which my record doesn't.

The rules of chess have the shape too. The current Laws of Chess of FIDE, the international chess
federation, say in Article 9.2.3 that two
positions are the same only if ``the same player has the move, pieces of the same kind and colour occupy
the same squares and the possible moves of all the pieces of both players are the same,'' and they spell
out that a king that could still castle and one that can't are in different positions, even on an
identical board. That passes the perfect-vision test. And the official text says why it passes: the
castling right changes which moves are legal. So the hidden part steers the game: it decides what can
happen next. In the machine I'm building, the record never steers. It never touches the
ordinary computing at all. Each of these got something right and missed something else.

The one that fit best, and I want to say clearly that it only fit best among the ones I found, was the
standing of a mathematical statement. Here's how it went for one statement, as far as I could follow it.

In 1611 Johannes Kepler, the emperor's mathematician in Prague, owed his friend and patron Johann Matthäus
Wackher von Wackenfels a New Year's present and, he said, had nothing to give. Wackher, Kepler wrote,
loved \emph{nothing}, for the games you can play with the word, so Kepler wrote him a little pamphlet about the nearest thing to nothing he could find,
a snowflake, which had landed on his coat as he crossed a bridge. Why six corners? Kepler couldn't say
in the end. But along the way he stacked equal balls in his head and asserted that one way of stacking
them, the way grocers stack oranges, packs them so tightly that, in the 1966 English translation, ``in
no other arrangement could more pellets be stuffed into the same container.'' He didn't prove it. He
said it.

Then the sentence sat. In 1831 Carl Friedrich Gauss, reviewing somebody else's book on a piece of
number theory, proved what amounts to the special case of stackings laid out on a regular grid. In 1900 David Hilbert put the general question of packing equal spheres
on his famous list of problems for the new century, without mentioning Kepler. In 1953 the Hungarian geometer
László Fejes Tóth showed how the whole thing might be cut down to a problem with finitely many numbers in it, and a decade
later he guessed that computers might one day finish it. Thomas Hales, a mathematician then at the University of Michigan, started on it in earnest in 1994,
and in August 1998 he and his student Samuel Ferguson announced a proof that leaned on a great deal of
computer work. The Annals of Mathematics gave the paper to a panel of twelve referees, led by Gábor
Fejes Tóth, László's son. They ran seminars on it for years. A journalist, George Szpiro, later reported
that by July 2002 they were 99 percent certain it was right; I couldn't find those words in anything the
referees wrote themselves. What Hales quotes is the editor's letter, saying the referees had checked many
local statements and found them correct, and had ``not been able to certify the correctness of the proof
\ldots because they have run out of energy to devote to the problem.'' The Annals printed the human part in 2005, and the whole
proof appeared in 2006. Hales, in his own words, ``growing out of my frustration, in an effort to bypass
the referees,'' started a project in 2003 to have the entire proof checked by a proof assistant, the
same kind of tool that checks this book. It was finished on 10 August 2014.

Lay those dates out on the table and look at what moved. The sentence never changed. Hilbert's version
of the question didn't even name the man who first said it. Whether it's true never changed, as far as
anyone can tell. What changed was how far it had been established, and it changed in stages, each one
paid for by somebody's work: a guess, a special case, a place on a list, a plan, an announcement, a
panel's reported ninety-nine percent and their exhaustion, a printing, a machine check. A perfect reader of the
sentence can't see which stage it's at. And it only ever moved one way.

Then I tried to break that one too, because by this point I'd watched a lot of good-looking examples
fall over, and there's an obvious place to push. Standing can fall. In 1852 a student named Francis
Guthrie, colouring a map of the counties of England, noticed that four colours always seemed to be
enough to keep neighbouring counties different. The question passed to his old teacher Augustus De
Morgan, who wrote to the Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton that a student had asked him for ``a reason for a fact which
I did not know was a fact,'' and that he didn't know it yet either. In 1879 Alfred
Kempe, a barrister who did mathematics on the side and sang counter-tenor, published a proof, and his
description of finding it is wonderful: ``After a somewhat arduous search, I have succeeded, suddenly,
as might be expected, in hitting upon the weak point.'' The journal's associate editor, William Story,
added a note saying Kempe had ``substantially proved'' the theorem, and tightened the counting part of
the argument. Eleven years later Percy Heawood, a lecturer at Durham who by one account brought his dog
to his lectures, showed that one step of what he called ``the now apparently recognised proof'' doesn't
work. Kempe swaps colours along two chains at once, and swapping the first can spoil the second.

So standing can fall, and I went back and forth on what that does to my picture. Where I've landed for
now: the check that got Kempe's proof accepted, Story's note, went through the counting and never
examined the double swap. A check that never looked at a step can't have said no to that step. In the
sense of the previous few pages, the part that fell was never earned in the first place. I'm aware
that's a convenient reading for me, and I'm wary of convenient readings, especially my own. Take it as
where I ended up. It isn't a settled answer. It is, though, the reason the machine later in this
book only lets its record go up after a passing, sound check and a matching commitment. It supports
nontrivial claims whose checks can fail. It does not require every certified claim to be nontrivial.

And then the part I didn't expect. The four-colour statement was true all along. Kenneth Appel and
Wolfgang Haken, two mathematicians at the University of Illinois, proved it in 1976 with a computer, and the proof was met with suspicion for years; a
cleaner version came in the 1990s; and in 2005 Georges Gonthier, a computer scientist at Microsoft Research in Cambridge, finished a proof of the whole thing
checked by Coq, the program that checks this book. So here's a statement that stayed true the entire
time while its standing went up in 1879, came down in 1890, went up again in 1976 against a lot of
doubt, and went up further in 2005. The fall wasn't a fall of the truth. It was a fall of how far the
truth had been established, and it was the right fall to have, because what had been established was
less than anyone thought.

Laying all of that out together is what changed my picture. If there are stages, then at each one
there's a line, and the line has two sides: not this far yet, and at least this far. Each line amounts to
its own yes-or-no question, and the answer to each can only ever change from no to yes, so long as the
check behind it could have failed. Maybe the switch wasn't wrong. Maybe it was just incomplete, the first of many lines, and the
real shape is a direction with lines drawn across it. I've gone
around many times on whether the lines create the direction or the direction comes first and the lines
are just places where you cut it, and on whether yes and no are even different from each other until
something draws the line between them. I don't have an answer to that. The one part I could actually
settle is that a single switch isn't enough once there are three or more stages, and that is proved
(Section~\ref{sec:direction}). Everything else in this paragraph is me thinking out loud.

Flatland, where this hunch started (Section~\ref{sec:origin}), turned out to belong in the first batch. It's a novel Edwin Abbott published in 1884, narrated by a square who
lives in a flat, two-dimensional world (Section~\ref{sec:windows} says more about him and it). When a sphere passes through the flat world, the narrator sees a line whose ends fade wrong and whose
length keeps changing, and only when he feels it does he find a circle, a perfect one. Then the
sphere tells him it will rise, and he watches it dwindle to a point and vanish, and come back larger
and larger. The hidden direction
leaks into his view, faintly, and a sharp enough flat observer could in principle work out where the
sphere is. In this machine, as far as I can make out, you could move a state all the way along the
established direction without changing a single bit of the ordinary machine. That may be exactly why the
ordinary machine can't see it. It may also be why, if the direction is worth having, someone has to build
it in on purpose and keep it on purpose. Whether keeping it costs anything is what the rest of this
chapter tries to find out.

None of these people were writing about what I'm writing about, and none of them is the reason any of
this is true or false. Reading them didn't make anything truer. It raised how far I'd established a few
things for myself, and I could still be wrong about every one, the way the people who read Kempe in 1880
were. I went through them because I needed something to test the feeling against, and most of what I
tested failed. The failures told me what the thing isn't: not hidden, not free, not reversible, not
steering. What's left after all that is mostly a list of what it isn't, and I'm still not certain I've
described what it is.

\subsection*{Computing already had a word for it}

Here's the slightly embarrassing part. Computing already has a word for this and uses it every
day. Anyone who's used a database has seen it: COMMIT.

A database does a pile of tentative work, and then there's one moment, the commit, written to a log,
after which the change counts. Jim Gray, who more or less built the theory behind that, opens his
1981 paper on it by saying the idea comes from contract law, and his example is a wedding. People
negotiate, somebody asks, two people say ``I do,'' and from then on it's binding. If it was a mistake, you don't erase
it. You do another transaction to fix it, the way a bad contract gets a second
contract. Nobody reaches for a time machine.

The wedding was a philosopher's example first. The Oxford philosopher J. L. Austin, lecturing in 1955, said ``I do''
\emph{makes} a marriage. It doesn't \emph{describe} one, and sayings like that aren't true or false. They can misfire
(the wrong person says it, a step gets skipped). They can't be false. That's a commit exactly.
Writing the commit record doesn't report that a question got closed. Writing it \emph{is} the closing.
And a commit can't be false. It can misfire: committed without the check, committed about the wrong
pocket. Gettier and Peirce again, from a third direction. Then somebody else reads the record, and
for them it stops being a performance and turns into a report: ``this was checked and closed.'' A
report can be false. On the small machine in Part IV it can't be, about the machine's own history:
if its flag is up from a clean start, some claim was checked and closed, and that claim held of that
edition when it was checked. That's the one place in the book where a commit and the truth get tied
together, and it took a proof to do it.

Robin Milner, building a proof checker in the 1970s, ran out of memory, so he decided to keep only
the finished theorems and throw the proofs away, like a teacher rubbing out the blackboard to make
room. The obvious worry is forgery: if the proofs are gone, what stops someone just writing a
theorem down? His answer was beautiful. Theorems got their own type in the programming language, and
the only way to make one was through the rules of logic. You couldn't forge one because the language
wouldn't let you build it any other way. He named that language ML, for Meta Language. I wanted to
call my machine the meta machine. I'm choosing to treat that as a coincidence. Calling it a sign would be more my
style, so this is more restraint than I usually manage.

Bitcoin is the loud modern version. Its records can't be changed without redoing all the work that
came after them, and a computer that drops off the network and comes back trusts the longest chain
as the story of what happened while it was gone. That's Turing's clerk again, coming back to a note.
The difference is that the clerk's note costs nothing to forge and Bitcoin's costs a mountain of
work. It's the clearest case I know of somebody making a settled fact expensive to fake, and they got
there by paying for a search. The settling itself carries no price.

That's a different job from the one this book's price does, the mark it charges for raising a
record. I'll name that price the toll when I state it, a few pages on, and I'd rather say this now,
before you read the toll as a deterrent. One mark deters nobody. Bitcoin's work is tied to something
scarce, electricity and hardware; a mark in this book is tied to nothing. Eric Budish, an economist
at the University of Chicago, built a model in 2025 of what that tie has to cost. As I read him, for
Bitcoin's kind of trust to hold, the honest work has to stay expensive at every moment compared with
what an attacker could win, and the bill grows in step with the value being protected. A flat mark can't do that job, and it isn't trying to. What makes a raised record mean something, on the
machine where it means anything, is an order rule: check, then commit, then certify. That rule would
work just as well at a price of zero. The price is there because, on the premises of the chairs a
little further on, a finite machine that prices its merges can't avoid it. Scaring
anybody off has nothing to do with it. The machines I actually build don't meet those premises, so on them the price is a
choice made to match (Section~\ref{sec:smallest} says why).

And Bitcoin wasn't first. Pull on its footnotes: three of the eight
references in the paper that started it point to Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, who in 1991
worked out how to stamp a document with a time nobody could fake later, by chaining each stamp to
the ones before it. A company built on their idea, Surety, printed a short fingerprint of its chain in the classified
ads of the New York Times once a week from 1995, and it was still doing it in 2018. I found that in
a piece the journalist Daniel Oberhaus wrote that year, which says the ad runs under ``Notices \&
Lost and Found.'' Think about that for a
second. To make a record nobody could quietly rewrite, they put it somewhere a million people would
keep a copy of without even meaning to. A physicist named Wojciech Zurek has spent decades arguing that the world does the same thing with a measurement, copying the result into so many places that nobody can take it back. I'll get to him properly near the end of Part III.

There are more fences like these: logs that can't quietly change, certificates you can check. Later
in the book I take five of
them apart. I lean on all of them. They work. I want that said plainly, because the next thing isn't
``they're broken.''

The next thing is where they sit. The database's commit is bits in a log, kept by a database
program, on a machine whose own step will overwrite those bits the moment some instruction says to.
Milner's guarantee is a type checker; it holds inside programs written in his language and nowhere
else. Bitcoin is a protocol on ordinary computers that will do whatever they're told. Every one of them is a program or a rule, on top of a
machine that can't tell my two computers apart. The machine underneath keeps nothing and charges
nothing for what got settled.

The obvious comeback: so put the rule one level lower, in the operating system, or what security
people call a reference monitor, the small always-on piece everything has to pass through. Yes.
Exactly that. A monitor that wouldn't let any program raise its record without paying would be doing
the thing I'm talking about. In this book's words it would be \emph{implementing} the model, and I'd
count that as agreement. What I care about isn't who builds the fence. It's what the fence has to
obey, wherever it's built, and whether that's forced or just a good idea.

That comeback has a history, and it's older than me by a lot. In 1972 James P. Anderson's planning
study for the US Air Force described a reference monitor: a piece every access has to pass through,
that can't be tampered with, and small enough to check. In 2000 Fred Schneider, a computer scientist at Cornell, argued that a monitor that only watches a
run as it goes can enforce only rules whose breaking shows up at some finite point, the kind
computer scientists call safety rules. ``No certificate without an
earlier passing check and a commit'' is one of those. And in 2015 Arthur Azevedo de Amorim, a computer scientist then at the University of Pennsylvania, and six
coauthors built monitors that check a rule at every single instruction, and proved them correct in
Coq, the same proof checker this book uses. So putting a rule under every program, so nothing can
get around it, is their move. I didn't invent it. What I'm putting under that move is narrower: a record that
has to be paid for, on the small machine one that has to be earned, and a reason, from counting,
why a finite machine that prices its merges can't make the price of a record that never comes down zero.

\subsection*{What settling looks like}

The chapter on what structure is (Section~\ref{sec:structure}) ends with a pile of things sorted
into buckets. Settling a question is that, plus one more thing.

Picture every state the machine could be in as a field of dots. A yes-or-no question about the state
splits the field into two rooms: yes and no. That's a sorting, the smallest one there is. And
remember the no pile: if one of the rooms is empty, there's no sorting at all, just a field. Now the
extra thing that makes it a settlement: once the machine is in the yes room, \emph{no step it can take
leads back out}. The door opens one way. A settled question is a sorting plus a door that only
swings in.

At its best, what goes through the door is a relation: these numbers are in this order, these two
things belong together. There's a chimpanzee named Sultan, later in the book, who fitted two short
sticks into one long one and reached the food. Nothing new got added to the cage. Two sticks became
one tool. That's what I'd want the door to be for.

But the door doesn't care, and this is the honest edge of the whole picture. Hook the door to a
check that says yes to everything and the machine walks through, settled, and wrong. Settled whether
true or false, like Peirce said. A door that only swings one way tells you a question was closed. It
doesn't tell you it was closed right. Price and correctness are two different books, and I keep
both, separately.

One more edge, the one Gray's wedding already hinted at. What stays shut for good is that the
question got closed, about that edition of that thing. Whether the claim is still true is another
matter. Change the list after the commit and the record still says, truthfully, that the old
edition was checked and closed. And if the claim turns out bad, the fix is another act on top, a
second record that says ``withdrawn.'' The first one never quietly comes back down. So ``entitled
to lean on it right now'' is three things at once: closed, not withdrawn since, and the thing
unchanged.

\subsection*{Why it has to cost}

This is the part I'm proudest of, because once you've picked a record that stays, the choosing stops
and the counting takes over. And the counting is chairs.

Take any machine with a finite number of states. Its step is a function: give it a state and a move,
it gives you back one state. Pick a yes-or-no reading of the state and make it permanent: no step
ever turns a yes back into a no. Now suppose some step takes a state that reads no and lands it on
one that reads yes. Then that step has to land two different states on one. It \emph{merges}.

Do it with chairs. Draw a box on the floor, three chairs inside, one chair outside by the door. Four
people, one per chair: the four states the machine could be in. The three inside already read yes.
One step moves everybody at once, each to the chair the rule sends them to. Nobody inside may leave,
because yes is permanent. The person by the door has to come in, because this is the step that flips
them to yes. Now finish the move, one person per chair. You can't. Four people, three inside chairs:
somebody shares. Maybe the newcomer ends up on a lap, maybe two insiders squeeze onto one chair;
either way, two people end on one chair, and from where everyone's sitting you can't tell which two.
That's the pigeonhole principle, which is old and not mine, and the checked version, with exactly
those three conditions (finite, permanent, one flip), is in the chapter ``Why the toll isn't
arbitrary.'' No physics in it anywhere. Counting.

(How old is it? I went looking. A French Jesuit, Jean Leurechon, used it in 1622 to argue
that two people somewhere must have exactly the same number of hairs on their heads, which is the
kind of thing you can be completely sure of and never check. The first name for it I can find came two centuries later, from the German mathematician
Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet, who used it in print in 1842 without naming it and in later work
called it the drawer principle, the \emph{Schubfachprinzip}; the pigeons came later still.
Benoît Rittaud and Albrecht Heeffer, who wrote a short paper in 2014 on what came before
Dirichlet, looked for a source for the year 1834 that turns up next to his name and found none,
and neither have I. Is 1622 the bottom? I can't
tell you. History is like that: it's where you start digging.)

Turn it around and it gets better. A \emph{reversible} computer, one where every step can be run
backwards, never merges anything, because a step you can undo never puts two people on one chair.
Bennett, the same Bennett, showed in 1973 that any computation can be done reversibly if you give it
room to keep its history while it works. But give a reversible computer a finite memory and, however
much it computes, it can never raise a flag that stays up. It can always back up to before the
flag. Settling needs exactly the kind of step a reversible computer refuses to take. (Where does
the merged state go, physically? Out of the machine and into the room, as heat; the machine and
the room together never merge. Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} comes back to that.)

Now the physics, as an assumption with its name on it. Rolf Landauer, at IBM, 1961, said that a step
that can't be run backwards, that merges, ``requires a minimal heat generation.'' That's the rule
people call Landauer's principle. On a finite machine, settling something for good takes a merge,
and if Landauer's right, a merge costs heat whenever the machine doesn't already know which of the
merged states it was in. So on that assumption, a device that has to settle things correctly
without knowing its own state ahead of time can't do it for free.

And here's the rest of his sentence, the one I promised at the start. That heat, he wrote, ``serves
the purpose of standardizing signals and making them independent of their exact logical history.''
That's my two computers, in 1961. Ordinary machines spend their merges, and their heat, on
\emph{forgetting how the bits got there}, on purpose, so a 1 is a 1 no matter what path made it. That's
why the sorter and the copier end up identical, and why the comparing wing goes dark. And the very
same kind of step, a merge, is what it takes to close a door for good.

So here's the deepest thing I can say about settling. Not every forgetting settles anything: wiping a scratch pad closes no
question. But on a finite machine, every settling forgets. The step that closes a question for good
lands two states on one, somewhere, maybe not where you happen to be standing, and afterward nothing
can tell which one it was. A verdict keeps the decision and lets go of the arguing. An ordinary
computer pays for the forgetting and keeps nothing to show for it. What I want to know is what a
machine looks like that pays for the same forgetting and keeps the receipt.

Every assumption in that is a way out, and you should know where they are. Give the machine
unlimited memory and it never has to merge; it can write its history down forever, and the chapter
``Why the toll isn't arbitrary'' builds exactly that machine. Let the flag come back down and the chairs lose their grip.
And the heat isn't owed by every run. Landauer's principle, in the general form Part II adopts,
charges for what you didn't know, so for one run from a known start, with its controls timed from
outside, the premise supplies no positive heat floor (which doesn't show the device gives off none); the floor
bites for a device that has to cope with states it can't tell apart, which is how devices get
built (Theorem~\ref{thm:known-state}). The toll still charges its mark on that run, because the
toll is a rule about the move, and the move doesn't know who's watching. And Landauer's principle is physics. No proof in this book reaches it. In 2012 a group in Lyon
erased one bit held in a tiny bead, kept in place by a laser, and found the average heat it gave off
coming down toward Landauer's floor as the erasing was slowed. The principle has serious
critics too, the philosopher John Norton among them. So the counting is proved and the price is an
assumption, and I never let those two swap places.

\subsection*{Somebody got there first, goddamn it}

Bennett also says looking can be free. His famous move with Maxwell's demon (the whole story's later
in the book) is that you can write down which side of a box a molecule is on without paying
anything, as long as you write on a blank page. What costs is wiping the page to make room for the
next one.

I'd been sitting on this idea that \emph{committing} is what costs, and learning doesn't, and I thought: this
one's mine, I finally had an original thought. Then I found Carlo Rovelli's 2024 paper, ``The
Thermodynamic Cost of Choosing.'' Nope. Somebody got there first, goddamn it. A real physicist, with
a real paper, saying that making a choice that sticks costs at least the same heat Landauer charges
for erasing a bit. He even quotes a German saying, \emph{Wahl ist Leiden}, to choose is to suffer, and at
that point what are you going to do but laugh.

And then, taking him apart properly, it got good, because he seems to contradict Bennett. Bennett
says measuring can be free; Rovelli says any measurement costs. So which is it? Look at what Rovelli
calls a choice. A coin in the air hasn't chosen anything; it has to hit the ground and stop. And
then the sentence I'd put on my wall: ``stabilization must be irreversible, otherwise it is not
stabilization.'' Bennett's free measurement is one that could still be undone; that's \emph{why} it's
free. Rovelli's choice is one that's been made to stay; that's why it costs. The way I read them,
they're standing on opposite sides of the same door: learning on Bennett's side, committing on
Rovelli's. (Bennett's demon still pays in the end, when it wipes the page.) Neither of them puts it
that way, so push on it. But if it holds, it's the best sign I've got that the line I keep drawing
between knowing and settling isn't something I made up.

Push on it, then, with his paper open, and it gives in four places: his choice is unpredictable,
it's a branching where mine is a merge, it's stable only for a while, and he stands against
Bennett's free measurement, where I'd have put him beside it (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing} goes through all four). So
the two-sides-of-one-door picture is my reading. He doesn't draw it, and the piece of it that's really his is
the one sentence about stabilizing. That sentence I'll still put on my wall.

So he's my closest neighbour, and here's the difference, exactly. His is physics: a price in heat,
at a temperature, for a choice that sticks. Mine is a rule in a model of computation: a charge in
the machine's own count, on the step that flips a permanent reading on, with no temperature anywhere
in it. Same instinct, different place. I'll take it. It's annoying to be second. It's worse to be
alone and wrong. And he's the closest only on choosing. On copying there's an older neighbour, in
the physics of molecules, and Section~\ref{sec:narrowing} gets to it.

\subsection*{What the Thiele Machine is}

So here's what I built, and which parts I was pushed into and which parts I chose, because you
should know which is which.

The Thiele Machine is a model of computation, the way Turing's machine is: math you can reason
about. You can't buy it in a box. It has a few parts. A state. A step that moves the state. A record: a
yes-or-no reading of the state that says whether something's been established. A charge on each kind
of move, added up on a counter that only climbs. One rule, which I call the toll: the step that
flips the record from no to yes has to cost at least one mark on that counter. And a window, what an
outside observer gets to see, which is there because the two computers already showed you the
problem: the usual window, the bits, can't see the record. The toll's first name, the one I gave it
before I understood it, is No Free Insight.

One what, and why one? One mark, in the model's own count. One because it's the least a whole-number
count can charge and still not be free, and the toll only says \emph{not free}. The model doesn't say a
mark is worth a joule or a dollar; whether it's worth anything physical is Landauer's assumption,
named, and nowhere else. And one is just the floor: Part II shows that if you charge one mark per
halving, a step that squeezes a lot together pays at least the logarithm of the squeeze, roughly how
many times it halves the number of states it can tell apart. Don't read that backwards, though. One
mark isn't one halving. A single state flipping into a big room of states that already read yes
squeezes things together very little, much less than a halving, and the whole-number count rounds
that up to one.

What was I pushed into? That on a finite machine, a record that never comes down can only be raised
by a merge: counting, proved. That merges cost: physics, assumed. What did I choose? To put the
count \emph{inside the step}, as part of what a step is. Nothing forces that, and a log off to the
side was always the other place it could go. It's my claim about where the account belongs, and the rest of the book is the case for
it.

About the name. I named it after myself, on purpose. Half of that is a joke and half of it is a
