stake in the ground. Turing got a machine, so here's mine. The longer story,
meta machines and all, is in ``How I got here'' (Section~\ref{sec:origin}).

The names work the way Turing's do, and I'm going to be a little annoying about them. \emph{The Thiele
Machine}, capital letters, is the model and nothing else. \emph{A Thiele machine}, lower case, is any
particular system proved to fit the model, the way one rule table is a Turing machine; a two-box toy
on a sheet of paper counts. A Thiele machine is \emph{Thiele-complete} when the machine under the
record can compute anything a Turing machine can, for free and without ever touching the record;
a record that
goes up stays up; and, from
a clean start, the record goes up only after a check of some claim passes,
by
a checker proved to
mean what it says, then a commitment to that same claim with nothing
it's about changed in between, then a certificate, with exactly one mark charged for each
of those three acts; and at least
one claim on the machine has a check, commit
and certificate that raise the record on some inputs and leave it down on others. And a
\emph{universal} Thiele machine is one fixed program that runs other machines as guests, with
each guest's record earned again by the host's own steps and each guest's toll paid on the host's
own ledger. Nothing is left to the guest's good manners.

The first bar, being a Thiele machine at all, is low, and I'd rather you hear
it from me. A machine that charges one mark for every step it takes, whatever the step does,
obeys the toll for any record you like; a clock is enough to make something a Thiele machine. If
Thiele-complete only meant a Thiele machine that can compute anything, a clock bolted to a
computer would pass that too, and so would a machine whose record never goes up. That's why
Thiele-complete asks for more, and both of those fail it, by theorem: a clock charges for
computing, and Thiele-complete says computing is free; and a machine whose record never goes up
fails the clause asking for at least one claim whose check, commit and certificate raise the record
on some inputs and leave it down on others (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). The small
machine of Part IV meets it, and so does the same machine over any properties with an exact test for telling two of them apart and
a checker
proved to mean what it says, as long as one of them is true of some number and false of another, sorted lists included. And every machine that meets it has the same
blind spot built in, also by theorem: the part a Turing machine would call the whole machine, the
line it's on and the numbers it holds, can't tell you its record or its ledger.

\subsection*{The two computers, put back together}

Here's the two-computer story again, rebuilt as Thiele machines, with the record and the counter
written out, so you can watch it happen. You don't have to take my word. The prices are the ones on the smallest
machine I build later: one mark each to check, to commit, and to certify (raise the record), and
nothing for ordinary work like moving numbers around.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.205\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.097\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{step} & \textbf{sorter does} & \textbf{record} & \textbf{counter} & \textbf{copier does} & \textbf{record} & \textbf{counter} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
start & nothing yet & no & 0 & nothing yet & no & 0 \\
1 & sorts (lots of ordinary steps) & no & 0 & copies in the typed list & no & 0 \\
2 & checks ``sorted'' on this list, this edition: passes & no & 1 & (no check) & no & 0 \\
3 & commits to ``sorted,'' about this list, this edition & no & 2 & tries to commit: nothing checked, refused & no & 1 \\
4 & certifies & \textbf{yes} & 3 & tries to certify: nothing committed, refused & no & 2 \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

At the end, the bits on both machines are still the same sorted list. Everything else differs. The
sorter's record is up and its counter reads 3. The copier's record is down, and it's paid 2 for two
refusals, because on that machine a refused attempt still costs what it costs. (Read those as two
separate attempts. Written as one stored program, the copier would stop at its first refusal and
pay 1.) Nothing the copier
can do raises its record without first running a passing check of the claim it then commits to. And no
outside window that only shows the list can tell you which is which; the difference is all in the
part the window doesn't show. Walk that warehouse now and there's finally a lamp that's lit in one
and dark in the other.

Now how literally to take that table. It's a picture of the chain, and the chain is what's proved.
The small machine's own checks are three questions about one counter: is it zero, is it even, is it
at least some number. What its proofs need from the questions is a checker proved to say yes
exactly
when the answer is yes, and an exact test for telling two questions apart. That's enough for ``sorted'': a version of the machine that takes
any questions with checkers like that proves the same chain once for all of them, and with a list
packed into one counter it certifies a sorted list for three marks and refuses an unsorted one
forever (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). Without a proved checker for ``sorted,'' the chain would be honest about a
counter and only by convention about your list, which is Gettier's pocket again, one level down.

And a lamp for whom? The record is bits too. It's a lamp on the machine, for anybody walking that
warehouse. Hand somebody a printout of it across a desk and you're back at the sticker on the
windshield: they have to trust whoever hands it over, or have some way to check the box that says
it ran. That crossing is a different problem with its own tools, signatures, attestation and proofs
a stranger can check, and this book doesn't solve it. Section~\ref{sec:windows} says what those
tools rest on, and the small machine's record, like any record kept in a machine's state, carries
nobody's signature. What the step changes is the question, from ``did it run?'' to ``do I trust
the box that says it ran?'' That's a smaller question. It isn't no question.

Now the honest half. Take away the small machine's rules and keep only the bare toll, and the copier
has an easier move: pay one mark, flip the record to yes, done. The toll is satisfied. The receipt
is real. It's a receipt for nothing. The bare toll prices the closing of the door. The check
behind it goes unpriced.

\subsection*{What putting it in the step buys}

So here's the hardest objection, and I'd rather make it myself. You defined a flag and a charge,
then proved the charge gets paid when the flag goes up. That's your definitions agreeing with each
other.

On the bare model, that's fair, and the copier's receipt for nothing is the proof. What makes the
record mean \emph{established} is the small machine's step, which won't let a commit through unless a
check of that very claim passed, meeting the first three of the four conditions from Gettier's
pocket, with the fourth, an honest checker, proved about the checker separately. And what it proves
isn't about one program. It's this: on \emph{every} list of instructions anybody can write, starting
clean, if the record is up, then somewhere earlier a check of some claim, about some edition,
passed; then a commit of that same claim; then the certificate; with nothing touching the
thing between the check and the commit.

From a clean start, a raised flag guarantees that some claim went through a passing check, a
matching commitment about the same edition, and a successful certification. The flag retains
that historical fact. The channel names the latest earned commitment, which need not be the
commitment on which the flag first rose. The final state does not, in general, identify the claim
certified at that first rise or the step at which it occurred. And the flag doesn't say the
claim still holds, at the certification or at the end, since the counter can change after the
commitment.

That ``every'' is the whole answer to what the step buys. A log kept by a program gives you a fact
about that program: if the program's right, the log's right. The database's guarantee holds for work
that goes through the database. A rule in the step gives you a fact about every program the machine
can run, the buggy ones and the hostile ones too, because there's no way to run anything on it that
isn't a string of its steps. That's what moving the rule down a level changes. Not what can be
computed. \emph{Which} programs the guarantee covers: this one becomes every one. Most of the rest of the
book is how far that ``every'' goes and where it stops.

Two limits on that ``every,'' said now so you don't have to find them later. First, it's every program.
It isn't every everything. The guarantee covers any list of instructions, run from a clean start, one step at
a time, on a step that does what its definition says. Hostile programs, yes. A hostile start
(a table of facts nobody checked, a reset), hostile hardware (a soldering iron on the flag's bit,
a second writer the step can't see) or a hostile reader, no; Section~\ref{sec:scope} lists the
whole fence. That's the same shape as the database's guarantee, true if the layer underneath is
faithful, with a much bigger class of programs inside it.

Second, the flag and the counter on their own are what people who verify programs call ghost state:
erase them and every program computes exactly what it did before (Section~\ref{sec:counter} has
where that idea comes from). What isn't ghost on the small machine is
the table of checked facts, which the step reads and refuses on, at run time, for every program. And
the move of putting a rule under every program isn't mine either. It's the reference monitor's,
and its history is a few sections back.

\subsection*{What it isn't}

It isn't more computing power. Anything a Thiele machine computes, the
machine under its record
computes without it. The book proves that over any machine at all, an honest record is a switch the machine's own
events flip once and nothing flips back; it watches the computing and adds nothing to it. It isn't
faster. It isn't quantum. It says nothing about which problems are hard.

And an ordinary computer can keep a record like this. Give a Turing machine a spot for the record
and a track for the counter, write its rules so it never sets the spot without bumping the counter,
prove that, and it \emph{is} a Thiele machine. It's no counterexample. What an ordinary programmable
computer, as built, doesn't do is make its own step enforce a record \emph{for the programs it runs}.
When it runs another program, that program's record is just data in memory the program can write,
and a buggy program can flip it for free, because the host's step has no opinion about it. Could it
be built otherwise? Sure. A universal machine with one fixed table, the kind Turing built, could
have that table written so it mirrors each guest's record and charges for the raise, and it would
qualify. Nothing about ordinary computers stops that. They just aren't built that way. That gap,
between the machine doing the stepping and the program it runs, is where the databases and the proof
checkers and Bitcoin built their fences, and it's the gap the universal Thiele machine later in the
book closes, first for the programs of the small machine it's built on, and then for every Thiele
machine whose workings a program can compute.

There's a cheap version of a universal machine, so here's which one this is. A host with a move
that means ``run one guest step'' runs any guest because I wrote it that way, and the book has one
of those, as the simple picture. The universal Thiele machine doesn't get that move. It's one fixed
program, written in the small machine's own six kinds of instruction on a host with more counters,
and it fetches, decodes and carries out each guest instruction itself, the way Turing's universal
machine does. The theorems are about that program: it halts exactly when its guest halts, with the
guest's answer in its counters; its flag goes up exactly when the guest's would, by its own check,
its own commit and its own certificate; its ledger matches the guest's mark for mark; and the
machine it runs on is Thiele-complete (Section~\ref{sec:universal-host}). Its guests are the small
machine's programs, which compute everything. Add one move that pays a mark and does nothing else,
and the same kind of program runs every Thiele machine
whose next move, step, prices and reading are computed by programs: it halts when the guest's run stops, its flag goes up exactly when the guest's reading
has said yes, on a chain whose check is the guest's own reading, and its ledger is the guest's prices plus at most two marks at the raise when the guest's reading starts at no (when
it starts at yes, the host has to raise its flag at once and pays three on a ledger of nothing), a surcharge no program on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the guest's whole ledger at the raise is below three (Section~\ref{sec:presented-universal}). A Thiele machine whose
reading no program decides isn't covered, and I say exactly where the edges are.

\subsection*{What's proved, what's argued, and what I just believe}

Every claim in this book has a status and I'll tell you which, every time. Here's the whole list at
once, so you know what I'm on the hook for.

Checked by a proof assistant, with every assumption printed, for any system with the named parts:
anything that obeys the toll pays at least one mark to get from not-established to established
(short enough that you'll prove it yourself on paper in Part II). With finitely many yes-states and a record
that never comes down, every move that raises it merges states, which is the chairs; consequently
every schedule that prices merges charges that move, and every run from no to yes has positive total
cost. The price is an assumption with a name. Finding out can be free: you can learn
something from a step that merged nothing and cost nothing, so the toll lands on committing. A window that shows a certifying step and a quiet one
alike, before and after, can't price
certification exactly, however clever it is. And over any machine, an honest record is a one-way
switch on an event, with two choices left free: the price list and which event.

On the smallest machine I could build, six instructions on two counters: the chain in the table
above (check, commit, certify, same claim, same edition), for every program anybody can write, that one included, with
claims about any property that comes with a checker proved to mean it and an exact test for telling properties apart, ``sorted'' included
(Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). From a clean start, a raised record always went through a
passing check,
then a commit, then a certificate, of exactly the same claim
about exactly the same edition; nothing
gets into its list of checked facts
without a check writing it. Every run from a clean start that ends with the flag raised has
incurred at least three marks of instruction cost, and this bound is attained: check ``this counter is zero,'' commit to it, certify, and when the
counter is zero that pays exactly three; when it isn't, the check traps with the flag down and
nothing after that ever raises it. The machine doesn't stop you asking a question that can't come
out no, and I say so where it matters. It's Thiele-complete in the strong sense from a few pages
back, and that sense has teeth: every clock-style machine, one that charges for computing, fails
it, and every machine that meets it hides its record and its ledger from its own window, both by
theorem. Its computing is that of the two-counter machines of Marvin Minsky, one of the founders of artificial intelligence at MIT, which Minsky proved can compute
anything a Turing machine can. And there's a universal Thiele machine on top of it: one fixed
program, with no guest step built in, that runs every program of the small machine, halts when
the guest halts, raises its own flag exactly when the guest's would, on its own earned chain, and
keeps a ledger equal to the guest's. With one paid move added, one fixed program runs every
computably presented Thiele machine, a machine from anywhere whose choice
of next move, step, prices and decided reading are programs: halting matched, its record carried as a latch and raised on the host's own
earned chain about the guest's own reading, its prices matched to within a surcharge of at most two when
the guest's reading starts at no, which can't be avoided in general.

Argued only: that an account of computation \emph{should} carry what was established, and what it
cost, in how it steps. The proofs show that it hangs together, what it follows from, and what it
costs (six instructions and three marks, on the small machine); whether it ought to be adopted is
argued, and it's a claim about what matters, which no proof checker can check.

Guessed at, with the ways to kill it written down: that the event worth recording is certification,
because its records are the ones that get copied and relied on all over the place (the pointer
conjecture, Part III).

Not proved, and I'll say so every time it's tempting: any physical price for one mark, anything
about a physical device running any of this, or anything about which problems are hard.

Which of the proved part is new? Not one big thing, and I'd be suspicious of me if I said otherwise.
By my own sorting at the back (Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine}) it's four smaller ones, each with its
neighbours standing right there. The toll derived from finiteness, permanence and a price on
merging: the pigeonhole principle, Landauer and Bennett on merging, and the finite heart of
the German mathematician Ernst Zermelo's 1896 recurrence argument, about whether a closed box of gas has to come back around to where it started, are all next to it. A window that shows a certifying step and a
quiet one alike, before
and after, can't price certification exactly: an old fact about functions, the
1956 thought experiments of Edward Moore, at Bell Labs, on what you can learn about a machine you
may only watch from outside, and the engineer Rudolf Kalman's observability, the same question
asked of control systems. What I put in is a price. An honest permanent record, over
any machine, is a latch on one event: the 1918 flip-flop and write-once memory are its neighbours.
And the small machine, a definition of Thiele-complete that a clock can't meet, and a universal
Thiele machine written as one fixed program: a record that's priced, and earned, under the reference
monitor's every-program move (Anderson in 1972, Schneider in 2000, Coq-checked monitors from Azevedo
de Amorim and coauthors in 2015), carried to every program of the small machine and, with one paid
move added, to every computably presented Thiele machine. That fourth one is built and checked;
the idea under it isn't new. The first three are small exact statements I didn't find stated before, where I looked. The
two-player game check later in the book is careful engineering on known mathematics. It doesn't make a fifth.

\subsection*{At the bottom: what I suspect and can't prove}

This is underneath the proofs, so read it with the lights on. None of it is a theorem, and I'm not
going to dress it up as one. It's why I care, and I'm telling you going
in, so you don't catch me
sneaking it in later.

Physics has a word for the moment a question closes: \emph{measurement}. And the people who thought
hardest about it keep describing it in this chapter's shape. They ran together for me until I put
them on one picture. Flip a coin in a crowded room. Before it lands, it could go either way. After,
it's settled, somebody chalks it on a board, and the result gets copied out into the world, the
light and the air, so many times that it can't be taken back and everybody who looks agrees. Five
pieces: the question, the landing, the chalk mark, the copies, the agreeing. Each person leans on a
different one. Wojciech Zurek has spent decades on how the copying works. Rovelli's coin has to hit
the ground, so his piece is the landing.

Niels Bohr, the Danish physicist whose institute in Copenhagen was where quantum mechanics got
argued into shape, leans on the mark. In a 1954 talk he said seeing anything at that scale depends
on an apparatus that works irreversibly, like permanent marks on a photographic plate: a door that
swings one way. I found that line quoted in a recent paper and haven't seen the page in Bohr's book
myself. John Wheeler, the Princeton physicist who named the black hole, went further in a 1989 talk
in Tokyo and leaned on the question: every physical thing gets its existence from yes-or-no
questions answered and registered, boiled down to ``it from bit.'' As I read him, the coin has no
face until something asks and something writes the answer down. How literally he meant that, I can't
tell. And Peirce, way before any of them, leans on the agreeing: the kind of settling worth trusting
is the kind that has to answer to everybody. Laid out like that, they pair up. Bohr and Rovelli lean
on a step that only goes one way, in the plate and in the coin. Zurek and Peirce lean on many
onlookers who agree, one with light and one with people.

Lay that next to everything above and the parts line up: a check that could have come out either
way, a result that's now settled, a price paid in forgetting, a record that stays. I suspect that
isn't a coincidence. I suspect the event this book prices on a machine is the same kind of event
physics calls a measurement, showing up in a different place. The forgetting is my step. Bohr only
says irreversible, and getting from a record that stays to a merge is the chairs, on a finite
machine. Push on it and it gives at Zurek. In Zurek's picture the world settles a result by copying
it, and copying merges nothing (Section~\ref{sec:pointer} pushes on that). As I read it, that's
Bennett's free measurement, writing on a blank page. So physics' own word lands on both sides of
Bennett and Rovelli's door: the chalk on the paying side, the copies on the free side. The landing
I'd put with the chalk, and when Section~\ref{sec:narrowing} pushes on Rovelli's paper it slides
toward the free side, the side of finding out. So two pieces already stick out, and I'll leave them
sticking out. Which picture a settling on a
machine matches is part of the suspicion, and the suspicion doesn't settle it. That's as far as I'll
take it here: a suspicion.

Now let me point the biggest gun I can find at it, and that's John Bell, the Northern Irish physicist at CERN whose 1964 theorem comes back in
Part IV. In 1990 Bell wrote a short,
furious essay against the word ``measurement,'' with a list of words he said have no place in a
physics that wants to be precise. On the list: system, apparatus, environment, irreversible,
information, and measurement, which he called the worst of all. I used half of them in the last few
paragraphs without even trying. Bell would have taken my suspicion apart in an afternoon, and he'd
have been right to, because every piece of it leans on words physics hasn't pinned down. Nothing in
this book proves any of it. The proofs are about models and machines, and whenever physics shows up
in them it shows up as an assumption with a name on it. The suspicion is why I went looking. It
isn't what I found.

\subsection*{Where this goes}

So here's the picture, put back together. Two machines can hold the same bits and differ in what
they've established, and you can't see it even walking the floor between them, because it was
never kept. The difference isn't information; information theory says the sort added nothing new.
It isn't depth; depth belongs to the bits, and a copy has just as much. It's an event: a check that
could have said no, about the claim, then a question closed for good, with no promise the
answer's true. The could-have-said-no part lives in the procedure. Two end states with the same
bits and nothing else kept can't tell it apart, so only a record written into the state can carry
it. On a finite
machine, a record that never comes down can only be raised by a merge, a kind of forgetting, the
same kind ordinary computers pay heat for so their bits forget where they came from. If Landauer's
right, that costs, for any device that has to settle things without already knowing which state
it's in. The Thiele Machine puts the record and the charge in the step itself, and what
that buys isn't more computing. It's a guarantee about every program. A log kept by one program
covers only that one.

Every time I thought I'd found something new on the way down, somebody had a name for part of it
already, and that last sentence is no exception: a rule under every program is the reference
monitor's move, from 1972. Fine. What I think is put together here is smaller and more than one
thing: the four small things I listed under what's proved, each with its neighbours
named. There's no one big one.

And the stuff from the start, the audit, the proof, the ledger, the test sheet, the sticker, the
confident AI? Here's the straight answer on which of those this helps. The sticker is a question of whether a piece of paper is
genuine, and nothing here touches it. The ``all tests passed'' sheet fits only if the test is a
checker proved to mean what it says, in the machine's own language; a set of tests that can miss a
bug certifies ``this procedure said yes,'' which is true and smaller. An audit and a ledger get the
test sheet's answer: kept by a program on an ordinary computer, they're bits the program wrote, and
they fit only where the step underneath keeps the record and refuses to raise it without the check.
A proof is the case this book is built on. A proof checked by a proof assistant is a check that could
have said no, and the checker vouches that the proof fits its statement; whether the statement says
what you meant is still yours to read. The AI that talks as if it's sure of
itself isn't addressed at all. What the book gives you is a record on the machine itself, with a
proof of what a raised one means. Getting that record to somebody across the room who has to
believe it is a separate job, and Section~\ref{sec:scope}, under ``Outward consequences,'' says how
little of the outside world I've reached. If you came for a tool, that's a short list. If you came
for the question, this is where it starts.

The rest of the book is me trying to break all of it. First where I came from, then the word I couldn't define when I
started, structure. Then the smallest thing that could carry the bill, on a sheet of paper, with one
rule I'll hand you without a reason, and then the chapter where I find out whether I had to pick it.
If it breaks there, the book ends there. I'd rather know.

\clearpage

%===========================================================================
\phantomsection\section*{Before the book: the short version}
\label{sec:shortversion}
%===========================================================================

\emph{The book in one paragraph.} The Thiele Machine is an abstract model of computation. Its core is a
state, a step rule, a cost for each move and a yes-or-no certification reading, with one rule: the
step turning the reading from no to yes costs at least one unit (I call that rule the toll,
and its first name, the one I gave it before I understood it, is No Free Insight; Part II
builds it). On top of that core go a counter that adds up the costs and only climbs, and a window
that says what an observer sees. Here's what's proved,
in Coq (a proof assistant: software that checks every step of a proof), with every premise
printed. Any system that follows the toll pays something to get from uncertified to
certified. With finitely many yes-states and a reading that is never taken back, every move that raises the
reading merges states; consequently every schedule that prices merges charges that move, and every
run from no to yes has positive total cost. That's the universal certification result, and
Landauer's principle (the physicist's rule that forgetting costs heat) is a named premise for
pricing merges. A measurement that forgets
nothing can be priced at zero. A window that shows a certifying step and a
quiet one alike, before and
after, can't price certification exactly. Over any base machine, an honest permanent record is
a latch on an event (a switch the event flips once and nothing flips back). And no decider
whose flip a substrate can
represent decides which programs admit a shortcut, given a recursion theorem (the fact
that a program can act as though it held its own code). ``Admits a shortcut'' there is a label for any
property of programs that two programs doing the same thing always share, and that some programs have
and some don't; Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} says why the label is all the argument gets to see. A substrate is the model's bare
shape, a kind of state and a
rule for stepping; each theorem adds whatever extra pieces it
asks for, and here
the extra pieces are programs written as states and that recursion theorem.
All of that is about the model: any system with the named pieces. One machine carries the
model in this book, and it's a Thiele machine in the sense a few pages on pins down: six
instructions on two counters, where commitments are earned and universality is proved. It's
Thiele-complete under a definition no clock meets (computing free and unable to touch the record, a record that stays up once it's up and, from a clean start,
is earned, each of the
three acts priced at exactly one, and one claim whose check, commit and certificate raise the record on some inputs and not on others), every machine that meets that definition hides its record and
its ledger from its own window, and one fixed program in its own instruction kinds, with no step
of any guest built in, runs every program of it with halting, flag and ledger matched exactly:
a universal Thiele machine. Add one move that pays a mark and does nothing else, and one fixed
program runs every Thiele machine whose next move, step, prices and
reading are computed by programs, the reading decided on every state: halting matched, the guest's reading carried as a latch on the
host's own earned flag, and the guest's prices matched to within a surcharge of at most two marks
when the guest's reading starts at no, which can't be avoided in general. The lambda calculus L gets a recursion theorem by proof, and so
does the machine that universal program runs on, with Rice's theorem beside it. On the two-counter
machine itself Rice's theorem holds on every input, Kleene's holds with inputs written as powers of two, for the function the program computes though not for the facts it records,
and with plain inputs Kleene's is false, which is proved too. An integer check
on eight counts is earned on the small machine's host: a flag raised from a clean start can stand on a passing check of the
counts, and the check passes exactly when every question pair was sampled and a fixed moment matrix
is positive semidefinite, which forces Tsirelson's bound, the ceiling quantum mechanics puts on the
score of a two-player game (Part IV builds the game, the matrix and the check from zero; it's there
as a check with a striking result, to show the toll charges the same however deep the check is. It isn't there
as a physics tool). Under the stated covering and payment conditions, the index-bit narrowing bound applies to the record moves of
every Thiele-complete machine; a finite machine with eight states (four slots and a flag) runs on the small machine and, after
a two-mark setup, pays
exactly its own charges; and on every Thiele-complete machine no checker that sees only the clean
start and the final window is both sound and complete about the record. Not proved: a physical price for one mark, any separation of complexity classes, that
certification is the event worth recording (that's a conjecture), or anything about a physical
device running any of it. Of all that, what I'd call new is several small things. There isn't one big one. They are the
toll derived from finiteness, permanence and a price on merging; a window that can't price it
exactly; the latch shape of a permanent record; and a
priced record, earned on the small machine, under the reference monitor's every-program move,
carried by one fixed universal program to every program of it and to every computably presented
Thiele machine, which is built and checked though the idea under it isn't new. Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine} puts each beside the work it leans on.

I didn't invent a machine. I found one. That's how I see this work, and I'll be straight
about the difference between that conviction and a theorem before I do anything else.

That sentence walks straight into one of the oldest fights in mathematics, so here's a short
trip into it first. G. H. Hardy, a Cambridge number theorist who wrote \emph{A Mathematician's Apology} in 1940 to
defend doing mathematics for its own sake, came down on
the found side about as hard as anyone ever has: mathematical reality, he wrote, lies outside
the people who study it, and the theorems they like to call their creations are really just
notes on what they saw there. The German mathematician Leopold Kronecker supposedly split the difference: God made the
whole numbers, and everything else is the work of people. Supposedly, because push on that
line and it gets thin fast. It comes down through Heinrich Weber, another German mathematician, in a memorial piece written
after Kronecker died, pointing back to a lecture from 1886, and that's the only source I could find anybody citing. A great line with one witness. (The first chapter of Part II stops early on to ask how
many witnesses a claim ought to need. The answer is more than one.) So does any of this
settle whether I found the Thiele Machine or made it up? No. A proof checker doesn't settle
it either; Coq checks a proof the same whether you think the theorem was out there waiting or
you think you built it. That's why it's labelled a conviction. What it changes is how I hold
the thing: like something that was already there, which means I can be wrong about its shape
and the shape won't care. And to be exact about what ``found'' covers: the parts the counting
forces on you, the latch shape and the merge. The event to record, the price list, and putting
the count inside the step are choices, mine, and ``The point'' said so where it sorted what
I was pushed into from what I chose.

What the Thiele Machine is. An abstract model of computation. A machine the way Turing's
machine is a machine: mathematics you can reason about. It isn't a device. It isn't a CPU or an
instruction set; those are things you build to carry it, and Part IV builds one, as small as I
could make it. The model is small. A state. A step rule. A record. A counter that only climbs. A rule for
which steps have to pay. And a window: what an observer is allowed to see. Like a Turing
machine, it's a precise way to say what a computation is. Unlike a Turing machine, it
computes nothing new. It adds what a computation \emph{establishes}, and what establishing it
cost. The event it accounts for happens on any computer, whether anybody keeps track of it
or not. What Turing's model doesn't have is a place for the record of that event, or
anything that enforces one. A Turing machine can be programmed to keep the record, and then
it obeys the toll and it's a Thiele machine in its own right. But when it runs some other
program's record as data on its tape, nothing in its own step enforces it
(Section~\ref{sec:machine-vs-program}). The event's physical cost comes in only under
Landauer's premise, with its name on it. The record exists only if something keeps it, and
keeping it, priced, is what the model adds.

What this book is. An argument, made with that model, about what an account of
computation should preserve. Turing's account, and every account built on it, describes a computation by what it reads and
writes. I think that account is a shadow, and that there's another axis, holding what the
computation established and what that cost. Here's the argument in five steps, each with
where it stands.

\emph{Holding a sorting costs something; standing behind one might.} That's Part I: one word,
structure, pushed on with you through as many of the people who wrestled it before me as I
could reach. It finds three
different acts that people run together. Building and storing a sorting you can read back
costs work and space. Forgetting where things came from costs heat, if Landauer is right.
And standing behind a sorting, vouching for it, is a third act, and nobody I read had put a
price on it. The nearest was Rovelli's price on a choice that sticks, and his is a choice nobody
could predict, which Section~\ref{sec:narrowing} shows is a different act. Whether vouching has a
price is the question the rest of the book takes up.

\emph{Establishing is not free.} If the step that turns uncertified into certified has to pay,
every run from uncertified to certified has paid. Proved, for any system that follows that
rule, whatever its states and steps. And the rule isn't arbitrary: on any system with
finitely many states, a certificate nothing takes back can only be switched on by a step that
merges two states. That part is pure counting, proved. If merging is charged for, the way Landauer's
principle charges for it in its worst case, the rule follows. That part is proved with the
charge as a named premise, its critics named, and every premise refusable with a
counterexample built. Learning isn't what costs: a measurement that forgets nothing can be
priced at zero by an honest price list, and an observer still learns from it. Proved. What
can't be free, on those premises, is committing to what you learned in a record the machine
can't take back.

Two more things belong to that step. First, which steps a price on merging has to charge,
when move names can be told apart:
exactly the ones that merge. On a finite machine, every step that writes a record nothing takes
back is one of
them, and a step that switches a certificate on escapes the price only
when the same step switches one off somewhere else. The tidier guess, that the priced steps
are exactly the permanent records, is false, and three states show it. No theorem picks out
a wider class of events every account must price. With one mark per halving, the step that
writes a permanent record costs at least the base-two logarithm of how much it squeezes
together (how many times it halves the number of states it can tell apart), and, from an even spread over the states in play, the same
bound
holds in bits of Shannon entropy, the standard measure of information. Proved, with
the price as a premise. Second, where the machine I built stands, and that's a fact Part IV settles. The small machine of Part IV isn't a finite
machine of that kind: its counters have no top, so it isn't finite, and some of its free steps merge states too. On it the toll is a design
choice the chairs don't force. What the chairs do reach is a finite piece: an eight-state machine,
four slots and a flag, on which every premise is a theorem and the toll follows outright
(Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). And the small machine runs that piece: seen through a window that shows only the
line number, read modulo four, and the flag, a program of the small machine, after a two-mark setup, does what the
eight-state machine does,
one move at a time, and from then on pays exactly what the eight-state machine
charges (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, with the construction in
Section~\ref{sec:part3-on-machine}).

\emph{A window can hide what was paid.} Two runs can look identical through the usual window
and differ in what they established and paid, and nothing reading only the window gets the
difference back. The machine I built has such a pair for the window a Turing machine would point at
it, the line and the counters, and every machine that meets the definition of Thiele-complete has
one through its own window: two runs from one clean start that end looking the same, one certified
and one not. Proved, both. And when two single steps look the same through a window, before and
after, and only one of them certifies, no price read off that window charges the certifying step
exactly. Proved, for any window with such a pair of steps.

\emph{Leaning on a fact takes a paid history.} A computation is entitled to lean on a structural
fact when it holds the object, a checked relation, and a paid event on its record. Defined,
for the model, with a counting fact beside it: narrowing a list of rivals down takes at least
the yes-or-no questions that name the survivors. The cost floor that ties those questions to
steps a run actually paid for holds for any system with a counter, once somebody supplies three
things: the list of rivals before, the list of survivors after, and a tree of yes-or-no questions
with enough leaves to cover the narrowing. Then if a run paid at least as many charged steps as that
tree is deep, those payments cover the index bits, the questions it takes to point at one entry of
the first list less the ones it takes for the second (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}). No run is shown to have to pay them. On every
Thiele-complete machine, the small machine included, the paid steps are the record moves, each
exactly one mark, and a run from a clean start that ends with the record up, having narrowed a list
that way, carries an earned chain and pays at least the index bits in record moves
(Section~\ref{sec:part3-on-machine}); and when the questions are counted as the run's own checks,
the floor needs no tree to be supplied, with a limit stated where it's proved.
Entitlement is a license to lean on a claim. It doesn't prove the claim is true.

\emph{So the axis belongs in the step.} An account of computation should carry what was
established and what it cost as part of how it steps. Bolting it on after isn't enough.
Proposed. The proofs around it show it hangs together and what it costs; whether it should be
adopted is argued, and no test settles it. What's proved around it: over
any base machine, an honest record is a latch on an event, with two free choices, the
price list and the event; no decider whose flip a substrate can
itself represent decides which
programs admit a shortcut (in the label sense given above), given a recursion theorem, by the same self-referring trick, the
diagonal, that put a hole in the foundations for arithmetic built by the German logician Gottlob Frege (Part I tells that
story); and which event deserves the record is a conjecture, with its refutations listed.

Certification is one point I could pin down. It gave me a law I could state, a machine I
could build and run, and proofs I could put in front of someone who didn't share my
intuition. It's one witness in a larger argument about structure and observation. It isn't
the argument.

How the book is laid out. Part I is the picture: how I got here, and what structure is.
Part II is the axiom: the smallest thing that could carry a bill, and why its one rule
isn't arbitrary. Part III is the logic: the counter, the windows, entitlement, insight, the
latch, the whole direction, the exact shadow, the diagonal, five real systems, and a conjecture. Parts I to III never use my
machine; every claim in them is about any system with the pieces it names, and the pictures
are toys. Part IV builds one machine, the smallest honest machine I could make: two
counters, six instructions, a table of checked facts, a ledger and a flag. On it a flag raised from a
clean start
provably went through a passing check, a commitment and a certification of the same claim, in
that order, and it computes everything Minsky's two-counter machines can, so whether it halts
is undecidable. There Thiele-complete gets its definition, the one a clock fails, and the
universal Thiele machine gets built as one fixed program that runs every program of the small
machine and earns its own flag, and then, with one paid move added, every computably presented
Thiele machine. Then a check worth earning, the two-player game and its integer test, and what
the counter has to do with physics. Part V is how to check all of it and how to break it. The
vocabulary I had to learn is at the back.

If you want the argument without the whole tour, read ``The point'' and this short version, then
Section~\ref{sec:toll}, Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, Section~\ref{sec:latch},
Section~\ref{sec:smallest} and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}. If physics is your thing, add
Section~\ref{sec:narrowing} and Section~\ref{sec:landauer}. If you mean to check me, add
Section~\ref{sec:falsification} and Section~\ref{sec:ledger}. The appendices are reference:
everything in them is there to be looked up when a claim points at it. Nothing gets cut for
that. It's a map. Nobody's on a diet.

One more thing before the book starts, because people get it backwards. I used language models to
write the code and the proofs in this project, and I trust language models about as far as
I can throw them, which is exactly why every formal declaration is checked by a proof
assistant that doesn't care who or what wrote it. Coq rejects a wrong proof the same whether
a tenured professor or a model hands it over, and it accepted these, with none of my own
axioms anywhere in them, re-checkable by the procedure in Part V. Being self-taught and
using modern tools didn't make this looser. It's the reason I made a machine check the
formal corpus, and then built an auditor to read over the checker's shoulder for every way I
might have cheated, on purpose or by accident (Part V says what it looks for). It doesn't
trust me either. Good.

I think there's something foundational here. The results in this book have statements,
premises, and proof terms. The larger claim is a conjecture. No theorem proves it. I built the
machine so that the work could be done in public, with something firmer than my confidence
to argue over. If you're the skeptical sort, and I hope you are, the two places to aim are
the appendix that sorts what's mine from what isn't (Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine}) and the
chapter of ways to break it (Section~\ref{sec:falsification}).

%===========================================================================
\phantomsection\section*{Let me be straight with you}
\label{sec:straight}
%===========================================================================

\emph{What this project is.} An argument about what an account of computation should preserve,
made with an abstract model built to carry it. Its central proposal is that what a
computation established, and what establishing it cost, belong in how it steps. The working
form of that proposal is structural entitlement: a computation is entitled to lean on a
structural fact when it holds the object, a checked relation, and a history that earned
it. The model, its laws, and the instructions of any one build are different things, and I
keep them apart. The generic
flag-raising step pays to set a flag; it checks nothing. A claim that something is actually
\emph{true} needs explicit witnesses and a checker proved sound, and some results here are of
that kind; the generic accounting law isn't one of them. It's a law about marks.

\emph{The universal certification result.} The universal certification result is this: when the
yes-state set is finite and the reading is permanent, every move that raises the reading merges
states. Consequently, every cost schedule satisfying merge pricing charges that move at least one
mark, and every run from no to yes costs at least one. This is a theorem over all systems
satisfying those premises. It isn't a property peculiar to the implementation in Part IV
(\code{nec\_f\_perm\_flip\_merges\_yes\_finite} and \code{nec\_f\_toll\_from\_merges\_yes\_finite},
NecFMerge.v). Three layers stay separate through the book. The first is the structural fact that a
permanent raise merges states, which needs no prices at all. The second is the pricing premise,
merge pricing, which turns that fact into a ledger bound. The third is the small machine of Part IV,
which enforces earned certification on top of both.

\emph{The proved core, in three steps.} Anything that follows the toll pays something to get from
uncertified to certified. A window that shows two states as the same, when they disagree on
the counter or on some other question, can't answer that question on every state. Those two
are about any system with the named pieces, and so is the third, argued in three lines in
Part III: a checker that only sees a window where two states collide can't be both sound and
complete about the claim that separates them (Section~\ref{sec:windows}).
All three are
statements about named laws and named windows, and the third is checked too, over abstract
transcripts and then for every Thiele-complete machine (Section~\ref{sec:windows}). An ordinary machine can keep a richer encoding, or enforce the same invariant
through its own transition table. What I'm proposing is about why the extra distinctions
matter. It isn't a theorem that every Turing-equivalent system lacks them. And if you want the
list of what I think is new, it's the short one at the end of ``What's proved, what's argued,
and what I just believe'' in ``The point,'' the same four things the short version names,
and nothing bigger.

\emph{The layers, once.} The core definition (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}) is a certification
system: states, moves, a step, a cost for each move, a yes-or-no reading, and the toll. Everything
else is added on top, and each theorem names what it adds. First come extra structures and
requirements: a ledger that sums the costs, a window, permanence of the reading, a price on
merges. Then an earned implementation, the small machine of Part IV, with a checker proved sound
and a provenance theorem. Then an interface, Thiele-complete, that any machine can be read through.
Then a universal interpreter for a stated class of guests. The bare definition doesn't ask the step
to be computable, so when I say the record adds no computing power, I mean relative to a fixed
base.

\emph{Substrate versus scaffolding.} Two layers run through the book, and confusing them makes
the theorems quietly stop meaning what they say. The \emph{substrate} is the shape: a kind of
state and a rule for stepping. Different theorems ask that shape for different extra pieces,
and the pieces aren't the same. The universal floor (the ``pays something'' result above)
asks for a certification reading and the toll on it. The counter's uniqueness (only one
count fits a chosen start and price list) asks for a starting value and a schedule of
increments; Part III gives the argument, a short induction that works for any system with
those two pieces, and on the small machine of Part IV the ledger is the sum of the charges by
theorem (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). The diagonal asks for a way to write programs as states and a recursion theorem for
the transformations the substrate can express, and needs no toll at all. ``Substrate-level''
doesn't mean one fixed plug that every theorem shares. A theorem only gets to use the parts
it asks for. Ask it what it needs and it'll tell you, and whatever else is lying around the
workshop isn't the theorem's. So each result is stated over exactly the extension it uses. The substrate with the extension a theorem names is what I
mean by \emph{the model}, and the name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. The \emph{scaffolding} is
everything that holds the shape up so you can touch it, and when I say \emph{my machine}, \emph{the
small machine}, \emph{the machine I build} or \emph{the build}, this is what I mean: the machine
of Part IV, with its two counters and their versions, its table of checked facts, its channel,
trap, ledger and flag, its six instructions and their prices, the host with a register for every
whole number, the universal programs that run on that host, and the Coq files that define all of
it. The build fills in several extensions at once and borrows, for any one theorem, only
the extension that theorem names. Let that line blur and a theorem stated over one extension
starts reading as if it carried premises it never uses. ``Substrate'' never means the build,
and it never means the side of a simulation doing the stepping; for that I say ``the machine
doing the stepping,'' as against ``the program it runs.''

So here's how the book keeps the two apart. Parts I to III are about any system with the
pieces each result names, and their pictures are toys you can hold (two boxes on a sheet of
paper, chairs in a room, a row of dots). My machine isn't one of them; it first appears in Part IV.
Every Part III claim that has a machine instance gets that instance in Part IV, with
its own checked name, and Part III says so in one sentence at most. When the origin story,
a few pages on, says the shape ``was the substrate the entire time,'' it means this layer, the model's shape.
It doesn't mean any piece of the build. Same story with two more of its words. When it says ``the
machine'' about the thing it named the Thiele Machine, or calls that thing a meta machine, it
means the model; ``my machine'' is the build, and the build doesn't show up until Part IV.
And when it lists what the model asks for (a state, a step, a record, a ledger, a window), read the
ledger and the window as two of the extra pieces: a result asks for them only if it uses
them.

Part IV has one piece of scaffolding, and I'd rather you know up front how small it is.
Section~\ref{sec:smallest} builds the smallest honest machine I could: two counters, six
instructions, a table of checked facts, a ledger and a flag. Earned commitments are proved there
(a flag raised from a clean start was
checked, then committed, then certified, on the same
edition, with nothing touching
that thing between the check and the commit), and so is universality, through Minsky's two-counter machines and a halting result
borrowed from the Coq undecidability library. Then one fixed program, on a host made of the same
kinds of instruction with more counters, runs every program of it, and with one paid move added,
every computably presented Thiele machine. None of that is the model. It shows the model fits in
six instructions.

The names again, this time with every part pinned down, because I'll hold to them for the rest
of the book. \emph{The Thiele Machine}, with
capitals, is the model and nothing else. \emph{A Thiele machine}, lower case, is any particular
system proved to be an instance of the model's core definition, a certification system with
its five parts and its toll (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}), the way one rule table is a Turing
machine. The toys on paper in Part II count, the same way trivial Turing machines do. The
small machine counts too, with its toll proved, and Part IV names the theorem. A Thiele
machine is \emph{weakly} Thiele-complete when its base is Turing-universal, and that bar is
nearly empty: a machine that charges one for every step is a Thiele machine for any record, so a
clock bolted to a computer clears it, and so does a machine whose record never rises. So
\emph{Thiele-complete} asks for four things (Definition~\ref{def:u34-thiele-complete}). A
universal base whose moves are free and can't touch the record, and a record that stays up once it's up. A record that, from a clean start, rises
only after a
passing check of a claim, then a commitment to that same claim with nothing it's about changed in
between, then a certificate, with the checker proved to mean what it says. An exact toll: one
mark for each of those three acts and nothing for anything else. And a claim whose check, commit and certificate
raise the record
on some loaded starts and leave it down on others. Every clock-style machine fails the definition, because it charges for computing, whatever its
record, and every machine that meets the definition hides its record and its ledger from its own window, both by theorem. The small machine
meets it, and so does the same machine over any properties with an exact test for telling two of
them apart and a proved checker, as long as one of them can come out both ways, sorted lists
included. A
\emph{universal} Thiele machine is one fixed program that runs any machine of a stated class as
a guest, with the guest's record earned again and its toll paid by the host's own steps. Part IV
builds one, $U$: a fixed program in the small machine's own six kinds of instruction, on a host
with more counters, with no step of any guest built in. Its guests are the small machine's
programs, so every computation runs on it, and it matches each guest's halting, answer, flag and
ledger exactly, raising its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate. Then $U_P$, the
same program with one more handler for a paid move that does nothing else, takes as its guests
every computably presented Thiele machine, one whose next move (picked by a driver), step,
prices and reading are computed by programs, with the reading decided on every state. It matches the guest's halting, raises its
own flag on its own earned chain exactly when the guest's reading has said yes, and keeps the
guest's prices to within a surcharge of at most two when the guest's reading
starts at no, which no program on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid in general.
And a computer that runs the small machine, your laptop say, isn't a Thiele machine. It
implements one, inside bounds, the way a laptop implements a Turing machine.
Push on that comparison, because it's loose, and the looseness is the
point. Does a laptop implement a Turing machine? Not exactly. Turing's tape never runs out,
and a laptop's memory does; strictly, a laptop is a very large machine with finitely many
states, and it behaves like a Turing machine only on computations that fit. Nobody minds,
because the bound is known and most computations people care about fit inside it. That's the
same deal any device running the small machine gets: its counters stop somewhere, and the
theorems speak only for runs that fit. The bounds aren't fine print. They're the whole
difference between implementing a model and being one.

How much can a difference in width matter? There's a famous answer, and it's worth the
detour. On 4 June 1996 the first Ariane 5 rocket lifted off and broke apart about forty
seconds after its engines lit. The inquiry board, chaired by the mathematician Jacques-Louis
Lions, traced it to one conversion in the inertial reference software: a sixty-four-bit
floating-point number, an alignment value called BH that's tied to horizontal speed, squeezed
into a sixteen-bit signed integer. On Ariane 4, where the software came from, that value
could never get big enough to overflow, because of how that rocket flew in its first forty
seconds. Ariane 5 flew differently. The value got too big, the backup unit failed on it, the
main unit failed the same way about seventy milliseconds later, and the function doing the
converting didn't even serve a purpose on Ariane 5; it was kept for commonality with the old
rocket. The board's report says the assumption that made the conversion safe had been agreed
on and never exposed to outside review. A width premise that holds on one machine is a fact
about how that machine gets used. The code doesn't carry it, and yet it travels with the code without
anybody noticing. The only defence I know is the dull one: write the premise into every
statement that needs it, where the next person will trip over it.

\emph{What ``new model of computation'' means here.} It adds something to how a machine runs:
structure it keeps, and an account of what that structure cost. It doesn't add computable
functions. It's an abstract model the way the Turing machine is, but it doesn't hand you a
new primitive to compute with; whatever base machine sits under it still does all the
computing. When I say ``shadow'' I mean the particular window I name. Other ways a
conventional machine could store things aren't covered. Enforcing the law, storing it, and
letting an observer see it are three separate questions, and the book keeps them separate.

Which leaves a fair question hanging: if it computes nothing new, does it even get to call
itself a model of computation? I think so, and not only on my say-so. Computer science has
long kept models that compute exactly what Turing's does and differ only in what they count,
how long a step takes, what reaching into memory costs, because the counting is the reason
to have them. Part III lays the toll over a register machine of that kind, and over a Turing
machine and a lambda calculus, and none of them computes one function more afterward
(Section~\ref{sec:latch}). What each of them gains is a record and a bill.

\emph{What this project is not.} Not a solution to P versus NP, and not a complexity-class
separation of any other kind. Not a theory of everything. Not a claim that computation is
physics, or that physics is computation. Not a physics result: the game result (the
integer check and Tsirelson's bound from the short version) is pure mathematics, and
Landauer's principle enters only as a premise with
its name on it. Nothing here derives it. Not a quantum computer or a claim about quantum behaviour. Not a verified chip or a
verified device of any kind; a checked model and a checked machine, on paper and in Coq. Not a
claim to priority on any idea in
it. Not closed on every question: the ones I couldn't settle are listed at the end.

\emph{What I do and don't know about prior work.} I came to this with no formal training in the
fields it turned out to need, and I've read what I could reach, with every tool I had. The
prior-work map below is orientation. It doesn't pretend to be scholarship. For each piece of this book it says who did
the thing it leans on, and what, if anything, this development adds. I'd welcome correction
on any row.

There's a law about rows like these, and it's a joke that keeps turning out true. In 1980 the
statistician Stephen Stigler proposed that no scientific discovery is named after the person
who first found it, and then credited the idea to the sociologist Robert K. Merton, who had
been writing about fights over scientific priority since 1957. So Stigler's law is an example
of itself, which is either the best joke in the history of science or a very tidy accident.
Is it a law? No. It's a pattern. Nobody proved it. But this book has already tripped over it
once, in the opening chapter: the pigeonhole principle wears Dirichlet's name, and
Leurechon had it two centuries earlier. And I put my own name on a machine. By Stigler's law, that makes it
somebody else's. The table below is my best attempt at finding out whose.

What I compare each time is what a result is \emph{about}. Landauer's bound is about heat, a
physical cost under a thermodynamic model. No Free Lunch (an optimisation result, in the
list below the table) is about averages over a whole spread of problems. The toll is a floor on one kind of step, the step that turns a
certification reading on. Rise-only pricing adds a second rule on top: charge nothing on a step that doesn't turn it on. So the
comparisons are about the shape of each result. They aren't claims about who got somewhere
first, and they don't show that certification is the only event worth pricing.

\emph{Three kinds of exact.} The word exact does three jobs in this book, and each job keeps one
name. \emph{Rise-only pricing} charges at least one mark on every step that raises the reading and
nothing on any other step; its tightest bill, one mark per raise and nothing else, is the
\emph{exact schedule}. \emph{Instruction-exact pricing} charges every instruction a fixed listed
price. On the small machine of Part~IV that's one mark each for CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY and
nothing for the rest, and the definition of Thiele-complete calls it the \emph{exact toll}. CHECK
and COMMIT raise no flag, so the small machine is instruction-exact without being rise-only, and
no rule is broken by that. \emph{Simulation-exact accounting} is a host whose ledger equals its
guest's ledger at every point where the two runs match, as the universal program $U$'s does. A
machine can meet any one of the three and fail the others.

The right-hand column uses words the book only builds later (the latch, the fibre, the
universal program, the integer check, the matrix test), so read it as a list of places to go.
You aren't meant to follow it yet.

Everything in the right column is stated with its premises in the body of the book, and
everything in the middle column is cited where it's used. The table is the short form. The
long form is Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine}, which takes each row, says what was
already known with sources, and sorts what's added into new result, new proof,
mechanization, implementation, synthesis, or conjecture. Most of the right column is
mechanization, implementation, and synthesis.

A few more labels I went and looked up are neighbours. Some of them also sit in
the table above,
and one, the reference monitor, is the move the small machine's step makes. I list them
so you can see why I don't think the toll is one
of them under a new name. Each is a claim inviting correction.

\begin{itemize}
\item Linear logic (Girard 1987) treats an assumption as a resource that gets used up. It
constrains what a program, or a proof, may consume. The toll constrains the model's step
function instead. Same instinct, different layer.
\item Foundational proof-carrying code (Appel 2001) checks safety proofs against the smallest
trusted base it can: a logic plus the machine's semantics. Here no proof rides along with
the program. The step rule writes the receipts as the run goes.
\item Session types (Honda 1993) constrain how programs talk to each other so the conversation
can't go off script. The toll is about what one computation has paid to establish.
Different problem.
\item No Free Lunch (Wolpert and Macready 1997): averaged over every problem, whatever an
optimiser gains on some problems it gives back on others. That's an average over a whole
problem space, and the edge is paid for elsewhere. The toll charges one step in one run,
with no refund anywhere.
\item Kolmogorov complexity (Kolmogorov 1965): the structure in an object is the length of the
shortest program that prints it. That's a property of a finished string, with no steps and
no moment of paying. The toll is a law about a step.
\item Cook and Levin (Cook 1971; Levin 1973): checking can be cheap while finding looks
expensive, and whether finding is really harder is the open P-versus-NP question, a gap in
how difficulty grows with size. The toll puts a fixed floor under the one step that
commits, however easy or hard the finding was.
\item The thermodynamic cost of choosing (Rovelli 2024): settling a binary choice at temperature
T gives off at least kT ln 2. That's the closest thing to the toll itself I've found, because it
charges a commitment. An object or an average isn't what it prices. But it's physics, indexed to a
temperature, and its choice is unpredictable, a branching, and stable only for a while, where
the toll's commit is a deterministic merge that stays. The toll charges the commitment in a model of computation, with no
temperature in it. Closest neighbour. A different chair.
\item Persistent copies (Ouldridge and ten Wolde 2017; Ouldridge, Govern and ten Wolde 2017):
making a copy that stays correlated with its original after the two come apart has a
thermodynamic bill. The nearest physics I've found to ``learning free, committing priced.'' It's
heat for a correlation, in chemistry; the toll is a count in a model of computation.
\item Thermodynamics of finite automata (Ouldridge and Wolpert 2023): if the smallest automaton
for a language has a letter that sends two states to one, recognising that language on a
device that repeats one local step produces entropy, and if the smallest automaton only
reshuffles, recognition can be free. That's the chairs with a physical price on them, and one
of their worked examples is the latch's language turned inside out. It's the closest neighbour
of all to the road the toll is derived on; Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} says exactly
what's left over for me.
\item CerCo, the Certified Complexity project of Amadio and coauthors, builds a verified C compiler that carries the object
code's execution cost back up to annotations on the source. There the cost decorates the
program and survives compilation. Here it lives in the model's step rule.
\item Reference monitors and execution monitors (Anderson 1972; Schneider 2000; Azevedo de
Amorim and coauthors 2015). A small piece every action passes through, enforcing a rule on
every program. Schneider argued that a monitor watching a run can enforce only rules whose
breaking shows up at a finite point, and ``no certificate without an earlier passing check and
commit'' is one of those; the micro-policies check a tag rule at every instruction, proved in
Coq. That's the move the small machine's step makes, so this one is the house itself. What's added is the edition-bound check-then-commit with a paid, permanent record on top,
and the derivation of why the payment can't be zero. Kevin Hamlen, Greg Morrisett and Fred
Schneider (2006) went on to sort which rules monitors, program rewriters and static checkers can
each enforce, and they differ, which is one reason this book doesn't claim that every enforcement
mechanism is a Thiele machine underneath.
\item Trusted components in replicated services (Chun and coauthors 2007; Levin and coauthors
2009; Veronese and coauthors 2013; Decouchant and coauthors 2022; Clement, Junqueira, Kate and
Rodrigues 2012): a small record inside each replica that a replica taken over still can't make
say two things, with a proof of exactly what that buys. The record is theirs. The toll isn't in
their picture.
\item Ghost state (Owicki and Gries 1976; Filliâtre, Gondelman and Paskevich 2014): variables
added for a proof that can be erased without changing what the program computes. The flag and
the counter are ghost in that sense. The small machine's table of checked facts isn't, because
the step reads it and refuses on it, for every program.
\item Verifiable computation and proof-carrying data (Parno, Howell, Gentry and Raykova 2013;
Chiesa and Tromer 2010): a short proof, checkable by a stranger, that a computation's output is
right. That establishes the claim for the stranger, and anyone with the inputs can make one,
the copier included. The record here is about one machine's own history. A proof like that is
one way to carry the local record out of the box.
\item Commitments and entitlements (Brandom 1994): talk as score-keeping, tracking who is
committed to what and who is entitled to it. Brandom's entitlements can be defeated and can be
passed on by testimony. Here entitlement is priced, step by step, and a copy carries it only as
far as the copy is genuine. Same words, different machinery.
\item Correspondence assertions (Woo and Lam 1993; Gordon and Jeffrey 2003). In protocol
verification, ``this end event must be preceded by a begin event for the same thing'' is a
correspondence assertion, and a type system can prove a protocol keeps it against any
opponent. ``No certificate without an earlier commit, and no commit without an earlier check
of the same claim'' has that shape. Theirs is proved about programs by typing. Mine is enforced
by the step, which is the LCF comparison again, at the level of single instructions.
\item Monotonic parallel composition (\AA{}man Pohjola and Parrow 2016) and persistence in the
pi-calculus (Palamidessi, Saraswat, Valencia and Victor 2006). \AA{}man Pohjola and Parrow
separate models where a neighbouring process can never stop a step from models that can solve
consensus, and test-and-set, an instruction that writes a cell and reports what was there, is
on the consensus side. Palamidessi and coauthors compare messages that are used up with
messages that stay, and the end of their study is a reduction from Minsky machines. A store
that can refuse permanently, which is what the version rule does to a stale commit, looks like
the non-monotonic side. I haven't written that encoding, so take it as a pointer. It isn't a claim.
\item Constructor theory (Deutsch and Marletto 2015; Marletto 2016; Marletto, Vedral and
coauthors 2022; Violaris and Marletto 2022): physics as which tasks a device that runs in a
cycle can do, with irreversible meaning possible while the inverse isn't. It's the nearest
physics I know to ``committing costs'' stated for a cycling device. It's quantum and
approximate, and the chairs are classical, finite and exact
(Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}).
\item Accountability and fault detection (Haeberlen and Kuznetsov 2009; K\"usters, Truderung
and Vogt 2010; Treitz and K\"unnemann 2026): when an outside party can tell who misbehaved.
Their windows are this book's windows, and the trust they leave over, an honest log or a
trusted step, is left over here too (Section~\ref{sec:windows}).
\item Transferability (Easwaran 2009): a deductive proof lets you learn from someone you don't
trust because you can check every step, and a probabilistic proof doesn't. That's the argument
for carrying the object and re-running the check (Section~\ref{sec:windows}).
\end{itemize}

And then the silly question that list raises, which I'm going to chase anyway: why is an
optimisation theorem named after lunch? Wolpert and Macready borrowed an old saying, ``there
ain't no such thing as a free lunch,'' and the saying is older than almost everyone who gets
credit for it. American saloons in the 1800s put out a free lunch for anyone who bought a
drink, and the drink paid for the lunch. A Washington newspaper was already saying in 1909
that somebody has to pay for a free lunch; a newspaper fable by Walter Morrow had the whole
line in 1938; a book by Pierre Dos Utt already had the squeezed form, TANSTAAFL, as its title in
1949; Robert Heinlein's 1966 novel \emph{The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress} made that squeezed form
famous; and the economist Milton Friedman put the saying on the cover of his 1975 book of essays on public policy. I'd have credited
Heinlein or Friedman. As far as anything I could find goes, neither coined it. Stigler's law again,
at lunch. Here's what it changes. No Free Insight is named like a cousin of the saying, and the
family resemblance misleads in one way. The saloon's lunch was paid for somewhere else, in the price of the beer, and that's
Wolpert and Macready's shape: a gain here, handed back over there. The toll isn't that.
Nothing gets paid somewhere else. The step that raises the flag pays, on the spot.


\part{The picture}

%===========================================================================
\section{How I got here}
\label{sec:origin}
%===========================================================================

What I am is curious, past the point of good sense.

I pick a thing up and cannot set it down until I have turned it over enough times to see how it holds together, and this time it did not let go.

I am not a programmer and I was never formally taught any of this.

I was not trying to build a formally verified CPU, and the one I came close to building later, on the way here, is not part of this book.

I would not have known what one was if it bit me.

I was trying to build a 3D renderer.

There was no plan behind it.

Just a pull to make something real with my own hands, and the kind of stubbornness that will not let a thing go until it stands up on its own.

I have worked on it in off hours every day since.

Once I started digging in, two things came clear fast. I knew nothing about computers, and the field was already saturated, every obvious road paved and crowded. So I needed an angle nobody else was standing on, and the angle I had wasn't a strategy. It was just the only way my head works. I did not know what compositional meant. I had never heard of category theory. I called the thing I was building digital DNA, because that is what it felt like in my hands, and I thought about it in the only language I had: gravity pipes and directions and vectors, things that were linear and somehow not linear at the same time, structure that flowed and joined and came apart without my owning one proper word for any of it. I built a custom rendering pipeline out of those intuitions, by feel, throwing out pieces that did not sit right even when I could not have told you the rule they were breaking. And then, the way I always do, I went looking for what I was actually doing, and found out it already had a name. An old one. A deep one. What I had been reaching for in the dark was composition. It was category theory, a whole field I had never once heard of, sitting there describing the exact shapes I had been shoving around. The moment that landed, the rendering pipeline stopped being a rendering pipeline and started turning into a categorical engine, and I started swallowing the real theory as fast as I could find the words for things I had already built.

The method underneath was crude and it held. I wrote a long structured spec in JSON (a plain-text format for describing data) as a context document, fed it to Copilot, and had it build one Python file per concept, one at a time, each with its own tests, and I would not move to the next until I could watch the current one actually run. Category. Object. Morphism. Functor. Monoidal product. It came together in pieces and never in chapters, the way a picture resolves out of static. The Yoneda lemma (a result buried deep in category theory) was the piece that made the rest snap into place, the night I quit borrowing other people's runtimes and started writing my own around it, with Z3 (a constraint solver out of Microsoft Research) wired into the middle.

Then within weeks I found out the engine I had built to draw pictures was general enough to run a physics simulation on the exact same primitives, without my rewriting any of it. I wrote Newton's laws as a program in it, half expecting nothing, and it ran. I want to be careful about what that was and what it was not, because this is exactly the kind of thing that gets misread. It was not me deriving physics, and I am not claiming the machine explains gravity. It was the compositional structure being general enough to express a physics simulation the same way it had expressed a renderer, and that generality is what told me the structure was the point and the pixels never were. Somewhere in those weeks I crossed from debugging why one pixel would not show up to understanding that I had quietly built a categorical computing engine, and that the rendering had only ever been the first thing I aimed it at. The pixel did eventually show up, for what it is worth.

I kept going, because by then I could not not keep going.
