Do it for one day. Keep two columns of every dollar that moves, and total them at night. Now
have a friend secretly change one entry in one column. The totals disagree; you catch it. Now
have them change the matching entry in both columns. The totals agree. You've caught nothing.
Push on that and you've found what double entry actually is: a trap for slips. A
careful liar walks straight through it. Did Pacioli see that? I can only get at it secondhand. The scholar Forrester, in a paper on the University of Strathclyde's accounting-history pages, reads him as reporting that in many places the
books were taken to the local consul to be authenticated before a single entry went in. The
stamp is a witness again, from outside. The two columns are the discipline; the stamp is the
claim that someone other than you will stand behind the fact that these are the books.
No other set gets that stamp. Keep both halves separate in your head. One is a method. The other is a
commitment.

And then I found the place where this got turned into a motto. The Royal Society, founded
in London in 1660 and still running, picked as its motto \emph{Nullius in verba}: take nobody's
word for it. (Where did they get it? From somebody's words, naturally. It's half a line of the
Roman poet Horace, from a verse letter to his patron, saying he isn't bound to swear by the
words of any master. So the society that takes nobody's word for it took its motto from a poet
and cut the line to fit. That's not a contradiction, and it's a nice picture of the method:
borrow what's useful, say whose it was, and don't swear by it.) The historian Steven Shapin wrote a paper about what that meant in practice,
and the answer is more interesting than the slogan. Robert Boyle, pumping the air out of a
glass globe to see what happens to a candle or a bird, had three problems: the machine, the
report, and the witnesses. He solved the third by having gentlemen present who'd sign their
names, and the second by writing the report so richly that a reader who wasn't there could
picture the scene and count as a witness anyway. Shapin calls that virtual witnessing, and he
notes, dryly, that the air pump was very expensive, seventeenth-century big science. So there
\emph{was} a cost. It just wasn't a cost of declaring the fact. It was the cost of the instrument
and of getting enough people into the room. Hold on to that distinction. The rest of the book hangs on it.

\subsection{A demon, and the step that pays}

Now the strangest entry, and the one that gets closest. In 1867 the physicist James Clerk
Maxwell, in a letter to his friend the Scottish physicist Peter Guthrie Tait, imagined a ``very observant and neat-fingered being'' sitting
at a tiny door between two halves of a box of gas, letting fast molecules through one way and
slow ones the other, so that one side heats up and the other cools with no work done, which
is supposed to be impossible. The being got called Maxwell's demon, and physicists have been
arguing about it for a hundred and fifty years, which should tell you something.

In 1929 Leo Szilard, a young Hungarian physicist working in Berlin, cut the demon's box down to a single molecule, and that made information part of the accounting.
The tempting move, and the one Szilard's own accounting made, is to put the whole bill on finding out which side the molecule is on.
Bennett separated finding out from restoring the memory for another round: measuring onto a
blank record can, in principle, be thermodynamically reversible, and resetting an unknown
record is a different operation. That does not make a real measuring device free to build
or run. It says that learning and resetting do not carry the same unavoidable entropy
cost, and I'm about to pick a step to charge, so I need that distinction before I do.

Bennett's version of the rule, in a 2003 paper you can read, is that what must cost is ``the
erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths.'' Erasing, or taking two possible
situations and making them one. And in the same paper he lists copying unknown data onto a blank
place to write among ``the most important logically reversible operations,'' the kind he says can, at least in principle, be run thermodynamically reversibly. So, in the one place in all of this where a record is priced by
physics, the unavoidable erasure charge belongs to \emph{forgetting} the unknown record. Making
a record carries no such charge of its own. Read
that twice. It's not what I expected either.

I'll put the rest of the lineage quickly, because it all points the same way. Regulators who
make brokers keep records on media that can't be rewritten (the SEC required exactly that, write
once and read many, from 1997 until 2022, when it allowed an audit trail as the other way to comply)
are pricing the hardware. The act itself stays free. Haber and Stornetta in 1991, the timestamping that
Bitcoin's footnotes lead back to in the opening chapter, chained time-stamped
records together with hashes so that changing an old entry breaks every entry after it (and
Ralph Merkle's hash tree, from his 1979 Stanford thesis on secrecy and authentication, lets one short value vouch for a great many records); try it with five lines and a made-up sum, change line two, and watch every number below
it move. That makes a change \emph{visible}. It doesn't make it cost. Proof-of-work, which the
computer scientists Cynthia Dwork
and Moni Naor proposed in 1992 to make junk mail expensive and which Bitcoin later chained, is the
one framing where a record genuinely costs, and what it charges for is a search: how many
tries it took to find a lucky number. An empty block costs the same work as a full one. So the
work prices the search. The moment anything becomes certified costs nothing extra. Robert Floyd
and Tony Hoare, two computer scientists asking how you'd prove a program does what it's
supposed to, attached claims to points in a program in 1967 and 1969 (``whenever you get here, this is true''), and
the claim is backed by a proof that's paid for off the machine. And the certificates of
complexity theory, which go back to Stephen Cook's 1971 work on NP, are strings designed to be cheap to check:
hand me the certificate and I can confirm the claim quickly. Whether they're also expensive
to \emph{find} is the famous open question of the field, P versus NP, and nobody knows; what's
settled is only the cheap half. That's the opposite of a price on vouching: the whole design
goal is that checking a claim costs nearly nothing. And from statistics, a ledger that runs the
other way: Dean Foster and Robert Stine's alpha-investing (2008) runs a long string of tests
against a budget of allowed false alarms, where every test spends some of the budget and every
discovery, a rejection that stands, pays some back. That's the other way round from a toll on vouching:
the test pays, and a discovery that stands gets paid.

\subsection{What they all agree on, and who they rule out}

Lay them down, and this time what shows through is not one thing. It's five different jobs
that the word ``record'' has been doing, and I'd been letting one word carry all five. Each
has a corpse next to it, and the corpses are different too.

Durability: the record can't be silently undone. The bulla, the write-once disk, the hash
chain, Bennett's card that has to be wiped. The corpse is the editable log, and the company
that kept its debts off the books: Enron hid its debt in side entities set up to keep it off
the balance sheet, which is how the Justice Department described the scheme in 2002, and its
auditor, Arthur Andersen, shredded the paper. Andersen was convicted for the shredding that
year, and the Supreme Court threw the conviction out in 2005 over how the jury had been
instructed; either way, those books recorded nothing. But notice this job doesn't need a
witness at all. A copy will do: a hash chain nobody signed is still hard to change quietly, so
long as somebody else holds the latest link, because a chain with no copy anywhere can be
rewritten from end to end and recomputed, and nobody would know.

Authenticity: the record came from who it says it came from. Seals, the signature only a
key-holder can make, the consul's stamp. The corpse is the forged charter and DigiNotar.
This job is about custody of a stamp, and it's a different job from durability; a perfectly
authentic entry can still be erased, and a perfectly durable one can still be a forgery.

Evidence: enough independent people stand behind the claim that lying is expensive. Two
witnesses, seven seals, Boyle's gentlemen. It rules out anonymous assertion, and it rules out
``the universe keeps the receipt'': information spread
into the environment is not a record anyone can read or rely on. This one is about numbers
of people and their risk. Paper has nothing to do with it.

Accounting: the record checks itself for slips. The two columns. And here's a thing to keep
straight: the second column is \emph{not} an outside witness. It's you,
checking you. It catches a dropped digit. A careful liar gets past it, as you saw. It
belongs on this list as its own job, separate from the seven seals.

Cheap checking: a record whose correctness can be confirmed for much less than it cost to
make. Cook's certificates, the signature, the hash. This one isn't universal,
and I thought it was. Whether checking needs to be cheaper than making depends on who you're
worried about and how much a wrong record costs you; plenty of records are checked by
redoing the whole thing, and that's fine when the thing is small.

Now the thing none of them says. Not one of these jobs is
pricing the act of certifying. Bennett prices merging and erasing, which a certifying step
might or might not be. Proof-of-work prices a search the designer chose. Bookkeeping prices
a discipline. Witnesses and seals price showing up and guarding the stamp. I looked, with
everything I had, and that's where it ran out. If the bill exists, nobody in this lineage
wrote it down, and that's either because it isn't there or because the one person who did
write it down is on a shelf I never found. So I'm going to have to try it myself, on the
smallest thing I can build, and let you watch. And I'll have to be honest about which of the
five jobs the small thing even attempts, because the answer is going to be none.

\subsection{The smallest thing that could carry the bill}

Take a sheet of paper. Draw two boxes and label them NO and YES. That's the reading, a
single yes-or-no question asked of the state, and I'm going to be careful about what the
question is, because after five thousand years of seals and witnesses the word ``vouch'' is
carrying a lot and this toy carries almost none of it. The question is only: ``has the
designated flag been set.'' Not ``is some claim about a grouping true.'' Not ``did anyone check.''
There is no claim in this toy, no evidence, no checker, nobody standing behind anything. There
is a flag. Whether a flag can ever be made to \emph{mean} that something was checked and can be
relied on is a real question, and it's not this section's; I'll build toward it later, and
until then please read YES as ``the flag is up'' and nothing more. Where the state is: which
box you're in. That's the whole state, one bit. Then draw a line under the boxes for tally
marks. The marks sit outside the state. They're the running total you keep beside it as
you play, the way you'd keep score beside a board game.

Now give yourself three moves. STAY: you don't move, no mark. WORK: you don't move either (it's
a stand-in for every ordinary step a machine takes), no mark. VOUCH: from NO you move to
YES; from YES you stay in YES; either way you make one tally mark, because in this toy the
price belongs to the move's name; where you were standing doesn't enter into it. Play. Start in NO, make
any sequence of moves you like, and stop in YES. Count the marks. Now try to reach YES with
zero marks. You can't, and you can see exactly why: the only move that crosses from NO to YES
is VOUCH, and VOUCH makes a mark. Now erase the mark from VOUCH's rule and play again.
YES for free, every time. That's the entire content of what I'm about to call a rule, and I
want you to see how little it is before I dress it up: I've decided that the move which
crosses the line makes a mark, and nothing else about the machine forces that. It's a choice.
The next section is about whether I had to make it.

Why tally marks, by the way? Because they're about the oldest receipt there is. The real
ones, the English treasury's notched sticks split down the middle, get their own story in
Part III (Section~\ref{sec:counter}), fire and all. The tally on your paper is nothing like
those. Nobody holds the other half. You keep it, beside the board, and you could rub a mark out
and nobody would ever know. Hold on to that, because by the end of this section it's the reason
the toy does none of the five jobs a record does.

Here is the same toy, stated once, carefully, because this is the one place in the book where
I state it and everything later points back here. The thing on your paper has five parts.

A set of states. (Here: NO and YES, and nothing else.)

A set of move names. (STAY, WORK, VOUCH.)

A step: for each state and each move name, where you land.

A cost for each move name: a whole number of marks, zero or more. (Zero, zero, one.)

A reading: for each state, yes or no.

That's it. Add the one rule below and I'll call it a certification system; in the checked
record the rule is a sixth field, so nothing counts as one without it. And I want to be
exact about what's not in it. There's no counter stored inside the state that's forbidden
from going down; the marks are the side tally from the board game, and the tally only ever
grows because the costs are whole numbers, zero or more. (A machine could keep the
total inside its state too; that's an extra part beyond the five, and Section~\ref{sec:counter} builds it.) There's no window, no observer
who sees only part of the state; that's a later question and it gets its own section. And
the cost depends only on the move's name; where you are when you make it doesn't matter, which is a
real simplification, and I'll flag it where it counts.

One rule, which I'll call the toll. For every state and every move: if the reading is NO
before the move and YES after it, the move's cost is at least one mark. That's all. It says
nothing about any other move. It says nothing about how big a mark is in anything you could
measure. One mark is one mark; what a mark is worth, why the smallest charge is one (why not two,
or a half?), and whether I had any right to decide that, come next, and I'm not sure of
all of it.

And one theorem, which is the only thing the toy actually proves, and you've already proved
it by playing. Take any run of moves that starts in a NO state and ends in a YES state. Then
the marks it made add up to at least one. Here's the argument in words, and it's short enough
that you can hold the whole thing. Walk the run move by move, reading the box at each step.
It read NO at the start and YES at the end, and every move either leaves the reading alone or
flips it, so at some move it went from NO to YES. The toll says that move cost at least one.
Every other move cost zero or more. Add them up: at least one. Notice what the argument did
not need. It didn't need the reading to \emph{stay} YES afterward; if a later move flipped it back
to NO and another flipped it to YES again, that's two tolls, and the argument still goes through. It didn't need the
machine to be finite. It didn't need to know what any move does besides what the reading says
before and after. It needed exactly one thing: the toll.

That's the whole theorem. Here it is once more in the exact form, because from here on the
book carries two layers side by side: what I mean, in words, and what's stated and checked,
in symbols you can hold me to. The symbols are few. $\mathbb{N}$ is the whole numbers 0, 1, 2,
and so on. $S$ and $I$ are just names for ``the set of states'' and ``the set of move names.''
Writing $\mathrm{step} : S \times I \to S$ means ``hand it a state and a move name and it hands
back a state.'' A \emph{run} is a list of move names, $t = [i_1, \ldots, i_n]$, played from a start
$s_0$, one after another. The double arrow $\Longrightarrow$ reads ``then'': the thing on its
left forces the thing on its right. And ``by induction on the run,'' in the proof, is the
formal name for the way you'd check it by hand: settle the empty run, then show that one more
move at the front can't break what you've settled.

\begin{definition}[Certification system]\label{def:certsys}
A \emph{certification system} consists of a set $S$ of states, a set $I$ of move names, a step
function $\mathrm{step} : S \times I \to S$, a cost $\mathrm{cost} : I \to \mathbb{N}$, and a
reading $\mathrm{cert} : S \to \{\mathrm{no}, \mathrm{yes}\}$, subject to one rule, the
\emph{toll}: for every state $s$ and move $i$,
\[
\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no} \text{ and } \mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s,i)) = \mathrm{yes}
\;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1.
\]
The run of $t = [i_1, \ldots, i_n]$ from $s_0$ ends at $\mathrm{run}(t, s_0)$, the result of
applying the steps in order, and its total cost is
$\mathrm{cost}(t) = \mathrm{cost}(i_1) + \cdots + \mathrm{cost}(i_n)$, with the empty run
costing 0.
\end{definition}

Defined as the record \code{CertificationSystem} (UniversalCertificationCost.v).

\begin{theorem}[The universal floor]\label{thm:universal-floor}
In any certification system, every run that starts at a state reading no and ends at a
state reading yes has total cost at least 1: if $\mathrm{cert}(s_0) = \mathrm{no}$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{run}(t, s_0)) = \mathrm{yes}$, then $\mathrm{cost}(t) \ge 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By induction on the run. If $t$ is empty, the run ends where it starts, at a state reading
no, so the hypothesis ``ends at yes'' can't hold and there's nothing to prove. Otherwise
$t = i :: t'$ (the first move, then the rest); let $s_1 = \mathrm{step}(s_0, i)$. If
$\mathrm{cert}(s_1) = \mathrm{yes}$, the first move is a crossing, the toll gives
$\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$, and the rest cost at least 0, so $\mathrm{cost}(t) \ge 1$. If
$\mathrm{cert}(s_1) = \mathrm{no}$, the rest of the run starts at no and ends at yes, so by the
induction hypothesis $\mathrm{cost}(t') \ge 1$, and $\mathrm{cost}(t) = \mathrm{cost}(i) +
\mathrm{cost}(t') \ge 1$. Nothing else is used: not finiteness, not that the reading stays
yes, not what any move does beyond the reading before and after.
\end{proof}

Where to check it: the record's six fields are \code{cs\_state}, \code{cs\_instr}, \code{cs\_step}, \code{cs\_cost},
\code{cs\_cert}, and the toll \code{cs\_cert\_costs}; the theorem is \code{universal\_nfi\_any\_substrate}, in the
same file; and the checked proof is the induction above, step for step. One honest edge:
the theorem does not assume that a YES state exists. If no state ever
reads YES, no run meets the theorem's hypothesis, so it's true of every run and tells you
nothing about any of them, which is a mathematician's way of saying
it's true and useless. The toy on your paper has a YES box, so it isn't useless there. It
would be natural to assume the system has to have at least one NO state and one YES state;
the checked statement has no such clause, and that's on purpose, because a theorem that
applies to no run is still a theorem and the toy is where you supply the runs.

The theorem also runs backwards, and that direction is one line. Suppose every run from a state
reading no to a state reading yes costs at least one, whichever state you start from. A single
move is a run of length one, so a move that takes no to yes costs at least one, which is the
toll. The floor from every start and the toll are the same rule (\code{nec\_f\_floor\_iff\_a2}),
and nobody has to choose between them. From one fixed start that reads no, the floor asks for
the toll only at
the crossings you can reach without paying anything (\code{nec\_f\_floor\_at\_iff\_free\_reach});
a crossing you can only reach by paying has already cost at least one by the time you get there.

And the bound of one is the smallest case of a count. Under the toll a run costs at least the number
of times it takes the reading from no to yes, with no permanence assumed
(\code{nec\_f\_cost\_ge\_rises}). That bound for every run is again the same rule as the toll
(\code{nec\_f\_rises\_iff\_a2}). And it is reached for every count: on a one-bit machine whose set
costs one and whose reset is free, setting and resetting $k$ times from no takes the reading
from no to yes $k$ times and costs
exactly $k$ (\code{nec\_f\_bit\_rises\_exact}). All of these are in NecFFloor.v.

And one more edge, because it's the first thing to bite when you ask a machine to stand behind
more than one thing. The definition has \emph{one} reading in it. One question, one flag, one
toll on its crossing. Once the flag is up, a second claim has nowhere to go: raising a flag
that's already up doesn't move anything. So a second claim needs a reading of its own, and a
third claim a third: one reading per claim, each with its own toll. Part III builds that
properly, as a family of flags, one per threshold, each charged when it goes up
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing}), and the same theorem sends the bill for finiteness: a record
held in $k$ bits that only ever turns bits on can take at most $k + 1$ different values, so it
can go up at most $k$ times. A finite machine can keep only so many things up for good in its
whole life. That's the opening chapter's ``you can't keep all of it,'' turned into a count.

\subsection{What this does and doesn't buy}

I want to be very plain about how small this is, because the temptation is to look at the
word ``theorem'' and feel something has been established about the world. Nothing has. What's
been established is that \emph{if} you adopt the toll, \emph{then} the flag can't be raised for free,
in any system with those five parts that obeys it, no matter what the states and moves are. The ``if'' is
doing all the work. I chose the rule. A reasonable person could ask why, and the only honest
answer right now is ``because that's the thing I wanted to be true,'' which is not a reason.

Notice also what it doesn't ask about how strong the thing is, in either direction. A system
is \emph{Turing-complete} when it can imitate a Turing machine, and no stronger than one when a
Turing machine can imitate it. The theorem asks neither. Stronger than a Turing machine,
weaker, dead even: none of it reaches the floor. Bring the five parts, charge the toll on the
crossing, and you're in scope. The floor doesn't check what you can compute, because it was
never about what you can compute. It's about what a move is allowed to do for free.

Which brings up the objection a theorist makes in about four seconds, so I'll make it first.
The toll is a floor, and a floor is easy to meet. Charge one mark for every move, whatever it
does, and the toll holds for any reading you like, since every crossing is a move and every
move costs one. So any computer with a step counter beside it, and any yes-or-no question at
all about its state, is a certification system. A clock passes. Nothing about that is a loophole. It's
what the definition says, and it means the definition, on its own, doesn't tie the marks to
certifying anything. It only says a crossing can't be free. (It's also why ``a base that can
compute anything plus a flag that obeys the toll'' would be a cheap thing to call Thiele-complete,
and why the definition that gets that name, in Part IV, asks for free computing and an earned
record, which no clock meets; Section~\ref{sec:smallest}.) Two things later in the book do the tying. One is a ceiling: demand that a run's
total never exceed the number of times the flag went up, and together with the floor exactly
one bill survives, one mark per raise and nothing on any other step
(Section~\ref{sec:windows}); a clock fails that the first time it charges a step that raised
nothing. The other is order, on the smallest machine I build:
there, from a clean start, the flag can't go up
unless a passing check of a claim came first, then a commitment to that same claim, and a
clock can't fake that, because it's about which moves happened, and a clock only makes marks
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned}).

And the other side of that: nothing is in scope just for being a computation. A Turing
machine's run isn't an instance of this theorem because it's a run. It becomes one when
somebody supplies all five parts for it, says which states read yes, and proves the toll for
that cost. Until then the theorem says nothing about it, and I won't pretend it does.

That's also where the other axis from the Flatland night ended up, once I checked it. It isn't
a direction an ordinary computer can't reach. Hand a Turing machine a reading, charge the toll
on its crossing, and it's in scope like anything else. The possibility was always there. What
the usual rules leave out is the price.

The same goes for a system with no reading at all. If nothing in it answers ``is the flag
up,'' then nothing in it can say, from the inside, that anything is entitled to be relied on.
Whatever entitlement it ends up with gets carried in from outside, by somebody who signs
their name to it, and nothing in the system priced it. Smuggled entitlement isn't entitlement for the system, no matter whose name is on it. Be careful which way that cuts,
though. Whoever reads the signature can be perfectly entitled on their own account; that's what
an auditor has, and it's honest as long as it's called the auditor's. It isn't the system's. On
the smallest machine I build later, the reason to believe its checker says yes only when the
claim is true is exactly that kind: a proof, checked outside any record the machine keeps, and
I'll say so when I get there (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). What outside entitlement never is,
is something the system itself earned.

And here's a question I'll only start on here: bolt two certification systems together, and do
you get one? Run them side by side, each move being a move of one or the other, and add up
the marks. It depends on the reading you give the pair. Take a reading that can only go up
when one of the parts' readings goes up, like ``either flag is up'' or ``both are'': then any
crossing of the pair is a crossing of a part, that part's toll charged it, and the pair obeys
the toll. Take ``the first flag is up and the second is down,'' and it doesn't: that reading
turns on when the second flag falls, and nothing charges a fall. The first two readings are checked: read through ``either flag is up'' the pair is a
certification system whose floor is one. Read through ``both are,'' a run that starts with both
flags down and ends with both up costs at least two, and two is reached when each part can
raise its own flag for one (Section~\ref{sec:parts}).
From a start with one flag already up, one raise is enough, so two is a floor for the clean start
only. The third is still an argument on this page. A related
composite is checked too, a host machine running a guest, read through ``the host's
own flag or its copy of the guest's'' (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-host-instance}). Whether every way of
building one machine out of others keeps the toll is a bigger question, and Section~\ref{sec:parts}
takes it as far as I could: some ways do, some provably don't, and it says which.

So why bother with the toy at all? Not because the lineage was looking for it. The bulla
was after durability, the seven seals after evidence, the consul's stamp after authenticity,
the two columns after catching slips; none of them was trying to put a price on the moment a
flag goes up, and I shouldn't pretend they were. The reason is narrower. Everywhere in that
lineage where somebody \emph{did} locate a cost, it sat on a step next to the flag. The flag itself
went unpriced: Szilard on the measurement, Bennett on the wiping, proof-of-work on the search, Boyle
on the instrument and the room, Foster and Stine on the test. The toy is the first thing I could build where the cost sits
on the crossing itself, and it proves that if you price that step, the floor follows
everywhere, for any machine with the five parts. That's not an answer. It's the question made
exact enough to be wrong. And of the five jobs a record does, the toy attempts none of them. Not even durability:
the flag can be lowered by any move you care to write, and the marks that don't go away are
kept by \emph{you}, the scorekeeper, beside the board. The machine keeps none of them. What the toy has is a
scorekeeper's receipt for the crossing. Whether the machine can be made to keep that receipt
itself, where a step could reach in and change it, is Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s question. Authenticity, evidence,
accounting, cheap checking: none of them is in here, and I'll say so again when it's tempting
to forget.

And here's what I'll owe you by the end. Whether the toll is a choice or a necessity: the
next section, and I'll tell you now that the answer surprised me. What a mark is worth in
anything physical: later, and only partly. What an observer who sees only a window can and
cannot recover, including whether they can even tell which step paid: its own section. And
whether a full-size machine, the kind you could actually run a program on, can be made to obey
the toll without cheating, and what that machine looks like, and what it costs to vouch for
structure in it: that waits for Part IV, on purpose, and takes most of the rest of the book,
and I'm still not sure I pulled it off.

For now you have a sheet of paper with two boxes, three moves, one rule you were handed
without a reason, and one theorem you proved yourself in about a minute. Don't let go of it.
It's the smallest version of everything that follows, and if it's wrong here, it's wrong
everywhere.

%===========================================================================
\section{Why the toll isn't arbitrary}
\label{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}
%===========================================================================

I handed you a rule without a reason. The move that raises the flag makes a mark, because I
said so. If that's all it is, this book is a long way of describing a preference, and you
should treat it the way you'd treat someone telling you their favourite colour is a law of
nature. So this section is me trying to find out whether I had to pick it. I'll tell you the
shape of the answer up front, because I don't want you reading forty paragraphs to find out
whether there's a point: on a machine with a finite memory, where the flag once raised stays
up, the step that raises it has to forget something, and forgetting is the one step Landauer's
principle puts a price on, when what's forgotten wasn't already known (that last clause takes
a lot back, and I'll show you exactly how much). Three ``ifs'' in that
sentence. Every one of them
is a door you can walk out of, and I'm going to show you each door, because the doors are
where the actual content is.

\subsection{A closed room with no spare chair}

Do this one with real objects, because the whole section rests on it and it's about ninety
seconds of work. Draw a box on the table and call it the certified room. Put three chairs
inside the box and one chair outside, by the door. Four people, one per chair; the people are
the states your machine could be in, and the three inside are the ones whose flag is already
up. One move of the machine moves everybody at once: each person stands up and goes to the
chair the rule sends them to. Two rules. First: nobody inside the room may end up outside,
because the flag, once up, stays up. Second: the person by the door must end up inside,
because this move is the one that raises their flag.

Now try to finish the move with one person in each chair.

You can't. Three people start inside and have to stay inside, so they take the three inside
chairs between them, with nobody left out, because nobody may leave. The person from the door
has to come in. There is no fourth chair inside. Somebody shares. Two of the machine's
possible states land on one state, and after the move you can no longer tell, from where
everyone is sitting, which of the two it was. The move forgot something.

That's the whole argument, and I want to name the piece of mathematics that did the work,
because it's old and it's not mine. If you put things into fewer boxes
than there are
things, some box gets two. People call it the pigeonhole principle; it's the one from the
opening chapter, where Jean Leurechon used it in 1622 to argue that two people somewhere have
the same number of hairs, and the first name for it I could find came from Dirichlet, who used it in 1842 and later called it the drawer principle. It's the kind of fact a child accepts and a
mathematician spends a career finding new uses for. Here the use is: a step that forgets
nothing is a one-to-one shuffle, a one-to-one shuffle of a finite set of chairs hits every
chair, so the inside chairs are all taken by insiders, so there's no room for the newcomer.
Finite. Permanent. Flip. Those three and nothing else, and the conclusion is ``two states
became one.''

The checked version of the chairs is a theorem a few lines down, and it needs one word first.
``Injective'' is the mathematician's word for ``forgets nothing'': a step is injective when two
different starts always give two different ends. The theorem says exactly what the chairs
said and takes exactly the three premises: a duplicate-free list that
names every state (finite), a reading that no step ever turns off (permanent), and one state
that reads NO before the step and YES after it (the flip). There is no price in it anywhere.
It is pure counting. I'll come back to what counts as physics, but notice that nothing so far
has been.

Here are the words, exactly. For this whole section the setting is the five parts from
Section~\ref{sec:toll} without the toll: states $S$, move names $I$, a step, a reading, and (later) a cost.

\begin{definition}[Finite, permanent, injective]\label{def:fin-perm-inj}
The machine is \emph{finite} when there is a list of states with no repeats that contains every
state. The reading is \emph{permanent} when no move ever turns it from yes back to no: for all
$s$ and $i$, $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{yes}$ implies
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s, i)) = \mathrm{yes}$. A move $i$ is \emph{injective} (forgets
nothing) when different starts give different ends: $\mathrm{step}(a, i) =
\mathrm{step}(b, i)$ implies $a = b$. A move that is not injective \emph{merges}.
\end{definition}

Defined as \code{finite\_states}, \code{permanent} and \code{step\_injective} (PermanentCertification.v).

\begin{theorem}[A permanent flip merges]\label{thm:perm-flip-merges}
On a finite machine with a permanent reading, if $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no}$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s, i)) = \mathrm{yes}$, then the move $i$ merges.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $i$ were injective. Let $C$ be the list of states that read yes; it is finite and
has no repeats. By permanence, $\mathrm{step}(\cdot, i)$ sends every member of $C$ into $C$.
Being injective, it sends the members of $C$ to members of $C$ with no two landing on the
same one, so its images are as many as $C$ itself, and a list of that many distinct members
of $C$ is all of $C$. So the yes-state $\mathrm{step}(s, i)$ equals $\mathrm{step}(c, i)$ for
some $c$ in $C$, and injectivity gives $s = c$, so $s$ reads yes. It reads no. That's the
contradiction, and it's the chairs.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{permanent\_flip\_is\_not\_injective} (PermanentCertification.v). The proof there
uses the standard-library fact that a duplicate-free list of $n$ members inside a list of
$n$ is the whole list, which is the pigeonhole in the form Leurechon would recognise.

Is that new? No. It has been sitting in two places for a long time, one in physics and one in
the theory of automata, and a physicist will recognise it on sight, so start there. In 1876 Josef Loschmidt pointed out,
against Ludwig Boltzmann's account of how a gas settles down, that the laws of mechanics run
just as well backwards: reverse every molecule's velocity and the gas retraces its steps, so
mechanics alone can't make entropy only ever climb. Twenty years on, in 1896, a young
assistant of Max Planck's in Berlin pushed harder. He took Henri Poincaré's recurrence
theorem of 1890, which says a bounded mechanical system comes back as close as you like to
wherever it started, again and again, and used it to argue that nothing in such a system can
climb forever: give it time and it comes back down. The assistant was Ernst Zermelo, the same
Zermelo who'd patch Frege's floor twelve years later. Boltzmann answered the same year, not
very politely, that the times you'd have to wait for a return are so enormous that nobody
would ever see one. (Jos Uffink, who wrote the Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on Boltzmann's
statistical physics, calls that reply drenched in sarcasm and bitterness, and calls Zermelo's
own paper a careful logical argument.)

Now look at the chairs again. A step that forgets nothing, on a finite set, is a reshuffle:
it moves everybody around in loops, and every loop comes back to where it started. A flag
that goes up and stays up is exactly a quantity that climbs and never comes back down. So a
reshuffle can't carry one, which is Zermelo's objection with the infinities taken out. On a finite set the loops are enough, and
Poincaré's theorem isn't needed. And the wait is at most as many
steps as there are chairs. Nothing enormous. Zermelo was aiming it at the second law. Flags never came into it. The quantum version came in 1957, when P. Bocchieri and A. Loinger proved the same return
for a closed quantum system whose energies come in separate levels, so going quantum isn't a way
out of the room either, not for a closed system that never sheds anything.

The second place stings more, because it's in computer science. Somebody got here first, again.
Picture a finite machine that reads letters, one move per letter. If every letter just reshuffles
the states one for one, automata theorists call it a permutation automaton, and the sets of inputs
such machines can pick out are called group languages. Jean-Éric Pin's 1992 paper on reversible
automata, machines whose letters act as one-to-one maps, sorts out exactly which languages those
machines recognise, and in that world the chairs are folklore. Here's the short version. Start at
a state that reads no, and collect every input that ends at a yes. Because yes is permanent,
adding letters to the end of a collected input keeps it collected. A group language with that
property is either empty or everything, and everything would include the empty input, which ends
where it started, at no. So it's empty: no run of reshuffles raises the reading. That's
Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} with the moves as letters. Pin's paper is where I'd send you
to check the automata side. It isn't about flags or prices, and I'm not claiming it says
anything about them.

And if you like your facts in the most general clothes going, category theorists have this one
too. Treat the moves as a monoid acting on the states, and a permanent reading as a set of states
the moves never leave. In the topos of that monoid's actions, the truth value of ``reads yes'' at
a state is the set of move sequences that carry it into the yes-states. Every move can be undone
exactly when the monoid is a group, and exactly then is that topos Boolean, which makes every
such truth value all or nothing. Morgan Rogers
lays out that fact in his 2019 and 2021 papers on toposes of monoid actions. On a finite set, a
move that merges nothing can be undone, so it's the chairs again, in a third language. Does it
change anything here? No. It's the same fact wearing a bigger coat, and I mention it so nobody
thinks the chairs are mine.

Going quantum doesn't get around the automata version either. Alex Brodsky and Nicholas
Pippenger (2002) showed that a quantum finite automaton that measures only once, at the very
end, accepts with bounded error exactly the group languages, the reshuffle kind. One that's
allowed to measure after every letter, and to stop on what it sees, does better: it accepts
every piecewise testable language, and ``has seen a $b$ somewhere'' is one of those. A
measurement that can stop the machine is a record that stays, and it's the extra thing that
lets the bigger class in.

The third place is the closest, and it isn't old at all. In 2023 Thomas Ouldridge and David Wolpert
derived the thermodynamics of a finite automaton built the way real computers are:
the same physical step run again and again, each time touching only the part of the machine
that changes. They sorted languages into two kinds by the smallest automaton that recognises
each one. If that automaton has a letter that sends two states to one, every automaton for the
language has such a letter too, and on their derivation
recognising the language on a device like that produces entropy, waste no cleverer design gets back, unless the inputs are so finely arranged that only
one of the merged states ever actually turns up. If the smallest automaton only reshuffles, they find the language
can be recognised with no entropy produced at all. One of their worked examples is
the strings with no $b$ in them, which is my flag turned inside out: the runs that raise it are
exactly the strings that have seen a $b$. So the chairs, a real price on them, and the escape
when you already know which chair you're in are all in their paper, three years before this
book. Their price is derived from the physics of the device. Mine is assumed.

There's a fourth neighbour, and I'd call it
a cousin, because it speaks another language. Constructor theory is David Deutsch and Chiara Marletto's programme for stating
physics as which transformations a device that runs in a cycle can and can't bring about, and
in it a task is irreversible when it's possible and its inverse isn't. Marletto's version of
thermodynamics (posted in 2016) leans on exactly that: tasks that are possible while their
transposes aren't. Marletto, the physicist Vlatko Vedral and coauthors (2022) made an irreversible task out
of the quantum homogeniser, a machine of reservoir qubits that interact by partial swaps,
and ran it with photons. Maria Violaris and Marletto (2022) then argued that the same machine, run
in a cycle, can turn a pure qubit into a mixed one
and can never turn a mixed qubit back into a pure one,
even though every interaction in it is reversible, and that this suggests erasure may cost something beyond Landauer's bound. The chairs are a classical,
finite, exact cousin of that sentence: a set of states a step can't leave, a task that's
possible, and no way back. Theirs is quantum and approximate and aimed at physics' price;
mine is counted, and assumes its price. Deutsch and Marletto's paper on information (2015)
has a neighbour of the chairs argument in its section 8.6: measuring one observable
disturbs another irreducibly, and nothing can undo the disturbance afterwards while the
outcome stays in an information variable. That's a second, theory-independent way of saying
that a record that stays makes the step irreversible.

So what I can claim here is narrower again, and I'd rather say exactly how. Is even the pricing
form Ouldridge and Wolpert's? In physics, on their derivation, yes: a
merge the language can't avoid costs entropy. What I didn't find in their paper is the price as a named rule about a move, one a
machine charges on a ledger whether or not anybody's physics is right (put a price on merging
and the flip has to pay it, which is the next subsection), and what I get out of that rule: the
toll, as a theorem about the ledger, the merge-or-revoke split for a single move, the exact
match between ``forced to be priced'' and ``merges,'' the squeeze bound counted in whole marks
and its entropy form, a built machine walking out of each door, and all of it checked. The core
move is older than the computer, it had two homes before it got to mine, and its physical price
had a third.

\subsection{Now charge for forgetting, and the toll falls out}

Here's the step I'd been circling since the kindergarten buckets. In the last section I told
you Bennett's rule as he states it: what has to cost is erasing a bit or merging two paths a
computation could have taken. I didn't ask you to believe it. I'm not going to ask you now
either. I'm going to write it down as a rule you can accept or refuse, in the smallest form
that does any work: \emph{any move that forgets something costs at least one mark.} Any move that
is not injective has cost at least one. That's it. Note what it does not say. It says nothing
about certifying. It says nothing about flags. It's a price on forgetting and only on
forgetting.

Put the two together. The room says: on a finite machine with a permanent flag, the move
that raises the flag forgets something. The price says: a move that forgets something costs
at least one. So the move that raises the flag costs at least one. That is the toll, the rule
I handed you without a reason, and now it has one. The proof is two lines: the first theorem
says the flipping move merges, the premise says merges are priced, done. I'll keep saying
``premise,'' because that's what it is, and because the next section of this book
is about what happened to some very smart people who put a price where a premise goes and
then treated it as a law of nature, and about half of this one is me trying not to do that.

\begin{premise}[Merge pricing]\label{prem:merge-pricing}
Every move that merges costs at least one: for all $i$, if $i$ is not injective then
$\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$. (Checked name: \code{merging\_steps\_priced}.)
\end{premise}

\begin{theorem}[The toll from finiteness, permanence, and merge pricing]\label{thm:toll-derived}
On a finite machine with a permanent reading whose cost satisfies merge pricing, every move
that turns the reading from no to yes costs at least one. That is, the machine with that cost
is a certification system in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:certsys}, and the universal floor
(Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-floor}) applies to it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A move that flips the reading merges, by Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}; merge pricing
charges it at least one.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{a2\_from\_merging\_price\_and\_permanence}; the packaging of such a machine as a
certification system is \code{certification\_system\_from\_merging\_price}, and the run-level floor
for it is \code{permanent\_certification\_trace\_floor} (PermanentCertification.v).

The theorem asks for more than it uses. Only the yes-states need to be finitely many: with a
permanent reading and finitely many states reading yes, the rest of the machine as large as you
like, merge pricing still gives the toll (\code{nec\_f\_toll\_from\_merges\_yes\_finite}). And merge
pricing asks for more than the toll needs. Under those same two conditions the toll holds exactly
when every move that flips the reading somewhere and merges is priced
(\code{nec\_f\_a2\_iff\_flipping\_merges\_priced}). Merge pricing gives that
(\code{nec\_f\_merging\_priced\_weakens}), and the eight-state machine described later in this
section, with its jump made free, meets the toll without merge pricing
(\code{nec\_f\_a2\_without\_merge\_pricing}). All four are in NecFMerge.v.

One more way to see the same thing, because it answers a rival I'd otherwise owe you. The
rival says: leave certification alone. Price \emph{erasure}, and keep an honest flag that reports
when something was erased. Fine; but a system can set its certificate at cost zero with its
erasure flag reporting nothing, exactly because the certifying move merged two states and
the flag didn't say so (\code{commit\_without\_erasure\_system\_is\_not\_honest}). Make the erasure
flag honest, so that it reports every move that forgets, and on a finite machine with a
flag that stays up the erasure law sends the same bill the toll does
(\code{honest\_erasure\_accounting\_implies\_a2}). The toll isn't a rival to
honest erasure accounting. It's what honest erasure accounting says about the certifying
move.

So, is the toll arbitrary? Here's the honest version. The toll is a consequence of three
things: a finite memory, a flag that stays up, and a charge on forgetting. If you accept all
three, you don't get to refuse the toll; it's forced. If you refuse any one of them, the toll
goes back to being my preference. So the question ``did I have to pick it'' has turned into
three smaller questions, which is what progress usually looks like: a better set of things to argue about. Let me take the three doors in order, and for each one,
build the thing that walks out through it, because a premise you can't see the counterexample
to is a premise you're taking on faith.

\subsection{Door one: keep everything, and nothing ever has to merge}

Take a strip of paper that never runs out of boxes. The machine's whole state is the strip.
Each move writes a 1 in the next empty box, and the flag is up as soon as any box has a 1 in
it.
Check the three premises. Permanent: once there's a 1, there's always a 1. Flip: the empty
strip reads NO, and after one move it reads YES. Forgets nothing: every move can be undone by
erasing the last 1, so two different strips never become the same strip. So here is a machine
that raises a flag, keeps it up, and never merges anything. The room argument has no grip on
it, and the toll doesn't follow. The checked version is \code{unbounded\_history\_escapes}, and its
state is a list of bits of any length, which is the formal way of saying the strip has no end.

If the endless strip feels like a cheat, it's a famous one. David Hilbert, in a lecture course in the winter of 1924--25, told a story about a hotel with infinitely many rooms, every one of them taken,
where a new guest still gets a room: everybody moves from room $n$ to room $n+1$, and room 1
comes free. That's the chairs argument losing its grip, told as a joke about a front desk.
And here's the part worth checking: Hilbert never published it. The hotel became famous
because George Gamow put it in a popular book in 1947, and for a long time it wasn't clear Hilbert had told it at all. The historian of science Helge
Kragh first guessed that Gamow had made it up. Then Tilman Sauer, a historian of science who
had co-edited a volume of Hilbert's lectures on the foundations of physics, pointed him to Hilbert's lecture
notes, which had just been printed in 2013, and in 2014 Kragh took his guess back in a paper called
``The True (?) Story of Hilbert's Infinite Hotel.'' Keep the question mark. Even Kragh's own paper
puts the lecture in January 1924 in one place and January 1925 in another. Still, this time a story
everybody repeated turned out to have a real lecture behind it. I've learned not to count on that
happening. Bring it back to the table. In the room, the person from the door had nowhere
to sit because the chairs ran out. In Hilbert's hotel they never do, so everybody shifts one
over and nobody has to share. The strip machine is that hotel. The argument stays the same.
What the hotel shows you is that it was about running out of chairs all along.

What walked out the door is the finiteness premise. Now cut the strip to eight boxes and run
it for real: eight boxes, nine moves. On the ninth move there's nowhere to write. To keep going you have to reuse a box, and
the moment you reuse a box two different histories end on the same strip, and you're back in
the room with a shared chair. Keeping the whole history is exactly the move Bennett made in 1973, when he showed
that any computation can be done without forgetting if you let it keep a copy of everything it
did; Landauer, back in 1961, had already written that for a machine able to run a program that doesn't stop, the
space to hold every intermediate result ``cannot be there.'' The history escape is real. It
costs you a memory that never fills. Every machine you can buy has a memory that fills.

One thing I have to say plainly, because the file is more careful than I'd like to be. The
theorem shows the strip machine has the other two properties and forgets nothing. It does
not contain a sentence saying ``and this machine is infinite''; that's something you and I can
see about a list of unbounded length, but no Coq statement says it. And it contains no cost
at all. ``Certifies for free'' is written in a second theorem, \code{history\_escape}
(AxMerge.v): there the strip is counted as a number, each move adds one at a cost of zero,
nothing merges, merge pricing holds, and the toll fails. So I'm marking the place where the words outrun the file.

\emph{Which state is being counted.} Whether a move merges depends on what the state keeps. The
strip keeps its history, so nothing merges; cut it to eight boxes and the reuse merges.
Section~\ref{sec:landauer} proves the general form (Theorem~\ref{thm:u24-history}): keep the
previous state alongside the current one and every fixed-instruction step is one-to-one. So a merge
price is a fact about a move on a stated state space. Each price derived in this book is derived
on the whole state its definition gives, and three things go with it: which state that is, what
lies outside it (nothing outside it is charged), and whether the move is one primitive instruction
or a composite run of several. Relabelling the states one-to-one changes no price, since it sends
merges to merges and one-to-one moves to one-to-one moves. Adding history to the state, or
projecting part of the state away, changes the machine being modelled, and the price can change
with it.

\subsection{Door two: let the flag come back down}

Take one coin. The rule is: turn it over. Heads is YES, tails is NO. Every move is undoable
(turn it over again), so nothing is forgotten. Tails goes to heads: that's a flip, NO to YES.
And heads goes to tails: the same move takes the flag back down somewhere else. Two states,
finite as it gets, and the move that raises the flag forgets nothing, so a schedule that
charges only for forgetting is allowed to charge it nothing. The file states that the one move
forgets nothing
(it is injective) and its on-then-off behaviour (\code{revocable\_certificate\_escapes}); that the coin is
finite and that the price may be zero are written in \code{toggle\_escape} (AxMerge.v), which
prices the turn at zero, meets merge pricing, and fails the toll.
The thing that walked out the door is permanence.

Now here's a fact that I think is sharper than the premise it replaces, and it was the thing
in this section that surprised me. Drop permanence entirely. Keep only finiteness. Take any
move that raises the flag anywhere. Then one of two things is true: the move forgets something,
or the same move lowers the flag somewhere else. There's no third option, and the proof below
is a search: go through the finitely many YES states looking for one this move turns to NO.
Find one, and that's the revocation; find none, and the move is permanent at least for
itself, which is all the room argument needs. So a flag that goes up for free is a flag the same move can take back. A
flag that nothing takes back is paid for. You can't have a free raise that stays raised, not on
any finite machine, not with any price schedule that charges for forgetting. That's a narrower sentence than ``every certificate
costs.'' It's true, and I'll take it.
The broad one would only be mine.

\begin{theorem}[Merge or revoke]\label{thm:merge-or-revoke}
On a finite machine (no permanence assumed), if $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no}$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s, i)) = \mathrm{yes}$, then either $i$ merges, or there is a
state $t$ with $\mathrm{cert}(t) = \mathrm{yes}$ and $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(t, i)) =
\mathrm{no}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Check every yes-state on the finite list for one that $i$ sends to no. If there is one, that
is the second alternative. If there is none, then $i$ keeps every yes-state at yes, which is
permanence for the single move $i$; the argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} uses
permanence only for the move it is about, so it applies, and $i$ merges.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{flip\_merges\_or\_revokes}, with the single-move form of the room argument as
\code{permanent\_at\_flip\_is\_not\_injective} (PermanentRecordPricing.v).

I'll give you the three-card version too, because it shows that a move can
be forced to be priced without writing anything permanent, and I don't want you to think the picture is tidier than it is. Three cards, T0, T1, T2, with a star on T1.
The rule: T0 goes to T1, T1 goes to T2, T2 goes to T1. T0 gains the star (a flip). T1 loses
it (a revocation). T0 and T2 both land on T1 (a merge). So this move is priced, by the
forgetting rule, and yet it writes nothing permanent; it takes a star away in the same breath.
``The priced moves are exactly the permanent records'' is false, and the file proves it false
with these three cards. What's true is one direction: on a finite machine whose move names can be decided equal or different, every permanent raise is a priced move.
The other direction has the three cards standing in it. And ``priced'' here has an exact
meaning worth one sentence: a move is \emph{forced to be priced} when every schedule that charges
for forgetting charges it, and that holds exactly when the move forgets something, with no finiteness needed at all. A way
to tell two move names apart is enough.

\begin{definition}[Forced to be priced]\label{def:forced-priced}
A move $i$ is \emph{forced to be priced} when every cost function satisfying merge pricing
(Premise~\ref{prem:merge-pricing}) charges $i$ at least one.
\end{definition}

Defined as \code{forced\_priced} (PermanentRecordPricing.v).

\begin{theorem}[Forced price is merging]\label{thm:forced-iff-merge}
If any two move names can be decided equal or different, then a move is forced to be priced
exactly when it merges. No finiteness is needed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $i$ merges, merge pricing charges it at least one, whatever the cost function. If $i$
does not merge, define the cost that is $0$ on $i$ and $1$ on every other move (this is where
telling move names apart is used). It satisfies merge pricing, since every merging move is
some move other than $i$ and costs one, and it charges $i$ nothing, so $i$ is not forced.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{forced\_priced\_iff\_merges} (PermanentRecordPricing.v).

\begin{corollary}[Permanent records are forced]\label{cor:permanent-forced}
On a finite machine whose move names can be decided equal or different, a move
that never turns the reading off and turns it on somewhere is
forced to be priced. (By Theorem~\ref{thm:merge-or-revoke} it merges; by
Theorem~\ref{thm:forced-iff-merge} it is forced.) The converse fails: the three cards are
forced, because they merge, and they revoke.
\end{corollary}

Checked as \code{forced\_priced\_iff\_merges}, \code{permanent\_record\_write\_is\_forced\_priced}, and the
three-card counterexample \code{forced\_price\_without\_permanent\_record} (PermanentRecordPricing.v).

\subsection{Door three: forget for free}

The third door is the easiest to describe and the hardest to argue about, so I'll describe
it and then spend the rest of the section on the argument. Take two sheets of paper, one
blank and one stamped. One move: stamp whatever you're handed. Finite, two states.
Permanent: stamped stays stamped. Flip: blank goes to stamped. Forgets: both sheets end up as
the same stamped sheet. Everything the room argument needs is here, and the move merges. Now
set the price of that move to zero. The toll fails, and you can watch it fail: the flag went
up for nothing.
That's \code{free\_merge\_escapes} (PermanentCertification.v), and what walked out the door is the charge on forgetting. (The
same file shows that a price of one on that move satisfies all three premises,
\code{priced\_reset\_satisfies\_premises}, so the premises can hold together; door three is about
whether they must.) Nothing in counting stops you from setting that price to zero. Only a
claim about the world does. The nearest such claim is Landauer's, and I have to be exact
about the gap between the two: the premise as written charges \emph{every} forgetting move,
whether or not you knew which state you were in, and Landauer's own heat, as the coin under
the cup below will show, is owed only for what you didn't know. So the premise is Landauer's
claim taken in its worst case over what the machine might be holding, and that's the
version the counting needs.

Here is what Landauer said, in 1961, as exactly as I can put it. I went past the
summaries and read the paper itself. A logical operation with no single-valued inverse (a step that
forgets, in this book's words) must produce heat, ``typically of the order of kT'' per operation, where
k is Boltzmann's constant and T is the temperature; and for the specific case of resetting
one bit whose value you don't know, the minimum is kT times the natural log of 2, about 0.69
kT. I want you to hear two things in that. First, ``of the order of'': he was not handing out a
number to three decimals. Second, and this surprised me, he did not measure anything. The
paper is argument, with models. He writes that he can ``show, or at least very strongly
suggest'' the conclusion, and that his reasoning gives ``no guarantee that this minimum is in
fact achievable.'' That's the founding paper of the whole subject, and it's a careful man
saying ``I think this is right and here's why.'' I like him more for it.

Was it measured, eventually? Yes, and only recently. In 2012 a group at the École Normale
Supérieure in Lyon, Antoine Bérut and Sergio Ciliberto's lab working with Eric Lutz, trapped
a single glass bead, two millionths of a metre across, in a
double well made of laser light, and used the two wells as the two values of a bit. Then they
erased the bit, by lowering the barrier, tilting the trap, and raising it again, many times
over, slower and slower, and measured the heat each time. The average heat came down toward
Landauer's kT ln 2 and sat there as the erasure got slower. On average. Single runs went
under it; the bound is about the average, and any one erasure can beat it. And if you only succeed in
erasing half the time you owe nothing, which the paper's formula shows and which I think is
the most honest line in it. Others have done it since with different devices. So: predicted
in 1961 by argument, seen in a laboratory fifty-one years later.

And is it settled? No, and I'd be lying by omission if I left that out, because the people
who doubt it are not cranks. John Norton, a philosopher of physics, has argued since 2005
that the usual proofs of the principle quietly assume what they're trying to prove, and that
the kinds of process they assume, combined, could be made to break the very law the
principle is supposed to guard. An earlier objection, made in 1999 by Norton and his Pittsburgh colleague John Earman, also a philosopher
of physics, was that the principle can't be independent of the second law. Charles Bennett, who did more
than anyone to build the subject, rated that one ``in my opinion the one of greatest merit,''
and then disagreed with it. Others replied to Norton; Norton replied back. The Stanford Encyclopedia
entry on the topic, written by a philosopher of physics who works on exactly this, ends
without a verdict. I've read what I could of both sides and I'm not qualified to referee them, and I'm
not going to pretend the laboratory settles a question about what the principle means in
general, because measuring one bead doesn't do that.

So here's what I did with it, and I think it's the only honest thing to do. The charge on
forgetting is written into the checked work as a \emph{named premise}. It's a definition the
theorems take as an assumption, and nowhere is it proved as a general fact, because it isn't
provable from counting; for particular machines with particular price lists it's checked
(the stamp at cost one, above), which is a different thing. If Norton turns out to be right, every theorem in this section still holds; they
just have one premise fewer that the world agrees to. If Landauer's side turns out to be
right, the premise is physics. Either way, nothing in this section says a device does
anything until someone measures the device. The counting is mine to prove. The physics is a
door I've labelled, and what opens it is a measurement. A proof can't.

Labelled, though, isn't the same as unplaced, and a hedge isn't a position, so here's mine.
Earman and Norton's objection is a dilemma. Either an information-theoretic exorcism of the demon
assumes the second law, which they call the \emph{sound} horn, and then it adds nothing the
second law didn't already give; or it rests on a new principle tying information to entropy, the
\emph{profound} horn, and nobody has given that principle independent grounds. A named premise
is the sound horn, on purpose. That's where Bennett ended up in 2003, and Norton's ``Too Good to
Be True'' (written in 2025, published in 2026) says the careful literature almost always accepts
that horn, and argues that whatever succeeds there is ordinary thermodynamics relabelled. I'll
take that. Ordinary thermodynamics, relabelled onto a ledger, is all this section asks of the
physics. And on the counting I'm on Norton's side outright. His 2018 paper ``Maxwell's Demon Does
Not Compute'' exorcises the demon with Liouville's theorem and nothing else, no information and
no computation: dynamics that keeps every patch of states the same size can't crowd a big set
of states into a small one. The counting core of this section, that a step losing nothing can't
carry a no-state into a set that stays up, is that point in finite, discrete form. And if you
want the best case for the premise itself, the one I found is James Ladyman, Stuart Presnell,
Anthony Short and Berry Groisman (2007): from one of the standard statements of the second law, the one named for Kelvin, they derive
that a logically irreversible operation can't be carried out thermodynamically reversibly by any
of their L-machines. That's the merge-pricing premise with an argument under it, and if you want
to argue with the premise, that's the paper to argue with.

One question a physicist asks before any of that, and it's a good one: the laws underneath
never merge anything. Classical mechanics carries each exact state forward to exactly one next
state and could carry it back again, and Liouville's theorem adds that a patch of states keeps
its size as it moves; quantum mechanics is unitary, which is one-to-one too. So when this
section says a step merged two states, where did the difference go? Out of the machine. The
merge is in the machine's own description, the states its reading is about. The machine
together with everything around it still runs one-to-one, and the distinction the machine
forgot survives. It gets pushed out into the surroundings, mostly as heat. The
surroundings are door one's endless strip. That door is always open for the universe as a
whole and shut for the machine, because the machine isn't the universe and its memory fills.
Read that way, Landauer's premise is the claim that pushing a distinction out of a finite
machine into its surroundings costs heat, and that's all it claims. Which also means the bill
is heat \emph{handed over}. None of it has to be heat \emph{wasted}. Takahiro Sagawa's 2014
analysis says that a step
that forgets can, in principle, be run slowly enough that no entropy is produced overall: the
heat leaves the machine, the room's entropy goes up by what the machine's went down, and
nothing is lost that didn't have to be. So on the premise the forgetting step can't be free,
but it doesn't have to be wasteful. When I call it a cost, I mean a transfer you can't avoid.
None of it is a loss you could have engineered away.

\subsection{How much: the price grows with the squeeze}

The toll says ``at least one mark.'' That's a floor for raising one flag. The room argument
says more if you let it. Say there are m people already inside and k more come in through
the door in one move. (That's a different k from the one in Landauer's kT; when the two meet,
below, Boltzmann's constant gets a little B hung under it, $k_B$, so you can tell it from a
head count.) All m plus k of them end up in m chairs. That's a squeeze, by a factor
of (m + k) over m, and if you accept a slightly stronger version of the forgetting price,
that each mark pays for at most one \emph{halving} of the number of distinguishable states, then
the move costs at least the number of halvings in that squeeze, which is the base-two
logarithm of (m + k)/m.

Back to door three's stamp, with four sheets this time: three blank, one stamped, and the
stamp-everything move. Four states go to one. Before the move, to say which sheet you had took
two yes-or-no questions (is it one of the first two? then which of those two?); after the
move, it takes none. Two bits gone. Two halvings. So that move costs at least two marks, and
two marks is enough: a cost of exactly two satisfies the halving rule (both facts are checked
for these four sheets, \code{quad\_stamp\_needs\_two} and \code{quad\_stamp\_cost\_two\_is\_priced}). The
general statement is m + k at most 2 to the cost times m, and next to it in the file sits a
logarithm form that rounds both logarithms up and is weaker for it (three states and one
newcomer round to the same two bits on both sides, and the rounded form says nothing). The
halving premise, like the one before it, is a definition used as an assumption. The units
are halvings. To turn a halving into joules of heat you multiply by $k_B T \ln 2$, and that
multiplication is physics; the counting stops before it.

That little $k_B$ deserves a short trip of its own, because it sits exactly where counting
turns into physics, and its name is a small history lesson. Ludwig Boltzmann's grave in
Vienna has $S = k \log W$ carved on it (that $k$ is the same $k_B$, before anyone hung a B
under it): entropy is a constant times the logarithm of the number of ways the parts could be
arranged. The idea is his. The constant, and the equation written that way, came from Max
Planck, in his work on radiation around 1900. In his Nobel lecture in 1920 Planck said the
constant ``is frequently termed Boltzmann's constant, although to the best of my knowledge
Boltzmann himself never introduced it,'' and guessed that Boltzmann never believed anyone could
measure it accurately. I'd assumed Planck named it after Boltzmann. His own words point the other
way: it was other people calling it that. Who first did, I couldn't pin down; one recent paper
points to Paul Ehrenfest in 1906, the year Boltzmann died, and I haven't checked that myself.
Ehrenfest was an Austrian physicist who had done his doctorate under Boltzmann in Vienna. So
the most famous constant in this corner of physics wears the name of a man who didn't write it
down. Does that change the bill? No. But look at the job the
constant does in that equation. Take it away and what's left is the logarithm of a count,
which is a number of halvings, which is what the squeeze bound hands you. The constant is the
exchange rate, and whether the world honours that rate for a merge is the premise. No
theorem here settles it.

Exactly, with one new piece of notation: for a list $D$ of states, write $|D|$ for how many
it has, and $\mathrm{img}_i(D)$ for the number of \emph{different} states the move $i$ sends them
to.

\begin{premise}[Halving price]\label{prem:halving}
Each mark pays for at most one halving: for every move $i$ and every list $D$ of states with
no repeats, $|D| \le 2^{\mathrm{cost}(i)} \cdot \mathrm{img}_i(D)$. (Checked name:
\code{compression\_priced}. It implies merge pricing, since a merge sends two different states to
one and so needs $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$.)
\end{premise}

There's a plainer way to read that premise, and it's worth having because it says what the
premise is \emph{about}. Look at one landing spot of move $i$ and count how many states land
there; call the biggest such count the move's worst pile-up. The premise holds exactly when
every pile-up has at most $2^{\mathrm{cost}(i)}$ states in it, which is to say the cost is at
least the base-two logarithm of the worst pile-up. One direction: take $D$ to be one whole
pile, which lands on a single spot, and the premise says the pile has at most
$2^{\mathrm{cost}(i)}$ members. The other: any list $D$ splits by where its members land,
each part fits inside one pile, so $|D|$ is at most the number of landing spots times the
worst pile-up, which is the premise. So the halving price asks a move to pay for the worst it
could ever do, whichever state it's actually handed. That's worst case on purpose, and it has
a home in physics. In the branch of thermodynamics that prices a single run that
has to succeed every time, with no averaging over many runs, Philippe Faist, Frédéric
Dupuis, Jonathan Oppenheim and Renato Renner derived in 2015, in that framework, what they give as
the least work any logical process needs, and when every input might occur and no error is allowed, their bound comes to
$k_B T \ln 2$ times exactly that logarithm. Take an AND gate as the example: three inputs
land on 0, so it needs at least $\log_2 3$, about 1.6, halvings' worth of work (two marks,
in whole numbers). The premise asks for that bound of a device that has to work whatever
it's handed, and it counts it in marks. Joules don't come into it.

\begin{theorem}[The squeeze bound]\label{thm:squeeze}
On a finite machine with a permanent reading and a cost satisfying the halving price, let
$m$ be the number of states that read yes, and let a move $i$ turn $k$ different no-states
to yes. Three numbers, then: $m$ counts every yes-state of the machine, reachable or not; $k$
counts a list of distinct no-states that the move turns to yes, and the move may turn others too;
and $\mathrm{cost}(i)$ is the price the cost assigns to the move. Then
\[
m + k \;\le\; 2^{\mathrm{cost}(i)} \cdot m, \qquad\text{and, when } m \ge 1,\qquad
\mathrm{cost}(i) \;\ge\; \log_2 \frac{m+k}{m}.
\]
The counting inequality holds as stated. When $m \ge 1$, it is equivalent to the displayed
logarithmic lower bound.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put the $m$ yes-states and the $k$ newcomers in one list; it has $m + k$ different members.
By permanence every yes-state lands on a yes-state, and by hypothesis every newcomer does
too, so all $m + k$ land among the $m$ yes-states: $\mathrm{img}_i \le m$. The halving price
gives $m + k \le 2^{\mathrm{cost}(i)} \cdot \mathrm{img}_i \le 2^{\mathrm{cost}(i)} \cdot m$.
\end{proof}

The four sheets are the case $m = 1$, $k = 3$, where the bound is reached. With
$k = 1$ the bound says $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$, which is the toll again
(\code{a2\_from\_compression\_price\_and\_permanence}). Checked as
\code{permanent\_flips\_compression\_bound}, with the rounded-logarithm form
\code{permanent\_flips\_log\_bound} and the counting-only cousin \code{permanent\_flips\_collapse\_at\_least}
(at least $k$ states collapse, with no price premise at all).

The bound is reached for every $m \ge 1$ and every cost $c$. Whenever $m + k \le 2^c m$, a finite
machine with a permanent reading and the halving price has $m$ yes-states and a move of cost
exactly $c$ that turns a listed $k$ distinct no-states to yes. The move turns every other no-state
of that machine to yes as well, $(2^c - 1)m$ of them in all. No cost meeting the halving price on
that machine charges the move less than $c$ (\code{nec\_f\_squeeze\_tight\_every\_k} and
\code{nec\_f\_grid\_cost\_least}, NecFSqueeze.v). So the least whole-number cost that meets the bound
is exactly $\lceil \log_2 \frac{m+k}{m} \rceil$ (\code{nec\_f\_least\_cost\_exists} and
\code{nec\_f\_least\_cost\_is\_ceiling}, NecFSqueezeLog.v).

Four more facts about the halving price, all checked, and the last one is a limit. First, the plainer
reading above is a theorem on a finite machine: the halving price holds exactly when no move has
a landing spot with more than $2^{\mathrm{cost}(i)}$ states landing on it
(\code{ent2\_compression\_priced\_iff\_fibres}). Second, for the eight-state machine
described later in this section that's a theorem about its own price list: no
move has a larger pile-up than $2^{\mathrm{cost}}$, so the halving price holds, and the toll follows
from it (\code{ent2\_frag\_compression\_priced}, \code{ent2\_frag\_toll\_by\_compression}); and the price
list is the least that meets the halving price, since any price list that does charges every move at
least what this one charges (\code{ent2\_frag\_cost\_minimal}). Third, the squeeze bound is met with
equality there: its stamp turns on the four states whose flag is down, beside the four whose flag is already up, and
$4 + 4 = 2^{1} \cdot 4$ (\code{ent2\_frag\_bound\_attained}). Fourth, and this is the limit, the small
machine of Part IV as a whole does not meet the halving price, whatever procedure you use to decide
whether two of its states are equal, because one of its free moves, the one that takes one off
a number the machine holds, lands two different states of the whole machine on the same
state (\code{ent2\_small\_not\_compression\_priced}; the pair is in
Theorem~\ref{thm:frag-merge-split}). So on that machine the toll is the rule I chose, as I said it was;
that the halving premise fails there is a theorem (CompressionSmall2.v).

\subsection{The same bill, written in bits, and when it's zero}

There's one more way to say all this, and I include it because it's the way physicists say
it and because it hands you the one case where the bill is exactly zero, which I find more
instructive than any case where it isn't.

Claude Shannon, in 1948, gave a number to ``how much you don't know'': if something could be in
any of n states and you have no idea which, your uncertainty is log base two of n bits, and
that's the most it can be for n states. If you push your uncertainty through a step that
forgets nothing, it stays the same; through a step that merges two states you might have
been in, it drops. Now run the room. Before the move, you might be in any of the m + k states
in play. After it, you're in one of m. So your uncertainty afterward is at most log2 of m,
whatever you believed before. If you started with no idea at all, every one of the m + k
states equally likely, your uncertainty was exactly log2 of (m + k), and the move removed at
least log2 of (m + k)/m bits: the same number as the halving count, now in Shannon's units.
Landauer's principle, in the form physicists write it, then says a step that removes that
many bits from the state gives off at least $k_B T \ln 2$ of heat per bit. Put the two
together and the flip gives off heat, and the exact statements below say how much and under
which side conditions, one of which (the temperature has to be taken as zero or above) is
easy to skip and shouldn't be.

Why does Shannon's number share a name with the physicists' entropy at all? There's a story
about it. Shannon wanted to call it uncertainty, and the mathematician John von Neumann
told him to call it entropy instead, for two reasons: the same formula already lived in
statistical mechanics under that name, and nobody really knows what entropy is, so in an
