argument he'd always have the upper hand. It's a great story. It comes from Myron Tribus, who spent years tying information theory to
thermodynamics, who
said Shannon told it to him in 1961, and who printed it, with Edward McIrvine, in \emph{Scientific American} in
1971. Then in 1982 an interviewer, Robert Price, asked Shannon about it, and Shannon said he
didn't think von Neumann had told him any such thing. So it's a
legend with one witness, and the person the witness quoted doesn't remember saying it. What
doesn't hang on the story: the two formulas really do have the same shape, and it still
takes Landauer's premise, a named assumption, to turn a count of bits into heat.

Exactly, with the notation built first. A \emph{spread} (probabilists say distribution) is a way
of giving each state a chance $p(x) \ge 0$, with the chances adding to 1. Its Shannon
entropy, in bits, is
\[
H(p) \;=\; -\sum_{x:\,p(x) > 0} p(x)\,\log_2 p(x),
\]
where the big sigma means ``add up, over every state $x$ with a chance above zero,'' and each
term is a state's chance times the bits it would take to single that state out. That comes to
$\log_2 n$ when $n$ states share the chance evenly and less when the chance is lopsided. Pushing a spread through a move $i$ gives the spread of where you land:
$q(y) = \sum_{x:\,\mathrm{step}(x,i) = y} p(x)$. The bits the move \emph{removes} are
$H(p) - H(q)$.

Start with the half of the claim that costs nothing, Bennett's half. A move that forgets
nothing sends each state somewhere different, so the chances just get carried to new
addresses, one for one. Nothing piles up and nothing spreads out. The uncertainty is the same
number before and after.

\begin{theorem}[A move that forgets nothing removes no bits]\label{thm:u04-injective-entropy}
Let the states be finite, listed once each, and let $f$ send states to states with
$f(a) = f(b)$ only when $a = b$. Then for every assignment of chances $p$, the pushed spread
$q$ has $H(q) = H(p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
An injective map on a finite list of distinct states is a reshuffle of that list: every state
is hit exactly once. So $q(f(x)) = p(x)$ for every $x$, and the sum defining $H(q)$ is the sum
defining $H(p)$ with its terms in a different order.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{step\_entropy\_invariant\_if\_injective} (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v). That's
why a price on removed bits can leave every reversible move free, which is the shape the
toll needs: the bill lands only where something was forgotten.

\begin{theorem}[Entropy after a permanent flip]\label{thm:entropy-ceiling}
On a finite machine with a permanent reading, let $m$ be the number of states that read yes,
and let a move $i$ turn $k \ge 1$ different
no-states yes. For any spread $p$ whose chance lies on those $m + k$
states, the spread after the move has $H(q) \le \log_2 m$. For the even spread on the
$m + k$ states, the move removes at least $\log_2 \frac{m+k}{m}$ bits.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
After the move, all the chance sits on the $m$ yes-states (permanence for the old ones,
the hypothesis for the new). There is at least one yes-state: the image of a state that
flips. Thus $m\ge1$. Write $q_1,\ldots,q_r$ for the positive output probabilities,
where $r\le m$ and their sum is $1$.

For $y>0$, $\ln y\le y-1$: the derivative of $y-1-\ln y$ is $1-1/y$, so its minimum
is $0$ at $y=1$. Apply this with $y=1/(m q_j)$, multiply by $q_j$, and add:
\[
-\ln m-\sum_{j=1}^{r}q_j\ln q_j
\;\le\;\sum_{j=1}^{r}(1/m-q_j)=r/m-1\;\le\;0.
\]
Dividing by $\ln2>0$ gives $H(q)\le\log_2 m$. The even input spread has
$m+k$ probabilities each $1/(m+k)$, hence $H(p)=\log_2(m+k)$. Subtracting the
output bound gives the claimed loss $\log_2((m+k)/m)$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{permanent\_step\_entropy\_ceiling} and, for the even spread, \code{permanent\_flip\_uniform\_entropy\_drop} (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

\begin{premise}[Landauer's principle, as a premise]\label{prem:landauer}
A step that lowers the entropy of the machine's state by $\Delta H$ bits, at temperature
$T$, gives off heat $Q \ge k_B T \ln 2 \cdot \Delta H$, where $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant.
(Checked name: \code{landauer\_heat}, with $k_B T$ as one variable.)
\end{premise}

\begin{corollary}[Heat floor of a permanent flip]\label{cor:heat-floor}
Under Premise~\ref{prem:landauer}, with $k_B T \ge 0$, the flip of
Theorem~\ref{thm:entropy-ceiling} from the even spread gives off at least
$k_B T \ln \frac{m+k}{m}$; with $k_B T > 0$ that is strictly positive.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:entropy-ceiling} gives an entropy loss of at least
$\log_2((m+k)/m)$ bits. Multiply by the nonnegative factor $k_B T\ln2$ and use
Premise~\ref{prem:landauer}. The identity $\ln2\,\log_2 x=\ln x$ gives the displayed
floor. Here $m>0$ and $k>0$, so $(m+k)/m>1$ and its logarithm is positive; if
$k_B T>0$, the heat floor is strictly positive too.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{permanent\_step\_entropy\_ceiling}, \code{permanent\_flip\_uniform\_entropy\_drop},
\code{entropy\_le\_log\_support}, \code{permanent\_flip\_heat\_floor}, and \code{permanent\_flip\_heat\_positive}
(PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

How big is that? Take the case where the squeeze is two, one state flipping in beside one that
was already yes, so $m = k = 1$ and the floor is $k_B T \ln 2$. At room temperature, about 300
kelvin, that's roughly three zeptojoules: three thousandths of a billionth of a billionth of a
joule. And that's the \emph{biggest} bill a single flip gets from this corollary. With $k = 1$ the floor is $k_B T \ln \frac{m+1}{m}$, and it shrinks as more states
already read yes: with a thousand of them it's about a thousandth of $k_B T$, some seven
hundred times less than the case of two. So one mark is not one halving. It's one halving
exactly when the squeeze is two; for any thinner squeeze the physics asks for less than a
halving, and the toll still charges a whole mark, because marks come in whole numbers (that's
the rounding the entropy road to the toll leans on, a little further down). Whatever the size,
it's a bill only if you grant the premise; nothing on this page measured anything. And even
granted, it's a bill nobody will ever see on a meter: real logic gates spend many thousands of
times more than this on every switch, even the frugal ones. One 2023 tally of the numbers puts
switching a single CMOS gate at a hundred attojoules at the low end, over thirty thousand
times this. The point of the number isn't that
certifying is expensive. It's that, on the premise, it isn't zero.

Physicists have a name for a step with no way back, and that logarithm has turned up in their
work before. Y\^uto Murashita, Ken Funo and Masahito Ueda (2014) studied processes where some
histories of the reversed process have no forward history at all. They call that
\emph{absolute irreversibility}, and they derived that the entropy
such a process produces averages at least $-\ln(1-\lambda)$, where $\lambda$ is the chance of those orphaned reverse
histories. Their first example is a gas let out of a box that held a fraction $l$ of the room,
where the bound comes to $\ln(1/l)$. Now picture the even spread of my flip played backwards:
the chance sitting on the $m$ yes-states spreading back out over all $m+k$, a gas let out of a
box holding $m/(m+k)$ of the room. Their bound for that is $\ln\frac{m+k}{m}$, the same
logarithm as the heat floor, in units of $k_B T$. So is my squeeze a special case of their
bound? No, and the reason is worth a minute, because the match is a good trap. The even spread
gives a real chance to every state the flip starts from, so no forward history is missing: the
flip itself isn't absolutely irreversible at all, and their $\lambda$ for it is zero. The heat
floor is ordinary Landauer heat, the bill for squeezing a spread over $m+k$ states into $m$ of
them, the same kind of bill as any reset into a smaller set. The two logarithms match because a
squeeze's Landauer heat equals the entropy produced by the free expansion that undoes it, and
that free expansion, the flip played backwards, is the process their bound is about. A mirror.
Neither result descends from the other. Their idea does reach the flip, just somewhere else: on a device
whose rates never change, raising the flag from a state it knows, which turns up at the end of this
section. Gonzalo Manzano, G\"ulce Karde\c{s}, \'Edgar Rold\'an and David Wolpert (2024) carried
absolute irreversibility over to computations, with one-way transitions and machines that stop
at random times, worked on finite automata, and the same $-\ln(1-\lambda)$ term sits in their
second-law bounds.

The even spread is the easy case, and you might worry the heat depends on picking it. It
doesn't. Any spread that gives a real chance to every yes-state and to the state that
flips will do.

\begin{corollary}[Positive heat for any full spread]\label{cor:u04-full-support-heat}
On a finite machine with a permanent reading, let move $i$ turn a no-state $s$ yes. Take any
spread $p$ that gives positive chance to $s$ and to every yes-state. Under
Premise~\ref{prem:landauer} with $k_B T > 0$, the heat the move gives off is strictly positive.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
After the move, $s$ and the yes-states all land among the yes-states, and there is one more
of them than there are yes-states, so two distinct states with positive chance land on the
same state. That merge removes a positive number of bits
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u04-point-sum} below), and a positive temperature times a positive number of
bits is positive heat.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{permanent\_flip\_full\_support\_entropy\_drop\_positive} and
\code{permanent\_flip\_full\_support\_heat\_positive} (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

There's a third road to the toll here too, and it's the same shape as the merge road, with
bits in place of marks for forgetting.

\begin{definition}[Entropy-priced]\label{def:u04-entropy-priced}
On a finite machine, a cost is \emph{entropy-priced} when, for every move $i$ and every spread
$p$, the cost of $i$ is at least the bits the move removes:
$\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge H(p) - H(q)$, where $q$ is $p$ pushed through $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The toll from entropy pricing]\label{thm:u04-entropy-toll}
On a finite machine with a permanent reading and an entropy-priced cost, every move that
turns the reading from no to yes costs at least one. So the machine with that cost is a
certification system (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}), and every run from a no-state to a
yes-state costs at least one.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let move $i$ turn $s$ yes, and let $m$ be the number of yes-states; $m \ge 1$, since
$\mathrm{step}(s, i)$ is one. Take the even spread on the $m$ yes-states and $s$. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:entropy-ceiling} with $k = 1$, the move removes at least
$\log_2 \frac{m+1}{m} > 0$ bits, so the cost of $i$ is a whole number above a positive
number, which makes it at least one. The run-level floor is the universal floor
(Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-floor}) applied to that system.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{a2\_from\_entropy\_price\_and\_permanence}, with the packaging
\code{certification\_system\_from\_entropy\_price} and the run-level floor
\code{entropy\_priced\_trace\_floor} (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

Now the zero. Put a coin under a cup without looking. Rule: set it heads up. You might have
had tails; now you have heads; one bit of what you didn't know is gone, and that's the bit the
principle charges for. Now lift the cup, see heads, put the cup back, and apply the rule
again. Nothing you didn't know changed. No bit was lost. And the principle, applied to a state
you already knew, demands nothing: the premise holds exactly when the heat is zero or more,
which is to say it sets no floor at all. The principle
charges for \emph{uncertainty removed}. The shape of the move doesn't enter. This is the generalized
form of Landauer's principle, worked out by Owen Maroney in 2009, in a paper he wrote at the
Perimeter Institute in Canada (he has been a philosopher of physics at Oxford since 2011), and by Sagawa in 2014, and Landauer
himself had the seed of it in 1961: for a row of bits all already ONE, he wrote, there's no need
to carry out any operation, so no entropy changes and no heat is given off, and resetting a row
all ZERO to ONE involves no entropy change either, because neither row carries any
information.

\begin{theorem}[A known state gets no heat floor from the premise]\label{thm:known-state}
On a finite machine, if the spread puts all its chance on one state $s$, then any move removes
zero bits, and Premise~\ref{prem:landauer} for that move holds exactly when $Q \ge 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A spread on one state has entropy 0, and so does its image, which is again on one state. So
$\Delta H = 0$ and the premise reads $Q \ge 0$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{known\_state\_step\_removes\_no\_entropy} and \code{known\_state\_flip\_forces\_no\_heat} (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

Be careful with that one, because it's easy to overread. ``The premise sets no heat floor for a known
state'' does not mean a stamping machine run on a known-blank sheet gives off no heat.
A fixed device that merges states dissipates on known input too; Bennett calls that
wasteful, because entropy goes out into the room with nothing taken from the data. What the
theorem says is only that the \emph{premise} sets no floor there. The floor comes from what you
didn't know. That's a sentence about the bill. The device is a separate matter. And notice that the
toll still charges the known-state stamp one mark, because the toll is a rule about the
\emph{move}, and the move doesn't know what the observer knows. That's the worst-case gap from
door three showing up again, and it's the price of having a rule a machine can follow
without asking who's watching.

There's a second piece of fine print on that theorem, and it's about who works the controls.
The generalized principle can charge a known state nothing because it lets the step be driven by
a protocol that changes in time: lower this barrier, tilt that well, raise the barrier again,
each at the right moment. Something outside the step keeps that time, an outside clock or an
outside hand, and the premise doesn't bill it. Take the hand away and the bill changes. Paul
Riechers, Alexander Boyd, Gregory Wimsatt and James Crutchfield (2020) analysed what happens
when the control is \emph{time-symmetric}, the same played forwards or backwards, which covers a clocked pulse and any device
whose rates never change. On their analysis, every move that doesn't come back to
where it started when you apply it twice, which they call \emph{nonreciprocal}, costs at least
$k_B T \ln(1/\varepsilon)$ on top of the change in free energy, to run with error at most
$\varepsilon$. A flip that stays up is always nonreciprocal: apply it twice from the no-state
and you're still at yes. So, if they're right, under that kind of
control the known-state stamp isn't free after all, and the more reliable you want it, the more it costs. Their class is bigger than mine,
though. Erasure is nonreciprocal, and so is a counter of three or more values that steps forward
and wraps around, which merges nothing, so their bound is about what the
controls are allowed to do, records or no records. So read Theorem~\ref{thm:known-state} with its control written in:
Landauer's premise sets no positive heat floor for a known state when the step can be driven by a protocol timed
from outside it. The same goes for Theorem~\ref{thm:forced-iff-merge}. On a machine whose move names can be decided equal or different,
the moves every
merge-pricing schedule must charge are exactly the merging moves, and that's true against merge
pricing; measured against time-symmetric control, the forced moves would be, on this argument
and unchecked, the nonreciprocal
ones, the wrapping counter included. Which moves the physics forces a price on depends on what
the controls can do.

A deterministic run from a known start has a known state at every step. For such a run, the
adopted entropy-loss premise reduces to $Q \ge 0$: it supplies no positive heat lower bound.
That does not establish that a particular device attains zero heat. The chairs guarantee a
collision among the already-yes states together with the entering no-state. They do not
guarantee that the entering state takes part in the collision (a four-state machine where it
doesn't is \code{nec\_f\_collision\_avoids\_s}, NecFMerge.v). For an input distribution
supported only on no-states, this counting argument alone therefore forces no positive entropy
loss. Whether other states in that support merge depends on the move. The operation-level
ledger toll still follows under merge pricing.

So here's what this section actually earns.
A device with finitely many states that has to raise a flag and keep it up
correctly \emph{from every state it might be
in}, including states where it can't tell whether the
flag is already up, can't do it for
free at any temperature above zero, on Landauer's premise; that's the design envelope, the worst case. A particular run from
a start it knows can, on the same premise, as long as something outside the step does the
timing. What stays forced in every case is the toll as a
rule about the move, because the rule can't ask what the run knows. Wherever this book says
that settling something for good can't be free if Landauer's right, it means the device
sentence. It never means the run sentence.

Here's the general case, and it's the one that shows you where the bits go. Split the bill
state by state. Each state $x$ you might be in carries its chance $p(x)$ along to where it
lands, $\mathrm{step}(x, i)$, and finds whatever other chance landed there too. If nobody else
landed there, it owes nothing. If others did, it owes the difference between how crowded its
landing spot is and how much of the crowd it brought.

\begin{theorem}[The bits removed, one term per state]\label{thm:u04-point-sum}
On a finite machine, for any move $i$ and any chances $p(x) \ge 0$, with $q$ the pushed
spread,
\[
H(p) - H(q) \;=\; \sum_{x:\,p(x) > 0} p(x)\,\bigl(\log_2 q(\mathrm{step}(x,i)) - \log_2 p(x)\bigr).
\]
Every term is zero or more, so a move never adds bits. If two different states $x \ne x'$,
both with positive chance, land on the same state, the sum is strictly positive.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Group the sum for $H(q)$ by where things land: the chance $q(y)$ at a landing spot is the
sum of the $p(x)$ that land there, so
$H(q) = -\sum_{x:\,p(x) > 0} p(x) \log_2 q(\mathrm{step}(x,i))$. Subtract from $H(p)$ term by
term. Each term is non-negative because the landing spot holds at least what $x$ brought,
$q(\mathrm{step}(x,i)) \ge p(x)$, and the logarithm keeps order. If $x$ and $x'$ share a
landing spot, that spot holds at least $p(x) + p(x') > p(x)$, so the term for $x$ is
strictly positive.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{entropy\_drop\_as\_point\_sum}, \code{entropy\_drop\_nonneg}, and
\code{entropy\_drop\_pos\_of\_support\_merge} (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

\subsection{What you're entitled to, and what you're not}

Let me total it: what have you earned the right to conclude, and what is still a door?

You've earned this: on any machine with finitely many states, a move that raises a flag
either forgets something or takes a flag down somewhere else. Pure counting, no physics, no
premise beyond finiteness, and the half of it where nothing comes down is the four chairs.
You've earned this: on a finite machine, if a flag, once up, stays up, then raising it
forgets something, and a move that raises k states collapses at least k of them. Counting
again. And you've earned this: if forgetting
is charged for, the toll follows, and if forgetting is charged per halving, the size of the
toll follows too; each of those derivations hands back a system with the five parts and the
toll, so Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s floor applies to it as it stands.
That's the rule from Section~\ref{sec:toll}, now derived, with every premise named, for any
finite machine with a flag that stays up. In that section I only declared it.

Here's what you haven't earned. I'm listing it so you don't assume it. You haven't
earned that forgetting costs anything in the world; that's Landauer, it's measured for beads
and argued over for the general case, and in the checked work it's an assumption with a name.
And even granting it, Landauer charges a run that knows where it is nothing at all (the lifted
cup), so what the physics forces is a floor on a device that has to work whatever it's
holding. Any one run can come in under it.
You haven't earned that any machine you'd actually want to build is of this kind, either,
and there are two easy ways to miss. A machine that keeps its running total inside its own
state, as a number with no ceiling, has infinitely many states, so the finite premise fails
for it as a whole. And you can't patch that by giving the total a ceiling. A total that only
climbs, held in finite memory, eventually either stops at its top, and then two different
histories leave the same top value, which is a merge, or rolls back over to zero, and then it
doesn't only climb. So any running total a finite machine keeps for itself has a horizon:
it's honest up to its width and no further. And a machine whose price list charges the step that raises the flag, but lets
some other step merge two states for nothing, raises the flag honestly and still doesn't
charge for forgetting in general, so the merge-pricing premise fails for it. Either one puts
a machine outside these theorems as stated, though a finite piece of it can still sit
inside. The machine I build later (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}) misses in both ways. It keeps
counters with no ceiling, so it's infinite outright, and some of its ordinary steps, counting a
counter down among them, can land two different states on one for free. So for it the toll is a
rule I chose; the chairs force it only on finite machines that price every merge, and it isn't
one.

A finite piece can still sit inside, and here's the smallest one I could build where every
premise is a theorem. None of them is left as a hypothesis. Four slots times a flag, eight states. Three
moves: stamp (set the flag, go to the next slot, cost one), jump to slot $a$ (cost two), next slot
(cost zero). It's finite (\code{fin\_finite}) and permanent (\code{fin\_permanent}); the next-slot
move forgets nothing (\code{fnext\_injective}); the stamp and the jump merge
(\code{fcertify\_merges}, \code{fjump\_merges}); merges are priced
(\code{fin\_merging\_priced}), and priced per halving (\code{fin\_compression\_priced}). So this
section's two conclusions hold on it outright (\code{fin\_a2\_from\_merging\_price},
\code{fin\_a2\_from\_compression\_price}, FiniteCertMachine.v). The counting lemma underneath,
that a duplicate-free list with at most $K$ preimages per image has at most $K$ times as many
members as images, is proved generically (\code{fiber\_bound\_compression}). Merge pricing alone
would take any price of at least one for the jump. The jump's price of
two is what the halving price asks, since the jump squeezes four states into one. One more fact
about it, also checked: each move's price is exactly the number of halvings in its largest
squeeze. For a move that costs $c$, no state is landed on by more than $2^c$ states, and some
state is landed on by exactly that many (stamp squeezes at most two states into one, jump to a
slot squeezes four, and next-slot squeezes nothing).

The machine Part IV builds runs this eight-state machine. Seen through a window that shows only a line
number, read modulo four as the slot, and a flag, a short program of that machine, once a
two-instruction setup has run, does what the
eight-state machine does, one move at a time, and pays exactly what the eight-state machine charges
(Section~\ref{sec:part3-on-machine} has the construction and the exact statements). The machine as a
whole is still not merge-priced: some of its free steps merge states, so the finite piece is a piece,
and the machine around it keeps the choice the chairs don't force.

And you haven't earned anything about \emph{what} the flag means. Four chairs don't know what they're certifying. The bill is for raising a flag that
stays up. Whether raising that flag ever amounts to standing behind a structural fact, the
``vouching'' I keep promising and keep not delivering, is a question for the machine of Part IV,
and here it has moved exactly this far: on a finite machine that charges for every merge, if that flag stays up, it was paid for.

One last thing, because it should nag at you. The toll is forced by the
premises, but the premises were chosen, and ``permanent'' in particular was chosen by me. Why
should a certificate stay up? Why not let it come down, pay nothing, and be honest about it?
That's a fair question, and merge or revoke is the start of an answer (the three-card machine only showed that
the converse of Corollary~\ref{cor:permanent-forced} fails): on a finite machine that charges for every merge, a flag that
goes
up for free is a flag the same move takes back somewhere, and a record that can be silently
taken back is the thing the bulla and the hash chain and the write-once disk were all built
against. ``Permanent'' here is exactly that: the flag can't be lowered. The toy in Section~\ref{sec:toll} didn't
have it; the lineage in Section~\ref{sec:toll} was built around it; I chose it. Whether that was the
right job to pick out of the five is something you can argue with me about, and I'd want you
to.

And ``permanent'' is an idealization, which I should say before a physicist does. No physical
record lasts forever. A bit held behind an energy barrier leaks over it at some rate, however
slow, and a closed finite system comes back around, which is Zermelo's point from the chairs.
The theorems in this section need permanence on every state, including states the machine
never visits, forever. Weaken that to ``the flag stays up on the states that actually turn up,
for as long as anyone cares,'' and merge-or-revoke tells you what goes wrong: the move could
take the flag down somewhere nobody ever looks, and then it isn't forced to merge at all. A
version of the toll stated in chances and time spans would be a different theorem, and I
don't have it.

One piece of it I can hand you, argued here on the page. The checked files don't have it. Take
one move and repeat it from one start, forever. On a finite machine the states that run passes through are
finitely many, so it falls into a loop. If the move forgot nothing on those states, it would
be a reshuffle of them, and a reshuffle brings every one of them back around, the start
included, where the flag was down. So if the flag goes up along that run and stays up from
some point on, the move merges two states \emph{the run itself visits}. The shared chair is
one the machine actually sits in. And it doesn't touch the known-state point above: a merge
among states the run visits still costs Landauer nothing if the run knew where it was and
something outside timed the step.

Runs that mix different moves split two ways, and the answer is short enough to give here,
argued on the page like the last one. If the moves are picked from outside, in any order at
all, the answer is no. Take two states, one reading no and one reading yes. Move $a$ swaps them;
move $b$ does nothing. Run $a$ once and then $b$ forever: the flag goes up at the first step and
stays up for good, and neither move merges anything anywhere. The swap would take the flag down
from the yes-state if it ever ran there; on this run it never does, and that's exactly the
weakened permanence this paragraph is about. But if the machine is closed, picking its next
move from its own state, the run is the orbit of one map, the step with whatever move the state
picks, and the single-move argument applies to that map as it
stands. Now say the moves come in a
pattern that eventually repeats, one word $w$ of moves over and over. Suppose the flag is down at some step after the
repeating starts, and goes up and stays up after that. Count the repetitions from a step where the flag was down (start
$w$ at that letter if you have to) and run the same argument on the composite of $w$'s moves, at the states where such a repetition begins. It merges two
of those states, both visited; follow the two through the letters of $w$, and the first letter
where their paths meet merges two states the run visits at that letter's place in the pattern.
So: moves picked from outside, no; a closed machine or a repeating program, yes.

And one limited piece of the chances-and-time-spans version, also argued here and not checked,
because it shows exactly where the known-state escape stops. Take a device with no outside hand
at all: a little random process hopping among finitely many states at rates that never change,
with the usual physical conditions (every hop has a reverse hop, and the rates obey local
detailed balance), able to get from any state to any other. Left to run, it settles into a
long-run spread $\pi$ and spends stretches with the flag up and stretches with it down; call
their mean lengths $T_{\mathrm{up}}$ and $T_{\mathrm{down}}$. Start it in a no-state you know.
Then the entropy it produces from then on is at least $\ln\bigl(1 + T_{\mathrm{up}}/T_{\mathrm{down}}\bigr)$,
in units of $k_B$. The argument is three lines once the pieces have names. With fixed rates, the
entropy produced is at least the drop in relative entropy between the device's spread and
$\pi$; that's half of Massimiliano Esposito and Christian Van den Broeck's split of entropy
production (2010). A start known to be in state $s$ has relative entropy $-\ln\pi(s)$, which is
at least $-\ln\pi(\mathrm{no})$, where $\pi(\mathrm{no})$ is the long-run chance of the flag being
down, and the relative entropy runs down to zero as the device settles. And the long-run
chances of up and down stand in the ratio of the mean stretch lengths, because the crossings up
and the crossings down balance, so $-\ln\pi(\mathrm{no}) = \ln\bigl(1 + T_{\mathrm{up}}/T_{\mathrm{down}}\bigr)$.
Read it this way: each doubling of how long the record stays up, against how long it sits down,
costs about one more $k_B\ln 2$, and a record that stays up forever on a fixed-rate device costs
without bound. That's Murashita, Funo and Ueda's absolute irreversibility landing on the flip
at last, with $1-\lambda$ the long-run chance of the starting state. It isn't new physics:
nothing in it needs a record, since an autonomous reset to a fixed state obeys the same bound,
and the time-symmetric-control result above covers the same ground with an error rate in place
of the time ratio. And it isn't the theorem I said I didn't have. It's a first honest step
toward it, and it pins down where ``the premise sets no heat floor for a known state'' needs its outside clock.

The next section is about a different door entirely. Forgetting has had its section; the
question now is whether \emph{finding out} costs, because the demon's whole trick was that it knew which way the
molecule was going, and I owe you a straight answer on whether knowing is free.

%===========================================================================
\section{Learning is free, committing is not}
\label{sec:narrowing}
%===========================================================================

I ended the last section owing you an answer about knowing. The bill so far sits on
forgetting: on a finite machine, a flag
that stays up was paid for because raising it merged two states. But
there's a thing that looks like the opposite of forgetting and feels like it ought to cost
at least as much, probably more. Finding out. Every time a machine rules out a possibility, it knows more than
it did. If forgetting a bit costs, does learning one cost too? I had a strong feeling about
this, and you probably have it too, so here it is first: learning is the expensive part. Most
physicists had that feeling as well, for a long time. It's why the demon took a hundred and fifteen
years to exorcise. Or didn't. ``Exorcise'' is the word the people who think it worked like to
use. John Earman and John Norton, the doubters from the last section, called their two-part
paper on it ``Exorcist XIV: The Wrath of Maxwell's Demon,'' and I read that Roman numeral as a
joke about how many times the demon has been declared gone. So hold the word loosely. This section is me finding out where the feeling
goes wrong. I'm going to tell you the version where the exorcism worked, because it's the version that says
where the bill goes, and the door from the last section stays open behind it.

\subsection{A small being at a small door}

You met Maxwell's demon in Section~\ref{sec:toll}, in one paragraph. It gets a whole section here, because the step
it seemed to pay for and the step it actually pays for are what this section is about.

In December 1867 James Clerk Maxwell, who had published his equations for
electricity and magnetism two years before, in 1865, and to my mind had as good a claim as anyone to being the most important
physicist alive, wrote a
letter to his friend Peter Tait describing a problem he couldn't get rid of. Take a box of gas
at one temperature, with a wall down the middle and a tiny door in the wall. Now imagine, he
said, a ``very observant and neat-fingered being'' sitting at the door, who can see individual
molecules coming. When a fast one approaches from the left, it opens the door and lets it
through. When a slow one approaches from the right, same. Otherwise it keeps the door shut.
It never pushes anything; it only opens and closes a frictionless door at the right moments.
After a while the right side is hot and the left side is cold, and you've got a temperature
difference you could run an engine off, made out of nothing but \emph{looking}. That's supposed to
be impossible. It's the thing the second law of thermodynamics says can't happen, and the
second law is the law physicists are least willing to give up; Arthur Eddington, the English
astronomer, wrote in a 1928 book of popular lectures that a theory
found to contradict it has nothing for it but to collapse in deepest humiliation, and nobody
has had to test that yet.

Maxwell put it in his textbook in 1871, and it got named Maxwell's demon, though not by
Maxwell. William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, called it a demon in \emph{Nature} in 1874, and
Maxwell, in an undated note to Tait headed ``Concerning demons,'' tried to take the name back:
``Call him no more a demon but a valve.'' Nobody listened, which is probably for the best,
because ``Maxwell's valve'' would not have lasted a century. But keep his correction, because
it's exactly right and it's the whole problem: the being does no work. It opens and shuts a
door. So physicists
spent the next century trying to find where the being was cheating. I want you to feel the
pull of the obvious answer, because I felt it and so did most of them: the being has to
\emph{see} the molecules. Seeing costs. Case closed. In 1929 Leo Szilard built a one-molecule
version of the box and did the arithmetic, and said the second law survives if finding out
which side the molecule is on costs at least as much entropy as the being gains. In 1951 the French physicist Léon
Brillouin made it concrete: to see a molecule you have to bounce light off it, and the way the
philosopher of physics Jeffrey Bub sums up the result, finding out that way costs at least
k ln 2 of entropy for every bit, which is kT ln 2 of heat, Landauer's number before Landauer, and there was your toll on
looking. For thirty years that was the answer. Information costs because getting it costs.

That's a price on one way of looking, and it doesn't show that every possible way of
making a record has to pay it. A device can burn energy without that being a law.

Szilard is worth one more minute, for a reason that has nothing to do with the demon. Four
years after the one-molecule engine, in September 1933, by his own later telling, he was
waiting at a traffic light on Southampton Row in London, having just read a newspaper report
in which Ernest Rutherford, the physicist who had announced the atomic nucleus in 1911, called the hope of getting power out of atoms moonshine, and as the light
changed it occurred to him that an element which gave off two neutrons when it swallowed one
could keep a reaction going by itself. That's the nuclear chain reaction, thought up crossing
a street. It's his memory of himself, and Richard Rhodes's history of the bomb opens with it, in a
first chapter called ``Moonshine,'' which is where most
people meet it, so hold it as the man's own story. A timestamp it isn't. Does it change
anything about the demon? No. What it adds is a picture of the man: the same mind looked at one
molecule in 1929 and one neutron in 1933, and both times the question was what a single small
step forces downstream.

\subsection{Bennett moves the bill}

In 1982 Charles Bennett, who'd already shown in 1973 that computation can be done without
forgetting, took the demon apart one step at a time. The being looks at a molecule and writes
down which side it's on. Is writing that down a merge? Picture the being's notepad, which
starts blank. After looking, the notepad says ``left'' or ``right.'' Two possible worlds before
(molecule left, pad blank; molecule right, pad blank). Two possible worlds after (left,
``left''; right, ``right''). Nothing merged. Two in, two out, and you can read the before off the
after. Copying what you see onto a blank page forgets nothing, and a step that forgets nothing
is a step Landauer doesn't charge for. Brillouin had priced one particular way of looking
(bouncing light) and took it as the price of getting information at all. Bennett gave a way of looking that, on his account, doesn't pay it.

So where is the bill? The being has one notepad and a lot of molecules. After the first
molecule the page is full. To do the next one it has to wipe the page. And \emph{wiping} takes two
possible worlds (pad says ``left''; pad says ``right'') to one (pad blank). That's the merge.
That's the step with no way back. The demon pays every cycle, and what it pays for is making room to see again, and the amount it pays is at least what it gained, and the second law
sleeps soundly. That's the rule from his 2003 notes I quoted in Section~\ref{sec:toll}: erasing and merging cost,
and copying onto a blank place to write doesn't.

Section~\ref{sec:toll} separated making a record from resetting it. Now you can see
exactly which step pays, and why the other one was tempting, because looking \emph{feels} like the active part.
It's the thing the being does. Wiping feels like housekeeping. The housekeeping is where the
money goes. If there's a sentence in this section I'd want you to carry out of it, that's the one, and the idea in it is Bennett's.

\subsection{Two different things called ``narrowing''}

Here is what I had to get straight in my own head before any of this made sense, and I'll give
it to you as a picture because that's how I eventually got it.

Draw the machine's possible states as a row of dots. Now draw a second row above it: the
dots that \emph{you}, standing outside, still think it might be in. Those are two different rows.
The first is a fact about the machine. The second is a fact about you, about what you've
seen and what you've ruled out. Both rows can shrink. They shrink for different reasons, and
only one of them costs.

The machine's row shrinks when two of its states land on the same state. That's a merge.
That's what the price charges. Under the halving rule from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, a run can't shrink the
machine's own row by more halvings than it paid for. That's the theorem just below, and
it's the Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} squeeze bound run forward along a whole program. That section took it one step at a time. No new idea;
the same chairs.

Exactly. Write $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ for the index-bit count of $n$: the smallest whole number
$k$ with $2^k \ge n$, the number of yes-or-no questions it takes to pick one of $n$ things. It is $0$
at $n = 1$, and I set it to $0$ at $n = 0$ too, a convention for empty lists, since the logarithm
of zero isn't a number. Wherever I write an ordinary logarithm without the rounding, its argument
is positive. For a run $t$ and a list $D$ of
starting states, let $\mathrm{img}_t(D)$ be the set of states the run can end in, starting
from somewhere in $D$, and write $|\mathrm{img}_t(D)|$ for how many there are (in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} the
symbol for one move already meant the count; here I need the set and its size both). Let
$\mathrm{cost}(t)$ be the run's total cost.

\begin{theorem}[The machine's own narrowing is priced]\label{thm:machine-narrowing}
If the cost satisfies the halving price (Premise~\ref{prem:halving}), then for every run $t$
and every list $D$ of starting states with no repeats,
\[
\lceil \log_2 |D| \rceil \;\le\; \mathrm{cost}(t) + \lceil \log_2 |\mathrm{img}_t(D)| \rceil .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By induction on the run. A single move of cost $c$ shrinks a list with no repeats by at most
a factor $2^c$ (that's the halving price), which costs at most $c$ in rounded logarithms; the
states reachable after the rest of the run from the shrunk set are exactly those reachable
after the whole run from the original. Add the costs.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{run\_narrowing\_priced\_log} (KnowledgeNarrowing.v). The run itself is the witness;
nothing else is handed in. That will matter in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, and I'll say why at the end of this
section.

Your row shrinks when you see something that some of your candidates couldn't have shown you.
You cross those candidates off. Nothing happened to the machine. It didn't merge anything; it
didn't know you were watching; it would have done the same thing with nobody in the room. The
physicist Edwin Jaynes had a name for mixing these up, and I think it's one of the most useful
names in all of science: the mind projection fallacy, treating what you know about a thing as
if it were a property of the thing. Your list of candidates is in your head. The machine's
row is in the machine. The halving price is about the machine's row, and crossing a candidate
off yours doesn't move it.

And here I have to be fair to Jaynes, because he'd argue with where I just took his phrase. In
a 1965 paper on Gibbs's and Boltzmann's entropies he wrote that entropy is ``an anthropomorphic
concept'' (a phrase he credited to the physicist Eugene Wigner), and by that he meant a property
of the particular experiments you or I choose to do on a physical system. On his account the
system alone doesn't carry it. So for Jaynes the second law is
about what's known too, and the line I'd have liked to draw, that the second law has opinions
about the machine and none about you, is exactly the line he'd refuse. Who's right is one of
the oldest fights in statistical physics, Jaynes's reading against Boltzmann's, and I can't
settle it. I don't have to. The spreads in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s entropy
theorems are spreads over the states the device might be in when the step runs, and every
theorem there holds whether you read those chances as ignorance or as physics; ``the floor
comes from what you didn't know'' is the same sentence in either reading, with ``you'' being
whoever built the spread. What I need from the fallacy is only this: the two
rows are different rows, and only one of them is the machine's.

\subsection{The demon on a sheet of paper}

Build it, because the whole claim is four dots and two arrows and you should see it merge or
not merge with your own eyes.

The machine has a hidden bit (think of it as the molecule's side) and a display (the
notepad). Four states: write them as pairs, hidden then display. 00, 01, 10, 11. Two moves.

MEASURE copies the hidden bit onto the display, by adding it in the way that a light switch
adds: if the hidden bit is 1, flip the display; if it's 0, leave it. Draw the arrows. 00 goes
to 00. 01 goes to 01. 10 goes to 11. 11 goes to 10. Look at the arrowheads: every state has
exactly one arrow landing on it. Nothing merged. MEASURE forgets nothing.

WIPE sets the display to 0 whatever it held. 00 goes to 00; 01 goes to 00 as well. 10 goes to
10; 11 goes to 10 as well. Two arrows land on 00 and two on 10. That's a merge, twice over.
Under any price that charges per halving, WIPE costs at least one. MEASURE is allowed to cost
zero.

Now be the observer. You can see the display and not the hidden bit. What you're shown, the
display here, is what I'll call a \emph{window}: the part of the state an outside observer gets
to see. Section~\ref{sec:windows} is about windows in general; here the window is just the display. The display starts
blank, so your list of candidates is \{00, 10\}: two possibilities, one bit you don't know. The
machine runs MEASURE. You look at the display. If it shows 1, the only candidate that could
have produced it is 10. If it shows 0, only 00. Your list went from two to one. You learned
the hidden bit. The machine's price for that move: zero. Its own row of possible states went
from \{00, 10\} to \{00, 11\}, still two; nothing it could have been got merged with anything
else. You narrowed. It didn't. That's the measuring half of Bennett's argument on four dots,
and WIPE's charge is the wiping half. So the demon just broke something: one bit gained,
nothing charged. Here's the thing it broke, written out so you can see exactly where the
crack runs: for every list of starting candidates, every run, and every actual start in the
list, the index bits the observer gains (log2 of the candidates before minus log2
of the candidates after, both rounded up) are at most what the run was charged. Four dots, and that
sentence is false.

\begin{definition}[What an observer knows]\label{def:knowledge}
Fix a window $w$ from states to what can be seen. Given a list $\Omega$ of candidate starting
states, a run $t$, and the actual start $s_0 \in \Omega$, the observer's \emph{knowledge}
$K(\Omega, t, s_0)$ is the list of candidates $s \in \Omega$ whose run shows the same thing
through the window at every step as the actual run does.
\end{definition}

Defined as \code{knowledge} (KnowledgeNarrowing.v).

If that definition looks familiar, it should. It's the standard way logicians of knowledge set
it up: what you know is whatever holds of every case you can't tell apart from the actual one,
given everything you've seen (Fagin, Halpern, Moses and Vardi's \emph{Reasoning About
Knowledge}, 1995, builds a whole subject on it, runs and observations included). And it's the
logically omniscient kind from the opening chapter, the kind where knowing some facts means
knowing everything that follows from them, for free. I'm using it on purpose, flaw and all.
This section is about learning, and learning in that sense is exactly the thing that's allowed
to be free. Settling is the separate act with a price, and nothing in this definition settles
anything.

\begin{theorem}[An observer can learn for free]\label{thm:observer-free}
There is a four-state machine (the demon), a cost satisfying the halving price, a run of cost
0, and candidates with $|\Omega| = 2$, for which $|K(\Omega, t, s_0)| = 1$. So the claim
``for every $\Omega$ with no repeats, every $t$, and every $s_0$ in $\Omega$: $\lceil\log_2|\Omega|\rceil - \lceil\log_2|K(\Omega,t,s_0)|
\rceil \le \mathrm{cost}(t)$'' is false for that machine and that cost. In the same machine,
every cost satisfying the halving price charges WIPE at least one.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The machine and run are the four dots above: MEASURE is a bijection, so cost 0 satisfies
the halving price; the observer's two candidates show different displays after MEASURE; WIPE
sends two pairs of states to one each, so the halving price needs its cost $\ge 1$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{observer\_narrowing\_can\_be\_free}, \code{demon\_observer\_learns},
\code{demon\_machine\_spread\_kept}, \code{measure\_forgets\_nothing}, \code{wipe\_merges}, and
\code{wipe\_costs\_at\_least\_one} (KnowledgeNarrowing.v).

The demon is the picture. The smallest case is smaller. The claim as written already fails on a machine with
two states and every move free, because the observer's very first look tells the two apart, and it
never fails on a machine with one state (\code{nec\_f\_two\_state\_observer\_free},
\code{nec\_f\_one\_state\_observer\_priced}, NecFNarrowing.v). That's why the interesting version is
learning \emph{after} the first look, which is where the three states of
Theorem~\ref{thm:three-states} come in. And WIPE's price needs less than the halving rule: merge pricing
alone charges it at least one (\code{nec\_f\_wipe\_under\_merge\_pricing}).

I have to be exact about one thing the file is exact about. The halving rule is a floor. It
says merges cost at least this much; it does not say anything costs zero. So what the theorem
exhibits is \emph{one} price schedule that meets the halving rule and charges MEASURE nothing. A
different schedule could meet the rule and still charge MEASURE; nothing in counting forbids
overcharging. The claim is ``learning is not \emph{forced} to cost.'' It isn't ``learning is free on every
machine,'' and on a given machine a schedule may still charge it. That's weaker than the section title. The title is the short form you'd say before
checking the fine print, so the title stays and this paragraph stays next to it.

The physicists had this freedom on the books long before me. Paul Fahn (1996), doing the entropy
accounting of Szilard's one-molecule engine step by step, argued for a symmetry between the measuring step and the erasing step: on his account,
which of the two you hand the bill to is partly a choice of bookkeeping, and the
total is what's fixed. Sagawa and Ueda (2009) derived a bound on that total, with the split
depending on the memory. So, on their accounts, ``a schedule could charge MEASURE instead'' is a known freedom in how the books are kept.
I didn't find a loophole. And the other reading is very
much alive. Ruth Kastner (2025) argues that Brillouin was essentially right after all: once the
physics of a real measurement is put back in, it's measurement that pays and
foils the demon, erasure drops out of the bill, and Bennett's free copy fails as physics. The theorem above is about price
lists, so it stands either way. What hangs on her is whether a real demon can look for nothing,
which is the same door the next paragraph's doubter pushes on.

And the doubter from the last section cuts this side too, so I owe it to you, since I leaned
on him there. In 2013 John Norton argued for a no-go result: at the scale of molecules, thermal
jiggling keeps any process that's supposed to be thermodynamically reversible from ever
actually finishing, and finishing it takes more entropy than Landauer's amount. If he's right,
Bennett's free measurement isn't free in practice either, because it's one of those
processes. The theorem above survives that, because it's about price lists: a schedule that
meets the halving rule isn't forced to charge the copy, whatever a real device spends. What
wouldn't survive is the physics I've been hanging on it, that a real demon can look for
nothing. If Norton is right, the line between learning and committing keeps its counting and
loses its physics. I can't referee that one either.

\subsection{Who holds the pen changes the bill}

Now the part that I think is the most beautiful fact in here. You find it by playing
with the four dots. Thinking about them won't get you there. Run MEASURE \emph{twice}. The first copies the
hidden bit onto the display. The second adds the hidden bit in again, and adding a bit twice
with a light-switch add gets you back where you were: the display is blank again. Check the
arrows: 10 to 11 to 10. The display went full and then blank, and nothing merged, and the
price was zero both times. So a display that was blank before the first MEASURE \emph{can} be put back to blank for
free, by a second MEASURE. Just not by WIPE.

What's the difference? MEASURE \emph{consults the hidden bit} when it clears the display. It knows
what's written there, because it has access to the thing it was copied from, and so it can undo the
copy. Nothing gets erased. WIPE doesn't look. It sets the display to 0 regardless,
and ``regardless'' is exactly the many-to-one. Bennett has the general form of this in the 2003
notes: he lists the ``erasure of one of two copies of data known to be identical'' among the
logically reversible operations, because you're removing a duplicate, and no information is
destroyed. And it goes further than Bennett in
work that came after him: the quantum physicist Lídia del Rio and colleagues argued in 2011 that the cost of erasing a
system depends on how much the eraser already knows about it, down to zero and in the
quantum case past zero. The bill for clearing a record is sent to whoever clears it, and it's
smaller the more they know. Try it with a card under a cup and a sticky note. Write the
colour on the note, then erase the note \emph{without lifting the cup}: two possible notes
become one blank, a merge. Now do it again, but lift the cup, check the
note matches, and then erase: nothing unknown was destroyed. Same blank note. Different bill.

\subsection{The smallest machine that teaches for free, and the one that can't}

Two more small facts, and then the point. The demon measures what you learn by comparing the
start to the end, but an observer's very first look already rules things out before any step
runs, so the fairer question is: after that first look, can a \emph{step} teach you more, for
free? Yes, and the demon still does it. And the smallest machine
that can is three states in a ring: U goes to V, V goes to W, W goes to U, and the window
shows ``true'' only at W. Start with candidates \{U, V\}; both show false. Take one step. From U
you now see false; from V you now see true. One step told them apart, and a ring forgets
nothing, so a zero price meets the halving rule, and the file takes it.

Two states can't do it, ever, with any arrows, and this is the one that needs no price
premise at all. If a machine has only two states and you can't tell them apart at the first
look, then the window shows the same thing on both, and those two are \emph{all the states there
are}, so the window shows the same thing everywhere, forever, and you never learn anything.
Try to draw a counterexample. You'll draw the
same two dots a few times and give up, and the giving up is the proof. Three is the smallest
number of states on which two states that look alike at the first look can come apart at a
later look, and that's what teaching is.

\begin{theorem}[Three states are the minimum for free teaching]\label{thm:three-states}
Call a machine a \emph{free teacher} when it has a cost satisfying the halving price, a list of
candidates with no repeats containing the actual start, and a run of cost 0 after which the
observer knows strictly more than after the first look, $|K(\Omega, t, s_0)| <
|K(\Omega, [\,], s_0)|$. There is a free teacher with exactly three states, and there is none
with two or fewer.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Three: the ring $U \to V \to W \to U$ with the window true only at $W$, candidates
$\{U, V\}$, one step, cost 0 (a ring is a bijection, so cost 0 satisfies the halving price).
Two or fewer: two candidates that agree at the first look are, on a two-state machine, all
the states there are, so the window takes one value everywhere and no later look can
separate them. This half never uses the price at all.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{free\_incremental\_narrowing\_with\_three} and
\code{no\_free\_incremental\_narrowing\_below\_three} (KnowledgeNarrowingMinimal.v), and the
demon-against-the-first-look form as \code{demon\_refutes\_incremental}.

\subsection{What the toll prices, said at last}

Now I can say, more precisely than I could two sections ago, what the mark in Section~\ref{sec:toll} is a mark
for. Not for learning. What you know can be narrowed at no cost, with nothing merged, on
some machines under some honest price lists, and the demon is one. Not for
looking, not for copying, not for finding out. The mark
is for the one thing in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} that couldn't be done without merging, on a machine with finitely
many states: raising a flag that stays up. Learning is the demon writing on a blank pad, which merges nothing. What the demon
pays for is the wipe, a step with a shared chair. The mark in Section~\ref{sec:toll} is paid for the same
reason, because raising a flag that stays up also has a shared chair, but it's a different
step: the demon machine has no flag, and its file prices merges; commitments never appear in it. Same
chair. Different room.

This is also where I settle up with Rovelli, my closest neighbour from the opening chapter,
because I put him and Bennett on opposite sides of one door, and I owe you how much of that is
mine. All of the reconciliation is mine. Rovelli's paper doesn't make it, and in four places
his own framing points somewhere else. He reserves ``choice'' for an outcome that is stable and
\emph{not predictable}, and he rules out a thermostat because it runs on a predictable
mechanism; the commit in this book is a step a rule fixes in advance, so by his own definition
his result doesn't cover it. His choice is a branching, one possibility splitting into two,
and he calls choosing in a sense the inverse of erasing, because branching is the inverse of
merging; the toll comes from a merge, the opposite shape. His stability is for a while: he says
stabilization means something only on times that aren't too long next to the time it takes
things to thermalize, and past that nothing stays chosen; my permanence is forever (and the
last section owned up that forever is an idealization). And he doesn't stand beside Bennett at
all: he holds that any measurement is dissipative, credits the point to the philosopher of
science Hans Reichenbach, and
doesn't cite Bennett. So what Rovelli and I share is a sentence, that a choice that sticks
costs something like Landauer's bill. There's no shared mechanism. Push on it and his coin hitting the
ground, a fact gained from something nobody could predict, sits closer to what this section
calls learning than to committing. I still think it's the same instinct. That's my reading,
and he doesn't make it; you now have everything you need to disagree with it.

And on one point Rovelli isn't the nearest physics. The nearest I've found is in biology. Thomas
Ouldridge and Pieter Rein ten Wolde (2017) derived what they call the fundamental costs of making a
\emph{persistent} copy of a polymer, one whose sequence stays correlated with its template after
the two have physically come apart, and of destroying one. On their account a copy like that is a state
out of equilibrium, and making it has a thermodynamic bill they measure efficiency against. A companion
paper the same year, with Christopher Govern, does the same kind of accounting for the molecules a
cell uses to read out the state of its receptors, which is a measurement in all but name. The way
I read them, the copy that has to stay is the one with the bill, and that's the closest thing in
physics I've found to the line this section draws between finding out and committing. The
differences, so it doesn't get borrowed for more than it is: theirs is heat, in chemistry, for a
correlation between two molecules, and their title has the destruction of copies in it too, so
their copies don't last forever; mine is a count in a model of computation, for a reading that
never turns off, with no temperature anywhere. Same instinct again, from a different direction.

The chemistry has the sharp form of it, too, and it came two years later. Jenny Poulton, Pieter
Rein ten Wolde and Thomas Ouldridge (2019) studied minimal models of polymer copying, and in
those models, when the copy grows at equilibrium, with the weakest chemical driving, a persistent copy's
accuracy and the efficiency of making it both vanish; only driving the growth out of
equilibrium, paying, buys a copy that still carries information about its template after the
two let go. That's finding out against committing, in chemistry, with the bill attached, and I'd
rather say plainly that biology had the distinction before I did. What stays different is the
kind of thing the record is: theirs is a correlation in a chemical ensemble, mine is a reading
enforced by a step in a model of computation.

Two more neighbours have ``learning'' and ``commit'' in their titles, so the slogan shouldn't be
read against them by accident. Sebastian Goldt and Udo Seifert (2017) did the stochastic
thermodynamics of a neural network learning a rule, and argued from it that learning has a thermodynamic cost: on
their account, the entropy the network produces bounds how much it can learn. That doesn't contradict
this section, and here's why. Their learner isn't copying onto a blank page. Its weights are a
driven thermal system, jostled by noise and dragged toward what the data push them to, and what
they price is that physical process. This section's free learning is narrower: one way of
finding out, a copy onto a blank, is \emph{allowed} to cost nothing. Nothing here says every
way of learning is cheap, and theirs isn't. From statistics, Aur\'elien Garivier, Tor Lattimore and Emilie
Kaufmann (2016) gave a proof that in a two-armed bandit with Gaussian rewards, a
strategy that explores first and then commits for good ends up, as the horizon grows, with at
least twice the regret of the best strategy that keeps deciding as it goes. That's the closest
published sentence I've found to ``committing isn't free'' with a number on it. Their price is
reward lost, which is a different unit from a mark on a ledger, so it's a cousin. A twin would
have to count marks.

So here's exactly what ``No Free Insight,'' the name I gave the toll before I understood it,
covers, because I don't want the name doing work it hasn't earned.
Insight in the sense of \emph{finding out} can be free. The insight the toll prices is the kind
you've \emph{committed to}, written into a record the machine can't silently revise. Whether that
narrower thing deserves the name is a fair thing to argue about; I kept the name because it's
the question I started with, and because the narrowing is the finding. I don't count it as a retreat.

It also tells you how to read a bound that's coming. Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} counts what it takes to narrow a
list of candidates down to a shorter one: at least as many yes-or-no questions as it takes to
point at the survivors among their rivals, a counting fact that holds for anything with a
list in it. Turning that count into a \emph{bill}, saying a run actually paid that many marks, is
a different claim, and when the book makes it, for any certification system in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, the payment goes in as a hypothesis: a decision tree (a branching chart of yes-or-no questions, which Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}
builds) no deeper than the number of paid steps the run took is handed in, along with the
lists themselves and
the fact that the tree's leaves cover the narrowing. This section is the reason it has to go in that way. The narrowing alone
doesn't force anyone to pay; the demon just showed you a narrowing that cost nothing. So
wherever narrowing gets a price in this book, the payment is a premise, and I'll keep calling
it one.

And one more boundary. This whole section is about a machine that's finite and deterministic
and a watcher who crosses candidates off a list. There's no quantum anything in it. This narrowing has nothing to do with ``observation
collapses the state'': the
narrowing here is bookkeeping in the watcher's
list, the machine never notices, and the result would be the same if the watcher were a
filing cabinet. In 2010 a group in Tokyo (Toyabe, Sagawa, Ueda, Muneyuki and Sano) did
run a real demon, a tiny particle walked up a staircase of potential by feedback on what a
camera saw, and the energy it gained
was paid for by the information the camera took, with no violation of anything. The demon is
real, it works, and it pays. Where it pays is the part that took a century.

What I still owe: everything so far says ``at least one mark'' and I've been keeping the marks
on the side of the page, a running total you tally as you go. What happens when the machine
keeps that total itself, inside its own state, where a step could in principle reach in and
change it? That's the counter, and it's the next thing I have to build.


\part{The logic}

%===========================================================================
\section{The counter}
\label{sec:counter}
%===========================================================================

Everything so far has kept the marks on the side of the page. You played the toy, you made a
tally as you went, and the tally lived in your hand. The machine never saw it. That's fine for a
toy. For anything that's going to run on its own, with nobody tallying, the total has to live
somewhere the machine can reach, which means the machine can, in principle, reach it. So
this section is about what a counter has to be before you're allowed to call it a receipt.
I mean the counter of \emph{any} machine whose state carries
a running total that every step bumps by whatever a price list says that step costs. Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s
five parts don't need one (there the total was a sum you did on the side), so this is one
piece added to the five, and the facts below are about anything that has it. I'll give
you the answer first, because it's short, and then spend the section on why each word is
there: a receipt is a total that lives in the state, that only climbs, that equals the sum
of what was charged, and that nothing else could have been.

\subsection{A stick, split down the middle}

The oldest receipt I could find that you can still hold is a piece of wood. From about 1100,
under Henry the First, until 1826, the English treasury recorded what it was owed on tally
sticks: a strip of hazel, notched across with cuts of set widths (the treasury's own handbook
from around 1180, the \emph{Dialogue of the Exchequer}, gives them: a thumb's width for a
hundred pounds, a swollen barleycorn for a pound, a bare cut for a penny), then split lengthwise so that each half carried the
same notches. The payer kept one half, called the stock, which is one story for where the word
stockholder comes from. The treasury kept the other. When the time came to settle, you laid the two halves
together, and only the two original halves fit, because wood splits along a grain nobody can
copy. Add a notch to your half and the other half shows a gap where the partner should be. Try
to remove a notch and you find that wood can't be uncut. When they finally stopped using them,
the clerks burned centuries of old tallies in the furnaces under the House of Lords,
overheated the flue, and burned down the Palace of Westminster, which I mention because it's
the best fact I picked up for this book and because it tells you how many of them there were.

Do it: notch a strip of card once for every coin you hand a friend, split it, keep half each.
Try to cheat, either direction. The three things you'll find are the three things I want.
The total is the notches, added up, and nothing else (I'll call that conservation). You can
add a notch but you can't take one away (it only climbs). And two halves that were notched
together must agree; a half that disagrees is a forgery, and the wood says which one (there
is only one honest count). The treasury didn't have the words. They had the stick.

Economists read the same stick another way, and they're not wrong either. Alfred Mitchell-Innes
(1913) made the exchequer tally his star witness that money is credit: the crown paid the people
it owed by ``raising a tally'' on some branch of its revenue, a wooden acknowledgment of debt. A
receipt to me, money to him, and it's the same piece of wood. Narayana Kocherlakota (1998) later
proved a version of his point: in a wide class of economies where nobody can be held to a
promise, anything money lets people do, a memory of everyone's past dealings lets them do too.
His title says it in three words: money is memory.

\subsection{Why it has to climb}

Start with the second property, because it's the one that does the most work and the one
people fight hardest. Why can't the counter ever go down?

Because of what the toll is for. The floor it buys, back in Section~\ref{sec:toll}, says a run from NO to YES
costs at least one. That
sentence is a \emph{floor}: it says the run paid at least this much. If the counter could come back
down, a run could pay the toll, get its flag, and then take the payment back, and the floor
would be a floor on nothing; ``this run cost at least one'' would be true of a run that ended
having cost nothing. So a counter that can fall is an accountant you can lean on to revise the
books, and a floor stated in terms of it isn't a floor. The counter only climbing is not a flourish. It's what makes ``at least'' mean something.
This ledger records cumulative charges, each a whole number of marks and none negative, so it
never decreases. A refundable balance, one that pays money back, would be a different accounting
object with a different invariant, and the floor here says nothing about it. (In Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s abstract theorem the total is
a sum of whole numbers and climbing comes for free; this paragraph is about why a total
\emph{stored in the state}, where a step could in principle write it, has to be designed so that
no step ever lowers it.)

The same rule turns up in two places that have nothing to do with each other, pointing in
opposite directions, and that's a big part of why I trust it. In 1978 Leslie Lamport asked how
a set of computers that pass each other messages, with no shared clock, could ever agree on
what happened before what. His answer is a counter per machine with two rules: add one before
you do anything, and when a message arrives carrying the sender's count, jump your own counter
above it (never below your own). Those counters, he showed, respect cause and effect: if this
caused that, this has the smaller number. And they do it ``with no actual timing mechanism,''
his words; they're clocks only in name. Try it with three people passing notes and you'll see
it work in two minutes, and then let one of them reset their counter to zero after reading a
note, and watch a reply come out numbered \emph{before} the note it replies to. A counter that
goes down can't be leaned on for order.

Where did Lamport get it? In the notes he keeps on his own papers, he says the timestamps came
from an earlier note by Paul Johnson and Bob Thomas on keeping copies of a database in step,
whose algorithm wasn't quite right: it let things happen in an order that broke cause and
effect. What let him see the fix, he says, was special relativity, which teaches that the one order of events everybody agrees on
is the order of what could have caused what. And he
passes on a line from Jim Gray, the same Gray as the commit at the start of the book: Gray had
heard two opinions of the paper, that it was trivial and that it was brilliant. Lamport's
answer is that he can't argue with the first and isn't inclined to argue with the second.
His account stops at relativity, so the chase does too. The picture it leaves is a good one: a number that's
allowed to climb and never to fall is enough to write ``this came after that'' with no clock
anywhere.

Now the other direction. In 1949 Alan Turing, and in 1967 Robert Floyd, each asked how you
prove a program \emph{stops}. The answer, both times: find a quantity that goes \emph{down} on every step
and can't go down forever (a whole number that can't go below zero, say). If every step
lowers it and it can't fall forever, the steps can't go on forever. Up-only gives you order.
Down-only gives you stopping. They're different rules (one needs the jump-above-the-message
step, the other needs a floor it can't fall below). They have the same shape, seen from the
two ends: a one-way quantity is something you can build on, and a two-way quantity is a
number that happens to be written down somewhere.

And the real-world case where a counter was allowed to go down, and got gamed exactly there:
Ethereum, one of the largest blockchains, charges ``gas'' for every step of a program, and for
years it \emph{refunded} gas when a program freed up storage. Someone noticed you could fill
storage when gas was cheap, hold it, and cash the refunds when gas was dear, and a token was
built to do exactly that, and the real work in a block could reach nearly twice the block's
stated limit. In 2021 a change called EIP-3529 cut the refunds sharply (none for
self-destruct, a smaller one for clearing storage, and a cap of one fifth of the gas used).
The written reasons are the gas token and those overfull blocks. I read both as the same
lesson: a counter that goes down was being leaned on at the place where it went down.
Ethereum's gas comes back in Section~\ref{sec:models} as one of five small models of systems people actually run, and
it's the only one of the five that prices a write at all, and it's instructive that the part
they had to fix was the part that could fall.

\subsection{Conservation: the total is the charges and nothing else}

The first property is the plainest one. The counter after a step is the counter
before plus what that step was charged. Add up a whole run and the middle values cancel out,
the way a sum of differences collapses to last minus first, and the total is the sum of the
per-step charges. Why state it?

Because it's the property that fails quietly. Say a machine charges one for raising a flag,
and also, somewhere in its error handling, forgets to add the charge when the step fails
halfway through. Or charges two in one code path and one in another for the same move. Or
has one step that writes the counter directly. Then the counter is \emph{mostly} the sum of the
charges, and ``mostly'' is the whole gap between a receipt and a note that says ``trust me, about
this much.'' Conservation is the sentence that there is no ``mostly'': every step, every outcome,
every error, adds exactly its charge, and a step that fails is charged the same as one that
succeeds, because the charge is on the attempt. For a machine built the way I'm describing,
that sentence is the rule the counter is updated by, so it can't fail by definition. What can
fail is the claim that a real machine \emph{is} built that way, and checking that means going
through every move it has, the failure branches included, one at a time, which is dull and is
the whole job. The run-long form, counter at the end equals counter at the start plus the sum
of the charges, then follows from the one-step rule by the cancelling sum; it's below. It's
the kind of theorem that looks boring and is the one you'd most want if you were going to
rely on the number.
One thing it doesn't say: that every mark bought something. The ledger is exact about what
was spent. What the spending was worth is another question, and whether a mark bought a real narrowing is
Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s question, and it needs a witness on top of the ledger entry.

\subsection{Only one honest count}

Here's the property that surprised me by being provable at all. Suppose you fixed the
schedule: this move costs one, that move costs zero, and so on, for every move. And suppose
someone else keeps their own books: their own function from states to totals, which starts at
zero and, on every step, goes up by exactly what the schedule says. Could their books disagree
with the machine's counter, somewhere, on some state you can actually get to?

No. And the proof is the tally stick. Both totals start at zero. On every step both go up by
the same amount. So on every state you can reach by steps from the start, they're equal.
That's it; it's an induction, the one-step-at-a-time argument from Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s floor.
The mathematician's word for this is \emph{initiality}: the counter is the one bookkeeping that
all the others, if they're honest about the schedule, turn out to be. Given the schedule, the
count is forced. Two things about that sentence I had to be careful with, and they're worth
saying before the symbols. It doesn't assume the other books climb: climbing follows from the
schedule, since the schedule never charges a negative amount, so ``only one honest count'' and
``it only climbs'' aren't two separate demands on the other bookkeeper. And it holds on
\emph{reachable} states only. A state you can't get to from the start is one where it says nothing
about whether the other books agree, which is the right thing for a receipt to say.

Here are the properties exactly. First the piece being added to Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s five, a counter and a
price list, and then the two facts about it. The counter gets the Greek letter $\mu$ (mu),
which is what the checked work calls it.

\begin{definition}[A counter kept by a price list]\label{def:u06-counter}
A \emph{counter machine} has a set of states, a set of moves, a step function
$\mathrm{apply}$ that takes a state and a move, a start state $s_\mathrm{init}$, a
schedule $c$ giving each move a cost in $\mathbb{N}$, and a counter $\mu$ from states
to $\mathbb{N}$, such that $\mu(s_\mathrm{init}) = 0$ and
$\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mu(s) + c(i)$ for every state $s$ and move $i$, with no
exceptions. A \emph{run} of a list $t$ of moves from $s$ applies them in order, and
$c(t)$ is the sum of their costs. A state is \emph{reachable} when it is the start or is
$\mathrm{apply}(s, i)$ for a reachable $s$ and some $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Conservation]\label{thm:conservation}
In a counter machine, for every state $s$ and every list $t$, $\mu$ at the end of the run of
$t$ from $s$ equals $\mu(s) + c(t)$. In particular $\mu$ never decreases along a run.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $t$. For the empty list both sides are $\mu(s)$. For a list $i$ followed by $t'$,
the one-step rule gives $\mu(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = \mu(s) + c(i)$, and the induction
hypothesis from $\mathrm{apply}(s, i)$ adds $c(t')$. Since every $c(i) \ge 0$, the counter
never falls.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Only one honest count]\label{thm:initiality}
In a counter machine, let $B$ (for ``books'') be any function from states to $\mathbb{N}$ with
$B(s_\mathrm{init}) = 0$ and $B(\mathrm{apply}(s, i)) = B(s) + c(i)$ for all $s$ and $i$.
Then $B(s) = \mu(s)$ for every reachable state $s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By induction on why $s$ is reachable. At the start both are 0. If $s = \mathrm{apply}(s', i)$
with $B(s') = \mu(s')$, then $B(s) = B(s') + c(i) = \mu(s') + c(i) = \mu(s)$, the last step
by the counter's rule.
\end{proof}

Those two proofs are the whole of it, and they're about any counter machine. Coq checks them
over arbitrary states, as \code{nec\_f\_conservation}, with \code{nec\_f\_counter\_monotone} for
the climb, and \code{nec\_f\_initiality} (NecFCounter.v), and here they're on
the page, where you can check every line. The machine I build later is one of these, and on
it the run form is a checked theorem: the ledger after any list of instructions is the start
