plus the sum of their costs (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}). The uniqueness half holds even with
the books' rule asked only of reachable states (\code{nec\_f\_initiality\_reachable\_rule}).

I want to flag what initiality does \emph{not} do, because the fact is smaller than the word.
It doesn't pick the prices. The schedule is an input: somebody decided that raising the flag
costs one and adding two numbers costs zero, and nothing here says that decision was right
(Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} is where I argued the floor isn't arbitrary; the rest of a schedule has to be defended by
whoever writes it). It doesn't turn marks into anything physical. And it isn't the category
theorist's ``initial object,'' though the word is borrowed for a related reason.

There \emph{is} a universal property nearby, and I'll say exactly how far it reaches so the
borrowed word doesn't reach further. Take any other machine that understands the same
moves (call it the \emph{target}), and pick a state of it to start from. Walking a list of moves
through it, one at a time, is the one and only way to send lists to its states that starts
where you said and keeps in step as the list grows by one. Programmers call that walk down a
list, one item at a time, a \emph{fold}, and I'll borrow the word. That's an induction on the list from its
end, the same shape as the proof just above, and it never looks at the other machine's
reading or its prices, which tells you how much the toll is doing here: nothing. It's a fact
about \emph{lists of moves}; states haven't come into it yet.

Coming down from lists to the states of the machine running them is where it gets
interesting, and where the borrowed word stops. Two different lists can leave a machine in the
same state. If they leave the target in two different states, there's no single place
to send that state. That's the whole obstruction, and it's exact: the map from states exists
on the reachable ones precisely when equal states always come from lists that agree on the
other side. Call that the \emph{descent} condition, because it's what
lets the fold come down from lists to states. A toll doesn't force it. Take the one-bit machine whose set costs one and whose
reset is free. It obeys the toll, yet a single set and a reset followed by a set leave its
bit in the same state. A target that keeps its whole history as its state tells those two
runs apart, so nothing comes down. So the fold is unique on lists, and that's what the word ``initial''
earns. It doesn't make anybody's states initial among everything that obeys the toll, and I
won't say it does. The fold and the descent condition are checked over any machine: the fold
is the one such map (\code{nec\_f\_fold\_unique}), descent holds exactly when each reachable
state goes to one target state (\code{nec\_f\_descent\_iff\_functional}), and a map the fold
factors through gives descent (\code{nec\_f\_factor\_gives\_descent}), all in NecFCounter.v; the
history-keeping machine is the example that shows where descent fails
(\code{nec\_f\_descent\_fails\_for\_history}).

And the borrowed word has a home. I didn't build it, so I'll point at it. That lists
of moves are the starting object, and that a machine's behaviour factors through its reachable
states exactly when a condition like descent holds, is the theory of minimal realization. Joseph
Goguen put it as a universal property in 1973, in a paper whose title says it outright,
``Realization is universal,'' and Thomas Colcombet and Daniela Petri\c{s}an redid automata
minimization in the same functorial terms in 2020. Their machines can have any output at all,
which is the honest point: the fold and the descent condition never use the record, so the toll
is doing nothing here, just as I said.

\subsection{The toll is an old trick with a new name}

Now a thing I first took as a let-down. It would be nice to have a new kind of
cost argument. This isn't one. The toll is a case of a technique that
algorithm people have used since 1985 and that a mathematician studying the stability of
motion had, in a different costume, in
1892. I'm telling you it's old so you don't think I invented it.

The trick is called the potential method, and here's the whole of it. Give every state a
number, call it the potential, that measures how much ``owing'' is stored up in that state.
Then look at each step and ask: does the cost of the step, plus the change in potential it
causes, ever come out negative? If it never does, you've got a bound: any run costs at least
the amount the potential \emph{dropped} from start to finish, because the drop had to be paid for
by the steps along the way. The computer scientist Robert Tarjan set it out in 1985, crediting the potential view to
Daniel Sleator. Tarjan's use goes the
other
way (potential as prepaid credit, to bound a run
from above): he used it to analyse data structures that
are occasionally expensive and usually cheap; and the decreasing-function idea underneath it
is the one the Russian mathematician Aleksandr Lyapunov used in 1892 to prove that a system settles down. Do the coin version,
which runs Tarjan's way, as a ceiling: a stack of coins, PUSH adds one and costs one, POP-ALL removes them all and costs as
many as it removed, potential equals the number of coins. PUSH costs one plus one potential;
POP-ALL of k coins costs k and drops the potential by k, net zero. So any sequence from an
empty stack costs at most twice the number of pushes, however many expensive pops are in it.
That's the method. Three lines.

Push on that 1892 for a second, because a date like that hides a lot. Lyapunov wrote the idea up
as his doctoral thesis, in Russian. A French translation came out in 1907, made by a French
naval engineer, \'Edouard Davaux, and corrected by Lyapunov himself. The English one came
out in 1992, a hundred years after the original, and it was translated from the French: a
translation of a translation. So for most of the twentieth century a reader with only English
met the idea secondhand or not at all. Did the algorithm people of 1985 get it from him? I can't
tell you, and nothing here needs them to have. Whether anybody walked from one to the other on
purpose is a question I'd like answered. What I do have is a picture: the same
idea, a number that only goes one way along a run, turned up in a thesis about whether a moving
system settles down and in a paper about data structures, close to a century apart.

Now point it at the flag. Potential: one if the flag is down, zero if it's up. A step from
down to up drops the potential by one, so for the step's cost plus potential change to be
non-negative, the step has to cost at least one. That's the toll, exactly, and the two are the
same statement: the toll holds for a machine if and only if every step has non-negative
amortized cost under the flag potential (``amortized cost'' is just that sum, the step's cost
plus the change in potential). Then the universal floor from Section~\ref{sec:toll}, ``any run from NO to YES
paid at least one,'' is just the potential method's standard conclusion, the drop in
potential from one to zero, and every system with the five parts that obeys the toll is an
instance (the checked record carries the toll as a field, so that's every certification
system). Two more facts fall out of the same picture. Under the toll, a run raises the flag
at most as many times as its total cost; each raise uses up a unit and a unit isn't used
twice. And if you demand the upper-bound version too, that the potential before a step covers
its cost plus the potential after, then the two together hold exactly when raising the flag
costs exactly one, everything else costs zero, and the flag never comes down; that's the
sharpest version of
the schedule, and notice that Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s toy doesn't meet it: the toy's VOUCH move, played from
YES, makes a mark
although it raises nothing, which the floor allows and the exact version forbids. (These
two theorems let the price depend on the state as well as the move's name, which is wider
than Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s per-name cost; a per-name cost is a special case.) Two older tools sit beside
these, named for completeness: running a list of moves in a ``writer'' that accumulates a
number returns the final state and the run's cost (\code{run\_writer\_is\_run\_and\_cost}), and a
per-move schedule is a ``grade'' fixed before the run (\code{run\_graded\_is\_run}); neither
embeds those frameworks' full type systems, and the files say so. The writer is the move
the programming-language researchers Norman Danner and Daniel Licata make in their cost semantics, a translation that carries a cost alongside
a program's result (Danner, Licata and Ramyaa, ICFP 2015; Danner and Licata, \emph{Journal of
Functional Programming}, 2022). The grade is Shin-ya Katsumata's: a computation carries its resource
as a grade, and the grades compose as the computations do (``Parametric effect monads and
semantics of effect systems,'' POPL 2014). Dominic Orchard, Vilem Liepelt and Harley Eades put grades into the
types of a working language (``Quantitative program reasoning with graded modal types,'' ICFP
2019). Read against them, the counter is a grade carried in the state by the step rule. No type
carries it. And what does that difference even mean? A cost that lives in a type gets checked
before the program runs, by whoever checks the types; a cost that lives in the state gets
written during the run, by the step itself. Same number, different moment of truth.

So is mine an embedding of their frameworks, or something weaker? Half of it is exactly theirs,
and the other half is left out on purpose. The counter \emph{is} their writer: a step that moves
the rest of the state without looking at the counter, hands back its cost, and has the cost added
on is a computation in the writer over whole numbers with addition, and running a list of moves in
that writer gives back the final state and the total cost, nothing more and nothing less
(\code{run\_writer\_is\_run\_and\_cost}). Every system in this book whose step never reads its own
counter has that shape. What doesn't come along is the part of their frameworks that works before
anything runs: the type systems that carry grades, Danner and Licata's bounding relation and the
recurrences they extract for a program's cost. That isn't a hole waiting for a patch. It's the
moment-of-truth difference I just named. Putting the count in the step is choosing the other
moment, so the grade here is written by the step at run time and never checked ahead of it.

How close do the two moments come? Close enough to say exactly, in a limited form, argued here
and not checked. Take a small structured language over a machine with this kind of counter:
sequencing, branches whose two arms carry the same grade, and paid acts each graded with their
charge, and grade every program the way Katsumata's discipline does, adding grades along the
program. On loop-free programs the two agree on the nose: on every run that doesn't trap, the
counter rises by exactly the grade. The argument is conservation set beside the grade rule; the
counter's rise is the sum of the charges along the run, and the grade rule adds the same charges
in the same order. Loops break the agreement, and in one direction only. A loop that runs a
paid
check once for every unit
in some register, where the check
always
passes and is charged one,
costs that register's value on
entry, and no fixed whole number is an exact grade for it; a grade that's a function of the
inputs, the kind cost-aware type theories like calf (Niu, Sterling, Grodin and Harper, 2022)
allow, gets exactness back. So the counter carries their semantics exactly, agrees with fixed
grades wherever a fixed grade can be exact, and where a run's cost depends on its data it holds
the exact number that a fixed grade can only bound. What has no counterpart in the step is the
checking ahead of time: a type checker turning a program away before it runs.

There's one more neighbour, closer than any of those, and I'll name it before
somebody names it at me. A number the step keeps up to date and nothing else ever reads is
what program-proof people call an \emph{auxiliary variable}, or \emph{ghost} state. Susan Owicki
and David Gries added auxiliary variables to parallel programs in 1976, because some true facts
about such a program can't be proved without one, under the rule that an auxiliary variable
never steers the program. Jean-Christophe Filliâtre, Léon Gondelman and Andrei Paskevich, in
2014, worked out when ghost code can be erased without changing what the program computes. By
that test this section's counter is ghost whenever no step consults it, and
Section~\ref{sec:latch}'s honest extensions are built exactly that way: the base moves the same
whatever the ledger and the record say. So what does putting it in the step buy, if the number
is ghost anyway? Two things, as far as I can see. The number is there while the machine runs,
where a window can show it (Section~\ref{sec:windows}), and not only inside a proof somebody
wrote afterwards. And the rule that keeps it is one rule for every run of every program. An
annotation covers only the one program somebody happened to prove. Whether a record stays ghost depends on
what else the step does with it; the machine in Part IV has a part that isn't ghost, its table
of checked facts, and that's where I'll say why. One last relative, from the graph side: Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s floor is a
cheapest-path bound in a system with weights on its moves. Every path from the no-states to the
yes-states crosses the line between them, and every edge across that line weighs at least one.
Weighted automata go back to Marcel-Paul Schützenberger in 1961, and priced timed automata, which
add clocks, were set out in 2001. The floor is about the smallest case of what they compute.

Exactly, for any certification system with states $S$, moves $I$, step, per-name cost, and
reading:

\begin{definition}[Potential, amortized cost]\label{def:potential}
A \emph{potential} is a function $\Phi : S \to \mathbb{N}$. A step has \emph{non-negative amortized
cost} under $\Phi$ when $\mathrm{cost}(i) + \Phi(\mathrm{step}(s, i)) \ge \Phi(s)$. The
\emph{flag potential} is $\Phi_\mathrm{cert}(s) = 1$ if $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no}$ and $0$
if it reads yes.
\end{definition}

Defined as \code{amortized\_nonneg} and \code{cert\_potential} (CostSemanticsComparison.v).

\begin{theorem}[The toll is the potential method]\label{thm:potential}
(1) The toll holds exactly when every step has non-negative amortized cost under
$\Phi_\mathrm{cert}$. (2) For any $\Phi$ with non-negative amortized cost and any run $t$ from
$s$, $\mathrm{cost}(t) + \Phi(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) \ge \Phi(s)$. (3) Hence, under the toll,
a run from a no-state to a yes-state costs at least $1 - 0 = 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Check the four combinations of the reading before and after: only no-to-yes has
$\Phi_\mathrm{cert}$ dropping, by one, so the inequality there is exactly
$\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$; in the other three it holds for any cost. (2) Induction on the run,
adding the per-step inequalities so that the middle potentials cancel. (3) Apply (2) with
$\Phi_\mathrm{cert}$, which is 1 at the start and 0 at the end.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{a2\_iff\_nonnegative\_amortized\_cost}, \code{potential\_telescoping}, \code{nfi\_by\_potential},
and \code{certification\_system\_is\_potential\_method} (CostSemanticsComparison.v), with the
state-dependent-cost results \code{flips\_le\_cost} and \code{a2\_and\_aara\_iff\_exact}
(CostFrameworks.v).

So what's new, if the method isn't? Only where it's pointed. The potential method is a way of
proving things about costs. What this book adds is a claim about \emph{which} potential, the
flag, and about what happens to that claim when you can only see a window of the state. The
method is Tarjan's and Sleator's. The reading is mine, and I'm about to find out what it can and can't
survive.

The flag potential has relatives in physics-flavoured mathematics too, which I
found after the fact. Resource theories study what you can turn into what when some
operations are free: Bob Coecke, Tobias Fritz and Robert Spekkens gave the general definition in
2016, Fritz worked out its algebra in 2017, and Tomáš Gonda and Spekkens catalogued the numbers
that never go up under free operations, which they call monotones, in 2023. Read with ``certified''
as the resource and one mark as the currency, the flag potential is the kind of cost monotone
they build, measured in that currency, and the floor is its simplest case. Does that make the toll a resource theory? Only
in the trivial way: the conversion costs exactly one mark and that's the whole theory. It's a
neighbour to know about. I don't count it as a result.

\subsection{What the counter is, said once}

A receipt is a total that lives in the state, only climbs, equals the sum of the charges on
every path including the failures, and is the only such total for its schedule. Each of
those had a home before this book: the stick for a total that lives in the state, Lamport's clocks for climbing, Turing's and Floyd's ranking functions for
the same one-way rule run downward, the telescoping sum for conservation, the
induction for the single honest count. None of them is physics. None of them says
what the charges should be. What they say is that once you've chosen the charges, the
counter is the arithmetic. It's no second opinion. And the toll on top of it is the
potential method with the flag as potential, which is to say a trick from 1985 wearing the
question from Section~\ref{sec:structure}.

Here's one thing the counter can't do just by existing: if you can only see \emph{part} of the state, can you
tell what the counter is? Can you even tell, from outside, which step paid? The stick works
because you can lay the two halves together. What if you're only ever shown one half, through
a window, and the window doesn't show the notches?

One piece of that has a short answer, and I'll give it now so the next section can start
from it. A window, for now, is just the part of the state an outside observer is shown (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}'s
display was one, and Section~\ref{sec:windows} is about windows in general). Call a window \emph{counter-complete} when
some rule, applied to what the window shows, returns the counter on every state;
\emph{flag-complete} likewise for the flag. Say a window \emph{forgets the counter} when changing the
counter and nothing else never changes what the window shows, and likewise for the flag.

The short answer: a window that forgets the counter is never counter-complete, whatever else
it shows, and a window that forgets the flag is never flag-complete. Take any state and make
two copies of it, one with the counter set to 1 and one with it set to 2, everything else
held still. The window shows the same thing for both, so any rule gives the same answer for
both, and one of the two answers is wrong. The flag is the same argument with yes and no. On
the stick: a window that shows you the wood's colour and its
length, and hides the notches, can't tell you what's owed, and staring harder at the colour won't help. (The argument needs a
state space where the counter can be changed on its own, the rest held still; that's what
``forgets'' quietly assumes. The machine I build later is such a space, and it has a checked
pair of its own: two runs with the same window, one paid and one not
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-separation}).)

Be careful what that doesn't say. It says neither part can be dropped. It doesn't say a
window showing both is the smallest window that works, because nothing here orders windows,
so there's nothing for it to be smallest in. And it's about reading the counter back. Which step paid is the
harder question, and it's the next section's.

%===========================================================================
\section{Windows and shadows}
\label{sec:windows}
%===========================================================================

I left you with the stick split in half and asked what happens if you can only ever see one
half through a window that doesn't show the notches, and with a harder question under that
one: can you tell, from outside, which step paid? This section is about windows. It's a
section where the mathematics is so small that I'm going to state it in
full and then spend most of the pages on what it's \emph{not}, because the smallness is the
trap: the fact is a one-liner and it's tempting to climb over it with cleverness, and
you can't, and seeing why you can't is the content.

\subsection{A cave, and the people who got good at it}

This one is Plato's, and the part I need is near the end. In the seventh book of the \emph{Republic}, Plato has
Socrates, the main speaker of the dialogue,
describe prisoners chained in a cave since childhood, facing a wall, with a fire
behind them and people carrying objects along a walkway between the fire and their backs.
All the prisoners have ever seen is the shadows on the wall. To them, Socrates says, the
truth would be nothing but those shadows. Further on, Socrates reads the story out himself: the
cave is the world of sight, and the climb out of it is the soul's climb toward what's really there.
So a real world hidden from anyone who only looks is in the story on purpose, and Plato put it
there. It still isn't the part I need.

What I need comes a little before that reading, when one prisoner, freed and taken up into the
daylight, thinks back to the cave. The prisoners,
Socrates says, hand out honours to whoever is quickest at spotting the shadows as they pass
and best at guessing which comes next. Read that again. The prisoners \emph{get good at it}. They
build a whole science of shadows, with experts and prizes, and it works, on shadows. What
they can't do is say anything about a carried object that leaves no mark on the wall. Not
because they're stupid. Because the information isn't on the wall. Skill inside a window
doesn't reach past the window, no matter how much skill. That's the fact. Plato dressed it as
a lesson about education, and it is one, but strip the dressing and it's a sentence about
functions, and it's going to be the whole section.

\subsection{The shadow of a cube}

Do this one tonight with a lamp. Hold a cube face-on to the light: its shadow is a square.
Now hold up a square of card the same size: same shadow. A person who sees only the wall
can't tell you whether what's casting the shadow has any thickness at all. Ask them, and
they'll tell you, truthfully, that they can't know, and if they're honest they'll also tell
you that no amount of staring at that square will change it.

Now turn both a quarter turn. The card's shadow collapses to a line. The cube's stays a
square. Now the wall-watcher knows. What changed? Not their cleverness. The \emph{window}. A
second look from a different angle is a bigger window than one look, and what bought it was
the turn. Edwin Abbott wrote a novel about a window like this in 1884,
\emph{Flatland}. A Flatlander never sees a shape. Abbott's narrator says it in his first section: nothing was
visible to them, or could be, except straight lines. Put a coin flat on a table and lower your
eye to the table's edge, and the coin turns into a line; that's the whole view. What gives a
Flatlander anything more is fog. A line that's near is bright and a line that runs off into the
fog goes dim, so a trained eye can read a triangle or a pentagon off how fast the brightness
fades toward the ends. The training takes time and money, and in
the story only people with money get
it. That's a window that got bigger, and it was paid for in time.

Then a sphere comes through the narrator's plane. What his eye gets is a line whose ends fade
too fast for any flat figure he knows, changing size in a way no flat figure could. He only
settles that it's a circle by feeling it, and the circle grows from a point to its widest and
shrinks back to nothing as the sphere rises through. From one slice he can't put a sphere
together. From the slices one after another, seen and felt and argued over, he starts to.
The escape from a window is never ``think harder.'' It's always ``a different window,'' and a
different window always costs something: a turn, a second look, training, time.

Who was Edwin Abbott? Not a mathematician by trade. He was headmaster of the City of London School
for twenty-four years, a clergyman, and the author of more than forty books, a Shakespeare
grammar among them. He put \emph{Flatland} out under the name ``A Square.'' His full name was
Edwin Abbott Abbott, two A's, and the pen name may be a joke on that, A squared;
nice if true, but take it as a lead. Here's the part I like best, from a sketch
of his life on the geometer Thomas Banchoff's pages: \emph{Flatland}, by far the most read thing
he wrote, isn't mentioned at all in his obituary in the London \emph{Times} or in his entry in the
\emph{Dictionary of National Biography}. The official record of the man was a window too: it
showed the headmaster and the grammarian and left out the one book people still read. That
changes nothing in the argument. It's the argument, acted out by an obituary. (\emph{Flatland} already turned up in Section~\ref{sec:origin}, where the hunch behind this book started, and in Section~\ref{sec:point}, which first told the sphere's visit.)

\subsection{The whole fact, in one paragraph}

Here's the mathematics, and I promise it's all of it. You have a set of states, the real
things. You have a window, which is a function that takes a state and gives you what you can
see of it: the shadow, the slice, the half-stick without notches. And you have a question
about the state, which is also a function: it takes a state and gives an answer. The thing
you want is a \emph{decoder}: a rule that takes what you can see and gives the right answer to
the question, every time. When does one exist?

Think about two states that cast the same shadow. The decoder sees the same shadow for both,
so it gives the same answer for both. So if the question has \emph{different} answers on those
two states, the decoder is wrong on at least one of them, and there's nothing it can do about
it, because it never saw the difference. That's the whole fact. If a decoder exists, then the
question must already give the same answer on every pair of states that look the same through
the window. Mathematicians call the set of states that cast one particular shadow the \emph{fibre}
over that shadow (think of the shadow as a point on the wall and the fibre as the bundle of
all the things that could have cast it), and the sentence is: a decoder exists only if the
question is constant on every fibre. That's the theorem just below, and the ``only if'' is the
direction that bites. The other direction, ``if the question is constant on
fibres then a decoder exists,'' is true too, but it needs you to be handed, for every possible
shadow, one actual state that casts it, so you can look up the answer there, and the handing
is not free either, since someone has to supply a representative for every shadow. (You can always fill a gap with a default
answer. The default doesn't recover what was really there.)

Exactly. Let $S$ be any set of states, $V$ any set of views, $w : S \to V$ a window, and
$q : S \to A$ a question with answers in any set $A$. A \emph{decoder} is a function
$d : V \to A$ with $d(w(s)) = q(s)$ for every state $s$. The question is \emph{constant on
fibres} when $w(s) = w(s')$ implies $q(s) = q(s')$.

\begin{theorem}[Decoders need constant fibres]\label{thm:fibre}
If a decoder exists, the question is constant on fibres. Conversely, if the question is
constant on fibres and you are handed, for every view $v$, a state $r(v)$ with
$w(r(v)) = v$, then $d(v) = q(r(v))$ is a decoder.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $w(s) = w(s')$ then $q(s) = d(w(s)) = d(w(s')) = q(s')$. Conversely,
$d(w(s)) = q(r(w(s)))$, and $r(w(s))$ has the same view as $s$, so by constancy its answer is
$q(s)$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{decoding\_requires\_fiber\_constancy} and \code{selected\_representatives\_give\_decoder}
(ObservationPolicy.v), for arbitrary types.

Try the smallest case, by hand, because it'll keep coming back. A state
is a pair: a position, 0 or 1, and a hidden flag, up or down. The window shows the position
only. Two moves from (0, down): one sets the position to 1 and raises the flag; the other
sets the position to 1 and leaves the flag alone. Both land on position 1. Now write down
every possible decoder from ``what I see'' to ``is the flag up'': there are exactly four
functions from two positions to two answers. Check each against both results. None of the
four gets both right, because both results show position 1 and one has the flag up and one
doesn't. That exhaustive check is the theorem on this example; the general statement is the
one-line argument above, and that's what's checked. There's no fifth function hiding
somewhere.

\subsection{People who found this on their own}

The fact is so plain that it got discovered separately in every field that has to deal with
seeing part of something, and I want to lay them beside each other, because that's the kind
of evidence I trust: people who'd never met kept walking into the same wall.

In 1956 Edward Moore, working on the small switching machines that became computer
hardware, asked when an experimenter who can only feed a machine inputs and watch its
outputs can tell two of its internal states apart. His answer gave a precise meaning to
``indistinguishable from outside,'' and a theorem with a sting in it: even when every pair of
states can be told apart by \emph{some} experiment, there are machines where no single experiment
tells you which state you started in. What you can always do is run an experiment after
which you know which state you're in \emph{now}. In 1960 Rudolf Kalman,
whose filter went on to aerospace and industry, asked the same question for continuous
systems, called it \emph{observability}, and gave a test (a matrix rank, which you can compute)
for whether watching the output over time pins down the internal state. His unobservable
states are exactly a fibre: states whose difference never reaches the output, and never will,
however long you watch. That second half took me longest to take in. More samples of the same
window only repeat the same fibre. Try it on a car: if your only instrument is the speedometer, two
cars a mile apart at the same speed read the same forever, and nothing on that dial will ever tell
you which mile marker either one started at. Read the mile markers instead and, over time, you
recover both position and speed. Same car, different window.

Where did Kalman's filter go first, before aerospace and industry at large? Toward the Moon. In the autumn
of 1960 Kalman called an acquaintance, Stanley Schmidt, at NASA's Ames Research Center, and came
to visit, not knowing what Schmidt's group was working on. The group, a branch with eight people
doing the analysis, was stuck on how a spacecraft going around the Moon and back could work out
where it was from what its crew could measure through an optical sight: a few angles to the Earth
and the Moon. That's a window problem with a capsule in it. The state is position and velocity,
the view is a handful of angles, and the job is to keep a running best guess at the state from a
sequence of views. Kalman presented his new filtering paper to them, and with real work (their
problem wasn't linear and his theory was) it fit, and it went into the feasibility studies for
navigating Apollo. Leonard McGee, of Schmidt's group at Ames, and Schmidt, telling the story in 1985, call it a fortunate
sequence of events and say the solution might have gone undiscovered but for that meeting. What
it changes: it shows the limit from the useful side. The filter didn't make the angles show more.
It made a sequence of views, over time, pin down the state, and it can only do that when the state
is observable from those views, which is Kalman's own condition. That's the mile markers. A
cleverer speedometer would never have got there.

In 1977 Patrick and Radhia Cousot built a whole discipline of program analysis, called
abstract interpretation, on throwing information away \emph{on purpose}. You run the program over
coarse descriptions of its values, and the exact values never enter. And you accept that the answer you get
has to be true of \emph{every} real value the coarse description could stand for. That last
sentence is fibre constancy as a design rule. And in 1970 Edgar Codd, inventing the relational
database, made programs independent of how the data is stored, and the relational systems
that followed gave users \emph{views}, deliberately partial windows onto the stored data. A
decade after Codd, in 1981, two database researchers, Fran\c{c}ois Bancilhon and Nicolas Spyratos, gave the view-update problem an exact semantics. The problem is this: if a user changes what they
see through a view, which of the many underlying states that cast that view should the
database move to? Several are legitimate. The fibre, from the writing side.

And Parnas, from Section~\ref{sec:structure}, hid things on purpose: a module is characterised by the design decision
it \emph{hides} from its callers. Hiding is a window. The caller can't later read back what was
hidden, including the things it later wishes it could check, and that's the price side of
the coin whose benefit side Parnas was selling. None of these people were doing philosophy.
They were trying to build filters, databases, compilers, and modules, and the wall is the
same wall in each.

One more, from information theory. Oliver Kosut, at Arizona State, and J\"org Kliewer, at the
New Jersey Institute of Technology, two information theorists, asked in 2018 when a receiver
on a channel with a possible attacker, and no shared key, can always either get the message
right or notice the attacker. The answer is all or nothing: the rate is zero, or it's everything
the channel would carry with no attacker at all, and which one depends on a condition they call
\emph{overwritability}, that the attacker can make what the receiver sees look exactly like an
honest transmission of some other message. That's a printer, a way to put the same thing in the
window without the event behind it. The fibre fact is their condition in its plainest form, with
the probabilities taken out.

And one from machine learning, where the two computers turn up with a lawyer attached. Four
machine-learning security researchers at the University of Toronto and the Vector Institute, Anvith
Thudi, Hengrui Jia, Ilia Shumailov and Nicolas Papernot, asked in 2022 how a company could prove a
trained model had forgotten someone's data, and found that the same model can come out of
different training sets, so the finished model can't show whether a point was used or removed.
The only claim they found you can audit is about the procedure that was run. Same wall: the
finished state is a window, and what happened is in the run.

Philosophers who study testimony, which is the trade of being told things, have the same wall from
the other side. Read one after another they blurred into a list of opinions for me, and the list
didn't tell me anything until I built a picture that showed where each one sits. So here's the
picture first.

Somebody passes you a note across a room. It says the answer to question seven is 42. What crossed
the room? Ink. Whatever made the writer believe 42 stayed on their side: the working-out, how careful
they were, whether they knew or guessed. Pull that apart and there are five things in play: the
claim on the paper, the writer's head, whatever process got the writer there, the trip across the
room, and your head at the other end. Every position I found puts its weight on one of those five.
Once I saw that, they stopped being a list and became a map, and the map has connections the list
hid.

The two ends of it are Locke and Burge, and they're the same dial turned opposite ways. The
philosopher John Locke, in the first book of his \emph{Essay} in 1690, says believing something
because someone with authority said it isn't knowing it. If the reason didn't cross the room, you
don't have it. Tyler Burge, a philosopher of mind and knowledge at UCLA, argued in 1993 that you're
entitled to accept what you're told, if it's presented as true and it makes sense to you, unless you
have a reason not to. Locke says only ink crossed, so you've got nothing. Burge says the ink comes
with a default, and the default holds until something knocks it over. I get the pull of Burge.
Nobody could get through a day checking every note. But a default anybody can trigger by writing
something sensible is a free record, the thing this book keeps refusing, so on that dial the book
sits at Locke's end. And sitting there has a price: staying there means carrying the check across
the room every time.

Jennifer Lackey, a philosopher at Northwestern who has spent much of her work on testimony, cuts the wire between the writer's head and what arrives. Her case, from 2008, is a teacher who doesn't believe the theory
she's required to teach, and her students come away knowing it anyway. I went back and forth on
whether those students really know it, and I haven't settled it. But look at where the case cuts. If
it's right, what arrives at your end never had to be believed at the other end, and the writer's head
drops out of the map. Sanford Goldberg, also at Northwestern, moves the weight one more place over,
onto the process. In 2010 he argued that whether your word justifies me can depend on how reliable
the processes behind your word were, which sit outside my head. That one took me a few reads. What I
think he's saying is that part of my reason for believing you lives in you, in machinery I can't
see, and he's fine with that. I'm not, quite, and why I'm not is why this book exists: machinery I
can't see is machinery I can't check. Christoph J\"ager and Nicholas Shackel, philosophers at
Innsbruck and Cardiff, built a model of degrees of belief in 2025 in which the writer knowing is neither
necessary nor sufficient for the reader to know. That lands where Lackey's teacher landed, from a
completely different direction, a story on one side and a calculation on the other. Agreement like
that I trust more than either piece alone, as long as I remember a model only shows what can happen
inside its own rules.

Then two sets of people who drew arrows. Wesley Holliday, a logician then at Stanford, put testimony
into a logic of belief change in 2009, with an authority graph recording whose word each agent takes
and rules for what hearing a speaker does to a belief. I've only read a summary of Holliday's paper,
so I'm taking that on somebody's word, which is a funny thing to admit in this paragraph. Security
people had drawn the same kind of arrow two decades earlier. In the logic of authentication of
Michael Burrows, Martin Abadi and Roger Needham (1990), two computer scientists at Digital's research
lab in Palo Alto and one at Cambridge, if I believe an authority has jurisdiction over a statement
and I believe the authority holds it, I believe it. Set that beside Burge and it's his default with
one change: the authority is named before the note arrives. That one change is the whole difference.
Burge's default trusts whoever is writing. Theirs trusts only a writer you picked in advance.

Kenny Easwaran is the one who goes after what crosses the room itself. He's a philosopher who works on
probability and on how mathematicians know things, and in 2009 he took up a question I'd never have
thought to ask. The philosopher Don Fallis had pressed it in a series of papers: why will
mathematicians accept a proof that's long and complicated, or partly carried out by a computer,
and turn down a probabilistic one that can be far more certain? That looked backwards to me at first. More certain
should win. Easwaran's answer is a property he calls \emph{transferability}. A deductive proof puts the
reason on the paper. Every step crosses the room, so you can learn from the writer without trusting
the writer. A probabilistic proof leaves the reason behind and sends only the writer's word about
what the dice did. Once I saw it that way it stopped looking backwards, and it's the cleanest
statement I found of what this book does: make the reason cross the room, carry the thing, and run
the check on your own side. That reading is mine. His subject is proofs passed between mathematicians, so if it's wrong, it's
wrong on me.

Now push on my own spot on the map, because it gives. The book carries the check across the room,
but the check runs on a checker, and I trust the checker because it was proved honest once, outside
every run. That's a jurisdiction rule. It's Burrows, Abadi and Needham's arrow with the checker as the
named authority, so I'm not sitting at Locke's end as cleanly as I'd like. What I can say is that my
authority was picked in advance, that it's a single named thing while Burge trusts every writer, and that its honesty is a proof you
can rerun yourself. That's a smaller trust than Burge's, and a different kind from Goldberg's, because
the machinery is out where you can look at it. It isn't zero, so
I'm pointing at it here
myself.

Only Burrows, Abadi and Needham write about machines passing messages, and even
they write about the computers as if the computers held beliefs. The rest are about what survives the trip from one head
to another. Either way it's the copier's problem, with philosophers' names on it and, in one
case, computer scientists'.

Distributed-systems people hit the wall too, and one pair of them measured how far it goes. Their
papers were a pile of acronyms to me until I put them all in one room. People at desks work from one
rulebook and pass slips to each other. Nobody sees into anybody's head; all anyone gets is the slips
handed to them. Somebody may be cheating. What can the honest ones do about it with nothing but slips?

Andreas Haeberlen, then at the Max Planck Institute for Software Systems in Saarbr\"ucken, and Petr
Kuznetsov, then in Berlin, asked in 2009 which faults an outside observer can
detect at all. As I read their answer, it sorts cheating by where it sits. A cheat can break the
rulebook without changing any slip. A cheat can write a slip an honest player could have written too,
for all anyone holding it can tell. A cheat can fail to send a slip that's due, an omission fault, or
send one the rulebook would never produce, a commission fault. The first two, they argue, no algorithm
can detect. The last two can be caught, and they put a floor under how many messages the catching
costs, which I liked for obvious reasons. My first guess was that the classes ranked how bad a fault
is. They don't. They rank how far the fault gets toward a slip, and the first two are a fibre: an
honest room and a crooked one that hand out the same slips. That's the fibre fact with an auditor
attached.

Their group's PeerReview system (Haeberlen, Kouznetsov, the same Kuznetsov spelled another way, and
Peter Druschel, the institute's founding director, 2007) is the ladder up to that wall:
every node keeps a secure record of the messages it sent and received, and a checker replays
the record against a reference implementation, a copy of the rulebook it can run, which exposes the
faults a correct node got to see. That's close to the whole-state escape from the three escapes
below, built: ship the log, and the checker re-runs it. Close, because a log of slips stands in for a
whole state only if the rulebook can rebuild what a desk did from them, and only if the checker's
copy of the rulebook is the right one.

The next three ask what you can say once you're at the wall. Ralf K\"usters, Tomasz Truderung and
Andreas Vogt, three security researchers at Trier, asked what a verdict should hold. They gave in
2010 a general definition of accountability, a verdict naming who misbehaved, and argued, with a
proof inside their own definitions, that verifiability, the property that an outsider can check a
result, is a restricted form of it. The way I read the restriction: verifiability says something went
wrong, and accountability points at a desk. Radha Jagadeesan, Alan Jeffrey, Corin Pitcher and James
Riely, programming-language people at DePaul in Chicago and, for Jeffrey, Bell Labs, asked when the
verdict comes. They built in 2009 an operational model of systems that enforce a policy after the
fact by audit, and studied the trade between the power of the auditor, the cost of the audit and
what's asked of the agents. Robert K\"unnemann, Ilkan Esiyok and Michael Backes, at the CISPA
security center in Saarbr\"ucken, in 2019 made the idea a mechanized check, with Certificate
Transparency (CT), the public logging of the certificates web browsers trust, among their examples. As I understand it, they did it by turning accountability into a
property of the trace, the whole run. That's Thudi and his coauthors' wall again: what happened is in
the run.

In September 2026 Timo Treitz, a student at Saarland University, and K\"unnemann gave CT the full
treatment (Section~\ref{sec:models} has my fragment of it) and found, in their model, that plain CT
gives accountability only if the log is assumed honest, an assumption the SCT auditing extension
(SCT is the signed certificate timestamp a log hands out) can drop and the gossiping extension can't. In my room, CT hands PeerReview's log of slips to a third party
to keep. An honest log is the commitment bit from the three escapes below, with a
name on the contract: somebody's promise that the bit is set when, and only when, the claim
holds, trusted at the step.

Turn the room on me and it gives twice. A flag raised for free that never reaches the window is
Haeberlen and Kuznetsov's first class, and no auditor outside catches it; that's the clerk's trouble,
next. My way out is PeerReview's, and it trusts a copy of the rulebook too: the checker, proved
honest once, outside every run. And every verdict in this book is accept or reject on one claim. It
never points at a desk. In K\"usters, Truderung and Vogt's terms that's the restricted form, and the
rest of accountability isn't here.

\subsection{The clerk with two photographs}

Now point it at the counter, because that's why this section is here. Suppose you want to
bill for raising the flag, exactly: at least one mark for every step that raises it, and
nothing for a step that doesn't. And suppose the person doing the billing is a clerk who
sees only a \emph{window} on the state, a photograph before the step and a photograph after.
The clerk's bill is a function of the two photographs. Can the clerk bill exactly?

Not if the window has the wrong kind of blind spot. Here's why, and it's the cube again.
Suppose there are
two steps that give the clerk the same before-photo and the same after-photo, and one of them
raised the flag and the other didn't. (The two-move toy above is exactly such a pair; so are
``a stamp goes onto a document inside a closed drawer'' and ``someone opens and closes the
drawer.'') The clerk has one bill for that pair of photographs. If the bill is at least one,
it overcharges the step that didn't raise the flag. If it's zero, it undercharges the step
that did. Any bill that never misses a raise bills something that wasn't a raise, and no
bill from those photographs is exact. The fix is the plain one: put the flag in the
photograph. If the window shows the reading, then ``one when the reading goes from down to
up, zero otherwise'' is exact, and such a window has no pair like the one above. That's enough.
It isn't the only way: a window can hide the flag and still have no colliding pair, in
which case a bill from the photographs can be exact; what ShadowPricing.v proves the other way is
only that a colliding pair rules exact pricing out. And ``exact'' here means rise-only pricing: at least
one on every step that raises the flag, nothing on any step that doesn't. That's all the
clerk's problem needs, and the bill ``one for a raise, zero otherwise'' meets it
(\code{step\_price\_is\_exact}). So it's exact about \emph{which} steps get charged. It isn't exact about \emph{how much}, and it
doesn't pick out one bill: ``two for a raise, zero
otherwise'' meets it too. Pinning the bill down takes one more demand, a ceiling: over any
run, the total never exceeds the number of raises. With the floor and that ceiling there's
exactly one bill left, one per raise and zero otherwise; that's an if and only if, proved for
any system whose bill is decided step by step (\code{exact\_commitment\_pricing\_characterization},
CommitmentPredicateAdequacy.v). These are stated for any states and any steps. The window version, the cube theorem with a
price in place of a decoder, comes next.

Same clerk, now in symbols, so you can check every word I just used. Take the five parts
of Section~\ref{sec:toll} with a window $w : S \to V$, and say a step $(s, i)$
\emph{raises} the flag when $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no}$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s,i)) = \mathrm{yes}$. A \emph{price} is any function of a state and
a move. It \emph{meets the floor} when every raise costs at least one, and \emph{never overcharges}
when every non-raise costs zero; together, it is \emph{exact} (about which steps are charged;
the amount is pinned only by the whole-run ceiling above). A \emph{window price} is one computed
from the two photographs only: $\mathrm{price}(s, i) = b(w(s), w(\mathrm{step}(s, i)))$ for
some bill $b : V \times V \to \mathbb{N}$. A \emph{collision} is two steps $(s_1, i_1)$ and
$(s_2, i_2)$ with $w(s_1) = w(s_2)$ and $w(\mathrm{step}(s_1, i_1)) = w(\mathrm{step}(s_2,
i_2))$, the first a raise and the second not.

\begin{theorem}[No exact window price across a collision]\label{thm:shadow-price}
If the window has a collision, every window price that meets the floor charges at least one
on some step that is not a raise; so no window price is exact. If instead the reading is a
function of the view, $\mathrm{cert}(s) = r(w(s))$ for some $r$, then the window price
``one when $r$ goes from no to yes, zero otherwise'' is exact, and the window has no collision.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Across a collision both steps get the same bill $b(v, v')$. The floor makes it at least one
because the first step is a raise; the second step, not a raise, pays it. If the reading is
$r$ of the view, the window price reads the raise directly, and two steps with the same
photographs either both raise or both don't, so there's no collision.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{shadow\_floor\_overcharges}, \code{shadow\_cannot\_price\_exactly},
\code{window\_showing\_reading\_prices\_exactly}, and \code{window\_showing\_reading\_has\_no\_collision}
(ShadowPricing.v), for arbitrary types.

So the exact price of raising the flag lives in the step itself, or in a window with no
colliding pair, and a window that shows the flag is the plainest such window. A window that
contains a pair like that one can't carry it. Whether a particular
machine has such a pair, for a particular window, has to be checked machine by machine and
window by window; the theorem only tells you what a pair does once you've found one.

There's a tidy way to say what the best window prices are, and it isn't mine. Give each pair of
before-and-after photographs the highest charge of any step that casts that pair, and you have
the cheapest window price that never undercharges; give it the lowest, and you have the dearest
one that never overcharges. Those two are the ``there is'' and ``for all'' of logic taken along
the window, which F. William Lawvere, an American mathematician best known for his work in category
theory, the mathematics of maps between structures, showed in 1969 (``Adjointness in foundations'')
are the two adjoints of pulling a statement back along a map. Four researchers at the University of
Calgary, Robin Cockett, Isabelle Geng, Carlo Maria Scandolo and Priyaa Srinivasan (2023), used the
same move, as Kan extensions, to extend resource measures along a map. In those terms the theorem
says that an exact window price exists exactly when the two coincide on every pair of photographs,
and a collision pulls them apart. That restatement is mine, and nothing checks it.

Control engineers have been hunting pairs like that for a long time, under other names.
Discrete-event systems is the field of machines that jump from state to state on events, some
of which an outside observer sees and some of which it doesn't. In 1995 five engineers, Meera Sampath, Raja Sengupta,
St\'ephane Lafortune and Demosthenis Teneketzis of the University of Michigan and Kasim
Sinnamohideen of Johnson Controls, asked when such an observer can always work out, from
what it sees, that a hidden fault event has happened, within a bounded number of further
steps. They called that \emph{diagnosability} and gave a test for it on finite machines.
Anooshiravan Saboori, then a doctoral student at the University of Illinois, and Christoforos
Hadjicostis, the engineer who supervised his doctorate there, asked in 2007 the question the other way round, for secrets: a system is
\emph{opaque} when an observer can never be sure it's in a secret state, because some run
outside the secret always looks the same. Read the raise as the hidden event and the window as
what the observer sees. Then a collision is the raise failing to be diagnosable with no delay
allowed, and a window that can't tell the flag is the flag's state being opaque to it
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-no-oracle}, later, is that, for the small machine). That's my reading; they
don't put it that way. Their versions are richer than mine: they allow delays, look at whole
runs, and come with algorithms. What this section adds is only the price: what a bill computed
through the window does across one such pair.

Why can't the clerk just watch the step itself? A clerk who does, who sees the whole state
before and the move, bills exactly with no trouble at all: ``one for a raise'' is a function of
exactly those two things, and it's the step price above. So the collision bites an observer who
doesn't see the step, or who's handed an account of the step and can't trust the account. That
second kind is the opening chapter's trace problem come back. If the names of the moves arrive in
a log the program wrote, the program can write whatever names it likes, and a clerk reading that
log is reading one more window, one the program painted. Seeing the move means being underneath
the program, where the step is.

\subsection{The three escapes, and what each one costs}

Suppose you're the person outside, and you want to be convinced that a run paid. The window
you've got doesn't show the counter. Here's how bad that is, in the smallest setting I can
build. Take a counter machine from Section~\ref{sec:counter}, give its states a position and a flag as well, and give
it a window that shows the position and nothing else. Now take two runs from the same start,
with the position at 0, the flag down and the counter at 0. Run $A$ makes one move that
raises the flag, costs one, and lands at position 1; its counter reads 1. Run $B$ makes one
move that does nothing but step to position 1, at cost zero; its counter reads 0. Call the
pair of photographs, position 0 then position 1, the \emph{transcript}. Both runs leave exactly
that transcript. A \emph{verifier} is a rule that takes a transcript and says accept or reject.
It is \emph{sound} when every transcript it accepts comes only from states where
the claim holds, and \emph{complete} when every transcript from a state where the claim holds is
accepted. The claim is ``the counter is 1.''

No verifier on these transcripts is both, and the proof is three lines. Suppose one were both.
Run $A$ ends with the counter at 1 and leaves the transcript, so completeness says the
verifier accepts it. Now soundness, on that same accepted transcript: every state that leaves it satisfies the claim, and run $B$'s end state
leaves it. So run $B$'s counter is 1. It is 0. That's the cube again, with a
verdict in place of an answer: a verifier sees only what the window kept, and two states that
the window can't tell apart get one verdict between them.

Now dress the transcript up. Take any richer kind of transcript, with a way to squash one
down to its bare photographs, and say a verifier on the rich ones \emph{only looks at the bare
part} when two rich transcripts that squash to the same photographs always get the same
verdict. If some rich transcript left by run $A$ and some rich transcript left by run $B$
squash to the same photographs, then no verifier that only looks at the bare part is sound
and complete either: it gives those two the same verdict, completeness makes that verdict
accept, and soundness then lies about run $B$. Notice what that needs. The pair has to survive
into the richer kind of transcript; a design whose extra part tells $A$ from $B$ doesn't meet
the premise, and the argument says nothing about it. So it doesn't classify every transcript
design. What it says is that a verifier that only reads what the bare window keeps fails on
that pair.

Economists got to the same wall by another road. Jerry Green and Jean-Jacques Laffont (1986)
asked what a mechanism can do when people can claim about themselves only
what their situation lets them back up, and Jesse Bull and Joel Watson (2007) built that into
mechanism design as \emph{hard evidence}. In their terms, an audit can tell apart only the cases
the evidence on offer tells apart. That's the cube with a ledger in it.

What can you do? Here are three things that work, and nothing says they're the only
ones; as far as I can tell, cryptography uses all three. Each rests on something you have to trust, and I'll say
what, because ``a price'' in the counter's sense is not what any of them costs.

You can be shown the \emph{whole state}. Then there's nothing to decode; you read the counter off
the state. The price is trust: you have to believe the state you were shown is the state
there was.

You can be shown a \emph{commitment}: the ordinary window plus one extra bit that is set when,
and only when, the claim holds (here, that the counter reads exactly one).
Reading that bit gives a verifier that is sound and complete for that claim, \emph{if} the bit is
binding (set only when the claim holds) and honest (set whenever it holds). The trust is in
those two ``ifs,'' which are a contract about who can set the bit. The contract can be met,
and a bit anyone can set breaks it, which is the one-line version of why an unsigned log is
just another window. Nothing in that picture has a hardness assumption in it; whether a real
commitment scheme meets the contract is a question for cryptography, and this book doesn't take
it up.
(A clash of words I should own: ``commitment'' here is the cryptographers' word, something
bound to a claim, which in their schemes also hides the claim until it's opened, and this bit
doesn't bother hiding anything. The opening chapter's commit is a different act, the closing of
a question. Same word, two jobs. The sealed envelope has an exact theory of its own. Three
information theorists, Andreas Winter, then at Bristol, and Anderson Nascimento and Hideki Imai,
then at Tokyo, found in 2003 the best rate at which a noisy channel can carry commitments, and the
cryptographers Claude Cr\'epeau, Rafael Dowsley and Nascimento (2020) worked out how
that rate drops as the committer gets some control over the noise, which is the opening
chapter's ``take the pen away from the program'' with a formula on it.)
In 1999 the cryptographers Bruce Schneier and John Kelsey worked out how to make a log that an
intruder who takes over the machine can't quietly rewrite, and the honest scope in their paper is
the honest scope here: it protects what was written \emph{before} the break-in, through keys, and
nothing after. Two cryptographers at the University of California, San Diego, Mihir Bellare and
Bennet Yee, had named that property \emph{forward integrity} in a 1997 report and proved their
scheme has it. Point it at an AI agent that keeps its own log of
what it did, and the line moves to the very start: an agent that writes the wrong thing from its
first step is on the far side of the break-in for the whole log. A 2026 preprint on tamper-evident
audit trails for such agents, built from hashes anchored on a public blockchain, is even called
Agent Flight Recorder (by Laurent Bindschaedler, of the Max Planck Institute for Software Systems,
and Quentin Botha and Christoph Siebenbrunner, of the Vienna University of Economics and
Business), which is the opening chapter's
word, and the opening chapter's fingerprint paragraph is the part of this book that applies to it.

Or you can \emph{ask}. Interaction: the outside party gets to put a question and gets an answer
that pins the thing down. The price is the honesty of the answerer; a liar's answer is
another shadow. Moore's experimenter chose inputs; the zero-knowledge proofs of the cryptographers
Shafi Goldwasser, Silvio Micali and Charles Rackoff in 1985 are the refined form, where a verifier
is convinced by a conversation designed to cut exactly the line between true and false and nothing
else, with a mathematical guarantee against a cheating prover. I mention zero-knowledge to say what
I'm \emph{not} claiming: the asking in this section is one round, with one fixed question (``tell me
your counter''), and nothing in it models a cheating prover; the honesty is assumed, and nothing
enforces it. That's a toy of the real thing, and I'm not going to let the real thing's
reputation stand behind the toy. (Joseph Halpern, Yoram Moses and Mark Tuttle, computer scientists
who work on reasoning about knowledge in distributed systems, gave zero knowledge a knowledge-based
analysis in 1988, which is where I'd start for the logic of it.)

The real thing even has a cave in it, which after Plato I can't resist. In a paper for the 1989
CRYPTO conference called ``How to Explain Zero-Knowledge Protocols to Your Children,''
two cryptographers, Jean-Jacques Quisquater of Philips Research and Louis Guillou of the French
telecommunications lab CCETT, with their families and Tom Berson of Anagram Laboratories on the
byline, told it as Ali Baba's cave: a ring-shaped tunnel with a magic door at the back that opens only
for a secret word. Peggy goes in down one side while Victor waits outside; then Victor walks to
the fork and shouts which side she should come out of. If she knows the word, she always can. If
she doesn't, she gets away with it only when Victor happens to call the side she went in. Play
it at the table with a coin for Victor's shout: one round, a cheat gets through half the time;
twenty rounds, about one time in a million. And here's the part that belongs in this section. In
the story, Victor ends up convinced, but a video of the whole thing
convinces nobody else, because a staged run, where the two agreed beforehand which sides he'd
shout, makes exactly the same recording. The recording is a window, and the real run and the fake
one cast the same shadow. That's the cube in the cryptographers' favourite bedtime story, and it's
why the real thing has to ask live, many times, against a prover who might be lying: everything
my one round leaves out.

Each escape is a window with something added: the whole state, a bound bit, an honest
answer. None of them is ``a smarter verifier on the old window.'' Cleverness lives on the
wrong side of the projection. What's true of any machine is the cube.

Here are the three constructions exactly, for the pair above, with the relations written down.
The relation matters: it says which state a transcript is allowed to describe. If it quietly
assumes a truthful answer, then a verifier sound for it is sound only against honest answerers,
and it says nothing about a liar. Write $A$ and
$B$ for the states runs $A$ and $B$ end at, $\mu$ for the counter, and $\tau$ for their shared
transcript.

\begin{definition}[Three richer transcripts and their explanations]\label{def:u21-escape-relations}
Keep the states $A,B$ and their shared bare transcript $\tau$, with
$\mu(A)=1$ and $\mu(B)=0$. Write $E_0(s,t)$ for
$t=\tau\;\land\;(s=A\;\lor\;s=B)$. The claim is $\mu(s)=1$.

A \emph{full-state transcript} is a finite list $t$ of states. Define
$E_S(s,t)$ to mean that $t$ is nonempty and its last entry is $s$.
The verifier rejects the empty list; otherwise it accepts exactly when the last
entry's counter is $1$.

A \emph{commitment transcript} is a pair $(t,b)$ of a bare transcript and a Boolean.
For any chosen explanation relation $E_C$, the \emph{commitment contract} is the pair
of implications, for all $s,t,b$:
\[
E_C(s,(t,b))\land b=\mathrm{true}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mu(s)=1,
\]
\[
E_C(s,(t,b))\land\mu(s)=1\ \Longrightarrow\ b=\mathrm{true}.
\]
These are binding and honesty, respectively. The verifier accepts exactly when
$b$ is true. One relation meeting the contract is
$E_H(s,(t,b))\iff E_0(s,t)\land(b=\mathrm{true}\iff\mu(s)=1)$.

A \emph{response transcript} is a pair $(t,r)$ of a bare transcript and a natural
number. Define $E_I(s,(t,r))\iff\mu(s)=r$. The verifier accepts exactly when
$r=1$. This relation imposes no condition on the bare component $t$; the response
alone carries its entire truth condition.

Each construction assigns verification the constant abstract cost $1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Three conditional escapes]\label{thm:u21-escapes}
The full-state verifier is sound and complete relative to $E_S$. For every $E_C$
satisfying the commitment contract, the commitment verifier is sound and complete
relative to $E_C$. The response verifier is sound and complete relative to $E_I$.
Each has cost $1$ under the stipulated cost assignment. The honest relation $E_H$
satisfies the commitment contract; the unchecked relation
$E_U(s,(t,b))\iff E_0(s,t)$ does not.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For the full-state verifier, an explaining state is precisely the last entry. Reading
that entry's counter therefore accepts exactly when the explaining state's counter is
$1$. An empty transcript is rejected and has no explaining state.

For the commitment verifier, acceptance says $b$ is true. Binding then gives the claim
for every explaining state, which is soundness. Conversely, honesty says that any
explaining state satisfying the claim has a true bit, which the verifier accepts.
The equivalence in $E_H$ gives both implications directly. Under $E_U$, however,
$B$ explains $(\tau,\mathrm{true})$ even though $\mu(B)=0$. That violates binding.

For the response verifier, explanation gives $\mu(s)=r$. Acceptance adds $r=1$,
so $\mu(s)=1$. Conversely, $\mu(s)=1$ and explanation give $r=1$, hence acceptance.
The three cost claims follow from the assigned constant.
\end{proof}

Checked, for any pair like $A$ and $B$, over arbitrary types of states, claims, transcripts and
explanation relations; nothing in it uses more about the two states than their claim values and
their shared transcript. The collision argument is \code{ver\_collision\_blocks}, the richer-transcript
one is \code{ver\_no\_factor} (a verifier sound and complete for the claim under an explanation relation
cannot be one that
only looks at the bare part, once two transcripts with the same bare part
are explained, one by a
state with the claim and one by a state without it), and the three escapes are
\code{ver\_full\_state\_escape}, \code{ver\_commitment\_escape} (under the contract, with
\code{ver\_honest\_meets\_contract} and \code{ver\_unchecked\_breaks\_contract} for the two relations),
and \code{ver\_response\_escape} (VerifierSmall.v). The cost $1$ in the definition above is not in
any of those statements; it is a number I wrote down, and no proof reads it.

On a real machine the collision is a theorem, and it doesn't depend on the toy. Give a run from a loaded start (Part IV's word for a start at line 1
with the two counters set to $a$ and $b$, written $(1, a, b)$) the \emph{bare transcript} made of $a$, $b$ and the base window the run
ends with, and say a state \emph{explains} a bare transcript when some run from that start ends
at it showing that window.

\begin{theorem}[No bare verifier on a Thiele-complete machine]\label{thm:ver-complete}
Let a machine be Thiele-complete through an interface
(Definition~\ref{def:u34-thiele-complete}). (1) No function from bare transcripts to Booleans is
both sound and complete, under that explanation relation, for the claim ``the record is up.'' (2)
There is a clean loaded state such that no function from bare transcripts to Booleans is both
sound and complete for the claim ``the ledger is at least 3 above what it was at that start.''
(3) For the small machine of Part IV, whose moves CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY and whose counter move DEC are defined there: a run CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY from the loaded
start $(1, 0, 0)$, which ends with the ledger at 3, and three DECs of a zero counter from the same start, which end with the ledger at 0, end with the
same window, and no function on bare transcripts is sound and complete for ``the ledger reads
3.''
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tc-window}(2) gives a loaded state and two runs from it that end with the
same window, one with the record up and one with it down, and, from one clean loaded state, two runs with the same window, one whose ledger rose by at least 3 and
one made of free base moves that leaves the ledger where it started (that theorem's proof builds it; \code{complete\_two\_runs} states it).
 Both end states explain the same bare transcript. A verifier
complete for the claim accepts that transcript, since a state where the claim holds explains it;
a verifier sound for the claim then makes the claim true of every state that explains it,
including the one where it's false. That's (1), and (2) is the same with the ledger: the paid run's end state satisfies the claim, and the free run's doesn't. For (3) the
two runs are written out in the statement: three moves land on line 4 in both runs with both
counters at 0, and the same two-state argument applies.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{ver\_complete\_no\_record\_verifier}, \code{ver\_complete\_no\_ledger\_verifier} and
\code{ver\_small\_no\_ledger\_verifier} (VerifierSmall.v), the first two from
\code{complete\_hides\_record} and \code{complete\_two\_runs} of ThieleCompleteWindow.v. Put with the
three escapes, the whole picture is one statement for every Thiele-complete machine,
\code{ver\_corollary}, and for the small machine \code{ver\_small\_corollary}: the bare-transcript
verifier doesn't exist; the collision survives into any richer transcript that keeps it, so no
verifier that only reads its bare part works either; a verifier on full states exists; one on the
bare transcript with a committed bit exists, sound and complete when the bit is honest, and the
unchecked bit breaks the contract; and one on a truthful response exists. The collision is a
premise of the richer-transcript half, and the contract is assumed; no fourth way is claimed to
be impossible, and no hardness is proved.

In the three escapes the collision is gone, and no trick did it: the extra information pulls $A$ and $B$ apart.
The full-state transcript shows the counter outright. The honest commitment for $A$ carries a
true bit and the one for $B$ a false bit. The honest responses are $1$ and $0$. In none of the
three is the verifier asked to tell identical inputs apart, which was the impossible job.

Now the limit, and I'd rather say it before you find it. A list of states has no
authentication built into it, so nothing in it stops a liar from handing over whatever the
verifier wants to see. The commitment contract is assumed, and the unchecked bit above is what
happens when the assumption is dropped. The response relation only allows a truthful counter
value, so asking a question here does not buy resistance to a cheating prover. And the cost
$1$ is an abstract price I wrote down. It doesn't measure what it takes to authenticate a
state, check a cryptographic proof or send a response. What these three show is which extra
distinctions a verifier can use. They are not an adversary model, a security parameter or a
hardness reduction.

So what would it take to make that commitment bit binding for real, against somebody who wants
to cheat? Cryptographers had to face that one in the open, and the place I'd point is a short
paper the computer scientist Manuel Blum, whose Turing Award was for complexity theory and its use
in cryptography, presented at the CRYPTO meeting in 1981, ``Coin Flipping by Telephone.'' His
setup: Alice and Bob have just divorced, they live in different cities, and they want to flip a
coin over the phone for who gets the car, with nobody they both trust to do the flipping. If
Alice flips and announces, Bob has to take her word. If Bob calls it first, Alice can lie about
how it landed. Blum's way out is for one side to commit first: send something that fixes the
choice without showing it, and open it only after the other side has called. And what keeps that
commitment binding isn't anybody's promise. It's a bet that a certain kind of big number is hard
to factor. Push on that and you're standing on the honest edge of this subsection. In Blum's
protocol, binding is earned, on the condition that factoring is hard. Here it's written into the
contract and assumed outright, and the unchecked bit above shows what's left without it. That's
why I won't say these escapes beat a cheater. Blum's paper is the kind of thing it would take,
and nothing like it is in this chapter.

Now point the three escapes back at the record this book is about, because that's where they
bite hardest. A record kept in a machine's state is bits too. Hand someone outside a copy of
those bits with a note saying ``the flag is up,'' and they're reading a window: the run that
really raised the flag and a box built to print that it did cast the same shadow. So putting the
record in the step answers ``was this earned?'' for whoever can see the state and trusts the step
that wrote it. For anybody else it moves the question, from ``did it run?'' to ``do I trust the
box that says it ran?'' Crossing that line takes one of the escapes: the whole state, from a box
you already trust; a bound bit, which in practice means a signature over the record or a quote
from measured hardware (and Section~\ref{sec:models} shows a quote vouches only for what was
measured); or asking, against a box that might lie, which is the cryptographers' business. One
more relative deserves its name here, \emph{verifiable computation}: the box hands back its
answer with a short proof that the answer is right, which a checker can verify without redoing
the work (Pinocchio, built in 2013 by the computer scientists Bryan Parno, Jon Howell, Craig Gentry
and Mariana Raykova), and proof-carrying data passes proofs like that along a whole chain of
parties who don't trust each other (the computer scientists Alessandro Chiesa and Eran Tromer,
2010). That's the strongest export there is, and notice what it exports: the claim. The history
stays behind. The proof shows the answer is right for that input.
It doesn't show which machine did the work, or when, and any box with the input can make one.
Nothing in this book supplies any of these escapes. The model's record is local to the machine
that keeps it, and the small machine of Part IV keeps its record in its state with no signature
on it at all.

\subsection{What this isn't}

Three things this isn't, and I'd rather take them off the table now.

It isn't mysticism. Nothing here says the window is false or the state is unknowable. The
wall is a function, the objects are its inputs, and the only claim is that the function isn't
one-to-one on the thing you asked about. A richer window recovers it. Plato's prisoners could
have turned around.

Rice's theorem is the neighbour this looks most like. It isn't Rice's
theorem, though it rhymes with it. The logician Henry Rice, in a paper
of 1953, proved that no program can
decide any interesting property of what another program \emph{does} from its code, and a cousin
of the fact here is that a run which hasn't halted yet looks, so far, exactly like one that
never will. But Rice is about what's \emph{computable}. The cube is about what's \emph{there}. The
cube theorem holds for a toy with two states and nothing to compute; the obstruction is
missing information, and cleverness doesn't come into it. I'd be overclaiming if I let the famous
theorem lend its weight to the small one.

And it isn't ``with enough data you can recover anything.'' Kalman's unobservable states stay
unobservable for all time. The question is never how much of the window you've got. It's
which window.

The counter lives in the state, and whether anyone outside can read it depends entirely
on what they're shown, and a window with a pair like that in it can't price the flag
exactly, with any rule, ever. Which raises the question I've been pushing in front of me since the
buckets. Fine, the flag went up and was paid for and I can see it in the right window. What
does that \emph{entitle} me to? A paid flag is a paid flag. What's the claim behind it, and when
am I allowed to lean on it?

%===========================================================================
\section{Structural entitlement}
\label{sec:entitlement}
%===========================================================================

I keep writing the word ``vouch'' and then taking it back. Let me stop doing that and say what
it would take. A reading went from NO to YES, the toll charged the move that did it (Section~\ref{sec:toll}),
maybe the reading stays up (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} says what it costs to make it stay), and the right window
shows it (Section~\ref{sec:windows}).
Now: what is a later step \emph{allowed to do} because of that? That's a different question from
``is the thing true,'' and the gap between those two is the subject of this section, and I'd
argue it's the subject of most of the arguments people have about evidence, so give me the
long way round.

\subsection{The coin that moved}

Here's an experiment you can run on a friend, and I'd ask you to actually run it, because
the feeling of it is the point. Put a coin under one of three cups while they watch. Say,
cup one. Send them out of the room. Move the coin to cup three. Then, and this is the trick,
put a \emph{second} coin under cup one. Bring them back and ask: ``Is there a coin under cup one?''

They say yes. They're right; there is. And they have a reason: they watched you put it there.
True, and believed, and justified by what they saw. And it's not knowledge, and you can feel
that it isn't, because their reason points at a coin that left. The coin that makes them
right is not the coin they're thinking of.

That's the trap from the opening chapter, done with cups: Edmund Gettier's three-page paper from
1963, ``Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?'', which broke a definition of knowledge in about the
time it takes to read it. The definition was
that you know something when it's true, you believe it, and you've got good reasons. Gettier took
it from two philosophers of the 1950s, Roderick Chisholm and A.~J. Ayer, and the only place he
mentions Plato is a footnote saying Plato ``seems to be considering'' something like it in the
