\emph{Theaetetus}. I'd assumed people had leaned on that definition since Plato. As far as I can
find, they hadn't. The Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on the analysis of knowledge calls the idea that
it was ever widely held ``a bit of a convenient fiction,'' and Julien Dutant, a philosopher at King's
College London, wrote a 2015 paper called ``The Legend of the Justified True Belief Analysis''
arguing that the older tradition asked for something stronger: a mark on the belief that can't be
wrong. I've read only summaries of Dutant's paper, so take that last part as his, secondhand. Gettier's two cases, and the cups, show a
belief that passes all three tests and still isn't knowledge, because the reasons and the
fact aren't connected; they just happen to agree. Bertrand Russell had a related case in 1948:
somebody looks at a stopped clock at the one moment it happens to be right, and they're right
about the time, and they know nothing.

Is 1963 the bottom? Not even close, and 1948 isn't either. The Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on
the analysis of knowledge, which is where I'd send you to check me, gives a case from the
eighth-century Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara: you're looking for water on a hot day, you see
water ahead, it's a mirage, and when you get there you happen to find water under a rock. And one from Peter of Mantua, a logician of the late fourteenth
century who died in 1400 and whose \emph{Logica} survives in manuscript: Plato is running right next to you, you take him
for Socrates, so you believe Socrates is running, and Socrates is in fact running, in Rome, where
you can't see him. Older still? Maybe. This is where the trail goes cold, which isn't the same as
where it ends. What it changes is how much
I trust the shape. People in different centuries, languages and traditions kept building the
same trap by hand: a reason that points at one thing, and a truth that happens to be sitting on
another.

What's missing is a wire from the reason to the fact. Ask your friend what they'd need, to
be \emph{entitled} to ``there's a coin under cup one,'' and they'll tell you: lift the cup. Not
``remember putting it there.'' Lift it, now, and look. That lifting is an event, it happens on
the record, and after it the reason and the fact are the same object.

\subsection{Plato nearly had it}

Who was Theaetetus, though? The dialogue is named for a real person, and I wanted to know who. He was a mathematician. In the dialogue he's a teenager, and he tells
Socrates that his teacher Theodorus had been showing them, one case at a time, that the side of a
square of area three, or five, and so on up to seventeen, can't be named by any fraction: the
Pythagoreans' diagonal from Section~\ref{sec:structure}, done again case by case. The young man's
idea was to stop going one case at a time and find one word for all of them. Euclid's tenth book,
on lengths that share no common measure, is thought to be largely his work, and he's credited with
being the first to study the eight-faced and twenty-faced solids, the two Plato assigned to air
and water in the \emph{Timaeus}. The dialogue opens with him being carried home to Athens from the army at Corinth,
badly wounded and sick with the dysentery going round the camp, barely alive; the usual date is
369 BC. And the conversation itself has come down as a record. Euclid of Megara (not the geometer) says he
took notes as soon as he got home, filled them out later, and had Socrates correct them whenever
he came to Athens, and he has the result read aloud. So the dialogue about what turns a true
belief into knowledge survives as a checked record of what was said. That changes nothing in
the argument. I just like that the book about knowledge is named for the man who took the diagonal
and made it general.

I want to be fair to the \emph{Theaetetus} here, because it's easy to be quick with the ancients
and they deserve better. Socrates, in that dialogue, doesn't just say ``true belief
plus reasons.'' He tries three different senses of what the ``account'' behind a true belief
could be: a statement you can say aloud; a list of the thing's parts; and, third, the mark
that sets this thing apart from everything else it could be confused with. He tries each,
and each fails, and the dialogue ends with nobody knowing what knowledge is, which is one of
the more honest endings in philosophy. But the third sense is the one I'd underline. An
account as \emph{the thing that distinguishes}: the test that gives the real case a value no rival
gives. He couldn't make it work because he had no way to say what the account had to be
attached \emph{to}. Two and a half thousand years later, here's this book's guess: the thing it
has to be attached to is a state, and the account is an object sitting in it. I'm not claiming
that settles Plato. I'm claiming he was pointing at the right thing, and that's my reading of the
dialogue, which you can check against it in an afternoon.

Push on that once more, because Socrates gives his own reason for dropping the third account,
and it isn't the one I just gave. If the account means \emph{knowing} the mark that sets the thing
apart, then knowledge has been defined as true belief plus knowledge of something, and the word
you were trying to define is back inside its own definition. A circle. Does a check get out of
it? It gets the word out: a test that ran and found the mark isn't defined in terms of knowing.
Whether the test was any good is still a real question, and it's the question the rest of this
section puts a price on. So I'd say the circle moves. It doesn't vanish. It moves somewhere you
can look at it, which is the most I'd claim.

\subsection{The shape, said once}

So here's what I mean by entitlement, and it has three parts, and I'll try to earn each.

A run is entitled to a claim when three things are present. First, an \emph{object}, carried in
the state: a grouping, a relation between groups, a counter, a package of constraints. That's a
thing you could
print. A belief doesn't count. Second, a \emph{checked relation} between that object and the
claim: a test that was actually run, with its result on hand. ``A test exists'' doesn't count. Third, an
\emph{event on the record} that says this object was put there and paid for, so that anyone
auditing the run can point back at the moment the claim was marked.

Said as a definition, so the rest of the section has something to point at:

\begin{definition}[Entitlement]\label{def:u08-entitlement}
A run is \emph{entitled} to a claim when three things are on hand: an \emph{object} carried in the run's
states; a \emph{checked relation} between that object and the claim, meaning a test that was run
and whose result is on the record; and a \emph{paid event}, a move of the run at which
the object was put in place and which the price list charged at least one. In a certification
system (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}) a move that takes the reading from no to yes is such a
move, because the toll charges it. This is the book's word; there's no Coq definition of it.
\end{definition}

Without the third part, the object may be sitting right there and the claim may be true, and
the run still hasn't \emph{earned} it. That's the cups: the coin is under cup one; the reason is
disconnected from it; nobody lifted the cup. Put it on Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s sheet of paper, the one with the
NO box, the YES box and the tally line, and grow the toy by one thing: the state is now the box
you're in plus whatever is written on the sheet beside it. Next to the boxes, write a note:
``coin under cup one, checked.'' Writing the note is a WORK move, and WORK costs nothing. The note is an object, it's
on the paper, and it might even be true. What it doesn't have is a crossing on the record: no
move took the reading from NO to YES when the note went down, and there's no mark under the
line for it. The note is raw data, forged in one write, and the five parts allow a system that
lets you write one, because nothing in them says what an ordinary move may put in
the state. A note put down by the move that crosses has a receipt, and the receipt is the
event. One limit on that word ``receipt'': the crossing records that something was paid for at
that moment. What the crossing move actually looked at before it crossed is up to whatever
the move does, and the five parts don't say.

And here's the part to hold on to. Nothing in the five parts makes a later move \emph{read} the
reading. The step function is handed the state and a move name, and it's allowed to ignore
the YES box completely; plenty of systems will. So when I say a run is \emph{entitled}, I mean what
someone auditing the run may conclude from the reading and the receipt. The system doesn't
have to enforce it, and unless somebody builds it to, it won't.

This is a good place to line up the three things the word \emph{established} has had to mean
so far, because they blur easily, and a blur here would make the book look like it proves more
than it does. The yardstick is the opening chapter's four conditions for a check being about
this very claim: the same property, the same thing, the same edition, and an honest check.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.21\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.226\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.226\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.226\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{What's asked} & \textbf{Bare toll} & \textbf{Entitlement} & \textbf{Earned certification} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
A check ran & not required & a test result on the record & a passing check before the commit, on every run from a clean start \\
Same property & not asked & not asked & enforced by the step \\
Same thing & not asked & not asked & enforced by the step \\
Same edition, nothing written between & not asked & not asked & enforced by the step \\
Honest check & not asked & not asked & proved of the checker, once, outside the record \\
Could have failed & not asked & not asked & not policed \\
Paid for & at least one mark & at least one mark & at least three marks for the chain \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

After the column of questions, the first column is Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s bare toll: a paid crossing, and nothing says a check
happened at all (Section~\ref{sec:insight} has a remark saying exactly that). The second is this
section's entitlement. The third is the small machine of Part IV, whose step won't let a commit
through without a passing check of the same property, on the same thing, at the same edition, for
every program from a clean start (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-commit-earned}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned} for a run that ends certified), whose checker comes with a
proof that it says what it means (Lemma~\ref{lem:u34-eval}, Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-soundness}), and
whose certified runs from a clean start cost at least three (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-min-price}). Even there two things are missing, and the
first is in the table, where you'll see it. The step doesn't police whether a
check could have failed: a property every value has is a perfectly legal check, sound and useless.
And in all three columns the status belongs to whoever reads the record. The machine doesn't know
anything. What its flag means is assigned from outside, by whoever says what each property means.

Why does the honest check carry so much? The philosopher Linda Zagzebski, who works on knowledge
and the virtues of a careful mind, argued in 1994 that any account of
knowledge whose justification leaves even a small gap between having good reasons and being right
lets a Gettier case through: take a case where bad luck makes the reasons point the wrong way, then
add a stroke of good luck that makes the belief true anyway. The first three conditions plus an
honest check close that gap by construction, and only one half of honesty is needed for it, the
half that says no when the property is false. Saying yes whenever it's true is extra. A check that
can be wrong, a test suite that sometimes passes broken code, puts you straight back in her gap,
and then the record certifies something smaller and still true: this procedure said yes.

And who certifies that the check is honest? Not the record. Honesty is a fact about what the check
does on every input, and the opening chapter already said a finished state can't hold that kind of
fact. It has to be carried by a proof about the checker, done once, outside every run, and
nothing on the record pays for it. So an established claim is two things stuck together: a run
property the record carries and a program property a proof carries, and the proof is entitlement
for the auditor. The machine gets none from it. Section~\ref{sec:smallest} shows where that chain of reasons
stops on a real machine.

The engineering version of this was already built, in 1996 and 1997. The computer scientist George
Necula, then at Carnegie Mellon, called it
\emph{proof-carrying code}: when you ship a program to a host that doesn't trust you, you ship a
\emph{proof} with it that the program obeys the host's safety rules, and the host \emph{checks the proof that arrived} before running anything. Not your reputation. Not ``a proof exists
somewhere.'' The one in the box. A quarter century earlier Stephen Cook's certificates had the
same bones, from Section~\ref{sec:toll}: a claim comes with a witness that's cheap to check, and the checker
checks \emph{that} witness. And the Scottish philosopher David Hume, in 1748, arguing about
miracles in his \emph{Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding}, laid out the thing
the receipt replaces. He weighed testimony against evidence, and wrote that ``a wise man, therefore,
proportions his belief to the evidence.'' The way I read him, the whole of his argument is
a method for how much to trust a witness when you have no receipt. The move in this book is to stop weighing. A claim
on the record is either backed by its object and its paid event, or it's testimony from
outside, and a run that leans on testimony hasn't earned it itself. It can inherit it, but only
as far as the copy it leans on is genuine, which is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s problem of a
record shown from outside.

Robert Brandom, a philosopher at the University of Pittsburgh, built a whole account of language on two words this book leans on, commitment and entitlement,
and his \emph{Making It Explicit} (1994) is where I'd send anyone who suspects I invented the pair. In
his picture, as I read it and as his reviewers describe it, people talking keep score on each other: what each speaker is \emph{committed} to, what they've put
themselves on the hook for, and what each is \emph{entitled} to, what they're licensed to claim.
You can be committed without being entitled (a reckless assertion), many claims count as entitled
by default until someone challenges them, and entitlement can be borrowed: I can claim a thing on
your say-so and defer to you when I'm challenged. Lay mine beside his and the differences are the
content. His score is kept by the other people in the room; here it's a reading in the state. His
entitlement often comes by default; here it's an event that has to happen and is charged. And his
deferral is my testimony, which I've just let back in on a leash: borrowed entitlement is only as
good as the copy is genuine. The leash has an older formal cousin, the jurisdiction rule of
Burrows, Abadi and Needham's logic of authentication (Section~\ref{sec:windows}), where you take a
statement on an authority's word only if you already believe the authority has jurisdiction over
it. It came first, presented in 1989 and printed in 1990, years ahead of Brandom's book of 1994, and its words are \emph{believes} and
\emph{jurisdiction} where his are \emph{commitment} and \emph{entitlement}.

There's a whole field that would want a word here too, the logic of belief revision, which asks
how a reasonable mind should change what it believes when something new comes in. Its nearest
neighbours are worth naming, and I couldn't keep them apart until I put them back on the table with
the cups. Your friend believes the coin is under cup one. They can learn something that doesn't
clash with that, say cup two is empty, and just add it. They can lift cup one, find nothing, and
have to change their mind about a table nobody touched. Or you can tell them you moved the coin.
The last two felt alike to me at first. They aren't. In one the friend was wrong. In the other the
friend was right, and then the table changed.

Krister Segerberg, a Swedish logician at Uppsala, built a logic of
irrevocable revision in 1998: accepting something so that it can't be given up. That's the firmness
question taken to its end. Isaac Levi, a
philosopher at Columbia who spent a career on how beliefs get fixed and unfixed, split adding a
belief into a deliberate kind and a routine kind (I cite his 1991 book; the split goes back to his
1980 one). Deliberate is reasoning your way there. Routine is
where you take on whatever a procedure you committed to in advance hands you, the way you'd accept a
reading off a thermometer you've already decided to trust, or what's under a cup when you lift it.
What I think the split rests on is when the trust goes in: once, before the data comes. A passing
CHECK is routine in exactly that sense, with a checker proved honest once, outside every run.

Neil Tennant, a logician at Ohio State, and G\"osta Grahne, a computer scientist at Helsinki, I first
filed as two separate complaints. They're one move made from opposite sides. The target is the
best-known impossibility in that field, the Swedish philosopher Peter G\"ardenfors's 1986 theorem
that a natural rule for conditionals, the one his paper calls the Ramsey test, can't live with
rational revision. Tennant argued in 2008 that it goes through only by treating some additions as
revisions: the friend who learned cup two was empty gets counted as having changed their mind.
Grahne, working on updates and counterfactuals, argued in 1998 that G\"ardenfors's theorem bites
only revising, so the friend whose coin was moved is out of its reach. Side by side, they squeeze
the theorem from both ends into one case: being wrong about a table nobody touched.

The line this book leans on hardest is between two kinds of change. Revising is changing what you
believe about a world that stayed put. Updating is changing it because the world moved. Two computer scientists, Hirofumi Katsuno and Alberto Mendelzon, drew that line for knowledge bases in a
1991 paper on the difference between updating a knowledge base and revising it; database researchers had been
working on updates with incomplete information since the mid-1980s, Arthur Keller and Marianne Winslett among them. Grahne's result stands on it. And look at what the
friend sees: an empty cup one is the same empty cup whether they misremembered or you moved the
coin. The evidence alone can't tell revising from updating; that's a fibre. What tells them apart is a count of how often the cups were touched.
The machine in Part IV keeps that count as an edition number for each thing,
and its version rule treats every write as an update: a write moves the edition
number, so every fact about the old edition stops counting for the new one.

And Alexandru Baltag, Bryan Renne and Sonja Smets, three logicians at Amsterdam, gave a logic
in 2014 that keeps apart three things Gettier's cases blur: justified belief, explicit knowledge and
conclusive evidence. The friend who watched has justified belief; the friend who lifted the cup has
conclusive evidence. Explicit knowledge I read as knowing with the justification written out beside
it, the way the record keeps its check, and I'm less sure of that one. Put them together and they say
something exact about this book's record. A record that's never wrong and never corrected would be a dogmatist's dream if its sentences were about the present.
They aren't. Each says a property held of a thing at one
edition, and that sentence stays true after the edition number moves on.
The record can be infallible and never corrected only because its sentences are edition-stamped.
Strip the stamps, and the first write would turn it into a liar that can't take anything back.

Push on that and it gives twice. The record is Segerberg's irrevocable acceptance every time, with no
revising in it. If a check was dishonest, the only fix that fits a record like this is a second record on top
saying ``withdrawn,'' the way a revocation list works, so the infallibility leans on the checker,
proved once, outside. And the record is never wrong partly because it only talks about past
editions. Whoever reads it wants now, and getting from ``held at that edition'' to ``holds now''
crosses every update since. The record doesn't make that step for you.

And the logicians the opening chapter named in passing, the ones who taught the logic of knowing
to count. Here they are properly, and this time I want to see what each price rests on. Ho Ngoc
Duc, in 1997, gave the logic of knowing an operator for ``true after some train of thought'': an
agent doesn't know every consequence of what it knows now. It can come to know any of them by
taking steps of reasoning. Steps. I took that at first for the thing I was after, until I saw which
way it points. His operator points forward, at what the agent could come to know. A record points
back, at what was checked. One arrow, read from opposite ends. And Sergei Artemov and Roman Kuznets, in 2014, turned logical
omniscience into a question of cost: a logic escapes it when every valid claim that something is
known comes with a proof whose size is bounded by a polynomial in the size of the claim. The usual
modal logics of knowledge can't pass that test unless NP equals coNP, which most people would bet
against, and justification logic passes it for knowledge stated together with its justification,
because the size of the justification pays for the search. That last clause
took me a few reads. What I think it means is Cook's certificate from the proof-carrying-code
paragraph above: put the
justification inside the claim, and the hard part, finding it, was paid before the claim was
written. Their price rests on an open bet, and it's a price on looking. A price, of a sort. Steps and a
price are both there, then, in their own form. What I still don't find in them is the one I care
about: a single act that closes a question for good and is charged as that act. Their steps are
steps of reasoning, and their price is on finding a proof. Neither is on settling. I couldn't get
past the journal's paywall to Artemov and Kuznets's paper, so my account of it comes from
how other people describe it.

Push on mine the same way and it gives. A check is one of Duc's trains of thought, so my act is the
last step of his train, where the walking stops. What I've added is a direction and a charge on
stopping. And the charge rests on a choice. I put it inside the step, and nothing forced me to.

Three things entitlement is \emph{not}. It isn't permission: an access
control system says who may write to what, and that's granted from outside and says nothing
about truth; a process with permission to write the note still has no entitlement. It isn't
``true, therefore usable'': that's the cups. And it isn't ``sound by luck'': a shortcut that gives
the right answer because the inputs happened to cooperate is the stopped clock. The count
below has one condition aimed at it, and I'll tell you what the condition says and how much it
actually catches.

\subsection{What narrowing costs: count the rivals}

Now the number, because a book about a bill has to say how much. Here's the idea in a form
you can do with three playing cards. Shuffle cards marked 1, 2, 3 face down. Sort them using
only questions of the form ``is this one bigger than that one?'', and count the questions.
There are six orders the cards could be in. Each question has two answers, so after one
question you've split the six into at most two piles, after two questions at most four, and
you need to get down to one. Four is less than six, so two questions can't always do it, and
three can, and you can draw the tree of questions on paper and see it: six leaves, three
deep. The number of questions you need is at least the base-two logarithm of the number of
possibilities you started with, rounded up: that's log2 of 6, which is a bit under 3, rounded
to 3. Donald Knuth, a computer scientist at Stanford, gives this, in the volume on sorting of his
\emph{The Art of Computer Programming},
as the lower bound for all comparison sorting, and the shape of
the argument is just: a tree $f$ questions deep has at most $2^f$ leaves, so it can't tell
apart more than $2^f$ cases.

And then the obvious next question: is the floor always the price? Try five cards. There are 120
orders, log2 of 120 is a bit under 7, so you need at least seven questions, and seven is enough,
though not by the obvious method. Finding the way is a good evening with a deck of cards (Knuth
has it, under the name merge insertion, from the mathematicians Lester Ford and Selmer Johnson in
1959). Now twelve
cards. They can be in 479,001,600 orders, log2 of that is about 28.8, so the count says at least
29. Ford and Johnson's method takes 30, and in 1965 Mark Wells, a mathematician at Los Alamos who
built a programming language for exactly this kind of combinatorial search, showed by a computer
search that nothing does better:
twelve cards need 30. The floor was 29. The price is 30. So the count is a floor and only a floor;
it never promises the floor can be reached, and the bound later in this section has to be read
exactly the same way.

Ralph Hartley, an electronics researcher at the lab that became Bell Labs, writing in the Bell
System Technical Journal in 1928, before
Shannon, measured information exactly this way: the logarithm
of the number of possibilities, no probabilities, just a count. That's the measure here, and
I'll say plainly it's Hartley's. Shannon's would need a distribution over the list,
and there isn't one. There's just the list's length.

Here's the same count with something you can hold. Put three coins under three cups. Each coin
is heads or tails, so there are eight possible rows under the cups. Someone hands you two
answers: heads under the first cup, tails under the second. Lift the first cup and compare. A
matching answer leaves four possible rows. Lift the second and compare. A match leaves two. The
last coin can still be either way. The list really shrank: eight, four, two. Nothing in that
count needed a claim about which way the last coin faces.

This is a parlour game, and an old one. In \emph{A Christmas Carol}, in 1843, Scrooge's nephew
Fred plays a game called Yes and No at his Christmas party: he thinks of something, and
everybody else asks questions he may only answer yes or no. He's thinking of an animal, a
disagreeable, savage one that growls and grunts and lives in London, and the answer is Uncle
Scrooge. Most people know the game as twenty questions, and twenty is a good number for it:
each yes-or-no answer can at best cut the field in half, and twenty halvings take a million or
so possibilities, $2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$, down to one. Push on that, though. The halving only
happens because Fred answers truthfully about what's actually in his head. Lie once and the
count still shrinks; it shrinks around the wrong animal. That's the cups again: the four and
the two are real because you lifted the cup and compared. Being told what was under it wouldn't
have made them real.

Now put it on a run. Say a run comes with a list of states that are ``still on the table,''
the candidates, and a shorter list, with some ruled out. Call the first the prior and the
second the posterior, and I want you to hear those as \emph{a list you could print}. They aren't
``the space of possible worlds.'' Picture the ruling-out as observations, each observation that
ruled something out being one branch point in a tree like the card tree. And here's the claim: if that tree is no
deeper than the number of paid steps the run took, and the tree has enough leaves to cover
the narrowing in a way I'll spell out in a moment, then the counter rose by at least log2 of
the prior's length, rounded up, minus log2 of the posterior's length, rounded up. At least as many marks as \emph{index
bits} the list lost, where the index bits of a list are the yes/no questions it takes to point
at one entry of it, the card count again. That's the bound.

``Paid step'' needs its own sentence. It means a step the price list charges at least one for.
In a certification system the toll guarantees that every crossing of the reading is one; a
price list is free to put a floor under more steps than that (a look, a send, a check), and
the count takes every paid step there is. The tree is a bare shape, branches and leaves with
nothing written on them, and ``no deeper than the number of paid steps'' is a count along the
run that happened. It isn't a walk down the tree. A paid step doesn't have to have asked any
question at all.

Notice, too, what the bound does and doesn't say about the run. It takes the two lists, the
tree and the covering as given. It doesn't say the run produced the posterior from the prior;
nothing in it reads the lists off the run. What it says is that, given lists, a tree and a
covering that someone supplies, the paid steps of the run cover the rounded drop in list
length. That's Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}'s warning come due: watching can narrow for free, so the payment can't be
dug out of the narrowing. It goes in as a premise, the tree's depth against the paid steps,
and I'll keep calling it one.

\subsection{What ``narrower'' buys: a stronger test}

Before the count, one link that's pure logic, and Plato's third account is the whole of it.
Take a list of candidates and an observation, a function that says what each candidate looks
like from outside. The list's \emph{membership test} accepts an observation when some candidate on
the list shows it. Shrink the list, and the test can only get pickier: anything the short
list's test accepts, the long list's accepts too. The word for that, and it runs backward
from English, is \emph{stronger}: the stronger test is the one that lets \emph{fewer} things through.

Pickier, though, isn't the same as strictly pickier, and the cards show the gap. Take all six
orders as the prior, and as the posterior the three where card 1 sits left of card 2:
1-2-3, 1-3-2 and 3-1-2. First observation: ``is 1 left of 2?'' Every survivor says yes, and
the removed 2-1-3 says no, so the prior's test accepts yes and no, the posterior's only yes.
Strictly stronger. Second observation, same two lists: ``is the first card a 3?'' Now 3-1-2
says yes and the other two survivors say no, and among the removed orders 3-2-1 says yes and
2-1-3 says no. Both tests accept yes and no. Same strength, even though three orders are gone.
What made the difference is a removed candidate whose observation \emph{no survivor shares}. That's
Plato's mark, the thing that sets this case apart from everything it could be confused with,
turned into a function. Narrow the list and keep one distinguishing removed candidate, and
the test is strictly stronger; narrow it without one, and the test may not have moved at all.

\subsection{The count, exactly}

Here are the words and the count, for any system with Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s counter. A \emph{list} is a finite list
of candidates, repeats allowed, and $|\Omega|$ is the length of the list $\Omega$, repeats
counted. $\lceil \log_2 x \rceil$ is the base-two logarithm of $x$ rounded up: the smallest
$k\in\mathbb{N}$ with $2^k \ge x$. At $x=0$ it is $0$, the convention for empty lists set in
Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}. And $a \mathbin{\dot{-}} b$ is subtraction on whole numbers that stops at
zero, so $3 \mathbin{\dot{-}} 5 = 0$.

\begin{definition}[Decision tree]\label{def:u08-dtree}
A \emph{decision tree} is a leaf, or a branch with two subtrees. Its depth is $0$ for a leaf and
one more than the deeper subtree for a branch; its leaf count $L(T)$ is $1$ for a leaf and the
sum of the two counts for a branch. Nothing is written on a tree: no question, no answer, no
candidate.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[A tree is no wider than two to its depth]\label{lem:u08-tree-width}
For every decision tree $T$, $L(T) \le 2^{\mathrm{depth}(T)}$, and so
$\lceil \log_2 L(T) \rceil \le \mathrm{depth}(T)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on the tree. A leaf has one leaf and depth $0$, and $1 \le 2^0$. A branch with
subtrees of depths $d_1, d_2$ has at most $2^{d_1} + 2^{d_2} \le 2 \cdot 2^{\max(d_1, d_2)}$
leaves, which is $2$ to its own depth. The second half: $L(T) \le 2^{\mathrm{depth}(T)}$ means
$\mathrm{depth}(T)$ is one of the $k$ with $2^k \ge L(T)$, and the rounded-up logarithm is the
smallest of them.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{decision\_tree\_leaves\_le\_pow2\_depth} and \code{decision\_tree\_log2\_up\_leaf\_bound}
(DecisionTreeBound.v). Both are stated over the tree type alone, a leaf or a branch, with
nothing about any machine in them.

\begin{theorem}[Paid narrowing, counted]\label{thm:u08-count}
Take a system with a counter $\mu$ and a price list $c$ that obey conservation
(Theorem~\ref{thm:conservation}): each step raises $\mu$ by exactly its charge. Let $\Omega$ and
$\Omega'$ be lists with $|\Omega'| > 0$, let $T$ be a decision tree with
$|\Omega| \le L(T) \cdot |\Omega'|$ (the tree \emph{covers} the narrowing), and let $t$ be a run from
$s$ ending at $s'$ in which at least $\mathrm{depth}(T)$ steps are charged at least one each.
Then
\[
\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \mathbin{\dot{-}} \lceil \log_2 |\Omega'| \rceil \;\le\; \mu(s') - \mu(s).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The rounded-up logarithm respects order, so the covering gives
$\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \le \lceil \log_2 (L(T) \cdot |\Omega'|) \rceil$. It is also
subadditive on products of positive numbers,
$\lceil \log_2 ab \rceil \le \lceil \log_2 a \rceil + \lceil \log_2 b \rceil$, because
$2^{\lceil \log_2 a \rceil} \cdot 2^{\lceil \log_2 b \rceil} \ge ab$. So
\[
\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \mathbin{\dot{-}} \lceil \log_2 |\Omega'| \rceil \;\le\; \lceil \log_2 L(T) \rceil \;\le\; \mathrm{depth}(T),
\]
the last step by Lemma~\ref{lem:u08-tree-width}. By hypothesis at least $\mathrm{depth}(T)$
steps of the run were charged at least one, and no step is charged less than zero, so the sum
of the charges is at least $\mathrm{depth}(T)$. By conservation that sum is
$\mu(s') - \mu(s)$.
\end{proof}

For any system with a counter that obeys conservation it is two checked theorems, put together
by hand; nothing in Coq joins them. \code{nec\_e\_cs\_count\_any} (NecEEnt.v) proves it over any
certification system with the sum of the charges of a run in place of the counter's rise, and
without needing $|\Omega'| > 0$; and \code{nec\_f\_conservation} (NecFCounter.v), stated over any
counter machine kept by a price list, says that sum is the counter's rise. A system that is both
gets the theorem. The bill form is also part of
Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-cs} below. The tree
half is the checked lemma above; the rest is arithmetic on three whole numbers, the two lengths
and the leaf count, and on the counter. Notice what's missing from the hypotheses: anything tying the
lists to the run. That's the honest shape of the bound.

Three honest small prints, all of them visible in the statement. Both logarithms round up
separately, and the subtraction stops at zero, so when the prior and the posterior round up to
the same number of index bits (four candidates narrowed to three, say) the bound says nothing.
The lists are plain lists, repeats allowed, so ``index bits'' is a difference of rounded list lengths
with repeats counted; a list can get shorter by dropping a duplicate without losing a single
candidate, and ``a candidate was ruled out'' and ``the list got shorter'' are two different
claims. And the difference isn't the number of questions anyone asked.

The covering condition, $|\Omega| \le L(T) \cdot |\Omega'|$, is the nearest thing the count
has to an anti-stopped-clock clause, and I have to be exact about how near. Picture each survivor standing for a little crowd
of the prior's candidates, itself included, a
crowd no bigger than the tree has leaves. Then the condition says every candidate in the prior fits in some
survivor's crowd. That limits how much can be deleted per leaf you paid for. It doesn't say
why anything was deleted. So the condition rules out deleting too much for the tree you've
paid for. It doesn't rule out deleting for no reason. A run can satisfy every hypothesis of
the count and have ruled nothing out on purpose; the count prices the size of the drop. It says
nothing about the honesty of it. And the covering can't just be dropped. On the small machine one yes-or-no
question with a big constant in it
narrows $2^n$ candidates to one, $n$ index bits, for a ledger of
three,
so for any $n \ge 4$ the bound is false without it (Section~\ref{sec:part3-on-machine}).

Here's a side trip worth taking, because it looks like it breaks the count and doesn't. Two
information theorists, Rudolf
Ahlswede and Gunter Dueck (1989), noticed that asking ``is it this one?'' is a different job from
asking ``which one is it?'' If each receiver only wants to know whether the message is theirs, a
noisy channel used $n$ times can serve a number of receivers that grows like two raised to two to
the $nC$, with $C$ the channel's capacity, where naming the message only gets you two to the
$nC$. That's identification, and on its face it says checking can be exponentially cheaper than
naming. But their tests are allowed to say yes wrongly once in a while. Make the yes sound, a
test that never says yes to the wrong message, which is the only kind of check this book lets
raise a record, and the double exponential collapses. The argument is two lines of pigeonhole.
I argue it here, and nothing checks it. Each receiver's test, to be any use, says yes on some
output its own message can produce, and soundness means no other message can produce that output;
so those outputs are all different, one per receiver, and there can't be more receivers than
outputs, $|Y|^n$ for an output alphabet $Y$. Single exponential, the same order as naming. So for a
check that never lies, the card count is the right scale after all, and the cheap trick needs a
check that can be fooled.

\subsection{What you've got}

A paid flag is not a true claim; Section~\ref{sec:windows} left it at ``a paid flag is a paid flag,'' and Section~\ref{sec:insight} will say
it flatly. What a paid flag with an object and a checked relation behind it gives you is
\emph{entitlement}: anyone auditing the run may treat the claim as established, and can point at
the event where that became legitimate. (Nothing in the five parts makes the system itself
read the flag; I said that above and I'm saying it again because it's the sentence most likely
to get lost.) Entitlement costs at least the index bits of narrowing it commits to, given
lists, a tree and a covering somebody supplies, and given a run that paid for the tree's
depth. The cups say why entitlement and truth are different. Plato says what the checked
relation has to do: distinguish. Necula says how to build it. Hartley says what to count.

Put the three pieces on one hypothesis list (narrow the list with a test that separates, find
the paid event, count the bill against a tree the run paid for) and you get a single statement, structural entitlement, once
over any certification system and once, under the
longer name structural entitlement represented, for every Thiele-complete machine, the small machine included
(Section~\ref{sec:part3-on-machine}). The first one reads as follows.

\begin{theorem}[Structural entitlement, over any certification system]\label{thm:ent-cs}
Take a certification system (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}), a state $s$ that reads no, and a run
$t$ from $s$ that ends in a state that reads yes. Take a type of candidates, a type of
observations with an exact equality test, an observation $\mathrm{obs}$ of each candidate, and a
\emph{decoder} $d$ that turns a run into an observation (what its record shows). Take lists
$\Omega$ and $\Omega'$ of candidates and a decision tree $T$ such that:
(H1) $\Omega'$ strictly narrows $\Omega$: every member of $\Omega'$ is in $\Omega$, and some member of
$\Omega$ isn't in $\Omega'$;
(H2) some dropped candidate $w$, in $\Omega$ and not in $\Omega'$, shows an observation different
from every survivor's;
(H3) the decoded run $d(t)$ is shown by some survivor;
(H4) $|\Omega'| > 0$ and $|\Omega| \le L(T) \cdot |\Omega'|$;
(H5) at least $\mathrm{depth}(T)$ steps of the run are charged at least one each.
Then (1) the membership test of $\Omega'$ is strictly stronger than the membership test of
$\Omega$; (2) some step of the run took the reading from no to yes, and that step was charged at
least one; and (3) the sum of the charges of the run's steps is at least
$\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \mathbin{\dot{-}} \lceil \log_2 |\Omega'| \rceil$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) is the cards' argument: the dropped $w$ shows something no survivor shows, so the posterior
test says no where the prior test says yes, and every survivor was in the prior, so nothing the
posterior accepts is refused by the prior. (2) The run starts at no and ends at yes, so at some
step the reading goes from no to yes, and the toll charges that step at least one. (3) is the
proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:u08-count} with the sum of the charges in place of the counter's rise:
the covering and Lemma~\ref{lem:u08-tree-width} bound the index bits by $\mathrm{depth}(T)$, and the
sum of the charges is at least the number of steps charged at least one. On a system that obeys
conservation the sum of the charges is the counter's rise.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{ent\_narrowing\_strengthens}, \code{ent\_cs\_count} and \code{ent\_cs\_entitlement}
(EntitlementSmall.v); the tree lemma underneath is also there, as \code{ent\_leaves\_le\_pow2} and
\code{ent\_log2\_leaves\_le\_depth}. Theorem~\ref{thm:u08-count} is the same count with the counter's
rise, so for a system that obeys conservation it's the special case. Three things in the hypotheses
feed nothing, and I'm naming them here so you don't have to find them: (H3) isn't used
by any of the three
conclusions; from (H1) only the inclusion is used, and the gap goes unused; and in (H2)
the words ``not in $\Omega'$'' go unused, since a candidate whose observation differs from every survivor's can't be a survivor itself. And (H4)'s $|\Omega'| > 0$ is used in that proof but can be dropped too: the covering forces it once the prior has a member (\code{nec\_e\_cs\_entitlement\_stronger}, NecEEnt.v).

A statement like that is true by packaging: it takes the hypotheses in and hands the
conclusions back, and the right word for it is a checklist. A checklist for leaning on a claim.
It discovers nothing about leaning.

And a checklist isn't nothing. On 30 October 1935, at Wright Field, northeast of Dayton, Ohio,
the Army was evaluating Boeing's new four-engine bomber, the Model 299. Shortly after take-off it
plunged back onto the field and caught fire; that's how the wire report of that day has it, and the
later histories add that it pitched up and stalled first, which is what elevators locked in a raised position
would do. Two men died of their injuries, the Army's pilot, Major Ployer Hill, and
Boeing's chief test pilot, Leslie Tower. The airplane was fine. The crew had left the gust locks
on, a locking mechanism worked from inside the cockpit that holds the control surfaces still while
the plane sits on the ground. There's a
famous line that a newspaper called it too much airplane for one man to fly. I couldn't find that
line in any paper from 1935; the earliest place I could find it is a New Yorker article from December 2007 by Atul Gawande, a
surgeon who writes about how people get complicated work right, and he names no newspaper, so take
it as a lead. What I can find is what came after. The answer was a card: a list of
things to check, in order, every time, and the crews of the airplane worked through written
checklists for each phase of flight. The most careful history of it I found is by Walter Boyne, a
retired Air Force colonel and a former director of the National Air and Space Museum. By his
account it wasn't the first written routine for a pilot; those go back
before the First World War. And it's this crash, he says, that made the checklist the way a crew flew. The airplane went
on to be the B-17. Nothing on that card was a discovery. Every item on it was something the pilots
already knew. What the card did was make sure none of it got left out when it mattered. That's
what putting entitlement's hypotheses on one list does: it finds nothing new about leaning on a
claim, and it makes the hypotheses impossible to drop quietly.

Before any machine, I owe you the word the toll is named after, the ``insight'' in ``No Free
Insight'' (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}), because I've been using it as if it meant one thing.

%===========================================================================
\section{What insight is}
\label{sec:insight}
%===========================================================================

I named the rule in this book ``No Free Insight,'' and the name ran ahead of any careful account
of what insight is. The book has been narrowing it ever since: not learning (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}), not
looking, not copying. It's time to say what's left, and to say it in a way that someone who
studies actual insight, in actual heads, wouldn't laugh at. So who are those people, and what
did they find? Here's what I ran into, pushed on as I go. Where a story reached me
secondhand, I treat it as a lead to check.

\subsection{Sultan and the sticks}

In 1913 the psychologist Wolfgang Köhler went to Tenerife to run a research station with a
colony of chimpanzees, and the First World War then kept him there until 1920, five years longer
than planned, with the chimpanzees to watch.
The famous one is Sultan. Food is outside the cage, out of reach; two sticks are inside, each
too short, but one fits into the end of the other. Sultan tries each stick, fails, sulks,
plays with the sticks, and then, by Köhler's account, at a moment you can see, joins them and
reaches the food. Köhler's words were \emph{Einsicht} and \emph{einsichtig}, which came into English as ``insight,'' and
the whole school of psychology he belonged to, the Gestalt school, said that's what thinking
is: a \emph{restructuring}, the moment two sticks stop
being two sticks and become one tool. Stacking up tries until one works was, for them, something
else. Karl Duncker gave the human version, in German in 1935
and in English in 1945, five years after he died at thirty-seven; he'd spent his last years
working with Köhler at Swarthmore. You can set it up yourself: a candle, a box of tacks, matches,
and the task of fixing the
candle to the wall. Almost nobody sees that the \emph{box} is a shelf, until they do. And then he found that if you hand people the box \emph{empty}, with the tacks poured out beside it, they
solve it far more readily. Same objects. What changed was which relation among them was on the table.

I like both of these for the same reason: the insight didn't add an object. Sultan had both
sticks the whole time. The box was there the whole time. What arrived was a \emph{relation}, which
is to say a piece of structure in Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s sense, and the arrival was sudden. Hold that, because the thing the toll prices also arrives in one step, and at its
best it's also a relation.

\subsection{It isn't a feeling}

But here's the finding I'd hand anyone who thinks insight is a feeling, and it comes from
someone who measured it. In the 1980s the psychologist Janet Metcalfe asked people to solve
problems while rating, every fifteen seconds, how ``warm'' they felt, how close to the answer.
On ordinary problems, algebra for instance, the warmth climbs steadily and peaks at the
answer, which is what you'd expect. On \emph{insight} problems, riddles of the candle-box kind, the
warmth stays flat, flat, flat, and then the answer arrives, and if anything the people who
felt warmest beforehand were \emph{more} likely to be wrong. She put that last finding in the
title of a 1986 paper: premonitions of insight predict impending error. The feeling of being close is not a
gauge of being close. Try it yourself: write a number from one to seven every fifteen seconds
while doing a long sum, then while doing a riddle, and compare the curves.

And the most famous insight story there is fits Metcalfe uncomfortably well. Archimedes, a mathematician who died in 212 BC, asked by Hiero, the king of
Syracuse,
whether a goldsmith had cheated him on a crown, gets into a bath, sees the water rise, and
runs home naked shouting ``eureka,'' I've found it. That comes from Vitruvius, a Roman writer
on architecture, writing about two centuries later. Is it true? Galileo Galilei, then a young Italian mathematician, at twenty-two,
in 1586, took it as known that Archimedes caught the goldsmith. What he didn't buy was the method.
Water spilling over the side, as Vitruvius tells it, was to him ``a crude thing, far from
scientific precision,'' and he guessed some writer had set down a rumour. So he wrote a little
tract, \emph{La Bilancetta}, proposing a balance weighed in air and in water instead, which he
thought was probably what Archimedes actually did, since it rests on Archimedes's own results.
Whether there was ever a bath, or a shout, nobody can check now. What survives is a story two
centuries late, wrapped around a real man and probably a real problem. Notice what the legend kept:
the bath, the shout, the running home naked. The feeling. What it left shaky is the part that
would count as the check, the test that could have caught the goldsmith. The bit everybody
remembers is the bit that tells you least.

So any account of insight that keys on the sensation, the ``aha,'' is keyed to something that
the data says is unreliable. Whatever insight is, it isn't the feeling of having it. That's a
relief, because a system of states and moves doesn't have feelings, and a word that only
meant a feeling would be cheating if I hung it on one. The version this book can price has to be keyed to an \emph{event}, and the
question is which.

\subsection{What happens when a computation learns}

Here's the split, and I'll say what the toll does with each part, and then I'll say who
decided the split. Keep Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s sheet of paper in front of you: the NO box,
the YES box, the tally line, and the three moves STAY, WORK and VOUCH.

The first thing: \emph{raw observation}. Something comes in and gets written down. A counter
ticks. Nothing is claimed about what it means, nothing is marked as resting on it, and the
reading doesn't move because of it. Later moves can read what it wrote, but that reading is a
move of its own. This is the demon's pad in Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}, and it's what the statistician Dennis Lindley
measured in 1956 as the information provided by an experiment, the words of his title, and
defined as the expected drop in your uncertainty: a real quantity,
and a quantity about what was \emph{seen}. It can be free. The toll says nothing at all about a
move that doesn't cross from NO to YES, so a price list may charge it zero: on the paper,
STAY and WORK cost nothing, and Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}'s watcher narrowed a whole row of candidates without paying
a mark. ``Can be'' is the honest word. A price list is allowed to charge for looking anyway, and
whether looking costs anything in the physical world is a different question that this sheet
of paper doesn't touch.

Lindley's measure has a back story, and it runs through Bletchley Park. I. J. Good, who was Alan Turing's main
statistical assistant at Bletchley Park in 1941, wrote in 1979 that Turing had worked out the
expected weight of evidence an experiment would give, to judge one of the codebreaking
procedures before running it, and so partly anticipated Lindley by about fifteen years, in work
that stayed secret. Turing measured evidence in \emph{bans}, logarithms to base ten, with a tenth
of one called a deciban, and the name came from the town of Banbury, where tens of thousands of
the sheets used in that procedure were printed. It's the same base-ten unit other people call the
hartley, after the Hartley from the last section. And Good adds that Turing didn't know the
logarithm he was using had already appeared in 1878, in a paper by Charles Sanders Peirce, the
same Peirce from the opening chapter, who'd called it the weight of evidence. Peirce is as far
back as Good takes it. What it changes: nothing in the argument, but it shows how well trodden this
first kind of thing is. For a century and a half careful people have measured what an
observation tells you, and every one of those measures is about what was seen. That's the side
of the line the toll leaves alone.

The second thing: \emph{certified insight}. Some move turns the reading from NO to YES. Here is
where the toll lives. In any system with the five parts that obeys the toll, that move costs
at least one mark, and every run that starts at NO and ends at YES pays at least one somewhere
along the way, which is Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s universal floor. What's being charged for, at its best, is
exactly the Gestalt thing: a relation, committed to. One tool, claimed, out of two sticks. ``At
its best,'' because Section~\ref{sec:toll} was careful about what YES means: the flag is up, and nothing more. A
crossing that writes down which relation it's committing to carries Sultan's tool with it. A
bare crossing, VOUCH on the paper, commits to no relation at all, and it pays exactly the
same.

The third thing isn't a kind of event. It's an observation about the price: it's \emph{flat},
whatever is certified. Say the YES state also shows something striking, a deep relation, a
result nobody could have guessed, Sultan's two sticks become one tool. The toll charges the
crossing at least one. It doesn't charge the striking crossing more, because the floor's proof
never looks at anything but the reading before and after. On the paper: VOUCH from NO makes
one mark whether you were thinking of Duncker's box or of lunch. Meaning is not cost. The
depth of what's certified adds meaning. It doesn't add a mark.

The candle box has a footnote that says the same thing from the other side. In 1962 the
psychologist Sam
Glucksberg ran Duncker's problem with money on it: some people were told they could win five or
twenty dollars depending on how fast they solved it. With the tacks in the box, the people
chasing the money did worse than the people who weren't. With the box empty the problem was easier
for everybody, and the accounts I've read don't agree on what the money did there, so I'll leave
that half alone. Paying more didn't buy the insight, and on the hard version it got in the way.
That's a fact about heads. It says nothing about records, and I won't push it further than that. But it's a
nice mirror for the paper. On the paper a deeper crossing isn't charged more, and in Glucksberg's
room a bigger prize didn't bring the crossing sooner. In neither place does the price measure the
depth.

Here they are, exactly, for any certification system (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}). Runs are
written as lists, the way Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s proof wrote them: $[\,]$ is the empty run, and $i :: t$ is the
run that starts with move $i$ and carries on with the run $t$.

\begin{definition}[Certified insight event, raw observation]\label{def:u09-events}
In a certification system, a step from state $s$ by move $i$ is a \emph{certified insight event}
when it turns the reading on: $\mathrm{cert}(s) = \mathrm{no}$ and
$\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{step}(s, i)) = \mathrm{yes}$. A move $i$ is \emph{raw observation} when no
step by it, from any state, is a certified insight event.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[What the toll prices, and what it doesn't]\label{rem:u09-three}
Read off Definition~\ref{def:certsys} and Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-floor}; there is no further
Coq theorem at this generality. (1) The toll puts no bound on the cost of a raw-observation
move; on Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s board STAY and WORK are raw observation and cost $0$. (2) Every certified
insight event is charged at least $1$, by the toll, and every run from a state reading no to
one reading yes has total cost at least $1$, by the universal floor. (3) The price is flat:
the floor's proof uses nothing about the end state but its reading, so adding any hypothesis
about what else the end state shows leaves the bound at $1$ and cannot raise it. A system that
wants to charge more for a deeper certification has to write that into its price list, move
by move; the toll doesn't do it for anyone.
\end{remark}

So the account comes down to two facts and a warning. Looking can be free. Turning the reading
on can't. And putting something remarkable behind the reading doesn't make it cost any more.

Who decided the split? Not the costs alone. The toll prices exactly one thing, the crossing.
A price list is free to put a floor under more moves than that (a look, a send, a check) and
free to leave other moves at zero, so the sorting into raw observation and certified insight
is by whether the reading moves, and that sorting is this book's. The part that's \emph{forced} is
the floor under the crossing, and Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} is the argument for it; anything a price list charges
beyond that is a choice, and any concrete machine owes you its whole table so you can see
which choices it made.

\subsection{Test, then commit, and nothing forces the second to follow the first}

The philosopher Karl Popper said a theory earns its standing by being \emph{exposed}: you make a
conjecture, you try to kill it, and what survives a real attempt counts for something, where
``real'' means the test could have failed. His word for that earned credit is \emph{corroboration}. I've leaned on that idea through this whole book, and here's
where a certification system has a version of it, and here's where the version is weaker
than Popper and I have to say so.

Add a fourth move to the paper: CHECK. It looks at something (a sum, a coin under a cup, a
formula against a row of values), and it can come out pass or fail, and it doesn't move the
box. Charge it whatever you like; charging it on the attempt, pass or fail, fits Popper,
because what made his test count was that it was really run and could have failed. That's
the test. It's raw observation in the sense above,
because it never turns the reading on. VOUCH is the commit. So the honest protocol is two
moves: test, then commit, and the costs are separate, one for the checking work and one for
the crossing.

But nothing in the five parts makes the second move wait for the first. The step is handed
the current state and a move name; the toll looks only at whether the reading crossed. Play
VOUCH from NO with no CHECK anywhere before it, and you land in YES and make one mark, the
same box and the same mark as the player who checked first. The two tally lines differ by
exactly what the CHECK was charged, and if you charged it nothing they don't differ at all.
The mark for the crossing is the same mark either way. The receipt says a commitment was paid
for. It does not say it was earned. Popper's corroboration needs the test; the toll doesn't.

You can build a system that makes the commit wait. Let CHECK leave a mark in the state when it
passes, and write the step so VOUCH only crosses when that mark is there. That's a design,
written into the step function, and it's a perfectly good one. Nothing in the five parts or
the toll asks for it. That's a real gap between the word and the bare system, and the only
honest thing is to leave it visible: the toll prices the commit, and whether the commit was
preceded by a test is a fact about the run, or about a design somebody chose. The five parts don't
guarantee it.

\begin{remark}[Nothing makes the crossing wait]\label{rem:u09-no-wait}
Read off Definition~\ref{def:certsys}; there is no Coq theorem. The toll constrains
$\mathrm{cost}(i)$ for moves that cross, and nothing else; the step function is any function
of the current state and the move. So a certification system may have a move that crosses
from a state no check has touched, and the toll still holds. On Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s board extended with
CHECK, the run $[\mathrm{VOUCH}]$ from NO crosses with one mark, and so does
$[\mathrm{CHECK}, \mathrm{VOUCH}]$. Making a crossing depend on an earlier check is a
condition on the step function, which a particular system can impose and the definition does
not.
\end{remark}

\subsection{What the word means}

Insight, in the sense this book prices, is a relation committed to, in a move that flips a
reading from off to on, and that move costs at least one mark, in any system with the toll,
for any relation, whatever its depth. (And one edge from the paper: a bare crossing that
commits to nothing pays the same mark, so ``a relation committed to'' is what the crossing is
at its best. The toll doesn't guarantee it.) Three boundaries, each from a different place.
From Metcalfe: it isn't a feeling, and a system's version has to be an event. From the proof:
the price is flat; a shallow commit and a deep one both cost at least one, and cost is not
depth. A system can pay heavily to check a trivial claim, and Duncker's box, a real insight, is
still one small commit. And from the two-move protocol: a paid flag proves nothing on its own.
Price and correctness are separate books.

Which leaves a suspicion I'd have in your place. Everything so far has been one reading on one
sheet of paper, with a rule I chose and a count I bolted on. Is the shape of that record
something I picked, or is it what any honest record has to look like, on any machine at all?
That's the next section: take \emph{any} machine that steps, bolt a record onto it, and see what
shape it's forced into. How a concrete machine hangs actual claims on its parts, a checked
property of one counter at one edition, and where those sit in the state, comes in Part IV.

%===========================================================================
\section{Records over any base: the latch}
\label{sec:latch}
%===========================================================================

For the whole book so far I've been building up a thing with a flag and a counter, and a
fair reader is entitled to suspect that the whole apparatus is special pleading for one
machine, the one I keep promising to build. So here's the section that answers the suspicion
with no particular machine in it at all, and sees what's left. Take \emph{any} machine that steps deterministically: a Turing
machine, a register machine (a few numbered boxes that each hold a whole number, and a
program that adds, subtracts and jumps), a lambda calculus (Alonzo Church's way of computing by nothing
but plugging expressions into expressions; Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} builds one), anything. Call it the base. Now bolt a record onto it, under rules I'll state,
and ask: what can the record be?

The answer is one shape, and I'll show you the shape first because it's a thing you can
build from a cup and a die.

\subsection{A cup and a die}

Put a cup upside down on the table. The rule: the first time a coin lands in front of it,
turn it right side up. There is no rule for turning it back over. Now roll a die, and put a
coin down on every six. Roll twenty times. The cup turns over on the first six and stays
turned over. Write down which roll did it. That number, the roll that turned the cup, is
where the record happened, and the cup afterward is the record.

That's a \emph{latch}. Electrical engineers have had the circuit since 1918, when two British
physicists teaching engineering in London, William Eccles, a radio pioneer, and Frank Jordan,
applied for a patent on a two-valve arrangement that holds whichever state you last put it
in; it became the flip-flop, and the registers and caches in the device you're reading this on
descend from it. Cut its reset wire and what's left has one input, ``set,'' and the rule \emph{new state = old state or set}: once set, it stays set. The cup is that circuit:
a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off.

(Eccles and Jordan didn't call it a flip-flop. Their 1919 paper calls it a \emph{trigger relay}.
Where the newer, sillier name came from I can't source, so I'll leave it at that.)

Is a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off only a picture, or did anybody ever build one on
purpose? Somebody did, and for a reason that's very close to this book's. In the mid-1950s Wen
Tsing Chow, an engineer at the Arma division of the American Bosch Arma Corporation in Garden City,
New York, was asked by the United States Air Force, in the accounts of his career I could find, for
a more flexible and secure way to hold
the fixed numbers, the targeting constants, inside the guidance computer of the Atlas missile.
What he and his Arma colleague William Henrich patented (filed in 1957, granted in 1962, under the
plain title ``Storage matrix'') was a grid with a connection at every crossing, where you set the numbers by
taking out the connections you didn't want, physically or by burning them out with too much
current. The word \emph{burn} is right there in the patent, and people still say they burn a
chip. The descendants are called programmable read-only memories, PROMs, and a fuse blown in
one stays blown: there's no current you can send to grow it back. A whole memory built out of
cups with no reset wire, because somebody wanted numbers nobody could quietly change later. Does
that prove anything here? No. The theorem below doesn't care what a cup is made of. But it's
good to know the shape wasn't invented for a sheet of paper. Somebody needed it, for stakes a
good deal higher than a die.

Now the claim, stated loosely and then exactly: \emph{every honest record over any base is a cup with no reset wire, turned by some event the base passes through.}

\subsection{What ``honest'' has to mean}

Here's where the content is, and I'll give you the five rules, because the theorem is only as
strong as they are.

A machine \emph{extends} a base when there's a map from the bigger machine's states down to the
base's, and that map starts in the base's start states, reaches every one of them, moves in
step with the base (one step up top is one step down below, through the map), and agrees
about halting. The bigger machine may carry as much hidden state as it likes beyond the base.
That's the ``any base'' part: the base doesn't get to see the extension, and the extension
doesn't get to change what the base does.

The extension carries a \emph{record}, a yes/no reading, and a \emph{ledger}, a counter. It's an
honest extension when five things hold. One: the record's next value depends only on the
base's current state and the record's current value. (I'll call this \emph{driven by the computation}. It says the record answers to what the machine is doing. A clock on the
wall or someone's hand doesn't get a say.) Two: the ledger never goes down (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). Three: the step that turns the
record on costs at least one; that's the toll (Section~\ref{sec:toll}). Four: once on, the record stays on;
that's permanence (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). Five: some run from a start state actually reaches a step that
turns the record on; otherwise the record is decoration.

Here are the words exactly. On/off is true/false, $\lor$ is ``or'' (on when either side is
on), and $\mathrm{next}^k$ is $k$ steps.

\begin{definition}[Base, record-carrying machine, cover]\label{def:u11-base}
A \emph{base} $B$ is a set of states with a step function $\mathrm{next}_B$, a set of starting
states, and a halting predicate. A \emph{record-carrying machine} $M$ is a set of states with a step
function $\mathrm{next}_M$, a set of starting states, a \emph{record} $\mathrm{rec}$ from states to
Booleans, a \emph{ledger} $\mu$ from states to whole numbers, and a halting predicate. The cost of a
step is $\mathrm{cost}(m) = \mu(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) \mathbin{\dot{-}} \mu(m)$. A \emph{cover} of $B$
by $M$ is a map $\pi$ from states of $M$ to states of $B$ that sends starting states to starting
states, has every starting state of $B$ as the image of some starting state of $M$, commutes
with the steps, $\pi(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = \mathrm{next}_B(\pi(m))$, and agrees about halting:
$m$ halts exactly when $\pi(m)$ does.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Honest extension, latch]\label{def:u11-honest}
$M$ with cover $\pi$ is an \emph{honest extension} of $B$ when
(R1, driven
by the computation) there is one function $f$ such that, for
every state $m$,
$\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = f(\pi(m), \mathrm{rec}(m))$; for every state $m$, (R2, ledger)
$\mu(m) \le \mu(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; (R3, toll) if $\mathrm{rec}(m)$ is off and
$\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$ is on, then $\mathrm{cost}(m) \ge 1$; (R4, permanence) if
$\mathrm{rec}(m)$ is on, so is $\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; and (R5, a reachable write)
some starting state $m_0$ and some $k$ have $\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M^k(m_0))$ off and
$\mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M^{k+1}(m_0))$ on. An \emph{event} is a function $h$ from base states to
Booleans, and its \emph{latch} is the step $(b, r) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\, r \lor h(b))$. $M$
\emph{factors as the latch of} $h$ when, for every state $m$ (reachable or not),
\[
(\pi(\mathrm{next}_M(m)),\ \mathrm{rec}(\mathrm{next}_M(m))) = (\mathrm{next}_B(\pi(m)),\ \mathrm{rec}(m) \lor h(\pi(m))).
\]
\end{definition}

Now the theorem. Under those rules, the base state and the record move \emph{exactly} as a latch:
the record switches on at the first base state where some event holds, and never off, and
the event is read off the extension's own rule by asking it what it does when the record is
off (stated exactly below). Everything else the extension carries, all the hidden
state, shows up only in its ledger; it can't leak into the record's behaviour.

I promised the content was in the definition, and here's what that means: the proof is a
short case split on whether the record is already on, and it uses only \emph{two} of the five
rules, ``driven by the computation'' and ``permanent.'' The ledger, the toll, and the reachable-write clauses play no part in it. A
latch is what you get from ``answers only to the base'' plus ``never comes back down,'' full
stop. The other three rules matter for the \emph{converse}: for any base and any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at one unit per write, \emph{is} an honest extension.
Put the two together and you've got: honest records are exactly
latches. One shape, no others, over any base.

\begin{theorem}[The record is a latch]\label{thm:u11-latch}
Let $B$ be any base and $M$ an honest extension of it through $\pi$, with $f$ the function of
(R1). Then $M$ factors as the latch of the event $h(b) = f(b, \mathrm{off})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The base half of the equation is the cover's step clause. For the record, split on
$\mathrm{rec}(m)$. If it is on, permanence (R4) makes the next value on, and
$\mathrm{on} \lor h(\pi(m))$ is on. If it is off, (R1) makes the next value
$f(\pi(m), \mathrm{off}) = h(\pi(m)) = \mathrm{off} \lor h(\pi(m))$. Only (R1), (R4) and the
cover are used; (R2), (R3) and (R5) are discarded.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_holds} (StructuralRecordAxis.v), with the definitions
\code{BaseMachine}, \code{BaseCover}, \code{computation\_driven}, \code{HonestBaseExtension} and
\code{latch\_factorization} (StructuralCoreAnyBase.v), and the clauses (R2) to (R5) as
\code{ledger\_carried}, \code{rc\_a2} (StructuralCore.v), \code{record\_permanent} and \code{reachable\_record\_write}
(StructuralCoreCover.v).

One thing about that proof deserves a second look, because it cuts both ways. It never asks what
the base is. The cover decides that: whatever the map sends down is base, and the record's rule is
allowed to read all of it; whatever stays up top is extension, and (R1) keeps the record's rule
from reading it. Draw the line low, so the base is only the computation's own working state, and
(R1) is a real demand. Draw it high, put every table and every refusal bit into the base, and (R1)
is easy to meet, and the latch shape comes out exactly the same. So the theorem holds wherever
you draw the line, and that's exactly why it can't tell you where a record's meaning lives. The
meaning lives in what the event $h$ reads, and that's in the base by construction. The pieces
above the line, the record and the ledger, are the ones that never steer anything; the pieces that
make a flag mean something sit below it, where this theorem doesn't look. So when the machine in
Part IV arrives, ask it first which parts it puts above the line.

\begin{theorem}[Every reachable latch is an honest record]\label{thm:u11-converse}
Let $B$ be any base and $h$ any event. Let $\mathrm{Latch}_h$ have states $(b, r, x)$, starting
states $(b, \mathrm{off}, 0)$ with $b$ starting in $B$, step
$(b, r, x) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\ r \lor h(b),\ x + \delta)$ with $\delta = 1$ when $r$
is off and $h(b)$ is on and $\delta = 0$ otherwise, record $r$, ledger $x$, halting as $b$
halts, and cover $(b, r, x) \mapsto b$. Suppose some starting $b_0$ and some $k$ bring
$\mathrm{Latch}_h$ from $(b_0, \mathrm{off}, 0)$, in $k$ steps, to a state whose record is
still off and whose base state satisfies $h$. Then $\mathrm{Latch}_h$ is an honest extension
of $B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(R1) holds with $f(b, r) = r \lor h(b)$. (R2): each step adds $0$ or $1$. (R3): a step that
turns the record on has $r$ off and $h(b)$ on, so it adds $1$. (R4): $\mathrm{on} \lor h(b)$ is
on. (R5) is the supposition. The supposition asks for the first time $h$ holds on some run;
any run from a start that reaches an $h$-state has such a first time, though the checked
statement uses only the first-time form.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{latch\_core\_honest} (RecordAxisDiscrimination.v).

A reversible base needs one more thing to carry a record, and the next theorem says exactly what. If
the base never merges two states, keep every earlier record value in a growing history beside
the latch, and the whole step merges nothing either; but on a finite state space a permanent
record can't be written by a step that merges nothing at all. A step that merges nothing is
called \emph{injective}: no two states go to the same next state. And $r :: H$ is the history $H$
with $r$ put on the front, as in Section~\ref{sec:insight}.

\begin{theorem}[Records on reversible machines]\label{thm:u11-reversible}
(1) Let $B$ be a base whose step is injective. The machine with states $(b, r, H, x)$, step
$(b, r, H, x) \mapsto (\mathrm{next}_B(b),\ r \lor h(b),\ r :: H,\ x + \delta)$ ($\delta$ as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse}), starting states with $r$ off, $H$ empty and $x = 0$, has an
injective step, and under the supposition of Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse} it is an honest
extension of $B$. (2) On a finite state space, a single injective step with a permanent
reading never turns that reading from off to on.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Equal images have equal base parts, so equal base states by injectivity; equal histories
$r :: H$, so equal records and histories; and equal ledgers once the equal $\delta$ is
subtracted. Honesty is the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse} with the history carried
along. (2) is Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} of Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} with a single move.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{history\_latch\_injective}, \code{history\_latch\_honest} and
\code{finite\_reversible\_cannot\_write} (RecordAxisDiscrimination.v), the last from
\code{permanent\_flip\_is\_not\_injective} (PermanentCertification.v).

So a base that never merges can still carry a record, if it's allowed to grow a history that
never ends. A machine with finitely many states can't carry one without merging: on a finite machine the record's first write is a merge, and
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} already put the price on that.

Process-calculus people ran into the same thing from the other side. Vincent Danos and Jean
Krivine, two theoretical computer scientists in Paris, wanted to pin down what a transaction is. They
took in 2005 a reversible version of CCS, Robin Milner's calculus of processes that talk to each
other, where every step can be rolled back, and modelled a transaction as a process that wanders
freely through everything that can be undone until it performs an action declared irreversible,
which is the commit. The way I read it, they start from steps that all come undone and ask what has
to be added before anything sticks, and the theorem above starts from a record and asks what the
step under it must be. In their calculus, as in the theorem, a permanent effect needs a step with no
way back, and the calculus has to say which steps those are. The word I tripped on was
\emph{declared}. Theirs are labelled. Mine, I thought, are picked out by counting, since on a finite
machine the first write merges whatever anyone calls it. Push on that and it gives. I choose the
event $h$, and on a base that grows its history forever the write merges nothing
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-reversible}), so there my permanence is declared too.

There's an arrow of time in that theorem, and I should say where it came from, because I put it
there by hand. Every starting state has the record off. That's the only reason a raised record
means the event happened: it was down at the start, and only $h$ lifts it. Turn the cup up before
the first roll and it tells you nothing about the die. So the clean start is an assumed ready
state, a past hypothesis in miniature. The past hypothesis is the physicists' name for an assumed
low-entropy beginning of the universe, which several of the accounts below lean records on.
Whether every trusted record leans on it is their argument, and I'm not settling it. Nothing in
this book derives one; every theorem here about records assumes its small version and starts from there.

When I went looking for who else had found the arrow hiding in the start, I got five papers that
read like five unrelated answers. They lined up once I asked each one the same thing: what does
the cup being down at the start rest on? There are two places to put it. You can put it at the
beginning, as a fact about how things started. Or you can put it in the structure of what causes
what. David Wolpert, then a physicist at Los Alamos and the same Wolpert as the free-lunch theorem,
sorted memory systems in 1992, and one of his kinds works only because it begins in a prepared
state set up by a process that runs one way, which is how it leans on the second law. That's the
cup put down by somebody before the game, at the first place. Wolpert and Jens Kipper, a
philosopher at Rochester, put in 2024 that sorting on a formal footing, and they say plainly that
they have no formal proof this kind can only remember the past. I trust them more for that
sentence. What I think they're saying is that a prepared start buys you a memory, and getting its
direction too takes something they can't yet prove.
