Aram Ebtekar, an independent researcher in Vancouver, and Marcus Hutter, who works on the theory of
general artificial intelligence at Google DeepMind and the Australian National University, built in
2024 a reversible toy world, imposed a past hypothesis on it, coarse-grained it, and got records of
the past and none of the future. As I read their route, the clean start doesn't go straight to the
records. It goes through a causal structure first, and the arrows come out of that. Thomas
Blanchard, a philosopher of science at Cologne, got in 2024 the same lopsidedness of knowledge out
of the causal Markov condition, a condition on causal structure. So Blanchard starts at the second
place, which is the middle of Ebtekar and Hutter's road. That took me a while to see, because one
is a toy world and the other is philosophy of causation. They go from the start to causes to
records; he goes from causes to records. The fit is my reading, and it's mine to defend. And Carlo
Rovelli, two years before his paper on the cost of choosing from the opening chapter, studied traces in ``Memory and entropy'' (2022)
and concluded that a memory turns low entropy into available information. He's at the first
place, and he says what the beginning gets spent on. Read against the latch, that's the blank the
record uses up: the flag can say yes once because it started at no.

So does the latch explain why records point backwards? No.
I'll say that plainly, so it doesn't look
like it does. The step runs forwards and the runs start clean, and a theorem built on those two can
only hand the arrow back. Push further and it gives in a second place. The history that grows
forever looked like a way around the clean start. It starts empty, so it leans on the same blank.
Under a step that forgets nothing, on a finite set, no permanent record can ever be written, past or
future, which is Zermelo again. On the map the book sits at the first place, with Wolpert and
Rovelli, and it sits there by assumption. Ebtekar and Hutter at least imposed their start on a
world with its own dynamics and watched what came out. I wrote mine into the definition.

Constructor theory, which Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} brings in as a neighbour of the
chairs, has a paper on time (Deutsch and Marletto, 2025) saying that laws stated as which transformations
a device can and can't bring about can't mention time at all, so duration has to come from
relations between physical systems, clocks, that have their own dynamics. What I think they're
saying is that whenever you want a duration you point at a second system and count what it did.
That's the position this book is in by construction. The step count is the only time in it, and it
comes from the machine's own steps. The next subsection has a record turned at the fifth tick of a
hidden clock, and (R1) throws it out, which read beside them is a rule about which system may be
the clock: the one being recorded. Push on it, though. Their laws have no step in them, and the
paper's work is getting duration and dynamics out of clocks and timers. I put a step,
$\mathrm{next}_B$, into the definition of a base. So I'm in their position only at the far end of
their argument, where a clock already exists. The base is my clock, and I assumed it.

Physicists have built this latch on paper too, in quantum mechanics, and it behaves the way the
last theorem says. The question that sorted them for me is where the cup puts what it forgets,
since a closed quantum system with separate energy levels comes back (Bocchieri and Loinger,
earlier) and the theorem left only
two ways out: a history that never ends, or a merge. Klaus Hepp, a mathematical physicist at ETH
Zurich, wanted a measuring device inside quantum mechanics itself, and studied in 1972 a particle
that flips spins in a long chain as it passes, now called the Coleman-Hepp model (I know Hepp's
paper only from accounts of it), and John Bell (1975) took it apart: the record is exactly definite
only for an infinitely long chain, which is the reversible escape above, a history that never
ends, in quantum clothes. Jonathan Halliwell, a theoretical physicist at Imperial College London,
used in 1999 a two-state detector that flips once when a particle crosses a point and is kept from
flipping back by a large environment, which is a latch with the environment holding the history.
His abstract calls it \emph{effectively} irreversible, and I like that he puts the word
\emph{effectively} right there where you can see it. And Murray Gell-Mann, the
physicist who named the quark, and James Hartle, of the University of California at Santa Barbara,
gave in 1995 the property a name inside their framework of decoherent histories: the permanence of
the past, past alternatives that stay settled as the story is extended into the future. They name
(R4) for whole histories and leave the cup to others. So Hepp's chain, as Bell read it, is exact and infinite, and
Halliwell's detector is finite and only effectively permanent. Mine is finite, exact and permanent at once, and it
gets there by letting the first write merge. Push on that and it gives: I never say where the
merged state goes. Hepp's chain had to be infinite. Halliwell had to put his in an environment.
Mine just goes, and the toll writes a unit in a counter. That's fine in a model of computation,
and it's exactly where this stops being physics.

\subsection{Both rules do work: the toggle and the clock}

A theorem with two hypotheses should have two counterexamples, one for each hypothesis
dropped, and it does, and they're the two ways a record goes wrong in the world.

Drop permanence. Take a base that just counts, and a record that flips at every step: on,
off, on, off. It's driven by the computation; it's not permanent; and it's not a latch of
any event. This is a \emph{toggle}, a piece of working state. A record you
can revoke is working state wearing a record's clothes, and if a revocation has to stick,
that's a \emph{second} latch (``revoked''), which is how certificate revocation lists actually work:
you add an entry; you never delete the certificate. Alin Tomescu, a computer scientist then at
MIT, and his coauthors (2019) built
append-only authenticated sets and dictionaries for transparency logs, and revocation fits that
shape exactly: a revocation goes in once and stays. The pair theorem (stated below) covers two
latches that can each read the other; do it with two cups where the
second only turns over on an even roll \emph{if the first is already up}, and you'll see the
second can never turn before the first.

Dialogue theorists built a version of that two-latch rule for arguments. Give each speaker a row of
cups, one for every claim they've made. Everybody I read in this field is answering two questions
about those cups: whose hand turns them, and can they come back down. C.\ L.\ Hamblin, an Australian
philosopher and logician who also came up with reverse Polish notation for early computers, wrote
\emph{Fallacies} (1970), and it has a chapter on formal dialectic where each speaker has a
\emph{commitment store}, a list of what they're on the hook for, and the rules of the dialogue
update it. The speaker doesn't. I know that chapter from other people's accounts of it. That's an
answer to the first question, and it's (R1) for arguments: the cup answers to what happened in
the dialogue, and the speaker's hand is kept off it. Henry Prakken, who works on AI and law at
Utrecht, built in 2005 dialogue games for argumentation on stores like that and made commitments
sticky: a claim can be retracted only when it has been challenged, and claims and backtracking
carry a price. He also floats a convention that once a player has retracted a proposition, that
player can't take it on again, which is a revocation that stays revoked, the way an entry on a
revocation list does. That's an answer to the second question, and it took me a second pass to see
that it's two answers. A cup can come down, and coming down costs. And once it
has, the taking-back is itself a cup that stays up. Erik Krabbe, an argumentation theorist at
Groningen, names in 2001 the awkward part of that: retraction is frowned on, and yet resolving a
dispute takes somebody retracting a doubt or a point of view, so the rules have to say when taking a
commitment back is allowed. As I read him, he's standing between the two ends of the second
question. A store that never gives can't settle a dispute. A store that gives freely isn't a store.
The part of all that I'd keep is Hamblin's, that the store belongs to the rules. It doesn't belong
to the speaker. Take the pen away from the program. And this book answers Krabbe with a price: a
take-back is a second cup, ``revoked,'' and turning it costs at least one like any other write, so a
retraction is allowed, permanent and paid for. That's Prakken's convention with the toll attached.
Where mine gives is his first condition. He lets a claim come down only when it's been challenged,
and nothing in my latch asks why the second cup turned. The pair theorem lets the second cup's event read the
base and the first cup, and nothing in it requires a challenge to be there.

The same field has a notion that looks a lot like earning. In the abstract argumentation of Phan
Minh Dung, a computer scientist at the Asian Institute of Technology in Bangkok (1995), arguments
attack one another, and the \emph{grounded} semantics starts from the arguments nobody attacks and
keeps adding the ones they defend. Look at how it's built: things go in and never come out, which
is a row of cups turned one at a time. Pietro Baroni and Massimiliano Giacomin, at Brescia,
introduced in 2007, and Martin Caminada, then at Aberdeen, revisited in 2014, \emph{strong
admissibility}: a set is strongly admissible when every argument in it is defended by others in the
set that don't lean back on it, so the support bottoms out. That's the argumentation form of an
earned claim. Above the bottom, nothing in it is in by default, which puts it at the far end
from Burge's default on the testimony map in Section~\ref{sec:windows}. Caminada argues it plays a vital part in the dialogue games that decide
grounded acceptance. I've read Caminada's paper; Dung's and Baroni and Giacomin's I know through
what later papers say about them. Notice the bottom, though. An argument nobody attacks gets in
on a check that can't fail, and this book says a check that can't fail establishes nothing. Now
turn that on my own cups, because it lands. My first write needs only that $h$ holds, and what $h$
reads sits in the base, where the latch theorem doesn't look. I charge a unit for it. A unit is a
price. It isn't a check. So my earned records bottom out the way Dung's do, in something let in
without an argument, and the one difference is that mine pays to get in. Whether a machine's
earned record certifies exactly the strongly admissible sets is the kind of statement I'd have to
prove before I said it, and I haven't.

A record that's allowed to change its mind isn't lawless, though. It's somebody else's subject.
Count how many times the cup may be turned. Once, from down to up, is the latch. More than once and
you're somewhere else, and the people who went there sort it two ways: by how many turns are
allowed, and by how long the game runs. The philosopher Hilary Putnam, then at MIT, and E. Mark
Gold, a computer scientist at a research lab in Santa Monica, in back-to-back papers in 1965, looked
at questions a machine answers by guessing and revising, where the answer is whatever the guesses
finally settle on. Putnam's paper says outright that you're never sure you have the correct answer.
That stopped me the first time. What kind of answer can't you ever be sure you have? The way I came
to read it: the cup's position at any moment is the current guess, the answer is where it ends up,
and nobody watching can tell when it's done moving. Yuri Ershov, a logician in Novosibirsk, sorted
those in 1968 by how many revisions they're allowed (that's how his hierarchy is described; I
haven't read his paper). Allow one, from no to yes, and you get exactly the sets a program can list.
That level I did check, in a modern account of the hierarchy by Rod Downey, Carl Jockusch, Timothy
McNicholl and Paul Schupp, four computability theorists, and it's a short exercise once you see
it. That's what a permanent record raised by a search catches. Allow two, three, and so on, and every
extra change buys new sets: the rungs of the ladder are all different. A record that can come back
down lives on that ladder. Now put Putnam's worry on my cup, because it lands. On the bottom rung a
yes is final the moment it appears, and a no never is. Down means not yet. A single cup of mine can
certify that something happened and can never certify that it didn't; a final no would take a second
cup, turned by finding a reason, and that's the pair of latches again. That's what the bottom rung
costs, and I'd rather name it. This book stays on the bottom rung. I'm pointing at the ladder. I'm
not climbing it.

The ladder doesn't stop at finite time, and the people who followed it past infinity have
names for the two kinds of record I just described. A definition that only ever adds, stage
after stage, and keeps everything it has at each limit, is an \emph{inductive definition}
(the long treatment is a 1974 chapter by Wayne Richter and Peter Aczel, two recursion theorists).
That's the latch run through the infinite, a cup that goes up at some stage and is still up at
every stage after. Let it take things back, and keep what stays put from some stage on, and you
have what John Burgess, a philosopher and logician at Princeton, called in 1986
\emph{quasi-inductive} definitions, which he met in the revision theories of truth that grew up
beside the logician Saul Kripke's 1975 theory of truth, which builds up the true sentences in
stages. Burgess's paper measures how complicated the truths of those theories get. I've read its
abstract. The place where he names them I haven't. What took me a few reads is that Burgess's rule at a
limit is Putnam and Gold's rule, keep whatever the guesses settled on, applied at every limit stage
along the way. That's my reading of how the two fit. If it's right, the split between a
cup that only goes up and a cup that settles is the same split at finite time and past it. A
permanent record is the first kind. A toggle that's allowed to settle is the second. Joel Hamkins
and Andy Lewis, two set theorists, let a Turing machine keep running through the ordinals in 2000.
At a limit a cell keeps its value if it settled, and reads 1 if it kept flipping back and forth
forever, and the trick they use again and again is the toggle: flash a flag on and off every time a
guess changes, and at the limit the flag is on exactly when the guess changed infinitely often. A
flag that can come back down is how that machine learns what no finite run could tell it. A
permanent one can't do that trick, because at a limit a cell that only ever goes up just stays up.
So past infinity the toggle is the clever one. A latch tells you a thing happened at least once.
Their flashing flag tells you it happened infinitely often. I threw the toggle out a few
paragraphs back anyway, and I'd do it again, because before the limit its reading can't be relied
on, and nobody using a machine of mine gets to wait for a limit. One finite-time fact belongs beside it, so nobody concludes too much
from permanence. Hao Wang, a logician then at Oxford, described in 1957 a machine whose only write
is to mark a square and which can never erase one, and it computes everything a Turing machine
does. Permanence of a machine's own memory costs it no computing power. What the book prices is a
permanent reading raised by a step that has to work whether or not the reading is already up, which
is a different thing. So the cost I named a paragraph ago is a cost in what a reading can claim.
Computing power doesn't pay it.

Drop ``driven by the computation.'' Take a base that counts, and a record that switches on at
the fifth tick of a \emph{hidden clock}, whatever the base is doing. It's permanent. The computation doesn't drive it. This is a \emph{timestamp}. A timestamp is not evidence. It says \emph{when}. It doesn't say \emph{what happened}, and a record
switched by an outside party or a clock records that party or that clock and leaves the computation
out. Try it with the die:
play twenty rolls with the rule ``turn the cup after roll seven no matter what,'' and notice
you've recorded nothing about the dice.

StructuralRecordAxis.v proves exactly the facts I named for each: the toggle is driven, isn't
permanent and isn't a latch; the clock is permanent and isn't driven. That each also keeps the other rules (the
ledger is the step count, the first switch-on costs one, a run reaches it) is true by
inspection, and isn't a separate theorem.

Permanent but undriven is a clock, driven but impermanent is a toggle, and a record is
the thing that's both. That's the whole discrimination, and I think it's the most useful
single sentence in this book for looking at systems other than the one I build, which is
why it's here.

The pair theorem and the two counterexamples, exactly. The base for both counterexamples is the
counter: states are whole numbers, the step adds one, every state is a starting state, and
nothing halts. Two more bits of shorthand: $\lnot r$ is $r$ flipped, and a statement in
square brackets, like $[k = 5]$, reads on when it's true and off when it isn't.

\begin{lemma}[Two records are two latches]\label{lem:u11-pair}
Let $c_1, c_2$ be two records on $M$, with cover $\pi$ onto a base $B$, such that: there is one
function $F$ with $(c_1(\mathrm{next}_M(m)), c_2(\mathrm{next}_M(m))) = F(\pi(m), c_1(m), c_2(m))$;
the ledger never goes down; a step that turns either record on costs at least one; and each
record is permanent. Then there are $h_1, h_2$ with
$c_1(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = c_1(m) \lor h_1(\pi(m), c_2(m))$ and
$c_2(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = c_2(m) \lor h_2(\pi(m), c_1(m))$ for every $m$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Take $h_1(b, r_2)$ to be the first part of $F(b, \mathrm{off}, r_2)$ and $h_2(b, r_1)$ the
second part of $F(b, r_1, \mathrm{off})$, then split on each record as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch}.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{record\_pair\_is\_two\_latches\_holds} (StructuralRecordAxis.v).

\begin{lemma}[The toggle]\label{lem:u11-toggle}
Let the toggle have states $(n, r)$, step $(n, r) \mapsto (n + 1, \lnot r)$, every state
starting, record $r$, ledger $n$, cover $(n, r) \mapsto n$ onto the counter. It is driven by
the computation, with $f(b, r) = \lnot r$; it is not permanent; and it factors as the latch of
no event.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
At $(0, \mathrm{on})$ the next record is off, which breaks permanence; and any latch gives
$\mathrm{on} \lor h(0) = \mathrm{on}$ there.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{toggle\_computation\_driven}, \code{toggle\_not\_permanent} and \code{toggle\_not\_latch} (StructuralRecordAxis.v).

\begin{lemma}[The clock]\label{lem:u11-clock}
Let the clock have states $(b, k, r)$, step $(b, k, r) \mapsto (b + 1, k + 1, r \lor [k = 5])$,
every state starting, record $r$, ledger $b$, cover $(b, k, r) \mapsto b$ onto the counter. It
is permanent and not driven by the computation.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Permanence: $\mathrm{on} \lor x$ is on. Not driven: the states $(0, 5, \mathrm{off})$ and
$(0, 0, \mathrm{off})$ have the same base state and the same record, and their next records are
on and off, so no $f$ of the base state and the record can give both.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{clock\_record\_permanent} and \code{clock\_record\_not\_driven} (StructuralRecordAxis.v). ``Driven'' is a condition on every
state. The clock makes every state a starting state, so the two states the proof compares are
both ones a run can begin at, even though a clock started at $(0, 0, \mathrm{off})$ would never reach $(0, 5, \mathrm{off})$.

\subsection{Is there only one such machine? No. One structure, two free choices.}

Here's a sentence I have to take apart: ``there's only one honest way to carry a record.'' Three different things
get squeezed into that breath.

First claim: given the toll and a fixed price list, is there one way to keep the books,
starting at zero and adding each move's price? Yes, on every state reachable from the start;
that's Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s initiality, and it assumes the price list.

Second claim: is every honest extension of a base \emph{the same machine}, charges and all? No,
and the counterexample is embarrassing in its simplicity. Take any honest extension and add
one more coin to the bill on every step, whatever the step is. Now walk the five rules. The
record still answers only to the base and its own value (R1); the bill never touches it. The
ledger still never goes down (R2); it climbs faster, if anything. The step that turns the
record on still costs at least one (R3), because the toll is a \emph{floor} and a surcharge only
raises the price. Once on, the record stays on (R4), and the same run still reaches the write
(R5). So the billed machine is honest, and it isn't the machine you started with: wherever
the original sat still for free, the billed one pays a coin a tick for sitting still. Do it
with the cup and the die. Charge a coin for every roll, six or not. The cup turns over on the
same roll as before. You've changed the bill and nothing about the record. A machine that
charges for CPU time is honest and isn't the one that doesn't.

But the billed machine isn't a different \emph{structure}. It's the same record, steps and
halting with a different
price list. So the claim worth keeping is sameness \emph{up to the price schedule}: compare two
machines by their record, their halting and their steps, through their maps down to the
base, and don't compare charges. Fix which event the record is, and the bill stops mattering;
a flat surcharge, or any surcharge that depends on the current state, sits on the same
structure. That's the first free choice. The walk above is the whole argument, and it's
checked over an arbitrary base, with any surcharge that depends on the current state: the
billed machine is honest (\code{nec\_w\_billed\_honest}), has the same latch event
(\code{nec\_w\_billed\_same\_latch}), steps along with the original on record, halting and base
(\code{nec\_w\_billed\_same\_up\_to\_schedule}), and pays each step's cost plus the surcharge
(\code{nec\_w\_billed\_step\_cost}), all in NecWArgued.v.

And then the second free choice, and this one still surprises me. \emph{Which event} is the record?
Nothing in the five rules picks it. The converse above already says so, if you read it
twice: for any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at one unit per
write, is an honest record. Do it with the die. One cup turns over on the first six. Another
turns over on the first one. Both are cups with no reset wire; both are honest. Roll a one
first, and until a six turns up the two cups disagree about whether anything has been
recorded. So \emph{which permanent reading counts as the record} is a second thing nobody forces
on you. The price list is one free choice. The event is the other. That second choice is the
question Section~\ref{sec:pointer} is about: what, if anything, makes certification the event worth
recording. ``The ledger passed one'' is an event too, and so is anything else the base can reach.

\begin{corollary}[The event is a free choice]\label{cor:u11-event-free}
Let $B$ be any base and $h_1, h_2$ two events, each meeting the supposition of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse}. Then $\mathrm{Latch}_{h_1}$ and $\mathrm{Latch}_{h_2}$ are both
honest extensions of $B$. If some base state $b$ has $h_1(b)$ on and $h_2(b)$ off,
then one step from $(b, \mathrm{off}, 0)$ leaves the first record on and the second off.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Honesty is Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-converse} applied twice. The step is the latch's own rule:
$\mathrm{off} \lor h_1(b)$ is on and $\mathrm{off} \lor h_2(b)$ is off.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{nec\_w\_event\_free\_choice} (NecWLatch.v), whose proof is
\code{latch\_core\_honest} (RecordAxisDiscrimination.v) applied to each event.

Now let the cup wobble. Say whatever turns it over sometimes does and sometimes doesn't, with
odds you could write on a card. Does fixing the price list fix the odds? No, and the
counterexample is two cups with the same price tag and differently loaded coins. Here's the
setup, said carefully. Let a record be a single bit that moves at random: from each value, a list of weighted next values, every weight positive,
never empty, never leaving on once on, and with the write from off to on charged at least one.
Call such a record an \emph{honest probabilistic record}.
Call two such records \emph{the same schedule} when the same moves are possible and every move is charged the same, and \emph{the same in probability} when the weighted lists are equal.

\begin{theorem}[The schedule doesn't fix the probabilities]\label{thm:u11-probabilistic}
(1) There are two honest probabilistic records with the same schedule that are not the same in
probability. (2) There is an honest probabilistic record that no deterministic latch on its
current value describes.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) From off, one record moves to off or on with weights $1$ and $1$, the other with weights $1$
and $2$; from on, both stay on with weight $1$; both charge $1$ for the write. Same possible
moves, same charges, different weights. (2) The first record moves from off both to off and to
on, while a latch $r \lor h(r)$ gives one value.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{schedule\_determines\_probabilities\_refuted} and
\code{deterministic\_latch\_handles\_branching\_refuted} (ProbabilisticRecord.v), with the definitions in
ProbabilisticRecordCore.v. These are finite-weight models on one bit with no base underneath;
they say nothing about any particular machine.

Third claim: is there one state space, up to renaming, that every honest record-carrier has
to have? I don't claim it. Nothing needs it.

\subsection{Bases from outside, and a relation I have to be honest about}

The theorem is stated for any base, and the checked work instantiates it on three models of
computation that other people built: a small Turing machine (any program); a register machine
of the kind the computer scientists Stephen Cook (of the certificates) and Robert Reckhow described in 1973, with unit-cost indirect addressing (any
program); and a lambda calculus (call-by-value, meaning an argument is worked out before it's
plugged in, and made deterministic by letting a term with no step left to take step to
itself). On each, the latch form holds, by the one generic theorem applied to that base
(the checked names are listed with the formal statement below). So a register machine
with an honest record is a register machine plus a cup. So is a lambda calculus. (There's one
more instance, the machine I build later, where a particular flag is shown to
be an honest record and the same theorem makes it a latch, in
Section~\ref{sec:smallest}.)

Here are the three bases explicitly. A base needs a state, a next-state function,
a set of starting states and a halting predicate; the latch theorem asks for nothing
else about its instruction vocabulary.

\begin{definition}[Three concrete bases]\label{def:u11-concrete-bases}
The \textbf{tape base} has a finite Boolean list $t$, a head index $h$, a program counter
$q$ and a natural-number cost field. Reading beyond the list returns false. Writing
at $h$ extends the list with false cells if needed, then changes that cell.
Moving right increments $h$ and extends the list through the new head position.
Moving left decrements a positive $h$; at $h=0$, it prepends a false cell and keeps
the head at zero. A fixed finite program contains these instructions:

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{Next state} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
Write a bit & Perform the write and advance $q$ by one. \\
Move left or right & Perform the move and advance $q$ by one. \\
Branch to $j$ & Set $q:=j$ if the current cell is true; otherwise advance $q$ by one. \\
Halt & Leave the entire state unchanged. \\
ClaimTapeIsZero with parameter $\delta$ & Advance $q$ by one and do nothing else. \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

An out-of-range program fetch is Halt. Every state is allowed as a starting state,
and halting means the fetched instruction is Halt. The cost field is preserved by
every instruction in this base. In particular, its ClaimTapeIsZero instruction
neither erases the tape nor charges the cost field; the name supplies no extra
semantics.

The \textbf{random-access base} has a register function $X:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ and a
program counter $q$. For a fixed finite program its instructions are:

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{Next state} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
Constant $(i,c)$ & Set $X(i):=c$. \\
Add $(i,j,k)$ & Set $X(i):=X(j)+X(k)$. \\
Subtract $(i,j,k)$ & Set $X(i):=\max(0,X(j)-X(k))$. \\
Indirect load $(i,j)$ & Set $X(i):=X(X(j))$. \\
Indirect store $(i,j)$ & Set $X(X(i)):=X(j)$. \\
Positive branch $(j,a)$ & Set $q:=a$ if $X(j)>0$; otherwise advance $q$ by one. \\
Jump to $a$ & Set $q:=a$. \\
Halt & Leave the entire state unchanged. \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

Each register-writing instruction advances $q$ by one; its operands are evaluated
in the old state, and all other registers are preserved. A fetch outside the program
also leaves the state unchanged. Starting states have $q=0$ and arbitrary register
contents. A state is halted when it fetches Halt or is outside the program.
Unit cost here counts instructions. It has nothing to do with the certification ledger.

The \textbf{lambda base} uses the terms and weak call-by-value rule defined in
Definition~\ref{def:u12-L}. To compute its next state, first try to reduce the function
part of an application. If that part cannot step and is an abstraction, either
substitute an argument that is already an abstraction or take a step in the
argument. If neither applies, the term cannot step. Variables and abstractions
cannot step by themselves, and there is no reduction under an abstraction.
The base leaves a term unchanged when it cannot step and calls precisely those
terms halted. Every term is allowed as a starting state, including open terms.
\end{definition}

These definitions make the three examples bases in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:u11-base}. Applying the
latch theorem to them does not assert universality, an execution-time bound, or
a simulation between the three bases.

There's also a relation defined between bases, \emph{weak base equivalence}: two bases are
equivalent when some correspondence covers their start states both ways, related states agree
on an observation and on halting, and one step on one side is matched by some number of
steps, possibly zero, on the other. That ``some number of steps'' is the \emph{stuttering} idea
Leslie Lamport (the same Lamport as Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s message counters) put forward in 1983: a fine-grained machine and a coarse one shouldn't count as
different because one takes three ticks to do what the other does in one. The relation
carries no cost; a machine that multiplies huge numbers in one step and a Turing machine
differ in price. The relation never looks at price, so on what it does look at they can match. It's proved to be an equivalence relation, and the latch
form is preserved across it.

There is a limit to that statement. The ``preserved across it'' proof throws away its equivalence hypothesis; the latch holds
on every base regardless, so the preservation is true for a boring reason. And nowhere in the
checked work are \emph{two} of the bases actually related by this relation. The relation is
defined, it's an equivalence, and it is not used to connect the Turing machine to the
register machine to the lambda calculus, or any of them to the machine in Part IV. It would be
easy to read that list as if it did. What's proved is that each base, separately,
carries a latch. That's the honest sentence.

\begin{definition}[Weak base equivalence]\label{def:u11-weak-equiv}
Bases $B_1$ and $B_2$, with observations $o_1$ and $o_2$ into one common set, are \emph{weakly equivalent} when some relation $R$ relates every starting state of each to some starting state
of the other, and any related $x$, $y$ have $o_1(x) = o_2(y)$, the same halting, some $n \ge 0$
with $R(\mathrm{next}_{B_1}(x), \mathrm{next}_{B_2}^n(y))$, and some $n \ge 0$ with
$R(\mathrm{next}_{B_1}^n(x), \mathrm{next}_{B_2}(y))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Outside bases, and the relation]\label{thm:u11-four-bases}
(1) Weak base equivalence is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. (2) If two bases are weakly
equivalent, Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch} holds over one exactly when it holds over the other.
(3) Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch} holds over each of the three bases in
Definition~\ref{def:u11-concrete-bases}, for every fixed program where the base has one.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Reflexive with equality as $R$ and one step against one. Symmetric by reversing $R$.
Transitive by composing the two relations; a step on the first base is matched by $n$ steps on
the second, and those $n$ steps by some number on the third, by induction on $n$. (2) and (3)
apply Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch} directly. In (2) the equivalence hypothesis is discarded.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{weak\_base\_equiv\_refl\_holds}, \code{weak\_base\_equiv\_sym\_holds},
\code{weak\_base\_equiv\_trans\_holds} (through \code{weak\_match\_left\_runs} and \code{weak\_match\_right\_runs}),
\code{weak\_equiv\_preserves\_record\_latch\_holds} and \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_on\_tm\_holds}
(CrossBaseGranularity.v), \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_on\_ram\_holds}
(CrossBaseGranularityRAM.v) and \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_on\_l\_holds} (CrossBaseGranularityL.v), with
weak base equivalence and the tape base defined in CrossBaseGranularityCore.v, transitivity stated
in CrossBaseGranularityTransCore.v, and the random-access and lambda bases defined in their own files.

\subsection{Records with more than two values}

A cup has two positions. Some records have more: a counter of how many checks passed, a level
that only rises. The same reasoning goes through one threshold at a time. For each value $a$,
``the record has reached $a$'' is a yes/no reading, and each of those readings is a latch. What
doesn't go through is squeezing the whole record into one cup. ``Rises'' needs one word: the
values come with an order $\le$, ``is at or below,'' which needn't compare every pair (that's
what makes it a \emph{partial} order), and $[a \le x]$ is the yes/no reading ``$x$ has reached $a$.''

\begin{definition}[A growing record]\label{def:u11-growing}
Let the record take values in a set $A$ with a partial order $\le$ decided by a Boolean test. A
record $\rho$ on $M$, with cover $\pi$ onto a base $B$, is an \emph{honest growing record} when: there
is one function $f$ with $\rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m)) = f(\pi(m), \rho(m))$; it grows,
$\rho(m) \le \rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; the ledger never goes down and every step that changes
$\rho$ costs at least one; and some run from a starting state reaches a step that changes it.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Growing records are families of latches]\label{thm:u11-growing}
(1) For every honest growing record there is an $h$ with
\[
[a \le \rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m))] = [a \le \rho(m)] \lor h(a, \pi(m), \rho(m))
\]
for every value $a$ and state $m$: each threshold is a latch, whose event may read the current
value. (2) The thresholds determine the value: if $[a \le x] = [a \le y]$ for every $a$, then
$x = y$. (3) For a growing record, charging every change is the same as charging every threshold
that switches on. (4) One latch is not enough: a three-valued record that climbs
$0 \to 1 \to 2$ over a one-state base, each climb charged one, is honest, and no single Boolean
latch with a decoding from the base state and the latch reproduces it. (5) A chain of distinct
$k$-bit words, each word's set bits contained in the next one's, has at most $k + 1$ members.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Take $h(a, b, x) = [a \not\le x] \wedge [a \le f(b, x)]$. If $a \le \rho(m)$ already, growth
and transitivity give $a \le \rho(\mathrm{next}_M(m))$; otherwise the equation is the definition
of $h$. (2) Antisymmetry, with $a = x$ and $a = y$. (3) Growth plus antisymmetry turn ``the value
changed'' into ``some threshold switched on,'' and back. (4) Over one base state, a latch and a
decoding can produce at most two values, and the record takes three. (5) Each strict step up the
chain adds at least one set bit, and there are only $k$ bits.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{growing\_record\_decomposes\_holds}, \code{thresholds\_determine\_record\_holds},
\code{record\_price\_iff\_threshold\_price\_holds}, \code{one\_latch\_refuted} and \code{chain\_needs\_bits\_holds}
(GrowingRecord.v), with the definitions in GrowingRecordCore.v. The order need not be finite;
(5) is the finite-memory bound.

\subsection{What the base being free buys you}

The reason this section exists is to answer the suspicion I started with. The record isn't
special pleading for one machine. Over any base, under rules you can read, a record that
answers to the computation and never comes down is a latch on an event, and the proof
doesn't care what the base is. What a particular machine adds on top of the latch is a
\emph{choice of price list} and a \emph{choice of event}, and both are choices. The surcharged cup
shows the first: the bill can change and the record not notice. The two cups on one die show
the second: the rules are happy with either event. Any machine I build will have to make both
choices, and whether its choice of event is the right one is a question I'll get to
(Section~\ref{sec:pointer}), and won't claim to have settled. Before that, the opening chapter
promised more than two positions. Earlier in this section a record that rises got cut into one cup
per threshold; the next section asks how much of the rest of the book survives once a record has
more places to be than up and down.

%===========================================================================
\section{The whole direction}
\label{sec:direction}
%===========================================================================

Back in the opening chapter I said something I couldn't yet back up. I said \emph{established}
didn't feel like a switch to me. It felt like a direction with lines drawn across it, and the
switch was just the first line. Then I said the one piece of that I could settle was that a
single switch isn't enough once there are three or more stages, and I pointed here. So here's
where I pay that off, and where I find out how much of the rest survives being pushed on.

The cup of Section~\ref{sec:latch} has two positions. Everything the book has proved about the
toll so far (the floor, the merges, the squeeze, the windows) was proved for a cup. The question
for this section is blunt: if the record has more places to be than up and down, how many of
those results come along, and which ones break?

\subsection{A row of cups}

Get four cups and a pencil. Write five stages of a sentence on a strip of paper, left to right:
\emph{guessed}, \emph{announced}, \emph{refereed}, \emph{printed}, \emph{machine-checked}. Those
are close to the stages the Kepler story moved through in the opening chapter. Hales's referees ran seminars
on his proof for years and ran out of energy before they could certify it, so here
\emph{refereed} stands for that long reading, which is part of why the last stage exists. You
don't have to believe my version of that story to use them. Now put a cup between each pair of neighbours,
upside down. The first cup means ``at least announced,'' the second ``at least refereed,'' the
third ``at least printed,'' the fourth ``at least machine-checked.'' When the sentence reaches a
stage, turn over every cup up to that stage. Cups only ever get turned right side up. None of
them has a reset wire.

Two things to notice with the cups in front of you. Each cup by itself is exactly the cup of
Section~\ref{sec:latch}: it reads yes or no, and once yes it stays yes. And four cups were
enough for five stages. Try it with three. You can't: three cups that only ever turn up, in
order, give you at most four different arrangements along the way. I'll prove both of those in a
minute, and the proof is about as short as the experiment.

Now a harder strip. Some checks don't line up. A referee can read a proof, and a machine can
check it, and neither of those is above the other: a refereed proof hasn't been machine-checked,
and a machine-checked proof hasn't been refereed. Draw it as a diamond. \emph{Nothing} at the
bottom, \emph{refereed} on the left, \emph{machine-checked} on the right, \emph{both} at the top.
Moving up the diamond is still only ever moving up, but now there are two ways up from the
bottom, and the two middle points don't compare. That's what a \emph{partial} order allows: some pairs
simply aren't comparable. Put a cup on each point that isn't the bottom, one
for ``at least refereed,'' one for ``at least machine-checked,'' one for ``both.'' Each cup is
still a latch. The record is now a place on the diamond, and the three cups together tell you
which place.

Whatever the shape of the strip, a straight line of stages or a diamond or something with a
hundred points, I'll call the set of places the record can be the \emph{direction}, and each
question ``has the record reached at least this place?'' a \emph{line} across it. One line is
one cup.

\subsection{The order, said exactly}

The strip and the diamond each come with an order you can see by looking: whether one place is at
or below another. Said exactly, the order is a test. For any two places $x$ and $y$ it answers ``is
$x$ at or below $y$?'' with yes or no, and I write a yes as $x \le y$. The test has to obey two
rules: every place is at or below itself, and if $x \le y$ and $y \le z$ then $x \le z$. An order
that obeys just those two is called a \emph{preorder}. If it also obeys a third rule, that $x \le y$
and $y \le x$ together force $x = y$, it's a \emph{partial order}, and that third rule is called
antisymmetry. The two-point order, no below yes, is the cup. The whole numbers in their usual order
are a straight strip that never ends.

The cups say the same thing in their own terms. For a place $a$, the cup for $a$ asks ``has the
record reached at least $a$?'', so with the record at $x$ it's up exactly when $a \le x$, and I
write its answer as $[a \le x]$. In the row of cups I said the cups together tell you which place
the record is at. On the strip and the diamond you can check that with your eyes, and part (2) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing} already proved it whenever the order is partial, though I hadn't asked
what in that proof was doing the work. My first guess was that it held for every order.

Why bother with the bare preorder at all, when every strip on the table is a partial order? Because
I wanted to see what the third rule was doing, and the way to see what a rule does is to take it
away. Take a preorder with two places, call them \emph{left} and \emph{right}, where each is at or
below the other. There are two cups, one asking ``at least left?'' and one asking ``at least
right?'', and both are up at left and both are up at right. Look at the table and you can't say
where the record is. Now build a record that swaps between left and right on every single step and
charges nothing. Every rule I'm about to state is satisfied. The record never drops below anywhere
it was, because each place is at or below the other. No cup ever moves, so the toll in the next
subsection has nothing to charge. The record moved on every step and nothing on the table noticed.

\begin{theorem}[The cups fix the place, and only with antisymmetry]\label{thm:dir-lines}
(1) In a partial order, if two places $x$ and $y$ leave the same cups up, $[a \le x] = [a \le y]$
for every $a$, then $x = y$. (2) In a preorder that isn't a partial order this can fail: there's a
preorder with two different places that leave the same cups up, and a record over it, driven by
the computation and growing in that preorder, that changes on every step while no cup moves.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Look at the cup for $x$. It's up when the record is at $x$, since $x$ is at or below itself,
so it's up at $y$ too, and that says $x \le y$. The cup for $y$ gives $y \le x$ the same way.
Antisymmetry gives $x = y$. (2) Left and right above, with the record swapping every step.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{bp\_thresholds\_determine} and \code{thresholds\_fail\_on\_preorder} (AxCore.v), and
\code{indiscrete\_loses\_record} (AxLatch.v).

So in a partial order the cups are the place, and in the preorder I built they aren't. That second
half holds in every preorder that isn't partial, by one line of pencil that isn't in the Coq: if
$x \le y$ and $y \le x$ with $x \ne y$, then a cup that's up at either one is up at the other, by
transitivity. So the cups are the place exactly when the order is partial. My first guess was right on every
strip I could draw, and it was right because of a rule I hadn't noticed I was leaning on. On a
bare preorder, putting two places on the same rung tells the toll not to care about moves between
them, and it doesn't. I don't think that's a defect. It's the order telling you what you agreed to
count.

\subsection{The toll, over the whole direction}

One cup had one rule: the step that turns it right side up pays. Now there's a row of cups, or a
diamond of them, and a single step can turn over several at once. Here's the rule I'd guess first,
and it turns out to be the right one: \emph{a step that turns over any cup pays at least one.} A step
that turns over three cups at once still only has to pay one. The rule asks whether a step turned
something over. It doesn't ask how many.

What does that rule buy? The same thing one cup bought. Take any run, and suppose some cup is up at
the end that was down at the start. Somewhere along the run a step turned that cup over, and that
step paid. So the run paid at least one. Count the same way and you get more: the run paid at least
once for every step that turned anything over.

Now look at what that argument didn't use. It didn't care whether the cups sat in a row or a
diamond or something with a hundred points. It didn't care how many there were. It didn't even use
the fact that cups never get turned back down. If something could knock a cup back over, the
argument still works, because all it needs is the one step where that cup went up.

To say it exactly I want to put it in terms of places, so here's the translation. The cup at a place
$a$ is up exactly when the record is at or above $a$. Say a step takes the record from $x$ to $y$.
The cup at $y$ is up afterwards, since $y$ is at or above itself, and it was down before exactly
when $y$ isn't at or below $x$. And if $y$ is at or below $x$, any cup that's up at $y$ was already
up at $x$. So a step turns over some cup exactly when it lands somewhere that isn't at or below
where it started. The same reasoning says a run ends with some cup up that was down at the start
exactly when it ends somewhere that isn't at or below where it started.

\begin{theorem}[The toll over any direction]\label{thm:dir-toll}
Take a machine whose record is a place in any preorder, and say a step \emph{turns a cup over} when
it takes the record from $x$ to a place that isn't at or below $x$. (1) Every step that turns a cup
over costs at least one exactly when, from every start, every run that ends somewhere not at or
below its start costs at least one. (2) When that holds, a run costs at least the number of its
steps that turn a cup over. (3) It holds exactly when every cup, on its own, pays the toll of
Section~\ref{sec:latch}: for every place $a$, a step that turns the cup at $a$ from down to up costs
at least one. The floor of Section~\ref{sec:toll} is (1) with one cup.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) and (2) are the walk above. For the other half of (1), a run of one step that turns a cup over
ends somewhere not at or below its start. (3) is the translation above.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{ax\_floor\_iff\_a2}, \code{ax\_cost\_ge\_exits}, \code{ax\_view\_a2} and
\code{ax\_a2\_iff\_views} (AxCore.v, AxLatch.v), with the one-cup floor as \code{two\_point\_nfi}.
When the cups only ever go up, as on the strip and the diamond, a step that turns a cup over is
just a step up (\code{ax\_exit\_is\_strict\_rise}).

That surprised me a little. I'd filed the floor away as a fact about one bit. Nothing in it was
about one bit. It was about one cup going up, and anything you build out of cups has that.

\subsection{One line isn't enough}

Now the payoff I owe the opening chapter. Could a cleverer single cup do the job of all four? One latch, and some decoding that reads the record's place off the
latch and whatever the machine shows? Section~\ref{sec:latch} already shut that door in the
smallest case: over a machine with one visible state, a record that climbs through three places can't be
produced by one latch and a decoding, because one latch and one visible state make two outcomes and
the record has three.

So try a second guess, closer to the cup's own rule. The cup's rule was ``new value is old value
\emph{or} the event.'' The obvious rule for a whole row is ``new place is old place \emph{joined
with} the event's place,'' where joining two places means going to the lowest place at or above
both. On the row: the event names a place, and you turn up every cup as far as that place. Here's
where it breaks. Take the strip $0 < 1 < 2$, a cup at $1$ and a cup at $2$, over a machine with one
visible state, so the event has to be one fixed place. Let the record jump from $0$ straight to $2$,
turning up both cups in one step, and stay put at $1$ and at $2$. From $0$ the event has to turn up
both cups, so the fixed place is $2$. From $1$ the same event would turn up the second cup as well,
and the record stays at $1$.

What works is giving every cup its own event, and letting the event for a cup look at where the
record already is. That's exactly what Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing} said, and this is why it had
to say it. That leaves how many cups. In the row of cups I asked you to try five stages with three
and said you couldn't. Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing} (5) already bounded the chain from above.
Here's the count behind that again, with the matching example added, and with an arrangement of
$k$ cups read as a $k$-bit word, a one for every cup that's up.

\begin{theorem}[Lines a direction needs]\label{thm:dir-bits}
(1) A list of different arrangements of $k$ cups, each keeping up every cup the one before had up
(a chain of different $k$-bit words in which each word's set bits are among the next word's), has
at most $k + 1$ members, and for every $k$ there's such a chain with exactly $k + 1$. So a straight
strip of $n + 1$ stages needs exactly $n$ cups. (2) Over a machine with one visible state, take the
record on the strip $0 < 1 < 2$ that jumps from $0$ to $2$ and stays put at $1$ and at $2$. It
grows and is driven by the computation, and no rule of the form ``join the record with a fixed
place'' reproduces its steps.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Going from one arrangement to the next, which is a different one, turns up at least one more
cup, and there are $k$ cups, so there are at most $k$ steps and $k + 1$ arrangements. For the
matching chain, take no cups up, then the first, then the first two, and so on, packed to the
left: that's the row of cups. (2) Joining $0$ with a fixed place $g$ gives $g$, and from $0$ the
step has to give $2$, so $g$ is $2$. Joining $1$ with $2$ gives $2$, and from $1$ the step has to
stay at $1$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{chain\_bits\_exact} (AxLatch2.v) and \code{chain3\_not\_join\_latch} (AxLatch.v).

So five stages need four cups. One won't do it, and three won't either. The switch isn't wrong.
It's the first line, and a straight strip with more than two places needs more of them, exactly one
fewer than it has stages. A direction that branches needs at least as many cups as the steps in its
longest strict climb, and it can need more. Put three places above a bottom, none of them above another. The longest
climb is one step, and one cup can't tell four places apart.

People got here before me, and from a direction I didn't expect, which was programming for many
processors at once. Lindsey Kuper and Ryan Newton's LVars (2013), ``lattice-based data structures
for deterministic parallelism'' in their own title, are memory cells whose value only climbs in an
order, where a read can't ask for the value and can only ask whether it has climbed past a
threshold. That's a cup. What the cup buys them took me a couple of reads. As I understand it,
writers running side by side can push the value up in a different order on every run, and a cup
that's up stays up whatever the order was, so a program that only ever looks at cups can't see
the others' timing. Amin Timany and Lars Birkedal (2021), coming at it from proofs about programs,
show in Coq, as I read their paper, that any preorder at all can be carried as monotone ghost state
in a program logic. That's the closest thing I've found to the decomposition into lines being
checked by somebody else. The match is my reading, and if it's off, that's on me.

The two rest on the same thing, a value that only climbs and a question that only asks whether it's
past a point, and they use it for opposite jobs. In an LVar the threshold read steers the program.
Ghost state, as far as I understand the term, lives in the proof, and the running program never
reads it. Here the record is never allowed to steer anything, so I sit with the ghost state. Push on
that and it gives a little: Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s glance, the whole reason to keep a record,
is a read. What keeps me on that side is that a glance worth trusting gives the answer the long way
would have given. Their purposes aren't mine. But the shape is theirs first. What I can't find in
either is a price on crossing a line.

\subsection{Why crossing a line has to cost}

Part II showed that the cup's toll isn't an arbitrary rule. It's forced by three premises, and the
argument that ties them together was the
chairs: on a machine with finitely many states, a record that goes up and stays up has to seat two
states in one chair at the step that raises it (Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges}), and a step that
seats two in one chair is a step that forgets which one it came from. Does that survive the whole
row of cups? Mostly, and the parts that don't survive are the interesting ones.

The room needs a flag, and now there are many cups, so the first job is to pick one. My first guess
was the cup for the place where the record starts. That goes nowhere: the starting state
already has that cup up, so it's already inside the room, and there's nobody at the door. The cup
that works is the one the step turns over, the cup for the place $a$ where the record lands. It's up
after the step, since $a$ is at or above itself, and it was down before, which is what turning a cup
over means. So the room is every state with the cup at $a$ up, and the state the step
starts from is the one at the door.
If the move keeps everybody in the room inside it and seats nobody twice, the insiders fill the
inside chairs between them and there's no chair left for the newcomer. So one of two things
happened. Either two states shared a chair, or somebody who was in the room got moved out, which
means their cup at $a$ went back down. I'll call that second thing a \emph{revocation}.

\begin{theorem}[Turning a cup over merges]\label{thm:dir-merge}
On a machine with finitely many states and a record in any preorder: (1) if a move turns a cup over
at some state and lands the record at a place $a$, then either the move merges two states, or
there's a state with the cup at $a$ up that the same move takes to a state with the cup at $a$
down, which is a revocation; (2) if the record only grows, so that no cup ever goes back down, the
move merges; (3) if the record only grows, the toll holds exactly when every move that turns a cup
over at some state, and merges, costs at least one, so merge pricing gives the toll.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Gather every state with the cup at $a$ up. There are finitely many. If the move keeps each of
them there and is injective, it maps that collection into itself without two landing on one, so it
hits all of them, including the state it sends the starting state to; injectivity then says the
starting state was in the collection already, and it wasn't, because its cup at $a$ was down. So
either some state in the collection has its cup at $a$ knocked down, or the move isn't injective. (2) Growth rules out the
knocking down. (3) If the toll holds, every move that turns a cup over somewhere pays, merging or
not. The other way, a move that turns a cup over merges by (2), so the hypothesis charges it.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{ax\_exit\_merges\_or\_revokes}, \code{ax\_growth\_exit\_merges} and
\code{ax\_a2\_iff\_flipping\_merges\_priced} (AxMerge.v), with \code{ax\_a2\_from\_merge\_price} for the
derivation. It's the room again, once for every cup.

Each premise there can be knocked out, and I wanted to see each one go, because a premise you've
never seen fail is one you don't understand yet.

Knock out finiteness. Take the whole numbers as the states, which gives a row of cups that never
ends, and let the record be the state itself, one more on every step, at no charge. Every step turns
up one more cup. The step never merges anything: different numbers go to different numbers. Merge
pricing holds, because there are no merges to price, and the toll fails on every single step. The
room broke at the one place it needed to be finite. Everybody moved one chair along, and there was
always another chair. That's Charles Bennett's 1973 escape in miniature, the way I read it: a
machine that keeps its whole history never has to forget, so it never has to pay, for as long as it
has room for the history. With infinitely many states it always has room.

Knock out growth. Take a two-state machine whose record flips back and forth between two places, so
a cup goes up on one step and gets knocked back down on the next. The two states just trade chairs,
so nothing merges, and the price list is honest about merges. The step that turns the cup up
pays nothing. It takes the other branch of (1): the state that had the cup up
gets moved to where it's down. It revokes.

Knock out the price on merges. A two-state machine that stamps every state with yes turns the cup
up wherever it was down, merges at the stamp, and charges nothing. Of course the toll fails; nobody
asked the merge to pay.

\begin{theorem}[Three ways out]\label{thm:dir-escapes}
(1) There's a machine with infinitely many states, a growing record and an honest merge price on
which every step turns a cup over and the toll fails. (2) There's a two-state machine with an
honest merge price whose record doesn't grow, which turns a cup over and fails the toll. (3)
There's a two-state machine with a growing record whose merges aren't priced, which fails the toll.
\end{theorem}

Checked as \code{history\_escape}, \code{toggle\_escape} and \code{free\_merge\_escape} (AxMerge.v). So
the toll over a whole direction rests on exactly the three things the cup's toll rested on:
finitely many states, a record that doesn't come down, and merges that pay. Nothing extra got
smuggled in when one cup became a row, and nothing the one cup needed got left behind.

I'd half expected the diamond to need something new, some extra rule for the two middle cups that
don't compare. It didn't. Every cup gets its own room, and every room is the old one.

%===========================================================================
\section{The shadow, exactly}
\label{sec:shadow-exact}
%===========================================================================

Section~\ref{sec:windows} put the machine behind a window and asked what an outsider could tell.
It found that two states can look the same through the window and differ in what matters, and that
a price computed from the window can't be exact if the window has a collision
(Theorem~\ref{thm:shadow-price}). That was for one cup. With a whole row of cups in hand I can ask
the sharper version of the same question, which is also the one I actually care about. Take the
ordinary machine, the one with no cups and no ledger, and let it look at itself. What's the shape
of everything it can't see, and what does the toll cost in terms of that shape?

\subsection{The ordinary machine is a shadow}

Take any machine with a record and a ledger, and sweep both off the table, the cups and the
counter. What's left is a machine that steps the same way and knows nothing about either. Call that
the \emph{shadow}. Over any one state of the shadow there's a pile of full states, one for each
place the record could be, with its own cups up, and each value the ledger could hold, all of them
casting that same shadow. Section~\ref{sec:windows} already called the pile over a point the
\emph{fibre} over it. The shadow is one particular window, the one that shows everything except the
cups and the ledger.

The shadow has its own fibres, and every move has piles of its own too: the states a move sends to
one landing spot. I'll call those the move's \emph{landing piles}. A fibre is everything that looks
the same before anybody moves. A landing pile is everything that ends up in the same spot after one
move. Keep the two kinds apart, because the whole section turns on how they meet.

\subsection{Pricing from the shadow}

First the window question, over a whole row. A \emph{window price} charges each step from what the
window shows before and after it. It meets the floor if it charges at least one for every step that
turns a cup over, and it's \emph{exact} if it also charges nothing for any step that turns no cup
over. A \emph{collision} is two steps that look the same through the window, where one turns a cup
over and the other doesn't.

With one cup, the fix in Section~\ref{sec:windows} was to put the cup in the window. So my first
guess for a row was that the window has to show some of the cups. Try the smallest version: a
record in the whole numbers, and a window that shows only the first cup, the one that asks ``at
least one?'' Let the record rise on some steps and hold still on others. Once it's past one, that
cup is up before and after both kinds of step, so a step that turned over a cup further along looks
exactly like a step that turned over nothing. That's a collision. So then, I thought, the window
has to show every cup. That's wrong too, from the other side. Take a record in the whole numbers
that rises on every step, and a window that shows only whether the record is even, which on the row
is whether an even number of cups are up. You can't read the record off that window. Every step
changes the evenness, though, and every step turns a cup over, so charging one for every step is
exact.

\begin{theorem}[Window prices over a direction]\label{thm:dir-window}
(1) If the window has a collision, every window price that meets the floor charges at least one for
some step that turns no cup over, so no window price is exact. (2) On a machine with finitely many
states and moves, whose views can be told apart by a yes-or-no test, an exact window price exists
exactly when the window has no collision. (3) Along
any run, a window price that meets the floor charges at least the number of steps that turn no cup
over but look, through the window, like a step that does. When it can be decided, for each pair of
views, whether some step showing them turns a cup over, some window price meets the floor and, among
the steps that turn no cup over, charges one on exactly those, so that number is the least overcharge. (4) A window can
price exactly without showing where the record is: there's a record in the whole numbers, rising on
every step, and a window that shows only whether the record is even, which prices every step exactly
although no rule reads the record off it. (5) There's a record in the whole numbers and a window
that shows only the one cup ``at least one,'' and that window has a collision.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) The two colliding steps get the same bill. The floor makes it at least one because of the step
that turns a cup over, and the other step pays it too. (2) Without a collision, ``does some step
that looks like this turn a cup over?'' is a question about what the window shows, and on a finite
machine you can answer it for every pair of views; charge one exactly when the answer is yes. (3)
A step that turns no cup over but looks like one that does gets that step's bill, which is at
least one by (1)'s argument; add along the run. For the other half, charge one exactly when the
answer to (2)'s question is yes, which needs that question to be decidable, and count the
overcharge. (4) Every step changes the evenness, so the window
sees every step as a move, and every step turns a cup over. (5) The first cup, as above.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{ax\_window\_collision\_overcharges}, \code{ax\_window\_no\_exact\_price},
\code{ax\_window\_exact\_iff\_no\_collision}, \code{ax\_overcharge\_lower}, \code{ax\_overcharge\_tight}, \code{ax\_exact\_without\_position}
and \code{ax\_threshold\_window\_blind} (AxWindow.v).

Item (4) changed how I think about this. I'd assumed a window had to see the cups to price them. It
doesn't. It has to see them \emph{move}. A window that knows nothing about where you are, and knows
exactly when you've gone somewhere, can send the right bill every time.

\subsection{What a priced move destroys}

Now the fibres. Part II showed that the step raising a permanent flag on a finite machine seats two
states in one chair, and Theorem~\ref{thm:dir-merge} showed the same for a step that turns any cup
over, once the cups only go up. Which two? It matters a great deal. If they're in different shadow
fibres, then the ordinary machine lost something and the record didn't. If they're in the same
fibre, the ordinary machine lost nothing, and what got destroyed was only ever off the table: two
states that cast one shadow, told apart by their cups or their ledger, crushed into one.

My first guess was that it's always the second kind, because the cups are where everything
happens. It isn't always. It depends on whether the ordinary machine forgets anything on its own.

\begin{theorem}[The toll prices a collapse inside a fibre]\label{thm:dir-fibre}
On a machine with finitely many states and a growing record: (1) a move that turns a cup over
somewhere sends two different states to one landing spot; (2) if the shadow's step for that move
forgets nothing, sending different shadow states to different shadow states, then those two states
are in the same shadow fibre, and every landing pile of the move lies inside one fibre; (3) without
that premise it can fail: there's a two-state machine whose two states sit in different fibres and
whose shadow step forgets, so the merge at the step that turns the cup over lands two states from different fibres
and no fibre loses a point. (4) The halving price, which says a move of cost $c$ shrinks any
collection of states by at most a factor of $2^c$, holds exactly when every landing pile has at most
$2^c$ states, on a machine of any size.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) is the room of Theorem~\ref{thm:dir-merge}, with growth. (2) If two states land on one spot,
their shadows land on one shadow spot, and the shadow's step tells shadows apart, so the two states
cast the same shadow to begin with. (3) The stamp from the three ways out, with each state as its
own shadow: both states land on yes, and so do their shadows. (4) is the worst pile-up of
Premise~\ref{prem:halving}: one landing pile is a collection that lands on a single spot, and any
collection is at most the number of spots it lands on times the biggest pile. Neither half needs the
machine to be finite.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{ax\_exit\_collision}, \code{ax\_fibre\_collapse\_exit}, \code{ax\_step\_fibre\_in\_fibre},
\code{shadow\_merge\_escape}, \code{ax\_compression\_iff\_fibres}, \code{ax\_priced\_spots} and
\code{ax\_spots\_priced} (AxShadow.v, AxInfinite.v).

So on a machine with finitely many states and a record that only grows, when the ordinary machine forgets nothing,
the toll is a price on crushing a fibre: on taking
two states that cast one shadow, which only what's off
the table told apart, and making them one.
The last of those premises is the one I just showed you failing.

\subsection{How much gets destroyed, on average}

The halving price is a worst case. It prices the largest landing pile a move can have. The next question is
the average one: if I don't know which state the machine was in, cups and all, but I have some
spread of chances over the states, how much do I lose, on average, about which state it was, once
I know where it landed? That's what Shannon's conditional entropy measures (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}
built the entropy from scratch, so I won't do it again here). Write it in bits.

\begin{theorem}[The halving price in bits bounds the average loss]\label{thm:dir-bits-loss}
Take any spread of non-negative weights over the states, uniform or not. (1) If every landing pile
has at most $N$ states, the conditional entropy of the state given its landing spot is at most the
total weight times $\log_2 N$ bits. (2) So on a machine with finitely many states and the halving price, the average
information a move destroys is at most its cost in bits, times the weight. (3) The bound is reached:
the even spread on a pile of $2^c$ states loses exactly $c$ bits. (4) On a machine of any size and
for any spread, even one whose entropy is infinite, the same bound holds for every finite family of
landing piles of a priced move.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Inside one pile, Gibbs's inequality: the entropy of a spread over $n$ states is at most $\log_2 n$,
with equality for the even spread. Add over the piles, weighting each by its share. The halving
price makes $n$ at most $2^{\mathrm{cost}}$, and $\log_2 2^c = c$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{ax\_fibre\_gibbs}, \code{ax\_loss\_le}, \code{ax\_priced\_loss\_bits},
\code{ax\_priced\_loss\_tight} (AxProb.v) and \code{ax\_inf\_loss\_bits} (AxInfinite.v). These use Coq's
real numbers, and they lean on four standard-library assumptions, all named in
Section~\ref{sec:coq}: the two decidability principles that come with the reals, functional
extensionality, and excluded middle.

Where does it stop? My first guess was one place, a landing pile with infinitely many states, and
that the average would blow up there right along with the worst case. That's half right, and the
half that's wrong surprised me. No finite toll can price a move that sends infinitely many states
to one spot, and that's a theorem. But the average depends on the spread. Put weight $\tfrac12$ on
the first state, $\tfrac14$ on the next, $\tfrac18$ on the next, and so on, and the information lost
by crushing the pile never reaches 2 bits, however many of its states you count. Under that spread,
two bits of toll would cover the average, though nothing covers the worst case. So I went looking
for a spread that does blow up, and it took a nastier one: blocks of states, block $k$ holding
$2^{2^k}$ states and a share $\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}$ of the weight, which adds up to one. Under that
spread the loss grows past every bound. No toll covers it, on average or otherwise.

\begin{theorem}[An infinite pile]\label{thm:dir-infinite}
(1) A move that sends infinitely many states to one spot isn't priced by the halving price at any
finite cost. (2) Under the halving spread $2^{-(j+1)}$, the information lost by crushing the pile, counted over its
first
$n$ states, is less than $2$ bits for every $n$. (3) Under the block spread, the information lost
grows past every bound, so no cost covers it.
\end{theorem}

Checked as \code{ax\_collapse\_unpriceable}, \code{ax\_geometric\_loss}, \code{ax\_block\_mass\_n},
\code{ax\_block\_loss\_unbounded} and \code{ax\_block\_no\_toll} (AxInfinite.v).

And heat? Part II already said where the line is, and it's the same line here. Landauer's
principle, that crushing $c$ bits' worth of possibilities costs at least $c\,kT\ln 2$ of heat on
average, is a premise from physics, and a contested one (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). Nothing in
this section proves anything about heat. What the counting does give is this: under that premise,
on a machine with the halving price, a move's cost priced at $kT \ln 2$ per unit,
times the weight of the piles, is always enough
to cover the minimum the premise would
demand, for every spread and every finite family of landing piles. Checked as
\code{ax\_toll\_covers\_landauer\_minimum} (AxInfinite.v). If the premise falls, that sentence falls
with it, and every theorem above it stands, because none of them used it.

\subsection{What the shadow is}

Put the two sections together and here's the shape I've been circling since the Flatland night.
The ordinary machine is the shadow of a machine with a row of cups beside it. Over every shadow
state there's a whole fibre, a pile of states that differ only in their cups and their ledger, and
the ordinary machine can't tell them apart because nothing in its step ever looks at the cups. On a machine that pays the toll, a
step that
turns a cup over costs, whichever cup it is and however many it turns, and on a machine with finitely many states whose record
only grows, when the
ordinary machine forgets nothing, what that cost pays
for is exactly crushing two states of one
fibre into one. A window can send the right bill without seeing the cups, if it sees them move.
And on a machine with the halving price, where each unit of cost pays for at most one halving, the
bill in bits, times the weight of the spread,
is never less than what got crushed on average.

What I haven't shown is that any of this is out there in the world, that nature keeps a direction
like this over its own shadows. That's a belief of mine, and nothing in this book proves it. What
I've shown, and you can check, comes with its premises showing. A machine whose record is driven by
the computation and climbs a partial order is a row of cups, one latch for every line. If it also
has finitely many states, never lets the record come down, and prices its merges, it has to pay this
way. And when its ordinary machine forgets nothing, what it pays for is exactly this. It's less than the
Flatland night promised me. It's also the part of it that held when I pushed.

\subsection{Shortcuts}

Here's the question every machine with a record has to face, and no amount of good design makes it
go away. A cup is worth turning over because something later glances at it
and doesn't have to work the thing out again: that's Section~\ref{sec:structure}'s glance, reading
a block's bucket off the table without applying the rule from scratch. Call any move like that a \emph{shortcut}, and
call it \emph{sound} when it gives the answer the long way would have given. (That gloss is about cost, leaning on what
was done so nothing is redone, and the wall I'm about to show you doesn't look at cost at all;
the next section says exactly what it does look at.) So: can a machine \emph{decide}, from inside,
whether its own shortcuts are sound? That's a wall, and it's the same wall the logician Kurt Gödel and Turing hit, and
I have to show you that it's there before I show you anything that pretends to be on the other side
of it.

%===========================================================================
\section{The diagonal}
\label{sec:diagonal}
%===========================================================================

In Section~\ref{sec:structure} I said you'd watch the same move get made again and again as the book went on:
somebody says ``everything is X,'' it's true enough to do real work with, and then somebody
draws the diagonal. I owe you the diagonal itself now, because Sections~\ref{sec:latch} to~\ref{sec:shadow-exact} just handed a record, and a whole
direction of them, to \emph{any} system that steps, and the next thing anyone wants from a system with a record is for
it to tell sound shortcuts from unsound ones by itself. Before I let anything claim that, I
have to show you the wall every such claim runs into, and then show you exactly where a
system with a record stands relative to the wall. Not on the far side. Nobody's on the far
side.

\subsection{Five names and a table}

Do this first, with a pencil, because the whole family of arguments is this one trick and
you should own it. Write five friends' names down the left of a page. Next to each name,
write a five-digit string of zeros and ones, anything you like. Now build a new string: its
first digit is the \emph{opposite} of the first digit of the first row; its second digit is the
opposite of the second digit of the second row; and so on down the diagonal. Look at what
you've made. It differs from row one in position one, from row two in position two, from
every row at that row's own position. So it's nobody's string. Your table of five missed
something.

With five rows and five digits that's a cute fact. Georg Cantor, a mathematician working out how to compare infinite
sets, made the point in 1891 that it works for \emph{any} list, however long, even infinite: hand me a complete list of all infinite
strings of two symbols, I'll walk the diagonal flipping as I go, and I'll hand you back a
string that's on no row. So there is no complete list. There are more such strings than there
are places on any list, and that's where ``some infinities are bigger than others'' comes
from. (He wrote the two symbols as m and w, where I'd write 0 and 1, and that paper wasn't even his
first proof of the fact. The first was in 1874, by a harder road through the real numbers, and in
1891 he called the new one much simpler. The diagonal was him finding the easy way.)

Now look at what the argument \emph{did}, because it's going to do the same thing again and again,
in new clothes, and I want you to recognise it each time. (Not every name below is a
flipped diagonal in the table sense. Kleene's theorem is the tool that makes the diagonal
buildable, Rice's is the general form, the one from Ken Thompson, who built the
original Unix operating system at Bell Labs, is an attack that uses the same
trick, and the last, Lawvere's, is the theorem that makes them all one.) There was a table: rows are the things being
listed, columns are questions, each cell says ``does row i do column j.'' There was the
diagonal: the cells where a thing is asked about \emph{itself}. There was a flip: something with no
fixed point, like turning yes into no, applied along the diagonal. And the thing that got
refuted was \emph{the assumed object}, the complete list. Nothing outside the assumption was
