touched. Table, diagonal, flip, and the assumption eats itself. Hold those four.

\subsection{The same move, again and again}

Russell, 1902, from Section~\ref{sec:structure}: the collection of all collections that don't contain themselves.
That's Cantor's flipped diagonal with ``contains'' as the table, and Russell said as much, in
\emph{The Principles of Mathematics} in 1903. He got there, he wrote, by running Cantor's argument
on a supposed collection of everything, which ought to be the biggest collection there is. What got
refuted was the assumed object, the collection of everything, and Zermelo's fix was to stop
assuming it.

Jules Richard, 1905, in a short note in a French science review: some phrases (his were in French) define real numbers (``the ratio of a circle's
circumference to its diameter''); there are only countably many phrases, so list the numbers
they define in order; run Cantor's diagonal down their decimal expansions and you get a real
number no phrase defines, except that you just defined it, in the phrase that describes the
diagonal. The lesson I take from that one is the lesson this whole
section turns on: keep apart the language a system \emph{talks in} and the language you use to
talk \emph{about} it. Mix them and the diagonal bites you.

Richard's paradox has a cousin small enough to do at the table, and it comes with a footnote I
can't resist. Russell, the first to put it in print, in 1906, credited it to G. G. Berry, a
junior librarian at the Bodleian Library in Oxford. A paradox that has outlived empires, and it
came from the library desk. In the version in \emph{Principia Mathematica} it's about syllables. Take
the phrase ``the least integer not nameable in fewer than nineteen syllables.'' There are only
so many phrases shorter than nineteen syllables, so they name only so many numbers, so some
least number is left over, and the phrase picks it out. Now count the phrase: the, least,
in-te-ger, not, name-a-ble, in, few-er, than, nine-teen, syl-la-bles. Eighteen. In eighteen
syllables it has named the number that can't be named in fewer than nineteen. Same lesson as Richard's, in a smaller coat: ``nameable'' is a word about the
language, used inside the language, and that's where the bite is.

Kurt Gödel, 1931, with an improvement in 1936 by Barkley Rosser, a logician who had studied under
Alonzo Church at Princeton and whose trick lets the theorem assume only that the system is
consistent: the big one, and I'll say exactly
what it says, because every word of it is carrying weight. Take any consistent formal system with a mechanically checkable list
of axioms that can do a bit of arithmetic. Then there are sentences it can neither prove nor
refute. The engine is a lemma that lets you build, for any property you can write down, a
sentence that the system proves \emph{equivalent} to that property holding of the sentence's own
code number. Apply it to ``not provable'' and you get a sentence equivalent, inside the
system, to its own unprovability. Table: sentences by code. Diagonal: a sentence about its
own code. Flip: provable to not-provable. Two cautions the Stanford Encyclopedia stresses, and
I'll repeat them. The sentence doesn't literally ``say'' anything about itself. It's provably
\emph{equivalent} to a claim about its code, which is less mystical and more exact. And the
theorem doesn't say the sentence is unknowable. It says \emph{this one system} can't settle it.

And how did the world take it? Mostly, at first, it didn't. Gödel, twenty-four years old,
announced the first theorem during a round-table discussion on the last day of a conference in
Königsberg in September 1930, and by the account of Solomon Feferman, one of the editors of
Gödel's collected works, the room met it with general incomprehension. Except for one man. John
von Neumann pulled Gödel aside to talk about it, kept thinking about it, and a couple of months
later saw that the argument gave something more: a consistent system of this kind can't prove
its own consistency. He wrote to Gödel with it in a letter dated 20 November 1930. Gödel had
already got there. His paper had reached the journal three days earlier, with that
second theorem announced in it, and von Neumann left the credit with Gödel. It's the
``somebody got there first'' shape from the opening chapter, with one difference: here the man
who got there second was von Neumann.

Alan Turing, 1936. I'd always taken it that Turing proved the halting problem undecidable, and
here I had to go and look. The set theorist Joel David Hamkins and his coauthor Theodor Nenu went
back to the 1936 paper and report that the word ``halting,'' the modern statement, and the
self-referential proof everyone teaches are all, strictly speaking, absent from it. What Turing
proved undecidable were two other questions about his machines (whether a machine prints
infinitely many digits; whether it ever prints a given symbol). The second is \emph{equivalent} to
halting and the first is strictly harder. So their answer cuts both ways, and they say so: Turing
never stated the halting problem, and he essentially proved it, because his second question is a
short translation away from it. The name came later. Martin Davis seems to have been the first to
write ``halting problem,'' in a book of 1958, and Stephen Kleene had already stated the problem,
without that name, in his 1952 textbook \emph{Introduction to Metamathematics}. The textbook version is still right as mathematics, and here it is, on two index
cards. Card A is the Checker: hand it any program card and it announces ``halts'' or ``runs
forever.'' Card B is the Contrarian: ``Hand me to the Checker. If it says I halt, run forever.
If it says I run forever, stop.'' Hand B to A. Either answer is wrong. There's no Checker.
Table: programs by programs. Diagonal: a program run on itself. Flip: halt to loop.

Stephen Kleene, 1938, the logician whose textbook I just mentioned, and this is the one that turns the paradox into a tool, so slow down.
Everything above needs the self-referring object to \emph{exist}: Gödel's sentence has to be
buildable, the Contrarian has to be able to ``hand me to the Checker.'' Kleene's second
recursion theorem says: for any transformation of programs you can compute, there's a
program that behaves exactly as if it had been handed its own source code. Any program may
be written as though it already had a copy of itself in hand. He stated it almost in passing, in a paper
on something else, and proved it in the last two lines of one of its sections. I have that count
from Yiannis Moschovakis, a logician at UCLA and Athens who wrote a 2009 paper on it called
``Kleene's Amazing Second Recursion Theorem,'' and he calls it a little
gem. It's the reason ``programs that print their own source'' exist in
every programming language that can compute whatever
a Turing machine can (they're called quines, after a philosopher I'll come to in a moment; try ``Print the
following twice, the second time in quotes: `Print the following twice, the second time in
quotes:'\,'' and obey it). Self-reference in computation isn't a paradox. It's a construction.
The paradoxes happened only when someone assumed an \emph{unrestricted} collection or language;
the theorem happens when you build the self-referrer honestly.

And where does the word quine come from? Not from the philosopher himself. Douglas Hofstadter
coined it in 1979, in \emph{Gödel, Escher, Bach}, in honour of Willard Van Orman Quine, who had
made a long study of self-reference that works indirectly. Quine left a sentence you can take
apart at the table, from a 1962 essay on paradox. Here it is, all of it: ``yields falsehood when
preceded by its quotation'' yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation. Do what it says.
Take the part in quotation marks, put a quoted copy of it in front of itself, and look at what
you've built: it's the whole sentence, word for word. So the sentence says that it itself is
false. That's the liar paradox, but look at how it got there: no ``this sentence'' anywhere, no
pointing at itself, just an instruction to quote and copy, the same move as the print-twice
instruction above. That's Kleene's trick in plain English, and it's why the paradox and the tool
look so alike. The paradox is what you get when the copy asserts something about its own truth.
The tool is what you get when the copy just does something.

Henry Rice, 1953, whom you met briefly in Section~\ref{sec:windows}: the general form. Any property that depends only on what a program \emph{does},
whatever its text, and that's true of some programs and false of others, has no
algorithm that decides it for all programs. ``Does this program halt'' is one such property.
``Does this program ever output 7'' is another. ``Does this program contain an if-statement''
isn't, because that's about the text. One standard proof goes straight through Kleene.

And the one that's actually an attack: Ken Thompson, in his Turing Award lecture, published in 1984.
Build a compiler that, when it compiles the login program, plants a back door, and when it
compiles \emph{a compiler}, plants both habits into that one too. Then delete the trick from the
source. The compiled compiler still carries it, and recompiling a clean source with the
poisoned binary re-plants it, forever. Reading the source never reveals it. A locksmith
teaches an apprentice to cut a spare for every town-hall key and to teach \emph{that} to every
apprentice they train, and never to write it in the manual; years later the manual is
spotless and every locksmith in town cuts the spare. That's the recursion theorem with a
knife in it, and his moral was that you can't trust code you didn't write entirely yourself,
which is a sentence I'll come back to in Section~\ref{sec:coq} when I tell you what the trusted base of this
book is.

And Thompson wasn't first either, and he said so. Pull on the lecture's acknowledgment the way
the opening chapter pulled on Bitcoin's footnotes: he writes that he first read of the
possibility in an Air Force critique of the security of an early implementation of Multics, a
time-sharing system from the 1960s, and that he couldn't find a more specific reference to it,
and he asks anyone who can to send him one. The critique is Paul Karger and Roger Schell's 1974
security evaluation of Multics, which already described a trap door planted in a compiler that,
because the compiler is written in its own language, keeps itself alive. So the knife was in the drawer
ten years before the lecture was printed. Then the obvious next question: is there any way out, or is
``trust no binary you didn't build'' the bottom? There's a partial answer, and it took a while.
David A. Wheeler, in a 2005 paper and a 2009 dissertation at George Mason University, worked out
\emph{diverse double-compiling}: compile the suspect compiler's source with a second,
independently made compiler, use the result to compile that source again, and compare the
output bit for bit with the suspect binary. If they match, the binary really is what its source
says, unless both compilers were poisoned in the same way. The trust doesn't vanish. It moves,
from one compiler to the claim that two unrelated ones weren't rigged together. That's the shape
of every stopping point in this book. You don't reach the bottom. You reach a place where you can
say exactly what you're trusting.

Bill Lawvere, in 1969, proved a fixed-point theorem that, as I read it, makes all of these one theorem in disguise: if a set can be mapped
onto all the functions from itself to some target, then every function on the target has a
fixed point; so if the target has a function with no fixed point (a flip), no such covering
exists. Cantor, Russell, Gödel, halting, as instances of one shape. Noson Yanofsky retold it
in 2003 without the category theory. I mention it because ``it's the same wall'' is a claim I
make below, and I want you to know it's fair at the level of \emph{proof shape}, and that every
instance has its own boundary of \emph{who counts as a decider}, and that boundary is exactly
where most overclaims live.

\subsection{Four things it doesn't give you}

Before I point this at a system with a record, here are four conclusions the theorem doesn't reach.
Each one looks as if it follows, and I wanted to see exactly where each one stops.

``Gödel shows minds aren't machines.'' John Lucas, a philosopher who spent thirty-six years as a
fellow of Merton College, Oxford, argued it in 1961, in a paper called ``Minds, Machines and
Gödel.'' Roger Penrose, the Oxford mathematical physicist who later shared a Nobel prize for his
work on how black holes form, revived it twice, in two books, \emph{The Emperor's New Mind} in 1989
and \emph{Shadows of the Mind} in 1994. I'm sure of who argued it and when. Whether they're right is
the question, and the standard replies, as far as I can tell, have held up: the Gödel sentence is true \emph{only if the system
is consistent}, so a human who ``sees'' its truth has to know the system is consistent, which
is the hard part; and nobody can build the Gödel sentence of a system they can't specify, so
humans might be machines too complicated to diagonalise. The theorem has a conditional in it
and the argument drops the conditional.

And here's the part that's easy to miss: Gödel himself didn't go as far as Lucas. In a lecture
on the day after Christmas in 1951, at a meeting of the American Mathematical Society at Brown
University, he drew from his own theorems only an either-or. Either the human mind, even inside
pure mathematics, infinitely surpasses the powers of any finite machine, or there are problems
about whole numbers, of a certain simple kind, that no proof the human mind can conceive will
ever settle. Feferman, writing about that lecture, says Gödel privately believed the first half
and still stated only the disjunction, because he didn't have a knock-down argument against the
machine side. Gödel wrote soon afterward that he meant to publish the lecture, and never did; the
text sat among his papers until after his death. So the man whose theorem gets quoted for
``minds aren't machines'' stated an either-or and left the deciding to whoever came next. That's
the conditional again, kept, by the person with the most right to drop it.

``Undecidable means unknowable.'' Two senses share the word: a problem with no single
algorithm correct on every instance, and a sentence independent of one particular system.
Neither means nobody can know a given answer. Any single instance is decidable, trivially:
for any one program, one of ``say yes'' and ``say no'' is right. What's ruled out is one
\emph{inside} procedure that's right on \emph{every} case.

``Everything interesting is undecidable.'' Rice is about behavioural properties over \emph{all}
programs. It says nothing against checking the text, nothing against deciding for specific
programs, nothing against analyses allowed to say ``I don't know,'' nothing against finite-state
model checking or type checking. Real compilers are limited by cost and by choosing to be
sound-but-incomplete. The diagonal isn't what stops them.

``Self-reference is a paradox.'' It's a theorem with a construction. Kleene, quines, Thompson.

\subsection{Now point it at the record}

Here's the question Section~\ref{sec:shadow-exact} left open, with nothing in it but what Parts I to III have built. A
system steps; a record rides along and latches on an event (Section~\ref{sec:latch}); when the event is a
certification, Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} said the reading, with its object and its paid event behind it, is what lets an
auditor treat a claim as established, and for a claim that a shortcut is sound, that's what
makes the shortcut \emph{admissible}. So: can a system like that have, as one of its own programs, a procedure that
correctly decides, for every program, ``does this program admit a sound shortcut''? That
would be autopilot. Hand it any program and it says yes or no, and it's always right.

That's the question in plain words, and the checked statement is narrower, so here it is
before the proof. In the theorem, ``admits a shortcut'' is any property of programs with two
features: two programs that behave alike agree on it, and there's one program that has it
and one that doesn't. That's all the argument gets to look at. The diagonal doesn't see
soundness. Each system that wants the wall picks its own property, and whether that
property lines up with being entitled to soundness in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}'s sense is a separate fact about that system,
checked one system at a time if it's checked at all. A procedure that returns soundness
records for some programs, or only for restricted inputs, or with outside evidence, is not
what the wall rules out.

So in the theorem ``shortcut'' is a label. The plain-words gloss at the end of
Section~\ref{sec:shadow-exact}, leaning on a record so the thing isn't worked out again, is about
\emph{how} a program gets its answer, and how is exactly what extensionality throws away: the
theorem only gets to see what programs do, and it treats any two that do the same as one. A
question like ``is there a cheaper program that gives the same answers?'' isn't the theorem's
question, and a wall for it would need a different theorem. The nearest thing I know of is Manuel
Blum's speedup theorem, from 1967, and it goes somewhere stranger: there are computable functions
with no fastest program at all, where every program for the function has another that's faster on
all but finitely many inputs. That's a fact about cost. It isn't a wall about deciding, and nothing
in this book proves anything in that territory.

The answer is no, under premises. The proof is the two index cards, and I'll give you the
premises because they're the whole content. Suppose there were such a decider, one that says yes
exactly when a program admits a shortcut. Build the
flip: ``if the decider says yes about me, behave like a program that admits no shortcut; if
it says no, behave like one that does.'' If the system has a recursion theorem (a program
can be handed its own code), and if that flip is one of the transformations the system can
carry out, and if ``admits a shortcut'' depends only on behaviour (two programs that behave
the same agree on it), and if there's at least one program each way, then there's a program
that behaves exactly like its own flip, and whatever the decider says about it is wrong.
Both cases close in a line each. That's \code{structural\_shortcut\_undecidable}, which rules out a decider that says yes if and
only if a program admits a shortcut, stated for \emph{any}
substrate with those fields. (A substrate here is the bare shape the class asks for: programs, a run that may fail
to give back a state, a counter with a step relation it never goes down along, an
encoding of programs as data, a notion of ``representable'' transformation, and the recursion
theorem for those. Nothing about what the states are made of. The smallest checked
instance is the nat family below.) It's Rice's trick one floor over, and I should be careful
with that. Rice's theorem is stated for the functions Turing machines compute. This wall is
the same diagonal with different premises: it carries its own recursion theorem and its own
list of representable transformations, and it picks the property. So it isn't a corollary
of Rice as Rice stated it, and it doesn't show that any property is harder or easier to decide
than classical halting. And
here's something about its proof that I want you to have: it never touches the counter,
the toll, or the step relation. It uses the recursion theorem, representability of the flip,
the two witnesses, and extensionality, and nothing else. (The file's header calls the
substrates it covers ones that respect the toll. The
proof uses neither the toll nor the counter's climbing. It's the diagonal, clean.)

Here's the setting and the wall, with every word pinned down so you can poke at it.

\begin{definition}[Substrate]\label{def:u12-substrate}
A \emph{substrate} has a type of states, a type $\mathrm{Prog}$ of programs, and a run map that
takes a program and a state and either gives back a state or gives nothing. It has a counter
$\mu$ on states and a step relation along which $\mu$ never decreases; an encoding
$\mathrm{enc}$ of programs as states with a decoder $\mathrm{dec}$ such that
$\mathrm{dec}(\mathrm{enc}(p)) = p$; and a predicate $\mathrm{Rep}$ on maps
$f : \mathrm{Prog} \to \mathrm{Prog}$, the transformations the substrate counts as its own.
Two programs are \emph{equivalent}, $p \simeq q$, when $\mathrm{run}(p, s) = \mathrm{run}(q, s)$
for every state $s$. The last field is the \emph{recursion theorem}: for every $f$ with
$\mathrm{Rep}(f)$ there is a program $p$ with $p \simeq f(p)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Shortcut predicate]\label{def:u12-shortcut-predicate}
A \emph{shortcut predicate} on a substrate is a property $A$ of programs with two programs $y$ and
$n$ such that $A(y)$ holds, $A(n)$ fails, and $A$ is extensional: $p \simeq q$ implies
$A(p) \iff A(q)$. For a Boolean function $d$ on programs, its \emph{flip} is
$f_d(p) = n$ if $d(p)$ is true and $f_d(p) = y$ if $d(p)$ is false.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[No inside decider]\label{thm:u12-no-inside-decider}
Let a substrate carry a shortcut predicate $A$ with witnesses $y$ and $n$. Then there is no
Boolean function $d$ on programs such that $\mathrm{Rep}(f_d)$ holds and, for every program
$p$, $d(p) = \mathrm{true} \iff A(p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $d$ is such a function. Since $\mathrm{Rep}(f_d)$, the recursion theorem gives a
program $p$ with $p \simeq f_d(p)$. Split on $d(p)$. If $d(p)$ is true, then $A(p)$ holds by
correctness, and $f_d(p) = n$, so $p \simeq n$, and extensionality turns $A(p)$ into $A(n)$,
which fails. If $d(p)$ is false, then $A(p)$ fails by correctness, and $f_d(p) = y$, so
$p \simeq y$, and extensionality turns $A(y)$ into $A(p)$. Both cases are contradictions. The
argument uses the recursion theorem once, the two witnesses, extensionality, and nothing
about $\mu$, the step relation, or the encoding.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{structural\_shortcut\_undecidable} (StructuralUndecidability.v; the correctness it
rules out is $d(p)$ true exactly when $A(p)$), stated over the
class \code{Substrate} (Substrate.v) and its extension \code{WithShortcutPredicate}. Every field named
above is a premise; the theorem is about every substrate that supplies them.

So the wall is there. Now the honest part: \emph{who counts as a decider}. The theorem rules out
a decider whose flip the substrate can itself represent. It says nothing about a decider
standing \emph{outside}, and an outside decider can exist for the very same property, correct on
every program. That's the boundary of the sentence, and the boundary is
Richard's lesson: the language you talk about a system in is a different language from the one it
talks in.
You'll see it in miniature in a minute, on the nat family, with a pencil.

Two forms of the wall live in this section, and they're honest in different ways.

The \emph{nat family} (\code{nat\_self\_undecidable}): a tiny substrate built so that program two is the
Contrarian for a given candidate decider d, and for every d, d is wrong about program two. It's
a \emph{family}, one instance per d, and its recursion theorem holds by construction. It's the
index cards made formal and nothing more.

\begin{theorem}[The nat family]\label{thm:u12-nat-family}
Fix any Boolean function $d$ on $\mathbb{N}$. Let the substrate $N_d$ have programs and
states $\mathbb{N}$; program 0 returns 1, program 1 returns 0, program 2 returns 0 if $d(2)$
is true and 1 if it is false, and every other program gives nothing; $\mu$ is constantly 0;
$\mathrm{Rep}(f)$ holds when $f(p) = 1$ for every $p$ with $d(p)$ true and $f(p) = 0$ for
every other $p$; and $A(p)$ holds when program $p$ returns 1 on input 0. Then it is not the
case that $d(p) = \mathrm{true} \iff A(p)$ for every $p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The recursion theorem of $N_d$ holds with the fixed witness 2: for a representable $f$,
$f(2)$ is 1 or 0 according to $d(2)$, and program 2 returns exactly what that program
returns. The witnesses for $A$ are 0 and 1. The flip of $d$ is representable by the
definition of $\mathrm{Rep}$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:u12-no-inside-decider} applies to $d$ itself. Directly:
$A(2)$ holds exactly when $d(2)$ is false.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{nat\_self\_undecidable} (NatSubstrateInstance.v), with the built-in recursion
theorem \code{nat\_recursion\_theorem}; the general form, no decider whose flip is representable in
$N_d$, is \code{nat\_structural\_shortcut\_undecidable} in the same file.

Now push on it once more, because the nat family shows the outside decider in three lines,
and you can do them yourself. Stand outside $N_d$, knowing $d$. Write down a new decider
$e$: say yes on program 0, say ``not $d(2)$'' on program 2, and say no on everything else.
Check it against $A$. Program 0 returns 1, so $A(0)$ holds and $e$ says yes. Program 1
returns 0, so $A(1)$ fails and $e$ says no. Program 2 returns 1 exactly when $d(2)$ is false,
and that's what $e$ says. Every other program gives nothing, so $A$ fails and $e$ says no.
So $e$ is right about every program. Does that break the wall? No, and here's the bit that
matters: in $N_d$ a flip is representable only if it says 1 exactly where $d$ says yes, so
the flip of $e$ is representable only if $e$ and $d$ agree everywhere, and they disagree at
program 2. The correct decider exists; its flip just isn't one of the substrate's own moves.
(That one isn't a separate theorem in the Coq. It's three lines and a pencil, and you just
did it.) Undecidable from inside and decided cleanly from outside, at the same time, about
the same property. That's not a paradox. It's two different people asking.

And the one where the recursion theorem is \emph{proved} from the rules, with nothing assumed, which is why it exists:
\emph{L}, the weak call-by-value lambda calculus that Yannick Forster and Gert Smolka presented in
2017 as a model of computation in Coq, and which a group at Saarland has since used as the
seed of a whole library of undecidable problems. The development here builds its own copy of
L from the reduction rules, so the L results below assume nothing from that library. There,
\code{L\_recursion\_theorem} is a theorem with a proof, Rice's theorem follows (\code{L\_rice}), halting
follows (\code{L\_halting\_undecidable}), and the diagonal is reproved in the shape of the substrate
theorem (\code{L\_structural\_shortcut\_undecidable}), for any property of programs that depends only
on what they compute and that holds of one program and fails of another. The statement
mentions no shortcut. That's the diagonal for a fixed model with nothing assumed. It isn't an instance of the generic class
(the class wants a run map that always answers, with a state or with nothing, and L's evaluation
can run forever without ever answering), so it's the argument \emph{reproved}. The
generic theorem isn't \emph{applied} here. Both are true; they're different sentences.

Here's what that string of words means, because L is the strangest thing in this book that
computes, and the smallest. The lambda calculus is Alonzo Church's, from the 1930s, and it's
a programming language with one idea in it: functions. A term is one of three things. A
variable. A function, written $\lambda$ followed by its body, the body saying what to do with
whatever you hand it. Or one term applied to another, written side by side. Running a program
is one move, over and over: when a function meets an argument, put the argument into the body
where the variable was. No numbers, no memory, no instructions, and in 1937 Turing published a proof that
it computes exactly what his machines compute. ``Weak call-by-value'' is two house rules about
the order of moves: an argument is run down to a finished function (a \emph{value}) before it's
put in, and nothing runs inside a function that hasn't been handed anything yet. Variables
are written as numbers counting how many $\lambda$s back they were bound (a trick of Nicolaas
de Bruijn, who ran the Automath proof-checking project at Eindhoven from 1967 and comes back in
Section~\ref{sec:coq}; it means two variables can never get mixed up by sharing a name), and a term is \emph{closed}
when every variable in it is bound inside it, so it leans on nothing outside. Last piece: to
hand a program to a program, L needs a way to write any term as data, the way a program's
source is a string you can pass around. The one used here is the \emph{Scott encoding}, named for
Dana Scott, a student of Church's who went on to build mathematical models of the lambda calculus
itself. As far as I can trace it, the encoding first appeared in lecture notes of his from Berkeley
in 1962 that he never published. All you need about it is that every term $t$ gets one \emph{code}, written
$\ulcorner t \urcorner$, and the code is itself a closed value. Two tools get built on top of
that in the proof: a \emph{quoting} term $Q$ that takes the code of a term to the code of that
code (a program that prints its own source needs exactly this move), and a \emph{fixed-point
combinator}, a term that lets a function call itself, which is how $Q$ works its way through
a code of any size.

\begin{definition}[L, as built here]\label{def:u12-L}
A term of L is a variable (a de Bruijn number), an application $s\,t$, or an abstraction
$\lambda s$; the values are the abstractions. One step is weak call-by-value, left to right:
$(\lambda b)\,v$ steps to $b$ with $v$ substituted when $v$ is a value, a step inside the
left part of an application is a step of the application, and so is a step inside the right
part once the left part is a value. A term $s$ \emph{evaluates to} $v$ when $s$ reaches $v$ in
some number of steps and $v$ is a value; $p \equiv q$ when $p$ and $q$ evaluate to the same
values. Every term $t$ has a code $\ulcorner t \urcorner$, its Scott encoding, which is a
closed value. A map $f$ on terms is \emph{L-computable} when some closed value $s$ has
$s\,\ulcorner p \urcorner \equiv f(p)$ for every $p$. A term $D$ \emph{decides} a property $P$ of
terms when, for every $p$, $D\,\ulcorner p \urcorner$ reaches $\lambda\lambda.1$ (true) if
$P(p)$ holds and $\lambda\lambda.0$ (false) if it fails. $P$ is \emph{extensional} when
$p \equiv q$ and $P(p)$ give $P(q)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Recursion, Rice and halting for L]\label{thm:u12-L}
(1) For every closed value $s$ there is a closed term $t$ that reaches
$s\,\ulcorner t \urcorner$; hence every L-computable $f$ has a term $p$ with $p \equiv f(p)$.
(2) Let $P$ be extensional, with $P(y)$ and not $P(n)$ for closed terms $y$ and $n$. Then no
closed term decides $P$. (3) No closed term decides halting, the property of evaluating to
some value.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) A closed quoting term $Q$ takes $\ulcorner t \urcorner$ to the code of
$\ulcorner t \urcorner$; its constructors, recursive program and terminating induction are given in
Appendix~\ref{sec:quoting-construction}. A closed
term $\mathrm{mkapp}$ takes two codes to the code of their application. Let
$A = \lambda x.\, s\,(\mathrm{mkapp}\ x\ (Q\,x))$ and $t = A\,\ulcorner A \urcorner$. One step
gives $s\,(\mathrm{mkapp}\ \ulcorner A \urcorner\ (Q\,\ulcorner A \urcorner))$, and the argument
reduces to $\ulcorner A\,\ulcorner A \urcorner \urcorner = \ulcorner t \urcorner$. For the
second half, take $s$ computing $f$; then $t \equiv s\,\ulcorner t \urcorner \equiv f(t)$.
(2) Given a closed decider $D$, the flip
$\lambda x.\, D\,x\,(\lambda\_.\,n)\,(\lambda\_.\,y)\,(\lambda z.z)$ is a closed value; on the
code of $p$ it reaches $n$ when $D$ answers true and $y$ when $D$ answers false. Take its $t$
from (1). If $P(t)$, then $t \equiv n$ and $P(n)$; if not, $t \equiv y$ and $P(t)$. Both are
contradictions. (3) Halting is extensional; apply (2) with $y = \lambda z.z$ and
$n = (\lambda x.\,x\,x)(\lambda x.\,x\,x)$, which steps only to itself and so never reaches a
value.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{second\_recursion}, \code{L\_recursion\_theorem}, \code{L\_rice}, and \code{L\_halting\_undecidable}
(LRecursion.v), with the quoting term's specification \code{Q\_spec} and the substrate-shaped form \code{L\_structural\_shortcut\_undecidable} (no decider whose flip L can
compute says true exactly when the property holds) in the same file. The file uses only Coq's standard library.

That's the wall on paper, on a family built to fit it, and on one outside model with nothing
assumed. The machine built in Part IV fills in this same shape with nothing assumed either: on
its host machine, the one the universal program runs on, which has a counter for every whole number,
programs are numbers, Kleene's recursion theorem is a theorem, and so is Rice's, and the fixed point
can be taken to agree on what the program computes and also on the ledger and the flag
(Section~\ref{sec:small-diagonal}).

Here's the picture all of that fills in, lined up against Turing's, one column per axis.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.482\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Time axis} & \textbf{Structural axis} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
counts: steps & counts: $\mu$ \\
asks: does it halt? & asks: does it admit the shortcut? \\
the wall: no Turing machine decides halting & the wall: no decider whose flip is representable, under a recursion theorem \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

Read the table as two uses of one diagonal, each under its own premises. That's all it says.
The structural wall never uses $\mu$; the $\mu$ entry only says what that axis counts. The
nat result is a family indexed by the candidate decider, and L's results are about one fixed
model and properties that mention no shortcut. Neither hands you a second fixed undecidable
problem, and neither separates Turing degrees: a property can sit behind the wall from inside
and be decided cleanly from outside, as the pencil argument on $N_d$ showed. And ``admits the
shortcut'' in the right-hand column is the theorem's sense, any behavioural property with a yes and
a no. ``Has a cheaper way to the same answer'' is a second question, and the column has no wall for it.

\subsection{How to kill it}

Three ways, and I mean them as instructions.

One: produce, for some substrate with a shortcut predicate, a decider whose flip the
substrate can represent and that's correct on every program. That breaks the generic proof
at a named step, and I've named the steps.

Two: for the nat family, produce a d that correctly decides the predicate of the substrate
built from d.

Three: for L, produce a closed term that decides some extensional property holding of one
closed term and failing of another. That breaks \code{L\_rice}, which rests on the reduction rules
and Coq's standard library and nothing else.

An outside decider alone doesn't count against any of the three; the pencil argument on
$N_d$ is why.

\subsection{What this does to the book}

It does two things. It keeps me honest: nothing in what follows claims that a system with a
record can check its own shortcuts on autopilot, because that's a wall, the same wall, and I
showed you the bricks. And it tells you what a record \emph{can} do, which is the thing Part III
has been about since the counter: it can carry a shortcut \emph{with its receipt}, so that the question
``was this earned'' is answered by an event you can point at. No decider has to exist for that,
which is lucky, because on a system with a recursion theorem no inside one can. The
diagonal says such a system can't automate the judgement from inside, for any behavioural property with a yes and a no. The latch
says you can record the commitment. Those are different jobs, and a record does the second.

The diagonal has a famous cousin that seems like it ought to bite a record too, so let me walk
right up to it. Gödel's second theorem says a consistent system strong enough for arithmetic can't
prove its own consistency, and Martin Löb, a logician answering another logician's question, sharpened that in 1955: if such a system proves ``if this
is provable, it's true,'' it already proves the thing itself. So can a record vouch for itself, and
does Löb stop it? My first guess was that Löb stops it, since a record looked like a system talking about itself.
Here's where I landed instead, and mostly it's a relief. Hold two things side by
side: ``there's a receipt for this somewhere,'' and the receipt in your hand. Löb's theorem is
about \emph{provability}, the bare claim that some proof exists, the receipt somewhere. A record of the kind this book
keeps is a different animal: an event, a check of some claim that passed, a commitment to
it, and a certificate, at a definite step of the run. The receipt in your hand. It doesn't say
which claim or which step, as the two runs in Section~\ref{sec:small-diagonal} show; it says the
event happened. Sergei Artemov, the logician from the opening chapter, drew
exactly that line in 2001, between implicit provability (``there is a proof'') and explicit
evidence (``this is a proof''). As I read him, for explicit evidence the reflection step ``if
this is a proof of $F$, then $F$'' is harmless, while for the bare ``there is a proof'' it's what
Gödel and Löb forbid. Why, in my words: a receipt in your hand you can look at, and a receipt
somewhere you take on the system's own word. A record sits on the explicit side.

Push on that and it gives, because a receipt is only as good as whoever wrote it. Its trust rests
on the checker meaning what it says, and that gets settled once, from outside the machine. I don't
think it can be moved inside, and Gödel's second theorem is my reason. The theorem says a
consistent system strong enough for arithmetic can't prove its own consistency, and a checker
vouching for itself would be doing something close to that. That last step is my reading. The
theorem itself stops at consistency. So I didn't get rid of the receipt
somewhere. I moved it out of the machine and handed it to whoever reads the record. Try to move that proof inside the
system, so it can certify its own checker or a successor's, and you hit exactly the wall Eliezer
Yudkowsky and Marcello Herreshoff named the Löbian obstacle in 2013, writing about agents that
want to trust their own rewrites. As I understand their draft report, they came at it from the
far side, an agent wanting to trust a successor's proofs the way it trusts its own. Same arrow,
pointed forward, same wall.

One more thing falls out of the same picture, and it's a short argument with no checked
theorem behind it, so take it at that weight. Can a record rest on itself, the way the sentence ``this
sentence is certified'' would like to? Not if it's earned and permanent. The check that a
certificate stands on happened while the record was still down, because the record goes up only
after that check passes, and once up it never comes back down. So no claim whose truth needs the record already up can
be the claim a certificate stands on. Saul Kripke's 1975 theory of truth calls a sentence like
that, one that only ever leans on itself, ungrounded, and earned records are grounded in his
sense: every one bottoms out in a check that didn't lean on it. Caspar Oesterheld's 2019 work on
programs that cooperate by simulating each other needed a grounding step of the same kind to stop
an infinite regress. I haven't checked this in Coq, and I'm not claiming more than the paragraph
says.

One last distinction, because the two are easy to conflate and conflating them is the
easiest way to misread this book. There's a \emph{second} wall, nothing to do with the diagonal.
It's Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s kind of wall, a window with a colliding pair in it. Two states that differ in their
certification reading can look identical through a window that doesn't show that reading,
the stamp inside the closed drawer and the drawer opened and shut, and then no function of
the window recovers the reading (Theorem~\ref{thm:fibre}: a decoder has to give one answer on
everything the window lumps together). That's missing information. Nothing about it is undecidable; it holds for finite things with
nothing to compute; and it sits \emph{beside} Rice. None of Rice is underneath it. The property the diagonal uses (any behavioural property of programs with a yes and
a no) is a different kind of thing from the reading the window hides, and nothing here says
the two are the same. Two walls, two axes. The diagonal is about what no inside procedure can
decide. The window is about what no outside observer can see. I'll need both, and I'll try
not to call one by the other's name again. The machine I build later has a colliding pair of
exactly that kind (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-separation}).

%===========================================================================
\section{Five small models}
\label{sec:models}
%===========================================================================

A toll, a counter, two kinds of wall and a latch, and every one of them shown on paper, on
cups and cards and dice I made up. I've been building a toy and claiming it's the smallest
version of something people actually do. Time to go and look at what people actually do. I picked five systems that keep
records other people rely on, with real money or real security behind them, and asked each
the one question this book is about: \emph{is there a price on the moment the record is written?}
Not on the work around it. On the write. I'll tell you the answer first, because it's a
single sentence and it surprised me: of the five specifications, read through the
transcriptions I made of them, only one prices the write, and that one has a leak at exactly
the place Section~\ref{sec:counter} said a counter leaks, where it goes down.

Three things are easy to blur in a section like this, so I'll name them now and keep them
apart all the way through. There's the \emph{real specification}: the document real money and
real security run on. There's my \emph{transcription}: one mechanism copied out of that document
into Coq, small enough to check. And for some of the five there's a \emph{wrapper}: a tiny
abstract model that takes one premise as given and says what follows from it. A claim proved
at one level isn't a claim at the level above it. Near the end I'll walk one system, gas,
through all three, so you can see exactly where each claim stops.

What I built for each is a \emph{fragment}: a small Coq model of the one mechanism I'm asking
about, transcribed from the system's own specification where there was one, and nothing
more. Not the system. I'll say for each one what the fragment is and what it isn't, because
``Ethereum has been formalised'' is the kind of sentence that gets a book thrown across a
room, and rightly.

\subsection{Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back}

Ethereum and chains like it decide which blocks are final by having validators, people who've
locked up money (their \emph{stake}), vote on checkpoints: blocks picked out at regular numbered
rounds called \emph{epochs}. A vote isn't for one checkpoint. It's a \emph{link} from a checkpoint the
validator already trusts, the source, to a later one, the target, and every chain starts from
one first block, its \emph{genesis}, which counts as trusted from the start. In the design Vitalik
Buterin and Virgil Griffith published in 2017, called Casper, a checkpoint is \emph{justified}
when validators holding two thirds of the stake vote a link to it from a justified source,
and \emph{finalized} when it is justified and a two-thirds link runs from it to its direct child. The record is
``this checkpoint is final.''

What's priced? Two rules: don't vote for two different targets in the same epoch, and don't
cast a vote whose span, source to target, surrounds the span of another of your votes. Break
either and your deposit can be destroyed, which is called \emph{slashing}. The
theorem they prove, called accountable safety, says that if two \emph{conflicting} checkpoints
are ever both finalized, at least a third of the stake broke a rule and can be slashed. So
the price is on \emph{reversal}, on making the record contradict itself. The write itself,
finalizing, is free: honest validators finalize all day and nobody loses anything.

Do it with three validators. Let A and B vote one branch, B and C vote a competing branch.
Each pair is two of three. Both branches finalize. Now read the rule: B cast two different votes
with the same target epoch. B is the third that gets slashed; A and C are clean. That's what a fork costs
and who pays, and the checked work has exactly this instance (\code{casper\_fork\_exists},
\code{casper\_fork\_slashable}), so the theorem's premise isn't vacuous: forks of that kind can be
built, and the theorem fires on them.

The fragment: a transcription of a published Coq proof of Casper's accountable safety
(the casper-proofs development from Runtime Verification and the University of Texas at
Austin, itself based on Yoichi Hirai's proof in Isabelle, another proof checker; proofs redone on the standard library), with validator sets as predicates and
quorum intersection as a premise. A \emph{quorum} is a set of validators big enough to act, here
two thirds of the stake, and \emph{quorum intersection} is the arithmetic of the three-validator
example: two thirds plus two thirds is four thirds, so any two quorums share at least a
third. The fragment takes the overlap as given. It doesn't do that arithmetic. No deposits,
no rewards, no fork choice (the rule for picking a branch to build on), no connection to
anything else in this book. \code{accountable\_safety}: a finalization fork implies that a set of
validators the size of that overlap, at least a third of the stake, is slashed. And
\code{finalization\_without\_slashing}: a one-validator chain finalizes and nobody's slashed, which
is the ``write is free'' sentence in a degenerate setting, and only there.

Here's the fragment, small enough to read in one sitting. Every name below is from the transcription.

\begin{definition}[Casper setting and votes]\label{def:u13-casper}
A \emph{setting} has a type of validators, a type of block hashes with a parent relation and a
genesis hash, and two classes of validator sets, the ``two-thirds'' sets $Q_1$ and the
``one-third'' sets $Q_2$. It carries two premises: \emph{quorum intersection}, for any two sets in
$Q_1$ some set in $Q_2$ lies inside both; and \emph{at most one parent} per hash. A \emph{state} says,
for each validator, target hash $h$, target epoch $t$ and source epoch $u$, whether that
validator voted the link $(h, t, u)$. A link from $p$ at epoch $u$ to $h$ at epoch $t$ is
\emph{justified by} $q$ when $q \in Q_1$, every member of $q$ voted $(h, t, u)$, $h$ is the
$(t - u)$-th descendant of $p$, and $t > u$. Genesis is justified at epoch 0, and a block
reached from a justified block by a justified link is justified. Block $h$ is \emph{finalized} at
epoch $v$ with child $c$ when $c$ is a child of $h$, $h$ is justified at $v$, and the link
from $h$ at $v$ to $c$ at $v + 1$ is justified. A \emph{finalization fork} is two finalized blocks
$h_1 \ne h_2$, neither an ancestor of the other. A validator is \emph{slashed} when it voted two
different targets with the same target epoch (a double vote), or voted links $(h_1, t_1, u_1)$
and $(h_2, t_2, u_2)$ with $t_1 > t_2$ and $u_2 > u_1$ (a surround vote). The state is
\emph{quorum-slashed} when some set in $Q_2$ consists of slashed validators.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Accountable safety]\label{thm:u13-accountable-safety}
In every setting (so under quorum intersection and at most one parent), every state with a
finalization fork is quorum-slashed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let the fork be $h_1$ finalized at $v_1$ and $h_2$ at $v_2$. If $v_1 = v_2$, the two links into
epoch $v_1 + 1$ are each voted by a set in $Q_1$; quorum intersection gives a set in $Q_2$
that voted both; their targets differ, since equal children would give $h_1$ and $h_2$ the
same child and so, by at most one parent, $h_1 = h_2$. That set double-voted. If
$v_1 \ne v_2$, say $v_1 < v_2$, walk down the chain of justified links that justifies $h_2$,
by strong induction on the epoch gap. Every block on that chain is an ancestor of $h_2$, so
none descends from $h_1$. Some link in the chain starts at or below $v_1$ and lands above
$v_1$. If it lands at $v_1 + 1$, it and the finalization link of $h_1$ have distinct targets at
that epoch, and the intersection set double-voted. If it starts at $v_1$, its source is a
justified block at $v_1$ other than $h_1$, and the links that justified those two blocks give
a double vote the same way. Otherwise it starts below $v_1$ and lands above $v_1 + 1$, so it
surrounds the finalization link of $h_1$, and the intersection set made a surround vote.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{accountable\_safety} (CasperFFG.v), a transcription of the casper-proofs
Core/AccountableSafety file at a pinned commit with proofs redone on the standard library;
validator sets are predicates, and both premises are fields of the setting record, so they
are hypotheses of every theorem. The record reading is \code{conflicting\_records\_are\_priced}
(CasperRecordReading.v).

\begin{theorem}[The premise can hold, and the write is free]\label{thm:u13-casper-instances}
(1) In the three-validator setting where each validator has stake 1, $Q_1$ is the sets of
stake at least two thirds and $Q_2$ the sets of at least one third, the state where A and B
vote one branch and B and C the other has a finalization fork; B is slashed, A and C are
not, and $\{B\}$ is in $Q_2$. (2) In the one-validator chain setting, one vote finalizes
genesis and no validator is slashed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Both are computations on fixed finite data. In (1) B voted two different targets at epoch
1, which is the double vote; A's and C's votes are one link at epoch 1 from source 0 and one
at epoch 2 from source 1, which neither double-vote nor surround.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{casper\_fork\_exists} and \code{casper\_fork\_slashable} (CasperForkWitness.v), and
\code{finalization\_without\_slashing} (CasperRecordReading.v).

One thing that means for the record itself: finality is
revocable at a price, the price is named, and a final block can hold a false statement.

And the obvious next question: is the 2017 design what Ethereum actually runs? Partly, and the
paper's own title is the clue. It's called \emph{Casper the Friendly Finality Gadget}, and its
first sentence says it's a finality system that \emph{overlays} a chain still choosing its blocks
by proof of work. A gadget, bolted on top. In 2020 a larger group, Buterin among them, wrote up
\emph{Gasper}, which joins Casper's finality to a fork-choice rule called LMD GHOST, and on 15
September 2022, in the switch people called the Merge, Ethereum stopped choosing blocks by proof
of work at all and went over to proof of stake. So the checkpoints and the two slashing rules
above are one part of a system that holds real money today, and the transcription is of that
part's safety proof as the 2017 design states it. Everything between the two, the fork choice
and the rest of the running protocol, is the gap between my transcription and the running system, which I walk
through near the end of this section with a photocopied recipe and a kitchen. Does any of that move the price? No. Finalizing is still free for an
honest validator. What costs is contradicting yourself.

\subsection{Gas: the one that prices the write}

Every operation on Ethereum costs \emph{gas}, paid in ether by whoever sent the transaction. The
yellow paper, Ethereum's formal specification, gives the reason in one line: every computation is fee-bearing so the network
can't be abused and halting questions are sidestepped. The record I care about is a nonzero
slot in the shared storage, which every full node in the world (every computer keeping its own complete copy of the
chain) has to keep forever.

And here it is: writing a fresh storage slot from zero to nonzero costs twenty thousand gas,
by the table in the paper's appendix, plus twenty-one hundred for touching a \emph{cold} slot, one
the transaction hasn't touched yet (after the first touch it's \emph{warm}). As I read it, the point
is to discourage storage growth, since storage grows every node's database.
That's a price on the write, at the moment of the write, and it's the only one in the five.

Where does a number like twenty-one hundred come from? Somebody picked it, so the obvious next
question is who, and why, and the answer has a date on it. In September 2016, just as Ethereum's
developers were gathering in Shanghai for Devcon 2, their developer conference (the third one,
since they started counting at zero), attackers started filling
blocks with an operation that was cheap in gas and expensive in fact: it sent every node off to
read data from its disk, and nodes fell behind the chain. The first repair, a fork that October
called Tangerine Whistle, raised the prices of the operations the attack had leaned on. The
cold-slot charge came later, in a proposal by Vitalik Buterin and Martin Swende called EIP-2929,
switched on in the Berlin upgrade of April 2021, and the motivation it gives is still those 2016
attacks. So twenty-one hundred isn't a law of nature or a measurement of anything deep. It's a
scar: a price set after somebody found the place where the old price was wrong. That doesn't
change the argument; the write is still priced at the moment of the write. It does change how I
read the rest of that table: some of its numbers, at least, are somebody's answer to ``what did
this cost last time,'' which is a record of a different kind.

Now the leak, and it's Section~\ref{sec:counter}'s leak. Set a slot and then clear it \emph{in the same transaction} and
you get a refund. Count it through: first write twenty-two thousand one hundred; clearing it
costs a hundred and credits a refund of nineteen thousand nine hundred; net, twenty-three
hundred. That's \code{revoked\_write\_nearly\_free}, and \code{persistent\_write\_priced} is the other half:
leave it set and you pay at least twenty thousand. The write is priced.
The \emph{revoked} write nearly isn't. But I have to add what the fragment leaves out, because twenty-three hundred
on its own misleads: the realized refund is capped at one fifth
of the gas the whole transaction used (that's the 2021 change from Section~\ref{sec:counter}, the one that ended
the refund-hoarding token's advantage). So a real set-then-clear pays a lot more than twenty-three
hundred. How much more? The cap is a fifth of everything the transaction used, and that
includes the twenty-one thousand every transaction pays just for existing. Take a
transaction that does nothing but set and clear the slot: it uses 43,200 gas, so the cap is
8,640, so it pays 34,560, which is 13,560 on top of the base. (Look at the slot alone and
forget the base, which the rule doesn't do, and you'd get 17,760.) Either way it's far above
twenty-three hundred. The counter-level net is twenty-three hundred. The bill is not.

Here's the arithmetic the way the specification has it, so you can redo it with a pencil.

\begin{definition}[One slot in one transaction]\label{def:u13-slot}
A slot run records the slot's value at the start of the transaction (original), its current
value, whether it has been touched (warm), the gas charged so far, and the refund counter.
A store of a new value charges 2100 if the slot is cold, plus 20000 if the slot still holds
its original value, the new value differs, and the original is 0 (2900 if the original is
nonzero), and otherwise 100. It adjusts the refund counter by the specification's rules; in
particular, when the new value equals the original value 0, the refund grows by
$20000 - 100 = 19900$. The run starts fresh: original and current 0, cold, gas and refund 0.
The \emph{net} charge is gas minus refund.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Pricing the persistent write and the revoked one]\label{thm:u13-sstore}
(1) For every list of stores from a fresh slot, if the slot ends nonzero then the net charge
is at least 20000. (2) Storing 1 then 0 leaves the slot at 0 with net charge 2300; storing 1
alone has net charge 22100.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) By induction on the list, with the invariant: while the original value is 0, the net
charge is at least 0 when the current value is 0 and at least 20000 when it is not. Each
store keeps it, which is a finite case split on whether the slot is warm and which of the
original, current and new values are equal. A fresh slot satisfies it. (2) Direct
computation: $2100 + 20000 = 22100$ for the first store, $100$ for the second, refund
$19900$, and $22200 - 19900 = 2300$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{persistent\_write\_priced} and \code{revoked\_write\_nearly\_free} (EVMStorageGas.v),
transcribed from the execution specification's storage instruction and gas table at a
pinned commit. The end-of-transaction refund cap of one fifth is not in the fragment.

The fragment: one slot, one transaction, the gas and refund arithmetic transcribed from the
Ethereum execution specification at a named commit. No stack, no call context, no other
slots, and \emph{no refund cap}; the file says so.

Then the wrapper, which is a different kind of object, and the walk near the end is about
exactly that difference. It's a \emph{gas schedule} in the abstract: any states, any steps, a cost
per step, a yes/no commitment flag, and a charge predicate saying which steps get billed. It
formalises no EVM (the Ethereum virtual machine) at all. It is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s result
with the whole-run ceiling, the one that pins the amount as well as which steps pay, under a new
name, and the file says that too. Its two halves are worth reading separately. Leave one
committing step unbilled, and a one-step run commits for nothing
(\code{undercharged\_opcode\_admits\_free\_commitment}), so the floor fails outright; one missed commit
is enough. Bill one step that doesn't commit, and the schedule charges more than the number
of commits on that one-step run (\code{overcharge\_breaks\_exactness}), so the ceiling fails. And
the class isn't empty: in any system, the bill that charges one exactly on a step that raises
the flag and nothing on any other meets both halves (Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s step price).

And the wrapper itself, which is the cleanest thing in this section and has the least
Ethereum in it.

\begin{definition}[A gas schedule]\label{def:u13-gas-schedule}
A \emph{gas schedule} has states, instructions, a step, a cost $c(s, i) \in \mathbb{N}$ that may
depend on the state, a Boolean commitment flag on states, and a Boolean charge predicate
$\chi(s, i)$, with two premises: a charged step costs at least 1, and an uncharged step costs
0. A step \emph{commits} when it takes the flag from false to true. For a run $t$ from $s$, let
$c(t)$ be its total cost and $n(t)$ its number of committing steps. The schedule has the
\emph{floor} when $c(t) \ge n(t)$ for every run, and \emph{no overcharge} when $c(t) \le n(t)$ for every
run. It has \emph{unit pricing} when $c(s, i) = 1$ if $\chi(s, i)$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Gas schedule exactness]\label{thm:u13-gas-exactness}
For every gas schedule: it has the floor and no overcharge if and only if $\chi(s, i)$ holds
exactly when the step from $s$ by $i$ commits, and it has unit pricing. Moreover, (1) if some
committing step from an uncommitted state is uncharged, that one-step run costs 0 and the
schedule fails the floor; (2) if some charged step does not commit, the schedule
overcharges.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The equivalence is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s characterization with the whole-run ceiling, under another name. From right to left, each step's cost is 1 on a committing step and 0 otherwise, so a
run's cost counts its commitments. From left to right, apply the floor and no overcharge to
one-step runs: a committing step must cost at least 1, so it is charged; a charged step costs
at least 1 and may not exceed its commitment count, so it commits and costs exactly 1. Parts
(1) and (2) are those one-step runs read the other way.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{gas\_schedule\_exactness}, which proves both directions,
\code{undercharged\_opcode\_admits\_free\_commitment},
\code{undercharged\_opcode\_breaks\_certification\_floor} and \code{overcharge\_breaks\_exactness}
(GasMetering.v); \code{gas\_schedule\_exactness} is \code{exact\_commitment\_pricing\_characterization}
(CommitmentPredicateAdequacy.v) carried over unchanged.

Gas prices storage growth and computation. It says
nothing about whether what's stored is true.

\subsection{Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past}

A trusted platform module, the small chip on most laptop motherboards, keeps a handful of
registers that can only be \emph{extended}: the new value is a hash of the old value together
with a digest (a short hash) of whatever software just loaded. You can't set them; you can
only fold more in. A \emph{quote} is the chip signing those register values together with a
number the asker chose, a \emph{nonce}, so the asker knows the quote is fresh. Intel's SGX does the equivalent for an
\emph{enclave}, a walled-off region a program runs in. The record is the extended register.

What's priced? Nothing in the specification. Reversal isn't expensive. It's \emph{infeasible}: you'd
have to invert a hash or steal a key. That's the difference between a price and a wall, and
it's easy to blur. A price can come in three kinds. It can be economic, a fee or a deposit
the protocol takes (Casper and gas are here). It can be cryptographic, a reversal made
infeasible by a hardness assumption, which makes it a wall with no exact price on it (attestation and
transparency are here). Or it can be physical, energy spent, which none of these five
specifications touches. And the record's permanence is only as long as the register lives: a
platform's registers are cleared when it resets, so the permanence is per boot.

Why the registers, then, when something that lasts would make a better record? Because the quote is what a remote asker
reads, and the registers are what it signs. The same chip has longer-lived records, and they're
closer to the cup than anything else in this section. Version 2.0 of its specification has
storage slots of a kind it calls a bit field, changed only by a command that ORs new bits into the
old value: a bit can be set and never cleared, which is $r \lor h$ from Section~\ref{sec:latch},
on a laptop motherboard. It has counters that can only be incremented, and a counter's first
increment starts it at the largest value any counter on that chip has ever held, so deleting one
and making a new one can't wind it back. And those slots are rationed. Bryan Parno and his
coauthors, building a system called Memoir in 2011, noted that the specification of the day only
required a counter to be able to tick once every five seconds, and that the chip's storage was
expected to survive about a hundred thousand writes in its whole life, so writing once a second
would wear it out in under twenty-eight hours. Memoir writes to it twice per boot. Permanent,
finite and rationed: the honest record has a budget, the way Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-growing}'s chain
of $k$-bit words can only climb $k$ times. Phones and small controllers go one floor further down,
to fuses like the PROMs in Section~\ref{sec:latch}: a version number kept as a row of fuses, one
more blown at each security update, and boot code that refuses anything older. An industry guide
on it, Rob Smart's 2021 explainer for PSA Certified, a security certification scheme for chips and
devices, tells designers to make sure there are enough fuse bits to last the number of updates
expected over the device's lifetime, which is part (5) of that same theorem, written as a design
rule.

What all of this is for is \emph{rollback}. Memoir's example is a password checker restored to an
old saved state to undo a user's password change, and in 2017 a system called ROTE did the same
job for Intel's enclaves by having several machines vouch for each other's counters, with the
stated result that the only way left to break it is to reset every one of them to its start.
In 2016 Raoul Strackx and Frank Piessens's Ariadne got the cost of that job down to flipping a
single bit of non-volatile memory per state update, which they call the theoretical lower limit.
Notice who the attacker is in every one of these: whoever gets to put an old state back. A bad
program doesn't come into it. A record kept by the step can't see that attacker, which is why every guarantee
in Part IV about a record's earned history is stated from a clean start, and a restored start
is outside all of them. The per-step toll still holds after a restore. It just can't tell you what happened before it.

Replicated services put the same kind of record somewhere else: inside each replica, where a
replica that's been taken over still can't make it say two different things. Byung-Gon Chun and
coauthors' attested append-only memory (A2M, 2007) is a log a replica can only add to; Dave Levin
and coauthors' TrInc (2009) shrinks that to a trusted counter; MinBFT (Giuliana Veronese and
coauthors, 2013) uses a trusted counter to reach agreement with $2f+1$ replicas when $f$ of
them can lie, where the usual count is $3f+1$; and Damysus (Jérémie Decouchant, David Kozhaya, Vincent
Rahli and Jiangshan Yu, 2022) has a small trusted service, the Checker, that keeps a monotonic
counter of where the protocol is. Allen Clement, Flavio Junqueira, Aniket Kate and Rodrigo
Rodrigues (2012) worked out, with proofs, what such a record buys, and as I read their result it's
a good warning for this book.
On its own, stopping a replica from saying two different things doesn't lower the $3f+1$ bound
in an asynchronous network at all. Add signatures that a third party can check, and it turns any
protocol that survives crashes into one that survives liars, with no extra replicas. The way I
read it, a record helps the others only as far as they can check what it says, which is
Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s point from the other side.

There's a fourth kind under those three, and it's the one that always pays. It's the logical
kind: Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s room of chairs applies to any of these records. On a finite state space, a step
that switches a record on somewhere, and never switches it off anywhere, forgets something.
That needs no premise about money, keys or heat. The economic, cryptographic and physical
payments each need a premise of their own about their kind (a fee rule, a hardness
assumption, Landauer's principle), and they hold exactly where that premise holds.

\begin{theorem}[The logical level always pays]\label{thm:u13-logical-payment}
For any states $S$, instructions $I$, step and Boolean reading: if a duplicate-free list names
every state, the instruction $i$ never turns the reading from on to off, and $i$ turns it on
at some state $s$, then the step by $i$ is not injective.
\end{theorem}

Checked as \code{permanent\_write\_has\_logical\_payment} (PricingPhysicsAudit.v), from
\code{permanent\_at\_flip\_is\_not\_injective} (PermanentRecordPricing.v); the proof is
Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} with permanence required only of the one instruction $i$.

What the quote can do is say what was \emph{measured}.
It can't say the measured code is correct, and it can't say anything about runtime state
that was never folded in. A correctly measured buggy program attests beautifully. The
fragment proves that exact limit: one register, a hash about which nothing is assumed, a quote as a pair, and no
function of the quote decides a runtime flag the quote ignores
(\code{quote\_cannot\_attest\_unmeasured\_state}), which is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s cube again. And a companion shows
that a sign-and-verify interface \emph{alone} gives no authenticity (a scheme where verify always
says yes passes the interface), so a cryptographic premise has to be added; the fragment
doesn't model signatures, formats, or a freshness check (the nonce is just a field the
verifier fixes).

The same limit, turned outward, is the honest edge of the opening chapter's four conditions.
Every one of them is about a thing the machine holds: same property, same thing, same edition,
honest check. For a claim about the world (the oven is hot, the parcel arrived) there's no edition
the machine controls. Whatever reads the world is a window onto it, and ``nothing changed between
the check and the commit'' stops being something a step can enforce and becomes a premise about
the sensor. So a record can establish claims about the machine's own state, and claims about the
world only through named premises about whatever measured them. A correctly recorded sensor
reading certifies the sensor.

\begin{definition}[Platform and quote]\label{def:u13-quote}
Fix any functions $H : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ (the extend hash) and
$\delta : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ (the digest); nothing is assumed about either. A
\emph{platform} is a measurement log (a list of numbers) and a Boolean runtime flag. Its register
is the log folded from 0 by $H$. The \emph{quote} with nonce $n$ is the pair
$(\delta(\text{register}), n)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The quote cannot attest unmeasured state]\label{thm:u13-quote}
For every nonce $n$ there is no function $D$ from quotes to Booleans with
$D(\mathrm{quote}_n(P)) = \mathrm{flag}(P)$ for every platform $P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take two platforms with the empty log, one flagged true and one false. Their quotes are
equal, since the quote never reads the flag, so $D$ would have to return both values on one
input.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{quote\_cannot\_attest\_unmeasured\_state} (TPMQuoteGap.v). In the same file,
\code{quote\_decides\_measured\_claims} says any Boolean claim about the retained digest can be read
off the quote. The companion is \code{tpm\_interface\_authenticity\_refuted}
(TPMQuoteAuthenticity.v): a scheme whose verify always says yes satisfies the sign-and-verify
interface while accepting a signature no key produced.

\subsection{Certificate transparency: visible, unpriced}

The certificates that make your browser show a padlock are issued by hundreds of
authorities, and a bad or compromised one can issue a certificate for a domain it shouldn't.
Certificate Transparency makes authorities submit every certificate to public
append-only logs built as Merkle trees, so that anyone can check that a certificate was
logged and that the log never rewrote its past. It was specified in RFC 6962 in 2013 and revised as
RFC 9162 in 2021. I went looking for which one the running logs follow, and it's still 6962:
Mozilla's reference for web developers says browser implementations are based on 6962, and as late
as November 2025 Chrome's team was only proposing to drop its rule that every certificate carry a
timestamp from at least one 6962 log. The fragment I
transcribe is 9162's. A Merkle tree is Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s hash chain folded into
a tree: hash each certificate (those are the \emph{leaves}), hash the leaf hashes in pairs, hash
those in pairs, and so on up to one \emph{root} hash. To prove one leaf is in, the log hands you
only the few hashes sitting beside the climb from that leaf to the root, the \emph{path}, and you
redo the climb yourself. A second check, \emph{consistency}, shows that a bigger tree is a smaller
one with leaves added on the end and nothing rewritten. The record is a leaf in the tree.

Priced? Nothing. The RFC says it in its first section: logs let interested parties \emph{detect} misissuance
afterward. They don't \emph{prevent} it. And a log that shows different views to
different people (a \emph{split view}) can defeat the auditing, so logs are still trusted parties.
What it buys is visibility.

Which raises the obvious question: if nothing's priced, why does any authority bother logging?
Nothing in the RFC makes it. The answer is a browser. Chrome's team set the rule, enforced from
Chrome 68 in July 2018, that every certificate issued after 30 April 2018 had to meet its
transparency policy, and a
publicly trusted certificate that doesn't is simply not trusted by Chrome: the visitor gets a full-page warning in front of the site. So there is a price after
all. It isn't anywhere in the specification. It lives in one vendor's browser, and it's the price of being shown to that
browser's users at all. Is that the bottom? Not quite, because it means the strongest lever on
this record is a policy one company can change, which is a fact about who holds the stamp. The
tree has nothing to do with it. That policy changes nothing in the table at the end of this section, which asks what
each specification prices. But it's worth keeping two sentences apart: ``the specification
prices nothing'' and ``nothing is priced.''

Do the inclusion proof by hand, because it's the most satisfying ten minutes in this section.
Take the RFC's own seven-leaf example tree and verify that leaf d3 is in it from the path
the log hands you: three hashes and a rule about which side to hash on, depending on
whether your position is odd. Three hashing steps and you land on the root. The checked work runs the
RFC's own examples (\code{rfc9162\_example\_inclusion\_d3} and its siblings, including the awkward
lone-leaf case) through a transcription of the RFC's verifier control flow with a symbolic
hash. Verifier logic only: no signatures, no gossip (auditors comparing
the views they were shown), no misbehaving log.

\begin{definition}[Inclusion check, RFC 9162 section 2.1.3.2]\label{def:u13-inclusion}
Given a leaf index $m$, a tree size $N$, a leaf hash, a root hash and a path, the check
rejects unless $m < N$. Otherwise it walks the path from the leaf with two counters starting
at $m$ and $N - 1$, hashing each path element on the left or the right according to the
counters as the RFC specifies and halving the counters, and accepts when the second counter
ends at 0 and the result equals the root. A \emph{symbolic hash} makes a leaf hash $\ell(x)$ and a
node hash $\nu(a, b)$ free constructors, so two hashes are equal only when they are built the
same way.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The RFC's own examples pass]\label{thm:u13-ct-examples}
With the symbolic hash, in the RFC's seven-leaf tree with leaves $d_0, \dots, d_6$ (writing
$d_k$ also for its leaf hash $\ell(d_k)$), the inclusion check accepts leaf 3 with path $[d_2, \nu(d_0, d_1), \nu(\nu(d_4, d_5), d_6)]$, and
likewise leaves 0, 4 and 6 with their paths; the consistency check from size 4 to size 7
accepts. For every input with $m = N$, the inclusion check rejects.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The examples are evaluation of the transcribed functions on constructor terms. The boundary
case is the first test, $m < N$, failing.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{rfc9162\_example\_inclusion\_d3}, its siblings \code{rfc9162\_example\_inclusion\_d0},
\code{rfc9162\_example\_inclusion\_d4} and \code{rfc9162\_example\_inclusion\_d6},
\code{rfc9162\_example\_consistency\_4\_7}, and \code{rfc9162\_inclusion\_boundary\_safe} (RFC9162Merkle.v).
The append-only history is list append, and \code{ct\_extension\_preserves\_entries} says appending
keeps every old entry.

\subsection{Proof-carrying code: no price, no permanence}

Necula's idea from Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}: ship untrusted code with a proof that it obeys the host's policy; the
host computes what would need to be true and checks the proof with a small checker. The
record is the checked proof, and it's held only for the moment of loading. Priced? No.
Checking is cheap by design, which is the whole point, and the producer paid to build the
proof off the host. Permanent? No; nothing's written. The fragment is a three-instruction
memory-bounds language with the policy ``every address is below the limit'': the checker
accepts exactly when the condition holds, and a certificate implies the condition. One example
is checked on top of that: a program that reads address two under a limit of two is rejected.
Not the paper's real case study, and no bridge to anything else in this book. And its limit: a
program that writes garbage to address zero passes if zero
is below the limit. The proof is of the stated policy and nothing else.

And what was the paper's real case study, the one my fragment isn't? Network packet filters: the
little programs an operating system runs on incoming network traffic to decide which program
gets to see which packet. They run inside the kernel, the most trusted part of the system, and
they have to be fast, so they're exactly the code you'd most like to take from a stranger and
least like to trust. In the 1996 paper that first set out the idea, Necula and Peter Lee wrote
several filters by hand in the assembly language of a DEC Alpha, shipped each with its proof,
and reported a one-time cost of 1 to 3 milliseconds to check the proof, after which the filter
ran with no checks at all. That's ``checking is cheap by design'' with a number on it. It changes
nothing about my fragment, which still isn't that case study, and it doesn't add a price: the
milliseconds are the checker's work, and nothing is being written down for them to be a toll on.

\begin{definition}[The bounds fragment]\label{def:u13-pcc}
Instructions are READ $a$, WRITE $a\ v$, and HALT. For a memory limit $L$, the policy allows
READ $a$ and WRITE $a\ v$ when $a < L$, and always allows HALT. The \emph{verification condition}
of a program is that the policy allows every instruction in it. A \emph{certificate} is a list of
per-instruction policy facts, one for each instruction in order. The \emph{checker} tests the
policy on each instruction and returns the conjunction.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The checker is the verification condition]\label{thm:u13-pcc}
For every limit $L$ and program $P$: the checker accepts $P$ exactly when the verification
condition holds; any certificate for $P$ gives the verification condition; and with $L = 2$
the checker rejects READ 2 followed by HALT.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The first two are induction on the program and on the certificate, one instruction at a
time. The third is a computation: $2 < 2$ fails.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{pcc\_checker\_accepts\_iff\_vc}, \code{pcc\_certificate\_implies\_vc}, and
\code{pcc\_unsafe\_program\_rejected} (NeculaPCC.v, definitions in NeculaPCCTarget.v).

\subsection{One example, three levels}

Before I lay all five side by side, let me walk one of them up and down the three levels from
the start of the section, because every claim in here lives at exactly one level and it's
easy to let a claim slide up a floor without noticing. Gas, since it's the one place all
three line up. Think of a restaurant's real recipe, my photocopy of one page of it, and a
cookbook chapter on what any recipe has to contain. I can check my photocopy line by line.
That tells you nothing about what the kitchen cooks tonight.

The real specification. Ethereum's execution specification says, in a document that runs real
money, what a storage write costs, what clearing it refunds, and how the refund is capped at
