the end of the transaction. None of what I checked is at this level. What the network
actually charges is whatever the clients people run actually compute, and the evidence for
that is the clients and the chain. This book has none of it.

The transcription. I copied one mechanism out of that document, one slot in one transaction,
gas and refund arithmetic only, at a named commit
(Definition~\ref{def:u13-slot}, Theorem~\ref{thm:u13-sstore}). What the result tells you: \emph{if} the
storage rule is what I copied, then leaving a fresh slot set costs at least twenty thousand,
and set-then-clear nets twenty-three hundred at the counter. What it can't tell you: anything
about the refund cap (not copied, which is why the bill came out so different from the counter
earlier), the stack, calls, other slots, or whether any client implements the rule as written.
The boundary of the claim is the edge of the copy.

The wrapper. The gas schedule of Definition~\ref{def:u13-gas-schedule} isn't Ethereum. It's any
system with steps, a cost per step and a yes/no commitment flag, plus one thing \emph{stipulated}:
a charge predicate, with the premise that a charged step costs at least one and an uncharged
one costs nothing. That premise is the whole of what the wrapper adds, and it's added by
hand; no specification supplies it. Given it, the theorem says the bill is exact, never
letting a commit go free and never billing a non-commit, exactly when the charge predicate is
the commit predicate at unit price. What that tells you is what exact pricing would have to
look like, in any system. It doesn't say Ethereum meets it, and Ethereum doesn't: real gas
bills computation that commits nothing, which the transcription shows in numbers. So the
wrapper prices a definition, the transcription prices a copied rule, and neither prices the
chain.

The other four sit on the same three levels, and only one more wrapper is spelled out in this
section. Casper's transcription is the accountable-safety proof above; its wrapper is a small
gadget with the stake at risk handed in. A finalize step that risks nothing turns the record
on for free, which breaks Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s toll (the file calls that free forgery), and one that risks at
least one unit has a floor (\code{nothing\_at\_stake\_is\_free\_forgery}, \code{slashing\_finality\_floor},
PoSFinality.v). It records exposure to loss (no collateral is destroyed in it), has no Casper
checkpoints in it at all, and is priced by stipulation, the same way the gas wrapper is.
Attestation, transparency and proof-carrying code have transcriptions that prove what their
verifiers do and no price theorem, because their specifications carry no price. Their
wrappers, which I don't spell out here, are Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s verifier argument told in each system's vocabulary,
with a colliding pair behind each one, and that argument is all they carry here.

How to knock down the four claims with the most weight on them, since the book's rule is that every claim gets a way to break it.
For the gas transcription: a list of stores from a fresh slot that ends nonzero with net
charge under twenty thousand. For the gas wrapper: a schedule that never lets a commit go free
and never bills a non-commit, whose charge predicate still differs from the commit predicate
at some step. For the finality gadget: a finalizing trace from unfinalized to finalized whose
charged stake is zero while the gadget claims a floor. For the attestation fragment: a
verifier reading only the quote's fields that decides a runtime flag the quote ignores.

\subsection{The same table, five ways}

Lay them out. Casper prices \emph{reversal} (slashing). Gas prices \emph{the write} (and refunds the
revocation, capped). Attestation and transparency price \emph{nothing}.
They make reversal
infeasible or visible. Proof-carrying code prices nothing and keeps nothing.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.242\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.344\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.344\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{System} & \textbf{What its specification prices} & \textbf{What the transcription checks} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
Casper finality & reversal, by slashing & a finalization fork means a slashable third \\
Gas & the write, refunded on revocation & a persistent write to an empty slot nets at least 20000 \\
Attestation & nothing; reversal is infeasible & the quote can't decide what it never measured \\
Transparency & nothing; misissuance is visible & the RFC's own inclusion examples pass \\
Proof-carrying code & nothing, and nothing is kept & the checker is the verification condition \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

Each row proves what its own transcription says. Reading a row as a claim about a deployed
system takes evidence from that system, and no row shows that certification is the one event
every model has to price.

So the thing my toy charges for, the moment the record is written, is charged for in one of the five
specifications I read, and in that one the designers had to patch the place where the charge
could be clawed back. I find that neither a vindication nor a refutation. It's a fact about
what people built, and what they built was mostly walls (hash chains, signatures) and
penalties for contradiction. Tolls on commitment were rare. Whether a toll on commitment is a
\emph{better} design than a wall is not something I can prove, and I won't pretend the five say
so. What I read in them, and it's a reading of five fragments I chose, is that the record
axis is real in each of them (each has a bit that goes one way) and that the price axis is
mostly empty.

That leaves the question Section~\ref{sec:latch} raised and Section~\ref{sec:pointer} has to face. Five systems, five different
events chosen as ``the record'': finalized, committed, attested, logged, checked. Is there
anything that picks out one event as \emph{the} one worth recording, or is it a free choice every
time? I have a guess. It's a conjecture, and I'll show you how to kill it.

%===========================================================================
\section{The pointer conjecture}
\label{sec:pointer}
%===========================================================================

Here's where I am. Over any base, a record that answers to the computation and never comes down
is a latch on an event (Section~\ref{sec:latch}), and the event is a
free choice (Section~\ref{sec:latch} again, the two cups on one die). Five real systems each picked a
different event (Section~\ref{sec:models}). The toll in this book sits on certification. Why that one? I don't have a proof. I
have a conjecture, and the honest shape of a conjecture is: here's the claim, here's where I
got the idea, here's what's checked, here's what isn't, and here's how to kill it. In that
order.

\subsection{The claim}

Of all the events a machine could put on its meter, the ones its price list charges for and
its counter adds up, certification is the one whose records
get \emph{copied}: checked, stored, and relied on across independent places that share no other
state. Rival events leave no such trail. If that's true, the choice of certification stops being free.
It's the one event the world around the machine keeps redundant copies of, and that's a
reason to price it and leave the others unpriced.

There's a second handle on the same question, and it comes from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}. The permanent-certificate
theorem never uses the word certification for anything special: given Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s rule that
forgetting is charged, it prices any yes-or-no reading that, once on, stays on, on a machine
with finite memory. So it points at a narrower
candidate: the events to price are the ones that write a record no later step can take back.
Certification is one of them. As an exact answer that candidate is false, because a merging
step can also revoke (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s three cards). Whether the records that proliferate are the permanent ones, and
whether proliferation picks out anything the merge criterion doesn't, is what the two handles
have to settle between them.

Two holes in that, which I can see from here, so you don't have to find them for me. The first
is a missing premise. Even if the world copies certification records more than any other kind,
``copied'' doesn't give you ``priced'' on its own. Something has to connect them, and the best
candidate I have is a premise about incentives: a record that many independent parties copy and
lean on is exactly the record worth forging, so it's the one where a price buys the most
protection. That's a reasonable premise. It's also a premise, and as I've stated the conjecture,
it's missing. The second hole is a circle. If ``certification'' just means ``the record other
people rely on,'' then of course it's the one that gets relied on and copied, and the claim says
nothing. So the event has to be picked out without mentioning reliance: here it's a reading going
up for good right after a check of the same claim passed, which you can find in a run without
asking who reads it. Whether the world copies \emph{that} event more than its rivals is then a real
question, and it could come out no.

That's the whole conjecture. Now the rest of what a conjecture owes you.

\subsection{Where the shape comes from, and how much of it survived}

The shape is from physics, and I want to tell you where exactly, because I borrowed a word
and I didn't get to keep the whole thing.

Quantum mechanics has a famous problem: a system can be in a blend of states, and when you
measure it you find one definite state, and nobody agrees on what ``measuring'' did. In 1981
Wojciech Zurek asked a sharper question: of all the ways a measuring device \emph{could} end up,
why does it end up recording one particular kind of quantity (the position of a pointer on a
dial, say)? Why never some blend? His answer, developed over twenty years and summarised in a
2009 paper called ``Quantum Darwinism,'' is that the \emph{environment} decides. The air, the light,
the table, everything the device touches, is constantly interacting with it, and only
certain states of the device survive that interaction; those are the \emph{pointer states}. And
more: the environment selects them, and then it \emph{copies} them. The light bouncing off a
dial carries the dial's reading to every corner of the room, redundantly, so that a thousand
observers can each read a different scrap of the environment and all agree on where the
pointer is, without touching the dial. Objectivity, on this view, \emph{is} redundancy: a
property is objective when many independent fragments of the world each carry it.

Zurek isn't the only one behind it. Fernando Brand\~ao, Marco Piani and Pawe\l{} Horodecki (2015)
published a proof that, as I read it, makes something like it generic: under any quantum dynamics at all, observers who learn
about a system only through its environment get at most classical information, about one and
the same measurement of the system. That's their theorem behind the word ``objective,'' and it's a
statement about separate fragments, which is exactly the part I didn't keep.
Xiao-Liang Qi and Daniel Ranard (2021), as I read their paper, sharpened it into a statement about every possible
evolution of system and environment: everywhere in the environment outside a region of fixed
size, whatever an observer can learn about the system is classical, read off one fixed
measurement. A statement about every evolution and every input is the quantum cousin of what the
definitions below ask of an observer, that it record the event in every state, including ones
that never happen to turn up.

That's the shape I borrowed. Certification is to a machine's ecosystem (the machine plus everything around it that
reads, stores and relies on its records) what the pointer
reading is to the room: the thing that gets copied everywhere. It's a good shape and I think
it's the right intuition. Here's what survived into the checked work, and I'm going to be
exact because the word ``redundant'' is doing less than it does for Zurek.

Zurek's redundancy is \emph{graded} (each fragment carries almost all the information, with some
small loss) and it requires the fragments to be \emph{disjoint}: different observers reading
different parts of the environment. The checked definition is the zero-loss case with \emph{no
disjointness at all}. An ecosystem is a state type, some number of observers, and one bit
per observer; an observer \emph{records} an event when its bit is true exactly when the event
holds; an event \emph{proliferates} when every observer records it. Nothing in that says two
observers draw on separate parts of the state. They could all be reading the same bit. The
file says so itself. So I kept the word and dropped the independence that makes Zurek's version
mean ``objective.'' That's a gap between the conjecture's prose and its formal object, and the
prose is where the conjecture lives.

The independence I dropped is exactly what the conjecture's closest published neighbour keeps.
Jess Riedel, Zurek and Michael Zwolak (2016) took histories of a closed quantum system, the
story a whole sequence of events tells, and asked which of them the world keeps records of in
many separate pieces of the environment. As I read their paper, redundant records in separate pieces make a history
consistent, so ordinary yes-or-no reasoning about it works, and they pick out a small set of
histories from the huge number that are merely consistent: in their words, an objective past.
That's ``what proliferates is what counts'' in quantum form, with the disjointness in it, and it
came before this book. Halliwell, in a second 1999 paper, ``Somewhere in the universe,'' had already carried, as I understand him, the link between records and
consistent histories from pure starting states to mixed ones, where the records still exist but
are necessarily imperfect.

There's a deeper mismatch in the borrowing, and it runs against the book, so it goes here. In
Zurek's picture the whole thing, system and device and environment together, evolves by quantum
mechanics' rule for closed systems, and that rule never sends two states to one; every step can
be run backwards. So, seen from the whole, the environment's copying is just that, copying: the
dial's reading gets written onto fresh light, nothing anywhere is forgotten, and it's Door one of
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} with the rest of the universe as the endless strip. That's the
operation this book says is free, Bennett writing on a blank page. The forgetting shows up only
when you look at the dial alone and ignore what the light carried off. Then a blend of pointer
readings decays into a plain either-or, and two different blends can decay into the same
either-or: two states, one result, a merge in the coarse picture. So the opening chapter's
``every settling forgets'' fits the dial's own view. From the whole it fails, and the thing
the conjecture leans on, proliferation, is the free half of the story. What that does to the
conjecture: if there's a price, it isn't on the copying. It's on whatever makes the copy final
from the dial's side, and the claim above, as written, points at the copy.

A published no-go cuts closer still. Philippe Allard Gu\'erin, Veronika Baumann, Flavio Del
Santo and \v{C}aslav Brukner (2021) gave an argument that, under assumptions that look natural in quantum
mechanics, an observer's own perceptions of her outcome at two different times can't share one
reality: no joint chance for the two, depending linearly on the starting state, reproduces what
unitary quantum theory predicts for each. A record that persists, for the one holding it, is
exactly what gets into trouble once the whole is treated as one-to-one. It isn't a theorem
about my machine, which isn't quantum. It's still the strongest published reason I know to hold
the word ``permanent'' loosely when a physicist is in the room.

Which leaves the question to ask of any borrowed shape: has anybody checked the original? For a
long time quantum Darwinism was a theory without a lab. Then, in 2018 and 2019, three groups
working separately, in Italy, China and Germany, went looking for its fingerprint, as Philip Ball's 2019 report in \emph{Quanta Magazine} tells it. The German
one, at Ulm, with Zurek among the authors, watched the spin of a single defect inside a diamond
and the carbon atoms around it, and saw the redundancy the theory predicts: the defect's state
turned up copied in its surroundings, and it didn't take much of the surroundings before more of
them told you nothing new. The other two did it with photons. Is that the bottom? Not by a long
way, and the people involved said so. Zurek himself pointed out that the photon experiments make
their copies artificially and that the diamond's environment is small, and others noted that all
three are schematic versions of a real environment and don't rule out rival accounts. So the
shape I borrowed has passed some first tests in a lab, at the scale of a handful of atoms or
photons, with the caveats written on it. None of that touches the conjecture here, which is
about machines and never rested on quantum physics. It changes the picture: what I borrowed is a
lead somebody is checking. It isn't settled, and I don't get to lean on it as if it were.

\subsection{What's checked}

Definitions, a toy, a survey, and two refutations of things that would have been stronger.

The definitions above, plus ``unique pointer among rivals'': the event proliferates and none
of a listed set of rival events does. Uniqueness is \emph{relative to the list}, necessarily,
since any event that holds on exactly the same states as a proliferating event proliferates
whenever it does: the same fact under another name, so someone has to say which names count
as rivals. And the conjecture itself,
as a schema: for every ecosystem in some class, its metered event is the unique pointer among
its rivals. The class and the rivals are inputs. Nothing about them is proved.

Here's the formal object, small enough to hold in one hand.

\begin{definition}[Ecosystem, records, proliferates, pointer]\label{def:u14-ecosystem}
An \emph{ecosystem} is a type of states, a number $N$ of observers, and for each observer $i$ a
Boolean fragment $F_i$ on states. Observer $i$ \emph{records} an event $E$ (a property of states)
when, for every state $s$, $E(s)$ holds exactly when $F_i(s)$ is true. $E$ \emph{proliferates} when
every observer $i < N$ records it. $E$ is the \emph{unique pointer among} a list of rival events
when $E$ proliferates and no rival in the list does. Given a class $C$ of ecosystems, and for
each member a designated metered event and a list of rivals, the \emph{pointer criterion holds}
for $C$ when every member's metered event is the unique pointer among its rivals.
\end{definition}

Nothing in the definition makes two fragments read different parts of the state, and
``metered'' is only a label: the definition has no metering in it.

\begin{conjecture}[The pointer conjecture]\label{conj:u14-pointer}
Let $C$ be the class of ecosystems that faithfully model deployed record-keeping
disciplines, observed through independent carriers (separate parts of the world, each
holding its own copy), with each discipline's certification
event as its metered event and the other events a step rule could meter as rivals. Then the
pointer criterion holds for $C$.
\end{conjecture}

The conjecture leans on four notions left without precise mathematical definitions: what it is to ``faithfully model'' a
system, which systems count as ``deployed,'' what makes carriers ``independent,'' and which
events ``a step rule could meter.'' That's why it's a conjecture. A theorem with a
missing proof would at least have its terms defined.

A toy: three observers on a replicated ledger, where certification proliferates and ``work
done'' doesn't. The file labels it a sanity check, and that's all it is. It isn't evidence.

\begin{theorem}[The toy]\label{thm:u14-toy}
Let the toy have states (a certified bit, a work count), three observers, and every fragment
equal to the certified bit. Then ``certified'' is the unique pointer among the one rival
``work at least 1''.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every fragment is the certified bit, so every observer records ``certified'' by definition.
For the rival, take the state with the bit false and work 1: the event holds and observer 0's
fragment is false, so observer 0 does not record it.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{toy\_cert\_unique\_pointer} and \code{toy\_work\_not\_proliferating} (PointerObservable.v).

A survey of twelve events, one checked theorem: for each of the five systems in Section~\ref{sec:models}, the
designated event (finalized, committed, attested, logged, checked) proliferates in the
observer map I wrote for that system, and a rival (proposer work, a scratch counter,
measurement noise, submission latency, prover steps) doesn't. The five together are one
statement (\code{five\_labeled\_models\_have\_selected\_pointer}), an instance of the schema above.
Plus a symmetric message-authentication code, which does \emph{not} proliferate, and a digital
signature, which does. Twelve rows. And a thirteenth that I think is the most important one: swap which bit
every observer copies, and the criterion picks the \emph{other} event. The criterion selects
whatever the observer map copies. The map is where the argument lives, and I wrote the maps.
So the five ``confirmations'' are five instances of one construction with the fields renamed.
I'm saying that twice on
purpose, so it can't slip past once.

\begin{theorem}[The survey, and the swap]\label{thm:u14-survey}
(1) In each of the five observer models (proof-of-stake, gas, attestation, transparency,
proof-carrying), the designated event proliferates and the designated rival does not; in the
symmetric-MAC model the authentic-tag event does not proliferate; in the signature model the
authentic-signature event does. (2) Let the states be pairs of bits (first, second), with
three observers whose fragments all equal the second bit. Then ``second is true'' is the
unique pointer among the one rival ``first is true''.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each confirmation holds by definition: each observer's fragment is true exactly when the
event holds.
Each refutation exhibits one state where the event holds and some observer's bit is down.
In (2) that state is (true, false).
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{twelve\_candidate\_measurements\_checked} and \code{swapped\_event\_is\_pointer\_checked}
(RecordProliferationSurvey.v, statements in RecordProliferationSurveyTarget.v); the five
designated models together are \code{five\_labeled\_models\_have\_selected\_pointer}
(PointerObservableReductions.v), an instance of the indexed form of the criterion,
\code{pointer\_criterion\_holds\_indexed}.

Two stronger claims, both refuted, and I'd ask you not to merge them because they fail for
different reasons.

The first stronger claim: \emph{every forgery-resistant commitment proliferates}. If that were
true, certification would be the pointer because it's the commitment. It's refuted in three
observer models (deniable authentication, where only the designated verifier's bit tracks the
event; a symmetric MAC, where the key holders share a secret and nobody else can check; an
object capability, an unforgeable token that grants access to whoever holds it) and
confirmed in two (a public log; a digital signature). Build the first
with three observers: give one a copy of the event's bit and the other two a constant false.
The one records it; it doesn't proliferate. The checked half is the map computation. Whether
my maps are \emph{fair} to the real designs is argued in prose, and you should argue back.

\begin{theorem}[One blind observer is enough]\label{thm:u14-blind}
(1) In any ecosystem, if some observer $i < N$ has $F_i(s_0)$ false at a state $s_0$ where
$E$ holds, then $E$ does not proliferate. (2) Let the deniable model have states (authentic,
verifier-accepts), three observers, observer 0's fragment the authentic bit and observers 1
and 2 constantly false. Then observer 0 records ``authentic'', and ``authentic'' does not
proliferate. The symmetric-MAC and object-capability models also fail to proliferate their
events; the public-log and signature models proliferate theirs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Recording would require $E(s_0) \iff F_i(s_0)$, and the left side is true while the right
is false. (2) Observer 0's fragment is true exactly when the event holds. Apply (1) with observer 1 and
the state (true, true). The other two refutations apply (1) to a blind observer of their own model, and the two confirmations hold by definition.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{blind\_observer\_blocks\_proliferation} and \code{labeled\_model\_verdicts}
(PointerObservableCounterexamples.v). The theorem is about the observer maps. That a third
party in deniable authentication really cannot be convinced is the modelling claim, and the
model has no transcript, key or verifier in it to check that against.

The second stronger claim: \emph{agreement plus accuracy plus locality imply permanence}. That is,
if all observers agree, each sees the event exactly, and each updates by the same local rule
with no coordinator, then the recorded event can't be undone. Refuted by the smallest thing
imaginable: one bit, two observers who both see it, and the rule ``flip.'' All three conditions
hold and true becomes false in one step (\code{toggle\_game\_refutes\_strong\_pointer\_necessity}). Do
it on paper; it takes a minute and it's humbling. What \emph{does} give permanence is durability,
``an observer's true view stays true,'' added as a premise, and then it follows in a few lines
(\code{durable\_consensus\_implies\_permanence}). So durability is the premise doing the work, and
durability is Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s permanence wearing a different coat. Agreement doesn't buy it. Do the
paper version again with one change, the rule ``stay true once true'' in place of ``flip,'' and
the bit can't fall, because the rule won't let it. The observers agreeing has nothing to do with it. (The
machine I build later has a reading that's durable in exactly this sense: its flag never comes
down, by its step rule (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}).) None of this rules out a narrower theorem with real assumptions about the network,
the adversary or durability; it rules out these two strong forms.

\begin{definition}[Observation game]\label{def:u14-game}
A \emph{game} has states, a number $N$ of observers, a Boolean event $e$, a Boolean view $V_i$ for
each observer, and a step map. For $i, j < N$ it has \emph{consensus} when $V_i = V_j$ on every
state; \emph{authenticity} when $V_i(s) = e(s)$ for every state and every $i < N$;
\emph{coordinator-free update} when one function $\ell$ on Booleans has
$V_i(\mathrm{step}(s)) = \ell(V_i(s))$ for every state and every $i < N$; \emph{durable views} when
$V_i(s)$ true gives $V_i(\mathrm{step}(s))$ true for every $i < N$; and a \emph{permanent event}
when $e(s)$ true gives $e(\mathrm{step}(s))$ true.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[What buys permanence]\label{thm:u14-toggle}
(1) It is false that every game with $N > 0$, consensus, authenticity and coordinator-free
update has a permanent event. (2) Every game with $N > 0$, authenticity and durable views has
a permanent event.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) The toggle game: states are Booleans, two observers, event and both views the identity,
step ``flip''. Consensus and authenticity hold trivially, the local rule is ``flip'', and the
state true steps to false. (2) If $e(s)$ is true, observer 0's view is true by authenticity,
stays true by durability, and authenticity turns it back into $e(\mathrm{step}(s))$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{toggle\_game\_refutes\_strong\_pointer\_necessity} and
\code{durable\_consensus\_implies\_permanence} (EcosystemGame.v, definitions in
EcosystemGameTarget.v).

\subsection{What isn't checked, and must stay that way on the page}

That certification \emph{in deployed systems} is singled out by redundant proliferation across
\emph{independent} carriers. The proposed criterion has no precise definition of ``independent'' or ``deployed,''
and no cost law connecting proliferation to price. Every correspondence between a Coq observer
map and a real system is a sentence I wrote. The conjecture is a conjecture, and anyone who
says the formal object proves it is reading more than is there.

\subsection{How to kill it}

Three ways, in the order I'd try them.

One: find a deployed discipline that prices a \emph{non}-proliferating event. A real system with
a toll on something nobody copies. That breaks ``the priced event is the copied one.''

Two: find a rival event that proliferates \emph{as well as} certification in a real ecosystem.
Then certification isn't unique and the conjecture's ``the one'' is wrong. Or do it in a model:
show that something like a multiplication count, or the number of times a Turing machine's head turns around, proliferates by the same
standard I used, so the criterion picks out more than one event and decides nothing.

Three: formalise an ecosystem honestly, with independence defined, where certification
\emph{fails} the test. The symmetric-MAC row is already most of the way there for a different
claim; push it.

The checked work has already refuted two stronger forms of its own claim, which I take as a
sign the method works and as a warning about the main claim.

\subsection{The end of the logic}

That's Part III, and the end of the logic that started in Part II. Here's what it earned. A toll on raising a flag is forced by three premises
(Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). Learning isn't forced to cost. Committing is (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}). The counter is arithmetic once the schedule is
fixed (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). A window with a colliding pair in it can't price the flag exactly (Section~\ref{sec:windows}). Entitlement is an object,
a check, and a paid event, and, given lists, a tree and a covering that someone supplies, and a run that
paid for the tree's depth, it
costs at least the index bits it commits to (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}). Insight is a committed relation (Section~\ref{sec:insight}).
A feeling doesn't qualify.
Over any base a record that is driven by the computation and never comes
down is a latch, with two free choices, the price list and the event
(Section~\ref{sec:latch}). With more than two places, a record that is driven by the computation
and climbs a partial order is a
row of cups, each one a latch; the toll over the whole row is the old toll on every cup, and a
straight strip of $n + 1$ stages needs exactly $n$ cups (Section~\ref{sec:direction}). When the
machine has finitely many states, its record only grows, and the
ordinary machine forgets nothing, the toll prices crushing two states of one fibre, and a window
can price exactly by seeing the cups move (Section~\ref{sec:shadow-exact}). No inside procedure whose flip a substrate can represent decides a shortcut property,
given a recursion theorem, which the nat family has by construction. L
isn't a substrate, and
on L the same diagonal is proved again
from a recursion theorem it has by proof. What a
record can do is carry the commitment (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}). Of
five specifications, read through my transcriptions, one prices the write (Section~\ref{sec:models}).
And which event to record is a conjecture with a borrowed shape and a listed set of
refutations (Section~\ref{sec:pointer}).

The obvious question to ask of all that is whether the toll is the only way. A theorem saying so
would be the best thing this book could hold: a short list of requirements that any account of
what a step costs has to meet, whatever field it comes from, with the toll and the counter the
only accounting left standing. I looked for that theorem, and the answer I can give you is no, and
the no is small enough to check on three states. Call them blank, once and twice, with once and
twice reading yes. The flip takes blank to once and leaves the other two where they are. The
smooth takes both once and twice to twice and leaves blank alone. The smooth forgets something, so
the price on merging from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} charges it a mark. It raises nothing, so the toll
leaves it free. Now try requirements that name no reading: no charge on a move that changes
nothing, none on a move that forgets nothing, the same bill when you rename the states, a total
that adds up along a run, a bill that looks only at the step, and one mark on the flip from blank. The toll, read as
the bill that charges the flip from blank and nothing else, meets every one of them on this machine.
So does the price on merging. They disagree on the
smooth, so that list doesn't pick between them. What picks the toll is a requirement that names
the record: over any run the total is never more than the number of times the reading went up.
With the floor, that leaves exactly one bill, one mark per raise and nothing else
(Section~\ref{sec:windows}), and it rules the price on merging out, because the smooth costs that price a
mark and raises nothing. (The three-state machine itself isn't in the Coq. It's three states and a
pencil.) So the uniqueness is real and it's small. It holds once you've said which
reading you're charging for, and which reading deserves the charge is the pointer conjecture,
which is still a conjecture.

The uniqueness theorems that do exist are about pricing information loss, and they're worth
a look because they say what kind of bill the price on merging is. John Baez, Tobias Fritz
and Tom Leinster (2011), mathematicians who work in category theory, the mathematics Lawvere's
diagonal theorem came from, asked what a measure of information loss has to look like. As I read
their paper, they proved that, for maps that preserve a probability measure,
Shannon entropy is up to a constant factor the only
measure of information loss that is functorial, convex-linear and continuous. J\'anos Acz\'el and Bruno Forte, mathematicians at the University
of Waterloo who worked on functional equations, and C.\
T.\ Ng, who had taken his doctorate there under Acz\'el in 1971, asked in a paper of 1974 which entropies deserve to be called
natural, and proved, by their account, that the entropies with
a short list of natural properties are exactly the linear combinations of Shannon's and Hartley's, where
Hartley's is the log of the count, so even for merges the choice between the average and the
worst case is a real choice. Both price merges. Neither prices raises, so neither picks out the toll, and
that's the three-state example in a bigger room. On the other side of the fence, Luciano
Pomatto, Philipp Strack and Omer Tamuz (2023), economists at Caltech and Yale who asked what
learning something should cost, proved, by their account, a uniqueness result for what it costs to
\emph{acquire} information, with constant marginal costs. That's a price on producing a
signal, a different bill from the free learning of Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}.

What none of that is: a machine. Every theorem so far quantifies over ``any states, any
steps,'' or is about a small copy of somebody else's system, or points forward at a thing I
keep promising. That's the abstract part of the book, and it's done. From the next page on I
stop saying ``any machine'' and build one, mine: the least I can make that still shows the whole
model, with every part named and every price written down, so that everything above finally has
something to bump into, and then one fixed program, run on a host with more counters, that runs every machine of the model
whose workings a program can compute. If a statement up there doesn't mean what I think it
means, that's where it'll show. Part IV is the thing. I want to see if it holds weight.


\part{The machine}

%===========================================================================
\section{The smallest honest machine}
\label{sec:smallest}
%===========================================================================

Parts I to III never built anything. They said ``any states, any steps,'' and whenever a
picture was needed, a board or some chairs or a cup stood in. Now I have to build a
machine, and the first worry I have about that is a slightly embarrassing one. I built a big
one first, the one from the origin story, with dozens of instructions,
some picked for reasons and some picked because I had to pick something, and theorems held of it.
What does that show? That the model works, or that I'm good at stacking instructions until the
proofs go through? A big machine is a wonderful place to hide a mistake. It's a garage so full
of stuff that you could lose a car in it.

So the machine in this book is a small one. The least I can build that still shows the whole
model, every piece of it, with nothing waved at. If the idea only stands up with dozens of
instructions holding it, the idea belongs to those instructions. The model can't claim it. If it
stands up on six, the six are the idea, and you can hold all of them in your head at once, which
is more than I can say for most things I've built.

\subsection{What the model actually asks for}

Here's what Parts II and III say the model adds to a machine. A \emph{record}: a flag that reads
no or yes, ``certified'' or not. A \emph{toll}: the step that raises the flag costs something
(Section~\ref{sec:toll}). A \emph{ledger}: the running total of those costs, a whole number that only climbs (Section~\ref{sec:counter}).
And Section~\ref{sec:latch} proved the thing this whole chapter stands on: over any base at
all, an honest record is a \emph{latch}, a bit that switches on at an event the base decides and
never switches off (Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch}). The record watches the base. It doesn't
compute anything the base couldn't compute without it.

Push on that for a second, because it cuts the job in half. If the record adds no computing
power, then all the computing power comes from the base, and the question ``how small can
the machine be'' splits into two questions that don't touch each other. For the base: what's
the smallest thing that can compute everything there is to compute? For the record: what's
the smallest set of pieces that makes the flag \emph{mean} something?

One honest asterisk on ``don't touch,'' because the machine below makes it matter. What's
blind is the flag and the ledger: the base never reads either of them. But the pieces that
make the flag mean something (a table of checked facts, a slot for a commitment, a trap that
stops a refused run) have to sit where the step can read them, which is in the base, and they
do steer the run: a failed check stops a program dead. The latch theorem holds wherever you
draw the line between base and record, which is exactly why it can't tell you where the
meaning lives. On this machine the meaning lives on the base side of the line, in the
bookkeeping, and the flag on top reports it.

The record question, the second of those two, is the one Part III left to the machine, on purpose. Section~\ref{sec:insight} said that
testing a claim and committing to it are two different acts, and that nothing in the five
parts of the model makes the second wait for the first. Read Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s definition again with that
in mind: a machine where you pay one unit and raise the flag over nothing in particular
obeys every rule in it. That machine is honest about the price and silent about what was
bought. A receipt for nothing. The toll alone can't fix that, because the toll is a rule
about \emph{cost}, and ``was this earned'' is a question about \emph{order}: did a check happen, of
this claim, before the commitment, with nothing changing underneath in between?

This machine is my attempt to make the order part of the machine, in the smallest place I
could find to do it. I'll show you the pieces, then the proofs, then the places it falls
short, which there are, and which I'd rather you hear from me.

\subsection{Where the counters come from}

The base first, and the base isn't mine. It's Marvin Minsky's. In a 1961 paper in the
\emph{Annals of Mathematics}, and then in his 1967 book \emph{Computation: Finite and Infinite
Machines}, Minsky studied a machine so bare it's almost a joke. Picture a few bins of
pebbles and a numbered list of instructions. There are only two kinds of instruction: put
a pebble in bin $c$ and go to the next line; or, if bin $c$ has a pebble, take one out and
jump to line $j$, and if it's empty, just go to the next line. That's it. No memory, no
tape, no arithmetic beyond plus one and minus one. When the line you're on has no
instruction, the machine stops.

What Minsky proved, by hand, is that two bins are enough to compute anything a Turing machine can
compute, as long as you're willing to pack the input in a strange way. The trick is to keep
many numbers inside one number, as the powers of different primes ($2^x 3^y 5^z$ holds
three numbers in one), and to do arithmetic on the exponents by multiplying and dividing
with the second bin as scratch space. It's slow. Exponentially slow. A
two-counter machine doing your taxes would finish sometime after the sun burns out. But
``universal'' is a claim about what's \emph{possible}. Pleasant doesn't come into it, and on that
claim two bins of pebbles are as strong as anything.

Who cares? Minsky did, because the question then was where the edge of computation sits and
how little machinery reaches it. You should, because it means the base of this chapter's
machine hides nothing: if it can compute everything with plus one, minus one and a jump,
then nothing about the record can be smuggling computing power in through some instruction
I made fancy. And I care because it's the smallest universal base I know of that is
already in a Coq library, so the hard part (proving that its halting question is
undecidable) is someone else's checked work. I don't have to ask you to take my word for it.

And the pebbles aren't only my picture. They were somebody's actual machine, the same year.
In one issue of the Canadian Mathematical Bulletin, September 1961, Z.~A. Melzak, a
mathematician at the University of British Columbia, described a
computer made of distinguishable holes and an unlimited supply of pebbles, with one
three-place operation, and a few pages later Joachim Lambek, a mathematician at McGill
University, trimmed it to two moves: put a
pebble in hole $X$; take one out of hole $X$ if there's one to take. He called it an
\emph{infinite abacus}, and early on he writes ``Our method is probably not new,'' which is
a hard sentence to beat. He also tells anybody who distrusts infinity not to worry
about all those holes, since any one computation only ever uses finitely many of them.
Is that two inventions or one? Lambek says his was a modification of Melzak's, so call it one
and a half, with Minsky's as a separate find the same year. And then Lambek went somewhere
you wouldn't guess: in 1986, with Philip Scott, a logician who had come to McGill to work with
him and later taught at the University of Ottawa, he wrote a book whose first part, as the
publisher describes it, shows that typed lambda
calculi and a certain kind of category are essentially the same thing. Pebbles to category
theory in one career, twenty-five years end to end. Does any of it change the argument? No. The
library and I use Minsky's version and Minsky's name. But a bare machine that several people
reach for in the same year looks like a shape that was sitting there. It doesn't look much like
anybody's invention.

The title of Minsky's 1961 paper is the clue I can't leave alone. It's about ``Post's problem of
tag.'' Who's Post, and what's tag? Emil Post was a logician, a fresh PhD from Columbia, who in
1921, on a fellowship at Princeton, was playing
with about the simplest rewriting game there is. Take a word of 0s and 1s. Look at its first
letter, chop the first three letters off the front, and stick something on the end:
\texttt{00} if the letter you looked at was 0, \texttt{1101} if it was 1. Repeat, and stop when
fewer than three letters are left. Try it at the table. Start from \texttt{1000}: you get
\texttt{01101}, then \texttt{0100}, then \texttt{000}, then \texttt{00}, and it stops. Start from
\texttt{100}: you get \texttt{1101}, \texttt{11101}, \texttt{011101}, \texttt{10100},
\texttt{001101}, and then \texttt{10100} again, and it goes round forever. Post wanted a rule
that tells you, for every starting word, which of those happens. He worked at it for months and
later called it hopeless, and as far as I can tell it still is: a hundred years on, nobody knows
whether that one little game, with that one rule, can be decided. Stephen Wolfram, the physicist
who built Mathematica, wrote a 2021
article on it that tells the Princeton story, and it's where I'd start. In his 1961 paper Minsky proved by hand
that tag games in general can compute anything, which is why Post's name is on it. It didn't settle Post's
own game. And the chase goes one step further. In 2008 Liesbeth De Mol, a historian and philosopher
of computing who wrote her doctoral work on tag systems, turned
the famous $3n+1$ problem (halve an even number, triple an odd one and add one, and ask whether
you always get down to 1) into a small tag game of the same kind. So is Post's game secretly as
hard as everything, or just stubborn? I can't tell you, and as far as the published work goes,
nobody can yet.

None of that changes the machine below. It changes the picture. The two-counter machine came
out of a hunt for the smallest thing that can't be predicted, and the smallest things are exactly
where the open questions are still sitting.

One word clash, before it bites. Minsky's machine is usually called a \emph{counter machine},
and its bins are \emph{counters}. Section~\ref{sec:counter} also had a counter: the ledger $\mu$, the number that only
climbs. Same word, two completely different things, and I'd love to say I set that up on
purpose. In this chapter, \emph{counter} means one of Minsky's two bins, called $A$ and $B$, and
the climbing total is always \emph{the ledger} $\mu$.

\subsection{The machine}

Here's the whole state. I'll say each piece in words first.

\begin{itemize}
\item Two counters, $A$ and $B$. Each holds a whole number, with no upper limit.
\item A \emph{version} for each counter, also a whole number with no limit. It starts at 0 and goes
up by one every time its counter is written. Think of it as the counter's edition number:
a new value is a new edition.
\item A \emph{line number}, which instruction comes next, counting from 1 the way the library's two-counter machine does
(more on that choice just below).
\item A \emph{fact table}: a list of facts. A \emph{fact} is three things stuck together: a property, a
counter, and a version. ``$A$ is even, as of edition 3'' is a fact. The table has room for
sixteen. Why sixteen? It's a pick, with no derivation behind it, and what the pick costs is
in the subsection near the end of this chapter on what the machine doesn't do.
\item A \emph{channel}: either empty, or holding one fact. This is where a commitment sits.
\item A \emph{trap}: one bit, down at the start. When it goes up, the machine has refused something,
and it stays up.
\end{itemize}

Counting lines from 1 looks like the least interesting choice in the chapter, and it's one of
the oldest arguments in programming, with a famous referee. Edsger Dijkstra was a Dutch computer
scientist, one of the generation that founded the field, and for over forty years he mailed
numbered notes to a few dozen colleagues. In 1982 he wrote one of them, EWD 831, titled ``Why
numbering should start at
zero.'' His case goes through ranges first. Of the four ways to write ``2 up to 12'' with
less-than signs, he picks the one that takes the bottom in and leaves the top out,
$2 \le i < 13$: two ranges that meet end to end then share one number written once, and the
length is just the top minus the bottom. Start a sequence of $N$ things at zero and it's
$0 \le i < N$, and each thing's number is how many things came before it. He reports that
programmers on the language Mesa, which allowed all four conventions, found the other three a
steady source of clumsiness and mistakes, and he points out that FORTRAN starts at one. Does that
settle it? It settles which convention is tidier, by an argument you can check. It doesn't settle
which convention somebody else's work used, and that's the trap: the library's two-counter
machine, which it calls a Minsky machine, numbers its lines from 1, and so does this machine,
because matching it line for line is worth more here than tidiness. Is zero the right place to
start counting? Dijkstra's title says it is, and I can't tell you more than that. What his note
carries is an argument about which way makes fewer mistakes. That part you can check for
yourself, and it's the more useful thing to have.

Everything in that list is the \emph{core}, the part the base moves. Outside the core sit the two
pieces from the model: the ledger $\mu$ and the flag. The machine never reads either of
them to decide what to do next. I'm not asking you to take that on trust. It's how the step is
written, and it shows up as a theorem below.

The properties a fact can name come from a tiny fixed language with three words: \emph{is zero};
\emph{is even}; and \emph{is at least $n$}, for any whole number $n$ you like. Each one comes in two
forms. There's the \emph{checker}, a little program that computes yes or no: compare with 0,
look at the last bit, compare with $n$. And there's the \emph{meaning}, the plain arithmetic
statement the checker is supposed to be checking: the number is 0; the number is two times
something; $n$ is less than or equal to the number. Why both? Because a checker is code, and
code can be wrong in ways that look right, and ``the checker says yes'' is only worth
anything once somebody has proved it says yes exactly when the meaning is true. That proof
is one line per property, and it's the first block below.

Why can a machine check a claim at all? Because a claim with a precise meaning is something you
\emph{evaluate}: plug in the values and turn the crank. George Boole worked out in 1847 that you
can do arithmetic on claims this way, treating ``and'' like multiplication and ``or'' like a kind
of addition. Why multiplication? Try it at the table. Write 1 for true and 0 for false, and
multiply: one times one is one, and anything times zero is zero. That's ``and'' to the letter.
Then the stranger thing Boole noticed. Say ``x and x'' and you've said nothing new; it's just x.
In numbers that's $x \times x = x$, and he made it a law of his system, and it's a law ordinary
numbers mostly break. Which numbers equal their own square? Two times two is four, no. A half
times a half is a quarter, no. Zero, yes. One, yes. That's the whole list. So when Boole wrote his
bigger book in 1854, \emph{The Laws of Thought}, he asked you to imagine an algebra whose letters
take the values 0 and 1 and nothing else. Every checker on this machine answers in that algebra.

And the 1847 book has a backstory worth a detour, which I found in the Stanford Encyclopedia of
Philosophy's entry on Boole. Boole was largely self-taught and spent
about fifteen years as a schoolmaster, and what pulled him back to logic, early in 1847, was a
loud public quarrel between Augustus De Morgan and the Scottish philosopher Sir William
Hamilton over who had first thought of a small technical idea in the old logic of
syllogisms. Two well-known men fighting over credit, and a schoolmaster watching from the side
picks up the subject and writes the little book this paragraph is about. Few people remember
what the quarrel was over. Every checker in this chapter runs on what the bystander wrote.

Then push on it, because Boole's ``or'' isn't quite the one a checker uses. His plus only made
sense for things that can't both hold at once, so ``x or y'' with both of them true had no
meaning in his system. William Stanley Jevons, an English economist who also worked on logic, read
``or'' as ``either or both,'' which gives ``x or x is x,'' the same trick as before. He wrote to
Boole in 1863 saying plus ought to work that way, and in 1864 he put it in a book called
\emph{Pure Logic}. Boole wouldn't have it, since it broke the
tie to ordinary algebra his whole system stood on. The ``or'' in every programming language I know
is the inclusive one Jevons argued for. Does that change anything about the checker? No; the crank turns the same way. It
changes the picture: the ``or'' a checker uses is the one the man who invented the algebra
turned down.

Hanging a checked claim on a point in a computation is an old move too. Tony Hoare, in 1969,
built a whole way of reasoning about programs out of it: attach a claim to a \emph{point} in a
program (``whenever execution reaches here, this is true''), and reason forward from claim to
claim. Robert Floyd had done it two years earlier on flowcharts. Their claims were checked on
paper by the person writing the proof. This machine's version is a property of one counter at
one edition, checked by a step while it runs.

And is two years earlier the bottom? Not even close, and the next step down is a paper this
book already leaned on. In June 1949, at a Cambridge conference held for the new EDSAC
computer, Alan Turing gave a talk three pages long, ``Checking a large routine,'' the same note
the counter chapter used for stopping (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). Stopping was the second half
of it. The first half is this move, twenty years before Hoare: the programmer should make
``definite assertions which can be checked individually,'' and the correctness of the whole
should follow from them. His example program computes a factorial using nothing but addition,
and his picture for why you'd bother is one you can do on the back of an envelope. Add up a long
column of four-digit numbers and hand someone only the total, and they have to redo the whole
sum at one sitting, because the carries tie every column to the one before it. Hand them the
total of each column as well, and the job falls apart into small checks they can do one at a
time. That's a claim hung on a point in the middle of the work, so the person checking never
has to hold all of it at once. The paper got its due mostly later: in 1984 two computer scientists, F. L. Morris of Syracuse
University and C. B. Jones of Manchester University, who had worked on it together at Oxford,
republished it, with its misprints corrected, as an early program proof by Alan
Turing. Theirs is the text I read, and the column of numbers is Turing's own example in it. Does any of that change the machine? No. It changes the date on the idea, and it tells
you something I like: the first person to ask how you'd check a program put the claims in the
middle of it. He didn't save them for the end.

Now the six instructions.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.242\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.344\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.344\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Instruction} & \textbf{What it does, when the trap is down} & \textbf{Cost} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
INC $c$ & Adds one to counter $c$, adds one to its version, goes to the next line. & 0 \\
DEC $c$ $j$ & If $c$ is above 0: subtracts one, adds one to its version, jumps to line $j$. If $c$ is 0: just goes to the next line. & 0 \\
HALT & Nothing. A program that reaches it stops. & 0 \\
CHECK $p$ $c$ & Runs the checker for $p$ on $c$'s value. If it says yes and the table has fewer than sixteen facts, writes the fact ($p$, $c$, $c$'s current version) into the table and goes to the next line. Otherwise, trap. & 1 \\
COMMIT $p$ $c$ & Looks in the table for exactly the fact ($p$, $c$, $c$'s current version), field by field. If it's there, puts it in the channel and goes to the next line. Otherwise, trap. & 1 \\
CERTIFY & If the channel holds a fact, goes to the next line, and the flag goes up. Otherwise, trap. & 1 \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

The first three are Minsky's machine, plus a HALT so a program can say it's done. The last
three are the record's. Read them as a chain: you can only certify with a commitment in the
channel, you can only commit to a fact in the table, and the only way into the table is a
check that passed. Three links, and each one costs.

One of what? One unit of $\mu$, the same unit as Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s toll. Why one? Why would ten be worse? Because one
is the smallest positive whole number, which is honestly the whole defence, and Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} is the
section where I tried to do better than that for the flag. That argument doesn't reach this
machine, though (the end of the chapter says why), so here the one is a choice, full stop.

Where does that one come from, though? It's older than Coq by about a century. In 1888 the German
mathematician Richard
Dedekind published a little book whose title asks what numbers are and what they're for, and in
1889 the Italian mathematician Giuseppe Peano published a booklet, written in Latin, that set out
the axioms for the whole numbers in the form people still teach: there's a first number,
and every number has a next one, and a few rules about how ``next'' behaves. I had the two of
them down as working independently. I went looking, and the Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on
Dedekind says Peano acknowledged Dedekind's priority, which is why the axioms often go by both
names. (Peano's booklet is also where the
sign $\in$ that you met in Section~\ref{sec:structure} comes from: he wrote it as a Greek epsilon,
for the Latin \emph{est}, ``is.'') Coq builds
its whole numbers exactly that way, out of zero and ``the next one'' and nothing else, so inside
Coq the number three really is S (S (S O)), the next of the next of the next of zero. What that
changes here is small and I like it: the one a CHECK costs isn't a number pulled from a hat.
It's one application of the smallest step the number system has. You can't charge less than one
S and still charge something.

The zeros matter just as much:
computing is free on this ledger. Plus one, minus one and jumping around cost nothing at all.
Only the three acts that make a claim cost, and each of them costs whether it passes or traps.
Failing is not a discount.

\textbf{The version rule.} Here's why versions exist, with numbers. Start with $A = 4$, version 0.
CHECK \emph{is even} $A$ passes, and the table gets the fact (\emph{even}, $A$, 0). Now INC $A$: $A$
becomes 5, and its version becomes 1. Now COMMIT \emph{is even} $A$. The machine looks for
(\emph{even}, $A$, 1), the claim about the current edition. The table only has (\emph{even}, $A$, 0).
No match. Trap. The old fact is still sitting in the table, still true about edition 0,
and completely useless for committing to anything about edition 1. A fact is about one
edition of one counter, and an edition never comes back, because versions only go up and
never wrap. That's the whole trick against stale evidence: you can't check a number, change
it, and then commit to the check.

That's the opening chapter's time-of-check-to-time-of-use bug, the file checked and then swapped,
and the database answer to it is Kung and Robinson's: at commit time, check that nothing you read
was written in the meantime, and back out if something was. The version rule is that check, done
by the step, on one counter. It also shows where the guarantee ends. It works because one step does
every write and every write bumps a version. A second writer that changed a counter without
bumping its version, a second processor or a device writing memory on its own, would walk
right around it, and none of the theorems below are about a machine with one of those.

Processor designers put a cousin of this check in silicon. Jensen, Hagensen and Broughton, at
Lawrence Livermore in 1987, described a pair of instructions now called load-linked and
store-conditional: the load reads a word and the processor starts watching it, and the store
goes through only if nothing has written that word since; otherwise it fails and the program
tries again. It's tempting to say CHECK is the load and COMMIT is the conditional store, and
it's wrong in two places. COMMIT doesn't write the counter it checked, and the thing doing the
watching, the fact, sits in a table the step keeps. No single processor holds it. The hardware
version does cover the second writer, because the watching happens on the memory everyone
shares, which is exactly the case the version rule leaves out.

The real kinship is older, and it's somewhere else. Picture the table and the counters shared
by many processors, with CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY each done as one indivisible step. Maurice
Herlihy (1991), a computer scientist who has spent his career on how many processors can share
memory safely, ranked shared objects by how many processors each one can bring to agree on a
single value with nobody ever waiting on anybody, and that object would sit at the top, able
to bring any number to agree. The reason isn't that COMMIT is a store-conditional. It's that
the object contains a sticky bit, the idea of Serge
Plotkin (1989), a Stanford computer scientist working on distributed algorithms: a cell the first writer jams for good
and everyone after can read. Put a write that kills every fact about a counter together with a
commitment other processors can see, and you have a sticky bit. The trap is another one. Take the version rule away,
let failures change nothing, and let checked properties only ever turn true, and everything in
the object only grows; then it drops to the bottom rung, the level of plain memory, which is
the shared-memory face of what the database researchers Joseph Hellerstein and Peter Alvaro
(2020), at Berkeley and Santa Cruz, call CALM, where
monotone means nobody has to coordinate. The toll changes neither answer. That split is argued
here on paper. No Coq proof stands behind it, and neither half is mine: the top is Plotkin's and the bottom is
the monotone fact that field already knows.

Process-calculus people have a statement of the same split. Johannes \AA{}man Pohjola and
Joachim Parrow (2016) prove on paper that no model whose parallel composition is monotonic, where a
neighbouring process can never stop a step, has a consensus process, and one of their examples
of a model that does is test-and-set, an instruction that writes a cell and reports what was
there, which is a sticky bit under another name. A store that can refuse permanently, as
the version rule does to a stale commit, sits on the non-monotonic side. I haven't written that
encoding either, so it's a pointer.

Security people know the pattern by a third name. A check that blesses a value, and a write
that takes the blessing away, is close kin to dynamic taint tracking, where a label rides along
with the data and a sanitizing step changes it; the labels go back to the computer-security
researcher Dorothy Denning's 1976
lattice model of how information is allowed to flow. How much a monitor like that has to
remember is a studied question too: Chamseddine Talhi, Nadia Tawbi and Mourad Debbabi (2008),
three security researchers at universities in Quebec,
worked out which rules a monitor can still enforce when its memory is bounded. The version rule
is one small, specific member of that family, done by the step.

Notice what \emph{isn't} a write. DEC on a counter that's already 0 doesn't change the counter, so
it doesn't change the version. It's a test that happens to move the line number.

\textbf{The fact table.} Facts go in and never come out. Nothing erases them and nothing
overwrites them. When the table is full, a seventeenth CHECK traps. It doesn't push an old fact out to
make room. That's a choice with a bill attached, and I'll put the bill in the
section on what this machine doesn't do.

\textbf{Traps.} Any failure puts the trap up and changes nothing else in the core; the ledger
still takes the instruction's cost. Once it's up, every
instruction leaves the core alone. A stored program stops at a trap. But I also prove
things about \emph{any} list of instructions, programs or otherwise, because an adversary doesn't
have to run my programs; they can feed the machine whatever they want. For those lists, an
instruction after a trap is still charged its cost, and still changes nothing.

Now the exact version.

\begin{definition}[Properties, checker, meaning]\label{def:u34-props}
A \emph{property} is one of: $\mathsf{Zero}$, $\mathsf{Even}$, or $\mathsf{Ge}(n)$ for a whole
number $n$. The \emph{checker} $\mathrm{eval}(p, v)$ computes yes or no: $v = 0$ by equality,
evenness by the parity function, $n \le v$ by comparison. The \emph{meaning} $\mathrm{holds}(p,
v)$ is the arithmetic statement: $v = 0$; there is an $m$ with $v = 2m$; $n \le v$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[The checker says what it means]\label{lem:u34-eval}
For every property $p$ and every whole number $v$, $\mathrm{eval}(p, v) = \mathrm{yes}$ if
and only if $\mathrm{holds}(p, v)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Split on the three properties. Equality with zero returns yes exactly at zero; comparison
with $n$ returns yes exactly when $n\le v$. For evenness, the parity checker returns yes
at $0$, no at $1$, and the same answer at $v+2$ as at $v$. Induction in steps of two gives
yes exactly at $0,2,4,\ldots$, the numbers $2m$. Those are precisely the three meanings.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{eval\_iff} (EarnedCore.v).

\begin{definition}[Core, state, claim, start]\label{def:u34-state}
A \emph{core} $k$ holds two counters $A$, $B$ and their versions (whole numbers), a line number,
a fact table (a list of facts, a fact being a triple of a property, a counter and a
version), a channel (empty or one fact), and a trap bit. Write $\mathrm{val}(k, c)$ and
$\mathrm{ver}(k, c)$ for counter $c$'s value and version. A \emph{state} $s$ is a core, written
$\mathrm{core}(s)$, with a ledger $\mu(s)$ and a flag $\mathrm{cert}(s)$. The \emph{claim} $p$ of
$c$ in $k$ is the fact $(p, c, \mathrm{ver}(k, c))$. The table's room is 16. The start
$\mathrm{start}(a, b)$ has counters $a$ and $b$, versions 0, line 1, an empty table, an
empty channel, the trap down, $\mu = 0$ and the flag down. A state is \emph{clean} when its
table and channel are empty and its flag is down.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Instructions, costs, the step]\label{def:u34-step}
The instructions are INC $c$, DEC $c$ $j$, HALT, CHECK $p$ $c$, COMMIT $p$ $c$ and
CERTIFY, with effects on a core with the trap down as in the table above. Passing any
check, commitment or certification requires the trap to be down. With that condition, CHECK
passes when $\mathrm{eval}(p, \mathrm{val}(k, c)) = \mathrm{yes}$ and the table holds fewer
than 16 facts, COMMIT passes when the claim $p$ of $c$ is in the table, and CERTIFY passes
when the channel holds a fact; a failing one sets the trap and changes nothing else. On a
core with the trap up, every instruction changes nothing. Costs: CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY
cost 1, the rest 0. One step on a state is
\[
\mathrm{exec}(s, i) = \big(\,\mathrm{cexec}(\mathrm{core}(s), i),\ \ \mu(s) + \mathrm{cost}(i),\ \ \mathrm{cert}(s) \lor \mathrm{fires}(\mathrm{core}(s), i)\,\big),
\]
where $\mathrm{cexec}$ is the core's step and $\mathrm{fires}(k, i)$ is yes exactly when
$i$ is CERTIFY and passes at $k$. For any list $t$ of instructions (a \emph{trace}),
$\mathrm{run}(t, s)$ applies them in order and $\mathrm{cost}(t)$ adds their costs. A
\emph{program} is a list of instructions numbered from 1; a program run fetches the instruction
at the line number and executes it, and stops when the trap is up, the line holds HALT, or
the line holds nothing.
\end{definition}

Defined as \code{cexec}, \code{exec}, \code{run}, \code{total\_cost}, \code{run\_prog}, \code{start} and \code{Minimal.EarnedCore.clean\_start}
(EarnedCore.v).

Read the step line slowly, because the rest of the chapter leans on its shape. The core
moves by its own rule and nothing else. The ledger adds the cost. The flag becomes ``it was
up, or this is a CERTIFY that passed.'' The core's move doesn't mention $\mu$ or the flag
anywhere. The base is blind to the record by construction.

A worked run, the shortest one there is. The program: CHECK \emph{is zero} $A$; COMMIT \emph{is
zero} $A$; CERTIFY. Start at $\mathrm{start}(0, b)$, for any $b$. Line 1: $A$ is 0, the checker
says yes, the table is empty so there's room, and the fact (\emph{zero}, $A$, 0) goes in.
$\mu = 1$. Line 2: the claim about $A$'s current edition is (\emph{zero}, $A$, 0), and it's
right there. Into the channel. $\mu = 2$. Line 3: the channel holds a fact, the flag goes up.
$\mu = 3$. Line 4 has no instruction, so the program stops. Three paid acts, in order, a flag
that's up, and a channel that names the last earned commitment, which here is (\emph{zero},
$A$, 0).

Now start the same program at $\mathrm{start}(5, b)$. Line 1: $A$ is 5, the checker says no,
the trap goes up, $\mu = 1$, and the program stops right there. The flag is down, and you can
run it as long as you like: it stays down. That second run is the point of the first. The same
three instructions certify from some starts and refuse from others, because the check could
have failed, and from most starts it does. A check like that has a no pile, which is the only
kind the opening chapter counts as establishing anything.

Could I have picked an even dumber claim? Sure, and the machine would have let me. CHECK
\emph{at least 0} $A$ passes on every number there is, so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY on it raises the
flag for 3 from every start (stop the presses: a number is at least zero). The step doesn't
police that. It checks order, aboutness and that the checker tells the truth; whether the
question was worth asking isn't something it looks at. A check that can't fail establishes
nothing, and this machine will charge you three and raise the flag for it anyway. Spotting
that is the reader's job, with the property in hand, and it's on the list at the end of the
chapter.

Others walked into the same line from communication. Three theoretical computer scientists,
Oded Goldreich, Brendan Juba and Madhu Sudan
(2012), built a theory of communication with a partner you may not understand, in which getting a
message across counts only as a way to reach a goal, and the central notion is \emph{sensing}: being able to tell, from what you see,
whether you're making progress. The sensing they ask for is \emph{safe}: when there's no progress
it says so, and so it never reports a success that didn't happen. Their main result, as I read it,
is that safe sensing, with a partner who could help if you spoke its language, is enough for one
strategy that reaches the goal with every such partner. A check that can fail and never lies,
standing in front of a verdict you can't take back. That's their theorem, in their setting, and
it's the same shape.

\subsection{It computes everything two counters can}

First the base, because if the base can't compute, nothing else here matters.

\begin{definition}[Two-counter program, compile, window]\label{def:u34-minsky}
A \emph{two-counter program} $M$ is a list of instructions, each either $\mathrm{MINC}\ c$ or
$\mathrm{MDEC}\ c\ j$. A configuration is a triple (line, $a$, $b$). One step of $M$: if
the line holds no instruction, $M$ has \emph{stopped}; MINC adds one to $c$ and goes to the next
line; MDEC subtracts one from $c$ and goes to line $j$ if $c$ is above 0, and goes to the
next line if $c$ is 0. $\mathrm{mrun}(n, M, x)$ is $n$ steps from $x$, staying put once
stopped. The \emph{compile} of $M$ replaces each MINC $c$ by INC $c$ and each MDEC $c$ $j$ by DEC
$c$ $j$. The \emph{window} of a core $k$ is the triple (line number, $\mathrm{val}(k, A)$,
$\mathrm{val}(k, B)$).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Step for step]\label{thm:u34-simulation}
For every two-counter program $M$ and every core $k$ with the trap down: $M$ has stopped at
$\mathrm{window}(k)$ if and only if the program $\mathrm{compile}(M)$ has halted at $k$;
and if $M$ steps from $\mathrm{window}(k)$ to $y$, then one program step of
$\mathrm{compile}(M)$ from $k$ lands on a core with window $y$ and the trap still down. So
for every $n$, $n$ program steps of $\mathrm{compile}(M)$ from $k$ land on a core whose
window is $\mathrm{mrun}(n, M, \mathrm{window}(k))$, with the trap down.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Look up the instruction at the line. If there is none, both sides stop. If it's MINC $c$,
the compiled INC $c$ adds one to $c$ and goes to the next line, which is exactly the
window's move (the version also moves, but the window doesn't show versions). If it's MDEC
$c$ $j$, split on whether $c$ is 0, and both sides do the same thing in each case. Neither
instruction can trap. The run statement is induction on $n$, one step at a time.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{simulation\_step} and \code{simulation\_run} (EarnedCore.v).

\begin{theorem}[Halting matches]\label{thm:u34-halting}
For every two-counter program $M$ and whole numbers $a$, $b$: $M$ stops after some number of
steps from $(1, a, b)$ if and only if the program $\mathrm{compile}(M)$ halts after some
number of program steps from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The start has window $(1,a,b)$ and its trap is down. Apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-simulation} after any number $n$ of steps: the two configurations
still have the same window, the trap is still down, and one is stopped exactly when
the other is halted. The same $n$ witnesses termination in either direction.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{halting\_correspondence} (EarnedCore.v).

Now the part that isn't mine. Proving that halting is undecidable for two-counter machines
is real work, and it's already done, checked, in a shared Coq project called the Coq
Library of Undecidability Proofs (presented by Yannick Forster, Dominique Larchey-Wendling
and coauthors at CoqPL 2020). The two-counter result in it is Larchey-Wendling's, reached
from his and Forster's work on Minsky machines (CPP 2019) by way of FRACTRAN, a model of computation invented by John Conway, the English mathematician best known for the Game of Life, which the library uses as a stepping stone. Their two-counter machine has the
same two instructions as Minsky's, with the same rule for zero. Andrej Dudenhefner, one of the
library's authors, writes that rule out in his 2022 paper on deciding questions about
two-counter machines: DEC on a counter at zero goes on to the next instruction, and otherwise
it takes one off the counter and jumps. So the only thing I have to
prove is that their machine and my INC/DEC fragment are the same machine, step for step,
and then borrow their theorem.

One honest wrinkle about what ``undecidable'' means in that library, because it isn't the
textbook sentence. Every function you can write in Coq is a program, so ``decidable'' there
means ``some Coq function answers it.'' Coq by itself can't prove that \emph{no} Coq function
answers a question without an extra assumption about what programs are. So the library
says the strongest thing it can without one: if anything decided this, then the questions
on which a single-tape Turing machine \emph{doesn't} halt could be listed by a program, which is
the classic thing that can't be done. That's their convention, and the theorem below
inherits it exactly.

\begin{theorem}[Halting is undecidable for this machine]\label{thm:u34-undecidable}
The library's two-counter machine agrees with the INC/DEC fragment: its step, its stop, and
its termination match those of the compiled program, so a library problem $(P, a, b)$ halts
if and only if the compiled program halts from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$. Consequently, the
question ``does program $P$ halt from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$?'' is undecidable in the
library's sense: a decider for it would make the complement of single-tape binary Turing machine
halting enumerable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The agreement is a case split on the library's instruction at the current line, and then
induction along the run, ending in Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-halting}. The compile map is then a
reduction from the library's two-counter halting problem, which the library proves
undecidable, and the library's own lemma carries undecidability across a reduction.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{mm2\_step\_iff}, \code{mm2\_stop\_iff}, \code{mm2\_terminates\_iff}, \code{mm2\_halting\_iff} and
\code{earned\_core\_halting\_undecidable} (EarnedCoreLinks.v), the last applying the library's
\code{MM2\_HALTING\_undec}.

What that buys, and what it doesn't. It buys: the base of this machine is a universal
machine in Minsky's sense, and nobody (in the library's sense) can predict in general what
it'll do. What it doesn't buy is a fast machine, or one where your input arrives
conveniently. The counters start holding $a$ and $b$, given directly; there's no encoding
layer in my files. Minsky's prime-power packing is how you'd get from ``any Turing machine''
to ``two counters,'' and that construction is his and the library's, and I use it as it stands.

Is ``given directly'' just a convenience, or does it bite? It bites, and somebody found
exactly where. In 1972 Rich Schroeppel, then at the MIT AI Lab, wrote a ten-page memo titled
``A Two Counter Machine Cannot Calculate $2^N$.'' He spells out the convention first: a counter
machine computing a function starts with $n$ in one counter and zero in the others. Then he gives
a proof that a two-counter machine started that way can't compute
$2^n$. His proof isn't checked in this book. Its checked cousin here is a theorem about
multiplying, near the end of the chapter (Theorem~\ref{thm:no-plain-recursion}). So the packing Minsky needs is precisely the thing two plain counters can't do for
themselves. Hand the small machine its inputs straight and there are functions of them it
can't compute; hand it the inputs already packed and it computes anything a Turing machine
can. That's no contradiction with the undecidability above, which ranges over every program
and every starting pair, packed ones included. The base hides nothing. It just needs its
input pre-chewed, and the chewing is somebody else's.

\subsection{It's a certification system, and the flag is a latch}

Now the record. Three facts first, all of them read straight off the step line.

\begin{theorem}[Ledger, toll, permanence]\label{thm:u34-toll}
For every state $s$ and instruction $i$, $\mu(\mathrm{exec}(s, i)) = \mu(s) +
\mathrm{cost}(i)$, and for every trace $t$, $\mu(\mathrm{run}(t, s)) = \mu(s) +
\mathrm{cost}(t)$. If $\mathrm{cert}(s)$ is down and $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{exec}(s, i))$ is
up, then $i$ is CERTIFY, it passes at $\mathrm{core}(s)$, and $\mathrm{cost}(i) \ge 1$. If
$\mathrm{cert}(s)$ is up, so is $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{exec}(s, i))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Read the ledger component of Definition~\ref{def:u34-step}: it adds exactly
$\mathrm{cost}(i)$. Repeated substitution along a trace gives the sum of its costs,
or, equivalently, induction on the length of the trace does. The flag's new value is
its old value or $\mathrm{fires}(\mathrm{core}(s),i)$. A false-to-true change therefore
requires that event, whose definition requires a passing CERTIFY. CERTIFY costs $1$.
