An already true flag stays true under the same disjunction.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{mu\_conservation}, \code{mu\_conservation\_trace}, \code{only\_certify\_certifies}, \code{a2} and
\code{cert\_permanent} (EarnedCore.v).

That third clause in the middle is Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s toll, for this machine. Which means this machine \emph{is}
one of the things Section~\ref{sec:toll} was about, and Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s theorem applies to it without my lifting a finger.

\begin{theorem}[An instance of the certification system]\label{thm:u34-instance}
The states, the instructions, the step $\mathrm{exec}$, the cost and the flag, with the toll
of Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}, form a certification system (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}). So
the universal floor (Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-floor}) holds here: if
$\mathrm{cert}(s_0)$ is down and $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{run}(t, s_0))$ is up, then
$\mathrm{cost}(t) \ge 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take the state and instruction sets of Definitions~\ref{def:u34-state} and
\ref{def:u34-step}, their step and cost, and the flag as the reading. These provide the
five data fields of Definition~\ref{def:certsys}. Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll} supplies its
one required rule. Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-floor} gives the claimed bound.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{earned\_cs} and \code{earned\_core\_floor} (EarnedCoreLinks.v); \code{earned\_core\_floor} is
\code{universal\_nfi\_any\_substrate}, the checked name of Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s theorem, applied to \code{earned\_cs}. The
same floor is proved directly, without the link, as \code{nfi\_floor} (EarnedCore.v).

Then Section~\ref{sec:latch}. Section~\ref{sec:latch} said: take any base, and any record that answers only to the base and never
comes back down, and the record is a latch. This machine has a base: a program together
with a core, stepping by the program step. And it has a record, the flag, with the ledger
riding along. So the question is whether it's an \emph{honest} extension in Section~\ref{sec:latch}'s five-rule
sense (Definition~\ref{def:u11-honest}), and if it is, Section~\ref{sec:latch} does the rest.

\begin{theorem}[The flag is a latch of the base]\label{thm:u34-latch}
Let the base have states (program, core), stepping by the program step, starting at
$\mathrm{start}(a, b)$'s core for any $a$, $b$, and halting when the program has halted.
Map each (program, state) to (program, core). Then the machine, run as a closed machine on
(program, state), is an honest extension of that base, and so its flag factors as the latch
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch}) of the event ``the next instruction is a CERTIFY that passes.''
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The rules of Definition~\ref{def:u11-honest} one at a time. Driven by the computation: the
next flag is the old flag or ``the next instruction is a passing CERTIFY,'' which is a
function of the base state and the old flag (that's the step line). Ledger: $\mu$ only adds.
Toll: Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}. Permanence: Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}. A reachable write: the
three-line program of the worked run raises the flag from a start. Section~\ref{sec:latch}'s theorem then gives
the factorization.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{earned\_core\_honest} and \code{earned\_core\_is\_latch} (EarnedCoreLinks.v), the latter
by \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_holds}; the step-level facts are \code{cert\_latch} and \code{base\_blind}
(EarnedCore.v).

So far, nothing new. The toll, the floor and the latch are things Parts II and III already
promised about any machine of this kind. The next subsection is the part neither of them could give.

\subsection{Commitments are earned}

Here's the shape before the words. Pick any run from a clean start, any list of instructions
at all, chosen by somebody who'd love to cheat. Look at the moment a COMMIT would pass.
Then, somewhere earlier in that run, there's a CHECK of exactly the same claim that passed
and paid, at the same edition of the counter, and between that CHECK and now, nothing
touched the counter. Not ``probably.'' Not ``on the programs I wrote.'' On every list of
instructions anybody can write.

To say ``nothing touched it'' exactly, one word.

\begin{definition}[Untouched]\label{def:u34-untouched}
A list of instructions $\mathit{mid}$, run from a state $s$, leaves counter $c$
\emph{untouched} when, for every way of splitting $\mathit{mid}$ as $t_1$, then $i$, then
$t_2$, executing $i$ at the core reached by running $t_1$ from $s$ leaves both
$\mathrm{ver}(\cdot, c)$ and $\mathrm{val}(\cdot, c)$ as they were.
\end{definition}

Defined as \code{untouched} (EarnedCore.v).

\begin{theorem}[A commitment was checked first]\label{thm:u34-commit-earned}
Let $s_0$ be clean and $\mathit{pre}$ any trace after which COMMIT $p$ $c$ would pass. Then
$\mathit{pre}$ splits as $\mathit{pre}_1$, then CHECK $p$ $c$, then $\mathit{mid}$, where:
the CHECK passes at the core reached by $\mathit{pre}_1$; CHECK $p$ $c$ and COMMIT $p$ $c$
each cost at least 1; $c$'s version after $\mathit{pre}_1$ equals its version after
$\mathit{pre}$; and $\mathit{mid}$, run from just after the CHECK, leaves $c$ untouched.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
COMMIT passes, so the claim $(p, c, \mathrm{ver}(c))$ for the current version is in the
table. By the no-forging invariant (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-no-forging} below), that fact was
written by a passing CHECK $p$ $c$ at some point $\mathit{pre}_1$, with the version $c$ had
then; since it's the current version too, the two versions are equal. Versions never go
down, and any instruction that changes a counter's value also raises its version, so an
instruction in $\mathit{mid}$ that touched $c$ would have left $c$'s version higher at the
end than at the CHECK. It isn't. So nothing in $\mathit{mid}$ touched $c$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{earned\_commitment\_provenance} (EarnedCore.v).

\begin{theorem}[A raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified]\label{thm:u34-cert-earned}
Let $s_0$ be clean and $t$ any trace with $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{run}(t, s_0))$ up. Then
for some $p$ and $c$, $t$ is
\[
\mathit{pre}_1,\ \ \mathrm{CHECK}\ p\ c,\ \ \mathit{mid}_1,\ \ \mathrm{COMMIT}\ p\ c,\ \ \mathit{mid}_2,\ \ \mathrm{CERTIFY},\ \ \mathit{post},
\]
where the CHECK passes at its state, the COMMIT passes at its state, the CERTIFY passes at
its state, $c$ has the same version at the CHECK as at the COMMIT, and $\mathit{mid}_1$ leaves
$c$ untouched.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The flag starts down, so some first instruction raised it, and by
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll} it's a passing CERTIFY. A CERTIFY passes only with a fact in the
channel, the channel starts empty, and only a passing COMMIT puts a fact there, so some
earlier COMMIT $p$ $c$ passed. Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-commit-earned} at that COMMIT gives the
CHECK, the equal version, and the untouched stretch.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{earned\_certification\_provenance} (EarnedCore.v).

And the failure side, so you can see the refusals are clean, with nothing left half-done:

\begin{theorem}[Unearned steps trap and change no claim]\label{thm:u34-failures}
If COMMIT $p$ $c$ would not pass at a core $k$, executing it puts the trap up and leaves the
channel and the table as they were. If CERTIFY would not pass at a state $s$, executing it
puts the trap up and leaves the flag as it was.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If the trap is already up, the core is unchanged and its trap remains up. Otherwise,
the failed COMMIT takes the failure branch of the instruction table: set the trap,
leave every other core field alone. A failed CERTIFY takes the same branch, and its
$\mathrm{fires}$ value is false. The flag update is then its old value or false,
which leaves it unchanged. The instruction's charge still applies to the ledger.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{unearned\_commit\_traps} and \code{uncommitted\_certify\_traps} (EarnedCore.v).

If that rings a bell, it should. It's Milner's move from the opening chapter: in LCF a theorem is
a value that only the rules of the logic can build, so nobody can just print one (Milner and two
colleagues on his Edinburgh project, Michael Gordon and Christopher Wadsworth, wrote the system up
in 1979, and Gordon, who went on to build the HOL prover at Cambridge, told its history in
2000). Here the thing nobody can print is one bit, and what guards it is one step rule. Milner's guard
was a type checker. Same architecture, much lower down.

A provenance theorem is also an itemised receipt, and the itemised receipt has a history that's
exactly this gap. James Ritty ran a saloon in Dayton, Ohio, and believed some of his staff were
pocketing money. On a steamboat trip to Europe in 1878 he watched a mechanism that counted the
turns of the ship's propeller, and wondered whether something like it could count the money
instead. In 1879 he and his brother John patented a ``Cash Register and Indicator,'' and they
sold a version under the wonderful name Ritty's Incorruptible Cashier. The first model was this
book's counter (Section~\ref{sec:counter}) with brass on it: press a key, the amount goes onto a
dial showing the day's running total. No drawer, no paper. At closing time you hold the dial up
against the cash. And that's all a total can do. It tells you \emph{that} the money is short. It can't
tell you which sale went missing or who rang it up. The paper came later. The patents passed to
other owners, first a Cincinnati salesman named Jacob Eckert, and in 1884 to John H. Patterson,
who renamed the business the National Cash Register Company, and the story told
about that company is that it added a paper roll: one copy kept for the shop's own books, one
handed to the customer. That last part I only have from histories of the company and of the
machine, so hold it the way you'd hold any company's story about itself. The order is right
either way: first a total that can tell you something's wrong, then a list that tells you where.
The ledger $\mu$ is the dial. Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned} is the list: which CHECK, of
which claim, about which edition, before which COMMIT. The theorem supplies that list about the
run. The machine doesn't keep it as data anyone can read back from the end state, and nothing
in the theorem gives a procedure for rebuilding it from there. A fact in the table holds a
property, a counter and a version number. That's neither the counter's value back then nor a
log of what happened in between.

Read Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned} once more for what it \emph{doesn't} say. Between the CHECK
and the COMMIT, the counter is untouched. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, it isn't
promised anything. You can check $A$ is even, commit to it, add one to $A$, and then
certify. The flag goes up, and what it stands on is a commitment about the edition that was
current when you committed. The certificate is historical: it says ``this was checked and
committed about this edition,'' and it says nothing about whether that's still true. I think
that's the right meaning for a
certificate (a birth certificate doesn't expire when the baby grows), but it's a meaning,
and you should know which one you're getting. So a certificate doesn't say the claim holds at
the CERTIFY, and it doesn't say the claim holds at the end of the run. A CERTIFY that rechecked
the version would give a different guarantee. That's a possible extension, and the historical
theorem doesn't need it.

\subsection{What a passing check means}

Provenance says a CHECK happened. It doesn't yet say the CHECK was \emph{right}, and that's a
separate question with a separate proof. A machine could have a perfectly ordered chain of
check, commit, certify, all standing on a checker that says yes to everything. So: what does
a fact in the table actually tell you about the counter?

\begin{theorem}[Checker soundness]\label{thm:u34-soundness}
Let $s_0$ be clean and $t$ any trace, and let $k$ be the core of $\mathrm{run}(t, s_0)$. For
every fact $(p, c, v)$ in $k$'s table with $v = \mathrm{ver}(k, c)$, the property holds of
the counter's current value: $\mathrm{holds}(p, \mathrm{val}(k, c))$. In particular, if
COMMIT $p$ $c$ would pass at $k$, then $\mathrm{holds}(p, \mathrm{val}(k, c))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Carry one sentence through every instruction: every fact in the table has a version no
higher than its counter's, and if its version equals its counter's, its property holds of
its counter's value. A clean start has an empty table, so the sentence holds there. A
passing CHECK adds a fact at the current version, and the checker said yes, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:u34-eval} the property holds. A write raises one counter's version, so every
old fact about that counter falls strictly behind and the second half no longer applies to
it. Nothing else changes a value or a version. The sentence holds after every instruction,
so it holds at the end. The part about COMMIT is the case where the claim is in the table at
the current version.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{checker\_soundness} and \code{committed\_claim\_holds} (EarnedCore.v), through the
invariant \code{sound} and its one-step form \code{sound\_step}.

So, on a run from a clean start, a live fact means
exactly this: one of three arithmetic properties holds of one counter's
current value. Not ``the program is correct.'' Not ``the number is interesting.'' The property,
of the value, now. That's all ``checked'' means on this machine, and it's enough to be true.
Three events stay separate here. The property holding of the value is one. A CHECK passing is
another: a CHECK of a property that holds still doesn't pass when the table is full or the trap
is already up. A certification is a third, and it needs a COMMIT and a CERTIFY after the CHECK.
So a CHECK that didn't pass says nothing about whether its property is false.

So who checked the checker? Nothing on the record did. From a clean start, the record
carries the run's half of
the story: a CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same claim about the same edition, then a CERTIFY. The
other half, that the checker says yes exactly when the property holds, isn't in any run. It's
Lemma~\ref{lem:u34-eval}, a proof about the little program the step calls, checked once by Coq
and priced by nothing on the ledger. So a claim established here stands on two legs: a fact
about this run, carried by the record, and a fact about the checker, carried by a proof that
whoever reads the record has to accept. That's the Münchhausen trilemma from the opening chapter
taking its third horn on purpose: the chain of reasons stops at a proof, named and on the page,
where you can decide whether you'd have stopped there too. And the entitlement it gives is the
reader's. The machine doesn't know anything. It keeps the order.

The question in that paragraph is older than any checker, and its most famous wording isn't
about what you'd guess. ``Who will guard the guardians?'' gets quoted about governments and police
and, lately, proof assistants. Where's it from? Plato's
\emph{Republic} has the worry, sort of: in Book III (at 403e), Glaucon, Plato's older brother and
one of the people Socrates is talking with, says it would be absurd for a guardian
to need a guardian, which is close in words and opposite in mood, a man calling the question
silly. The Latin, \emph{quis custodiet ipsos custodes}, is from the Roman satirist Juvenal's sixth
satire, and it's a joke about a husband. His friends tell him to bolt his wife in and set guards
on her; the line asks who'll watch the guards, since she'll start with them. And it gets better.
In 1899 an Oxford undergraduate, E. O. Winstedt, found extra lines of that satire in a medieval
manuscript in the Bodleian Library, lines the other copies lack, partly overlapping the familiar
ones, and the famous question sits in that tangle. Scholars have argued ever since about whether
those lines are Juvenal's at all. So the most quoted sentence about trusting the checker comes
with a doubtful source of its own. Does that change anything here? No. The only answer I know
that works is de Bruijn's (Section~\ref{sec:coq} has it): you never get rid of the last guard, you
make the last guard small enough to watch yourself. Lemma~\ref{lem:u34-eval} is one line per
property. Euclid had the instinct: five postulates you can hold in your head, and everything else
meant to follow from them.

That split, a fixed checker proved sound from outside and a process that only gets to act when
the checker says yes, has a name in the writing on self-improving programs. The AI researcher
Jürgen Schmidhuber, at the IDSIA lab in Lugano, described a
Gödel machine (2003) that rewrites its own code only after its built-in proof searcher has proved the
rewrite useful, and Benja Fallenstein and Nate Soares (2015), researchers at the Machine
Intelligence Research Institute in Berkeley, survey agents that reason about their
successors through formal proofs a fixed checker accepts. Same architecture, aimed at a different
question: they want to know when a machine may trust a smarter version of itself, and this
machine only wants to know whether a flag was earned. Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} says why the
checker's proof has to live outside.

Soundness rules out a lying checker. It doesn't rule out a pointless question: \emph{at least 0}
has a perfectly sound checker and an empty no pile, as the worked run showed.

\subsection{Nothing gets forged}

The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-commit-earned} leaned on an invariant I promised to show you.
Here it is. The fear it answers: could some clever sequence of instructions get a fact into
the table without a CHECK writing it? A DEC with a funny jump target, a COMMIT after a trap,
something I didn't think of? The answer is checked one instruction at a time, which is the
only way I trust myself to answer it.

\begin{definition}[Earned fact; no forgery]\label{def:u34-earned}
After a trace $t$ from $s_0$, a fact $f = (p, c, v)$ is \emph{earned} when $t$ is $\mathit{pre}$,
then CHECK $p$ $c$, then $\mathit{mid}$, where the CHECK passes at the core reached by
$\mathit{pre}$, $f$ is exactly the claim $p$ of $c$ at that core, and, if $f$ is live at the
end ($v$ equals $c$'s version after $t$), $\mathit{mid}$ leaves $c$ untouched. The trace has
\emph{no forgery} when every fact in the table after it is earned.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[No forging]\label{thm:u34-no-forging}
For every core $k$, instruction $i$ and fact $f$ in the table after executing $i$ at $k$:
either $f$ was already in $k$'s table, or $i$ is CHECK of $f$'s property and counter, it
passes at $k$, and $f$ is the claim it writes. Consequently, if a trace has no forgery, so
does that trace followed by any one instruction; and from every clean start, every trace
has no forgery.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The first part is a case for each of the six instructions: only a passing CHECK adds
anything, and it adds exactly its claim. For the second, a new fact is earned by the CHECK
that just wrote it; an old fact stays earned, and if it's still live after the new
instruction, its counter's version didn't move, so the new instruction didn't touch the
counter and the untouched stretch grows by one. A clean start has an empty table, which has
no forgery, and the step carries it along any trace.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{facts\_step}, \code{no\_forging\_step} and \code{no\_forging} (EarnedCore.v).

\subsection{A full table traps}

Sixteen facts of room, and no eviction. Two halves to prove: nothing ever leaves, and
nothing ever overflows.

\begin{theorem}[Bounded table, no eviction]\label{thm:u34-bounded}
Every instruction keeps every fact already in the table. If the table holds 16 or more
facts, CHECK $p$ $c$ puts the trap up and leaves the table as it was. If the table holds at
most 16 facts, it still holds at most 16 after any instruction.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With a raised trap no instruction changes the table. With the trap down, only CHECK
can change it, and a successful CHECK adds one fact without removing an entry.
Success requires a previous length strictly below $16$, so the new length is at most
$16$. At length $16$ or greater that branch is unavailable: CHECK raises the trap
and preserves the table. Every other instruction preserves it as well.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{facts\_keep}, \code{full\_table\_traps} and \code{facts\_bounded\_step} (EarnedCore.v).

Why trap? Why not make room? Because ``making room'' means deciding which fact dies, and a
fact that can die is a fact whose absence you have to explain later. A table that only grows
is a history you can read back, and the provenance proofs above lean on exactly that. The
bill for it is real, though, and it's in the subsection near the end of this chapter on
what the machine doesn't do.

\subsection{The window can't see the record}

Section~\ref{sec:windows} was about windows: a view of a state that shows some of it, and the theorem that a window
which can't tell two states apart can't price the step between them exactly
(Theorem~\ref{thm:shadow-price}). Here's the smallest pair I could build where the window is
Minsky's view of the machine (line number and the two counters) and the record is
everything else.

Run two traces from $\mathrm{start}(0, 0)$. The \emph{earned} run is CHECK \emph{is zero} $A$; COMMIT
\emph{is zero} $A$; CERTIFY. The \emph{idle} run is DEC $A$ 0, three times. In the idle run, $A$ is 0
every time, so each DEC just goes to the next line and writes nothing. Both runs end on line
4, with $A = 0$ and $B = 0$, both versions 0. Through the window, identical. One of them has
paid 3, holds a fact, could commit again, and has its flag up. The other has paid nothing,
holds nothing, can't commit, and its flag is down. Two photographs, same picture, different
people.

\begin{theorem}[Same window, different record]\label{thm:u34-separation}
The earned run and the idle run from $\mathrm{start}(0, 0)$ end at cores with the same
window and the same versions of $A$ and $B$, and with different ledgers, different flags,
different tables, and different answers to ``would COMMIT \emph{is zero} $A$ pass.''
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In the earned run, CHECK adds $(\mathsf{Zero},A,0)$, COMMIT puts that fact in the
channel, and CERTIFY raises the flag. The ledger is $1+1+1=3$. No counter is written.
In the idle run each DEC sees zero, so it advances the line without writing a counter
or raising a version. Its three costs are zero and it adds no fact or commitment.
Thus both final windows are $(4,0,0)$ with versions $(0,0)$. The earned table contains
the current zero claim and the idle table is empty, giving the stated difference in
whether another COMMIT would pass, as well as in the ledger and flag.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{receipt\_separation} (EarnedCore.v).

\begin{theorem}[No window oracle]\label{thm:u34-no-oracle}
There is no function $g$ from windows to whole numbers with $g(\mathrm{window}) = \mu$ at the
end of every trace from $\mathrm{start}(0, 0)$. Likewise there is no function from windows to
yes or no that gives the flag at the end of every such trace, and none that gives whether
COMMIT \emph{is zero} $A$ would pass.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Such a $g$ would have to give both 3 and 0 on the one window the two runs of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-separation} share. The same for the flag and the commit right.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{no\_mu\_oracle}, \code{no\_cert\_oracle} and \code{no\_commit\_oracle} (EarnedCore.v).

This is Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s shape, made of pebbles: the record lives off the window. Anybody who only
watches the counters and the line number, which is everything Minsky's machine \emph{is}, can't
tell you what was paid, what was committed, or whether the flag is up. Not because they
looked carelessly. Because it isn't there to see.

Two things the same in everything you look at and still two things: philosophy has an old fight
about exactly that, and it's worth a detour, because it tells you which side of the fight these
theorems stand on. Leibniz said that for real things it can't happen. There are no two
individuals indiscernible from each other, he wrote in 1716 to Samuel Clarke, the English
philosopher and theologian who was taking Newton's side against him in an exchange of letters,
and he told a story to go with it. A clever gentleman of his acquaintance, talking with him in
front of the Electress Sophia of Hanover, Leibniz's friend and patron, in the garden at
Herrenhausen she had helped lay out, thought he could find two leaves perfectly alike. She dared
him to. He ``ran all over the Garden a long time'' looking, and it was ``to no purpose.'' You can
run his search tonight with a handful of anything, leaves or coins or grains of rice: look hard
enough and every pair differs somewhere. Then in 1952 Max Black, a Russian-born philosopher
teaching at Cornell, pushed back with a universe you
can't build at the table. Nothing in it but two iron spheres, the same size, the same colour, the
same everything, some distance apart. Name a difference between them. There isn't one, and there
are still two of them. People have argued about Black's spheres ever since, and I'm not going to
settle it.

Here's why I don't have to. Leibniz's claim is about \emph{every} property a thing has. The
theorems above are about three: the line and the two counters. The two runs aren't indiscernible
in his sense at all: one has a fact in its table and its flag up, and the other doesn't, and Coq
tells them apart in a line. They're indiscernible to a window, which is a much cheaper thing, and
it's the thing that matters for a machine, because an observer of a machine only ever gets a
window. Leibniz's gentleman would always find his difference if he could look at everything. It
doesn't help him if all he's allowed to look at is three things about each leaf.

There's a horse in this, too, if you squint. In Germany in the early 1900s a mathematics teacher
named Wilhelm von Osten showed off a horse called Clever Hans, who answered arithmetic questions
by tapping a hoof, and got them right, in front of crowds. Same answers out as a horse that could
count: that's the idle run's matching window. Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst stopped looking
at the answers and started changing the conditions, and published what he found in 1907. Put
blinders on Hans, or have him asked by someone who didn't know the answer, and the arithmetic fell
apart. Hans was reading the questioner: tiny, unintended movements of the head and body as the
hoof reached the right number. That's the probe. Pfungst didn't argue with the answers. He asked a
question the answers couldn't fake, one that needed the real thing to be there, the way a COMMIT
needs a checked fact to be in the table: run COMMIT \emph{is zero} $A$ after each of the two runs,
and one passes and the other traps (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-separation}). And the part of the story I
like best: nobody was lying. Von Osten was never persuaded by Pfungst and kept showing his horse.
A matching window doesn't need a cheat behind it, which is why you want a probe. An accusation is
the wrong tool for it.

\subsection{The exact price is three}

Section~\ref{sec:toll} said a raised flag costs at least one. On this machine that's true and too modest. A
raised flag needs a CERTIFY, a CERTIFY needs a COMMIT, a COMMIT needs a CHECK, and each of
those is its own instruction costing one. So at least three. One of what: three units of
$\mu$, one per paid act, each one the ``one'' I picked back in the table. And three is the number
of links in the chain. It isn't a guess that happens to hold.

\begin{theorem}[The minimum price of a certificate]\label{thm:u34-min-price}
If $s_0$ is clean and $\mathrm{cert}(\mathrm{run}(t, s_0))$ is up, then $\mathrm{cost}(t)
\ge 3$ and $\mu(\mathrm{run}(t, s_0)) \ge \mu(s_0) + 3$. For programs: if the flag is up
after $n$ program steps from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$, then $\mu \ge 3$ there.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned} finds a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY at three different
places in $t$, each costing 1, and every other instruction costs at least 0. The ledger
statement is Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}. A program run is the run of the instructions it
actually executes, so the program form follows.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{certified\_run\_min\_cost} and \code{program\_certified\_min\_cost} (EarnedCore.v).

The three is three independent units, one for each part of a clean start. A flag that is down
buys the first: a run that raises it costs at least one (\code{nfi\_floor}). An empty channel buys
the second: with the flag down and the channel empty, a run that raises the flag costs at least two
(\code{nec\_s\_floor\_two}). An empty table buys the third, and that is the theorem above. Leave out
any one part and its floor fails, and a cheaper certificate is there: with the flag already up it
costs 0, with a commitment already in the channel 1, and with a live fact already in the table 2
(\code{nec\_s\_clean\_conjuncts\_each\_buy\_one}, \code{nec\_s\_min\_cost\_needs\_flag\_down},
\code{nec\_s\_min\_cost\_needs\_empty\_channel} and \code{nec\_s\_min\_cost\_needs\_empty\_table}). The
exact condition is \code{nec\_s\_floor3\_iff}: every run from a state that raises the flag costs at
least three exactly when the flag is down and one of two things holds: the trap is up,
or the channel is empty and
every fact in the table is about an older version of its counter. And three is paid exactly from
every clean start whose trap is down (\code{nec\_s\_witness\_from\_every\_clean\_start}). All of these
are in NecSClean.v, except \code{nfi\_floor}, which is in EarnedCore.v.

\begin{theorem}[Three is tight]\label{thm:u34-tight}
For all whole numbers $a$ and $b$, run the program CHECK \emph{is zero} $A$; COMMIT \emph{is zero}
$A$; CERTIFY for 4 program steps from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$. If $a = 0$, it ends with the
flag up and $\mu = 3$ exactly. If $a \ne 0$, it ends with the flag down and the trap up, and
for every $n$, $n$ program steps from $\mathrm{start}(a, b)$ leave the flag down.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $a = 0$, the checker for $\mathsf{Zero}$ says yes at $0$, so the first instruction adds
$(\mathsf{Zero},A,0)$ to the empty table and charges $1$. No counter changes, so the
second instruction finds that same fact, puts it in the channel and charges $1$. The
third finds the channel occupied, raises the flag and charges $1$. The line is now $4$,
beyond the three-instruction program, and the fourth program step adds no charge. The
final ledger is exactly $3$. If $a \ne 0$, the checker says no, so the first instruction
sets the trap and leaves the flag down. A program run takes no step once the trap is up,
so every later program step leaves the state, flag included, exactly where it is.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{earned\_run\_check\_can\_fail} and \code{earned\_run\_refused\_forever}
(EarnedCore.v), with the program named \code{earned\_run}, and the lemma
\code{run\_prog\_trapped} for a trapped run standing still. The version whose check can't
fail, CHECK \emph{at least 0} $A$; COMMIT \emph{at least 0} $A$; CERTIFY, certifies from every
start for exactly 3 (\code{min\_cost\_tight}, with that program named \code{witness}). So the
floor of three is reachable from any start at all, and that's the machine declining to police
trivial checks. On that program the machine establishes nothing.

That's the worked run from the start of the chapter, now as a theorem. The floor is 3, and a
run whose check could have failed pays exactly 3, so 3 is the price. The bound has no slack
in it.

Don't mistake that 3 for a measure of how hard a claim is to certify. It's the same 3 for every
claim, easy or hard, because only the three acts that make a claim are priced and the counters
work out whatever the check needs for free. A cost of certifying that grows with the claim
would have to price the checking itself, and that's a different question with its own
literature. Four theoretical computer scientists, Guy Blanc, Caleb Koch, Jane Lange and Li-Yang Tan (2022), studied one version of it
under the name the query complexity of certification: how many questions an algorithm has to
ask a black-box function to hand back a small certificate for its answer. Their count moves
with the function. Mine doesn't move at all.

And that's every piece of the model, standing on six instructions: a base that computes
everything two counters can, a ledger that's exact, a toll the universal floor applies to, a
flag that's a latch of the base, a window that can't see the record, and, from a clean start, a commitment that can't
happen unless a check of the same claim,
on the same edition, came first and was right. Every result above is closed: Coq reports no assumptions for any of them. That isn't
my say-so. EarnedCore.v and its link file, EarnedCoreLinks.v, each end by asking Coq to print the assumptions of each headline
theorem, and the build of Section~\ref{sec:coq} compiles them and fails unless every one comes
back closed. The
project-wide audit of Section~\ref{sec:coq} lists these files too, and every theorem in them comes
back closed there as well. The base
file uses nothing but Coq's standard library, so you can check it with nothing else
installed; the link file adds only the book's own abstract records and the library of
undecidability proofs.

\subsection{What it takes to be Thiele-complete}

The front matter promised a definition of Thiele-complete with teeth, so here it is. First,
why it needs teeth. The easy definition goes: a Thiele machine is Thiele-complete when its base
can compute anything a Turing machine can. It looks fine, and it's nearly empty. Take Minsky's
two-counter machine, charge one mark for every move, and pick any yes-or-no question about its
configuration as the record. Every move costs one, so every move that raises the record costs
one, so it obeys the toll. That's a Thiele machine with a universal base: a clock bolted to a
computer. A machine whose record never goes up passes too, since a toll on a raise that never
happens is never broken. Neither one earns anything, and a name both of them get for free isn't
saying much.

So the definition below asks for what the small machine actually does, written so that any
machine at all can be held up against it. You hand over a reading of the machine, a list of
things, and then the reading has to pass four clauses.

\begin{definition}[Thiele-complete]\label{def:u34-thiele-complete}
A \emph{machine} has states, moves, a step, a cost for each move and a yes/no reading of each
state, the \emph{record}. An \emph{interface} for it hands over: a \emph{universal base}, meaning
a two-counter configuration shown by each state (its \emph{window}), a class of \emph{live}
states, a move for each two-counter instruction, and a loaded state for each start $(1, a, b)$;
a type of \emph{claims}, each with a \emph{meaning}, a statement about a state; a \emph{checker}
that says yes or no to a claim at a state; for each claim, a relation ``the thing this claim is
about is unchanged'' between two states; a set of \emph{clean} states; a \emph{ledger}, a whole
number for each state; and a \emph{kind} for each move: a base move, CHECK of a claim, COMMIT of a
claim, or CERTIFY. The machine is \emph{Thiele-complete} when some interface meets four clauses.
(a) \emph{Universal base.} Each two-counter instruction's move is a base move; from every live
state it acts on the window exactly as the instruction acts on a configuration, and the state
stays live; each loaded state shows $(1, a, b)$, is live and is clean; no base move changes the
record; and a record that's up stays up under every move.
(b) \emph{Earned record.} Clean states have the record down. Every run from a clean state that
ends with the record up contains a CHECK of some claim $c$ that passes, then a COMMIT of $c$
with the thing $c$ is about unchanged at every state in between, then a CERTIFY, with the record
down just before that CERTIFY and up just after it. A passing check means its claim's meaning
holds of the state it checked, and a meaning that holds keeps holding while the thing it's
about is unchanged.
(c) \emph{Exact toll.} Base moves cost 0, each CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY costs exactly 1, and
each move adds its cost to the ledger.
(d) \emph{Non-vacuity.} Some claim $c$ has a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY such that those three
moves alone, from a loaded state, raise the record exactly when $c$'s meaning holds there; and
$c$ holds at some loaded state and fails at another.
A Thiele machine whose base is universal, with no more asked, is \emph{weakly} Thiele-complete.
\end{definition}

Defined as \code{thiele\_interface}, \code{thiele\_complete\_with} and \code{thiele\_complete}
(ThieleComplete.v), with the four clauses as \code{universal\_base\_clause},
\code{earned\_record\_clause}, \code{exact\_toll\_clause} and \code{non\_vacuity\_clause}, and the
easy notion as \code{weakly\_thiele\_complete}.

Read the four clauses as four plain sentences. (a) It computes anything a Turing machine can,
and the computing can't reach the record: the base moves are the two-counter machine, they
leave the record exactly
where it was, and a record that goes up stays up. (b) From a clean start, the record goes up only on
top of the small machine's chain: a check that passed, a commitment
to the same claim with nothing changed underneath, then a certificate. (c) Computing is free and each of the three acts costs one, so the ledger
counts the acts. The steps in between go free. (d) Somewhere there's a claim whose check could have said no. A
machine whose every claim is ``at least 0'' doesn't qualify, and neither does one with nothing
to certify.

And look where the checker's honesty sits. In (b), ``a passing check means its claim holds''
is a field of the interface, proved once, outside every run, exactly where it sat for the small
machine (Lemma~\ref{lem:u34-eval}). The definition doesn't ask the machine to vouch for its own
checker, and Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} says why nothing of arithmetic strength could.
Nor does it ask the checker to be something a machine could run. Clause (b) wants a yes or no for
every claim at every state, sound for the claim's meaning, and nothing in it says that answer has
to be computable. Every instance in this book has a checker that's an actual program, so anything
those machines certify could be listed by a program that runs them. Inside Coq with no extra
assumptions that's all there can be, since every checker you can write there is a program, the
same point I made about what ``undecidable'' means in the library. An oracle gets in two other
ways: read the definition as ordinary mathematics, where any function counts, or add an axiom
that hands Coq a function knowing which programs run forever. Hand the definition a checker like
that and it's still met, and the machine certifies claims no program could ever confirm. Nothing
in this book builds one. So ``a Thiele-complete machine certifies
exactly the claims a program could list'' is true only with ``and its checker is computable''
added, and the definition doesn't require that.

One word needs pinning before the theorems, using the three names set at the front of the book.
In clause (c), the \emph{exact toll} is instruction-exact pricing: each of the three acts, CHECK
and COMMIT included, costs exactly one, so the ledger counts the acts that make a claim. Back in
Section~\ref{sec:counter}, one of the cited results (\code{a2\_and\_aara\_iff\_exact}) is about
rise-only pricing in its tightest bill, the \emph{exact schedule}: one mark on the step that
raises the flag and nothing on any other step. Measured against the flag alone, the small machine
isn't rise-only, since CHECK and COMMIT raise no flag and cost one each; measured the way (c)
asks, it is instruction-exact. Neither is wrong. They answer different questions: does the ledger
count the acts, or does it charge the flag and only the flag? Simulation-exact accounting, the
third name, comes up with the universal program $U$ below.

\begin{theorem}[What every Thiele-complete machine has]\label{thm:u34-tc-consequences}
Let a machine be Thiele-complete through an interface. (1) It obeys the toll and has a
universal base, so it's weakly Thiele-complete; its base runs every two-counter program step
for step from every live state,
and halting from a loaded state matches halting from the configuration it shows. (2) Along any run, the ledger rises by exactly the number of
CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY moves in it. (3) A run from a clean state that ends with the record up
contains at least three of those moves and raises the ledger by at least 3. (4) Some CHECK fails
at some loaded state, on a claim that is false there, and some run from some loaded state raises
the record. (5) On a run from a clean state, the move that raises the record is a CERTIFY. (6)
Every move costs 0 or 1, and some move costs 0.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) A raise of the record isn't made by a base move, by (a), so it's a record move, which costs
one by (c). Running a program on the base is induction on its steps, each matched by (a).
(2) is (c), added up along the run. (3) Clause (b) finds a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY at three
different places, and (2) counts them. (4) is (d): the three moves certify exactly where the
claim holds, the claim fails at some loaded state, and the check can't pass there because (b)
says a passing check means the claim holds; at the loaded state where it holds, the three moves
raise the record. (5) Clause (b) puts the record down right before a CERTIFY and up right after
it, and the record never comes down, so that CERTIFY is the first and only move where it rises.
(6) Every move is a base move or a record move, and (a) supplies base moves.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{thiele\_complete\_is\_weak}, \code{base\_runs\_every\_program},
\code{base\_halting\_correspondence}, \code{ledger\_counts\_record\_moves},
\code{certificate\_costs\_three}, \code{check\_can\_fail}, \code{some\_run\_certifies},
\code{only\_certify\_raises}, \code{complete\_costs\_at\_most\_one} and
\code{complete\_has\_free\_move} (ThieleComplete.v).

The second half of (6), that some move costs 0, is the one that kills the clock.

\begin{theorem}[A clock is a Thiele machine and isn't Thiele-complete]\label{thm:u34-clock}
Take the two-counter machine, let every move cost 1, and take as the record any yes/no
question about its configuration whatsoever; or take a flag that switches on, and stays on, the
first time any chosen test of the configuration says yes. Either way the machine obeys the toll
and has a universal base, so it's weakly Thiele-complete, and it is not Thiele-complete. More
generally, no machine whose every move costs at least 1 is Thiele-complete.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every move costs one, so any raise costs at least one: the toll holds for any record. The
machine's own moves are the two-counter instructions, which gives the universal base. But a
Thiele-complete machine has a free move, by Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tc-consequences}(6), and this
one has none.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{clock\_weakly\_thiele\_complete}, \code{clock\_not\_thiele\_complete},
\code{latch\_clock\_weakly\_thiele\_complete} and \code{latch\_clock\_not\_thiele\_complete}
(ThieleComplete.v).

That's short, and it's short because clause (c) does exactly the job it was written for: it
says computing is free, and a clock charges for computing. The other clauses earn their keep
too, and that's worth checking, because a definition with a clause nothing needs is a
definition hiding something.

\begin{theorem}[Each clause does work]\label{thm:u34-tc-clauses}
(1) Take a free two-counter base with a ledger beside it, and one extra move TICK that costs 1
and raises a flag. It obeys the toll, and read with TICK as CERTIFY it meets the universal base
clause and the exact toll clause; it is not Thiele-complete, and more generally no machine with a
move that raises the record from every state is. (2) Take a free two-counter base and a record
that never rises. It obeys the toll and meets clauses (a), (b) and (c); it is not
Thiele-complete, and more generally no machine whose record never rises is.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) From a clean state, TICK alone raises the record. Clause (b) would need a CHECK, a COMMIT and
a CERTIFY inside that one-move run, and one move can't be three. (2) Clause (d) needs a run
from some loaded state that raises the record, and none does.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{paid\_latch\_weakly\_thiele\_complete}, \code{paid\_latch\_meets\_base\_and\_toll},
\code{paid\_latch\_not\_thiele\_complete}, \code{one\_move\_record\_excluded},
\code{silent\_weakly\_thiele\_complete}, \code{silent\_meets\_base\_record\_toll},
\code{silent\_not\_thiele\_complete} and \code{never\_certifies\_excluded} (ThieleComplete.v).

The paid latch is the receipt for nothing from the opening chapter, wearing a universal base:
honest about the price, silent about what was bought. The definition throws it out.

Now the other direction. A definition nobody meets is as useless as one everybody meets.

\begin{theorem}[The small machine, the generic one and the sorted one are Thiele-complete]\label{thm:u34-tc-instances}
(1) This chapter's machine is Thiele-complete, read with INC and DEC as base moves, CHECK $p$ $c$
and COMMIT $p$ $c$ as record moves on the claim ``$p$ holds of $c$,'' CERTIFY as CERTIFY, the
window as (line, $A$, $B$), ``unchanged'' as ``same value and same version of $c$,'' clean
states as clean starts and the ledger as $\mu$. (2) So is the same machine over any property
language with an exact equality test and a checker proved to mean what it says, as long as some
property is true of one number and false of another. (3) In particular the machine whose
property is ``this counter, read as a list, is sorted'' is Thiele-complete. (4) Every
Thiele-complete machine is a certification system (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}) and obeys the
universal floor; for this chapter's machine, that system agrees step for step and cost for
cost with the one of Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-instance}, and for the generic machine with the
generic machine's own.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Clause (a) is Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-simulation} together with the step line: INC and DEC never
touch the flag, and the flag never comes down. Clause (b) is
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned} with checker soundness (Lemma~\ref{lem:u34-eval}), and a meaning
about $c$ keeps holding while $c$'s value doesn't move. Clause (c) is the price table. Clause (d) is
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tight} with the claim ``$A$ is zero,'' which holds at $(0, b)$ and fails at
$(5, b)$. (2) and (3) are the same argument with the property language left open, and the
sorted claim holds of the list numbered 18, which is $[1, 2]$, and fails of 20, which is
$[2, 1]$. (4) is (1) of Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tc-consequences} and Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s floor.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{earned\_core\_thiele\_complete}, \code{earned\_generic\_thiele\_complete} and
\code{sorted\_machine\_thiele\_complete} (ThieleComplete.v), and \code{thiele\_complete\_floor},
\code{earned\_complete\_agrees} and \code{generic\_complete\_agrees} (EarnedGenericLinks.v).

And here's the thing every machine that meets the definition can't help doing. It's
Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s shape again, only this time it isn't about one machine. It's about all of
them.

\begin{theorem}[Every Thiele-complete machine hides its record and its ledger from its window]\label{thm:u34-tc-window}
Let a machine be Thiele-complete through an interface, and let its window be the two-counter
configuration its universal base shows. (1) For every state $s$ there's a loaded state and one
free base move from it that lands on a state with $s$'s window, with the record down and the
ledger unchanged. (2) There's a loaded state and two runs from it that end with the same window,
one with the record up and one with it down; and likewise two runs from one loaded state that end
with the same window and ledgers at least 3 apart. (3) So no function of the window gives the
record at the end of every run from every loaded state, and no function of the window gives the
ledger. (4) The same holds of the certification system built from the machine.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tc-consequences}(4) gives a loaded state and a run from it that raises the
record, and (3) says that run paid at least 3. Say it ends with window (line $\ell$, $x$, $y$).
Two-counter instructions can steer any configuration to any other: empty $A$, fill it to $x + 1$,
empty $B$, fill it to $y$, then one DEC of $A$ that jumps to line $\ell$. Those are base moves,
so from the same loaded state they reach the same window, cost nothing, and leave the record down,
by (a) and (c). That's two runs, one window, two records and two ledgers, which is (2). A function
of the window would have to give both answers on that one window, which is (3). For (1), load
$(x + 1, y)$ and take just the last DEC. (4) is (3) read through the certification system,
whose runs are the machine's.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{complete\_every\_window\_printed}, \code{complete\_hides\_record},
\code{complete\_hides\_ledger}, \code{complete\_no\_record\_oracle},
\code{complete\_no\_ledger\_oracle} and \code{thiele\_complete\_hides} (ThieleCompleteWindow.v),
and \code{complete\_cs\_window\_blind} (EarnedGenericLinks.v).

Notice how little that took, and say it out loud so nobody mistakes it for more. It's the fibre
fact from Section~\ref{sec:windows} plus one observation: a universal base can print any window
for free. Which is the point. The window here is everything a Turing machine would call the
machine, the line and the counters. On a Thiele-complete machine, that's never enough to tell you
what was established or what it cost, and it can't be, because computing is free and can't touch
the record. A richer window, one that shows the flag, is a different window, and nothing above
says it fails.

\subsection{One machine that runs them all}
\label{sec:universal-host}

The small machine raises its flag only by checking, committing and certifying, and it pays
for that. The next question is whether one machine can stand in for all of them, the way
Turing's universal machine stands in for every Turing machine. Here's what I mean by that. A
\emph{universal Thiele machine} is one fixed machine running one fixed program that runs any
machine of a stated class as a guest, with the guest's record kept and the guest's toll
collected by the host's own steps. No program running on the host has to keep a convention for it.

And I want it the hard way. The easy way is to give the host a move that means ``take one step
of the guest,'' and then ``it runs any guest'' is true because I wrote it that way. There's a host
like that two subsections on, after the two programs, and it's useful as a picture.
It isn't Turing's kind of universal. Turing's universal machine has no instruction for ``do what the machine on the tape
would do.'' It has the same kind of instructions every other Turing machine has, and one fixed
table, and the table does the reading and the deciding and the carrying out. That's the bar
here: one fixed program, written in the small machine's own six kinds of instruction, with no
step of the guest built into anything.

Turing's own explanation is worth having in your head, because the program below copies its
shape. In the 1936 paper the universal machine's tape starts with the machine to imitate, written
out as a string of letters, its standard description, and after it the imitated machine's
complete configurations, one after another: where its head is, what state it's in, what's on its
tape. To take one step, the universal machine finds the last configuration, looks through the
description line by line, comparing, until it finds the line for that state and that symbol, and
then writes out the next configuration the way that line says. Then it goes back and does it
again. It leaves marks on squares so it doesn't lose its place. Every bit of that is ordinary
instructions on an ordinary tape, and nothing in its table knows any particular machine.

Turing's universal program came first on paper, and one that
people actually came to use arrived through the side door. John McCarthy, who had started the artificial intelligence project at MIT
with Minsky, was writing up his new language Lisp around 1960 and wanted to
show it was neater than Turing machines, so he wrote a universal function for it, \emph{eval},
the language describing how to evaluate itself, and argued it was shorter and easier to follow
than a universal Turing machine. In his own history of Lisp, that was for the paper, a thing to
read; the notation for writing programs as data was made up for the paper with no thought of
using it in practice. Then Steve Russell (S.\,R.\ Russell in McCarthy's account), a programmer on
that MIT project, noticed that eval could serve as an
interpreter and coded it by hand, and there was a running language with an interpreter that
nobody had planned. McCarthy adds that the surprise froze some decisions he'd made ``rather
lightheartedly'' for the paper. So the trick has a habit: written to be read, it ends up being
run. The program below goes the other way round, on purpose. It's written to run, and the
proofs check that what runs is what the page says.

\textbf{The host.} The program runs on a machine with the small machine's instructions and the
small machine's prices: INC, DEC, HALT for free, and CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY for one each, with the
same table of sixteen facts, the same channel, trap, ledger and flag. One change: it has a counter for every whole number,
each with its own version, where the small machine had two. No new kind of
instruction, no new price.

\begin{definition}[The host machine]\label{def:u34-multi}
The \emph{host machine} is the machine of Definition~\ref{def:u34-step} with one change: it has a
counter, with its version, for every whole number $r$ (a \emph{register}), and INC $r$, DEC $r$
$j$, CHECK $p$ $r$ and COMMIT $p$ $r$ name one register each. Its property language has one
property, $\mathsf{Slot}$. Write $\langle m, n \rangle$ for the number $(2n + 1)\cdot 2^m$; every
positive number is $\langle m, n \rangle$ for exactly one pair, and 0 is no pair. Number the small
machine's properties $\mathsf{Zero} \mapsto 0$, $\mathsf{Even} \mapsto 1$, $\mathsf{Ge}(n) \mapsto n + 2$.
The checker of $\mathsf{Slot}$ says yes at a value $x$ exactly when $x = \langle m, v \rangle$ and
the small machine's checker says yes to the property numbered $m$ at $v$; its meaning is the same
with $\mathrm{holds}$ in place of the checker.
\end{definition}

Defined as the machine of EarnedMulti.v, with \code{pair}, \code{unpair}, \code{pcode},
\code{heval} and \code{hholds} (UniversalCodes.v).

There's one place the guest's machine shows up in the host. The host's single property
knows how to read the small machine's three-word property language: ``this number is the pair
(property, value) and the property holds of the value.'' It doesn't know the small machine's
step. That's the counter version of Turing's universal machine knowing the alphabet its guests
write in.

\textbf{Two facts that force the design.} Why more counters? Because of two facts, and the program
looks the way it does because of them.

The first is about reading. On this machine the only way to find out what's in a counter is to
take pebbles out (DEC) and put them back (INC), and both of those are writes, so the counter's
version goes up. A fact is about one version. So a counter the program reads can never hold a
live fact, and the guest's counters are exactly the ones the program has to read, to decide which
way a DEC jumps and to check a property. The host can't keep the guest's facts on its copies of
the guest's counters.

The second says that even if reading were free, a fixed program couldn't. It's the pigeonhole.

\begin{theorem}[No host fact on an exact copy of the guest's counter]\label{thm:u34-nocopy}
Take any host property language with an exact equality test and any checker, a finite list $Q$
of host properties, and any translation of the small machine's properties into members of $Q$
whose host check passes whenever the guest's check passes on the same number. Then there are
$n \ne m$, with $\mathsf{Ge}(n)$ and $\mathsf{Ge}(m)$ translated to the same host property, such
that the guest program CHECK $\mathsf{Ge}(n)$ $A$; COMMIT $\mathsf{Ge}(m)$ $A$ traps within two
steps from every start, while on every host state with the trap down and room in its table, and
some register holding a number at least $n$, the translated CHECK and COMMIT on that register both
pass and put the committed claim in the channel.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A fixed program mentions finitely many properties, so $Q$ is finite, and the translation sends
the infinitely many $\mathsf{Ge}(0), \mathsf{Ge}(1), \ldots$ into it: two of them land on the
same member. The guest's COMMIT asks for $\mathsf{Ge}(m)$, and its table can only hold
$\mathsf{Ge}(n)$, so it traps (or its CHECK already trapped). The host sees one property twice:
its CHECK passes, since the guest's would, and its COMMIT finds exactly what that CHECK wrote.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{pigeonhole\_collision} and \code{no\_exact\_copy\_host} (UniversalNoCopy.v), with
the same statement on the host's certification system as \code{multi\_cs\_no\_exact\_copy}
(UniversalInterpreterLinks.v).

So the host keeps the guest's facts somewhere else: in \emph{slots}, extra registers used for
nothing but holding facts, one per checked fact, each holding the pair (property number, value)
that the guest checked. The pigeonhole doesn't bite a slot, because the property lives in the
slot's number. The instruction doesn't have to carry it: CHECK $\mathsf{Slot}$ on a slot asks about whatever pair
is sitting there, and there are infinitely many pairs. A slot is written only when the program is
moving a fact into it. And when the guest writes the counter a fact was about, the program gives
every slot about that counter a nudge, one INC and one DEC, which leaves the number alone and
pushes the version up, so the host's facts go stale at exactly the moment the guest's do.

\textbf{The program.} Here's $U$ the way Turing would describe it, one register at a time and then
one job at a time. Registers 0 and 1 hold the guest's $A$ and $B$. Register 2 holds the guest's
whole program as one number: each instruction gets a number (an opcode paired with its operands,
INC as 0, DEC as 1, HALT as 2, CHECK as 3, COMMIT as 4, CERTIFY as 5), and the list of them is
packed with $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$, the empty list as 0. Register 3 is the guest's line.
Registers 4 to 13 are scratch. Registers 14 and 15 count how many CHECKs on $A$ and on $B$ have
passed. Registers 16 to 47 are \emph{mirrors}, sixteen for each guest counter, and registers 48 to
79 are the slots, sixteen for each guest counter, because the guest's table holds sixteen. Register
80 is a dead end that's never written.

Each guest step goes like this. At line 1 the program copies the program number and the guest's
line into scratch, putting the originals back as it goes, because copying a counter on this
machine means emptying it into two others and refilling it. If the guest's line is 0, or past
the end of the program, it stops. Otherwise it peels instructions off the front of the copy, one
per line, until it holds the one at the guest's line, and splits that into opcode and operands.
Then a chain of DECs on the opcode sends it to one of six handlers.

\begin{itemize}
\item INC $c$: INC the guest's counter $c$, nudge every slot about $c$ and zero its mirrors, add
one to the guest's line, back to line 1.
\item DEC $c$ $j$: DEC the guest's counter $c$. If it was 0, add one to the guest's line. If it
wasn't, nudge every slot about $c$, zero its mirrors, and set the guest's line to $j$. Back to
line 1.
\item HALT: stop.
\item CHECK $p$ $c$: let $k$ be the count of passed CHECKs on $c$. If $k$ is below 16, build
$\langle$number of $p$, value of $c\rangle$ in slot $k$ of $c$, run CHECK $\mathsf{Slot}$ on that
slot, set its mirror to the number of $p$ plus one, add one to the count and to the guest's line,
and go back to line 1. If $k$ is 16, run CHECK $\mathsf{Slot}$ on the dead end, which holds 0,
which is no pair, so it traps, just as the guest's seventeenth CHECK does.
\item COMMIT $p$ $c$: look through the sixteen mirrors of $c$ for one equal to the number of $p$
plus one. At the first match, run COMMIT $\mathsf{Slot}$ on that slot. With no match, run COMMIT
$\mathsf{Slot}$ on the dead end, which traps.
\item CERTIFY: run CERTIFY, add one to the guest's line, back to line 1.
\end{itemize}

Why the mirrors? COMMIT has to find the slot holding the claim, and it can't read the slot to
find out, because reading would make the fact stale. So beside every slot sits a mirror the
program is allowed to read: the property's number plus one while the slot's fact is live, 0 once
the guest has written the counter. If a guest CHECK fails, the host's CHECK on the slot fails too,
since the slot holds exactly the pair the guest checked, and both machines trap.

Count what costs anything. Fetching, unpacking, copying, nudging, branching: all INC and DEC,
all free, the way computing is free on the small machine. The only paid instructions are the
CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY sites, and each guest CHECK, COMMIT or CERTIFY makes the program run
exactly one of them. So the host's ledger lands on the guest's, mark for mark. And when the guest's
flag goes up, the host's goes up by the host's own CERTIFY, standing on the host's own COMMIT and
CHECK on a slot. It isn't copying a bit. It runs the same chain on its own registers.

\begin{definition}[The program $U$, and loading a guest]\label{def:u34-U}
$U$ is the fixed list of 3728 host instructions described above, starting at line 1 and
mentioning registers 0 to 80; exactly 69 of them cost anything. For a guest program $P$ and a
start $(x, y)$, the \emph{loaded host} $\mathrm{hload}(P, x, y)$ has register 0 at $x$, register 1
at $y$, register 2 at the number of $P$, register 3 at 1 and every other register at 0, every
version 0, line 1, an empty table and channel, the trap down, ledger 0 and flag down. Write
$\mathrm{grun}(m)$ for $m$ program steps of $P$ from $\mathrm{start}(x, y)$, and
$\mathrm{hrun}(n)$ for $n$ program steps of $U$ from $\mathrm{hload}(P, x, y)$.
\end{definition}

Defined as \code{U}, \code{hload}, \code{prog\_code}, \code{grun} and \code{hrun} (UniversalLayout.v,
UniversalSim.v, UniversalRun.v, and UniversalCodes.v for \code{prog\_code}), with the 69 paid sites listed exactly by \code{U\_paid\_sites}
(UniversalLayout.v).

\begin{theorem}[$U$ keeps pace with its guest]\label{thm:u34-U-sim}
For every guest program $P$, start $(x, y)$ and number of guest steps $m$, there's a number of
host steps $n$ such that one of two things holds. Either the host is back at line 1 with
$m \le n$ and \emph{related} to the guest: registers 0 and 1 hold the guest's $A$ and $B$,
register 3 holds the guest's line, the guest's trap is down, the two ledgers are equal, the two flags
are equal, and the host's table and channel hold, fact for fact, slot facts matching the guest's
facts and channel. Or both have stopped, with the same counters, the same trap, the same ledger,
the same flag, and matching tables and channels. And from any related pair where the guest hasn't
stopped, one guest step is matched by at least one host step that lands related again, or with
both stopped.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The one-step part is a case for each thing the guest can do at its line: stop; INC; DEC, taken or
not; CHECK, passing, failing, or with a full table; COMMIT, found or not; CERTIFY, passing or not.
For each, the matching stretch of $U$ is proved to land where the case says. The relation carries
the bookkeeping that makes the next case go through: each count register equals the number of
slots in use for its counter, each slot in use holds (property number, checked value), a slot's
fact is current exactly when the matching guest fact is, a live slot's mirror is the property's
number plus one and a stale one's is 0, and unused slots, unused mirrors and the dead end are 0.
A freshly loaded host is related to the guest's start. The run statement is induction on $m$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{hload\_rel} and \code{U\_step} (UniversalSim.v), and \code{U\_simulation}
(UniversalRun.v).

\begin{theorem}[Halting and answers match]\label{thm:u34-U-halting}
For every $P$, $x$ and $y$, the guest's run of $P$ from $\mathrm{start}(x, y)$ halts if and only
if $U$'s run from $\mathrm{hload}(P, x, y)$ halts. And whenever the guest has halted at step $m$
and $U$ at step $n$, the host's registers 0 and 1 hold the guest's $A$ and $B$, and the two traps,
the two ledgers and the two flags are equal.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-U-sim}: a halted guest is matched by a stopped host, and a host that has
stopped can't be back at line 1 with the guest still running, because line 1 isn't a stop. A
halted machine stays halted, so the two halting points carry the same values.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{universal\_halting} and \code{universal\_output} (UniversalRun.v).

\begin{theorem}[The host's flag is the guest's, and its ledger is exact]\label{thm:u34-U-flag}
(1) The guest's flag is up at some step of its run if and only if the host's flag is up at some
step of $U$'s run. (2) For every $m$ there's an $n$ at which the two are related, with $m \le n$, or both stopped,
with $\mu(\mathrm{hrun}(n)) = \mu(\mathrm{grun}(m))$. And for every $n$ there's an $m$ with
$\mu(\mathrm{grun}(m)) \le \mu(\mathrm{hrun}(n)) \le \mu(\mathrm{grun}(m + 1))$: in between
matching points, the host's ledger never gets ahead of the guest's next step.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Flags are equal at matching points and never come down. (2) Ledgers are equal at matching
points; inside the stretch of $U$ that runs one guest instruction, at most the one paid site of
that instruction runs, so the host's ledger sits between the guest's before and after it.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{universal\_flag\_iff} and \code{universal\_ledger\_exact} (UniversalRun.v).

That's a third sense of ``exact,'' and it's the plainest of the three: two ledgers, one number.

\begin{theorem}[The host earns its own flag]\label{thm:u34-U-earned}
If the host's flag is up after $n$ steps of $U$ from $\mathrm{hload}(P, x, y)$, then the
instructions $U$ executed contain, in order, a passing CHECK $\mathsf{Slot}$ on a slot, then a
passing COMMIT $\mathsf{Slot}$ on the same slot, with the slot untouched and its version unchanged
in between, then a passing CERTIFY; the slot held
$\langle$number of $p$, $v\rangle$ at the CHECK, with $\mathrm{holds}(p, v)$. And the guest's own
run from $\mathrm{start}(x, y)$ contains a passing CHECK $p$ $c$, then, with $c$ untouched and
its version unchanged, a passing COMMIT $p$ $c$, then a passing CERTIFY, with $c$ holding $v$ at
its CHECK.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-U-flag} the guest's flag rises too; find the guest step where it rises, a
passing CERTIFY, and the related host point just before it. The guest's channel there names a
fact, and the relation says the host's channel names the matching slot fact. The host's own flag
rises at its own first passing CERTIFY, and nothing paid runs between the related point and that
CERTIFY, so the host's channel hasn't moved: it names that slot fact. The host machine's version
of Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned} gives the host's CHECK and COMMIT on that slot. The record kept with the slot
says what pair it held and when, and the checker's meaning gives $\mathrm{holds}(p, v)$. The same
theorem on the guest's run, up to the step where its flag rose, gives the guest's chain on the
same $p$ and $c$, and the record says $c$ held $v$ at its CHECK.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{universal\_earned} (UniversalRun.v).

\begin{theorem}[The host is Thiele-complete, and $U$'s halting is undecidable]\label{thm:u34-U-complete}
(1) The host machine, with $\mathsf{Slot}$ as its property and one move per instruction, is
Thiele-complete (Definition~\ref{def:u34-thiele-complete}), and $U$'s run from
$\mathrm{hload}(P, x, y)$ is a run of it. (2) Read as a certification system it obeys the universal
floor; a run of $U$ that raises the host's flag costs at least 3 there. The system built from its
Thiele-completeness agrees with it step for step and cost for cost, so the same run costs at least
3 on that one too, and the universal floor of 1 holds there directly.
(3) $U$ halts from $\mathrm{hload}(P, x, y)$ exactly when $P$ halts from $\mathrm{start}(x, y)$, so
the question ``does $U$ halt from this loaded host?'' is undecidable in the library's sense of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-undecidable}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) The base is registers 0 and 1, run by INC and DEC; the claims are ``$\mathsf{Slot}$ holds of
register $r$''; the rest is the host machine's own versions of the small machine's theorems, and
for non-vacuity, register 0 loaded with 1, which is $\langle 0, 0\rangle$, the pair of
$\mathsf{Zero}$ and 0, against register 0 loaded with 0, which is no pair. (2) is
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tc-instances}(4) and Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-U-earned}. (3) is
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-U-halting}, and the identity map reduces the small machine's halting question,
undecidable by Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-undecidable}, to this one.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{universal\_thiele\_complete} and \code{U\_run\_on\_host\_machine} (UniversalRun.v),
and \code{multi\_cs\_floor}, \code{interp\_U\_certified\_floor}, \code{interp\_U\_complete\_floor},
\code{interp\_complete\_agrees}, \code{interp\_halting\_iff} and \code{interp\_halting\_undecidable}
(UniversalInterpreterLinks.v).

Put it together, plainly. One fixed program, 3728 instructions of the small machine's six kinds,
with no guest step built into anything, runs every program of the small machine from every start.
It halts exactly when its guest halts, with the guest's answer in its first two registers. Its
flag goes up exactly when the guest's would, by its own check, its own commit and its own
certificate. Its ledger is the guest's, mark for mark, wherever the two line up. And the machine
it runs on is Thiele-complete. Since the small machine runs every two-counter program, $U$ runs
every computation. That's the universal Thiele machine of this book, for the small machine's
programs; the next subsection carries it to every computably presented Thiele machine.

The fine print, before you take that anywhere. The guests start clean, from $\mathrm{start}(x,
y)$; the whole-run theorems are about loaded hosts, and only the one-step theorem is about any
related pair. The host's property reads the small machine's three-word language, so a guest with
a different property language needs a different host property; the host of the next subsection
has one, a single property that reads a universal claim language. Sixteen slots per counter is
the guest's table size. The host just matches it.
And it's slow: every guest step unpacks the program number from the front,
on a machine where copying a number means moving it a pebble at a time.

Enforcement in the step is the reference monitor's move from the opening chapter, Anderson's 1972
move: one mechanism everything has to pass through. What's put together here is a priced, earned
record under that move, carried to every guest by one fixed program. The move itself is
Anderson's. Kevin Hamlen, Greg Morrisett and Fred Schneider (2006) worked out, in their model, which policies
mechanisms like
that can enforce at all, and their paper is where I'd go to see why
enforcing a property of every run escapes the Rice-style walls that deciding one runs into.

Why make such a fuss about proofs that walk every case? Because the first universal machine had
bugs. It's the machine in Turing's 1936 paper, and nobody gets to call Turing careless. In 1947
Emil Post, in an appendix to a paper on a problem of Thue, pointed out that the construction
leaned on a convention it hadn't earned, and he patched a small defect in how the universal
machine writes out each complete configuration. Around the same time Donald Davies, who joined
the National Physical Laboratory in 1947, where Turing was designing a computer, worked through
the universal machine's tables and found more mistakes, much to Turing's annoyance, as the
accounts of Davies's life have it. (It's the same Davies who later named the
\emph{packet} in packet switching.) His corrections were finally printed in a collection edited by
Jack Copeland, a philosopher and historian of computing who runs an archive of Turing's papers,
\emph{The Essential Turing}, in 2004. They may be some of the first bugs
ever written, in a program for a computer that didn't exist yet. That's a lovely claim and a
hard one to check, so take it as a lead. I can't give it to you as a fact. What it changes here: a universal machine
is exactly the kind of construction where a careful person leaves a hole, $U$ has 3728 lines for
a hole to hide in, and its theorems are checked by Coq one case at a time, which is the kind of
check that catches Davies's kind of slip. It doesn't catch a definition that says the wrong
thing. That's why the definitions are on the page, for you.

\subsection{Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host}
\label{sec:presented-universal}

$U$ runs the small machine's programs, and through them every computation. But a Thiele machine
from somewhere else has its own states, its own moves, its own prices and its own reading, and
running it through the two-counter encoding keeps its computation and nothing else. So the
question Turing's machine raises for this book is the bigger one. Take any Thiele machine whose
workings can be computed. Is there one fixed program that runs every such machine as a guest,
keeping its halting, raising its own flag exactly when the guest's reading would rise, on an
earned chain of its own, and keeping a ledger equal to the guest's own prices, with the host's
flat ones nowhere in it? There is, within limits I'll list, and here it is.

First the class, said plainly. A \emph{computably presented} Thiele machine is a certification
system in Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s sense (states, moves, a step, a price for each move, a yes/no
reading) together with a \emph{driver} that picks the next move from the current state or says
stop, and a way of writing states and moves as whole numbers. ``Computably'' means four little
programs, written in the plainest language of computable functions there is, the one built from
zero, plus one, picking an argument, composing, recursion and search: one computes the driver,
one the step, one the price, and one the reading, and the reading's program answers yes or no
on every state there is. Run from a start $s_0$, the driver's moves give one run. Its
\emph{ledger} after $n$ moves is the sum of their prices, and its \emph{latch} after $n$ moves
says whether the reading has been yes at any state so far.

The host needs one thing the small machine doesn't have: a paid move that certifies nothing. Without it the host can only charge one per
CHECK, COMMIT or CERTIFY, and a guest whose moves cost seven can't be billed seven. So the host
machine gets a seventh instruction, PAY: it costs one, goes to the next line, and changes
nothing else; it never raises the flag. Read through the definition of Thiele-complete, PAY is a
check of a claim that never holds, so the host stays Thiele-complete with it
(\code{pu\_universal\_thiele\_complete}, UniversalPRun.v), and its floor of three for a flag
raised from a clean start
still holds with PAY present (\code{pu\_multi\_certified\_run\_min\_cost}, EarnedMultiPriced.v).

The program is $U$ with one more handler: a seventh branch on the guest's opcode, for PAY, that
runs the host's own PAY once. Call it $U_P$; it's 3735 instructions, with 70 paid sites, the 69
of $U$ plus the PAY. The guest it runs is a program of the small machine with PAY added, and that
guest is where the presented machine goes. Its four programs are compiled into two counters, by
the packing Minsky used, with the undecidability library's compiler from computable functions to
counter machines doing the hard part; the guest keeps the presented machine's state coded in its
counter $B$, takes one of its moves by running the compiled step, pays the move's price in PAYs,
and, when the compiled reading says yes, checks, commits and certifies. The host's one property
is fixed too: a claim is either one of the small machine's three words about a number, or ``run
reading program $r$ on the coded state $v$,'' and the host's checker evaluates that with one
fixed routine for every presented machine there is. So nothing in $U_P$ knows any particular
presented machine. The machine arrives as data, the way Turing's guests arrived on the tape.

\begin{theorem}[One host runs every computably presented Thiele machine]\label{thm:u34-presented}
Let $M$ be a computably presented Thiele machine and $s_0$ a start state. Load $U_P$ with the guest
compiled from $M$'s presentation and $s_0$ coded in. Then: (1) $U_P$ halts exactly when $M$'s run
stops. (2) For every $n$ such that $M$ hasn't stopped before move $n$, there's a host time $t$
at which the host's register for the guest's counter $B$ decodes to $M$'s state after $n$ moves,
the host's ledger is $M$'s ledger after $n$ moves plus a \emph{surcharge}, and the host's flag is
$M$'s latch after $n$ moves; and if $M$ stops at $n$, such a $t$ has $U_P$ halted as well. (3) The
host's flag is up at some time exactly when $M$'s reading is yes at some state of its run. (4) If
the host's flag is up at time $t$, the host's own instructions up to $t$ contain a passing CHECK on
a slot, then a passing COMMIT on the same slot with the slot untouched in between, then a
passing CERTIFY; and the slot held the claim ``reading program $r$ says yes of $v$''
for $M$'s own reading program $r$, that claim holds, and $v$ decodes to a state of $M$'s run where
the reading is yes.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Two layers, each proved on its own. The bottom layer is the compiler: for every presented
machine, its guest program's run passes through points that code $M$'s states in order, with the
guest's ledger equal to $M$'s ledger plus the surcharge and the guest's flag equal to $M$'s latch,
and the guest's own flag stands on an earned chain whose claim is $M$'s reading program applied to
the coded state where the reading first said yes. The top layer is $U_P$, proved the way $U$ was
in the previous theorems, with the PAY case added: it keeps pace with any guest of this kind,
halting and flag matched, ledger equal at matching points, and its flag earned on a slot. Compose
the two. The earned part takes one more step: the host's chain gives a guest CHECK that passed, and
a guest run that ends with its flag up has exactly one passing CHECK, the compiler's CHECK of the
reading on counter $B$. So the guest CHECK the host's chain points to is that one, and its claim is $M$'s
reading at the first state where it said yes.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{presented\_universal} (PresentedUniversal.v), whose five parts are also stated
separately as \code{presented\_universal\_halting}, \code{presented\_universal\_points},
\code{presented\_universal\_halt\_point}, \code{presented\_universal\_flag\_iff} and
