\code{presented\_universal\_earned}; the host layer is \code{pu\_universal\_halting},
\code{pu\_universal\_flag\_iff}, \code{pu\_universal\_ledger\_exact} and \code{pu\_universal\_earned}
(UniversalPRun.v).

Now the surcharge, because that's where the ledger stops being exact, and it can't be helped. The
host raises its flag the only way the host machine allows, by a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY, and
those cost three. If $M$'s first move that turns its reading to yes costs at least three, the host
pays the difference in PAYs and nothing more is owed. If it costs less, the host can't match it.

\begin{theorem}[Exact, within two, and no better]\label{thm:u34-presented-surcharge}
Let $M$, $s_0$ and the loaded host be as in Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-presented}, and let $M$'s reading
be no at $s_0$. (1) For every $n$ before $M$ stops there's a host time at which the host's ledger
lies between $M$'s ledger after $n$ moves and that plus two, with the state decoded and the flag
matched as before. (2) If moreover every move that first turns $M$'s reading to yes costs at
least three, the surcharge is zero and the host's ledger equals $M$'s exactly at those times.
(3) If $M$'s latch is up after $n$ moves while its ledger is below three, then no run of the host
machine from a clean start, under any program at all, ends with its flag equal to that latch and
its ledger raised by exactly $M$'s ledger.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) and (2): the guest pays $M$'s prices in PAYs, a unit at a time, except at the move where
$M$'s reading first says yes. There it has to run its CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY, three units, and
it makes up the rest of the move's price in PAYs, so it pays the larger of the price $c$ and
three. The price is at least one, because the move raised a reading (the toll), so the excess is
at most two, and none when $c \ge 3$.
(3): a raised flag on the host machine costs at least three from a clean start, whatever the
program, and $M$'s ledger is less.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{presented\_universal\_surcharge\_le\_two}, \code{presented\_universal\_exact} and
\code{presented\_universal\_no\_exact\_below\_three}, with the corollary for $U_P$ itself,
\code{presented\_universal\_U\_no\_exact\_below\_three} (PresentedUniversal.v). If the reading is
already yes at the start, the host has to raise its flag at once, and that costs three on top of
a ledger of nothing.

And one machine run all the way, so the class isn't empty. Its states are whole numbers, its one
move adds one and costs three, its driver always picks that move, and its reading is ``at least
three.'' The four programs are written out from the library's building blocks and proved to compute
those four things. Loaded into $U_P$ from 0, the host never halts, its flag goes up, at the host
time matching move $n$ its ledger is exactly $3n$ and its flag is up exactly when $n \ge 3$, and
the raised flag stands on a host chain whose slot claims the machine's own reading of a state at
least three (\code{pu\_demo\_computably\_presented}, \code{pu\_demo\_never\_halts},
\code{pu\_demo\_flag\_rises}, \code{pu\_demo\_exact} and \code{pu\_demo\_earned},
PresentedDemo.v).

Now the limits, each of which is in the statement, said plainly.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Readings that are decided.} The reading's program has to answer yes or no on every
state. A reading a program could only confirm, waiting forever on the no cases, isn't covered, and
neither is a reading no program computes at all.
\item \textbf{One run per start.} The driver picks the move, so the guest is deterministic. A
machine whose next move is somebody's free choice gets in only with that choice written into its
driver.
\item \textbf{The record is the latch.} The host's flag is up once $M$'s reading has been yes at
any state of the run, which is exactly the latch of Section~\ref{sec:latch}. A reading that goes
yes and then back to no is carried as ``it was yes once.''
\item \textbf{The ledger is exact up to the surcharge.} When the reading starts at no, at most two,
and zero when the first raising
move costs three or more; when it starts at yes, three. And no program on this host, run from a clean start,
can do better for a raise that costs less than three.
\item \textbf{Prices in whole units, paid one at a time.} A move that costs a million is a million
PAYs. Nothing here is fast, and the compiler's packing is Minsky's, so it's slower still.
\item \textbf{Proved; never run.} The demonstration machine's numbers come from theorems. Nobody
has run $U_P$ on it: the files it lives in aren't extracted, the compiled programs are far too big
for any machine to step through, and some of the library's pieces don't compute inside the checker
at all. Section~\ref{sec:running} says what was run.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{A simpler host, with the guest step built in}

There's a much simpler host than $U$, and I keep it in the book because it's easy to read and
it shows the copy rule in one line. Its universality is by construction: it has a move that runs
one guest step by calling the small machine's own step. So it isn't the universal Thiele machine
of this book. $U$ is. Read it as a picture of what $U$ does the long way, and as a host that
starts from any guest state at all, clean or not.

It carries a guest inside its own state: the guest's program as data, the guest's counters, its
table, its ledger, its flag. The host has one extra move, run one guest step. In that one move it
looks at the guest's flag, takes the step, looks again, and if the flag went from down to up, the
host's own copy of that flag goes up in the same move, and the host pays for it.

\begin{definition}[The host]\label{def:u34-host}
A \emph{guest} is a program $P$ of this chapter's machine together with a state $g$ of it
(Definition~\ref{def:u34-step}). A \emph{host state} $h$ has six parts: its own core
$\mathrm{core}(h)$, its ledger $\mu(h)$, its own flag $\mathrm{own}(h)$, the guest program
$P(h)$ held as a list of instructions, the guest state $g(h)$, and the \emph{mirror} $m(h)$, a
yes/no copy of the guest's flag. The host has two kinds of move. $\mathrm{OWN}\ i$ runs the
instruction $i$ on the host's own core, costs what this chapter's machine charges for $i$,
and raises $\mathrm{own}$ exactly when that machine's flag would rise. $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ b$
costs $b$. If the host's core is trapped it does nothing else. Otherwise it moves the host to
its next line and, if the guest's next instruction costs at most $b$, runs that instruction
on $g(h)$; in the same move the mirror becomes $m(h) \lor (\lnot\mathrm{cert}(g(h)) \land
\mathrm{cert}(g'))$, where $g'$ is the new guest state. The host's reading is
$\mathrm{own}(h) \lor m(h)$. Its stored program is $U_0 = [\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1;\ \mathrm{OWN}\
(\text{INC } A);\ \mathrm{OWN}\ (\text{DEC } A\ 1)]$: one guest step, then two moves that
bring the host back to its first line. (The Coq file calls it \code{U}; I write $U_0$ here so
nobody mixes it up with the universal program $U$.)
\end{definition}

Every instruction of the small machine costs at most one, so $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1$ runs every
guest instruction there is. Why charge the budget $b$? Why not the cost of whatever
instruction got fetched? Because charging the budget keeps the price a function of the move
alone, which is what the certification system of Part II asks for: you read the price of a
host move off the move, the way you read the small machine's prices off its table, without
peeking inside the guest. The bill for that is easy to see. A host that steps a free guest
instruction, an INC say, still pays one for the move.

So the host's ledger is closer to a clock than to a receipt for its guests: one unit per guest
step, whatever the step was. It never falls behind the guest's own bill (part (3) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-host-toll} below), and it matches that bill only when every guest step
happens to cost one. Could a cleverer host have simulation-exact accounting, a ledger equal to
its guest's? Not with a price read off the move alone. $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1$ is the same move whether the guest's next instruction is a free INC or
a paid CHECK, so one price can't match both. A simulation-exact host has to be built the
other way, with no guest step to put a price on: that's $U$, which pays only on the record moves
it runs itself, so its ledger equals its guest's (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-U-flag}).

And one thing about the definition before the theorems, so you know which of them carry
weight. $\mathrm{GSTEP}$ runs the guest's instruction by calling the small machine's own step on
the guest's state: the guest's step is a primitive of the host. So ``the host runs any guest''
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-universal}) is true by construction. The host was built to do exactly
that, and the proof is mostly unfolding. The theorems with something in them come after it.
From a loaded host, or any state where the two agree, the mirror always equals the guest's flag (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-mirror}). Nothing raises the
mirror unless the guest itself passes a CERTIFY inside a guest step the host paid for
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-no-free-host}). No $\mathrm{OWN}$ move, in any host program at all,
touches the guest's state or the mirror (the second sentence of that same theorem), and no host
move of either kind rewrites the guest's program (\code{hexec\_gprog}, UniversalThiele.v). And
the mirror is tied to the guest's earned chain: after any host run from a loaded
host, if the mirror is up, the guest's own run from its start contains a
passing CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same claim, then a CERTIFY (\code{host\_mirror\_earned}, UniversalThiele.v). So this
host runs any guest by construction and keeps the guest's record by theorem, as a copy of the
guest's flag. It never earns a flag of its own. $U$ does both the long way: it runs the guest
with its own instructions, and it earns its own flag.

\begin{theorem}[The host runs any guest]\label{thm:u34-universal}
(1) If the host's core is not trapped, then after $n$ moves $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1$ the guest state
is the guest program's own run of $n$ steps from $g(h)$, the guest program is unchanged, and
the host is still not trapped. (2) If the host's core is at line 1 and not trapped, then $3n$
steps of the program $U_0$ leave the guest exactly where $n$ steps of its own program put it.
(3) For every two-counter program $M$ and inputs $a$, $b$: $M$ halts from $(1, a, b)$ exactly
when the host program made of $\mathrm{OWN}$ moves of the compiled $M$ halts, from a host
whose core starts at $(a, b)$, whatever guest that host carries.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Induction on $n$: a host that isn't trapped stays untrapped through a guest step, and with
budget 1 the guest step is the guest's own step. (2) One pass of $U_0$ is a guest step, then
INC $A$ and DEC $A$ back to line 1, so it is (1) once per pass. (3) A host program made only
of $\mathrm{OWN}$ moves is the small machine, core for core, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-halting} does the rest.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{universal\_simulation}, \code{universal\_program\_simulation} and
\code{host\_thiele\_complete} (UniversalThiele.v).

\begin{theorem}[The copy is the record]\label{thm:u34-mirror}
Say a host state $h$ \emph{agrees} when $m(h) = \mathrm{cert}(g(h))$. Every host move takes an
agreeing state to an agreeing state, so every host trace and every stored host program
does too, and a freshly loaded host agrees. In particular, if $h$ agrees and is not trapped,
the mirror after $n$ moves $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1$ is the guest's flag after $n$ steps of its own
program.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
One move at a time. An $\mathrm{OWN}$ move touches neither the mirror nor the guest. A trapped
$\mathrm{GSTEP}$ touches neither. An untrapped one sets the mirror to the old mirror or the
crossing, and the guest's flag is a latch (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}), so if the old mirror
equalled the old flag, the new mirror equals the new flag. The last sentence is this
together with Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-universal}.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{record\_agreement\_step}, \code{record\_agreement},
\code{record\_agreement\_program}, \code{hload\_agrees} and \code{simulated\_record}
(UniversalThiele.v).

\begin{theorem}[The host's step collects the guest's toll]\label{thm:u34-host-toll}
(1) If $h$ agrees, is not trapped, and the guest step that budget $b$ allows takes the guest's
flag from down to up, then the mirror is down before $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ b$ and up after it,
the host's ledger rose by exactly $b$, and $b \ge 1$. (2) In the run of (1) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-universal}, from a host that agrees, if the guest's flag goes up between its steps $n$ and $n + 1$,
the mirror goes up between the host's moves $n$ and $n + 1$, and that move costs 1. (3) For every
host trace $t$, $\mu(g(\mathrm{run}(t, h))) + \mu(h) \le \mu(\mathrm{run}(t, h)) +
\mu(g(h))$: the host's ledger grows at least as fast as the guest's.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) The guest's flag rises only on a passing CERTIFY (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll}), which costs
1, and the budget let it run, so $b \ge 1$; the mirror was the guest's flag, so it was down,
and the move sets it to the crossing. (2) is (1) at the matching move. (3) Induction on $t$: a
guest step that runs costs the guest at most the budget the host paid, and every other move
leaves the guest's ledger alone.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{toll\_enforced\_by\_host\_step}, \code{every\_guest\_crossing\_is\_a\_host\_crossing},
\code{host\_pays\_for\_guest}, \code{host\_cost\_covers\_guest} and \code{simulated\_cost}
(UniversalThiele.v).

\begin{theorem}[No free host certification]\label{thm:u34-no-free-host}
If the mirror is down at $h$ and up after a host move $i$, then $i$ is $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ b$ with
$b \ge 1$, the host was not trapped, the guest's next instruction was CERTIFY, and the guest's
flag went from down to up in that move. A trace made only of $\mathrm{OWN}$ moves leaves the
mirror and the guest state exactly where they were. And the host's own flag rises only by an
$\mathrm{OWN}$ CERTIFY that passes on the host's core.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
An $\mathrm{OWN}$ move copies the mirror unchanged, and a trapped $\mathrm{GSTEP}$ does too, so
the rise is an untrapped $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ b$ whose guest step crossed; a crossing is a passing
CERTIFY, which costs 1 and needed the budget. The own flag moves by this chapter's step line.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{no\_free\_host\_certification\_step}, \code{no\_free\_host\_certification},
\code{no\_free\_host\_certification\_program}, \code{guestless\_runs\_leave\_mirror} and
\code{own\_record\_only\_by\_certify} (UniversalThiele.v).

\begin{theorem}[The host is a Thiele machine]\label{thm:u34-host-instance}
For every host state and move, if the host's reading goes from no to yes, the move costs at
least 1; the same holds for the mirror alone and for the own flag alone. So the host read
through $\mathrm{own} \lor m$, the host read through $m$ alone, and the guest class are
certification systems (Definition~\ref{def:certsys}), and any host trace that raises the
host's reading costs at least 1.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The mirror's half is Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-no-free-host}; the own flag's half is the small
machine's toll on the host's core. The trace form is Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s universal floor.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{host\_toll}, \code{host\_own\_toll} and \code{host\_mirror\_toll}
(UniversalThiele.v), and \code{host\_cs}, \code{host\_mirror\_cs}, \code{guest\_cs} and
\code{host\_nfi} (UniversalThieleLinks.v).

\begin{remark}[Two guests, run]\label{rem:u34-host-runs}
Load the guest CHECK \emph{is zero} $A$; COMMIT \emph{is zero} $A$; CERTIFY; HALT with both
counters at 0. After two moves $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1$ the mirror is down; after three it is up,
the guest's flag is up, the host's own flag is still down, and the host has paid 3. Under the
program $U_0$ the mirror is down at host step 6 and up at step 7, with 3 paid. The guest
CERTIFY; CERTIFY traps on its first step: after five moves $\mathrm{GSTEP}\ 1$ the mirror is
down, the guest is trapped, and the host has paid 5 for nothing.
\end{remark}

Checked as \code{demo\_certifies}, \code{demo\_program\_certifies} and \code{demo\_forgery\_fails}
(UniversalThiele.v).

That copy can't be faked. The proof walks every host move there is, and the copy only rises
in a guest step where the guest itself ran CERTIFY and passed. A host program that never
touches the guest leaves the copy exactly where it was. From a loaded host the copy always equals
the guest's
flag, and the host's ledger always grows at least as fast as the guest's, and a three-instruction
loop runs any small-machine program one guest step per pass. Here the mirror, the crossing test
and the charge sit in the host's step rule, so Theorems~\ref{thm:u34-host-toll}
and~\ref{thm:u34-no-free-host} hold for every sequence of host moves, including ones that never
run a guest. That's the simple version. Everything it gets from its built-in move, $U$ gets from
ordinary instructions, plus an exact ledger and a flag of its own.

\subsection{The machine versus the program it runs}
\label{sec:machine-vs-program}

All three hosts in this chapter come down to one distinction, and it's worth saying on its own,
because the two halves are easy to run together: \emph{the machine doing the stepping} (what the
machine is) and \emph{the program it runs} (what runs on it). The toll of Section~\ref{sec:toll}
is a property of the machine doing the stepping. A rule a program keeps holds as long as the
program keeps it.

Here's the picture I keep for it. Play Monopoly on the counter of a real bank. The game has a
bank of its own, with its own rules, and one of them is printed in the rules sheet: the Bank
never goes broke, and if it runs out of money the Banker may issue more by writing on any
ordinary paper. Inside the game that's fine; the players agreed to it. The real bank's teller,
standing right there, has no opinion about any of it. Push a thousand in Monopoly money across
her counter and her ledger doesn't move, because her rules are about her own money. The game's
money is nothing to them. The real bank is the machine doing the stepping. The game is a program it happens to be
hosting. A rule that lives in the game holds as long as the players keep to it. A rule that
lives in the bank holds whatever the players do.

(And since the game is on the table: its box told an origin story for decades, that an
out-of-work salesman named Charles Darrow invented it during the Depression. The board is
older. Elizabeth Magie, an American writer and game designer with an economic argument about
land to make, patented The Landlord's Game in 1904, with a square track, railroads and
a square that sends you to jail, and described it as ``a practical demonstration of the present
system of land grabbing with all its usual outcomes and consequences.'' Darrow sold his version to
Parker Brothers in 1935, and the company bought
Magie's patent for a few hundred dollars, five hundred by the accounts I found. A story told by the company selling the product is a
lead to check, every time. It changes nothing about banks. It's a good reminder of who writes
the story on the box.)

A fixed machine can enforce an invariant in its own transition table, and that includes a
Turing machine. Give its tape a ledger track and a certification cell, and write a table
that never sets the cell without bumping the ledger: that machine obeys the toll in its step
relation. It's an instance of the abstract certification system, so it can't be a counterexample to it.
What it doesn't do, built the ordinary way, is enforce the toll on the programs it runs. A
universal machine whose table was written only to interpret carries the simulated
certification bit as plain data on its tape. If the host is programmable, so that other code
shares that tape with the guest, any of that code can flip the bit without paying, because the
host's step has no opinion about it. So an ordinary programmable computer, as built, doesn't enforce the toll for its
programs. That's how it's built. It could. The simpler host above enforces it
by having its own step mirror the guest's bit and charge for its crossing
(Theorems~\ref{thm:u34-mirror} and~\ref{thm:u34-no-free-host}), and the universal programs $U$
and $U_P$ are fixed tables that go one better: they earn their own flag, by their own check,
commit and certificate, exactly when the guest's would rise, and pay on their own ledger what the guest pays, $U$ exactly and $U_P$ to within
a surcharge of at most two when the guest's reading starts at no (Theorems~\ref{thm:u34-U-earned}, \ref{thm:u34-U-flag}, \ref{thm:u34-presented} and~\ref{thm:u34-presented-surcharge}). That's a statement
about which reading a step rule prices. It isn't a claim that Turing machines can't price one.

Computing ran into this exact gap in hardware, and how it got out is worth the detour. In 1974
two computer scientists, Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg, asked when a machine can run guests, a whole operating system
inside another, efficiently and safely. Their answer is one sentence you could check against any
instruction set. Call an instruction \emph{sensitive} if it reads or changes the machine's own
settings, the things the host has to keep for itself, and \emph{privileged} if running it
outside the host's own mode makes the machine stop and hand control to the host, which is
called a trap. For the kind of machine they modelled: if every sensitive instruction is
privileged, a host can be built. The guest runs at full speed, and whenever it touches
something that matters, the machine itself stops it and lets the host decide. That's a host
whose step has an opinion.

Then the obvious next question: did the machines people actually bought pass the test? The most
common one didn't. In 2000 John Scott Robin, an Air Force officer, and Cynthia Irvine, a
computer-security researcher at the Naval Postgraduate School, went through every instruction
of Intel's Pentium and found seventeen that are sensitive and not privileged; POPF, which loads
the processor's flags, is the one usually pointed at. A guest could run them and the host would
never hear about it. The fixes came two ways: VMware rewrote the guest's code on the fly so the
troublesome instructions never ran as written, and in the middle of the 2000s Intel and AMD
added hardware support so they'd trap. Does that change anything here? Not the theorems. Popek
and Goldberg were after speed and isolation. A record and a price weren't their question, so their result isn't
mine and mine isn't theirs. It changes the picture, though. The universal programs sit where
they'd want a host to sit: the host's own steps collect each guest's toll and earn each guest's
record again. And an industry learned the same lesson the expensive way: a rule binds the guest
only if it lives in the step underneath.

The smallest checked version of ``a ledger beside an ordinary machine'' is a Turing machine
configuration with a counter next to it, where each step adds one, plus one more if it writes
a nonblank symbol. The counter doesn't disturb the machine.

\begin{theorem}[A counter beside a Turing machine changes nothing]\label{thm:u19-tm-lift}
Let a Turing machine with transition table $\delta$ step a configuration $c$ to
$\mathrm{tm}_n(\delta, c)$ after at most $n$ steps (stopping when $\delta$ has no entry). Pair
each configuration with a counter, and step the pair by stepping the configuration and adding
the step's charge. Then for every $n$, $\delta$ and pair $(c, m)$, the configuration part
after at most $n$ steps of the pair is $\mathrm{tm}_n(\delta, c)$. In particular this holds
from $(c, 0)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $n$. For $n = 0$ both sides are $c$. For $n + 1$, if $\delta$ has no entry at
$c$, both runs stop and both sides are $c$. Otherwise the pair steps to $(c', m')$ where $c'$
is exactly the Turing machine's next configuration, whatever $m'$ is, and the induction
hypothesis at $(c', m')$ finishes it.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{thiele\_simulates\_turing\_gen} and \code{thiele\_simulates\_turing}
(ProperSubsumption.v). The ``Thiele'' in those names is a local record, a Turing configuration
and a number. It isn't a Thiele machine in this book's sense, and the file says not to cite it
as one simulating Turing machines. A counter beside a machine is the scorekeeper's tally from
Section~\ref{sec:toll}: honest about the machine, and kept by whoever holds the pencil.

One limit on all of this, so it isn't read as more. Certification is one event. Other kinds
of observable a machine might carry would each need their own event, their own evidence and
their own cost law, and nothing here supplies those.

\subsection{Parts II and III, run on this machine}
\label{sec:part3-on-machine}

Parts II and III proved their counts and their collisions for any system with the named pieces,
and they left a promise: that the machine of this part would be put through them. Here it is. The eight-state
machine of Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} gets run by the small machine, price for price.
Structural entitlement, the count of what narrowing a list of rivals costs, is proved for every
Thiele-complete machine, with the small machine as a worked member, a larger search on the host
that has a counter for every number, and a run that shows the count's one awkward hypothesis, the
covering, can't be dropped. And the time a check saves gets an exact exchange rate, for the part
of the machine that has no record. (The no-bare-verifier result is in Section~\ref{sec:windows},
next to the collision it comes from.)

\textbf{The eight-state machine, run by the small machine.} Look at the small machine through a
window that shows two things: its line number read modulo four, which I'll call its \emph{slot} (the
eight-state machine's word from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, unrelated to $U$'s slot registers),
and its flag. Call a state \emph{live} when its trap latch is down, the fact ``$A \ge 0$'' about
$A$'s current version is in its table, and its channel holds a commitment, which is what CERTIFY
needs in order to run.

\begin{definition}[The eight-state machine, compiled]\label{def:frag-small}
Stamp is the single instruction CERTIFY. Next-slot is the single instruction INC $B$. Jump to
slot $a$, for $a$ one of $0, 1, 2, 3$, is the four instructions COMMIT ($A \ge 0$) $A$; COMMIT
($A \ge 0$) $A$; INC $B$; DEC $B$ $a$. The \emph{setup} is the two instructions CHECK
($A \ge 0$) $A$; COMMIT ($A \ge 0$) $A$.
\end{definition}

The two COMMITs in a jump change nothing but the line and the channel, and each costs one, which is
where the jump's price of two comes from. The INC makes $B$ positive, so the DEC takes one off and
jumps to line $a$ for nothing, and $B$ is back where it was.

\begin{theorem}[The small machine runs the eight-state machine]\label{thm:frag-small}
(1) For every live state $s$ and every move $m$ of the eight-state machine, running $m$'s
instructions from $s$ ends in a live state whose window is the eight-state machine's step of $s$'s
window by $m$, and the ledger has risen by exactly $m$'s charge: one for stamp, two for jump, zero
for next-slot. (2) The same holds for any list of moves: the window after the compiled list is the
eight-state machine's run of the list, the state is live, and the ledger has risen by the sum of
the charges. (3) So a run of compiled moves from a live state that takes the flag from down to up
has raised the ledger by at least one. (4) From any start $(a, b)$, the setup ends in a live state
with window (slot 3, flag down) and the ledger at 2; after it, any compiled list runs as on the
eight-state machine from (slot 3, flag down), with the ledger at 2 plus the sum of the charges; and
if the flag is up at the end, the whole run, setup included, contains the earned chain of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) By cases on the move. On a live state CERTIFY runs, because a committed claim is on the channel;
it raises the flag, moves the line on by one and charges one. INC $B$ moves the line on by one and
charges nothing, and it touches only $B$ and $B$'s version, so the fact about $A$ and the
commitment stand and the state stays live. In a jump, each COMMIT finds its fact in the table and
succeeds, charging one, and the INC and the DEC are free and end at line $a$, whose slot is $a$;
the flag isn't touched. (2) is (1) over the list, by induction. (3) The eight-state machine's own
toll (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}) says a run of its moves that takes the flag from down to
up is charged at least one, and (2) carries that charge across. (4) CHECK ($A \ge 0$) passes at
every value of $A$ and the COMMIT after it passes, which takes line 1 to line 3, slot 3, with two
marks paid; then (2) applies. A raised flag was raised by a CERTIFY, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned} gives the chain.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{frag\_runs\_finite\_machine}, \code{frag\_pays\_finite\_price},
\code{frag\_runs\_finite\_trace}, \code{frag\_certification\_paid}, \code{frag\_setup\_live},
\code{frag\_program\_runs} and \code{frag\_program\_earned} (FragmentSmall.v), with the room argument
for the eight-state machine itself as \code{frag\_fin\_toll} and \code{frag\_cert\_system} in the same
file. Three reservations, said now. The setup's claim is true of every value, so its CHECK can't
fail; it's there because the small machine won't CERTIFY without a checked, committed claim. It
isn't there as a test. And the jump's price of two is two paid COMMITs, a choice a program makes that the
machine allows and doesn't force. The window is a projection, too: the small machine's full state
keeps far more than eight states' worth.

And the whole small machine isn't the eight-state piece it runs. It merges some states for free.

\begin{theorem}[The small machine's merges]\label{thm:frag-merge-split}
(1) A move of the small machine that takes the flag from down to up is CERTIFY; CERTIFY merges two
different full states into one (a state with the flag down and the same state with the flag up land
on the same state), and it costs at least one. (2) DEC $A$ 2 also merges two different full states,
and it costs nothing. So it is false of the small machine that every move that merges is priced.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Only CERTIFY changes the flag, and it costs one. The two states with the flag down and up, and
a committed claim, are the same state after CERTIFY. (2) Take a core at line 1 with $A$ at 1 at
version 0, and the same core with $A$ at 0 at version 1. DEC $A$ 2 takes the first to $A = 0$ at
version 1, line 2, a write; it takes the second to line 2 with $A$ still 0 at version 1, because
DEC on zero is no write. Same state, price zero.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{frag\_small\_certify\_merges}, \code{frag\_small\_certifying\_step\_priced\_merge},
\code{frag\_small\_dec\_free\_merge} and \code{frag\_small\_not\_merge\_priced} (FragmentSmall.v). It's
the same fact as the last item of the list of what this machine doesn't do, which comes near the
end of
this chapter, now with names: the chairs argument needs a price on every merge, this machine's schedule puts the floor on
the flag only, and that's why the eight-state piece is a piece.

\textbf{Structural entitlement, for every Thiele-complete machine.} Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-cs} was
about any certification system and handed the run's payments in as a bill. For a Thiele-complete
machine (Definition~\ref{def:u34-thiele-complete}) the bill is known. Call the CHECK, COMMIT and
CERTIFY moves of a run its \emph{record moves}; each costs exactly one, so the ledger rises by the
number of record moves, and clause (b) says what a raised record must contain.

\begin{theorem}[Structural entitlement represented]\label{thm:ent-machine}
Let a machine be Thiele-complete through an interface. Take a clean start $s_0$ and a run $t$ from
it; a type of rivals and a type of observations with an exact equality test; an observation
$\mathrm{obs}$ and a \emph{representative} observation $r$ of each rival; a decoder $d$ from runs to
observations; lists $\Omega$, $\Omega'$ of rivals and a decision tree $T$. Suppose
(M1) $\Omega'$ strictly narrows $\Omega$, as in Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-cs}, and (M2) some dropped
rival shows an observation different from every survivor's; (M3) the run ends with the record up
and the decoded run $d(t)$ is shown by some survivor; (M4) $\mathrm{depth}(T)$ is at most the number
of record moves in $t$; (M5) $|\Omega'| > 0$; and (M6) the covering is by fibres: there is a map
$F$ from rivals to lists of rivals such that every rival $x$ of $\Omega$ lies in $F(u)$ for some
survivor $u$ with $r(x) = r(u)$, the lengths of the lists $F(u)$ over the survivors add up to at
least $|\Omega|$, and no $F(u)$ is longer than $L(T)$. Then (1) the membership test of $\Omega'$ is
strictly stronger than that of $\Omega$; (2) $t$ contains the earned chain of clause (b), with the
meaning of the claim true at the CHECK and at the COMMIT; (3)
$\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \mathbin{\dot{-}} \lceil \log_2 |\Omega'| \rceil$ is at most the number of
record moves of $t$; (4) the number of record moves of $t$ is exactly the ledger's rise; and (5) the
ledger rose by at least 3.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) is Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-cs}(1). (2) Clause (b) applied to a run from a clean state that ends
with the record up gives the chain, and a passing check means the claim's meaning holds, which
keeps holding while the thing it's about is unchanged. (3) The fibres cover: summing their lengths
gives $|\Omega| \le L(T) \cdot |\Omega'|$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-cs}'s count finishes it, with
the record moves, which are the paid steps, in place of the charged steps. (4) is clause (c)
added up. (5) is Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tc-consequences}(3).
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{ent\_representation} (EntitlementSmall.v), whose Coq statement is printed in
Section~\ref{sec:coq-statements}. It's a checklist, as I said in Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}, and the small print is the
same kind. (M3)'s second half feeds no conclusion: only the record's being up is
used. (M1) is used only for the inclusion. Its gap feeds nothing. And
the first clause of (M6), the representative observation, isn't used by the count either. What the machine adds to Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-cs} is conclusions
(2), (4) and (5): the payment is the machine's own three acts, each at exactly one, and a raised
record carries the earned chain.
The packaged form, a record of the fifteen things a shortcut has to supply, with a theorem that
every inhabitant lands in the bound, is \code{ent\_shortcut} and \code{ent\_every\_shortcut\_lands\_here}.
The count with the tree thrown away, in the form I use below, is \code{ent\_complete\_tree\_bound}.

Two further statements, about the run's own questions and about the record clause.

\begin{theorem}[A floor with no supplied tree]\label{thm:ent-questions}
Take a machine and an interface that meets the exact-toll clause (c) of
Definition~\ref{def:u34-thiele-complete}, so each record act costs exactly one. Call the \emph{questions} of a run the claims of its CHECK moves, and say two rival states
\emph{answer alike} when every one of those claims gets the same verdict at both (each verdict taken
at the rival itself, as it starts; the states the run passed through don't enter). If, for a list $\Omega$ of rival
states and a number $m > 0$, the rivals of $\Omega$ that answer alike with any one rival, itself
included, are never more than $m$, then
$\lceil \log_2 |\Omega| \rceil \mathbin{\dot{-}} \lceil \log_2 m \rceil$ is at most the number of CHECK
moves of the run, which is at most its number of record moves, which is the ledger's rise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A run's questions give each rival an answer list, and answer lists are lists of Booleans of length
equal to the number of CHECK moves, so there are at most $2^{c}$ answer classes among the rivals,
$c$ the number of CHECK moves. The classes have at most $m$ members each, so
$|\Omega| \le 2^{c} \cdot m$, and the rounded logarithms follow. The rest is clause (c).
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{ent\_questions\_floor} (EntitlementSmall.v). The tree has gone: it is the run's own
questions. There are limits, and they're the ones in the statement. The verdicts are taken at the
rivals as they start. The states the run had reached when it asked don't come into it, and a free branch, DEC on
zero, can still narrow a list for nothing. So this prices a narrowing that the paid checks
explain, and no more.

\begin{theorem}[What the record adds]\label{thm:ent-observed}
Let a machine be Thiele-complete through an interface. (1) From a clean start, the record is up
at the end of a run exactly when the run contains the earned chain, and a run with the record up
raised the ledger by at least 3. (2) Conclusions (1), (3) and (4) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-machine} hold without a clean start and without the record being up, for a
machine that only meets the exact-toll clause (c): the hypotheses (M1), (M2), (M4), (M5) and (M6),
and the decoded run being shown by some survivor, are all it needs.
\end{theorem}

Checked as \code{ent2\_record\_adds}, \code{ent2\_upgrade\_iff} and \code{ent2\_observed\_representation}
(EntitlementMore2.v). So the record doesn't make narrowing cost more. It adds the earned chain and
a floor of 3, and that's all it adds: a run that narrows without ever raising the record is still bound to pay
its index bits, and the floor of 3 no longer applies to it.

\emph{Weights, and the partition form.} Two more pieces of the same count, both checked. First,
suppose the rivals aren't equally many: give each a whole-number weight, a multiplicity, and call
the sum of the weights of a list its \emph{mass}. The count survives with masses in place of
lengths. If the prior's mass is at most $L(T)$ times the posterior's, the rounded index bits of the
two masses differ by at most $\mathrm{depth}(T)$; so for any certification system a run that paid at
least that many charged steps has a bill at least the drop, and for a Thiele-complete machine the
representation theorem goes through with masses and the same five conclusions. On such a machine
the ledger rises by the same number from every start, the number of record moves, so the expected
rise over a weighted prior is its mass times the record moves, and the drop in rounded bits times
the prior's mass is at most that expected rise, with no averaging argument. The weights are whole
numbers, cross-multiplied, and no probability enters. Checked as \code{ent2\_weighted\_bits},
\code{ent2\_wreduction\_covers}, \code{ent2\_weighted\_cs}, \code{ent2\_weighted\_representation},
\code{ent2\_rise\_independent}, \code{ent2\_expected\_rise\_exact} and
\code{ent2\_weighted\_expected\_bound} (EntitlementMore2.v). Second, the covering by fibres has a plainer form
that doesn't need the clause that the fibres add up to the prior. Say the rivals are
\emph{partitioned} by the representative observation when every rival looks like some survivor
under it and no observation class, counted inside the prior, has more than $L(T)$ members. The
fibre lengths then add up to at least the prior, because every rival is in the class of some
survivor, so a partition gives the covering, and the count holds under it. The converse is false:
there are coverings that aren't partitions. Checked as \code{ent2\_cover\_sum},
\code{ent2\_partition\_old\_iff}, \code{ent2\_partition\_to\_reduction},
\code{ent2\_partition\_bits} and \code{ent2\_reduction\_not\_partition} (EntitlementMore2.v).

\emph{A worked member on the small machine.} Eight rivals: the starts $(a, b)$ with $a \in
\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ and $b \in \{0, 1\}$, counter $A$ at $a$ and counter $B$ at $b$. The run is CHECK
(Even) $A$; CHECK ($A \ge 2$) $A$; COMMIT ($A \ge 2$) $A$; CERTIFY, from $(2, 0)$. The program
raises the flag from a rival exactly when $a$ is even and at least 2, so exactly from $(2, 0)$ and
$(2, 1)$, and the posterior is those two. The decoder reads one ``passed'' for each CHECK in the
run's receipts; the representative observation is ``$B$ is 0,'' which isn't constant; the fibres
are the four rivals that share $B$; the tree is the complete tree of depth 2.

\begin{proposition}[The eight-start member]\label{prop:ent-small}
For every $a$ and $b$, the run raises the flag from $(a, b)$ exactly when $a$ is even and at least
2. All hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-machine} hold, with eight rivals narrowed to two: the test
of the posterior is strictly stronger; the index bits are $3 - 1 = 2$; the run has 4 record moves
and the ledger rises by exactly 4; and the earned chain is in the run. The run's own questions
(Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-questions}) are its 2 CHECKs, so the floor is met with equality. With the two
CHECKs alone, the record stays down, the ledger rises by 2, and the bound $2 \le 2$ still holds.
\end{proposition}

Checked as \code{ent\_small\_certifies\_iff}, \code{ent\_small\_posterior\_is\_certified},
\code{ent\_small\_instance}, \code{ent\_small\_questions} (EntitlementSmall.v) and
\code{ent2\_observed\_small\_instance} (EntitlementMore2.v), with \code{ent\_earned\_complete\_with}
saying the small machine meets the definition through its own interface. It's a real narrowing.
The cups of Section~\ref{sec:entitlement} aren't sitting under it in a costume, and the posterior is exactly the set of
rivals the run certifies, so here a proof ties the lists to the run. Nobody supplies them.

\emph{A search through $n$ bits.} The same shape at a size you can't enumerate, on the machine of
Definition~\ref{def:u34-multi}, the one with a counter
for every number, with the small machine's property language
of Zero, Even and At-least-$n$, read at registers,
in place
of $\mathsf{Slot}$. That machine is Thiele-complete too (\code{ent2\_mmachine\_complete}, MultiThiele2.v). Hide $n = k + m$ bits, one in each of registers 0
to $n - 1$. The program asks $k$ questions, one per bit of the first $k$: CHECK ``at least 1'' of
register $i$ for a 1, CHECK ``is 0'' for a 0. Then it COMMITs the first claim and CERTIFYs. The
prior is every $n$-bit value; the posterior is the $2^m$ values that begin with the answers; the
tree is the complete tree of depth $k$.

\begin{theorem}[A search through $n$ bits]\label{thm:ent-search}
For $1 \le k \le 16$ and any $m$: from a world holding a value $v$ of at least $k$ bits, the program
certifies exactly when $v$ begins with its answers, so the posterior is exactly the set of rivals it certifies from; the
test of the posterior is strictly stronger than the prior's; the earned chain is in the run; the
prior has $2^{k+m}$ members and the posterior $2^m$, so the index bits are exactly $k$; the run has
exactly $k + 2$ record moves and the ledger rises by exactly $k + 2$; and the run's own questions
are $k$ CHECKs, so Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-questions} is met with equality. With the COMMIT and the
CERTIFY left off, the questions alone narrow $2^{k+m}$ values to $2^m$, the record stays down, and
the ledger rises by exactly $k$. And no run from a clean start that raises
the record contains more than 16 CHECKs
before its CERTIFY, so with 17 questions no start certifies.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each question is a CHECK of whether one register holds a given bit, which passes exactly when it
does; a failing CHECK traps. So the program certifies exactly when every answer is right, which is
when $v$ begins with the answers. The counting is the count of bit strings, and the representation
theorem applies with every hypothesis a theorem. The cap is the fact table: it holds sixteen facts,
never evicts, and a CHECK on a full table traps (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-bounded}), so a seventeenth
CHECK before the CERTIFY ends the run in a trap.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{ent2\_search\_certifies\_iff}, \code{ent2\_search\_posterior\_is\_certified},
\code{ent2\_bit\_search}, \code{ent2\_search\_lands}, \code{ent2\_search\_questions\_floor},
\code{ent2\_search\_observed}, \code{ent2\_questions\_cap} and \code{ent2\_no\_search\_past\_16}
(BitSearch2.v, BitSearchMember2.v, BitSearchObserved2.v). The sixteen belongs to the machine. The
program has no say in it: it's the same ceiling as the item ``Sixteen checks per run, ever'' in the list of what the machine
doesn't do, near the end of this chapter, and it's why this search has $k \le 16$ however many bits
are hidden. Unasked bits can be any number. The lists, the
tree and the fibres are supplied here, as in the representation theorem, and tied to the run only
for this member. The covering still prices only the size of the drop. Its reason goes unpriced.

\emph{The covering can't be dropped.} It's a hypothesis, and one might hope it's a nuisance one
could remove. It isn't, and the small machine shows it. Fix $n \ge 4$, take the $2^n$ starts with $A$
below $2^n$ as the rivals, and run the three-move chain on the claim ``$A \ge 2^n - 1$'': CHECK,
COMMIT, CERTIFY. It certifies exactly from $A = 2^n - 1$, so the posterior is one start, $n$ index
bits are gone, and the ledger rose by 3. So for $n \ge 4$ the claim ``the index-bit drop is at most
the ledger's rise'' is false for this run, and no tree of depth at most 3 covers the narrowing,
whatever the representative observation. One property with a big constant in it carries $n$ bits in
a single yes-or-no question; what the bound prices is a narrowing whose classes are balanced, a
tree with enough leaves. A narrowing of any other shape is outside it. Checked as \code{ent2\_uncovered\_posterior},
\code{ent2\_uncovered\_claim\_false} and \code{ent2\_no\_cheap\_covering} (CoveringNeeded2.v).

\textbf{The time a check saves.} The question is whether counter $A$ is at least $m$. There are two
ways to find out. The \emph{free} way uses base moves only, INC and DEC, which cost nothing. But a
base move reads $A$ one unit at a time: a DEC takes a unit off $A$ or finds it empty. After $n$
moves, a run that started with $A$ at least $n$ has never seen $A$ empty, so it can't have
behaved differently for different such $A$ except by a constant shift in $A$ itself. The \emph{paid}
way is one CHECK ($A \ge m$): one move, a ledger of one, and the line it ends on says which way it
went. Certifying the answer takes the whole chain, CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY.

\begin{theorem}[The time tax]\label{thm:time-tax}
(1) No program of two-counter instructions that runs fewer than $m$ moves has its final line number
and its final $B$ determine whether $A \ge m$ at every start; in particular none tells $A = m - 1$
from $A = m$. (2) A program of $m$ DECs and INCs (a ladder: DEC $A$ and on success go on to the next
pair, otherwise INC $B$) decides it in exactly $m$ moves, from the line number and $B$, and costs 0.
(3) The paid chain of three instructions raises the flag exactly when $A \ge m$ and has a ledger of
exactly 3, whatever $m$ is. (4) A single CHECK ($A \ge m$) decides it in one move from the line
number, with a ledger of exactly 1, whatever $m$ is. (5) So if a ledger unit is worth $\lambda$
moves, the paid route to deciding costs $1 + \lambda$ and the free route costs at least $m$, and the
paid route is cheaper exactly when $1 + \lambda < m$; the paid route to certifying costs $3 + 3\lambda$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Take the starts $(m - 1, b)$ and $(m, b)$. When $n < m$ both have $A \ge n$, so in the first $n$
moves no DEC finds $A$ empty in either run, and the two runs differ only by the shift of one unit
in $A$. They end at the same line with the same $B$, though $A \ge m$ holds of one and not the
other. (2) Run the ladder: each pair either takes a unit off $A$ and moves on, or finds $A$ empty
and falls through to the INC. The line after $m$ moves is $2m + 1$ exactly when all $m$ units
were there. It's all DEC and INC, so it costs 0. (3) is the price table: CHECK ($A \ge m$) passes
exactly when $A \ge m$, a failing CHECK traps and the flag stays down, and the three moves cost
three. (4) is the same price table with one instruction: a passing CHECK goes on to the next line
and a failing one traps. (5) is arithmetic on (1) to (4).
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{ent2\_free\_run\_shift}, \code{ent2\_free\_cannot\_decide\_fast},
\code{ent2\_ladder\_decides}, \code{ent2\_machine\_free\_cannot\_decide},
\code{ent2\_machine\_ladder\_decides}, \code{ent2\_ladder\_free}, \code{ent2\_chain\_decides} and
\code{ent2\_time\_tax} (TimeTax2.v), the first three for two-counter configurations and the next
three for the same programs compiled and run on the machine, with the certifying comparison
$3 + 3\lambda < m$ inside \code{ent2\_time\_tax}, (4) as
\code{nec\_e\_time\_tax\_one\_paid\_move}, and the lower bound and the one-move decider together as
\code{nec\_e\_time\_tax\_free\_needed}
(NecESearch.v); the deciding comparison $1 + \lambda < m$ is arithmetic on those. The exchange is sharper than a
comparison of two particular programs: the free side is a lower bound over every program of
INC and DEC, so no choice of program is involved, and the paid side is constant. The limits: the bound is for
programs that make no record move, INC and DEC with falling off the end as stopping. It doesn't
cover every Thiele-complete machine, because the definition doesn't forbid a base move that changes a
counter by more than one unit, and such a machine is a different machine, one the bound doesn't
speak for. And the two routes put their answers in different places, the free one in the line
number and the paid one in the flag; this compares two ways to answer one question. It doesn't
compare two certifications.

\subsection{The diagonal, on this machine's programs}
\label{sec:small-diagonal}

Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} left the diagonal standing on any substrate and on a little family built to fit
it, reproved it on L, which isn't a substrate because its evaluation can run forever,
and said what a machine has to supply to fill in the same shape, two things: programs that can be handed to programs as numbers, and a recursion theorem for the
transformations it can carry out. This machine's universal program reads a whole guest program out
of one register, with a numbering of programs that goes there and back
(Definition~\ref{def:u34-U}), and halting is undecidable here in the library's sense
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-undecidable}). What's left are the two classical results that turn a
universal machine into a place where the diagonal bites: Rice's theorem and Kleene's recursion
theorem. They come with a wrinkle I should put first, because it decides which machine they're
about.

The wrinkle is the one from earlier in this chapter, at the end of the subsection on what two counters compute. The small machine takes its inputs straight
into two counters, and Schroeppel's memo gives a proof that two plain counters can't even compute $2^n$ from $n$. Rice's
reduction has to keep a program's input safe while a copy of a halting instance runs. Kleene's
construction has to run an evaluator while keeping its input. Two counters have nowhere to keep it.
So the two theorems land where they're true and where I could prove them. The host machine of
Definition~\ref{def:u34-multi}, the one with a counter for every number that $U$ runs on, is a fine
programming system: its programs are numbers, an input sits in register 1, and there's room to
spare. On it both theorems hold in full. On the two-counter machine itself the story splits, and
I'll tell it at the end of the subsection: Rice's theorem holds on every input, by a trick for
keeping the input that I'll show you; Kleene's holds when inputs are written as powers of two, the
way Minsky packed them; and on plain inputs Kleene's is false, and that's a theorem too.

The host machine's programs are numbered the way $U$ numbers a guest's. Write $\langle m, n \rangle$
for $(2n + 1) \cdot 2^m$. INC $r$ is $\langle 0, r \rangle$, DEC $r$ $j$ is
$\langle 1, \langle r, j \rangle \rangle$, HALT is $\langle 2, 0 \rangle$, CHECK $r$ is
$\langle 3, r \rangle$, COMMIT $r$ is $\langle 4, r \rangle$, CERTIFY is $\langle 5, 0 \rangle$, and a
program is the list code: the empty program is 0, and an instruction $x$ followed by a program $t$ is
$\langle x, \mathrm{code}(t) \rangle$. Every number decodes to some program, and decoding a program's
code gives the program back. Say a host program \emph{outputs} $y$ on input $x$ when, started with $x$
in register 1 and every other register 0, with a clean table, it halts with $y$ in register 0.

Rice first, because it's the shorter road. Henry Rice, whom you met in
Section~\ref{sec:windows}, proved in his 1951 doctoral thesis, and published in 1953, that no program decides any
property of what programs \emph{do} unless every program has
it or none does. Properties of how a program is written aren't covered. The road from halting is a single detour. Take a property of what programs do,
a program $y$ that has it, and a program $n$ that doesn't. Given an instance of two-counter halting,
a Minsky program $H$ with starting counters $a$ and $b$, build a host program that first loads $a$
and $b$ into two fresh registers, then runs a copy of $H$ moved onto those registers, then empties
both, then runs $y$. If $H$ halts on $(a, b)$ the built program behaves like $y$ and has the
property. If $H$ runs forever the built program never stops on any input, and it behaves like the
program that loops, which lacks the property (if the looping program has it instead, swap the roles
of $y$ and $n$). Everything the built program does before $y$ is INC and DEC, which pay nothing and
touch no fact, channel, trap latch or flag. So a decider for the property would be a decider for
halting, and the library already says what that would cost: the complement of single-tape
Turing-machine halting would become something a program could list, the same synthetic sense of
``undecidable'' as Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-undecidable}. Two words carry the weight, and they're the
ones to check in the statement: what ``behaves the same'' sees, and where the program starts.

\begin{definition}[Behaving the same, on the host]\label{def:host-same}
A host program \emph{ends} in a state when it halts there, from the start with $x$ in register 1 and
the rest clean; a trap counts as stopping. Two host programs \emph{behave the same} when for every
input $x$, any state one ends in has a state the other ends in that agrees with it on every
register's value, the fact table, the channel, the trap latch, the ledger and the flag, and the same
the other way round. The line number and the versions aren't compared. A property of host programs
is \emph{extensional} when behaving the same carries it from one program to the other.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Rice's theorem on the host machine]\label{thm:host-rice}
Let $\Pi$ be an extensional property of host programs that some program has and some program lacks.
Then $\Pi$ is undecidable in the library's sense.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The reduction above. The prefix before $y$ leaves every register but the two fresh ones as it
found them, and empties those, so when $H$ halts the built program ends in whatever state $y$ ends
in from the same input, with the same ledger, table, channel, trap and flag. When $H$ doesn't halt,
the built program stops on no input. The reduction is from the complement of halting, so no excluded
middle is needed; the proof splits on the decider's own answer for the looping program.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{sm\_host\_rice}, with the reduction's two halves as \code{sm\_rice\_prog\_halts} and
\code{sm\_rice\_prog\_diverges} (SmHostRice.v). A property that depends only on the partial function
a program computes, whether it stops and what it leaves in register 0, is extensional, so it's
covered; the files also derive that case again from the recursion theorem below, as
\code{sm\_host\_rice\_fun} (SmKleene.v).

On the small machine itself the same road works from the clean start, and only from there. Say two
two-counter programs \emph{behave the same from the clean start} when, whatever state one halts in
from counters $(0, 0)$, the other halts in a state with the same counters, trap latch, ledger and
flag, and the same the other way round. The fact table isn't compared, because the prefix moves the
versions of $A$ and $B$ by fixed amounts and the facts carry versions. There is no input to keep,
since the program starts at $(0, 0)$, and $H$'s instance is loaded straight into $A$ and $B$.

\begin{theorem}[Rice's theorem for the small machine, from the clean start]\label{thm:guest-rice}
Let $\Pi$ be a property of two-counter programs that's carried from a program to any program that
behaves the same from the clean start, held by some program and lacked by some other. Then $\Pi$ is
undecidable in the library's sense. In particular ``halts from the clean start'' is undecidable.
\end{theorem}

Checked as \code{sm\_guest\_rice} and \code{sm\_guest\_halting\_clean\_undecidable} (SmGuestRice.v).
That's the clean start only. Every input is harder, because the standard reduction has to keep the
input safe while the halting instance runs, and two counters have nowhere obvious to keep it. The
way through is at the end of the subsection.

Kleene's recursion theorem is the deeper one, and it's a construction, which is
Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}'s point about Kleene's little gem (Moschovakis's phrase): the content
is the building, and the contradiction in Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} was just the last line. It
says: for every transformation $F$ of programs that some program can carry out on numbers, there's a
program $p$ that computes the same thing as $F(p)$. The shape of the building is the old one. From
the program that carries out $F$, build an \emph{evaluator} that reads a number, treats it as a
program's code, specialises that program to its own code, runs $F$'s program on the result, and runs
whatever program comes back. The specialising step is what logicians call s-m-n: fix one input of a
program and get a new program that needs one input fewer. Then the witness is the evaluator
specialised to its own code. Run on any input, it builds its own code, hands it to $F$'s program,
gets the code of $F(p)$, and runs that.

Here's each piece on the host machine, with its exact premise.

\begin{theorem}[s-m-n, and a universal program for host programs]\label{thm:host-smn}
(1) For a number $c$ and a host program $V$, let
$\mathrm{spec}(c, V)$ be $c$ copies of INC 2 followed by $V$ with its jumps moved to follow them.
Then for all $x, y$, $\mathrm{spec}(c, V)$ outputs $y$ on input $x$ if and only if $V$, started with
$x$ in register 1 and $c$ in register 2, halts with $y$ in register 0. (2) There is a host program
$W$ made only of INC, DEC and HALT such that, for all $c, x, y$, $W$ started with $x$ in register 1
and $c$ in register 2 halts with $y$ in register 0 exactly when the host program numbered $c$
outputs $y$ on input $x$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) The prefix writes register 2 $c$ times and nothing else, so it moves that register's version from
0 to $c$. A fact records a version, so after the prefix every later version of register 2, and the
version in every fact the run records about register 2, is $c$ more than in a clean run. A CHECK or a
COMMIT reads versions only to ask whether two versions of the same register are equal, and adding $c$
to both keeps the answer, so the two runs take the same steps. The run is $V$'s run from the stated
start, moved down by $c$ lines. (2) is the evaluator. A finite algorithm decodes a number into a program, runs it step by
step on given registers, and, searching over the number of steps, returns the output of the first
halting run. I wrote that algorithm out in Coq, turned it into a term of the lambda calculus L, and
ran the library's compiler from L to Minsky programs, which gives a program of two-counter
instructions that a host program can be read off from, instruction for instruction. The tools
supply the program that computes the evaluator. The fixed-point argument below is not theirs.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{sm2\_smn\_all} (SmSmnAll.v), an if and only if statement that carries no premise on register 2, and
\code{sm\_host\_universal} (SmKleene.v); the narrower form of (1), with the premise, is still there as
\code{sm\_smn}. The numbering is \code{sm\_hcode}, \code{sm\_hdecode} and \code{sm\_hdecode\_hcode}
(SmCodes.v). Be exact about one
thing: $U$ is not that universal program. $U$ runs two-counter guests, and a two-counter guest
given its input plainly can't run the evaluator. With inputs written as powers of two one can, as
Theorem~\ref{thm:tc-kleene} near the end of this subsection shows. $W$ runs host programs, and it can, because it's a host program on a machine
with registers.

\begin{theorem}[Kleene's recursion theorem on the host machine]\label{thm:host-kleene}
(1) For every host program $T$ there is a host program $e$ such that for all $x, y$: $e$ outputs $y$
on input $x$ if and only if, for some $d$, $T$ outputs $d$ on the number of $e$, and the program
numbered $d$ outputs $y$ on $x$. (2) So for every transformation $F$ of host programs that some host
program carries out on numbers (on the number of $p$ it outputs the number of $F(p)$, for every $p$),
there is a host program $e$ such that for all $x, y$, $e$ outputs $y$ on $x$ if and only if $F(e)$
does. (3) The same on numbers: for every function $f$ on numbers that some host program computes,
some number $e$ has the program numbered $e$ and the program numbered $f(e)$ output the same on
every input.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Let $E$ be the following program of INC and DEC, built the same way as $W$ from one finite
evaluator, with $T$'s number $t$ written in. On inputs $x$ and $c$ it computes the number of $\mathrm{spec}(c, P_c)$, where $P_c$ is the
program numbered $c$, runs $T$ on that number to get $d$, and then runs the program numbered $d$ on
$x$. Let $c_0$ be the number of $E$, and let $e = \mathrm{spec}(c_0, E)$. By (1) of
Theorem~\ref{thm:host-smn}, $e$ on input $x$ does what $E$ does on $x$ and $c_0$. And $E$ on
$c_0$ builds the number of $\mathrm{spec}(c_0, P_{c_0})$, which is the number of $e$, since $P_{c_0}$
is $E$. So $e$ hands its own number to $T$, gets $d$, and runs $d$ on $x$. (2) and (3) are (1) with $T$
carrying out $F$ or $f$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{sm\_second\_recursion}, \code{sm\_kleene} and \code{sm\_kleene\_codes}
(SmKleene.v). That fixed point is of the \emph{function}: $e$ and $F(e)$ stop on the same inputs and
leave the same number in register 0. Their ledgers, flags and fact tables can differ, because the
marks $e$ pays are the evaluator's. I'd like a fixed point that agrees on the record too, and the next two theorems say how
much of that can be had. The ledger and the flag can be had. Every register can't.

\begin{theorem}[The recursion theorem, up to the record]\label{thm:host-kleene-record}
Let $F$ be a transformation of host programs that some host program $T$ carries out on numbers.
Then there is a host program $e$ such that, for every input $x$, any state $e$ ends in has a state
$F(e)$ ends in that agrees with it on register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the number of
facts in the table, and whether the channel is empty, and the same the other way round. So $e$ stops
on $x$ exactly when $F(e)$ does, and the ledgers are equal exactly, with no surcharge. $T$ may itself
check, commit and certify.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The construction is Theorem~\ref{thm:host-kleene}'s, with a different evaluator. The first step is to
see that a record is small. From a clean start, a host program that stops has a record I can read off
five numbers, in this order: what it left in register 0; how many facts the table holds; what is
left of the ledger once the facts, the trap and the flag are paid for, which I'll call the commits;
1 if the flag is up and 0 if not; and 1 if the trap latch is up and 0 if not. The record obeys a short rulebook. The table holds
at most sixteen facts. The latch is a single bit. A commit needs a fact behind it, a certify needs a
commit, and the channel is empty exactly when no commit was paid. The ledger is the facts, plus the
commits, plus the flag, plus the trap, and that's all of it. Those are the only properties of a record
the replay will use, and I proved them by following the plain machine alongside the real one, one step
at a time.

The second step is five blocks, one for each number. Each block reads the code of $T$, runs $T$ on the
number of the specialised program, runs the program that comes out on $x$, and returns its number. All of
that happens on plain data: the blocks are programs of INC and DEC, built the way $W$ was, from an
evaluator written out in Coq, turned into a term of L and compiled to Minsky programs. So if $T$ has marks
of its own, they are simulated and never paid.

The third step is the payment. The evaluator puts 1 in a fresh register, which satisfies the host's one
property, and CHECKs it once for every fact. It COMMITs to that claim once for every commit. It CERTIFYs
once if the flag is up. It copies the first number into register 0. And if the trap latch is up, it
CHECKs a register that holds 0, which fails, and the host traps. Everything before the payments is INC and
DEC and costs nothing, and the payments cost what the record costs, so the ledger is exact. Specialise the
evaluator to its own number, as before.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{sm2\_kleene\_obs} (SmFixedPoint.v), with the five numbers as \code{sm2\_final\_numbers}
and the evaluator's specification as \code{sm2\_ev\_spec} (SmTally.v) and the replay program as
\code{sm2\_VG\_forward} and \code{sm2\_VG\_halt} (SmFixed.v), where the trap latch is up exactly when the fifth number is 1 and the flag exactly when the fourth is positive; \code{sm2\_kleene\_fun} gives back the
version that compares only the function. Two limits, and the second one is a theorem. First, $e$ pays
after it has computed everything. It is not the way $U$ runs a guest, mirroring every move: $e$ pays
the counts, CHECKs, then COMMITs, then the CERTIFY, whatever order $F(e)$ used, so the order of the
record's events isn't preserved, and for a program $F(e)$ that never stops, $e$ never stops and pays
nothing, though $F(e)$ may pay without bound. The relation says nothing about states in the middle of a
run. Second, no fixed point agrees on every register, or on what the facts name.

\begin{theorem}[No fixed point of full behaviour]\label{thm:host-no-exact}
There is a transformation $F$ of host programs, carried out by a host program, such that no host
program $e$ behaves the same as $F(e)$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:host-same}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $F(p)$ be the one-line program INC $r$, with $r$ one above the number of $p$. A host program carries
this out on numbers; I got it from the same route through L. None of it was written by hand. A program's number is at
least every register it names: the number of an instruction is above its register, and the code of a
list is above every instruction in it. So $e$ can't name $r$, the register $F(e)$ writes. On input 0 the
run of $F(e)$ ends with 1 in register $r$, and if $e$ stops at all, it ends with 0 there. If $e$ doesn't
stop, then it already differs from $F(e)$, which does. Either way they don't behave the same.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{sm2\_no\_exact} and \code{sm2\_reg\_bound} (SmNoExact.v). A variant of $F$ that also
CHECKs register $r$ and commits to it gives $F(e)$ a fact and a commitment about $r$ that $e$ can't
have, so no fixed point agrees on the fact table alone, or on the channel alone, or on the versions of
the registers (\code{nec\_e\_no\_fixed\_point\_facts}, \code{nec\_e\_no\_fixed\_point\_versions},
NecEHost.v). What survives is what Theorem~\ref{thm:host-kleene-record} states. Whether one more fixed
register could be added to that list I haven't settled either way, and I don't claim it.

And with the recursion theorem proved, the wall of Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} goes up on this
machine without a premise left over. Call a property of host programs \emph{functional} when it
depends only on the partial function a program computes.

\begin{theorem}[The diagonal on the host machine]\label{thm:host-wall}
Let $\Pi$ be a functional property of host programs that some program has and some program lacks.
(1) Read ``$f$ is representable'' as ``some host program carries $f$ out on numbers.'' Then no
function $d$ from programs to Booleans whose flip is representable is right about $\Pi$ on every
program: this is the argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:u12-no-inside-decider}, reproved for host programs, with its recursion premise a theorem here.
(2) No host program decides $\Pi$ outright: there is no program $D$ that, on the number of every
program, halts with a number in register 0 that's 1 exactly when the program has $\Pi$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) The flip, send programs that $d$ calls good to the program lacking $\Pi$ and the others to the
one having it, is carried out by a host program by hypothesis. Theorem~\ref{thm:host-kleene}(2) gives
a program $e$ that computes what its image computes; $\Pi$ holds of $e$ exactly when it holds of the
image, and the image lacks it exactly when $d$ calls $e$ good, so $d$ is wrong at $e$. (2) From
a deciding program $D$ build a host program that computes $D$'s flip on numbers, by the same route
through L and the Minsky compiler, reading the Boolean off $D$'s runs with the standard library's
unbounded search; then (1) applies. This one is an outright negation. The synthetic notion doesn't come into it.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{sm\_no\_inside\_decider} and \code{sm\_no\_host\_decider} (SmKleene.v, SmDecider.v).

Rice and Kleene are the ingredients the diagonal of Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} asks a substrate for,
and the wall they put up doesn't care about the record: the base does the computing and the flag
watches. A program's ledger and flag are among what ``behaves the same'' sees on the host,
so a nontrivial property of those is undecidable too, in the library's sense of Theorem~\ref{thm:host-rice}, and the fixed point is up to the record, as
far as the theorems above say and no further.

Now the two-counter machine itself, which I promised at the start of the subsection: Minsky's two
bins of pebbles and nothing else. Rice, first. Say a two-counter program \emph{behaves the same} as
another on a set $X$ of inputs when, on every input $n$ in $X$, started with $n$ pebbles in bin A and
none in bin B, one stops exactly when the other does, and then they agree on both bins, the trap
latch, the ledger, the flag, and on which property and which counter each recorded fact and the
channel are about. The versions are left out: they say which write a fact is about, and the trick
below moves them.

The trick is the whole problem. Rice's reduction has to keep the program's input safe while a copy of
a halting instance $H$ runs, and there's no third bin to keep it in. My first guess was bin B, and
that dies at once, because $H$ needs both bins. The second guess is Minsky's own packing: keep several
numbers in one bin as powers of different primes, $H$'s two counters as the exponents of 2 and 3, and
the input as the exponent of 5. That dies more quietly. To put the input there, the program would
have to turn $n$ pebbles into $5^n$, an exponential, and Schroeppel's memo, from earlier in this
chapter, gives a proof that two plain counters can't even build $2^n$ from $n$. I had no way to build $5^n$.

What works is to stop keeping the input beside the work. Turn $n$ pebbles into $6n + 5$, which is only
adding, and then multiply in $H$'s counters as powers of 2 and 3. $H$ runs by halving the pile and
splitting it in thirds and building it back up, and the $6n + 5$ rides along in the middle of every
one of those piles. It's odd, and counted off in threes it leaves two over, so no halving or thirding
ever reaches into it.

\begin{theorem}[Rice's theorem for the two-counter machine, on any inputs]\label{thm:tc-rice}
For any set $X$ of inputs, a property of two-counter programs that's carried from a program to any
program that behaves the same on $X$ is undecidable in the library's sense, unless every program has
it or none does, and then it's decidable. $X$ can be every input, the powers of two, or $\{0\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For every input: given a two-counter instance $H$ starting from counters $a$ and $b$, build a program
that turns the input of $n$ pebbles in bin A into $(6n + 5) \cdot 2^a \cdot 3^b$, runs $H$ inside the
exponents of 2 and 3, divides out every 2 and every 3 when $H$ stops, takes away 5, divides by 6, and
then runs the program that has the property. Because $6n + 5$ shares no factor with 2 or 3, the coding
never mistakes it for an exponent, and the input comes back whole. If $H$ halts, the built program
behaves the same as the one with the property on every input; if not, it never stops on any input. The
reduction is from the complement of halting.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{tc\_rice} and \code{tc\_rice\_dichotomy} (TcRice.v).

So $6n + 5$ is the place to keep the input that two counters seemed not to have. It isn't beside the
work. It's inside it, in a factor the work never touches. I like that one more than I can justify: the
input hides in the leftover that every halving and thirding walks straight past.

Kleene needs more than keeping an input. It needs a program that runs a program. So write a number
$x$ as $2^x$ pebbles and read a result as the exponent of 2, the way Minsky did. With inputs written
that way, there's one two-counter program, call it $U_2$, that, started on $2^x \cdot 3^e$, stops with $2^y$
exactly when the program numbered $e$ gives $y$ on $x$; specialising a program to a number is exact;
and the recursion theorem holds. ($U_2$ is a different program from the universal host program
$U$, which runs on the machine with a register for every number.) Checked as \code{tc\_universal} and \code{tc\_smn} (TcPacked.v).

\begin{theorem}[Kleene for the two-counter machine, inputs written as powers of two]\label{thm:tc-kleene}
(1) For every transformation $F$ of programs that some program carries out on program numbers, there's
a program $e$ that computes the same function as $F(e)$, with inputs and outputs written as powers of
two. (2) The fixed point is of the function only: there's such an $F$ for which no $e$ behaves the same
as $F(e)$ once the properties and counters of the recorded facts count.
\end{theorem}

The counterexample in (2) is short. Let $F(p)$ check that bin A holds at least the number of $p$ plus
one. A program can only record facts about properties it names, and every property it names is below
its own number, so no $e$ records what $F(e)$ records.

Checked as \code{tc\_second\_recursion}, \code{tc\_kleene} and \code{tc\_no\_fine\_kleene} (TcPacked.v,
TcNoFine.v).

Even with Schroeppel in hand, my first guess about Kleene was that the powers of two were a
convenience, and that plain inputs would only take more work. They don't take more work. With plain inputs, Kleene's theorem is false. A
transformation is \emph{carried out} if some program, started on $2^n$ where $n$ is the number of a
program $p$, stops with $2^m$ where $m$ is the number of $F(p)$.

\begin{theorem}[No plain recursion on two counters]\label{thm:no-plain-recursion}
(1) No program of $n$ lines stops with $c \cdot x$ pebbles in bin A, started on $x$ pebbles in bin A
and none in bin B, for every $x$, where $c = N! + 1$ and $N = 16(n+1)(2n+1)^{16}$. (2) So there's a
carried-out transformation $F$ such that no program $e$ computes the same plain function as $F(e)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(2) from (1): let $F(p)$ multiply bin A by $c$ for the length of $p$. A program carries $F$ out by
the same route through L as before, and a fixed point would multiply every input by a number fixed by
its own length. For (1), count the control states of a program of $n$ lines: its line, the trap latch,
whether the channel holds a commitment, and for each of at most sixteen facts its property, its counter
and whether it still concerns that counter's current version. There are at most $4(n+1)(2n+1)^{16}$, and
$N$ is four times that, so $c$ shares no factor with any number up to $N$. Now suppose a program does
multiply every input by $c$. On a large input, a bin far fuller than anything a CHECK names is seen
only two ways: whether it's empty, and whether its pebbles pair off evenly. So the run breaks into
stages, each a bounded cycle that moves the small bin up by some $g$ and the full one down by some $m$,
both at most $N$. Follow one input and the same input plus the product of the $m$'s through the same
stages, and compare the outputs: the growth is $c$ times the product of the $m$'s on one side and the
product of the $g$'s on the other. A number with no factor up to $N$ can't divide a product of numbers
up to $N$ unless it is 1, and $c$ is at least 2.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{tc2\_no\_mult} (Tc2Mult.v), from \code{am\_no\_multiplier} (Tc2Chain.v), which says
the same for any machine with finitely many control states whose counters are read only through zero
and parity above a threshold, and \code{tc2\_plain\_recursion\_false} (Tc2Plain.v), which gives a
carried-out $F$ with no $e$ equivalent to $F(e)$ on plain inputs, all closed.

The case split in the stages is decided by running for a bounded number of steps, so no excluded
middle goes in. For a long time I couldn't read Schroeppel's own memo. I went looking again and
found the scan. As I read it, his route is close in spirit: he trades a two-counter machine that
starts with one counter empty for a machine with one register that can only add,
multiply and
divide by fixed numbers and take one away, each of those built out of one of the program's loops, and that's the
stages here under another name. I haven't followed his proof line by line; this one is checked. The $c$ it uses is astronomically bigger than anything a real
multiplier needs, and finding the best bound is a question I leave alone.

So on two bins: Rice holds on every input. Kleene holds with inputs written as powers of two, for the
function. It fails for the facts. And with plain inputs Kleene fails outright. The last one is the
answer I didn't see coming. The powers of two weren't a convenience. On two bins they're the
difference between a recursion theorem and none.

\subsection{What the universal machine covers, and what it doesn't}

Here's what that covers, said plainly, a sentence at a time. The guests of $U$ are this
chapter's programs, every one of them, from every start. That's the stated class. It's the same
kind of class Turing's universal machine has: a fixed instruction set, and a finite program held
as data, here packed into one number the way Turing packed his into a description number. Each
guest keeps its computation, its halting, its answer, its record and its prices, exactly: the
host halts when it halts, its flag goes up when the guest's would, on a chain of its own, and its
ledger is the guest's.

The guests of $U_P$ are every Thiele machine whose driver, step, prices and reading are computed
by programs, with the reading decided on every state. Each keeps its computation and its halting;
its reading becomes the host's flag as a latch, raised on an earned chain whose claim is the
guest's own reading; and its prices become the host's ledger, exactly, except for a surcharge of
at most two at the move where the reading first says yes, when the reading starts at no. The
