surcharge is zero when that move costs three or more, and it can't always be avoided: when the
guest certifies with a ledger below three, no program on that host, run from a clean start, matches its ledger exactly (Theorems~\ref{thm:u34-presented}
and~\ref{thm:u34-presented-surcharge}). Picture a clerk who'll stamp anybody's receipt. He copies
it onto his own forms, bills at your rates to within two, and the stamp at the bottom is one he
earned by checking your own reading. He didn't copy it.

What's outside the class is outside the theorems. A machine whose reading no program decides
(an oracle checker, say, which the definition of Thiele-complete doesn't rule out) doesn't come in. Nor
does a machine whose next move is nobody's computation. Nor does a guest that starts with a table
of facts nobody checked: the guests start where their presentation says, and the host from a clean
start.

And here's why insisting on no built-in step is the point. A plain interpreter on an ordinary
computer runs guests too, but then the guest's record is data the interpreter's program updates
by convention, which is exactly the position of the ordinary programmable computer from the front
matter and Section~\ref{sec:machine-vs-program}. That's a fact about how such interpreters are built. It says nothing about what they can do: $U$ and
$U_P$ are fixed interpreters, and their record isn't kept by convention. Nothing in them raises the
host's flag except the host's own CERTIFY, and the host's step won't let that pass without a
COMMIT, or the COMMIT without a CHECK on a slot nobody has touched. The guest's record isn't data
the host updates. It's a record the host earns again, under the same rule, on its own registers.

\subsection{What it doesn't do}

Here's where it falls short, in plain words, because a small machine is only honest if its
edges are as visible as its middle.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The check price is flat.} CHECK costs 1 whether it's asking ``is this 0'' or ``is this at
least a billion.'' The property language is fixed and each property is one evaluation, so
``pays for its work'' here means that flat price, the same however hard the
question was. A machine that charged by the difficulty of the check would be a different
machine, and I haven't built it.
\item \textbf{DEC on zero isn't a write.} It doesn't change the counter, so it doesn't change the
version. That's the right call for versions (nothing changed), but it means DEC on zero is
a free way to move the line number without leaving any mark. The idle run in the window
section uses exactly that.
\item \textbf{After a trap, a trace still pays.} On programs, a trap stops the run. On arbitrary
traces, instructions after a trap are each charged their cost and none of them changes the
core. I chose to keep charging so that the ledger stays the plain sum of what was issued
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-toll} has no exceptions); the price of that choice is that a trapped
machine can still be billed for nothing.
\item \textbf{``Checked'' means what the property language can say.} On this machine that's \emph{is
zero}, \emph{is even} and \emph{is at least $n$}, and a live fact means one of those holds of one counter's
current value. It doesn't mean the program is correct, or that anything follows from the
property, or that the property was worth checking. So can a proved machine of this kind check
``sorted,'' the claim the opening chapter's table runs on? Yes, through an encoding. A copy of
this machine, instruction for instruction, with its property language left open, has provenance,
checker soundness, no forging and the floor of three proved once for every property language that
comes with an exact equality test and a checker proved equal to its meaning. Give it ``the list
this counter encodes is sorted'' as a property and it certifies a sorted list for three and
refuses an unsorted one forever (\code{sorted\_run\_certifies}, \code{sorted\_run\_certifies\_iff}
and \code{sorted\_run\_refused\_forever}, EarnedGeneric.v). The copy is written out again in its own
file, and no theorem derives it from this one; putting the two side by side is how you check
they're the same machine. What makes that a check of
the list is the proof that the checker means sortedness. Without that proof, ``sorted'' would be a number
some unconstrained code wrote into a counter, and the record would be honest about the counter
and silent about the list.
\item \textbf{The certificate is historical.} Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, the counter can
change, and the flag still goes up. The flag says a claim was checked and committed about
an edition. It says nothing about whether the claim is still true.
\item \textbf{One latch, and a channel that moves on.} The flag records that an earned chain
happened, once. After that it stays up, and later CERTIFYs change nothing. The channel is the
part that names a fact: with the flag up from a clean start, it names a fact that some earlier
passing COMMIT committed (\code{certified\_channel\_earned} and \code{channel\_names\_last\_commit}, EarnedCore.v). But a later commitment replaces it, so at the end
it names the last earned commitment, which needn't be the one the flag rose on. Two runs from
$\mathrm{start}(0, 0)$ show it, worked from the instruction table. First run: CHECK \emph{is zero}
$A$; CHECK \emph{is zero} $B$; COMMIT \emph{is zero} $A$; CERTIFY; COMMIT \emph{is zero} $B$.
Second run: the same five instructions with the last two swapped, so COMMIT \emph{is zero} $B$
comes before CERTIFY. Both end in the same state: both counters 0 at version 0, both facts in the
table, the channel holding (\emph{zero}, $B$, 0), the trap down, a ledger of five and the flag
up. In the first run the flag rose at step four, on the commitment about $A$. In the second it
rose at step five, on the commitment about $B$. So the flag is an ever-certified latch: it says
an earned chain happened at some step, and the end state doesn't say which claim or which step.
A receipt naming the claim the flag first rose on would need that claim kept where nothing can
overwrite it; a receipt with a time on it would also need the step number kept; and several
certifications that each last would need a record richer than one flag. None of those is built
or proved here. They're extensions. Several claims need a latch each.
\item \textbf{Sixteen checks per run, ever.} Facts never leave and the table holds sixteen, so a run
gets at most sixteen passing CHECKs in its whole life, and the seventeenth traps. A
certificate needs only one, so this costs nothing for the theorems, but it's a hard wall
for any program that wants to keep checking forever, and it's this machine's small version of the
opening chapter's ``you can't keep all of it.''
\item \textbf{The clean start matters.} Provenance, soundness, no forging and the price of three are
all stated from a clean start. Hand the machine a table pre-loaded with facts nobody
checked, and of course none of that follows. The theorems are about what the machine
produces. What you smuggle in at the door is outside them. Spell the door out once: the theorems
cover any list of instructions anybody can issue, from a clean start, on a step that runs as
written, with nothing else writing to the machine. They say nothing about whoever sets or
restores the start, about a reset, about a device that misbehaves, or about whoever carries the
flag's value to you.
\item \textbf{The universal programs have stated guests.} $U$ runs every one of this machine's
programs from every start, with halting, answers, flag and ledger matched exactly. $U_P$ runs every
computably presented Thiele machine, with its reading decided by a program, its record carried as
a latch, and its ledger matched to within a surcharge of at most two when its reading starts at
no, and of three when it starts at yes. When the guest certifies with a ledger below three, no program on
that host, run from a clean start, matches its ledger exactly. A
machine outside that class, with a reading no program decides, isn't covered by either. The
simpler host with the built-in guest step pays one per guest step whatever the step was, so its
ledger is at least the guest's and usually more; $U$'s is exact, and $U_P$'s is exact up to the
surcharge.
\item \textbf{Slow, and fed directly.} Universality is Minsky's, with the inputs placed straight in
the counters. Getting from an arbitrary Turing machine to two counters goes through his
exponential packing, which my files don't redo; the compiler behind $U_P$ uses the library's
version of it, and nothing about it is fast.
\item \textbf{The step doesn't police trivial checks.} CHECK \emph{at least 0} passes on every
value, so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY on it raises the flag for three from any start (the note after
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tight}). A check that can't fail establishes nothing, and the machine raises
the flag for it anyway. The step checks order, aboutness and an honest checker, and it leaves
``was that worth asking'' to whoever reads the record.
\item \textbf{The toll is a choice here; nothing forces it.} Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s argument
forces a toll on a finite machine that pays for every merge. This machine is neither. Its
counters have no ceiling, so it's infinite. And its free instructions merge states: take a core
at line $\ell$ with $c$ at 1 and version $w$, and a core at line $j - 1$ with $c$ at 0 and
version $w + 1$, everything else alike, and DEC $c$ $j$ sends both to line $j$ with $c$ at 0
and version $w + 1$, for nothing. So for this machine the price of one is a design choice the
chairs don't force.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{What this chapter adds up to}

So Part IV has one machine, and it isn't the model. It's a Thiele machine in the front matter's
sense, an instance of the certification system with the toll proved: \code{earned\_cs}
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-instance}). It's Thiele-complete, in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:u34-thiele-complete}, the sense no clock meets
(Theorems~\ref{thm:u34-clock} and~\ref{thm:u34-tc-instances}): it computes whatever a Turing
machine can, its computing is free and can't touch the record, and, from a clean start, its record is earned. And the
universal Thiele machine runs on a host made of its own kinds of instruction: one fixed program,
$U$, with no guest step built in, that runs every one of its programs with halting, flag and
ledger matched exactly and earns its own flag (Section~\ref{sec:universal-host}); and the same
program with one paid move added, $U_P$, that runs every computably presented Thiele machine,
carrying its reading as a latch, its prices to within two when its reading starts at no, and a flag earned on the guest's own
reading (Section~\ref{sec:presented-universal}).

If you ever find yourself wondering whether a property of this machine is the model's or just
the machine's, hold it up against Section~\ref{sec:toll}'s certification system, the latch of
Section~\ref{sec:latch} and the four clauses of Thiele-complete. What follows from those holds of
every machine that meets them; the rest (a table of sixteen facts, three properties,
a flat price of one) is this machine's choice. Six
instructions, and a seventh for a host that has to bill somebody else's prices. If the model
needs more than that, this is where it'll show.

What's left of Part IV: whether any of this depends on counters (Section~\ref{sec:every-model}),
how machines are built from parts (Section~\ref{sec:parts}), whether any of it actually runs
(Section~\ref{sec:running}), then a check worth earning, and then what any of this costs against
physics.

%===========================================================================
\section{Every model}
\label{sec:every-model}
%===========================================================================

Here's the worry I couldn't put down after the last chapter. Everything in it was built on
Minsky's two counters. The definition of Thiele-complete names a two-counter window in clause (a).
The universal program runs two-counter guests. So is all of this a fact about counters? Pick a
different machine to start from, a Turing machine with its tape, a register machine, Alonzo
Church's lambda calculus, and does the record still go on the same way, or did I just find a
trick that happens to work for one toy?

I chased it with a picture: a box with a panel bolted to its front. The box computes, with levers
for moves and a window showing what clause (a) asks to see, two numbers and a line number. The panel is the last chapter's earned layer: version tallies that click
when the box writes, a rack for facts, the flag, and the three buttons CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY at one mark
each. The worry is whether that panel only bolts onto the one box I built.

If it did, it would be a curiosity. The whole point of the opening chapter was that the second
computer is missing something \emph{any} computer could have. So this chapter tries to break that,
from both directions: the panel onto other boxes, and other boxes run inside mine.

\subsection{From any base up}

Start with the direction I care about most: the panel onto a box I didn't build. The box can be any
machine at all that has a universal base in the sense of clause (a), and in the picture that's two
things. It shows a two-counter window. And for each two-counter instruction it has a lever that acts
on the window as that instruction does. What else is inside, what its states look like, I don't get
to know.

My first guess was to keep whatever the box came with. Plenty of machines have a meter of their own,
or a light on the front that means something's done, so leave those where they are, bolt the panel on
beside them, and see what happens. It can't work, and the definition says why. If a lever can cost
something, computing isn't free. If a lever can switch on the box's own light, a record went up with
no CHECK behind it. Thiele-complete rules out both. So the meter and the light come off, along with
everything else the box already had: its costs, its record, all of it, except the states, the levers
and what each lever does to the state.

Then bolt on a panel cut down from the small machine's, and nothing else:
one version number for the whole box that every lever
raises, which is the tally, a table with room for at least one fact, and three new moves, CHECK,
COMMIT and CERTIFY, at one mark each, with every lever free. Call that the \emph{lift} of the
machine.

\begin{theorem}[Every universal base lifts]\label{thm:lift}
(1) The lift of any box with a universal base, over a claim language with an exact equality test and a checker proved to mean what it says, is Thiele-complete, as long as the claims its CHECK can
ask include one that's true at one loaded state and false at another, and the fact table has room
for at least one fact. (2) The claims ``this register is at least $n$'' and ``the program is at line $n$,''
read off the window, always include such a claim, so with those claims every universal base lifts.
(3) Conversely, every Thiele-complete machine has an interface meeting the four clauses under which
its base moves, taken alone, form a machine with a universal base. (4) The
panel leaves the box alone: from a state whose trap is down, a run of lever pulls in the lift moves
the box exactly as the box's own run does, and the trap stays down.
\end{theorem}

The proof of (1) is the small machine's proof with the bins swapped out for whatever the box has.
That's the part I'd braced for, and it turned out to be nothing. The chain CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY
never looked at anything but the tally and the claim. The levers never touched the panel. Neither
side of the proof ever needed to know it was looking at pebbles.

Checked as \code{lift\_thiele\_complete}, \code{lift\_window\_nonvacuous},
\code{lift\_window\_thiele\_complete}, \code{lift\_reduct\_universal} and \code{lift\_projection\_run}
(LiftCore.v, LiftConverse.v), all closed.

So the earned layer isn't something two counters do. It sits on top of any machine that can compute,
and it never needed to know which one. I'd half expected to be rewriting the proof once per model.

\subsection{What never lifts}

A theorem that says the panel fits every box is one I don't trust until I've watched it fail to fit
something. So I went looking for boxes it won't turn into a Thiele machine, and the first one I tried
was the one I was surest would work.

A Turing machine, with one fixed table. Each lever does one row of the table. That looked like the
obvious base to me, and it isn't one at all. Clause (a) asks for a lever for every two-counter
instruction, and there are infinitely many two-counter instructions, since a jump can go to any line.
A fixed table has finitely many rows, so it has finitely many levers, and it runs out of levers long
before it runs out of instructions. The first two items below are that failure in two forms, and
the others fail for other reasons. Each is proved.

\begin{theorem}[What doesn't lift]\label{thm:lift-fails}
(1) A box with only finitely many levers has no universal base, and no box with a universal base is
finitely branching, meaning that from every state all its levers together lead to only finitely many
different states. (2) The lift of a finitely branching box is never Thiele-complete, whatever claims
and fact table it gets. (3) Neither is the lift of a box whose step ignores the state it's in, where
each lever sends every state to the same place. (4) On a record axis where every place is at or below
every other, there is no Thiele-complete machine at all. (5) The lift's own non-vacuity clause holds
exactly when the fact table has room and some claim is true at one loaded state and false at another.
\end{theorem}

Checked as \code{lift\_finite\_moves\_not\_a\_base}, \code{lift\_ub\_not\_finitely\_branching},
\code{lift\_finite\_branching\_not\_complete}, \code{lift\_stateless\_not\_complete},
\code{lift\_ax\_indiscrete\_no\_machine} and \code{lift\_canonical\_nonvac\_iff} (LiftConverse.v,
LiftAxis.v), all closed.

So my first test case failed, and at first I read item (1) as saying a Turing machine can't be a
base at all. It says something narrower. A Turing machine \emph{with one fixed table} can't be one. A classic model comes in the other way round, with one lever for each whole program,
run to the end. Pull it and the box runs that program from start to stop in a single move. That's how
the register machine below comes in, and it's the honest reading of ``a Turing machine is a base'' too.
The levers are the programs. They aren't the rows.

Item (3) is a box with no memory. Pull a lever and it lands wherever that lever always lands,
whatever happened before. So a window on it can't tell INC $A$ followed by INC $A$ from INC $B$
followed by INC $A$, and a box that can't tell those apart can't keep two counters in its window.

Item (4) is the trouble with bare preorders from Section~\ref{sec:direction}, where the cups stopped telling you the place, showing up one level higher. If
every place on the axis is at or below every other, the flag has no up to go to. No step ever turns a cup over, nothing ever has to pay, and the earned chain has nothing to earn.

\subsection{The same thing, in seven models}

Now the other direction, the one the worry was really about. Put boxes with different insides in a
row: one with a tape, one rewriting lambda terms, one with bins. Is a panel riding on one of them the
same as a panel riding on another? The honest way to ask is whether the boxes agree on what they
compute.

My first idea was to wire the boxes to each other myself, two at a time, with a relation that says
one box's run keeps pace with another's. I even have such a relation. Section~\ref{sec:latch} defines
weak base equivalence, and then has to admit that it never connects any two of the bases it was built
for. Doing that box by box would be years of work, and somebody has already done the hard part, in a
form that doesn't need my relation at all. The Coq Library of Undecidability Proofs, built over
several years by Yannick Forster, Dominique Larchey-Wendling, Gert Smolka and many others, proves in
Coq that seven models of computation compute the same relations on numbers: the weak call-by-value
lambda calculus L, Turing machines, two kinds of Minsky machine, binary stack machines, John Conway's
FRACTRAN, and the
$\mu$-recursive functions. Conway's model I know only as a step on the library's road to two counters
(Section~\ref{sec:smallest}) and by its place on that
list, so I'll say nothing about it beyond that. I didn't re-prove the agreement. I lean
on their proof. Their proof is checked by the same proof assistant as mine, so leaning
on it costs me nothing in certainty. What I proved is the joint where my boxes meet theirs.

\begin{theorem}[The base doesn't matter]\label{thm:lift-models}
(1) A relation on numbers that's computable in any one of those seven models is computable in all
seven. (2) The box that keeps a whole two-counter configuration in one number, with one lever for
each instruction, has a universal base, its step is computable in all seven models, and its lift,
with a table of sixteen facts, is Thiele-complete. (3) A register machine of the kind Cook and
Reckhow described, where each two-counter instruction compiles to at most six of its own
instructions, has a universal base too, and its lift is Thiele-complete. (4) Any box on numbers
with a universal base lifts to a Thiele-complete machine, and its step, computable in one model, is
computable in all seven.
\end{theorem}

Checked as \code{lift\_num\_models\_agree}, \code{lift\_ex\_in\_all\_models},
\code{lift\_ex\_thiele\_complete}, \code{lift\_ram\_thiele\_complete}, \code{lift\_numeric\_base} and
\code{lift\_classic\_bases} (LiftModelsAll.v, LiftModels.v), all closed, with the library's own
equivalences carrying the part about seven models.

So the answer to the worry is that the record doesn't care. A box with a universal base, described in any of the models people have
used to say what computing is, takes the same panel, becomes the same
kind of machine, and pays the same three marks for the same three acts.

And the trip goes back down. So far the panel went
onto other boxes. Now put another box, panel
and all, inside mine. Section~\ref{sec:smallest} proved that the fixed program $U_P$ on the small
machine's host runs every computably presented Thiele machine. In terms of the seven models, that
reads: if the four relations that describe a machine (its driver, which picks the next move or says
stop, its step, its cost and its reading, on codes) are computable in any one of the seven, then the machine is computably presented,
and $U_P$ runs it, halting when it halts, with its flag, and with a surcharge of at most two when its reading starts at no.

Checked as \code{lift\_computable\_runs\_on\_U} (LiftHeadline.v).

So a Thiele machine described in lambda calculus runs, under one fixed program, on the small
machine's host. That's model independence in both directions: up, by lifting any universal base, and
down, by running anything presentable on one fixed program. When I saw both arrows close I stopped
worrying that I'd built a trick for one toy. A trick for one toy wouldn't survive being carried both
ways.

\subsection{Why two counters}

If the box doesn't matter, why did I build on two bins? Because I wanted the smallest box that holds
up, and the obvious smaller one has a single bin. Nothing earlier in this book says one bin is too
few. So before I'd let myself say two is the fewest, I tried one.

Watch what a program on one bin can see. While the bin isn't empty, it can't tell how full it is: a
stretch of lines that never finds the bin empty does exactly the same thing from a fuller bin, with
the extra pebbles riding along. So the only news a one-bin program ever gets is the bin running dry.
Between two of those moments it's just walking its own lines, and among more moments than there are
lines, two are on the same line, which is the pigeonhole again. Put those together and a one-bin
program either stops within a count you can write down in advance, or never stops at all.

\begin{theorem}[One counter is too few]\label{thm:one-counter}
(1) A program $P$ on one bin, started with $n$ pebbles in it, halts exactly when it has stopped
within $k(n + k + 1)$ steps, where $k$ is the number of lines in $P$. So whether it halts is
decidable. (2) Halting for the book's two-counter machine is undecidable. (3) So no translation
from two-counter programs to one-counter programs keeps halting, unless the complement of
Turing-machine halting could be listed by a program.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Two facts and a count. The two facts are the walk above: the extra pebbles ride along, and
among more moments than there are lines, two are at the same line. Counting with those two facts
gives the bound. (2) The library's undecidability of
Minsky-machine halting, carried over to the book's instruction set line by line. (3) A translation
that kept halting would make two-counter halting decidable by (1).
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{lift\_oc\_halts\_bound}, \code{lift\_oc\_halts\_dec}, \code{lift\_cm\_halting\_undecidable},
\code{lift\_no\_oc\_translation} and \code{lift\_no\_oc\_translation\_undecidability}
(LiftOneCounter.v, LiftModels.v), all closed.

So two counters are the fewest in exactly this sense: one counter can't compute everything, because
its halting can be decided, and two can. I like where the answer came from. The pigeonhole that left
no spare chair in the closed room is the same one that says why the box has two bins.

\subsection{What this chapter doesn't say}

A panel that bolts onto anything is an easy picture to hear too much in, so here are four things the
chapter might be heard to say, and doesn't. First, it doesn't prove ``a lift is Thiele-complete
exactly when its base is universal'' as one equivalence. It proves the upward direction, the converse
for every Thiele-complete machine's own base moves, and the two kinds of base that never lift.
Second, it doesn't contain a Turing machine's rule table running a tape. The Turing machines here are
the library's, and they enter through what they compute. Third, the lift's tally is one version
number for the whole machine. It doesn't keep one per register, the way the small machine keeps one
per counter. That's coarser, and it's enough for every theorem above. Fourth, it doesn't show that a
lifted machine is computably presented in general. The trip down needs the four relations, and for a
particular machine somebody has to supply them.

All of it is one closed statement too, if you want the whole chapter in one place. Checked as
\code{lift\_model\_independence} (LiftHeadline.v).

I went into this chapter looking for the place where the bins were doing secret work for the panel.
I didn't find one. Either there isn't one, or I didn't look hard enough, and the four items above are
where I'd send anybody who wants to look harder.

%===========================================================================
\section{Built from parts}
\label{sec:parts}
%===========================================================================

Back in Section~\ref{sec:toll} I asked a question and only got halfway: bolt two certification
systems together, and do you get one? Everything real is built out of parts. A computer is a
processor and memory and a disk, a bank is branches, a proof is lemmas. If the record and its toll
only held for one machine at a time and fell apart the moment you put two together, they'd be a
property of toys.

So put two Thiele machines on a bench, each box with its own panel, and wire them up the three ways
anybody wires machines. Side by side, with no wire between them at all, so that every move is a lever
pulled on one box or the other. End to end, with the first box's bins tipped into the second's when
the first is done. And one inside the other, with the inner box running as a guest on the outer one.
Some of it holds. Some of it provably doesn't, and the places where it doesn't were where I learned
the most.

\subsection{Side by side}

Two boxes on the bench, no wire between them. A move of the pair is a lever pulled on one box or the
other. The question is what the pair's record should be, and my first answer was the wrong one: a
single count of how many certifications the bench has made. One number, easy to read. I'll come back
to why it fails, because it's in the list of things that break. What works is to keep both panels
showing. The pair's record is the pair of records, a place for the left machine and a place for the
right one, compared one side at a time.

Since that record has more than two places, ``Thiele-complete'' in this chapter means the definition
of Section~\ref{sec:smallest} with the record allowed to be a place along a direction, the way
Section~\ref{sec:direction} set it up. The old definition had a single bit there, and at two places
this one is exactly the old one. Checked as \code{ax\_tc\_two\_point\_iff} (AxTwoPoint.v).

\begin{theorem}[Side by side]\label{thm:parts-product}
(1) The cost of any run of the pair is the left machine's cost of its moves plus the right
machine's cost of its moves, and the order in which levers on the two boxes were interleaved doesn't
change where the pair ends up or what it paid. (2) The pair pays the toll exactly when both machines
do. (3) Read through ``either flag is up,'' two certification systems side by side are a
certification system with floor one; read through ``both flags are up,'' a run that starts with both
flags down and ends with both up costs at least two, and two is reached when each part can certify
for one. (4) Two Thiele-complete machines side by side
are a Thiele-complete machine. (5) In that pair, call a side's \emph{floor} the place on its record axis where its clean states sit. A run from
a clean start that ends with each side at or above a point that isn't
at or below that side's floor makes at least six record moves and raises the ledger by at least
six, and six is reached. (6) The pair of records is the product in the precise sense: for any machine
mapping into both, preserving records, there's exactly one map into the pair that does both jobs.
\end{theorem}

Most of that is what you'd guess from the bench. Each box keeps its own ledger and nobody else pulls
its levers, so the bills add, and it can't matter which box you happened to work on first. The six in
(5) is two certifications of three marks each, one per box, with no discount for doing them on the
same bench.

Checked as \code{cmpz\_cost\_prod}, \code{cmpz\_interleaving\_invariant}, \code{cmpz\_prod\_a2\_iff},
\code{cmpz\_cs\_or\_floor}, \code{cmpz\_cs\_and\_floor}, \code{cmpz\_cs\_and\_tight}, \code{cmpz\_prod\_tc},
\code{cmpz\_prod\_joint\_certificate}, \code{cmpz\_prod\_joint\_certificate\_tight} and
\code{cmpz\_prod\_universal} (CzProd.v, CzCounter.v, CzCS.v, CzProdTC.v, CzCat.v), all closed. The machines that
preserve cost and record form a category with these pairs as products, and the pairing is a
symmetric monoidal structure, with the pentagon, triangle and hexagon laws checked (CzCat.v).

That last sentence is the most formal way I know of saying ``side by side composes, and nothing about
the order of the parts matters.'' It's a lot of category theory to confirm what the bench told me in
a glance, and I'm glad to have it anyway. A glance is where I'd have missed something.

\subsection{One after the other}

Now wire them end to end. Run the first box, and when it's done, tip its two bins into the second
box's start, for free, and run the second. That's how programs get chained everywhere, and my first
thought was that the tipping couldn't matter. It's plumbing. Pebbles go from one bin into another,
nobody checks anything, and plumbing has no business on a record. That turned out to be half right,
and the wrong half is item (4).

\begin{theorem}[One after the other]\label{thm:parts-seq}
(1) Running one Thiele-complete machine and then handing its two counters to another through free
loads gives a Thiele-complete machine. (2) For any two programs of the two-counter machine, it computes the composite:
some schedule leaves the first machine's window where the first program takes the input, and the
second's where the second program takes that result. (3) The hand-off keeps the toll when every
state it can load into sits at one level of the second machine's record. (4) If some load lands
the second machine at a record that isn't at or below another load's, the hand-off loses the toll:
it's a certification nobody paid for.
\end{theorem}

Checked as \code{cmpz\_seq\_tc}, \code{cmpz\_seq\_composes}, \code{cmpz\_ld\_a2\_if} and
\code{cmpz\_ld\_unclean} (CzSeq.v, CzLoad.v), all closed.

Item (4) is the one to remember. The tipping is free, so it had better not tip in anything that counts
as established. If pouring pebbles into the second box can land its panel somewhere that isn't at
or below where some other pouring would land it, the second machine gets a raised record without ever having checked anything. That's
a forged certificate wearing the costume of plumbing. My first thought was right about the pebbles.
It was wrong about where they land.

\subsection{What doesn't compose}

Here's the list of things I tried to build on the bench that fell apart, each with a proof that it
does. Every one of them started as a reasonable-looking wiring job.

\begin{theorem}[What breaks]\label{thm:parts-breaks}
(1) Read the pair through ``both flags are up'' as a single flag, and any run that raises it from
a clean start makes at least six record moves; the definition of Thiele-complete asks for a claim
that three moves can certify, so through the pair's own interface that reading fails the non-vacuity clause. (2) Two clocks side by side
are weakly Thiele-complete. They aren't Thiele-complete, so composing the easy notion composes
nothing.
(3) Give the small machine a second writer that changes counter A without raising its version, and
the run ``check that A is 0, let the other writer change A, commit, certify'' raises the flag, so
the earned-record
clause fails when the machine is read the small machine's way, with the second writer as a base move. (4) Two windows that each price their own machine exactly can
collide as a pair, so exact pricing isn't preserved by putting machines together. (5) Count the
pair's certifications with one number, and the count can't tell which side certified. The pair of
records can.
\end{theorem}

Checked as \code{cmpz\_and\_costs\_six}, \code{cmpz\_and\_not\_complete},
\code{cmpz\_or\_clocks\_not\_complete}, \code{cmpz\_shared\_raises}, \code{cmpz\_shared\_not\_earned},
\code{cmpz\_exactness\_not\_preserved} and \code{cmpz\_sum\_record\_loses} (CzProdTC.v, CzShared.v,
CzWin.v, CzCounter.v), all closed.

Item (1) is one flag for two boxes. It costs what two certifications cost, six record moves, and the
definition wants a claim that three can settle, so a single flag over both panels, read through
the pair's interface, is too expensive
to meet the definition.

Item (3) is the one with the most teeth, because it's the opening chapter's bug, the file checked and then swapped. On the
bench it's a second hand reaching into a bin while the box isn't looking. Two writers, one value, and
a check that's out of date by the time anybody leans on it. The small machine's version rule is
exactly the fix, and this is what happens without it: the commitment goes through on a claim about a
thing that changed underneath it. Database people and the people who build processors have been
fighting this one since at least Kung and Robinson's paper of 1981 and the Livermore report of 1987, and the opening chapter called it time of check to time of use.
Here it's a theorem about the record, and the version number is what makes it go away. The second
hand can still reach in. With the version, its reach shows on the tally, and the COMMIT traps.

Item (5) is my first guess from the side-by-side wiring, coming back to fail on schedule. It's why the
pair's record compares one side at a time. Squash the two records into one number and the record
forgets who did the work, and a record that forgets who did the work isn't one anybody can lean on.

\subsection{One inside another}

The last way to wire the bench: put one box \emph{inside} the other, as a guest on a host. Part of
this the book already has. Section~\ref{sec:smallest} showed the fixed program $U_P$ runs any
computably presented Thiele machine, and the small machine's own programs, with the record earned
again by the host. What's new is putting those links in a row, a box in a box in a box, and asking
what the outermost one pays.

My first guess was that it could pay less. A host that's clever about how it runs the guest might
skip some of the guest's bills. That would have been bad news for every toll in this book, and the
first item below says it can't happen.

\begin{theorem}[Nesting]\label{thm:parts-nesting}
(1) If a host that pays the toll simulates a guest faithfully, with a record map that reflects the
order, then every run of the guest is matched by a run of the host that costs at least the number
of the guest's steps that turned a cup over. (2) A small-machine guest on $U_P$ is carried with
surcharge exactly 0. A computably presented machine whose reading starts at no is carried, through
its compiled guest, with surcharge at most 2, and exactly 2 when moreover every move costs at most
one. One whose reading starts at yes is carried with surcharge exactly 3. (3) Links compose, and their surcharges add: a tower of
$k$ links has surcharge between the sums of their lower and upper bounds.
(4) A tower of presented machines, each level running the next on $U_P$, adds exactly 2 for every level above the first, on top of the first level's own surcharge,
provided every level's host run is itself presented by the next.
\end{theorem}

Checked as \code{cmpz\_sim\_cost\_ge\_exits}, \code{cmpz\_priced\_link}, \code{cmpz\_host\_link},
\code{cmpz\_host\_link\_le\_two}, \code{cmpz\_host\_link\_exact}, \code{cmpz\_host\_link\_start\_up},
\code{cmpz\_link\_compose}, \code{cmpz\_tower} and \code{cmpz\_tower\_presented\_exact} (CzCat.v, CzLink.v, CzTower.v,
CzSelf.v), all closed.

Item (1) is the cleanest sentence in the chapter. However you build the outer box, as long as it pays
its own toll and doesn't lie about the inner box's record, it pays at least what the inner record
climbed. Nesting can add cost. It can't take any away.

The premise in (4) is a real limit, and I want to say exactly what it is. Two links are
unconditional: from a presented machine to its compiled guest, and from that guest to $U_P$ running it. Going deeper needs the
host's own run, at each level, to be presented as a machine the next level up can run, and the
host keeps a register for every whole number, which doesn't have a one-to-one code in a single
number the way a presented machine needs. So the box that has to fit inside the next one has more
states than there are numbers to name them. For three levels and more, the theorem says what happens
\emph{if} each level is presented. It doesn't claim that it always is.

\subsection{What this adds up to}

Wired side by side, end to end, or one inside the other, a Thiele machine on the bench stays a Thiele
machine, and the tolls add the way money adds. What breaks, breaks for reasons you could name before
you saw the proof: a single flag for two claims costs two claims' worth, a clock is still a clock, a
shared value without a version can't be trusted, and a free hand-off can't be allowed to carry a
certificate. None of those is a surprise in hindsight. All of them are now theorems, and the
composition question from Section~\ref{sec:toll} has an answer. Two certification systems side by
side are one under both readings I checked, ``either flag'' and ``both flags.'' The ``both flags''
reading still fails the definition through the pair's interface, the second writer breaks the earned-record clause through the small machine's own reading, the clocks and the two counterexamples fail outright, and simulation in
general has a proved floor.

Three of my first guesses on this bench were wrong: the single count, the harmless tipping, and the
clever host that pays less. The last two leaned toward a record that says more than anybody paid for,
and the first toward one that says less than it should. I didn't see any of the three coming. The
proofs did.

%===========================================================================
\section{Running it}
\label{sec:running}
%===========================================================================

Everything so far is theorems. A fair reader is entitled to ask the rude question: does any of it
run? The Coq definitions are drawings, exact to the last part, and every theorem in this book is
about the drawings. A proof that the drawn machine does something isn't a machine doing it, and I'd be
suspicious of a book about a machine that never once got built and switched on.

So this chapter builds it twice from the same drawings, once by Coq's own machinery and once by hand,
switches both on, and compares them step by step. It says exactly what ran, exactly what didn't, and what you'd
have to trust to believe the parts that did.

\subsection{Taking the coat off}

The first build is made by Coq itself. Coq can turn a definition into a program in an ordinary
programming language. It calls that \emph{extraction}. In the drawings every part comes wearing a
coat of proof, and extraction takes the coat off: the proof parts are thrown away and what's left is
code that computes the same function. I extract to OCaml, an ordinary
programming language that Coq's extraction supports directly. Two files do it. One extracts the small machine, the host
machine with a register for every whole number, the host with PAY, both universal programs $U$ and
$U_P$ written out instruction by instruction, and the loaders. The other extracts the compiler below
and its runner.

Two things about that build are worth knowing before you believe a word of the rest. First, the code
that runs is the code the theorems are about. Coq won't extract some of the files directly (a
technical limit on files that rename modules), so the extracted functions are copies with plain
names, and each copy is proved equal to the original, by computation or by a short proof, inside Coq.
The two universal programs are printed by Coq as literal lists and proved equal to the programs in
the theorems. Checked as \code{rlz\_host\_program\_is}, \code{rlz\_phost\_program\_is} and
\code{rlz\_host\_run\_prog\_is} (Realize.v and RealizePriced.v).

Second, whole numbers, and here my first instinct was the wrong one. The quick way to build is to map
Coq's whole numbers onto the computer's own machine integers, which are fast. They're 63 bits wide
here, and the guest codes $U$ reads go up near $2^{100}$, so they'd wrap around without a
word of warning. Coq's whole numbers never overflow. A machine word does, and the book already told
you what that cost Ariane 5 (Section~\ref{sec:straight}). So the extraction maps Coq's whole numbers
to an OCaml library of unbounded integers, and each arithmetic operation is mapped by hand to that
library's version of it. Those are the hand-written substitutions in the trusted path: one line
that maps Coq's whole numbers onto the library's integers, a few that map Coq's Booleans,
decisions, lists, pairs, options and its one-value type onto OCaml's own, two that map Coq's
``and'' and ``or'' onto OCaml's, two in one file that map the hosts' one-value property types onto
OCaml's unit, and the arithmetic operations, seventeen in one file and
thirteen in the other. Each arithmetic line carries a one-line justification next to it: addition is addition, subtraction stops at zero the way Coq's does, division by zero gives
zero the way Coq's does. The rest is Coq's own definitions. The hand-written code outside that is two
drivers, which read input, print output, and count steps while they call the extracted step function
in a loop.

What you're trusting, if you trust a run: Coq's extraction, the OCaml compiler and the C tools
under it, the integer library, those mapping lines, the two drivers, and the Python code that
does the comparing. None of that is proved. Coq's extraction, the OCaml compiler, the C tools and the integer library are old and used by a lot of people. The mapping
lines, the drivers and the comparing code are mine, and they're small enough to read in one sitting. That's a reason to trust it. It isn't a proof.

\subsection{A second machine, written by hand, to check the first}

Switch the first build on and let it run, and what have you learned? Less than I first thought. A run
of extracted code only tells you the extracted code agrees with itself. If the extraction, or one of
the integer mappings, or a driver had slipped somewhere, a run on its own would never show it. So there's a second build, made by hand:
an implementation of the small machine and both hosts written separately in Python straight from the
Coq definitions, with every function naming the definition it copies. Then the two builds are made to
argue.

They're compared on the \emph{whole} state after \emph{every} step: the program line, every counter
and register and its version, the fact table in order, the channel, the trap latch, the ledger and
the flag. Against Coq itself, computing the same steps inside the proof assistant, the Python machine
is run on every small-machine program of one or two instructions over a 26-instruction alphabet and
every program of three over a 9-instruction one, 1,431 programs, each run from several starts (4,266 runs in all), 300 random ones, and a few thousand
more on each host. Against the extracted OCaml, the same exhaustive and random small-machine sets
again, $U$ and $U_P$ on tiny guests, and the runs below. They agree on every step of every
one. I also broke the machine on purpose, giving it a fact table one too small, a free
CHECK, a commitment that ignores versions, and a write that doesn't bump the version, and each break
gets caught.

That's evidence. It isn't proof, and Section~\ref{sec:coq} says why Dijkstra would want me to say so.
What it is, is three routes to the same numbers: Coq computing inside itself, the code Coq extracted,
and a machine written by hand from scratch. When they agree on every step of thousands of programs, a
slip in the extraction, the integer mappings or the drivers would have to be matched by the same
slip in a machine written separately by hand to hide. I can imagine that happening. I can't imagine
it happening often. The comparison doesn't test whether the definitions say the right thing, since
the hand-written machine copies them. That's what having them on the page is for.

\subsection{$U$ on a real guest}

Now the universal program, which is where I expected trouble. The guest I wanted to run first was
the obvious one, a guest that goes the whole way: CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY, flag up, run inside $U$ on
the built machine. Here's why that's not what ran. $U$ keeps the whole guest program as one number,
a number that grows like two raised to the sum of the codes for the guest's instructions (for a
guest of one instruction it's exactly a power of two), and it reads that number
the only way a counter can, one unit at a time. So its speed depends on the code, and the code grows
fast: a guest with one CHECK in it has code $2^{24}$, and a guest with the whole chain has a code near
$2^{100}$.

So I came down to what could finish. Here's what ran, on the extracted program, compared against the
Python guest at the end: the host stopped exactly when the guest did, and showed the guest's
counters, latch, ledger and flag.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrr@{}}
guest & host & host steps & time \\ \hline
count A down from 2 & $U$ & 25,953,317 & \\
one passing CHECK & $U$ & 402,654,059 & 618 s \\
one failing CHECK & $U$ & 201,327,155 & 305 s \\
one passing CHECK & $U_P$ & 402,654,059 & 617 s \\
one failing CHECK & $U_P$ & 201,327,155 & 313 s \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The first row's count is pinned exactly: if the build changed so that it moved by one step, the
comparison would fail. The times are from one ordinary computer and are only there to give you the
scale. That's about twelve host steps for every unit of the guest's code, for every guest step, which
is exponential in the size of the guest. A guest with one CERTIFY in it would have code $2^{32}$, about
fifty billion host steps, and at the measured rate of about 650,000 steps a second it would take
something like twenty-two hours, nearly a day. The guest I wanted, with the whole
chain, has a code near $2^{100}$, and no computer will ever finish it. So $U$ on a guest that
certifies is proved. It isn't run. I'm not going to dress that up. Runs this long only fit in memory
at all because the host's register store can be squeezed during the run without changing any state,
which is a theorem too. Checked as \code{rlz\_sched\_sound} (RealizeCompact.v).

Why so slow? Because a fixed program on a machine of counters has to keep the guest packed into
numbers, and counters only count. Whether every universal program on counters has to pay this much
is a real question, and this book doesn't answer it. What it claims is exactly what the table shows.
I'll admit the table stung a little. About ten minutes to watch one CHECK pass is a long time to stare at a
machine you built to be small.

\subsection{A compiler, all in Coq}

Running guests one CHECK at a time doesn't tell you whether the built machine can do anything you'd
recognise as a program. You'd want to hand it gcd, or a sort, written the way people write them, and
get the answer out, and writing gcd by hand in INC and DEC is no way to find out. So the last piece
in the drawings is a compiler. The source is a small language you could write by hand: whole-number
variables, addition, subtraction that stops at zero, comparisons, \emph{if}, \emph{while}, and
procedures that return several results, with the rule that a procedure can only call ones defined
before it, so there's no recursion. Every stage is a Coq function with a Coq proof: the procedures are
inlined, the result is flattened to assignments and jumps, that is compiled to Minsky's counter
machine through the library's own compiler, that to a program for the host machine, that to a
two-counter guest, and the guest to a run of $U_P$.

\begin{theorem}[The compiler is correct]\label{thm:running-compiler}
For every source program with no recursion, and every input: the program computes $y$ exactly when
the runner (the Coq function that gets extracted) halts with $y$ for some amount of fuel; exactly when the compiled host program
halts with $y$; exactly when the two-counter guest halts with $y$; and exactly when $U_P$ running that
guest halts with $y$, with its first counter at 0, its ledger at 0 and its flag down. The runner also
takes exactly as many steps as the host program does, with the rest of its fuel left over, and a run
that doesn't halt has used all its fuel.
\end{theorem}

Checked as \code{cmp\_final} (CmpFinal.v), with the runner as \code{cmp\_exec\_machine}, \code{cmp\_exec\_sound},
\code{cmp\_exec\_complete} and \code{cmp\_exec\_unhalted} (CmpRun.v) and the source language's own
interpreter as \code{cmp\_interp\_sound} and \code{cmp\_interp\_complete} (CmpLang.v), all closed. The
statement says nothing about how many steps the compiled program takes. It's about answers.

The runner and the compiler are extracted, and the build has been run on a set of programs I picked
to be annoying: gcd, factorial, a primality program written with procedures, an Ackermann tower, a sorting
network on a list packed into one number, and a tiny interpreter for another machine written in the
source language. Then 220 random programs that halt, 160 random programs with loops that might not,
programs that never halt run for a fixed budget, and programs mutated on purpose to make sure the
comparison notices. Each answer is compared with plain Python arithmetic, an independent Python
interpreter of the source language, Python machines running the compiled programs step for step, and,
for sixteen of them, Coq computing the same thing itself. Ackermann's function at $(3, 5)$ is 253; the
source program takes 64,768 operations to get there, and the compiled host program takes about 119
million steps. The extracted runner does a few million host steps a second, so that's well under a
minute.

That's about 1,800 host steps per source operation for Ackermann, and up to about a hundred thousand
for multiplication by repeated addition, because every addition copies a running total one unit at a
time. Counters are unary, and unary is slow, and the slowdown grows with the values. How it grows
with the size of the program I haven't measured. The last two stages, the two-counter guest and $U_P$ running it, are proved. They aren't
run, for
two reasons: the files that build the guest aren't extracted, and even if they were, $U_P$ on a
compiled guest would be slow for the same reason $U$ on a certifying guest is. Still, I like that 253. It came out of nothing but INC and DEC, and a proof
that they mean what the source meant.

\subsection{What wasn't built}

No chip. The drawings were never cut into metal. Earlier work on this project went into hardware, a
chip design for a much bigger machine, and none of it was carried over: there's no circuit for the small machine, no
simulation of one at the level of gates, and no board ever ran any of this. The small machine exists
as Coq definitions, as extracted OCaml, and as a Python program written by hand, and those three
agree on every step anybody has checked. That's the whole of what ``it runs'' means in this book.

I'd love to see it in metal some day. But builds that can be held against each other on every step are worth a lot to
me.
A board with nothing to hold it up against isn't, and that's the trade this edition made.

%===========================================================================
\section{The CHSH check}
\label{sec:chsh}
%===========================================================================

The small machine checks whether a number is zero, even, or at least something. That's a
fine way to show the chain, and a dull thing to certify. Here's a check worth earning, built
from zero, and then the one thing the small machine's host does with it, which is smaller and more
exact than ``it checks for quantum behaviour,'' a sentence that's tempting and wrong.
The short version, so you know where this is going: the check never computes the famous
number and never writes down the famous bound. It tests seven facts about integers in eight
counts. If they pass, a certain five-by-five table has a property called positive
semidefinite, and that property forces the famous number under the famous bound. The wall
is a consequence of the check. It never goes into it. Everything else is explaining those sentences.

But first, why is a quantum game in a book about records at all? Not for the physics. Nothing in
this section tests nature, and the check can't tell honest play from a made-up tally (the
guarantee paragraph below says exactly how). It's here for three reasons, all about the record.
It's a check whose content is striking enough to tempt anyone into thinking that certifying it
should cost more than certifying something dull, and on the small machine it doesn't: a flag raised
from a clean start costs at least three, and
exactly three at the cheapest, whatever the claim (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). It sets free observation
against a priced check: a round of the game is written down for nothing, and judging the pile is
one of the three paid acts. And it's an integer test small enough to be a property in the small
machine's sense, a checker that's a little program and a meaning that's a statement, with a
proof that the two agree, which is exactly what Section~\ref{sec:smallest}'s generic machine asks
of any property before it lets a flag stand on it.

\subsection{The game}

Two players, Alice and Bob, in separate rooms. A referee flips two coins and hands Alice a
question x, zero or one, and Bob a question y, zero or one. Alice answers a, zero or one;
Bob answers b. No talking during the game. They may agree on a plan beforehand, as detailed
as they like. They win a round when their answers
\emph{differ exactly when both questions were one}. In words: if either question is zero, match; if both are one, differ.

Try to win every time. A plan is a list: what Alice says to x equals zero, what she says to
x equals one, and the same two for Bob. Four bits. Now write the four requirements the
rounds impose: a0 equals b0 (both asked zero); a0 equals b1; a1 equals b0; a1 differs from
b1. Chain the first three: a0 equals b0 equals a1, and a0 equals b1, so b0 equals b1. But
the fourth says a1 differs from b1, and a1 equals b0 equals b1. Contradiction. One of the
four must break. So any plan loses at least one of the four question pairs, and if the
referee asks all four equally often, the best a plan can do is three out of four. Seventy-five percent. Do it the long way too: there are sixteen plans (four bits), and if you write
them all out and count wins you'll find eight win three rounds and eight win one, and none
wins four (the broken requirements always come in odd numbers, which you can see by adding
up the four equations and keeping only whether the totals come out even or odd, with ``equal'' as 0
and ``differ'' as 1: each of the four answers appears twice on the left, so the left sides add to an
even number, and the right sides add to one). Sharing a
coin before the game to pick a plan at random doesn't help; a mixture of numbers no larger
than three-quarters is no larger than three-quarters. Arthur Fine, a philosopher of physics at the
University of Washington, much of whose work is on the physicist Albert Einstein and the quantum theory, proved
in 1982 that the
whole ``pre-agreed answers, no influence between rooms'' story is \emph{exactly} the mixtures of
those sixteen lists, one scoreboard for all four questions at once; the sixteen are the
whole classical story. That one I don't have to take on his word: the form of his theorem that
speaks of the four averages is checked in this book, and the end of this section says how.

The number. Recode answers zero and one as plus one and minus one. For each question pair,
let E be the average, over many rounds, of Alice's answer times Bob's. The CHSH quantity is
S equals E00 plus E01 plus E10 minus E11. For one fixed plan each win adds one to S and each
loss subtracts one, so S is wins minus losses: a three-win plan has S equal to two, a one-win
plan has minus two. With equal question frequencies, the win rate is one half plus S over
eight. So ``seventy-five percent'' and ``S at most two'' are the same fact, and the second is the
one that got the name.

The ceiling is easy to reach and costs nothing to write down. Tally one round per question
pair with both players answering zero every time: after the recoding every answer is plus one,
so all four correlators are one. That's the plan that answers zero to everything,
which matches on every pair and so wins the
three pairs that ask for a match, $S = 1 + 1 + 1 - 1 = 2$. On the small machine's host a tally like
that is a few INCs on counters, and INC is free. Nothing in it says the rounds were played; anybody can
tally anything for nothing. The other side, that no finite mixture of plans beats two, is
Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-fine} in Appendix~\ref{sec:chsh-derivation}, one direction of Fine's result. The
full equivalence, in the form that speaks of the four averages, is checked too, as
\code{nec\_e\_fine\_iff}; the last part of this section states it.

\subsection{Where it came from, and why anyone cared}

So who started this, and why would anybody care whether two rooms can win a coin game? The names
come in a line, and the line didn't mean much to me until I saw that each of them moved the same
thing a notch: from an argument about what's real, which you can only agree with or not, toward a
pile of counts a referee can judge. Each one rests on a different piece of the game above.

The trail starts in 1935, with Einstein, by then at the Institute for
Advanced
Study in Princeton, and two younger colleagues there, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen, asking whether quantum mechanics describes
everything that's real about a pair of particles. Their argument: if measuring one particle lets you
predict the other's result with certainty, the result must already have been fixed, and the theory
leaves that out. What they rest on is the plan in each player's pocket, a pre-agreed list of
answers, the plan above. And the first thing worth checking is whether the paper even says what
Einstein meant. By his own account, not quite. Podolsky did the writing, and that June Einstein
wrote to Erwin Schrödinger, the Austrian physicist whose 1926 wave equation is at the heart of quantum mechanics, that the essential thing had been ``smothered by formalism.'' The person who
lays that letter out is Arthur Fine, the same Fine whose theorem closed the sixteen plans above, in
his encyclopedia entry on the argument. So Fine stands at both ends of the line: he checked the
founding paper against what its author meant, and he proved exactly what the plans can do. Even the
founding paper is a lead to check. It isn't a verdict.

For thirty years that was philosophy. In 1964 John Bell turned it into arithmetic: if each particle
carries pre-agreed answers and nothing travels between the rooms, certain averages can't exceed a
fixed number, and quantum theory predicts they do. What that rests on took me a few reads. His
inequality rules out the \emph{pair} of assumptions together, called local realism (answers exist
before you ask, and no influence across the gap). Either one alone survives it. And where does a
paper like that get published? In a brand-new journal called \emph{Physics Physique Fizika}, which
charged authors no page fees and in fact paid them by the word, ten cents a word, and which folded in
1968 after four volumes, or
three. I went looking for that count, and the sources don't agree on it: four is the
number the American Physical Society's archive of the journal gives, and Iulia Georgescu, writing
about the journal in \emph{Physics World} in 2026, says three. She's also where the ten cents comes
from. As Andrew Whitaker tells it in his biography of Bell, the journal gave out no free copies,
so Bell spent his payment buying copies of his own paper to mail to other physicists. A result
nobody else holds a copy of hasn't left the room yet, and Bell paid to send his across. In 1969 four
physicists, John Clauser, then a graduate student at Columbia, Michael Horne and Abner Shimony at
Boston University, and Richard Holt at Harvard, rewrote it as the four-average form above, S
at most two, which could be tried in a lab with imperfect equipment. It's called the CHSH inequality, after their initials. That notch rests on what a real lab can
deliver. Shimony was in philosophy and in physics at Boston University both, which is the whole line
in one man.

Then the obvious next question: did anybody actually try it? Stuart Freedman, a graduate student at
Berkeley, and Clauser, by then a postdoc there too, tried it in 1972. The physicist Alain Aspect's group at the Institut d'Optique in Orsay, with
two
colleagues there, Jean Dalibard and Gérard Roger, did it in 1982 with the measurement settings switched while the
photons were in flight, which in the game's terms, as I read it, is the referee handing out the
questions too late for any note about them to cross between the rooms. Before that, in 1975, Aspect
went to see Bell at CERN to tell him what he planned, and by Aspect's own account Bell heard him out
in silence and then asked, first thing, whether he had a permanent position. Aspect did. Bell's
reason, as Aspect tells it, was that most physicists would take the experiment for a waste of time,
or take him for a crackpot. I read that as the toll in its oldest form: a check that could have come
out the other way costs somebody something to run, and Bell wanted to know who'd pay. And in 2015
three groups of experimental physicists (Bas Hensen's in Delft, with electrons 1.3 kilometres
apart; Marissa Giustina's in Vienna; Lynden Shalm's at NIST, the National Institute of Standards and
Technology, in Boulder) closed the two main escape routes at once. In 2022 Clauser, Aspect and the Austrian
physicist Anton Zeilinger shared the Nobel Prize ``for experiments with entangled photons,
establishing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science.'' The
2015 tests came out of that line of work, and Zeilinger was one of the authors of the Vienna one. So
in under fifty years the subject went from a question you needed a permanent job to risk to a Nobel.
The lab number sits above two. A remaining escape, that the referee's coins were secretly correlated
with the particles, is a philosophical one and I'm not going to pretend it's closed.

Now put this book's check on the same line, because that's where my position gives. It sits past the
far end, at the counts. Those fifty years went into making the counts worth judging, rooms really
apart, questions really late, escape routes really shut, and my check starts after all of it. It's
handed eight counts and can't tell a lab's tally from one somebody wrote down for free. So the check is a referee of counts, and everything that made these
counts worth refereeing happened upstream of it.

What quantum play does: if the players share an entangled pair and choose what to measure
from their question, the best they can do is S equals two times the square root of two,
about 2.83, a win rate of about eighty-five percent. Boris Tsirelson, a Soviet mathematician who later taught at Tel Aviv University, in a 1980 paper called ``Quantum generalizations of Bell's inequality,'' proved that that's
a \emph{ceiling}: quantum correlations violate Bell, but only up to there. I cite that and haven't checked it here; what's checked below is the algebra.

And the wall above that, which is the one I find most instructive. In 1994 the physicists
Sandu Popescu and Daniel Rohrlich asked: what if you only demand that nothing can be \emph{signalled}, that Alice's
answers on their own have the same odds whatever Bob is asked, and the other way round?
Then you can write down a ``box'' (the PR box, after their initials) that wins \emph{every} round (its answers differ exactly when
both questions are one, by fiat, each answer alone a fair coin), S equals four, and nothing
about it lets either room send a message. So relativity alone doesn't explain the quantum
ceiling; the PR box obeys relativity and beats 2.83. The order is: two for plans, 2.83 for
quantum, four for no-signalling.

And the box has the same kind of history as everything else in this book: somebody got there
first. Popescu and Rohrlich's initials stuck, but the big review of the field by Nicolas Brunner
and four coauthors credits boxes like it to Peter Rastall, whose 1985 paper on locality and Bell's theorem appeared in \emph{Foundations of Physics},
and, separately, to Leonid Khalfin, a physicist at the Steklov Institute's Leningrad branch, and Tsirelson himself, both in 1985, nine years before. Then the question that really matters: if
relativity isn't what stops things at 2.83, what is? People have tried candidates. In 2005 the
computer scientist Wim van Dam, who works on the theory of quantum computing, argued, in a paper on
the implausible consequences of such boxes, that with enough PR boxes, Bob could work out any yes-or-no function of both
their inputs after Alice sends him a single bit, which would make the whole question of how much
two parties need to talk collapse, and that's a strong hint the boxes are too good to be real.
In 2009 Marcin Pawłowski, a physicist at the University of Gdańsk, and five coauthors proposed a principle they called information
causality: Bob can't get more information about Alice's data than the bits she actually sends
him. They argue that ordinary and quantum physics both obey it, and that any theory that beats 2.83
breaks it. How much of the rest of the quantum
boundary it
reaches is something I haven't checked. Which principle fixes the
whole quantum boundary, if any one does,
this book won't answer. The
check below is a fence at the middle step.

\subsection{Five sentences that are easy to say by accident}

Here they are, each with what I can stand behind
beside it.

``Faster than light.'' Nothing travels. Each room alone sees fair coins; the correlation shows
up only when you lay the two columns side by side afterward. ``Quantum means random.'' The
average S is fixed by the state; what's random is each single answer; the plans are the less
random side. ``A Bell violation proves nonlocality.'' It rules out local realism, both
assumptions together, and every real test has loopholes with names. ``A tally above two
proves nonlocality.'' No: S is a \emph{population} average, and one finite tally can land above two
by luck. Four rounds, one per question pair, with coin-flip answers, reach S equals four one
time in sixteen. That gap between a population bound and a finite sample is the problem
Yanbao Zhang, Scott Glancy and Emanuel Knill, at NIST in Boulder, work through for real Bell tests (Physical Review A, 2011 and 2013),
and the book doesn't solve it. The way they solve it is worth knowing, because it has the shape
of this book's record. Turn each round into a small bet that no local plan can expect to win,
even a plan that remembers every earlier round, multiply the bets as the rounds come in, and
the French mathematician Jean Ville's inequality, from his 1939 thesis, one of the works that
started the theory of martingales, says the chance the product ever climbs past one over $\delta$
is at most $\delta$. So a flag can go up for good the moment the product crosses, with its error
stated up front. It needs one thing the small machine doesn't have: settings drawn underneath the
program, where the program can't choose them. And how much can one round tell you? Wim van Dam, Richard Gill, a mathematical statistician who later held
the chair in that subject at Leiden, and Peter Gr\"unwald (2005) measured exactly that, in bits of evidence against every local plan. Of the
two-party proofs they compare, CHSH comes out the strongest, ``much stronger'' than the others in
their words, at about 0.046 of a bit per round, a few hundredths, so a convincing record takes
hundreds of rounds. Four won't do. The checked work proves only the narrow thing, that a tally above two is not
explained by \emph{one fixed plan replayed every round}
(\code{chsh\_violation\_rules\_out\_locally\_factorizable\_coupling}), and that narrow thing is what
the sentence has to stay. And ``the PSD test proves the data is
quantum.'' (PSD is short for positive semidefinite, the property of the five-by-five table from
the short version; the next part builds both.) It doesn't, and the direction matters. Passing
implies the five-by-five table, pinned in a way the next part explains, is PSD, and that
implies S squared is at most eight; both are proved. Whether the
correlators of a PSD table like that are the correlators of some quantum strategy is the
cited result of Tsirelson and of Lawrence Landau, whose 1969 Berkeley thesis was on the quantum theory of local observables, and Lluís Masanes, then at the University of Barcelona, who found the exact edge
for this game (next part), and I haven't proved it here. Failing says nothing about whether the play was quantum: the check is complete for
the pinned matrix, the quantum set is wider than that, and quantum behaviour can fail it. Every one
of the sixteen plans fails it (\code{nec\_e\_check\_refuses\_all\_plans}), and I'll show you why. What it guarantees is in one paragraph, once
the check is on the host machine.

\subsection{The five-by-five, and what positive semidefinite means}

Here's the mathematics the check rests on, and it's one idea: a table of numbers
\emph{could be a table of dot products}. Take a two-by-two symmetric table with a and c on the diagonal and b
off it. It's positive semidefinite (PSD) when a and c are at least zero and a times c minus
b squared is at least zero. Check two by hand: ones on the diagonal and one half off, the
determinant is three quarters, passes; ones on the diagonal and 1.2 off, the determinant is
negative, fails. The reading: PSD means the table could be the dot products of some arrows,
and 1.2 is too big a dot product for two arrows of length one. That's the whole idea,
generalised to bigger tables.

Now the table. Rows and columns labelled I, A0, A1, B0, B1 (the identity, Alice's two
questions, Bob's two). Diagonal all ones. The I row and column zero off the diagonal (that's ``zero
marginals'': the table takes each answer alone to average to zero, a fair coin; the counts
record no marginals and the check doesn't test this). A0 with A1 zero, B0 with B1 zero (no round asks
Alice both questions, so no tally holds that average, and the table sets it to zero). Those
zeros are choices. They pin
the table to one slice, and I'll come back to what they cost.
And the four Alice-Bob cells hold the four correlators E. That's a five-by-five with four free
numbers in it. It splits into the one in the corner and a four-by-four block made of an
identity and the two-by-two grid E of correlators, and PSD of that block is the same as
saying \emph{E shrinks every vector} (E is a contraction), which is three inequalities: one minus
E00 squared minus E10 squared at least zero; one minus E01 squared minus E11 squared at least
zero; and their product at least the square of (E00 E01 plus E10 E11).

Run it. All four correlators 0.6 except E11 at minus 0.6, S equals 2.4: the two diagonal
terms are 0.28 and 0.28, the cross term zero, passes; above two, below 2.83. All four at one
over root two (E11 negative): diagonals zero, cross term zero, passes with no slack, S equals
two root two exactly, the 2.83; nudge any entry's size up and a diagonal goes negative. The all-ones plan (one, one,
one, one): first diagonal is one minus one minus one, negative, \emph{fails}, though S equals two
and it's a perfectly legal classical play. The PR box (one, one, one, minus one): fails the
same way. A fence at the middle step, and a fence that keeps out every one of the sixteen
plans: each has all four correlators at plus or minus one, so the first diagonal is always
one minus one minus one. Of the classical plays, only diluted mixtures of plans get through.

That point, one over root two in size in every entry, is four real numbers, and no tally of rounds
ever lands on it. A tally's correlators are ratios of whole numbers, and the point needs each of
them to be one over root two, which would make root two a fraction, and you killed that fraction
with a pencil in Part I. That point and its mirror image, every sign flipped, are the only places
the bound is reached (Remark~\ref{rem:chsh-equality} in the appendix). So a passing tally always has
S squared strictly below eight. It can get as close as you like: the (17, 3) tally in the five
examples below has S squared equal to 7.84, and tallies of the same shape with a fraction nearer one
over root two get nearer still. Two root two is the least bound the check can promise, and no tally
the check accepts ever reaches it. Hold on to that corner; it comes back.

Picture what quantum play can reach as a field, and every test as a fence. In 2007 Miguel Navascués,
Stefano Pironio and Antonio Acín, in a paper called ``Bounding the Set of Quantum Correlations'' (NPA, after their initials),
came at the edge from outside, resting on necessary conditions. In their terms a table like this one
is the first rung of a ladder: bigger tables of expected products, each PSD, each a necessary
condition for quantum behaviour when its entries are left free, each rung tighter, and (their 2008
paper) converging to the quantum set (strictly, the set from commuting operators, which can differ
from the tensor-product set in general scenarios). Each rung is a fence with the whole field inside
it. The check's table is the first rung with the marginals and the two within-party entries pinned
to zero. Pinning is a stronger demand than the rung makes, so passing puts you inside the first
rung, and a quantum point can still fail. My fence cuts across the field. Lawrence Landau in 1988
and Lluís Masanes in 2003 came at the edge itself, for this two-questions-each case only. I'd have
drawn a flat wall at 2.83. The exact boundary they found is a curved surface (the arc-sine form)
touching 2.83 at one point. I cite it and haven't proved it.

So the obvious next question: if every rung is tighter than the last, does some rung finally land
exactly on the quantum set and stop? My first guess was yes, at least here. A 2026 paper by Anubhav
Chaturvedi, a quantum-information theorist at the University of Gdańsk, says no: no \emph{finite}
rung of the ladder captures the whole quantum set even in this simplest case. And for the four correlators alone, a 2008 paper by the same Navascués, Pironio and Acín works out that the first rung already lands on Landau and Masanes's curved edge. That looked like a
contradiction until I saw what each one fences. Landau and Masanes draw the edge for the four
correlators alone. Chaturvedi's is the full behaviours, each room's own odds included. So there's
the corner again from the other side: tallies never reach it, and, if his proof holds, rungs never close on the field. I
wanted that to be one fact. It's two. Mine is root two again, about which points a count can hit.
His is about the fences. His result backs, from
outside, the caution this book keeps about the ladder, that
no finite rung may close on the whole
quantum set. It says
nothing about my own check, though. My check's caution, that a quantum point can fail it, comes from
the pinning, and his paper never pins anything.

\subsection{The check, in integers}

Eight counts: for each of the four question pairs, one counting rounds where the answers
matched and one where they differed. A round is one bump to one count; nothing
about the round
is tested, and no marginals are recorded. Then the check reads the
eight and tests seven integer facts. For each pair, let N be same plus different and D be same
minus different (so E is D over N). The seven: the four N are strictly positive (every pair was
sampled; a pair with no rounds is rejected outright, and never read as a correlator of zero); A, which is N00
squared N10 squared minus D00 squared N10 squared minus D10 squared N00 squared, is at least
zero; B, the same with the other column, is at least zero; and with C equal to D00 D01 N10
N11 plus D10 D11 N00 N01, C squared is at most A times B. Those are the three contraction
inequalities with the denominators cleared. No division, no reals, no square root, no S.
Try it: counts (same, different) of (4, 1), (4, 1), (4, 1), (1, 4) give E of 0.6, 0.6, 0.6,
minus 0.6; N is five and D is three (minus three for the last); A is 175, B is 175, C is zero;
passes. That's the first example above, the S equals 2.4 one, in integers.

The theorem chain, in words: a passed check gives PSD of the five-by-five built from the
