counts; contraction and PSD are equivalent, both directions; and PSD forces S squared at most
eight. The names are in the statements below. The underlying algebra is one identity: four times
the sum of the four correlators squared, minus S squared, is a sum of six squares
(\code{chsh\_gap\_is\_sum\_of\_squares}), so if the row sums of squares are at most one, S squared is
at most eight (\code{tsirelson\_squared}), and the point one over root two reaches it
(\code{tsirelson\_tight}). That's Tsirelson's bound as \emph{algebra}, with no Hilbert space (the
mathematical home of quantum states) in it.

Here is the chain as three statements. The derivations are in Appendix~\ref{sec:chsh-derivation};
this is what they prove.

\begin{definition}[Correlators from the counts; the pinned matrix]\label{def:u23-pinned}
For eight counts and a question pair $xy$, let
$E_{xy} = (\mathrm{same}_{xy} - \mathrm{diff}_{xy}) / (\mathrm{same}_{xy} +
\mathrm{diff}_{xy})$, read as 0 when both are 0. For reals $E_{xy}$,
$M(E)$ is the symmetric five-by-five matrix on $I, A_0, A_1, B_0, B_1$ with ones on the
diagonal, $E_{xy}$ in the cells $(A_x, B_y)$ and $(B_y, A_x)$, and zero everywhere else
(Definition~\ref{def:chsh-five}). $M$ is \emph{PSD} when $v^{\mathsf T} M v \ge 0$ for every real
vector $v$, and $S(E) = E_{00} + E_{01} + E_{10} - E_{11}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The integer check implies the pinned matrix is PSD]\label{thm:u23-notrap-psd}
If eight counts pass the seven integer facts, then $M(E)$ for their correlators is symmetric
and PSD.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The four positivity facts make every denominator positive, so each $E_{xy}$ is $D_{xy}/N_{xy}$,
and dividing the other three facts by positive squares turns them into the three contraction
inequalities (Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-clear}). Contraction is equivalent to PSD of $M(E)$ by a Schur
complement on the four-by-four block (Corollary~\ref{cor:chsh-iff}).
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{column\_contractive\_check\_witness\_sound} with \code{npa\_psd\_iff\_column\_contractive}
(Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-check-sound} and Corollary~\ref{cor:chsh-iff} in the appendix).

\begin{theorem}[PSD forces the Tsirelson bound]\label{thm:u23-psd-tsirelson}
For all real $E_{00}, E_{01}, E_{10}, E_{11}$: if $M(E)$ is symmetric and PSD, then
$S(E)^2 \le 8$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A PSD matrix with unit diagonal has every three-by-three principal minor at least zero. On
rows $A_0, B_0, B_1$ that minor is $1 - E_{00}^2 - E_{01}^2$, and on rows $A_1, B_0, B_1$ it
is $1 - E_{10}^2 - E_{11}^2$, so the four squares sum to at most 2. The identity
$4 \sum_{xy} E_{xy}^2 - S^2 = $ a sum of six squares then gives $S^2 \le 4 \cdot 2 = 8$.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{npa\_psd\_implies\_tsirelson\_bound}, with the row
bounds \code{npa\_psd\_zero\_marginal\_implies\_row\_bounds} (CHSHColumnCheck.v), and the identity
\code{chsh\_gap\_is\_sum\_of\_squares} (TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v); this is
Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-psd-tsirelson} in the appendix.

\begin{corollary}[A passed check means the bound]\label{cor:u23-notrap-bound}
If eight counts pass the seven integer facts, their correlators satisfy $S^2 \le 8$. In fact
$S^2 < 8$, and passing tallies come as close to 8 as you like.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:u23-notrap-psd} supplies positive semidefiniteness of the pinned
moment matrix for these four correlators. Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-psd-tsirelson} in the
derivation appendix applies to every such matrix and gives $S^2\le8$. Its quadratic
form calculation is printed there. The score is a ratio of whole numbers, and no such ratio
squares to 8, so the bound is strict. The tallies whose four correlators are
$n/q, n/q, n/q, -n/q$ with $2n^2 \le q^2$ pass, and their scores $4n/q$ come as near
$2\sqrt 2$ as you like.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{nec\_e\_check\_strict}, with \code{nec\_e\_check\_never\_tsirelson} for
$|S| < 2\sqrt 2$, \code{nec\_e\_no\_sqrt8} for the fractions, and \code{nec\_e\_check\_sharp} for
coming as close as you like (NecEChsh.v).

\begin{remark}[Sound, and incomplete]\label{rem:u23-sound-not-complete}
The pinned matrix is stricter than the quantum question it is usually read against. PSD of
$M(E)$ gives the correlators a PSD completion, since the zeros are one choice of the two free
entries (\code{zero\_marginal\_implies\_elliptope}, ElliptopeCompletion.v). The converse fails.
The all-ones plan has a PSD completion (\code{deterministic\_strategy\_elliptope}), and every
deterministic plan is a quantum strategy, a standard fact I haven't proved here; yet its
minor on rows $A_0, B_0, B_1$ is $1 - 1 - 1 = -1$, so $M(E)$ is not PSD there, and a tally of
one matching round per pair gives $A = 1 - 1 - 1 = -1$ in the integer check, so the check
fails. The second failure is a named theorem on the machine: the tally of one matching round
per pair is refused forever (Proposition~\ref{prop:chsh-demos}). Every deterministic plan fails
the same way. The tally of one round per pair fails the check for each of the sixteen plans
(\code{nec\_e\_check\_refuses\_all\_plans}), so does a plan replayed over any number of rounds once
pairs 00 and 10 have been sampled (\code{nec\_e\_check\_refuses\_deterministic}, NecEChshInt.v), and
no deterministic plan's pinned matrix is PSD (\code{nec\_e\_deterministic\_not\_pinned\_psd},
NecEChsh.v). So a pass proves the bound, and a failure proves only that the tally's pinned matrix isn't
PSD or a pair went unsampled; it says nothing about whether the play was classical or quantum. The free tally from the start of this section is
exactly such a tally: it reaches $S = 2$ and the check throws it out.
\end{remark}

None of that algebra is new, and I don't want it to read as if it were. Tsirelson's bound has
been formalised before, in Isabelle/HOL by Mnacho Echenim and Mehdi Mhalla, computer
scientists at Grenoble (2023), and in Lean's mathlib, and
Navascués, Pironio and Acín already analyse this very matrix by Schur complement and discuss
the level above it. What I think is mine here is smaller: an integer decision procedure on
the counts, and a checked link from ``the check passed'' to PSD to the bound.

\subsection{The check, earned on the host machine}

Now put it on the machine. A check on the small machine is a property: a checker, which is a
little program that says yes or no, a meaning, which is a statement, and a proof that the two
agree. The version of the small machine with its property language left open
(Section~\ref{sec:smallest}, Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tc-instances}) takes any property language with an exact equality
test whose properties come
with those three things, and for every one of them a flag raised from
a clean start stands on a passing CHECK of
one claim, a later COMMIT of the same claim with its counter untouched in between, and a later CERTIFY, the three acts costing one each.
So here's the plan for the game. Pack the eight counts into one counter, as a list, the way the
sorted-list machine packs a list into one number (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). Let the checker be
the seven integer facts read off the unpacked counts. And let the meaning be what the facts are
for: every pair was sampled, and the pinned five-by-five is positive semidefinite. Then the proof
the generic machine asks for, that the checker says yes exactly when the meaning holds, is the
chain above with the denominators cleared in both directions, and
a flag raised on that machine from a clean start
means: these counts, at this edition of their counter, passed the check, somebody committed to
that with nothing changed underneath, and the correlators they give satisfy $S^2 \le 8$.
Here is that, stated exactly, and it's stronger than the chain above in one way I want to say once
and plainly. The earlier theorems said that a passed check makes the pinned matrix PSD. The check is
also complete for it: it passes \emph{if and only if} every pair was sampled and the pinned matrix
is PSD, because clearing the denominators works in both directions. The statement is over the machine of Definition~\ref{def:u34-multi}, the
small machine with a counter for every number,
with PCHSH in place of its one property, $\mathsf{Slot}$. A CHECK reads one counter, which is why the eight
counts have to travel in one.

\begin{definition}[The packed tally, and the property PCHSH]\label{def:chsh-packed}
Read a whole number as a list in the list code (0 is the empty list, and $2^x(2y+1)$ is $x$ followed
by the list $y$), and take as its \emph{tally} the first eight entries, in the order
$\mathrm{same}_{00}, \mathrm{diff}_{00}, \mathrm{same}_{01}, \mathrm{diff}_{01}, \mathrm{same}_{10},
\mathrm{diff}_{10}, \mathrm{same}_{11}, \mathrm{diff}_{11}$, a missing entry reading 0. Every number
is some tally. The property PCHSH has the checker ``the tally passes the seven integer facts'' and
the meaning ``every question pair was sampled, and the pinned matrix $M(E)$ of the tally's
correlators is symmetric and PSD.''
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The check is exact]\label{thm:chsh-exact}
(1) The seven integer facts hold of a tally if and only if every pair was sampled and $M(E)$ is
symmetric and PSD. (2) For every whole number $v$, the checker of PCHSH says yes at $v$ if and only
if the meaning holds of $v$'s tally. (3) Reading the number that packs a tally gives that tally
back. (4) If the facts hold, the score of the tally satisfies $S^2 \le 8$ and $|S| \le 2\sqrt 2$;
in fact $S^2 < 8$ and $|S| < 2\sqrt 2$, and passing tallies come as close to 8 as you like.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) The forward half is Theorem~\ref{thm:u23-notrap-psd}. For the backward half, PSD gives the three
contraction inequalities (Corollary~\ref{cor:chsh-iff}); with every $N$ positive, multiplying them
through by the squares of the denominators gives $A \ge 0$, $B \ge 0$ and $C^2 \le AB$, which is
Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-clear} read the other way. (2) is (1) with the packing, since every number is a
tally. (3) is the code and its decoder being inverse. (4) is (1) forward, then
Theorem~\ref{thm:u23-psd-tsirelson}; the strict form and the closeness are
Corollary~\ref{cor:u23-notrap-bound}.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{small\_chsh\_check\_iff}, \code{small\_chsh\_clear\_denominators},
\code{small\_chsh\_psd\_iff\_contractive}, \code{small\_chsh\_psd\_tsirelson},
\code{small\_chsh\_check\_tsirelson}, \code{small\_chsh\_eval\_iff} and
\code{small\_chsh\_tally\_of\_code} (SmallChshCheck.v, SmallChshMachine.v). The non-strict bounds of
part (4) are a single checked theorem, \code{small\_chsh\_check\_tsirelson}, with both bounds in one
statement. The strict form of part (4), and the closeness, are checked as
\code{nec\_e\_check\_strict}, \code{nec\_e\_check\_never\_tsirelson} and
\code{nec\_e\_check\_sharp} (NecEChsh.v).

\begin{theorem}[A raised flag stands on the check]\label{thm:chsh-earned}
On the machine above, let $\tau$ be
a trace from a clean start $s_0$
that ends with the flag up. Then,
for some counter $c$, \[ \tau \;=\; \mathit{pre} \cdot \text{CHECK PCHSH } c \cdot \mathit{mid}_1 \cdot \text{COMMIT PCHSH } c
\cdot \mathit{mid}_2 \cdot \text{CERTIFY} \cdot \mathit{post},
\]
and with $v$ the value of $c$ after $\mathit{pre}$: the tally of $v$ passes the seven integer facts;
every pair was sampled and the pinned matrix is symmetric and PSD; its score satisfies $S^2 \le 8$
and $|S| \le 2\sqrt 2$, and in fact $S^2 < 8$, though passing tallies come as close to 8 as you
like; and $c$ still held $v$ when the COMMIT ran. For any stored program run from a fresh start (counters set, every
version 0, line 1, the ledger at 0)
that raises the flag, the trace it executed contains a CHECK PCHSH $c$ that passed, and the tally
$c$ held when it ran passes the seven integer facts, has every pair sampled and the pinned matrix
symmetric and PSD, and has $S^2 \le 8$ and $|S| \le 2\sqrt 2$. Conversely,
from a fresh start in which a counter
$c$ holds the packing of a tally $t$, the three instructions CHECK PCHSH $c$,
COMMIT PCHSH $c$, CERTIFY raise the flag if and only if $t$ passes the check, and then the ledger
reads exactly 3; if $t$ fails, the trap goes up at the CHECK and no number of further steps raises
the flag.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A raised flag from a clean start has the earned chain (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned}, which
holds for this machine as for the small one): a passing CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same claim with
the counter's edition unchanged, then a CERTIFY. A passing CHECK of PCHSH at $c$ means the
checker says yes at $c$'s value, which is the meaning by Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-exact}(2), and the
bound is (4) of the same theorem. An unchanged edition means an unchanged value. For the converse,
the CHECK passes exactly when the tally passes; if it does, COMMIT and CERTIFY find their
facts and the three acts cost three; if it fails, the trap latch goes up, and a run takes no
step once the trap is up (as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tight}), so the flag never rises.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{small\_chsh\_flag\_implies\_tsirelson}, \code{small\_chsh\_program\_flag\_implies\_tsirelson},
\code{small\_chsh\_chain\_certifies\_iff}, \code{small\_chsh\_tally\_certifies\_iff},
\code{small\_chsh\_tally\_certifies} and \code{small\_chsh\_tally\_refused\_forever}
(SmallChshMachine.v); the first is printed in Section~\ref{sec:coq-statements}. The strict bound on
the passing tally's score is \code{nec\_e\_check\_strict}, and \code{nec\_e\_check\_sharp} gives
passing tallies as close to 8 as you like (NecEChsh.v). That's the one thing the
machine does with the check, as the section's opening said: a raised flag can stand on it. Five
tallies, each a theorem with its counts written out, show the check isn't vacuous and where its
edges are.

\begin{proposition}[Five tallies]\label{prop:chsh-demos}
Counts are given as (same, diff) for the pairs 00, 01, 10, 11. (4,1), (4,1), (4,1), (1,4) has
$S = 12/5$: the check passes, the flag rises, the ledger reads 3. (17,3), (17,3), (17,3), (3,17)
has $S = 14/5 = 2.8$, just under $2\sqrt 2$, with $S^2 = 7.84$: it passes, the ledger reads 3.
(9,1), (9,1), (9,1), (1,9) has $S = 16/5$ with $S^2 > 8$: refused forever, whatever follows.
(1,0), (1,0), (1,0), (0,1), the PR box, has $S = 4$: refused forever. (1,0), (1,0), (1,0), (1,0),
the all-ones classical plan, has $S = 2$: refused forever.
\end{proposition}

Checked as \code{small\_chsh\_demo\_12\_5\_certifies}, \code{small\_chsh\_demo\_14\_5\_certifies},
\code{small\_chsh\_demo\_16\_5\_refused\_forever}, \code{small\_chsh\_demo\_pr\_box\_refused\_forever}
and \code{small\_chsh\_demo\_all\_ones\_refused\_forever} (SmallChshMachine.v). The last one is the
check being stricter than the bound, as a named theorem: a perfectly legal classical play with
$S = 2$ is turned away.

What the theorem doesn't say stays what it was. The tally is \emph{placed}. Nobody plays it on the
machine: the
theorem starts from a counter that already holds the packing, and no instruction plays a round, so a
program can put any code in a counter for free. There are no marginals. The pinned matrix is stricter than the quantum set, so failing says nothing about
whether the play was quantum, and there is no margin for sampling noise at
Tsirelson's point.

A tally stays free. Each count is a counter, a round is an INC on one of them, and INC costs
nothing, so a pile of trials costs nothing to write down; the packing into one counter is a program's
business, and in the theorem the packed counter is simply there at the start. What costs is the
claim about the pile. Statistics are free; the claim about them is what costs.

So here, in one paragraph, is what the check guarantees. If it passes, then every question
pair was sampled, the four empirical ratios satisfy three polynomial inequalities, hence the
fixed five-by-five is PSD, hence S squared is at most eight. It does \emph{not} guarantee that
the tally came from honest play (a program can INC
whatever counts it likes
for nothing, including four rounds that put S at four). It does not guarantee any
marginal is zero (no marginals are recorded and none are tested). It does not, by anything proved
here, put a quantum state behind the counts. That the correlators of a passing tally are quantum
ones is the cited result of Tsirelson, Landau and Masanes, and I haven't proved it.
And it fails the tally of every single plan, honest classical play included. It has no margin
for sampling noise either. Honest play at Tsirelson's point aims at correlators of plus or minus
one over root two, and there every pair of squared correlators the check adds up comes to exactly
one, the edge of what it accepts. So an honest tally aimed at that point sits right on the line,
and ordinary luck over a finite number of rounds pushes it over a good share of the time, and the
check fails. That's my arithmetic about where the point sits. No theorem in the files says it. The
check certifies a \emph{shape} of the tally. What the shape means is a question for whoever
supplied the rounds.

And notice which way the fence faces. The most practical use anyone has found for a Bell test,
certified randomness, needs the opposite bound. Stefano Pironio and colleagues (2010) argued, and backed
with an experiment, that a Bell violation, with settings the devices can't choose, certifies that the outputs are random,
and a group of quantum cryptographers, Rotem Arnon-Friedman, Fr\'ed\'eric Dupuis, Omar
Fawzi, Renato Renner and Thomas Vidick (2018), made the accounting tight with what they call entropy accumulation. A string printed in advance
passes no such test, so it's the cleanest case I know, outside this book, of a check that can
fail, separating output that was established from output that was printed. That needs $S$
bounded from below, with an error probability. This check bounds $S$ from above and fails every
single plan, so it's a fence that keeps out the super-quantum and the fixed plan. As a
nonlocality test it's no use. The deployed version exists, too: Gautam Kavuri and colleagues, physicists at NIST and
the University of Colorado (2025), run a
public randomness beacon whose outputs each trace back through a Bell test to a public record,
the nearest working system I know to a certified claim written down for good. And records cut
both ways there. Jonathan Barrett, Roger Colbeck and Adrian Kent, working on quantum cryptography (2013), pointed out that a device
which keeps its own memory of earlier rounds can leak it through outputs it makes public later,
so reusing a device can undo a guarantee the user thought was settled. A permanent record in the
wrong box is an attack.

\subsection{A rational stand-in for an irrational number}

One number you'll see in the files: 5657 over 2000, which is 2.8285, and two root two is
2.82842... It's the four-decimal round-up, chosen so that rational code can test ``above the
Tsirelson bound'' without square roots, and it's safe because 5657 squared is 32,001,649 and
eight times 2000 squared is 32,000,000, so the fraction sits above root eight by about seven
hundred-thousandths (\code{rational\_tsirelson\_bound}). It's used in a few rational
theorems. It is \emph{not} used in the integer check, and the real-number theorems use root
eight.

\subsection{Two more tests, as mathematics}

The second rung: a nine-by-nine table on I, the four questions, and the four Alice-Bob
\emph{products}, with the correlators and five extra free numbers for three- and four-body
entries. Its PSD is again equivalent to a contraction-like condition (\code{q1ab\_psd\_iff\_column\_contractive}).
The check for it proves something stronger, that the matrix is positive definite, by a cascade of
two Schur steps down to a four-by-four that Sylvester's criterion closes.
Sylvester's name on a test about matrices fits in a way I enjoy, because the word
\emph{matrix} is his. In 1850, in the \emph{Philosophical Magazine}, the English
mathematician James Joseph Sylvester used it for an ``oblong arrangement of
terms'' out of which you cut square blocks and take their determinants, and \emph{matrix} was
already an old word for the place something grows from. That's exactly what the test does:
it cuts the top-left square blocks out of the big grid, one row deep, two, three, four (the
leading minors), and asks each one's determinant to be positive. Was he the first to state the
test? The name doesn't settle that; names stick to people for all kinds of reasons, and I'd
treat this one as a lead.
And a fact that's easy to list without noticing what it means: with all five extra numbers at
zero, the condition certifies a strict \emph{subset of the classical set} (the ball where the four
correlators' squares sum to at most one), forcing S at most two
(\code{q1ab\_check\_at\_gzero\_implies\_classical\_bound}); it can't certify anything above the
classical line. To get a point above two you have to supply the extras
(\code{q1ab\_certifies\_a\_superclassical\_chsh\_point}, S equals 2.4 with one extra at minus one
half). Appendix~\ref{sec:chsh-derivation} has the algebra.

The two sizes are one test. A single positive-semidefinite predicate takes the size
as a parameter, and the five-by-five and the nine-by-nine are it at two sizes.

\begin{definition}[The size-generic PSD test]\label{def:u23-genrealizable}
A \emph{claim} is a top index $n$ and a matrix $M$ indexed by naturals. It is \emph{realizable} when
$M_{ij} = M_{ji}$ for all $i, j \le n$ and $\sum_{i \le n} \sum_{j \le n} v_i M_{ij} v_j \ge
0$ for every real vector $v$. The CHSH claim of $E$ is top index 4 with the matrix $M(E)$ of
Definition~\ref{def:u23-pinned}; the level-1+AB claim uses top index 8 and the nine-by-nine
matrix.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[The level-1 test is the size-five case]\label{cor:u23-general}
For all real $E_{00}, E_{01}, E_{10}, E_{11}$: the three contraction inequalities hold if and
only if the CHSH claim of $E$ is realizable. The same holds at size nine for the level-1+AB
contraction condition and its claim.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Realizability at top index 4 unfolds to symmetry and PSD of the five-by-five, by computing the
finite sums, and that is equivalent to contraction by Corollary~\ref{cor:chsh-iff}. At size nine
the same unfolding meets Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-nine-iff}. Nothing new is proved about the
matrices; the point is that one predicate covers both.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{column\_contractive\_iff\_general\_realizable} (GenRealizability.v) and
\code{column\_contractive\_q1ab\_iff\_general\_realizable}.

The third thing: the \emph{elliptope}, the set of correlators for which \emph{some} choice of the two
missing entries (A0 with A1, B0 with B1) makes the five-by-five PSD. Every one of the
sixteen plans is inside it (\code{deterministic\_strategy\_elliptope}), mixtures stay inside
(\code{elliptope\_convex}), every point inside obeys $S^2 \le 8$ (\code{elliptope\_tsirelson}), Tsirelson's point is inside and reaches it (\code{nec\_e\_pinned\_tsirelson\_tight}, NecEChsh.v), the PR box is out
(\code{pr\_box\_not\_elliptope}), and it's strictly bigger than the classical set
(\code{beyond\_classical\_elliptope}). There's a decider for it with a soundness proof, in two
branches: a strict Sylvester check with the completion supplied, and a rational
factorisation certificate of the completed matrix, checked in integers. What's proved is
that a pass puts the correlators inside the set and that no choice of inputs gets the PR box
through (\code{elliptope\_check\_full\_sound}, \code{elliptope\_full\_gate\_never\_accepts\_pr\_box}), and, by
computation, that some named points pass, the all-ones plan and a point that the cited arc-sine
boundary puts exactly on the quantum edge among them (\code{gate\_accepts\_all\_ones},
\code{gate\_accepts\_pythagorean\_boundary}).
The file's header also argues that every point with a rational PSD completion has such a
certificate; that is a comment, and no theorem states it. It's a decider with a soundness proof, as
mathematics; none of the small machine's properties is the elliptope check.

\subsection{What isn't proved}

The arc-sine curve. That any of these sets equals what quantum mechanics can reach. That
any state or measurement achieves 2.83. Those are the cited external results, and the files
say so in their scope notes. Also: the finite-mixture theorem (\code{fine\_theorem} in the source)
proves only one direction, that a finite local model satisfies the bound, and its converse as
stated is false: a table with $S = 0$ that no local model produces (\code{nec\_e\_fine\_converse\_false}).
Fine's own theorem, in the form that speaks of correlations, is proved separately as an
equivalence: a table of four correlators comes from a local model exactly when each is between
$-1$ and $1$ and all eight CHSH inequalities hold (\code{nec\_e\_fine\_iff}, NecEFine.v). And one more thing about tallies, which the guarantee paragraph above already used: a free
tally is not thereby classical (the four rounds with S equal to four). The correlators (one,
one, one, minus one) are the PR box, which no classical play produces; the classical vertex this
section used, which fails the check like every plan, is (one, one, one, one).

That's the game, the number, the two walls, and the check. Last of the machine sections:
what all this costs against physics.

%===========================================================================
\section{The counter against physics}
\label{sec:landauer}
%===========================================================================

Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} did the physics argument once: on a finite machine a permanent flag merges states,
Landauer's principle (a named premise) prices merges, and the toll follows. I'm not going
to do it again. This section is about what a machine's counter, the small machine's $\mu$
included, has to do with any of that, and the answer is: less than the word ``Landauer'' in a
file name suggests, and I want you to hear the exact amount from me.

\subsection{The calibration is a unit conversion}

There's a function in the source that multiplies the counter by a chosen energy per mark,
and a theorem that a state with one mark, at the scale kT ln 2 per mark, carries kT ln 2 of
energy (\code{calibrated\_mu\_landauer\_energy}, proving the predicate \code{mu\_landauer\_calibration} for
every k and T). Read that for exactly what it is: a unit conversion, true by definition,
with the scale as a free input. Nothing in it picks the scale. The theorem would be just as
true with the scale set to a dollar a mark. I'd say that out loud, so the name
``Landauer'' in it does no work. What \emph{would} connect marks to joules is the premise in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary},
\code{landauer\_heat}, and that one is an assumption with a name that nothing proves. And even
as a scale, $k_B T \ln 2$ a mark is the floor for one particular squeeze, a halving.
Corollary~\ref{cor:heat-floor}'s floor for a flip that brings $k$ states into a room already
holding $m$, starting
from the even spread on those $m+k$ states, is $k_B T \ln \frac{m+k}{m}$, and for one newcomer into a big room that's far below a
halving, roughly $k_B T / m$. Price every mark at $k_B T \ln 2$ and you can overstate the floor
of a single narrow flip by a factor that grows with $m$.

Remember the constant from Boltzmann's grave in Part II, the exchange rate between a count and
heat? It has a newer chapter, and it makes the point sharper than I can. The $k_B$ in
$k_B T \ln 2$ turns a temperature into an energy, and for most of its
history it was a measured number, with error bars, pinned down by careful experiments. Since
20 May 2019 it isn't. That day the international system of units was redefined so that
Boltzmann's constant is exactly $1.380649 \times 10^{-23}$ joules per kelvin, by definition, and
the kelvin is whatever makes that true. So the conversion from temperature to energy has been a
convention since then, in the strictest sense: nobody can measure it wrong any more. What's still
physics is everything around it, whether wiping a bit at a temperature really sheds that much
heat, which is what the Lyon bead was measuring. The calibration theorem is the same kind of move
as that redefinition. It fixes a conversion, and the physics, if there is any, is somewhere else.

\begin{definition}[Energy at a scale]\label{def:u24-scale}
For a real number $c$ (joules per mark) and a state $s$, the energy of $s$ at scale $c$ is
$\mu(s) \cdot c$. The \emph{Landauer calibration} at $k_B$ and $T$ is the statement that every
state with $\mu(s) = 1$ has energy $k_B T \ln 2$ at scale $k_B T \ln 2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The calibration is a unit conversion]\label{thm:u24-calibration}
(1) For all real $k_B$ and $T$, the Landauer calibration at $k_B$ and $T$ holds. (2) For any counter, there are two real-valued functions of
the state that give 1 and 2 on every state with
one mark, so the counter alone fixes no energy value.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Substitute $\mu(s) = 1$: $1 \cdot k_B T \ln 2 = k_B T \ln 2$, by ring arithmetic, for any
$k_B$ and $T$, positive or not. (2) Take the two functions to be the energy at scales 1 and 2. At $\mu(s) = 1$ they give 1 and 2.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{calibrated\_mu\_landauer\_energy} (PricingPhysicsAudit.v), which proves
\code{mu\_landauer\_calibration} (PricingPhysicsTarget.v) for all $k_B$ and $T$, and
\code{mu\_has\_no\_intrinsic\_joule\_value} (PricingPhysicsAudit.v). The physics is the premise of
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, restated here once in the form the next theorems test. In words first: a \emph{dissipation}
hands each instruction a whole number of heat units, each unit worth kT ln 2. Landauer's
principle, in that currency, says an instruction that takes at least one state where some yes-or-no
property is false to a state where it's true, and never sends a true one back to false,
dissipates at least one unit. The calibration says no instruction dissipates more units than the counter charges
it. One word about that word: ``dissipation'' here means heat handed to the surroundings, in the
sense Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} took from Sagawa: a bill for where the forgotten bit goes.
It has nothing to do with waste, or with doing the job badly. Two premises, nothing proved about either,
and the only question is whether they can sit in the same room:

\begin{premise}[Landauer, in units of the counter]\label{prem:u24-landauer-pair}
A \emph{dissipation} is a function $\delta$ from instructions to naturals, counted in units of
$k_B T \ln 2$. Landauer's principle, in this vocabulary (Premise~\ref{prem:landauer} of Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}):
every instruction that collapses a yes-or-no property has $\delta(i) \ge 1$, where $i$
\emph{collapses} $P$ when some state with $P$ false is sent to a state with $P$ true and every
state with $P$ true is sent to one with $P$ true. The \emph{calibration}: $\delta(i) \le
\mathrm{cost}(i)$ for every instruction. Neither is proved anywhere; the theorems below ask
whether they can hold together.
\end{premise}

\subsection{The premises have to be able to hold together}

Here's the one piece of this section that I think is good physics discipline, and it's a
consistency test. Suppose you want to claim the counter tracks dissipation. You need two
premises: that every step you've chosen to count dissipates at least one unit, and an upper
calibration that bounds dissipation by the charge. Can those two hold at once? There's a
theorem saying exactly when (\code{calibrated\_model\_exists\_iff\_positive\_cost}): a model
satisfying both exists precisely when every operation you've chosen to count (the statement
below calls those \emph{eligible}) costs at least one. I should say how cheap that is. The model the proof builds takes the dissipation to be
the cost itself, so the theorem shows the two premises don't contradict each other. It
doesn't show that the counter tracks any dissipation. Still, it does bite on a schedule: if you count a
zero-cost step, no such model can exist. One place the checked files show the premises holding is a
one-bit reset, where resetting costs one and idling costs
nothing (\code{bit\_model\_has\_satisfiable\_calibration}); the small machine's flag-raising steps, below, are another.

Now point the test at the small machine of Section~\ref{sec:smallest}, counting every step
that collapses some yes-or-no property, and it fails. Its free instructions merge states (the
last item of the list at the end of that chapter has the pair: two cores that one DEC sends to
the same core, for nothing), so DEC A 2, which collapses the property ``$A$ is zero or the line
number is 2'', costs zero there, and (1) below says no dissipation can charge it one and stay under its cost.
That's checked as \code{nec\_f\_small\_premise\_pair\_fails}, with the free merge itself as
\code{nec\_f\_small\_free\_collapse\_is\_merge} (NecFPhysics.v). The machine prices the
certifying chain and leaves its other merges free, so the premise pair holds for the steps
the toll is about (\code{nec\_f\_small\_premise\_pair\_on\_flag}) and fails for the whole instruction set. That's the honest shape.

\begin{theorem}[When the premises can hold together]\label{thm:u24-consistency}
(1) For any set of operations, any predicate ``eligible'' on them, and any cost, a dissipation
with $\delta(i) \ge 1$ on every eligible $i$ and $\delta(i) \le \mathrm{cost}(i)$ on every
$i$ exists if and only if every eligible operation costs at least one. (2) On a one-bit
machine with a reset of cost 1 and an idle of cost 0, taking ``eligible'' to mean ``sends two
different states to one'', such a dissipation exists.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) If such a $\delta$ exists, $1 \le \delta(i) \le \mathrm{cost}(i)$. Conversely, take
$\delta = \mathrm{cost}$. (2) The reset is the only operation that sends two states to one,
and it costs 1; apply (1).
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{calibrated\_model\_exists\_iff\_positive\_cost}, with the definition
\code{calibrated\_positive\_model}, and \code{bit\_model\_has\_satisfiable\_calibration}
(ObservationPolicy.v).

But now the history escape from Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, pointed at a machine. Keep the previous state in a
history list (push it onto the front each step; below, $s :: h$ is the list $h$ with $s$ put
on the front) and every fixed-instruction step becomes injective, while the step you can see
stays the same; the line number can collapse to one place while the bigger state keeps
its past. The free merge, lifted to a machine with
history, isn't a merge. So ``this step merged, therefore it dissipated'' can't be said of the
visible step alone. It's a sentence about the whole state including whatever
history is retained, and a physical model has to say what's retained. The
permanent-certificate theorem in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} supplies that for the certifying step on finite memory.
For the rest of a machine's steps it's unsaid.

\begin{theorem}[Keeping history makes every step injective]\label{thm:u24-history}
Let the history step send a pair $(s, h)$, a state and a list of past states, to
$(\mathrm{apply}(s, i), s :: h)$. For any step function, the history step with a fixed
instruction is injective, and its first component is the original step.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Undoing the history step, by popping the list, returns the old pair, so two pairs with the same
image are equal.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{retained\_history\_step\_injective} (ObservationPolicy.v).

\subsection{The calorimeter protocol, as a specification}

Here is how one \emph{would} measure this, and it's here because it makes the boundary exact. Take a two-state
register with energies zero and a gap, a population p in the excited state, and the simplest
possible rate equation for how p changes in one time step (a rate for climbing into the
excited state, a rate for falling out of it, and the length of the step). For the canonical reset
(population one half to zero, with the rates chosen so the equation closes), the heat
delivered to the bath is exactly half the gap (\code{canonical\_reset\_heat\_exact}). Choose the gap
to be twice kT ln 2 and that heat is exactly kT ln 2 (\code{selected\_gap\_gives\_landauer\_heat}).

Read that twice, because the temptation is to read it as a derivation of Landauer's number
and it's the opposite. The gap was \emph{chosen} to make the heat come out as Landauer's number.
The same populations and rates with half that gap give half the Landauer value, and there's
a theorem exhibiting identical population dynamics with different heat
(\code{master\_equation\_does\_not\_fix\_heat\_scale}). The rate equation fixes the \emph{shape}; the energy
scale is a selected Hamiltonian (the physicist's name for the rule that says what energy each
state has), and selecting it is not deriving it.

\begin{definition}[The two-state protocol]\label{def:u24-calorimeter}
For a gap $\Delta$, the register's mean energy at excited population $p$ is $\Delta \cdot p$.
One step of the rate equation is
\[
p' = p + \delta t \, \big(k_{01} (1 - p) - k_{10} \, p\big),
\]
and the heat to the bath over a step from $p$ to $p'$ is defined as $\Delta p - \Delta p'$. The
canonical reset takes $p = \tfrac12$, $\delta t = 1$, $k_{01} = 0$, $k_{10} = 1$, ending at
$p' = 0$, and counts one logical event.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The heat is fixed by the chosen gap]\label{thm:u24-calorimeter}
(1) The canonical numbers satisfy the rate equation. (2) For every $\Delta$, the canonical
reset's heat is $\Delta / 2$. (3) For all $k_B$, $T$, the gap $\Delta = 2 k_B T \ln 2$ gives
heat $k_B T \ln 2$. (4) If $k_B > 0$ and $T > 0$, the gap $k_B T \ln 2$ gives heat strictly
below $k_B T \ln 2$. (5) There are two different gaps for which the same canonical populations
satisfy the rate equation and the heats differ.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
All five are field arithmetic on the definitions: $\tfrac12 + 1 \cdot (0 - \tfrac12) = 0$;
$\Delta \cdot \tfrac12 - \Delta \cdot 0 = \Delta/2$; and $\ln 2 > 0$ for (4). For (5) take gaps
1 and 2.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{canonical\_reset\_satisfies\_master\_equation}, \code{canonical\_reset\_heat\_exact},
\code{selected\_gap\_gives\_landauer\_heat}, \code{smaller\_gap\_refutes\_unconditional\_landauer\_floor} (given
$k_B > 0$ and $T > 0$) and
\code{master\_equation\_does\_not\_fix\_heat\_scale} (CalorimeterProtocol.v), with the
definitions in CalorimeterProtocolTarget.v.

What ties it to a machine: the protocol counts one logical event (the file defines that
count as the constant one), and one is what the small machine's CERTIFY charges, the last of
the three paid acts behind a raised flag (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). That's a match of two
numbers, both one by choice, and nothing more. There is no theorem mapping the
protocol's two register states to any machine state. The file's ``heat to the bath'' is the
register's mean energy before minus after, so it also assumes the bath receives what the
register loses, and no Coq says that. So a device test would have to measure the gap, the
populations, the rates, and the bath heat independently; separately establish
thermal admissibility and detailed balance (that the up and down rates stand in the ratio the
temperature dictates); and separately establish that the device's
physical reset \emph{is} the machine's certify event. The protocol is an executable experimental
specification. It is not a measured device, and it is not an unconditional conversion of
marks to joules, and anyone who tells you otherwise is reading a file name.

\subsection{What permanence adds to Landauer: nothing new, said plainly}

Here's a fair question: is there a prediction the permanent-certificate theorems make that
Landauer's principle alone doesn't? No, and the reason is short. The smallest case, one certified state and one
flipping in, is ``set a bit to one whatever it held,'' which is the reset Landauer described
and Bérut measured; Landauer's own name for it is ``restore to one.'' The general bound, kT ln((m plus k) over m) for squeezing m plus k
equally likely states into m, is what Landauer's principle gives for that squeeze, at kT ln 2 for
each bit removed. What the permanence
theorems add is the \emph{derivation}: which premises about a machine (finite, permanent) make
the certifying step a reset, so that Landauer applies to it. That's a result about the
machine. Physics gets nothing new from it, and that's the right size for it.

\subsection{What this section is}

A calibration that's a unit conversion; a pair of premises, consistent on
the steps the toll is about and inconsistent on the whole instruction set; a history that makes any step injective; and a
measurement protocol that's a specification with a selected scale. The physics in this book is
in Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, as a named premise with its critics named. Here there's
accounting, and I've tried to call every line by its right name. That's the end of the machine.
What's left is what it took to check any of this, and where the checking stops.


\part{Checking it, and its edge}

%===========================================================================
\section{What Coq is, and why}
\label{sec:coq}
%===========================================================================

Coq is a proof assistant, which is a phrase I had to go and look up. Underneath the phrase
it's a programming language, but one whose type system is strict enough to do a thing
ordinary languages can't: you write a proof down as a program, and the compiler refuses it
unless the program genuinely matches the statement you claimed. You can't talk it into a
maybe.

The name is a joke three ways at once, and it's worth knowing before you say it out loud in
English. \emph{Coq} is French for rooster. It's also a nod to Thierry Coquand, a French computer scientist and mathematician, now at the University of Gothenburg, who worked out the
logic it started from with
Gérard Huet, a French computer scientist at INRIA, and to that logic's initials, CoC, for the Calculus of
Constructions; and there's a French habit of naming research tools after animals. The English
slang reading did what you'd guess. By the development team's own account, some people, women
students especially, ended up never learning the tool because of its name. So in March 2025 it
got a new one, the Rocq Prover, after Rocquencourt, the Inria site where it was first built,
and after the Roc, the giant bird of legend, so the bird stayed. Everything in this book was
checked with Coq 8.18, from before the rename, so that's the name I use. The rooster changes
nothing about what got checked.

\subsection{Types as claims}

Here's the idea, and it's one idea. In a normal language a type says what kind of value a
variable holds: in Python, ``x is an int'' means x is a whole number. In Coq, types are
\emph{claims}. The type ``n is greater than zero'' is the type of \emph{proofs} that n is positive. A
function from ``n is greater than zero'' to ``n plus one is greater than zero'' is a proof that
if n is positive, n plus one is too, and the compiler checks that the function really has
that type, the way it would check that a function from integers to strings really returns
strings. This correspondence between proofs and programs has a name, Curry-Howard, after
two people who noticed it separately decades apart, and Coq's foundation, the Calculus of
Inductive Constructions, is a type system built to exploit it. Coquand worked it out with
Christine Paulin-Mohring, a logician and computer scientist best known for developing Coq,
on top of the Calculus of Constructions he and Huet had made; their paper on it was given in 1988
and printed in 1990, so the late 1980s is as close as I'd date it. The ``inductive'' part means you
define your own recursive types (numbers, lists, trees, machine states) inside the system. The numbers, lists and states this book uses are all defined that
way, inside the system, so the foundation is explicit; nothing is smuggled.

``Decades apart'' undersells it, and the gap is worth a side trip. Haskell Curry, an American logician at Penn State best known for combinatory logic, noticed in 1934
that the type of a function from $A$ to $B$ reads like the claim ``$A$ implies $B$,'' and that
the types his functions could have lined up with the claims you can prove; he and Robert Feys, a Belgian logician at Leuven, pushed it further in 1958.
William Howard, a proof theorist at the University of Illinois at Chicago, wrote the sharper version in 1969, and then it went
around as a photocopied manuscript until 1980, when it was finally printed in a collection of essays for Curry. (The Edinburgh computer scientist Philip Wadler's 2015 survey, ``Propositions as Types,'' tells this story.) So the sharpest statement of the idea under the tool this book is checked with spent its first eleven
years as a stack of photocopies. Is that the bottom? No. Reading a proof of ``if $A$ then $B$''
as a method that turns any proof of $A$ into a proof of $B$ is older still: the intuitionists
had it in the 1920s and 1930s, Brouwer, Heyting and Kolmogorov, which is why people also call
it the BHK interpretation. Where it really starts I can't tell you. It changes nothing in what
the checker checks. It changes how I'd tell the story: nobody sat down one day and invented
``proofs are programs.'' It kept getting noticed, by people coming from different directions,
until somebody wrote it down plainly.

The compiler checks whether the types line up. If your proof has a hole, it rejects the proof, unless you write ``trust
me'' (the keyword is Admitted), and then it marks the theorem as unproved. But here's the part that matters: the
compiler checks that the proof matches the \emph{statement}. It does not check that the statement
says what you \emph{meant}. Hand it a statement that means nothing and it'll prove it for you,
three characters, no complaint. So a proof being accepted is not the same as the thing being
true. It means this proof matches this statement, and whether that's the right statement is
on me. The machine can't tell. \hyperref[sec:point]{The point} said a short version of this and I'm saying it again because every section
since has leaned on it: the checked names in this book are a promise that the \emph{proof} is
there, and the sentences around them are my claim about what the statement \emph{says}, and the
second can be wrong while the first is fine, which is why so many sections of this book
stop to say exactly what a statement's hypotheses are.

\subsection{Why I used it}

Not to make anything true. I used it because I don't trust my own eye to catch a gap in an
argument I want to believe. I spent months convinced by my own reasoning, pushed the proof
through, and watched a key step come apart in my hands. The machine caught where I'd fooled
myself. That's what it's for. Gap-catcher. Not the proof. The proof is the argument, and an
argument has to close in a way a person can follow, or it hasn't closed at all, which is
why this book is written in prose. A list of theorem names can't close an argument for anyone.

Two precedents show that a proof assistant is a serious tool. Neither of them is a
toy. CompCert, Xavier Leroy's C compiler, written and proved correct in Coq: the assembly it
emits behaves as the source does, for programs with defined behaviour. And Georges
Gonthier's 2005 proof of the four-colour theorem, a century-old problem whose first
proof (in 1976) needed a computer to check fewer than two thousand configurations, by its own
announcement's count, and was distrusted for exactly that reason. Gonthier redid it in Coq, working
from a later version of the proof by Neil Robertson, Daniel Sanders, Paul Seymour and Robin Thomas
(1997), so that the \emph{checker} was the small, auditable thing and the cases were the program. That's de Bruijn's criterion applied to mathematics itself: the thing you have
to trust is the small kernel. The big proof only has to get past it. The name was given by Henk Barendregt, a
Dutch logician known for his work on the lambda
calculus and type theory, after Nicolaas de Bruijn, whose Automath project, begun in 1967, kept the part of a proof checker you have to
trust small: a system meets the criterion when its proofs can be checked by a small independent
program that a person could read.

The 1976 proof deserves its own side trip. Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken did it at the
University of Illinois, and the mathematics department changed the slogan on its postage meter
to ``Four colors suffice.'' The slogan it replaced had been on the department's mail since soon
after 1963, and it said that $2^{11213} - 1$ is prime, a prime Don Gillies, a professor at the
same university who helped design its ILLIAC II computer, had found in 1963 while checking that
machine out. Think about that for a second. For years
on end a mathematics department stamped its mail with results nobody could have checked by
hand, first one and then the other, and both were right. So was the distrust of the 1976 proof
wrong? I don't think so. The worry was never that the computer lied. It was that nobody could
read what had been checked, and a check you can't look at is hard to lean on. Gonthier's answer
was de Bruijn's: make the part you have to read small enough to read.

\subsection{What ``zero Admitted'' means}

``Zero Admitted'' is literal. Nowhere in the proof tree did I write ``trust me'' and walk on.
Every step the checker could see, it saw, end to end, with no ``and the rest is obvious.'' It's
a hygiene fact about the gap-catcher. It passes no verdict on the argument: it says I didn't let
myself skip a step where the machine was watching. It does not say the statements are the
right statements.

What it doesn't mean, listed. It doesn't mean the theorems prove physical reality; they
prove things about the machine as formalised, and whether that describes the world is
answered by experiments (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, Section~\ref{sec:landauer}). It doesn't mean Coq's own foundation is proved
consistent; it's believed consistent, and that can't be proved from inside, by Gödel (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}),
so the foundation is trusted, and ``trusted'' has substance: it's the same kernel CompCert and
the four-colour proof stand on, and a bug in it would take all of them down together, which
is a kind of safety in numbers. And it doesn't mean no axioms: the
proofs use a handful of standard-library assumptions, and the assumption audit names them:
functional extensionality on dependent functions (two functions that agree everywhere are
equal); two decidability principles that come with the standard library's real numbers, used
by the matrix proofs behind the game check; and, in some theorems, the law of excluded middle
(every proposition is true or false). The count, from the full audit:
the full-corpus probe covers 5,369 named theorems across 308 files: 4,882 close under the global Coq context outright, and 487 use only Coq standard-library assumptions.
Zero project-local axioms appear in any of the 5,369 dependency trees.
The small machine's files, under minimal/, are inside that probe too, and every one of their 1,417
probed theorems comes back closed under Coq's own rules, with no axiom at all. Among them are the small machine,
its
version for any property language, the simpler host, the definition of Thiele-complete and its
window theorem, the host machine with a register for every whole number, the numbers that write
a guest program down, and the pigeonhole (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}), and the files that run Parts II and III on that machine and the diagonal on its programs (Sections~\ref{sec:part3-on-machine} and~\ref{sec:small-diagonal}). Each also ends by printing the assumptions of
every headline theorem in it, and every one
of those lines says the theorem is closed. A lemma a closed theorem uses is closed with it. So for those files ``nothing assumed''
means exactly that, and two separate printouts say so. Only two small files under minimal/,
MuCore.v and Napkin.v,
sit outside the big audit, and they are built and checked on their own. The
universal program's own files, which lean on the vendored library's counter-machine blocks, sit
in the kernel tree with the other link files, and they also end by printing their headline
theorems' assumptions; so do the files of the priced host, the compiler from computable
functions and the theorem for every computably presented Thiele machine.
In plain words: every theorem in the audit either needs nothing at all or leans only on those
standard-library assumptions, none of mine. Those counts are of the sources at this
edition. Add a theorem and the counts move. The shape, nothing of mine assumed anywhere, is what every
edition has to keep.

\subsection{What you're trusting, in one place}

If you accept every checked theorem in this book, here is what you're still taking on trust,
all of it, so you don't have to collect it from five chapters.

\begin{enumerate}
\item The statements. The checker confirms a proof proves its statement. It doesn't confirm the
statement says what my sentence about it says. That's why the book prints the important
ones in full, premises and all, and why Appendix~\ref{sec:coq-statements} prints the Coq text
of the load-bearing ones beside a line on whether my sentence says exactly that, more, or less. A
machine check supplements that reading.
\item Coq's kernel and its foundation, and the standard assumptions above.
\item The tools under Coq. Coq's own program, the compiler it was built with, the operating
system it ran on and the processor under all of them are trusted. This is the list Ken
Thompson's lecture from Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} was about. I didn't write Coq, or OCaml, or
any of the rest, so by his moral I can't fully trust any of them, and neither can you. What I
can do is keep the list short and print it, so you know exactly which tools you're being asked
to believe have no spare key cut into them.
\item The tested parts. The tests are evidence that the programs around the proofs do what's
claimed on the runs tried. They can't show the programs always do. Edsger Dijkstra had a sentence for
this, and the version in his 1976 book starts by admitting he'd already said it many times:
program testing ``can be quite effective for showing the presence of bugs, but is hopelessly
inadequate for showing their absence.'' (I'm quoting it as John Harrison, who was then proving
floating-point hardware correct at Intel, quotes it in a 2007 survey, from that
book.) That's why this item says \emph{tested}. It never says \emph{proved}.
\item The physics. Anywhere a theorem has Landauer's principle or a calorimeter in it, the
physical premise is named and assumed (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, Section~\ref{sec:landauer}).
Nothing here derives it.
\item Whoever sets the start and whoever reads the record. Every guarantee about the record is
about programs run from a clean start on a step that does what its definition says. The
operator who chooses the start, a reset, a device running the machine, and anyone reading a
report they didn't watch being made are outside it (Section~\ref{sec:scope} lists the whole
fence).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Thompson's knife, again}

Every link on that list is a place where Ken Thompson's compiler from Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}
could sit unseen: a translator that plants something and re-plants it when it translates
itself. Coq's own binary, the compiler that built it, the operating system under both. I don't
believe any of them does. I can't prove it, and the discipline of this section is to say so.
``Formally verified'' doesn't cover a chain whose bottom is trust.

And a planted knife isn't the only way a trusted link goes wrong. Sometimes nobody plants
anything and the thing at the bottom is just wrong. In 1994 Thomas Nicely, a mathematics
professor at Lynchburg College who was computing with twin primes and their reciprocals, found
that his new Intel Pentium got some divisions wrong. The standard example is
4,195,835 divided by 3,145,727, which the bad chips got wrong in the fourth decimal place.
Intel's explanation was missing entries in a table inside the divider: five of them, it said,
dropped by a script. Intel set aside about \$475 million to cover it.

Push on the five. In 2024 Ken Shirriff, who reverse-engineers old chips from photographs of their
silicon and writes them up on his blog, went to die photographs of an affected chip, read the table's layout off the silicon, and counted sixteen
missing entries, left out by a mistake in the table's mathematical definition, of which only
five ever mattered. If Shirriff's reading of the silicon is right, and I haven't checked it, Intel's own explanation, repeated for thirty years, had the effect right
and the cause off, and it took somebody reading the actual silicon to say so. Floating-point
arithmetic went on to become one of the places where formal verification earned its keep in
industry; Harrison, who did that work at Intel, brings up this very bug in his 2007 survey
of it. Does any of that touch this book? Only at the bottom of the list above. Every proof here
was checked by a program running on some processor, and nobody here has read that processor's
tables off the silicon either. That's why the processor is on the list as trusted. I can't give it a
kinder word.

\subsection{The auditor on top}

Beyond the type checker, the project has a custom proof auditor I called the Inquisitor,
because a thing that reads every proof looking for ways you've cheated deserves a name you
won't forget. It reads every proof file, and its source names about eighty distinct rules. The main
families: no holes (no Admitted, no admit, no give-up, no unproved axiom or parameter in
project code); vacuity heuristics (no theorem whose conclusion is literally True or a
tautology; no theorem of the shape ``P implies P''; existence claims backed by a constant
witness get flagged, and a flag is a reason to look and nothing more, since some constructions
like a fixed interpreter program are \emph{supposed} to be fixed and get judged on what they
compute); physics-definition heuristics (no physical quantity defined as a placeholder
constant, no physics claim without an invariance condition); scope enforcement (the proof
tree is split into tiers, the kernel tier may not import from research-side files, and every
active file must reach the cost or semantics foundation through its imports, or it doesn't
get to claim the kernel's pedigree); and comment hygiene (no unfinished or historical
markers in maintained source). Its rules are heuristics. They point at places to look. They don't prove
a theorem means what it should, and they can't promise every empty premise got caught.

So none of this is foolproof, the checker and the auditor included, and I don't treat it as if
it were. That's the reason some of the theorems are runs. The worked examples in Part IV, the earned run that pays exactly three and the one that traps for good, and the two guests run on
the simpler host, are computed by Coq from the definitions. The demonstration machine on the priced
host is different: its numbers are proved, and nobody has
run it. A proof can be hollow in a way nobody spots. A definition that
has to produce the numbers on the page, run by the checker itself, is harder to fool, and when it
disagrees, it tells you where to look.

\subsection{Checking the companion formalization}

The mathematical claims are the statements printed in this book, with their stated
hypotheses and the arguments given here. Running software is an additional way to check
their formal counterparts. It isn't a prerequisite for reading the argument.

A reproducible check needs a fixed copy of the proof sources, dependencies and probes.
Changing that copy changes the object being checked; a later software result cannot
silently revise a theorem in this edition. The procedure below describes the companion
proof build. With Python 3, GNU make, Coq 8.18 and its standard library, CSDP, OCaml with
its ocamlfind tool, and MetaCoq 1.2.1 for Coq 8.18 (the vendored lambda-calculus files need it)
installed,
run this from the root of a checkout of the sources at a fixed revision. The revision this edition was checked against is
this one:

\begin{verbatim}
Companion sources:
  https://github.com/sethirus/The-Thiele-Machine
  branch handoff/native-recursion-2026-10-01
Revision used for this edition:
  7a3fc08dbc6168e4c749aa6fcfbbee6e68899884
  (last change to the proof sources:
   961a97da442b16204aab12affac64225f796223c)
Dependency snapshot:
  Coq 8.18.0 (Ubuntu 24.04 packages), MetaCoq 1.2.1
  (scripts/install_metacoq.sh), vendored Coq Library of
  Undecidability Proofs at upstream commit
  8880e198bdc44cba1bd901f1fee701a95fc440ae (coq-8.18
  branch; vendor/coq-undecidability/UPSTREAM.md)
Build command:
  python3 scripts/reproduce_coq.py
Audit report for this revision:
  artifacts/print_assumptions_all_proofs.json
  SHA-256 0e1d96d9588a7808024b60aadfa8a06e
          f5b60142bc5f2f10d61a753393c67210
  corpus digest be964110a7d5c31c316c02a1eeb9a4cb
                4d25b0b8865e3a7f0beda4f5179e56ec
Manuscript source for this edition:
  monograph/monograph.tex at the release commit; a file
  can't print its own checksum, so take it with
  git rev-parse RELEASE:monograph/monograph.tex
\end{verbatim}

The counts this book reports from the assumption audit (5,369 theorems in 308 files) are the ones
in that report, and they belong to that revision. A change to the proof sources changes the
corpus digest; the audit then has to be run again and its counts read afresh.
With those installed, run:

\begin{verbatim}
python3 scripts/reproduce_coq.py
\end{verbatim}

That copies the sources into a fresh directory and works only from the copy: it builds the
part of the vendored Coq Library of Undecidability Proofs the proofs use, regenerates the build
file, rebuilds every proof from source, and runs Coq's independent checker over every module the
project lists. Extra probe files that re-check named theorems can be added with \texttt{--probe};
none run by default. It reuses no compiled proof from the
checkout, and it writes its pass file only after every stage passes. A failed run resumes
from the snapshot it captured, and a change to the sources needs a fresh run:

\begin{verbatim}
python3 scripts/reproduce_coq.py --resume \
  --output artifacts/reproduction/RUN_DIRECTORY
\end{verbatim}

The run has to pass. Don't stop at the pass: read the theorem
types and their global dependencies, because a closed report doesn't make a theorem's own
premises go away.

That's the checker. What's left is to tell you how to break what it checked.

%===========================================================================
\section{How to break this}
\label{sec:falsification}
%===========================================================================

Every main claim in this book comes with the exact shape of the thing that would kill it. I
went to the trouble on purpose. A claim you can't break is a claim that wasn't saying
anything. So I'm handing you a loaded gun pointed at my own work, with every sentence sharp
enough to aim at. These are written as instructions: here is the trace to find, the
object to build, the theorem to exhibit. Build one and the proof tree falls, and I mean that
as an invitation.

The invitation is an old one, and people have put prices on it. Donald Knuth gives the first
person to find each error in his books one hexadecimal dollar, 0x\$1.00, which is \$2.56,
deposited these days at the Bank of San Serriffe, a bank that doesn't exist, since real
checks turned out to be an open door for fraud. Why pay strangers to find your mistakes? His
own page says it plainly enough: a careful reader makes the book better for everyone who reads
it next. This chapter doesn't come with a bank, real or made up. What it comes with is, for
every claim, a description of the exact object that would make it fall, so you know before you
start what counts as winning.

Before the list, the honest part about it. Most targets below are theorems Coq has checked,
and knocking one of those over head-on would take a bug in Coq's kernel. That can happen, but
it isn't where I'd put my money. The places a reader can actually win are aimed at me,
and there are three. None of them goes through Coq. A sentence of mine that says more than the Coq statement it cites
(Appendix~\ref{sec:coq-statements} puts the load-bearing ones side by side to make that easy). A Coq
definition that doesn't capture the English word it's named for: on the small machine, ``is at
least 0'' is a check that can't fail, and the step certifies it anyway, so ``certified'' there
doesn't mean ``found something out'' (Section~\ref{sec:smallest} says so, and that's the kind
of gap to hunt). And a list of premises that only its own example satisfies.

\subsection{The abstract claims (Parts II and III)}

\emph{The universal floor (Section~\ref{sec:toll}).} Build a certification system that satisfies the one-step toll
and give a run from uncertified to certified with total cost zero. \code{universal\_nfi\_any\_substrate}
falls. If you instead drop the toll, you've built a free-certification system. That's
a different system, and it counts for nothing against the theorem.

\emph{The toll from premises (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}).} Exhibit a finite, duplicate-free list of every state, a
certificate no step revokes, and an \emph{injective} step that switches it on.
\code{permanent\_flip\_is\_not\_injective} falls, and the derivation of the toll with it. An infinite
state space, a revocable certificate, or an unpriced merge is not a counterexample; the file
already builds one of each. For the squeeze bound, a finite permanent machine with a cost
meeting the halving premise where one step switches k states on beside m certified ones and
two to the cost times m is less than m plus k; \code{permanent\_flips\_compression\_bound} falls.
For merge-or-revoke, a finite machine and an injective instruction that switches a reading on
without switching it off anywhere; \code{flip\_merges\_or\_revokes} falls. A move that merges and
also revokes counts against nothing. It's the three cards. For the eight-state
machine, a move of it that merges two states and costs nothing; \code{fin\_merging\_priced} falls.

\emph{The bill in bits (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}).} Exhibit a finite machine with a permanent certificate, a move that
switches k states on beside m certified ones (k at least one), and a spread of probability
over those m plus k states whose image under the move has entropy above log base two of m.
\code{permanent\_step\_entropy\_ceiling} falls. For the general form, a step and a spread on
a finite list of every state under which
two different states, each with some probability, land on the same state while the entropy
doesn't drop; \code{entropy\_drop\_pos\_of\_support\_merge} falls. A heat measurement on a real device
below what the bound asks doesn't touch either theorem. It refutes the premise
\code{landauer\_heat} for that device, which is Landauer's principle, and that's a fight with
physics. The counting stays where it was. And a certifying step from a state already known that gives
off no heat isn't a counterexample: \code{known\_state\_flip\_forces\_no\_heat} says the premise sets no positive
floor there.

\emph{Learning is free (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}).} Show that the four-state demon's measure step merges two states,
or that its observer's candidate list doesn't shrink. \code{observer\_narrowing\_can\_be\_free}
falls. A different price schedule that charges the measure step is allowed and isn't a
counterexample. The claim is ``not forced.'' It never says ``always free.''

\emph{The counter (Section~\ref{sec:counter}; on the small machine, Section~\ref{sec:smallest}).}
Find a state of the small machine and an instruction such that the ledger after is anything
other than the ledger before plus that instruction's cost; the loud version is a ledger that
goes down. \code{mu\_conservation} falls. The uniqueness half, that only one bookkeeping starts
at zero and follows the schedule, is checked over any counter machine as
\code{nec\_f\_initiality} (Section~\ref{sec:counter}); a
reachable state where two such bookkeepings disagree makes it fall.

\emph{Windows (Section~\ref{sec:windows}).} Exhibit a window and a price computed from the observed before and after
that meets the floor and never overcharges, on a machine where two steps share their before
and after pictures and only one certifies. \code{shadow\_cannot\_price\_exactly} falls. A window that
shows certification is not a counterexample; the theorem says exactly that such a window
prices exactly. For the three escapes, a verifier of one of the three kinds that's wrong about
the pair, under its own relation; the argument after Definition~\ref{def:u21-escape-relations}
falls.

\emph{Entitlement (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}).} Produce a strict narrowing of a candidate
list, with a distinguishing observation, that does not yield a strictly stronger membership
test; the card argument falls. Or exhibit a run with a tree no deeper than its paid steps,
covering the narrowing, whose counter rose by less than the index bits lost;
Theorem~\ref{thm:u08-count} falls.
On every Thiele-complete machine: a run from a clean start that ends with the record up, meets the
hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-machine}, and has fewer record moves than the index bits it
narrowed, or has no earned chain in it; \code{ent\_representation} falls, and the weighted form
(\code{ent2\_weighted\_representation}) falls the same way. A narrowing with a big drop and a small
bill is not a counterexample unless a tree no deeper than the record moves covers it: the covering
is a hypothesis, and \code{ent2\_uncovered\_claim\_false} says why it has to stay one. On the host
machine, a run from a clean start that raises the record only after more than sixteen CHECKs; \code{ent2\_questions\_cap}
falls. On the small machine, a program of INC and DEC that runs fewer than $m$ moves and
whose final line number and $B$
determine whether $A \ge m$ at every start; \code{ent2\_free\_cannot\_decide\_fast} falls.

\emph{The latch (Section~\ref{sec:latch}).} Exhibit an extension of a base whose record is driven by the computation
and never switches off, and which is not a latch on any event. \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_holds}
falls. A record that switches off, or one driven by a hidden clock, is the file's own pair of
counterexamples. The file built those already.

\emph{The diagonal (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}).} Two routes. A decider for some substrate
with a shortcut predicate whose flip the substrate can represent and which answers
correctly on every program; the generic proof fails at a named step. For the nat family, a d
that correctly decides the predicate of the substrate built from d. L has its recursion theorem
by proof, so it gets a target of its own: a map on L's terms, computable by an L term, with no
term that behaves like its own image; \code{L\_recursion\_theorem} falls.
On the host machine: a host program that decides an extensional property of host programs that some
program has and some lacks, or a map of host programs that a host program carries out, with no host
program that computes the same function as its image; \code{sm\_host\_rice} or \code{sm\_kleene}
falls. On the small machine: a decider for a property of what two-counter programs do from the clean
start that some program has and some lacks; \code{sm\_guest\_rice} falls. A decider for such a
property over every input of two-counter programs; \code{tc\_rice} falls. A two-counter program that
multiplies every plain input by the number of Theorem~\ref{thm:no-plain-recursion}; \code{tc2\_no\_mult}
falls. A map of host programs that a host program carries out, with no host
program that stops when its image stops and agrees with it on register 0, the trap latch, the ledger,
the flag, the number of facts and whether the channel is empty, is a counterexample to
\code{sm2\_kleene\_obs}. A map whose fixed point disagrees with its image on some other register is not one:
some computable map has no fixed point that agrees with its image on every register (\code{sm2\_no\_exact}).

\emph{The pointer conjecture (Section~\ref{sec:pointer}).} It's a conjecture, so the three routes are its own: a
deployed discipline pricing a non-proliferating event; a rival event proliferating as well
as certification in a real ecosystem; an honest formalisation with independence defined
where certification fails the test.

One concession goes with it, and I make it in full. The window results, the separation of
the two runs, and the counter's uniqueness don't single out certification. Their
proofs use only that the step carries something the classical picture doesn't determine, so
the same shape of result holds for any such field. Nothing in Parts II to IV proves that
certification is the one event a model is \emph{forced} to price; Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} forces a price on every
merge, certifying or not. That's the conjecture, and Section~\ref{sec:pointer} is the case I make for it.

\emph{The five models (Section~\ref{sec:models}).} Each fragment has a theorem with a named falsifier: a finality fork
with nobody slashable; a gas schedule meeting floor and no-overcharge whose charging
predicate differs from the commit predicate on some step; one of the RFC's own example proofs
that the transcribed inclusion check rejects, or an input with leaf index equal to tree size
that it accepts; a program the bounds checker accepts whose verification condition fails. Each
kills one fragment. None of them, and I want this clear, says anything about the
real system beyond the fragment.

\subsection{The machine claims (Part IV)}

\emph{The small machine (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}).} Four targets. From a clean start, a
run that raises the flag without an earlier passing CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY of the same
claim, with the counter's version unchanged between the CHECK and the COMMIT;
\code{earned\_certification\_provenance} falls, and \code{earned\_commitment\_provenance} for
a COMMIT alone. From a clean start, a trace that leaves a fact in the table nobody checked;
\code{no\_forging} falls. From a clean start, a run that ends certified for a total charge
under three; \code{certified\_run\_min\_cost} falls, and a run at exactly three is not a
counterexample: CHECK ``A is 0'', COMMIT, CERTIFY from a start where A is 0 is one, and the
same program from any other start is refused forever (\code{earned\_run\_check\_can\_fail},
\code{earned\_run\_refused\_forever}). A check that can't fail certifying for three isn't a
counterexample either; the step doesn't police trivial checks, and the book says so. A two-counter machine and a
program whose run on the small machine disagrees with it step for step, or halts when it
doesn't; \code{simulation\_step} or \code{halting\_correspondence} falls.

\emph{Thiele-complete (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}).} A machine that charges at least one for every
move and still meets the four clauses; \code{complete\_has\_free\_move} falls, and with it \code{clock\_not\_thiele\_complete}, whose proof uses it. A
Thiele-complete machine and a function of its window that gives its record at the end of every
run from every loaded state; \code{complete\_no\_record\_oracle} falls. A clause none of the
excluded machines needs: drop it and show the paid latch or the silent machine still fails, and
\code{paid\_latch\_not\_thiele\_complete} or \code{silent\_not\_thiele\_complete} has been proved
by the wrong clause, which is worth a letter.

\emph{The universal program (Section~\ref{sec:universal-host}).} A program of the small machine and
a start on which $U$ halts and the guest doesn't, or the other way round;
\code{universal\_halting} falls. One on which the flags disagree, or the ledgers differ at a
matching point; \code{universal\_flag\_iff} or \code{universal\_ledger\_exact} falls. A run of $U$
whose raised flag doesn't stand on a passing CHECK, then COMMIT, of one slot, then CERTIFY;
\code{universal\_earned} falls.

\emph{Every computably presented machine (Section~\ref{sec:presented-universal}).} A computably
presented Thiele machine and a start on which $U_P$'s flag goes up while the machine's reading
never says yes, or the other way round; \code{presented\_universal\_flag\_iff} falls. With the
reading starting at no, a step the machine reaches at which every point of
$U_P$'s run that matches it has a ledger more than two above the
machine's; \code{presented\_universal\_surcharge\_le\_two} falls. A program on the host machine,
from a clean start, that matches a raise costing less than three exactly;
\code{presented\_universal\_no\_exact\_below\_three} falls. A machine whose reading no program
decides isn't a counterexample. It's outside the class, and the book says so.

\emph{The classical CHSH bound (Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).} Exhibit four fixed bits and a tally consistent with that
one plan, every pair sampled, scoring above two. \code{chsh\_violation\_rules\_out\_locally\_factorizable\_coupling}
falls, and so does known mathematics. A randomised plan landing past two by luck doesn't
count; the theorem is about one fixed plan, and Section~\ref{sec:chsh}'s coin-flip example shows the luck.

\emph{The integer check (Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).} The game check has two walls, and here's how to knock each one
over. A correlator that passes the three contraction inequalities whose
five-by-five is not PSD (forward), or a PSD five-by-five of that shape whose correlators
aren't contractive (reverse); \code{npa\_psd\_iff\_column\_contractive} falls. A correlator whose
pinned five-by-five is PSD (contractive, by the equivalence) with S squared above eight;
\code{npa\_psd\_implies\_tsirelson\_bound} falls. The PR box and the classical mixture (1, 0, 1, 0) are
\emph{not} counterexamples to any of these. Both fail contraction by plain arithmetic (the table
in Appendix~\ref{sub:chsh-five}), which is exactly what the theorems need them to
do.
On the machine: a raised flag from a clean start with no passing CHECK of the packed-counts property
before it, or whose counts give $S^2 > 8$; \code{small\_chsh\_flag\_implies\_tsirelson} falls. A
tally that passes the seven facts while its pinned matrix isn't PSD, or one with every pair sampled
and a PSD pinned matrix that fails them; \code{small\_chsh\_check\_iff} falls. The all-ones tally and
the PR box being refused are not counterexamples; those refusals are the point.

\emph{The nine-by-nine (Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).} A point and five extra numbers where the
contraction-like condition holds and the nine-by-nine isn't PSD, or the other way round;
\code{q1ab\_psd\_iff\_column\_contractive} falls. A point where the condition holds with all five
extras at zero and S is above two; \code{q1ab\_check\_at\_gzero\_implies\_classical\_bound} falls.

\emph{The elliptope completion (Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).} This one's a shape, so you're trying
to push a point in or out of it. Three targets, one per theorem, plus the decider beside it. Signs $a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1$,
each squaring to one, and a vector on which the completed matrix of that plan goes negative;
\code{deterministic\_strategy\_elliptope} falls. A correlator with some positive semidefinite
completion and S squared above eight; \code{elliptope\_tsirelson}
falls. Real numbers x and y that
