make the PR box's completed matrix positive semidefinite; \code{pr\_box\_not\_elliptope} falls. And
for the decider that sits beside it: inputs on which it says yes while the correlators have
no PSD completion at all (S squared above eight is one way to show that);
\code{elliptope\_check\_full\_sound} falls. The all-ones plan and (1, 0, 1, 0) aren't counterexamples here either, from the other side: the
completion admits them (\code{turing\_point\_elliptope} for the second), which is what the theorems
require.

\emph{The audit (Section~\ref{sec:coq}).} Run the assumption probe on any theorem the book cites
and find a project-local axiom or parameter in its dependencies, and the claim of zero of them
falls. For the small machine, its hosts and the universal programs, compile any of their files
and find a printed assumption line that isn't closed. Run the
Inquisitor and read what it says; it fails on high and medium findings. A new finding means
somebody looks. It doesn't automatically mean a theorem is false.

\subsection{What's mine and what isn't}

This is not a claim to have been first. Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine} does the sorting item by
item, with sources: what was known, what's added, and what kind of addition it is. Here's the
short form, and I'd welcome correction on any boundary.

\emph{Borrowed, with names.} As the opening chapter warned, I usually had the hunch first and
found these names after, and that order doesn't make any of it mine. Everything in Part I (every
source is cited where it's used), the category theory (Eilenberg, Mac Lane) included. Minsky's
two-counter machines and the Coq library that proves their halting undecidable and compiles
computable functions into them (Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors). Turing, Church, Kleene, Rice, Cantor, Gödel, the
diagonal pattern, Lawvere's unification, and the mechanized versions of them:
Michael Norrish's in HOL4, Mario Carneiro's in
Lean, and Yannick Forster, Fabian Kunze and Gert Smolka's in Coq. Bell, CHSH, Tsirelson, Stephanie Wehner's semidefinite proof of Tsirelson's bound (2006), NPA, Landau,
Masanes, Fine, the elliptope, and the machine-checked proofs of Tsirelson's bound that came
before mine (Echenim and Mhalla in Isabelle, and Lean's mathlib). Landauer, Bennett, Szilard,
Maxwell, and their critics. The potential method (Tarjan) and its mechanizations (Nipkow,
Charguéraud and Pottier), Lamport's clocks, Floyd and Hoare. Gettier, Necula, Cook, Hartley,
Shannon, Rissanen. Zurek. The guarantee about every program: the reference monitor (Anderson),
execution monitors (Schneider), and monitors checked at every instruction and verified in Coq
(Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors). The counting under the permanence results: Poincaré's
recurrence, as Zermelo used it. The seL4 and CompCert discipline. The facts under the permanence results are Landauer's own example and Shannon's
bounds, and ``set a bit to one whatever it held'' is my way of saying his RESTORE TO ONE.

\emph{Formal reconstructions.} The Coq development defines the state types, transition systems,
real-matrix predicates, encodings, and proof terms this book uses. When I say a theorem is
checked, I mean the stated proposition has a kernel-checked proof under its printed
premises. That doesn't make the underlying idea mine, and it doesn't make it new.

\emph{What this project proved, inside its stated interfaces.} The abstract floor, which is the
potential method with one particular potential. The derivation of the toll from finiteness,
permanence, and a named price, in counted states and in bits, with each premise's
counterexample built. The eight-state machine on which every one of those premises is a theorem.
The window that can't price the flag exactly, and the small machine's own colliding pair. The
latch form over any base, with its two counterexamples and converse. The small machine's earned record from a clean
start (checked, then committed, then certified, about
the same edition, nothing forged, three at least), its exact ledger, its universality through Minsky, the definition of Thiele-complete that
every clock fails and the window blindness of every machine meeting it, the universal program $U$ with its guest's halting and flag matched exactly, its ledger equal to
the guest's at every matching point, and its own flag earned, the priced
program $U_P$ that runs every computably presented Thiele machine with its reading latched, its
flag earned on the guest's own reading and its ledger within two of the guest's when the
reading starts at no, a surcharge no program on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid for a raise that costs less than
three,
and the simpler host's mirror, its isolation and its refusal to certify for free. The substrate
diagonal and the L results, with Rice's and Kleene's theorems on the machine's host and Rice's from
the clean start on the two-counter machine. The integer check, exact for every pair being sampled and the pinned matrix being PSD
(and so a sufficient test for the bound, which tells you nothing about quantum behaviour), the equivalence with
contraction, Tsirelson's bound from PSD, which is known mathematics checked again here, and the
check earned on the host, a raised flag standing on it. Structural entitlement for every
Thiele-complete machine, with its worked members, its floor that takes no supplied tree and its
proof that the covering can't be dropped; the eight-state machine run by the small machine; the time
a check saves; and the collision of every bare-transcript verifier on every Thiele-complete machine.
All of it with premises printed.
Of
that list, the toll derivation as a rule on a ledger (Ouldridge and Wolpert priced the same
merge in entropy first), the pricing form of the window fact, and the latch form are
the only pieces I'd call new statements, and only in the sense that I didn't find them stated
where I looked. The fourth thing I'd name is built and checked, and its idea isn't new: a
record that's priced, and on the small machine earned, under the reference monitor's
every-program move, which is old and isn't mine. Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine} names the same four the same
way, with the prior work beside each.

\emph{Interpretation, which is mine and not proved.} That structure is what a computation
establishes and the toll is the right thing to price. That certification is the pointer
event. That the record axis ``belongs in the step.'' Those are proposals, with the arguments
I've given, and the proposals are where I'd aim first if I were you.

%===========================================================================
\section{The claim ledger}
\label{sec:ledger}
%===========================================================================

Here's everything this book claims, one line each: what kind of claim it is, and where it
lives. ``Proved'' means proved under the premises printed in that section, and nothing more.
If a line here ever says more than its section does, the section is right and the line is
wrong. ``By unfolding'' after it means the proof does little more than read the answer off the
definitions, a case split whose every branch is a line: true, checked, and carrying almost
nothing the definitions didn't already say. If you're counting results, count those
differently. I mark them so they don't pad the list.

Ledger is a good word for it, and it's older than bookkeeping. Around 1400 a \emph{ledger} was a
book that lay permanently in one place, a big church breviary, say, from the old verb
\emph{leggen}, to lay; the account-book sense turns up in the 1500s. A book that stays put. That's
the job here too. The home sections are long and they wander, and this is the one place where
every claim lies still, so you can come back and find it where you left it.

\subsection{Claims about the model}

First the model. Every line in this table is about any system that has the pieces the line
names: a state and a step, plus whatever the result asks for, a reading and the toll, a
counter and a price list, a window, programs. None of them is about my machine, except the lines that run these results on it,
which say so and point to Section~\ref{sec:part3-on-machine}. The table
runs over several pages, in reading order.

Here's one way to use it, and it takes five minutes. Pick the sentence in this book you trust
least. Find its line. Read the Kind column before anything else. Then go to the home section
and check that the line says no more than the section does. If it says more, you've found my
mistake, and the end of this section says what I'd like done about it.

\subsection{Claims about the machine}

Part IV built one small machine and the hosts that run it, and the ledger keeps them apart from the
model. The machine is the small one of Section~\ref{sec:smallest}, two counters and six instructions, where commitments are earned
and universality is proved, with the definition of Thiele-complete that every machine can be
held against, the universal program $U$ on a host made of the same instruction kinds, and the
priced program $U_P$ that runs every computably presented Thiele machine. Every line in the
next tables is about those machines, or about every machine meeting that definition, or about
the game check and the physics section that close Part IV, and nothing else, under the premises
printed in its section.

\subsection{What I propose}

And then there's what I'm proposing. These are mine. They reach further than any theorem in
here, and nothing in the tables puts an unavoidable physical price on every observable change.

\begin{itemize}
\item That the axis belongs in the step (Section~\ref{sec:scope}, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}).
\item That the usual account of a computation is a shadow of the step (Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}).
\item That certification is the event worth recording, which is the pointer conjecture (Section~\ref{sec:pointer}).
\item That this is a structural account of computation, with a cost model as one part of it (Section~\ref{sec:scope}).
\item That the toll is the right thing to price. The alternatives are a wall or a penalty for contradiction (Section~\ref{sec:models}, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}).
\end{itemize}

And three things this book doesn't settle, with what would settle each. Whether Landauer's critics are
right, which would leave every theorem standing and one premise unowned by the world: that takes
measurements of real devices (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). Whether certification really is the
pointer event: that takes a definition of the systems the conjecture is about, and Section~\ref{sec:pointer}
gives three ways to kill it. And whether there's a smaller start than a partition: that takes a ruler
someone can state and a smaller structure measured by it (Section~\ref{sec:structure}).

That's the whole ledger. If you find a claim in this book that isn't on it, or a line that
says more than its home does, that's my mistake, and I'd want to hear about it.

%===========================================================================
\section{Scope}
\label{sec:scope}
%===========================================================================

This is the line around what I've proved. Inside it: an accounting law for one event, a
derivation of that law from premises each with its own counterexample, a set of windows
that provably lose it, a record axis that's a latch over any base, a diagonal that holds by
proof on L, a six-instruction machine on which commitments are earned and which computes what
two counters can, one fixed program in its instruction kinds, run on a host with more
counters and one paid move, that runs every computably presented Thiele machine,
and an integer check that implies a bound by algebra. Outside it:
everything that follows. This is the fence. I built it myself, so lean on it before you
trust it.

G. K. Chesterton, the English writer who has been called the prince of paradox, has a famous
fence, in a 1929 book called \emph{The Thing}. A reformer finds a
fence across a road, can't see what it's for, and wants it cleared away; the wiser one tells
him to go off and find out why it was put there, and only then come back and argue for tearing
it down. This section runs the other way round. Every post below comes labelled with what it's
there for, the overclaim it stops, so you don't have to go off and find out first. Pull up any
post you like. Just look at what walks through the gap when you do.

\emph{Physical interpretation of the counter.} The ledger is unique once the start and schedule
are chosen. That doesn't make it entropy, and it doesn't make it energy. A physical bridge
needs a model of which states carry information, premises that can all hold at once, and a
real argument tying the formal charge to dissipation. The permanent-certificate theorems
supply the first for an abstract finite machine with a permanent reading. The two premises
are shown able to hold together whenever every counted step costs at least one, and for a
one-bit reset. The small machine's free steps merge states and are charged nothing, which
breaks the bridge for its whole instruction set (Section~\ref{sec:landauer}), and the calorimeter protocol shows that population
dynamics don't fix the energy scale. No joule value attaches to one mark without thermal and
device premises (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, Section~\ref{sec:landauer}).
Once you pick the start and the price list, the number is forced by arithmetic, and
it isn't energy. What I'd need before it could be is the list at the top of this paragraph.

\emph{Class separation.} The witnesses show specific windows losing specific fields. They don't
stop a conventional simulator from keeping those fields in its encoding. No separation of
standard complexity classes follows from the collisions (Section~\ref{sec:windows},
Section~\ref{sec:smallest}).
I'll be blunt about why I'm careful here. Whether P equals NP is one of the seven problems the
Clay Mathematics Institute put a million dollars on, at a meeting in Paris in May 2000. One of
the seven has been solved since, the Poincaré conjecture, by the mathematician Grigori Perelman, who posted the proof as preprints in 2002 and 2003. P versus NP
hasn't. If a two-state collision on my machine settled it, I'd be owed a million
dollars. Nobody owes me anything. A window that loses a field is a fact about that window. A
complexity class is a fact about what every possible program can do within a budget, and
nothing in these collisions reaches that far.

\emph{Trace initiality, and what it doesn't settle.} The universal property of the trace fold is
about evaluating lists of instructions: pick where a target starts, and there's exactly one
way to fold a list into it (Section~\ref{sec:counter}, checked as
\code{nec\_f\_fold\_unique}). The counter's uniqueness
assumes a schedule. Exact pricing assumes an event, and a reference count that says what
charging too much means (Section~\ref{sec:windows}). Those results make the construction precise. None of them
shows that the schedule I chose, or the event I chose, is physically necessary.

\emph{Other observables.} Certification is one worked example. A family of other observations
might turn up other structural laws, but each would need its own events, its own evidence,
and its own cost rules, justified on their own terms. The window and oracle
results are about
what specific maps
keep, and nothing more.

\emph{Program predicates versus state observations.} The state-level collision (Section~\ref{sec:windows}'s wall) and
the program-level diagonal (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}'s wall) live in different domains. Linking them would take a
theorem of its own. The nat family and L (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}) keep their explicit
quantifiers and representability premises.

\emph{Entitlement bounds.} The count is handed its tree and its covering, along with the
payment condition. It doesn't dig the tree out of an arbitrary run, and it isn't a Shannon bound
on every trace (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}). On every Thiele-complete machine the payment is
the record moves, each exactly one mark, and a floor that takes no tree exists when the questions
are the run's own CHECKs; but its answers are taken at the rivals as they start, a free branch can
still narrow for nothing, the lists, tree and fibres are supplied except in the worked members,
and the covering can't be dropped. The search through $n$ bits is capped at 16 questions by the
machine's fact table, and the time tax is a lower bound for programs of INC and DEC only. Nothing here
extends it to every Thiele-complete machine (Section~\ref{sec:part3-on-machine}).

\emph{Quantum behaviour.} The fixed-matrix equivalence is about one completion with zero
marginals and zero within-party moments. The elliptope lets the within-party moments move,
at the level of correlators. Full behaviours with marginals, and operator realisations, need
identifications this book doesn't make. A sound check isn't complete for those bigger sets,
and the elliptope decider is mathematics. None of the small machine's properties is it
(Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).

\emph{The record axis.} The proved structural result is: a permanent record driven by a base
computation is a latch on an event; on a finite machine its write merges states; and the named
windows don't recover it. Certification is one instance. No theorem
selects it as the unique event every system must record (Section~\ref{sec:latch}, Section~\ref{sec:pointer}). A finite monotone
multi-valued record decomposes into threshold latches. One Boolean latch can't hold it.
Revocation, including revocation priced from the other side as in Casper, lies outside the
permanent-record axis; a price on revocation doesn't transfer to a price on the write (Section~\ref{sec:models}).
Probabilistic records don't inherit the uniqueness result either. Two honest random records
can have the same branches and the same charges and still give those branches different
weights, one choosing evenly and one two to one, so the schedule doesn't fix the
probabilities (\code{schedule\_determines\_probabilities\_refuted}). And no single deterministic
latch explains a record that can branch both ways from the same observation
(\code{deterministic\_latch\_handles\_branching\_refuted}).
Weak base equivalence is defined and is an equivalence; no two of the three bases of
Definition~\ref{def:u11-concrete-bases}, and none of them and the small machine, are related by it in
the checked work, and the latch form holds on each separately, so it doesn't tell
them apart (Section~\ref{sec:latch}).
A record driven by the computation that stays up is a latch, and on a finite machine its write merges states;
which event deserves the latch isn't proved; records that can come back down lie outside all
of this (they're limit computability's, and Section~\ref{sec:latch} points at Ershov's ladder),
and random ones lose the uniqueness.

\emph{Who it's safe against.} Every guarantee about the record is about programs: any list of
instructions, run from a clean start on a step that does what its definition says, one writer
stepping at a time. That covers the buggy program and the hostile one. It doesn't cover whoever
sets the start (a snapshot put back, a table loaded with facts nobody checked), a reset or a
power cycle, whoever picks the program, the wire that carries the report, someone who
flips the flag with a probe, the tools that built the step, or a second writer that changes a
counter without bumping its edition. Those are the operator, the device and the tool chain,
and they're outside this fence. A record read by someone who didn't watch it being made is only
as good as their reason to believe the box that shows it. The ways across that I know of, a quote
over measured state and a proof that travels on its own, are in Section~\ref{sec:windows} and
Section~\ref{sec:models}, and this book builds neither.

\emph{The diagonal on the machine.} What's proved for the small machine's programs is that
halting is undecidable in the library's synthetic sense, for them and for the universal program
(Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). L has its recursion theorem, Rice and halting by proof
(Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}). On the host machine, the one with a counter for every number, Rice's
theorem holds for properties that depend on everything a program ends with (every register, the
table, the channel, the trap, the ledger and the flag; the line number and the versions are left out), for
programs run on an input in register 1; s-m-n holds with no premise on register 2; and Kleene's recursion theorem
holds for the transformations a host program carries out on numbers, with a fixed point that agrees with
its image on stopping, register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the number of facts and whether
the channel is empty; for some of these transformations no fixed point agrees on every register. On the
two-counter machine itself Rice's theorem is proved on every input, with facts compared by what they're
about, their versions left out of the comparison; Kleene's is proved with inputs written as powers of two and refuted
with plain inputs (Section~\ref{sec:small-diagonal}).

\emph{The five models.} Each is a fragment transcribed from a specification, with a named
theorem and a named limit: the Casper transcription has no deposits or fork choice; the gas
fragment omits the refund cap; the attestation fragment has no signatures; the transparency
verifier covers control flow and leaves collision resistance out; the proof-carrying checker is
a
three-instruction memory-bounds language. None is a claim about the real system beyond its fragment
(Section~\ref{sec:models}).

\emph{The machine.} Part IV has one small machine, with the hosts that run it,
and here's its fence. The small machine of
Section~\ref{sec:smallest} (two counters, six instructions) is where commitments are
earned: from a clean start, a raised flag went through a passing check, a commitment and a certification of the
same claim, nothing is forged, and the cheapest certificate costs exactly three, a price reached
by a check that could have failed (the step doesn't police trivial checks: a check that can't
fail certifies for three too). It's also
where universality is proved, by matching Minsky's two-counter machines step for step and
borrowing their undecidable halting from the Coq library. It's Thiele-complete under a
definition every clock-style machine fails, and every machine meeting that definition hides its
record and ledger from its own window. The universal Thiele machine is one fixed program, $U$,
on a host with the small machine's instruction kinds and more counters, with no guest step built
in: it runs every program of the small machine from every start, halts when the guest halts, raises
its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate exactly when the guest's flag would rise,
and keeps a ledger equal to the guest's at every matching point. With one paid move added, one
fixed program, $U_P$, runs every computably presented Thiele machine: its step, prices and
reading computed by programs, the reading decided on every state, the run fixed by a driver. The
host halts when the guest stops, its flag is the latch of the guest's reading, raised on its own
earned chain whose claim is that reading, and its ledger is the guest's plus a surcharge of at
most two when the reading starts at no, a surcharge no program on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid for a raise
that costs less than three. A machine whose reading no program decides is outside. A simpler
host with a guest step built in runs guests by construction and keeps a mirror of the guest's
flag; its ledger only covers the guest's. The small machine's check price is flat, its fact table holds sixteen,
and its certificate is historical (Section~\ref{sec:smallest} lists the rest).

\emph{The comparison machines.} The small machines I built to compare against are fragments too.
The random-access memory result covers an addressed list memory with load, increment and
decrement on cells (\code{concrete\_ram\_write\_reads\_back} and its neighbours), and it's about that
machine. The register machine Section~\ref{sec:latch} puts the latch on (\code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_on\_ram\_holds}) is
a different small machine, the one with indirect addressing, and that theorem is about it. The reversible-machine
result covers arithmetic update cores: add and subtract, each undone by the other, with or
without wrapping at a modulus (\code{janus\_like\_unbounded\_inverse}, \code{janus\_like\_bounded\_inverse}).
None is a theorem about real memories or full reversible languages. The cost-semantics
results are local correspondences, short of full cost-framework embeddings: the trace's cost is a
writer cost and a grade, and the toll is the potential method with one potential (Section~\ref{sec:counter}).
Nobody's whole type system gets embedded either.

\emph{Outward consequences.} I looked for results about real systems that would need the record
axis. Five narrow ones are proved, each as a two-state countermodel: a certificate-transparency
client's local tree head can't decide whether the world's log is consistent
(\code{ct\_local\_view\_insufficient}); a quote check that matches only the composite digest accepts a
mismatched selection (\code{tpm\_selection\_binding\_is\_necessary}); a local suffix can't decide a
trusted anchor (\code{weak\_subjective\_suffix\_insufficient}); an acknowledgement without a durable
commit record can be lost (\code{wal\_ack\_requires\_durability}); and a current local log can't
decide what happened before it (\code{audit\_local\_snapshot\_insufficient}). Each reduces to a known
indistinguishability or durability argument. Five stronger candidates would need protocol or
hardware semantics I haven't formalised, and I've proved nothing about them. So none of this
yields a new outside result that both needs the record axis and is ready to use.


\emph{Where each result lives.} Every system that follows the toll, whatever its states: the
floor, at most as many certifications as cost, and the potential-method reading. Every
finite machine whose price covers merges: the toll for permanent records, and, when its move names can
be decided equal or different, which
instructions every such price must charge. Every finite machine paying per halving: the
machine's own narrowing bound. Every machine extending a base with a driven, permanent
record: the latch. Every window through which a certifying and a non-certifying step look
alike: no exact price from the window. Every machine meeting the definition of Thiele-complete: a free move, at least three
marks on any run from a clean state that ends certified, and a window blind to the record
and the ledger. Any eight counts: the integer check and its PSD bridge, which are mathematics.
This machine only: its six instructions and their prices, its sixteen slots, its own colliding
pair, and the encodings its universal programs use.

\emph{What I'm proposing beyond that.} That the axis belongs in the step; that certification is
the event worth recording; that this is a structural account of computation,
with a cost model as one part
of it. Those reach further than any theorem here, and no theorem here puts an
unavoidable physical price on every observable change. They're the argument, and the
argument is what the rest of the book was. What kind of claim is that? A proposal about which
distinctions an account of computation ought to draw, and no proof settles an ``ought''. The
proofs show the proposal hangs together, follows from premises I've named, and costs little
(six instructions on the small machine); whether anyone should adopt it is something I
argue for and can't prove.
Here's what would weaken it: if every use people have for the record turned out to be
recoverable from a log the program writes plus a correctness proof about the program, or if the
real systems keep choosing walls over tolls for good reasons, as the five in
Section~\ref{sec:models} mostly did.

%===========================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
%===========================================================================

I started with one word and a machine I couldn't explain. Here's where the word ended up,
and where the machine did.

Structure, by the end of Part I, was relations among things, kept under chosen changes, carried by
whatever stuff, always relative to a frame. The start I chose, the smallest one by the count
of names, was a sorting of a pile, and the thing nobody I read had priced was the moment you
stand behind the sorting. That was Part I, and it ended with a question.

The question got an exact form in Part II: five parts, one rule, one theorem you proved at
the table. Then the rule stopped being only my preference. With finitely many yes-states and a flag
that stays up, every move that raises it merges states, and if forgetting is charged for, the way Landauer's
principle charges for it in its worst case, the toll follows. That's a derivation under three
premises you can refuse one at a time, each with its counterexample built. It isn't a proof that
every computation has to adopt the rule; and the charge on forgetting is a named premise with
its critics named. Learning can be free; committing to a record that stays put can't be, on
those premises. That's as far as physics goes in this book, and I've tried to keep it exactly
that far.

Part III was the logic, and here's what it earned, in the order it was earned. The counter
is arithmetic once the schedule is chosen. A window in which a raising step and a quiet one
look the same can't price the raise exactly, by a fact about functions far older than the
machine. Entitlement is defined as an object, a checked relation, and a paid event; given
lists, a tree and a covering somebody supplies, a run that paid a charged step for every level
of the tree has paid for the index bits it commits to (no run is shown to have to pay them); on
every Thiele-complete machine the same count, for a run from a clean start, is a theorem about its record moves, with the earned
chain inside the run, and the count can't do without the covering; and it
is a license to lean on a claim. It doesn't prove the claim true.
Insight, in the sense the toll prices, is a committed relation. A feeling doesn't count. Its floor
is flat: at least one, however deep. The claim behind the flag is something a check could
have refused, and in the bare model nothing makes the commit wait for the check. Over any base,
an honest record is a latch, with two free choices, the event and the price list; ``only one
substrate'' is false and ``one structure, many price lists'' is true once the event is fixed. No
procedure the substrate itself can represent decides the shortcut predicate, given a
recursion theorem, by the same diagonal that broke Frege's floor, and the machine's answer is
to record the commitment. It leaves the judgement unautomated. Of five record disciplines I
modelled in fragments, one prices the write. And which event to record is a conjecture, with
its refutations listed.

Part IV built one small machine, two counters and six instructions, with hosts to run it, and on
it the model stands whole: from a clean start, a raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified, on the
same edition of the same counter, nothing gets forged, the cheapest certificate whose check
could have failed costs exactly three (the step doesn't police trivial checks), and it
computes everything Minsky's two-counter machines can, so its halting is
undecidable. Earned commitments and universality are proved there. So is what
Thiele-complete has to mean: a universal base that's free and can't touch the record, a record that stays up once it's
up, an earned
record, one mark for each check, commit and certificate, and some claim whose check can fail. Every clock,
every machine that charges for computing, fails it; the small machine meets it; and every machine
that meets it hides its record and its ledger from its own window. And so is a universal Thiele
machine, with its scope said plainly: one fixed program, $U$, written in the small machine's own
six kinds of instruction on a host with more counters, with no guest step built in, that runs
every small-machine program from every start, halts exactly when its guest halts, raises its own
flag by its own check, commit and certificate exactly when the guest's would, and keeps a ledger
equal to the
guest's at every matching point. And then the bigger version of the same thing: with one paid move added,
one fixed program, $U_P$, runs every computably presented Thiele machine, a machine from
anywhere whose driver, step, prices and reading are computed by programs. It halts when the guest
stops, raises its own flag on its own earned chain exactly when the guest's reading has said
yes, with the guest's own reading as the claim it checked, and, when the guest's reading starts at no, keeps the guest's prices
to within a surcharge of at most two, which no program on
that host, run from a clean start, can avoid for a raise that costs less than three. An ordinary programmable computer, as built, doesn't do that for the
programs it runs; $U$ and $U_P$ show a fixed interpreter can. All of it is proved in Coq with
nothing assumed: each file prints the assumptions of every headline theorem, and every line
comes back closed. Then a check worth earning, the two-player game with an integer test whose
pass forces Tsirelson's bound, and what the counter has to do with physics, which is less than
the word Landauer in a file name suggests. The places where the machine came up short of the
idea stayed on the page: its free steps merge states, so the toll on it is a choice the chairs
don't force, and a check that can't fail certifies for three like any other. Part V was how to
check it and how to break it. Every result carries the shape of the thing that would
kill it, gathered in one place (Section~\ref{sec:falsification}): a state of the small machine
and an instruction after which the ledger goes down; a contractive correlator whose pinned matrix isn't positive semidefinite; a
certification system that follows the toll and certifies at total cost zero; a function on
numbers that correctly decides the shortcut predicate of the substrate built from it. Any one
of them brings down the theorem it matches. I hunted. I came up empty. For a theorem Coq has
checked, that's no surprise: finding one would take a bug in the checker. The places a reader can really win are where my sentence says more
than the statement does, or a definition doesn't catch the word it's named for, and
Section~\ref{sec:falsification} starts with those.

If you asked what's new here, I wouldn't give you one thing, because there isn't one. There
are four, and each comes with its fence and its neighbours. First, the toll isn't only my
preference: on a finite machine a reading nothing turns off can only be turned on by a step that
merges states, so if merges are priced, raising it costs (Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges},
Theorem~\ref{thm:toll-derived}). The counting under it is the finite cousin of the recurrence
argument Zermelo threw at Boltzmann in 1896, and the price on a merge is Landauer's, as a
premise. Ouldridge and Wolpert (2023) had already put a physical price on that merge for finite
automata, so what's here is the toll as a rule on a ledger. Second, a window that shows a raising step and a quiet one the same can't price the
raise exactly (Theorem~\ref{thm:shadow-price}); that a price computed from what a window shows
can't tell apart two steps the window shows the same is elementary, and what's here is the
pricing form. Third, a record driven by the
computation that never switches off is a latch on one event, over any base
(Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch}); latches and history variables are old, and the theorem covers
only records that never come down. Fourth, a record that's priced, and on the small machine
earned (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned}), under the move of guaranteeing something about
every program. That move isn't mine at all. It's the reference monitor's (Anderson, 1972),
made precise for monitors that watch a run (Schneider, 2000), and verified in Coq for monitors
checked at every instruction (Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors, 2015). What's put together under
it here is built and checked, and its idea isn't new: the check bound to the edition it looked
at, the toll paid on top, and universal programs that carry both to every program of the small
machine and to every computably presented Thiele machine, earning their own flag as they go.
Appendix~\ref{sec:whats-mine} sorts all four with sources.

And two things I'd point at if you asked how far the checking reaches. Neither is a fifth new
thing.

In the game: an integer check on eight counts forces a five-by-five matrix to be positive
semidefinite, and from there the Tsirelson bound follows, and the chain never once reaches for
physics. No Hilbert space, no operators, no observables. The route through the matrix is the
first rung of a ladder Navascués, Pironio and Acín built in 2007. None of that route is mine, and
the semidefinite road to Tsirelson's bound is older than that. What's here is the check that runs in
whole numbers, and the checked link from ``the check passed'' to the bound. It's algebra you can
follow line by line, and the assumption audit on that link finds exactly three standard
axioms from Coq's own library (two that come with its real numbers, and functional
extensionality) and nothing of mine, which is how anyone can see
that no physics was smuggled in. And on the small machine's host a raised flag can stand on that
check: from a clean start a raised flag contains a passing CHECK of the packed counts, a COMMIT and
a CERTIFY, and the check passes exactly when every pair was sampled and the five-by-five is
positive semidefinite (Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).

In the model: the diagonal rules out a correct decider whenever its flip can be expressed
inside the substrate and the substrate supplies the fixed point; in L the fixed point is
proved from the reduction rules and the diagonal is Rice's theorem. On the small machine's host,
Kleene's recursion theorem and Rice's theorem are proved for its own programs, so the wall stands
there by proof, with its premise a theorem: no host program decides a property of what a program
computes that some program has and some lacks; such a property is undecidable in the library's
sense (Section~\ref{sec:small-diagonal}).

What this book doesn't settle, by my count. Whether the toll is the \emph{right} thing to price. The
five real systems mostly built a
wall or a penalty for contradiction.
Whether certification is the pointer event. Whether Landauer's critics
are right, which would leave every theorem standing and one premise unowned by the world.
And the question I'd most like someone to take from me: is there a smaller start than a
partition, by a ruler they can state? I said in Section~\ref{sec:structure} it would change this book. It would.

And the two computers from the first pages, the sorter and the copier, holding the same bits.
Walk the warehouse again. On an ordinary machine there's still no lamp for what the sorter did,
and nothing in this book changes that. On the small machine there is one: a flag and a counter
you can read off the state, and a theorem that, from a clean start, the flag can't be up unless
some claim went through a passing check, a commit about the same edition and a certificate, in that order, where a claim can be any
property, in a language with an exact
equality test, whose checker is proved to mean what it says, ``this counter, read as a list, is
sorted'' among them (\code{sorted\_run\_certifies\_iff} and \code{sorted\_run\_refused\_forever}, EarnedGeneric.v). That's the one lamp I set
out to light. It's a lamp for whoever can read this machine's state. A ``tests passed'' sheet
fits it only when the test is a checker proved to mean what it says; the sticker and the very
sure AI from the first pages ask something else, whether to believe a report you didn't watch
being made, and nothing in this book answers that (Section~\ref{sec:scope}). Whether every
machine ought to have that lamp is the argument. No proof here settles it.

So that's the Thiele Machine. An abstract model with five parts and one rule, an argument
made with it that the usual account of a computation is a shadow and the axis it leaves out
belongs in the step, and one small machine to check the argument against, with one fixed
program, written in its instruction kinds plus one paid move and run on a host with more counters, that runs every machine of the model whose workings a program can present.
The theorems are what they are, with their premises printed. The interpretation is mine, and
I've tried to say at every turn which is which, because the first time through I was the
only one checking, and I've met me, and that's not enough people. Now there's you.


\appendix

%===========================================================================
\section{Things I had to learn first}
\label{sec:vocab}
%===========================================================================

I came in with none of the formal fields this work turned out to need. By the time the
proofs compiled I'd needed enough of half a dozen of
them that I had to put down somewhere what those fields had words for. This appendix is that
place. None of it is the argument. It's what I needed to be able to make it. Everything
below is what I understood after I went and read about it; I'm not claiming to teach you
these subjects, and if you already know a part, skip it.

\subsection{Bits, bytes, and what a CPU sees}

A bit is one digit that's either zero or one, the smallest fact a machine can hold.
Everything else is bits stacked up. Eight of them make a byte, which lands you any number
from 0 to 255, and the first thing that genuinely surprised me is that the same byte is also
a letter: a convention called ASCII simply agrees to call 65 the letter A, 48 the digit 0,
32 a space. Nothing in the byte knows which it is. The meaning is a convention laid on top.

You can see the convention's seams with a pencil. Write 65 in binary: 1000001. Knock off the
first two digits and what's left, 00001, is 1, and A is the first letter. B is 66, which ends in
00010, two. Now lower case: a is 97, which is 1100001, the same pattern with one more bit
switched on, the one worth 32. Every capital and its small letter differ in exactly that bit.
That's on purpose. The first version of the code, in 1963, had no lower case at all; when lower
case arrived, in the 1967 revision, it was placed so the two cases differ by one bit, which made
matching them, and building keyboards and printers, simpler. Nothing in the byte knows it's a
letter, but somebody made the letters easy for a circuit to tell apart.

Everything in this subsection is about real CPUs. None of it belongs to the abstract model,
which has a kind of state and a step rule and nothing about widths or slots, and the small
machine of Part IV needs very little of it: its two counters have no width at all, and hold any
whole number.

A word is a chunk of bits the CPU treats as one unit, these days usually 32 bits (0 to about
4 billion) or 64 (0 to about 18 quintillion). The abstract model doesn't care which width.

A register is a named storage slot inside the CPU that holds one word, the fastest place to
read or write. Memory is a longer list of word-sized slots accessed by index, the address. The
program counter is one specific register that tracks where in the program the machine is;
after every instruction it moves on to the next instruction unless the instruction says jump. On the small
machine it's called the line number. A stack pointer is a register pointing at the top of a
region used for nested calls. A port is a named channel for talking to the outside world.

Modular arithmetic means counting wraps around: counting modulo 16, the numbers run 0 to 15, and 17
wraps to 1.
Bitwise operations work on the bits of a value one position at a time: AND is 1 only when
both bits are, OR when either is, XOR (exclusive or) exactly when they differ. A shift moves
every bit left or right, which multiplies or divides by a power of two. Popcount is the
count of one-bits in a value. Hexadecimal is base 16, digits 0 to 9 then A to F, written
with a 0x prefix: 0xFF is 255.

A trap, on a CPU, means execution jumps to a fixed handler and the program stops advancing, the chip's
``this went wrong.'' On the small machine a trap is one bit that goes up when an instruction
refuses, and then the core stops moving. An ISA, instruction set architecture, is the list of
every instruction a CPU recognises, each identified by an opcode, a numeric tag the CPU
decodes. The small machine's has six. The abstract model has none; it has a step rule.

\subsection{The notation the formal parts use}

I don't think in these symbols, and I had to learn to read them. The natural numbers are 0,
1, 2, and so on, written with a double-struck N; the integers add the negatives; the reals
are the whole number line. A function from a set A to a set B is written with an arrow. For
a finite set, vertical bars around it mean its size; for a number, its absolute value. A big
sigma is a sum over every member of a set. A delta before a quantity means the change in it.
An upside-down A means ``for every''; a backwards E means ``there exists.'' A double arrow is
implication; a double-headed one is ``if and only if.'' A small circle between two functions is
composition, apply the right one first. Angle brackets mean one of three things, and the sentence around them says which: a pair of numbers packed
into one, $\langle m, n \rangle$ (Section~\ref{sec:universal-host}); a dot product of two vectors; or, around a random quantity,
its
long-run average, which I picked up from the Bell-test papers. The quantum sense of a circled times never appears, because the game section
does its work in plain integer arithmetic. A superscript T on a matrix is its transpose, rows
and columns swapped, and I with a subscript n is the identity matrix.

\subsection{Coq, in just enough detail}

Coq is a proof assistant: a programming language whose type system is expressive enough that
proofs are programs and the compiler checks them (Part V has the long version). A Theorem is
a named statement followed by a proof; a Lemma is the same thing used for an intermediate
result; a Definition introduces a named value; an Inductive type is one with a finite list of
constructors, the only ways to build a value of it (Coq's natural numbers have two: zero, and
successor of another natural). A tactic is a step inside a proof: induction (base case, then
step), destruct (split into cases), reflexivity (prove a thing equals itself), simpl
(compute), lia and lra and nra (arithmetic solvers for integers, linear reals, and
polynomial reals), psatz (a certificate search for polynomial inequalities). Qed ends a
proof and asks Coq to check the whole chain. Admitted is the keyword for ``I claim this
without proof,'' and it appears nowhere in the active tree. A Hypothesis inside a Section is a
named premise that becomes an argument of every theorem that uses it when the Section
closes; ``closed under the global context'' doesn't make it go away. Print Assumptions lists
the global axioms a theorem depends on; on the kernel tier it shows only standard-library
ones. A total function always returns a value, and Coq requires every function to be total;
the small machine's step function is, traps included. ``Parametric in K'' means the proof
works for any K; the small machine's table size, sixteen, is a literal constant, and the proofs
are about that literal.

\subsection{Category theory beyond Part I}

Section~\ref{sec:structure} sketches objects, arrows, composition, identities, associativity,
and the identity laws. Beyond that: a functor is a structure-preserving map from one category to
another, sending objects to objects and arrows to arrows while respecting composition and
identities; think of it as a translation rule between two worlds of structure. An embedding
is a functor that throws nothing away, and faithful is the precise version for arrows: two
distinct arrows never land on one. Conservative is the version for inverses: if the
image of an arrow has an inverse, the arrow already had one, so the functor can't
manufacture an isomorphism (an arrow with an inverse) that wasn't there. The two properties
are different, and neither gives the other. Read the natural numbers under addition as a
category with one object and an arrow for each number, and the same for the integers. The
inclusion of the first into the second is faithful, since distinct naturals stay
distinct
integers. It isn't conservative: 1 has no inverse among the naturals, and its
image has one,
minus 1. The other way round, the functor from the integers
onto the trivial one-arrow group
is conservative, since every arrow of the integers already
has an inverse. It isn't faithful:
it sends every integer to the same arrow. An embedding needs faithfulness specifically. A
monoidal product combines two objects or two arrows into one, with a unit and laws that make
the combining behave. An initial object has exactly one arrow into
every object; the counter's uniqueness in this book is a uniqueness-on-reachable-states
fact, and no category-theoretic initial object is involved. Yoneda's lemma is where the categorical
engine first clicked for me, the night I stopped borrowing other people's runtimes, and
nothing in the formal development uses it.

\subsection{Bell-test vocabulary}

A correlation between two outcomes is the average of their product; with outcomes plus or
minus one it lies between minus one and one, plus one meaning always match, minus one always
differ. A correlator is one such average in a labelled setting, E00 for Alice's setting 0
and Bob's 0. The marginal of a joint distribution is the distribution of one side alone with
the other averaged out; zero-marginal means each side's outcome is plus or minus one equally
often on average. A local hidden-variable model is one where both outcomes are fixed by a
shared random variable agreed before the game plus each side's own setting; Bell's theorem
says no such model produces certain correlations quantum mechanics does. No-signalling means
neither side's marginal depends on the other's setting. Quantum-realisable means compatible
with some quantum state and measurements; the NPA hierarchy gives a ladder of necessary
tests, each a positive-semidefiniteness condition on a moment matrix, and no single rung is
known to be sufficient in general
(Chaturvedi's 2026 preprint argues none is, even for this game). The PR box is the no-signalling correlation that wins the game every
time, stronger than quantum mechanics allows. Cauchy-Schwarz is
the inequality that a dot product is bounded by the product of the lengths. The Tsirelson
bound is two root two, the largest game score quantum mechanics allows; the classical bound
is two and the PR bound is four. (If you go looking for Boris Tsirelson's 1980 paper, look
under Cirel'son, the spelling the journal printed, or you may not find it.) The elliptope is
the set of correlators that can be filled
out into a positive-semidefinite matrix.


\subsection{Other terms I use without rebuilding}

Provenance is the recorded chain of where an object came from; on the small machine, a
commitment's provenance is the passing check that came before it (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}).
Simulation, in computer science, is one system
imitating another's input-output behaviour; a Turing machine simulates any system of the model
whose step a program can compute, my machine included, by writing the whole state out on its tape, and the difference
this book is about is what a window on that tape shows. That's real, and it raises a fair
question: if a tape can stand in for the state, what was the
difference? The tape carries a picture of the state, the way a photograph carries a
fire, and a photograph of a fire keeps you exactly as warm as any other photograph. The counter and the toll live in
the step rule. An encoding copies the bytes, and the step rule isn't in them. A Turing machine built
with the toll in its own transition table is a different case: it's an instance of the
model, and it simulates nothing. What no machine can do is make a simulated rule binding just
by writing it down on tape.

Projection is a function that drops information on purpose. The window on the small machine
keeps three things, the line number and the two counters, which are what Minsky's machine
already has, and that's why projecting lands you back in ordinary computation. It drops
everything else, including the parts doing the new work: the versions, the table of checked
facts, the channel, the ledger and the flag. Nothing is wrong with it. It's a perfectly good
function. It just costs you what made the state more than a pair of counters. A quotient is the operation of declaring two things the same when
they agree on what you chose to look at and working with the classes instead. A projection
does exactly that. Dropping fields one at a time also glues together states that
the dropped fields kept apart. The fibre of a function over a value is
everything the function sends to that value. An injection sends no two inputs to the same
output; a surjection covers every output. Decidable means an algorithm always halts with a
yes-or-no answer; keep the claim and the algorithm apart, since the algorithm decides the
claim only once there's a proof that its answer matches. Polynomial time means running time
bounded by a power of the input size; P is the problems solvable that way, NP the problems
where a candidate solution can be \emph{checked} that way, and whether the two are the same is
open.

``Kernel'' wears three hats in this book, so here they are before one of them ambushes
you. First, mathematics: the kernel of a map is what it sends to the identity, and for a
projection the useful version is the relation ``these two states project to the same thing.''
Second, the proofs, where the hat comes in two sizes: the kernel tier, the part of the Coq
development where the model is written down and its main theorems live (Section~\ref{sec:coq}),
with the link files that tie the small machine to them;
and Coq's own kernel, the small checker that accepts or rejects every proof. Third, the
operating-system kernel, which I never use and mention only so you know it isn't meant. The
sentence around the word always says which one is.

\subsection{Matrices}

A matrix is positive semidefinite (PSD) when $v^{\mathsf T} M v \ge 0$ for every vector $v$;
the game check is all about one matrix being PSD. The determinant of a square matrix is a
single number that is zero exactly when the matrix squashes some direction flat. For a
two-by-two matrix with rows $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$ it's $ad - bc$. For a bigger one, expand
along a row: for each entry, delete its row and column, take the determinant of what's left,
multiply by the entry, alternate the signs, and add up; the recursion bottoms out at two by
two. A principal submatrix is what you get by choosing some of the indices and keeping only
those rows and the same columns; its determinant is a principal minor. A symmetric matrix is
PSD exactly when every principal minor is at least zero, every one of them, and the game check uses
the three-by-three ones (Appendix~\ref{sub:chsh-five}). The Schur complement turns a question
about a block matrix into a question about a smaller one. For a symmetric block matrix with
corner block $P$, off-diagonal block $Q$ and other corner $R$, it's $R - Q^{\mathsf T} P^{-1}
Q$, and when $P$ is positive definite the whole matrix is PSD exactly when that complement is
(Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-schur}). Positive definite matters; invertible isn't enough. Take $P = -1$
and every other entry zero: the complement is zero, which is PSD, and the whole matrix
isn't.

\subsection{Borrowed ideas the book pushes on}

These get their full story in the chapter that uses them; here's the one-line version for
when you've forgotten which one Landauer was.

The pigeonhole principle: put more pigeons than holes and some hole holds two. Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}'s room with
too few chairs is that, and so is the proof that a permanent flag can only be raised by a
step that forgets something. Landauer's principle (Rolf Landauer, 1961): a step that wipes
information, lowering the entropy of what a machine holds by some number of bits, gives off
at least Boltzmann's constant times the temperature times the natural log of two in heat per
bit. In this book it's always a premise with its name on it. Nothing here derives it (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}, Section~\ref{sec:landauer}).
Entropy, in Claude Shannon's sense: for a spread of chances over states, roughly the average number
of yes-or-no questions you'd need to pin the state down, so an even spread over $n$ states
has $\log_2 n$ bits. A spread, in this book, is just a list of chances that add up to one.
Maxwell's demon (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}): a little creature that watches molecules and sorts fast from slow,
seemingly for free; Charles Bennett's answer was that the measuring can be free and the
wiping of the demon's notes is what costs. The potential method (Robert Tarjan, 1985): pay
for a run with a quantity stored in the state, so a step's bill plus the change in the
stored quantity is what you count; Section~\ref{sec:counter} reads the toll as that method with one particular
potential.

The halting problem (Alan Turing, 1936, who essentially proved it without stating it in
this form; Stephen Kleene stated it in 1952, and Martin Davis seems to have been the first to name it, in 1958,
Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}): no program decides, for every program and input,
whether it stops. Kleene's recursion theorem (Stephen Kleene, 1938): for any transformation
of programs that can itself be computed, some program behaves exactly like its own
transform. Rice's theorem (Henry Rice, 1953): any property that depends only on what a
program does, and isn't true of all programs or of none, can't be decided by a program. The
diagonal is the move under all three: build the thing that does the opposite of what the
table says about it (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}). L is a small lambda calculus, a language made of nothing but
functions applied to functions, which Yannick Forster and Gert Smolka built in Coq and which
Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} uses as a tool. A hash is a short fingerprint of a longer piece of data, made so
that finding two inputs with the same fingerprint is supposed to be hard; a hash chain folds
each new record into the fingerprint of the last, and a Merkle tree folds them pairwise into
one root (Section~\ref{sec:toll}, Section~\ref{sec:models}).

\subsection{Words this book builds}

These are mine, or mine in the sense that I pinned them down for this book. Each is built
properly in the chapter named; this is only a reminder.

A few words first, because everything else hangs off them and each has exactly one meaning.
The \emph{model} (or the abstract model) is a kind of state and a rule for stepping, plus exactly
the extra pieces a given theorem asks for: a certification reading and the toll, or a counter
and a price list, or a window, or programs written as states and a recursion theorem. The
name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. Parts I to III live there, and every claim in them
is about any system with the pieces it names. A \emph{substrate} is the model's shape with
whatever extension a theorem names, and nothing else; the word never means my machine, and
never the side of a simulation that does the stepping (\hyperref[sec:straight]{Let me be straight with you}). \emph{My machine} (also the machine I
build, the build, the small machine, the smallest honest machine, Section~\ref{sec:smallest})
is the concrete machine of Part IV that fills in those pieces at once: two counters with their
versions, a table of checked facts, a channel, a trap, a ledger and a flag, six instructions
and their prices, with its hosts and universal programs. The \emph{scaffolding} is that machine
and everything built on it, and Part IV lives there. \emph{A Thiele
machine}, lower case, is any system proved to be an instance of the certification system
(Definition~\ref{def:certsys}), five parts and the toll; the paper toys are, and so is the
small machine. \emph{Weakly Thiele-complete} means a Thiele machine whose base is Turing-universal;
that bar is nearly empty, since a clock that charges one for every move pays the toll for any
record. \emph{Thiele-complete} means more (Definition~\ref{def:u34-thiele-complete}): a
universal base whose moves are free and can't touch the record, a record that
stays up once it's up and is raised from a
clean state only after a passing check, a commitment to the same claim and a certificate, one mark for each of those
three acts, and a claim whose check, commit and certificate raise the record on some loaded starts
and leave it down on others. Every clock-style machine fails it; the small
machine meets it; and every machine that meets it hides its record
and ledger from its own window. A \emph{universal} Thiele machine is one fixed program that runs
any machine of a stated class as a guest, with the guest's record earned again and its toll paid
by the host's own steps. The ones in this book are $U$ (Section~\ref{sec:universal-host}), a fixed
program in the small machine's instruction kinds, with no guest step built in, that runs every
small-machine program with halting and flag exact and its ledger equal to the guest's at every matching point, and $U_P$
(Section~\ref{sec:presented-universal}), the same program with one paid move added, that runs
every \emph{computably presented} Thiele machine, one whose driver, step, prices and reading are computed by programs with
the reading decided on every state, keeping its reading as a latch
and, when the reading starts at no, its prices to within two, a surcharge no program on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid for a raise that
costs less than three. The simpler host with a built-in guest
step runs guests by construction and keeps a mirror of the guest's flag. A computer running the
small machine isn't a Thiele machine; it implements one, inside bounds, the way a laptop
implements a Turing machine. When a word below belongs
to only one of the two layers, the entry says which.

A \emph{partition} is a sorting of a pile into groups, nothing in two groups and nothing left
over (Section~\ref{sec:structure}). A \emph{certification system} is a state type, moves, a step, a cost per move, and a
yes-or-no reading, plus one rule, the \emph{toll}: a move that turns the reading from no to yes
costs at least one (Section~\ref{sec:toll}). The files call that rule A2 in the numbering their
certification records use (Appendix~\ref{sec:assumptions}). A move \emph{merges} when two different starting states land on
the same end; one that never does is \emph{injective}, it forgets nothing. A reading is
\emph{permanent} when no move turns it from yes back to no (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}).

The \emph{counter}, which I also call the \emph{ledger}: in the model, a number carried in the state
that starts at zero and that every step raises by exactly that step's charge (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). My
machine has exactly one, the ledger $\mu$ (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). Two other things get called
counters, and each chapter says which: Minsky's two bins on the small machine, and the eight counts that
tally the game's rounds (Section~\ref{sec:chsh}). Neither is the ledger. A \emph{price list} says
what each move costs; the model takes it as given, and my machine's table of what each instruction
costs is in Section~\ref{sec:smallest}. A \emph{receipt} is a total that lives in the
state, only climbs, equals the sum of the charges on every path including the failures, and is
the only such total for its price list (Section~\ref{sec:counter} proves it for any system with a counter
and a price list, \code{nec\_f\_conservation}, \code{nec\_f\_counter\_monotone} and
\code{nec\_f\_initiality}; on my machine the sum is a checked theorem too, Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). In
the model there is just a \emph{certification reading}, yes or no (Section~\ref{sec:toll}); on
the small machine it's the \emph{flag}, set by a CERTIFY that passes and never cleared.

These belong to the small machine only (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). A \emph{two-counter machine} is Minsky's: two
counters holding whole numbers with no upper limit, and two instructions: add one, and
subtract one and jump if the counter is above zero, or else go on to the next line; already enough that nobody can decide in general whether
one halts. The small machine is a two-counter machine plus HALT and three instructions for the
record, six in all: INC, DEC, HALT, CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY. A counter's \emph{version} is its
edition number: it starts at 0 and goes up by one every time the counter is written, so an
edition never comes back. A \emph{fact} is a property, a counter and a version together, such as
``$A$ is even, as of edition 3''; the properties come from a fixed language of three, \emph{is zero},
\emph{is even} and \emph{is at least $n$}. The same theorems also hold for any property language
with an exact
equality test whose checker is proved to mean what it says, and one such language reads a counter as a list
and asks whether it's sorted (\code{sorted\_run\_certifies\_iff} and \code{sorted\_run\_refused\_forever}, EarnedGeneric.v). The \emph{fact table} holds up to sixteen facts, and the only way
in is a CHECK that passed; nothing ever leaves it. The small machine's \emph{channel} holds one
committed fact or nothing, and COMMIT puts a fact there only if the table has it about the
counter's current edition. With the flag up from a clean start it names a commitment earned
that way, and a later COMMIT
replaces it, as a two-commit run shows (\code{certified\_channel\_earned} and \code{channel\_names\_last\_commit}, EarnedCore.v). The \emph{trap} is a bit that goes up when an instruction refuses, and
then nothing in the core moves again. A commitment is \emph{earned} when a passing check put its
fact in the table first, about the same edition, with no write to that counter in between; on
the small machine every flag raised from a clean start is earned, and that's a theorem.
CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY cost one each and everything else costs nothing,
so from a clean start the cheapest certificate costs exactly three, and a check that could have failed reaches it: CHECK
\emph{is zero} on $A$, COMMIT, CERTIFY, from a start where $A$ is 0. The step doesn't police
trivial checks; \emph{is at least 0} passes every value and certifies for three too. The
\emph{host machine} is the small machine with a counter, called a \emph{register}, for every
whole number, and one property, $\mathsf{Slot}$, true of a number that packs a property of the
small machine together with a value it holds of. A \emph{slot} is a register of the host used for
nothing but holding one checked fact about the guest, and its \emph{mirror} is a register beside
it, safe to read, that says which claim the slot holds while its fact is live. $U$ is the fixed
program of 3728 host instructions that runs every small-machine program; it reads guest
instructions out of one register, keeps the guest's counters in two others, and puts every
checked fact in a slot, because on this machine reading a counter writes it. The universal
program's \emph{guest} is a program of the small machine, held as one number in a register of the
host and run one instruction at a time by $U$'s fetch and decode. $U_P$ is $U$ with one more
handler, for PAY, an instruction that costs one and does nothing else; its guests are programs
compiled from computably presented Thiele machines (Section~\ref{sec:presented-universal}).

A \emph{window} is any function that shows you part of a state (Section~\ref{sec:windows}); a \emph{shadow}, said loosely, is
what a window leaves you with. A
\emph{collision} is two steps that look the same through a window, before and after, where one
raises the flag and the other doesn't (Section~\ref{sec:windows}). \emph{Entitlement} is what a run has when it carries an
object, a checked relation between that object and a claim, and a paid event that put the
object in place: a license to lean on the claim. It doesn't prove the claim true (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}). A \emph{latch} is
a record that switches on the first time some event holds and never switches off (Section~\ref{sec:latch}). The
diagonal's \emph{substrate} (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}) is the model's shape extended with programs, a run that may give
nothing back, a counter that never falls, a way to write programs as states, the
transformations the substrate counts as its own, and its own recursion theorem for those; the
proof of the diagonal uses neither the counter nor the toll.

%===========================================================================
\section{Every assumption in one place}
\label{sec:assumptions}
%===========================================================================

This book leans on a small number of rules that nothing proves, plus a handful of record
types that carry rules as fields. I've named each one where it's used. Here they are side by
side, because a reader who wants to break this book should be able to see every place where
it says ``suppose,'' in one list, with what each ``suppose'' buys.

One thing to undo first, and it's my fault. The checked work numbers the rules its records
carry with bare labels, A2, A3 and so on, as if they were axioms. The book uses ``the toll''
for the rule that matters and avoids the bare labels; this appendix maps the labels for anyone
reading the files.

\subsection{The records that carry a rule}

\begin{definition}[Certification system]\label{def:app-certsys}
The record \code{CertificationSystem} (UniversalCertificationCost.v) has five data fields, a state
type, a move type, a step function, a cost per move in $\mathbb{N}$, and a yes/no reading,
and one proof field, \code{cs\_cert\_costs}: a move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at
least one. This proof field is the toll of Section~\ref{sec:toll}, and in this record's
numbering it is called A2. Every result stated ``for any certification system'' assumes it,
because the record cannot be built without it.
\end{definition}


\begin{definition}[Quantitative certification system]\label{def:app-qcs}
The record \code{QuantitativeCertificationSystem} (QuantitativeNoFI.v) extends a certification
system with a \emph{witness}, a function $W$ from states to $\mathbb{N}$, and a threshold
$N \in \mathbb{N}$, and adds two proof fields:
(A3, \code{qcs\_cost\_bounds\_witness}) $W(s) + \mathrm{cost}(i) \ge W(\mathrm{step}(s, i))$, the
witness grows by at most what the move cost; and
(A5, \code{qcs\_cert\_threshold\_witness}) a state that reads yes has $W(s) \ge N$.
An optional extension, \code{QuantitativeCertificationSystem\_full}, adds
(A4, \code{qcsf\_witness\_nondecreasing}) $W(s) \le W(\mathrm{step}(s, i))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The floor raised to a threshold]\label{thm:app-quantitative}
In a quantitative certification system, every run from a state with witness $0$ (this
starting condition is called A6) to a state that reads yes has total cost at least $N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Adding A3 along the run telescopes: the witness at the end is at most the witness at the
start plus the total cost, so at most the total cost. A5 says the end witness is at least
$N$. Neither A4 nor the toll is used.
\end{proof}

Checked as \code{universal\_nfi\_quantitative} (QuantitativeNoFI.v). A3 and A4 bound opposite
directions, and neither implies the other: witness 1, cost 0, witness 0 satisfies A3 and
breaks A4, and witness 0, cost 0, witness 1 does the reverse. The record is a general shape.
The small machine's own floor of three is proved directly (Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-min-price})
and never goes through it.

Here are the labels side by side, so none of them is left without a meaning.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.75\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Label} & \textbf{In the certification records} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
A2 & the toll: field \code{cs\_cert\_costs} of \code{CertificationSystem} \\
A3 & the witness grows by at most the cost: field \code{qcs\_cost\_bounds\_witness} \\
A4 & the witness never drops: field \code{qcsf\_witness\_nondecreasing} of the full record \\
A5 & yes needs a witness at the threshold: field \code{qcs\_cert\_threshold\_witness} \\
A6 & the run starts with witness zero: a hypothesis of \code{universal\_nfi\_quantitative} \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

\subsection{The premises the derivations take}

These are definitions used as hypotheses. Nothing proves them in general; each theorem that
uses one says so in its statement.

\begingroup\small
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.233\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.221\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.221\linewidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.221\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Premise} & \textbf{What it says} & \textbf{Where it's used} & \textbf{Checked name} \\
\midrule
\endhead
\bottomrule
\endlastfoot
Finite & a list with no repeats contains every state & the room argument, Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} & \code{finite\_states} \\
Permanent & no move turns the reading from yes to no & the room argument & \code{permanent} (and \code{permanent\_at} for one move) \\
Merge pricing & every move that merges costs at least one & the toll derived, Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} & \code{merging\_steps\_priced} \\
Halving price & each unit of cost pays for at most one halving of distinct states & the squeeze bound; narrowing along a run, Section~\ref{sec:narrowing} & \code{compression\_priced} \\
Entropy pricing & each move costs at least the bits it removes from any spread & the third road to the toll & \code{entropy\_priced} \\
Landauer's principle & removing $\Delta H$ bits gives off heat $\ge k_B T \ln 2 \cdot \Delta H$ & the heat floor; with $k_B T \ge 0$ (or $> 0$) as a separate hypothesis on each theorem & \code{landauer\_heat} \\
Recursion (generic) & every transformation the substrate can represent has a fixed point & the diagonal, Section~\ref{sec:diagonal} & field \code{recursion\_theorem} of the class \code{Substrate} \\
Commitment contract & a commitment bit is set only when the claim holds, and whenever it holds & the commitment escape, Section~\ref{sec:windows} & stated in Definition~\ref{def:u21-escape-relations} \\
Computably presented & four programs compute the driver, the step, the price and the reading, and the reading's program answers on every state & the universal host for presented machines, Section~\ref{sec:presented-universal} & \code{cg\_presentation} \\
Clean start & an empty fact table, an empty channel and the flag down & every provenance theorem about the small machine, Section~\ref{sec:smallest} & \code{clean\_start} \\
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

Three remarks on the table. First, the recursion premise holds by construction for the nat
family and by proof for L (Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}) and for the programs of the small machine's
host (Section~\ref{sec:small-diagonal}).
Second, the class
\code{Substrate} (Substrate.v) carries a different rule from the toll, \code{mu\_monotone}: the counter
never goes down on a step. Neither implies the other, and the diagonal uses neither. Third, merge pricing is Landauer's principle taken in its worst case over
what the machine might be holding: it charges every merging move, while the principle in its
general form charges only for uncertainty actually removed, when the step can be driven by a
protocol timed from outside it (Theorem~\ref{thm:known-state}). Under time-symmetric control,
Riechers, Boyd, Wimsatt and Crutchfield (2020) argue, even a known state pays for a move that
doesn't undo itself.

\subsection{The axioms of the checker itself}

Beyond the premises above, the checked proofs rest on Coq's own foundation and on a handful of
standard-library axioms, which the assumption audit lists theorem by theorem: functional
extensionality on dependent functions; two decidability principles for the real numbers (used
wherever real analysis is, for example in the game check of Section~\ref{sec:chsh}); and the
law of excluded middle, in some theorems. No axiom or
parameter of the project's own appears in the audited theorems. Section~\ref{sec:coq} says what that does and
doesn't mean.

%===========================================================================
\section{What's mine, and what isn't}
\label{sec:whats-mine}
%===========================================================================

Every chapter of this book leans on somebody, and I've named them where I lean. This appendix
does a different job, and it's the one where I'd most like to be caught out, and caught out
early. For each thing the book could be accused of claiming as its own, it says what was
already known, what this work actually defines, builds, proves, or connects, and what kind of
contribution that is. Six kinds, and they aren't the same claim: a \emph{new result} (a statement
nobody had); a \emph{new proof} of something known; a \emph{mechanization} (a known result checked by a
machine, here Coq); an \emph{implementation} (something built that runs); a \emph{synthesis} (known
pieces put together under one question); and a \emph{conjecture}. Every kind can be worth doing.
None of them is the others. And if you read down the list and notice that ``new result''
hardly shows up, good. You're reading it right.

Two warnings about my own evidence before the list. First, ``I didn't find it'' is a fact about
my searches. The literature is bigger than my searches. I searched with every tool I had, and some tools will
cheerfully invent a citation if you let them, so where it matters I say where I looked, and
you should assume it may well be sitting in a paper I'd need a few more lifetimes of homework
to read. Second, nothing below is inferred from how many theorems there
are, from the audit's clean bill, or from a good story about who came before. Those tell you
the work was checked. They don't tell you it's new. Thousands of checked theorems could,
in principle, be thousands of careful ways of agreeing with Tarjan.

\subsection{1. The universal floor and the potential method}

Known: the potential method of amortized analysis, a function on states whose drop bounds
the cost of a run, is Tarjan's (1985), and it has been mechanized more than once (Nipkow in
Isabelle/HOL, 2015 and 2019; Charguéraud and Pottier's time credits in Coq, 2019), built
into type systems for automatic resource analysis (Hoffmann and coauthors, 2011 onward), and
recast in cost-aware type theories (Niu, Sterling, Grodin and Harper, 2022). Mine: choosing
the potential that is one when a designated reading says no and zero when it says yes, so
that ``the crossing costs'' (the toll) and ``every run that crosses paid'' (the floor) are the
