potential method's two halves (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). Kind: a mechanization of a known
technique with a particular choice of potential. The choice is the point: it makes ``was
certified'' something the account must carry. The theorem is not new mathematics. If it
looks clever, that's Tarjan's cleverness; my part was picking which number to plug in.

Go back to Tarjan's paper and there's a sentence that sits right on the line this book draws.
He opens with the dictionary (to amortize is to put money aside at intervals, as in a sinking
fund) and then gives two views of the method. In the banker's view the computer is
coin-operated, and each operation is handed credits to spend or save; in the physicist's view,
which he credits to Daniel Sleator, every state has a potential and you count its changes.
Then he stops to say that the credits are only an accounting device: the programs that actually
run contain no mention of credits or debits. That's exactly right for what he wanted, a bound
proved about a program from outside. It's also exactly the gap. In his method the coins live in
the proof. The one move I chose was to put them in the step, where no program takes a step
without it being counted. Same arithmetic, different place.

\subsection{2. The toll from finiteness, permanence, and a price on merges}

Known: that steps which merge states (no single-valued inverse) are what Landauer's principle
charges for is Landauer's (1961), sharpened by Bennett (1973, 1982, 2003; the words ``the erasure of a bit
or the merging of two computation paths'' are from the 2003 abstract); generalizations and the dependence on the input
distribution are Maroney's (2009), Sagawa's (2014), Wolpert's; the critique is Earman and
Norton's and Norton's. Write-once memory is an old topic in coding theory (Rivest and
Shamir, 1982), where the question is reuse and price never comes up, and Chris Heegard (1985) worked out the capacity
of permanent memory with noise, again a question of how much fits. What it costs
doesn't come into it.
Statisticians priced permanence on finite memory in their own currency: in Hellman and Cover's
analysis of hypothesis testing with finite memory (1970), a machine that settles its answer by
falling into states it never leaves does worse than one that doesn't, so a decision held for
good costs memory states. Heat never enters their analysis. And the counting under the theorem is older than
any of that, twice over. Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} is the finite, discrete cousin of the
recurrence argument Zermelo, using Poincaré's theorem of 1890, turned on Boltzmann in 1896, here
aimed at a reading. Zermelo aimed it at entropy, and Bocchieri and Loinger gave the quantum recurrence in
1957. In automata form it is classical: a finite machine whose moves are all one-to-one
reshuffles recognises only group languages, and the inputs that raise a permanent reading form a
language that is never one of those unless it is empty (Pin's 1992 paper on reversible automata
is the reference I'd check; automata theorists treat the step as folklore), and going quantum
doesn't change it (Brodsky and Pippenger, 2002: quantum finite automata that measure once, at
the end, accept with bounded error exactly the group languages). The closest of all is recent.
Ouldridge and Wolpert (2023) give a proof that if the smallest automaton for a language has a step
that merges states, every automaton for it does, and argue that recognising it on a device that repeats
one local step produces entropy, while a language whose smallest automaton only reshuffles can
be recognised for free; one of their worked examples is the strings with no $b$, the complement
of the latch's language. That's the core with a physical price already on it. And the
logarithm in the heat floor matches the absolute-irreversibility bound of Murashita, Funo and
Ueda (2014), which Manzano, Karde\c{s}, Rold\'an and Wolpert (2024) carried over to computation.
The match is a mirror image. It isn't a special case of their bound: the squeeze is ordinary Landauer heat, whose logarithm
equals their bound for the free expansion that undoes it, and absolute irreversibility reaches
the commit itself only on a fixed-rate device starting from a known state.
Constructor theory states a cousin of the same core for devices that run in a cycle: Marletto,
Vedral and coauthors (2022) and Violaris and Marletto (2022) built an irreversible task out of
the quantum homogeniser and argued that erasure may cost more than Landauer's bound.
Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary} tells all of it. Mine: the price as a named rule on a
ledger, a premise that merges cost at least a mark, which turns ``the flip merges'' into ``the
flip costs'' on any machine whether or not anybody's physics is right, and the toll derived from
it (Theorem~\ref{thm:toll-derived}); what comes with that form, namely the characterisation of
the moves every merge-pricing schedule must charge, when move names can be decided equal or different (the merging moves, so the core again in
pricing words), the merge-or-revoke dichotomy for a single move, the squeeze and entropy forms
for a permanent flip, and a built counterexample for each premise; and the mechanization of all
of it (Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary}). Kind: the core is classical, and somebody else's: Zermelo's in
physics, folklore in automata theory, with Pin's paper as the place to check it. The pricing
form isn't wholly mine either: priced in entropy, for automata, it's Ouldridge and Wolpert's.
They derive the price from the physics. I assume mine. What's mine is the price as a named rule on a
ledger, the toll derived from it, its single-move and counted forms, the counterexamples, and
the mechanized proofs, and the physics is a named premise and is Landauer's. Searches: the core
turned up in the places just named, and its physical price in Ouldridge and Wolpert; I didn't
find the ledger form or the derived toll stated anywhere I looked, and nobody's search covers a
whole field, mine least of all; I found no mechanization of Landauer's principle in Coq,
Isabelle, or Lean.

\subsection{3. Learning free, committing priced}

Known: that measurement can be done at no fundamental cost and the cost sits in erasing the
record is Bennett's resolution of Maxwell's demon (1982), with the quantitative trade-off by
Sagawa and Ueda (2009). The closest physics I found to the line between learning and committing
is Ouldridge and ten Wolde's fundamental costs of persistent copies (2017; with Govern, 2017),
copies that stay correlated with their originals after the two come apart; theirs is heat for a
correlation in chemistry, and Section~\ref{sec:narrowing} says how it differs. The sharp
chemical form, that a persistent copy grown at equilibrium carries no information about its
template, is Poulton, ten Wolde and Ouldridge's (2019), and that the bill can be split between
measuring and erasing in more than one way is Fahn's (1996). Mine: the four-state demon and the three-state ring as checked
models, and the two-state impossibility (Section~\ref{sec:narrowing}). Kind: mechanization
and illustration of a known physical point inside my ledger. Not a new physical claim.
Bennett did the hard part in 1982; I built a toy with four dots on it and got Coq to agree
with him.

\subsection{4. Windows that can't price what they hide}

Known: a function of an observation is constant on the observation's fibres; that's
elementary, and the systems version of it is Moore's distinguishing experiments (1956),
Kalman's observability (1960), and the completeness question of abstract interpretation
(Cousot and Cousot, 1977; Giacobazzi, Ranzato and Scozzari, 2000); in control theory it is
diagnosability and opacity of discrete-event systems (Sampath and coauthors, 1995; Saboori and
Hadjicostis, 2007), where a collision is a hidden event no observer can diagnose without delay;
in economics it is the
hard-evidence view of mechanism design (Green and Laffont, 1986; Bull and Watson, 2007), where
what a mechanism can tell apart is limited by the evidence on offer; and its sharp form for
fingerprints is Naor and Rothblum's lower bound for checking a stored file (2005); in distributed systems it
is Haeberlen and Kuznetsov's (2009), that only omission and commission faults can be detected from outside,
and in philosophy it is Easwaran's transferability (2009). Mine: stating the pricing
version (no window price is exact across a collision), exhibiting a colliding pair for the
small machine's window, and the theorem that every Thiele-complete machine has two runs from one
clean start that end looking the same through the window its base shows, one certified and one
not (\code{complete\_hides\_record}; Section~\ref{sec:windows}, Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). Kind:
mechanization of an elementary lemma, plus specific facts about the machine and the definition.

\subsection{5. Structural entitlement and its bound}

Known: decision-tree counting bounds (a tree that tells $N$ cases apart has depth at least
$\log_2 N$); certifying algorithms that hand over checkable certificates (McConnell,
Mehlhorn, Näher and Schweitzer, 2011); proof-carrying code (Necula, 1997); the gap between
justified true belief and knowledge (Gettier, 1963). Mine: the definition of entitlement as an
object, a checked relation, and a paid event on the record, and the count that, given lists, a
tree and a covering, a run that paid for the tree's depth pays at least the index bits it
commits to (Section~\ref{sec:entitlement}). Kind: synthesis; the counting idea is standard, the
assembly and its vocabulary are this work's, the pricing policy is assumed (nothing derives it), and the
count is mechanized: in its bill form over any certification system, and for the record moves of
every Thiele-complete machine on a run from a clean start, with the earned chain in the run, a floor that takes the run's own
checks in place of a tree, and a counterexample showing the covering can't be dropped
(Section~\ref{sec:part3-on-machine}).

\subsection{6. The record axis is a latch}

Known: monotone, write-once state is old: the latch (Eccles and Jordan, 1918), sticky bits
(Plotkin, 1989), grow-only state in replicated data types (Shapiro and coauthors), history
variables and stuttering in refinement (Abadi and Lamport, 1991), append-only authenticated sets
for transparency logs, which fit revocation as a once-only event (Tomescu and coauthors, 2019),
and, in program logic, monotonic state, where a property witnessed once on state that only moves
forward can be recalled at any later point, with a soundness proof and a working home in
F$^\star$ (Ahman, Fournet, Hri\c{t}cu, Maillard, Rastogi and Swamy, 2018): the type-theory name
for a record that stays up. Past the finite case, inductive and quasi-inductive definitions
(Richter and Aczel, 1974; Burgess, 1986) and the flag trick of infinite time Turing machines
(Hamkins and Lewis, 2000) are the transfinite versions of a record that only grows and a
toggle, and Danos and Krivine's (2005) reversible calculus needs an action declared
irreversible in order to commit.
Mine: the exact statement
that a record driven by the computation that never switches off is, over any base, a latch
on one event, with its converse and a counterexample for each of the two conditions, and the
argument that honest records agree up to the price list while the stronger uniqueness fails
(Section~\ref{sec:latch}). Kind: a small structural lemma, I think not stated before in this
form (I found no prior statement in the searches I ran), built from old notions; the latch form
is mechanized, and so is the agreement up to the price list
(\code{nec\_w\_billed\_same\_up\_to\_schedule}).

\subsection{7. The diagonal and L}

Known: Kleene's recursion theorem and Rice's theorem; Lawvere's fixed-point form (1969) and
Yanofsky's retelling (2003); mechanized recursion theorems and Rice (Norrish in HOL4, 2011;
Carneiro in Lean; Forster, Kunze, Smolka and coauthors in Coq, including L itself, 2017, and
the Coq Library of Undecidability). Mine: the diagonal stated once over any substrate that
supplies a recursion theorem; and Rice and halting proved again for L from its reduction rules
(Section~\ref{sec:diagonal}); and the same two theorems built for the small machine's host, with
Rice's on every input of the two-counter machine and Kleene's with inputs written as powers of two,
and Kleene's refuted for plain inputs (Section~\ref{sec:small-diagonal}).
Kind: checked instances of known theorems of computability. They hold for any model with
universality and s-m-n, and the work is in building those for this machine.

\subsection{8. The game check}

Known: that positive semidefiniteness of a correlation matrix gives the Tsirelson bound is
Tsirelson's (1980) and Stephanie Wehner's semidefinite proof (2006), from a paper on Tsirelson bounds for generalized CHSH inequalities; the moment-matrix hierarchy, the
Schur-complement analysis of this very level-one matrix and the level $1+AB$ are Navascués, Pironio
and Acín's (2007, 2008); the arcsine characterization is Landau's (1988) and Masanes's (2003); and Tsirelson's bound has already been checked by machine, in Isabelle/HOL (Echenim
and Mhalla, 2023) and in Lean's mathlib. Rational sum-of-squares certificates are Helfried Peyrl and Pablo A. Parrilo's
(2008), from a paper on computing sum-of-squares decompositions with rational coefficients. Mine: a decision procedure in integer arithmetic on outcome counts; a checked
chain from ``the counts pass'' to ``the pinned level-one matrix is positive semidefinite'' to
``$S^2 \le 8$''; proofs of the contraction equivalence by explicit test vectors; and the
level-$1+AB$ cascade and an elliptope gate in whole numbers, with a soundness proof
(Section~\ref{sec:chsh} and its derivation appendix). Kind: mechanization, with a new proof of a
known equivalence in one slice. I found no prior formalization taking counts as input, and
that's a report on where I looked, and the literature is bigger than where I looked. The same check earned on
the small machine's host, a raised flag standing on it, is built and checked; the idea isn't new
(Section~\ref{sec:chsh}).

\subsection{9. Five record disciplines, one question}

Known: each system and its guarantee belongs to its designers: Casper (Buterin and Griffith,
2017), Ethereum's storage gas and refunds (EIP-2200, EIP-3529), extend-only TPM registers,
Certificate Transparency (RFC 9162), proof-carrying code. Mine: asking all five whether the
write is priced, with a small checked fragment of each (Section~\ref{sec:models}). Kind:
synthesis and an organizing reading; the fragments are not verifications of those systems.

\subsection{10. The pointer conjecture}

Known: Zurek's quantum Darwinism (2009), with Ollivier, Poulin and Zurek (2004) and
Blume-Kohout and Zurek (2006): preferred states are the ones whose records proliferate
redundantly in the environment. Mine: borrowing that shape for the question of which event
deserves a record, with definitions, a toy, and refutations of two stronger forms
(Section~\ref{sec:pointer}). Kind: conjecture. No claim about quantum physics.

\subsection{11. The counter as a receipt}

Known: one-way counters that give order and termination are old: Turing's 1949 note on
checking a large routine, Floyd's ranking functions (1967), Lamport's clocks (1978).
Carrying a run's cost beside its result is the writer cost of Danner, Licata and Ramyaa (2015)
and of Danner and Licata (2022), and the
graded effect semantics of Katsumata (2014), with a working-language version in Orchard,
Liepelt and Eades (2019). The receipt side of time credits is Mével, Jourdan and Pottier's
(2019): in their Coq-checked extension of the Iris logic every step uses up a credit and
produces a receipt, receipts prove lower bounds, and enough of them prove that a counter can't
overflow in any feasible time, which is the closest published neighbour of a total that only
climbs. Mine: putting three properties side by side (the total only
climbs, it equals the sum of the charges on every path including the failures, and it is
the only such total for a given price list), the argument for any system with a counter
and a price list, and the checked sum on the small machine (Section~\ref{sec:counter},
Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). Kind: synthesis; the abstract statements are checked over any
counter machine (\code{nec\_f\_conservation}, \code{nec\_f\_counter\_monotone} and
\code{nec\_f\_initiality}), and on the small machine the sum is too. Against the graded
frameworks the answer is split: the counter is their writer exactly
(\code{run\_writer\_is\_run\_and\_cost}), and their type systems, bounding relations and
before-the-run checking of grades are not embedded, because the grade here is written by the step
during the run (Section~\ref{sec:counter}). On loop-free programs the counter agrees with a fixed
grade exactly, and where a run's cost depends on its data it holds the exact number that a fixed
grade can only bound; that's argued in Section~\ref{sec:counter}, with no checked theorem
behind it, and cost-aware
type theories such as calf get exactness back with grades that depend on the inputs.

\subsection{12. The small machine}

Known: two-counter machines are Minsky's (1961, 1967), and the undecidability of their
halting is checked in the Coq Library of Undecidability (Forster, Larchey-Wendling and
coauthors, 2019, 2020). The guarantee about every program is older than any of this, and it
isn't mine either. It's the reference monitor (Anderson, 1972): a check that sits in the path of
every operation, so no program gets around it. Schneider (2000) worked out what a monitor that
watches a run can enforce: only safety properties, the kind a bad run breaks at some finite
moment, and ``no CERTIFY without an earlier earned COMMIT'' is one of those. Azevedo de Amorim
and coauthors (2015) verified, in Coq, monitors that check tags at every instruction. The shape
of ``earned,'' a certificate nothing can make except through the rules, is Milner's LCF, where a
theorem is a value only the logic's rules can build (Gordon, Milner and Wadsworth, 1979; Gordon,
2000); the small machine is that architecture at the level of single instructions. ``No certify
without an earlier commit'' is also a correspondence assertion in the sense of Woo and Lam
(1993), which Gordon and Jeffrey (2003) check with a type system, and a store of commitments
that the rules of a dialogue keep, each speaker's updated by the rules as the moves are made, is
Hamblin's (1970, chapter 8, on formal dialectic); the difference from all three is
again that here the step enforces it. A check that
blesses a value and a write that takes the blessing away is close kin to dynamic taint tracking,
whose labels go back to Denning's lattice model of information flow (1976), with the blessing
itself, controlled endorsement, given a type system and a security theorem by Cecchetti, Myers
and Arden (2017), and what a monitor
can enforce with bounded memory is Talhi, Tawbi and Debbabi's question (2008). A small monotone
record inside each replica of a replicated service is A2M (Chun and coauthors, 2007), TrInc
(Levin and coauthors, 2009), MinBFT (Veronese and coauthors, 2013) and Damysus (Decouchant and
coauthors, 2022), and Clement, Junqueira, Kate and Rodrigues (2012) worked out, with proofs, what such a record
buys and what it doesn't. The signature route to the same goal, which needs no trusted step,
is IA-CCF (Shamis and coauthors, 2021): replicas sign and log their protocol messages in the
ledger, so blame lands on individual members however many of them misbehave. And ``check once, issue a capability the system trusts, rely on it
later'' is built and deployed in Garg and Pfenning's proof-carrying file system (2010), whose
logic lets a policy's consequences change with time and state, and in Sirer and coauthors'
logical attestation for the Nexus operating system (2011), unforgeable statements about programs
used as credentials; those are the closest systems I've found to check, commit, certify. Mine: a
six-instruction machine on two counters, with a version
for each counter, a bounded fact table and a channel; its theorems that, from a clean start, a committed fact was checked
first about the same edition, that nothing is forged, that nothing is evicted,
that with the flag up from a clean start the channel names a fact an earlier passing COMMIT committed, and a later commit can replace it, as a two-commit run shows (\code{certified\_channel\_earned} and \code{channel\_names\_last\_commit}, EarnedCore.v), and that the cheapest
certificate whose check could have failed costs exactly three and no less (the step doesn't
police trivial checks, so one that can't fail costs three too); the same theorems for any
property language with an exact equality
test whose checker is proved to mean what it says, a sorted list read out of a
counter included (\code{sorted\_run\_certifies\_iff} and \code{sorted\_run\_refused\_forever}, EarnedGeneric.v); and the step-for-step match with
the library's machine, so halting is undecidable for it (Section~\ref{sec:smallest}).
Kind: an instance of monitor enforcement, implemented and mechanized, with two things on top
that I didn't find put together where I looked: the check is bound to the edition of the thing
it checked, and a toll is paid for the commitment. The universality and the
undecidability are borrowed, and the other properties are short consequences of the step
rule. Whether the design is new I can't say, and I make no claim beyond the proofs.

\subsection{13. The universal host}

Known: Turing's universal machine (1936), which runs any machine given as data, and the
universal register machines that run two-counter programs. Keeping a guest and the code running
beside it out of each other's state is what a virtual machine monitor promises (Popek and
Goldberg, 1974). Compiling computable functions into counter machines is checked in the Coq
Library of Undecidability. Mine: one fixed program, $U$, written in the small machine's own six kinds of
instruction on a host with a register for every whole number, with no guest step built in, that
runs every program of the small machine from every start, halts exactly when its guest does, raises
its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate exactly when the guest's would rise, and
keeps a ledger equal to the guest's at every matching point; its host machine is Thiele-complete,
and whether $U$ halts on a loaded guest is undecidable (Section~\ref{sec:universal-host}). Two
small facts force its shape, and they're stated there: reading a counter on this machine writes
it, and a finite program can't keep the guest's facts on a copy of the guest's counter, by the
pigeonhole. Beside it, a simpler host with a built-in guest step runs guests by construction and
keeps a mirror of the guest's flag, with the mirror, isolation and earned-chain theorems.
An ordinary programmable computer, as built, doesn't do this for the programs it runs, because
the code beside a program shares its memory and can flip anything; $U$ is a fixed interpreter
that does. Kind: implementation and mechanization of a design whose shape is Turing's universal
machine, with the record and the toll carried through. The universality is borrowed from the
small machine and from Minsky. And the same program with one paid move added, $U_P$, runs every
computably presented Thiele machine, with its halting matched, its reading carried as a latch on
the host's own earned flag whose claim is that reading, and its prices to within a surcharge of
at most two when the reading starts at no, which no program on the host, run from a clean start, can avoid for a raise
that costs less than three (Section~\ref{sec:presented-universal});
the compiler that carries the guest onto two counters is the library's. Kind for that part:
implementation and mechanization again. That a universal machine runs any computable machine is
Turing's; what's carried through here is the record, earned again, and the prices, exact up to
the surcharge, and I didn't find that put together where I looked.

\subsection{14. Thiele-complete, defined so a clock fails}

Known: Turing completeness, and the observation every theorist makes in four seconds, that a
toll alone is cheap: a machine that charges for every step pays any toll. Enforcement mechanisms
have been compared and sorted before, and they aren't one notion seen several ways: James Morris
(1973) separated access limitation from authentication in programming languages, and Kevin Hamlen, Greg
Morrisett and Fred Schneider (2006)
classified which policies execution monitors, program
rewriters and static analysis can each
enforce, and they differ; Wai Wong (1995), on a neighbouring track, recorded
and checked HOL proofs so a theorem could carry its derivation. Mine: a definition of
Thiele-complete with four clauses (a free universal base that can't touch the record and a record that stays up once it's
up, an earned
record, an exact toll on the three record acts, and some claim whose check can fail), the proofs that every
clock-style machine and a paid latch and a silent machine fail it while the small machine, the
same machine over any property language with an exact equality test, a proved checker and a property that holds of one number and fails of another, and the universal program's host meet it,
and the theorem that every machine meeting it hides its record and ledger from its own window
(Section~\ref{sec:smallest}). Kind: a definition with short consequences. The window theorem is
the fibre fact of item 4 plus one observation, that a universal base prints any window for free.
I'm not claiming the definition is the only reasonable one, or that LCF kernels, reference
monitors and proof-carrying code are all Thiele-complete machines in disguise; Hamlen, Morrisett
and Schneider's sorting says such mechanisms genuinely differ, and the book doesn't have a
theorem showing the definition holds up across such differences.

\subsection{What that adds up to}

Read straight down the list. The mathematics underneath this
book is mostly known, and some of it is very old. What's mine is the question (should an
account of computation carry what was certified and what certifying cost, as part of how it
steps), and the answer isn't one result. It's four, and I name them the same way wherever they
come up. The toll derived from finiteness, permanence and a price on merges (item 2; the
counting is classical, the finite cousin of Zermelo's recurrence objection and folklore about
permutation automata, and Ouldridge and Wolpert already priced it in entropy for automata, so
what's mine is the price as a rule on a ledger and the toll it gives, and the price is
Landauer's, as a premise). The pricing form of the window fact (item 4; the fact itself is elementary). The
latch form of a record that never comes down (item 6; latches and history variables are old).
And a record that's priced, and on the small machine earned, under the reference monitor's
every-program move (items 12, 13 and 14; the move is Anderson's, Schneider's and the micro-policy
authors', and what's added is the check bound to its edition, the toll on top, a definition of
Thiele-complete that a clock fails, and universal programs that carry both to every
small-machine program and to every computably presented Thiele machine, earning their own flag).
The first is a ledger
form of a core that's classical and already priced in physics; the second and third are small exact statements I didn't find
stated where I looked; the fourth is built and checked, and its idea isn't new. Under all four sits a
large body of mechanized proof that
ties those statements to one small machine and the programs that run on it. Around it is my best
attempt at saying which is which,
which you should check as hard as anything else in here. Item 2's core, the finite cousin of Zermelo's recurrence objection, was
folklore among automata theorists,
with Pin's paper as the place to check it, long before I found
it, and its price in physics was Ouldridge and Wolpert's. If someone shows me
its ledger form, the pricing form in item 4, or item 6
stated earlier, I'll move it up the list and be glad to, and a little embarrassed, in that order.

\section{Every result and where it is checked}
\label{sec:crosswalk}
%===========================================================================

Every numbered result in this book is in the table below, in the order it appears, with
the Coq names that carry it, the file each lives in, and what the last full assumption
audit printed for it. Four groups of rows are placed out of that order, beside the rows they
belong with: Definition~\ref{def:frag-small} and Theorems~\ref{thm:frag-small}
and~\ref{thm:frag-merge-split} beside the eight-state machine of Section~\ref{sec:a2-not-arbitrary},
the rows from Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-machine} to Theorem~\ref{thm:time-tax} beside
Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-cs}, Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-presented} and the two rows after it below the
host's rows, and Remark~\ref{rem:u23-sound-not-complete} below the small machine's five tallies.
``none'' means the theorem is closed: its proof uses nothing beyond
Coq's own rules. The other entries name the standard-library assumptions it uses: FE is
functional extensionality on dependent functions, RD is one or both of the two decidability principles
that come with the real numbers, and EM is excluded middle. ``def'' marks a definition, which
has nothing to assume.
The audit covers every file the project builds, the small machine's files under minimal/ and the
kernel tree under coq/kernel alike; only MuCore.v and Napkin.v, which are built and checked on their
own, sit outside it. The small machine's files, the universal program's files and the priced host's
files also end by printing the assumptions of their own headline theorems, and every one of those
lines says closed. ``+N''
after a file means $N$ other files under coq/ and minimal/ define or declare a name spelled the same way, section variables and hypotheses included (notations, module aliases and record fields aren't counted); the row gives
the file this result uses. A premise is assumed and never proved, so its row gives at most the Coq
definition that states it, marked ``def''. A conjecture has no Coq name, because the book states it
and doesn't claim it. The section that states each one says so.

This table is an index of companion formalizations. The statements, hypotheses and
arguments are in the numbered sections it points to. An audit status reports the
recorded check; running a later version does not change a claim in this book.

%===========================================================================
\section{The exact words of eighteen results}
\label{sec:coq-statements}
%===========================================================================

This book states its theorems in its own words, and Section~\ref{sec:coq} says why that's a
risk: the checker confirms a proof matches its statement. Whether my sentence matches the
statement is a question the checker never asks. So here are the statements themselves for eighteen of the results the argument
leans on hardest. Each is copied from its file with the comments taken out and nothing else
changed, and each comes with its file, a plain reading, and a line on whether the book's
printed version says exactly that, more, or less. You don't need to read Coq to use this. Put
the printed theorem next to the block and check that every premise in the block turns up in the
sentence. That's the whole test. These are the statements this book was checked against; if a
file differs later, the book means the one printed here.

\subsection{The universal floor}

{\raggedright \code{universal\_nfi\_any\_substrate}, coq/kernel/nfi/UniversalCertificationCost.v, with the record it quantifies over.\par}

{\footnotesize
\begin{verbatim}
Record CertificationSystem := mk_cert_system {
  cs_state : Type;
  cs_instr : Type;
  cs_step  : cs_state -> cs_instr -> cs_state;
  cs_cost  : cs_instr -> nat;
  cs_cert  : cs_state -> bool;
  cs_cert_costs :
    forall (s : cs_state) (i : cs_instr),
      cs_cert s = false ->
      cs_cert (cs_step s i) = true ->
      cs_cost i >= 1;
}.

Theorem universal_nfi_any_substrate :
  forall (CS : CertificationSystem)
         (trace : list (cs_instr CS))
         (s0 : cs_state CS),
    cs_cert CS s0 = false ->
    cs_cert CS (cs_run CS trace s0) = true ->
    cs_total_cost CS trace >= 1.
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: a certification system is a record of a state type, a move type, a step, a
cost and a yes-or-no reading, plus one more field, \code{cs\_cert\_costs}, which is the toll: a
move that takes the reading from false to true costs at least one. Since the toll is a field,
every system the theorem talks about has it. The theorem: start at a state reading false, run
any list of moves (\code{cs\_run} applies them in order, \code{cs\_total\_cost} adds their
costs), end at a state reading true, and the costs add up to at least one.
Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-floor} says exactly this; the rule that Definition~\ref{def:certsys}
calls the toll is the record's last field here.

\subsection{A permanent flip merges}

{\raggedright \code{permanent\_flip\_is\_not\_injective}, coq/kernel/nfi/PermanentCertification.v, inside a section that fixes the states, the moves, the step and the reading.\par}

{\footnotesize
\begin{verbatim}
Variables (S I : Type).
Variable step : S -> I -> S.
Variable cert : S -> bool.

Definition finite_states (all : list S) : Prop :=
  NoDup all /\ forall s, In s all.

Definition permanent : Prop :=
  forall s i, cert s = true -> cert (step s i) = true.

Definition step_injective (i : I) : Prop :=
  forall a b, step a i = step b i -> a = b.

Theorem permanent_flip_is_not_injective :
  forall all s i,
    finite_states all ->
    permanent ->
    cert s = false ->
    cert (step s i) = true ->
    ~ step_injective i.
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: \texttt{finite\_states} $\mathit{all}$ says the list $\mathit{all}$ has no repeats and every
state is on it, so there are finitely many. \code{permanent} says once the reading is true,
every move keeps it true. \texttt{step\_injective i} says move $i$ never sends two different
states to the same one. The theorem: on a finite machine with a permanent reading, a move that
takes some state from false to true isn't injective, so it merges two states.
Theorem~\ref{thm:perm-flip-merges} says exactly this, with ``merges'' meaning ``isn't
injective''.

\subsection{The toll from finiteness, permanence and merge pricing}

{\raggedright \code{a2\_from\_merging\_price\_and\_permanence}, the same file and section, with a cost on moves added.\par}

{\footnotesize
\begin{verbatim}
Variable cost : I -> nat.

Definition merging_steps_priced : Prop :=
  forall i, ~ step_injective i -> cost i >= 1.

Definition a2_holds : Prop :=
  forall s i, cert s = false -> cert (step s i) = true -> cost i >= 1.

Theorem a2_from_merging_price_and_permanence :
  forall all,
    finite_states all ->
    permanent ->
    merging_steps_priced ->
    a2_holds.
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: \code{merging\_steps\_priced} says every move that isn't injective costs at
least one, and \code{a2\_holds} is the toll. The theorem: finite, permanent and merges priced
give the toll. Theorem~\ref{thm:toll-derived} says this and one thing more, that the machine
with that cost is then a certification system the universal floor applies to. That second half
isn't in this statement. It's the definition right after it in the file
(\code{certification\_system\_from\_merging\_price}), which fills the record's toll field with
this theorem, so the printed form is true, and it leans on two Coq items: this theorem and that
definition.

\subsection{No exact window price across a collision}

{\raggedright \code{shadow\_cannot\_price\_exactly}, coq/kernel/nfi/ShadowPricing.v, inside a section that fixes the states, moves, step, reading and a window \code{obs}.\par}

{\footnotesize
\begin{verbatim}
Variables (S I O : Type).
Variable step : S -> I -> S.
Variable cert : S -> bool.
Variable obs : S -> O.

Definition flips (s : S) (i : I) : bool :=
  negb (cert s) && cert (step s i).

Definition shadow_cost (price : O -> O -> nat) (s : S) (i : I) : nat :=
  price (obs s) (obs (step s i)).

Definition meets_floor (cost : S -> I -> nat) : Prop :=
  forall s i, flips s i = true -> cost s i >= 1.

Definition never_overcharges (cost : S -> I -> nat) : Prop :=
  forall s i, flips s i = false -> cost s i = 0.

Definition shadow_collision : Prop :=
  exists s1 i1 s2 i2,
    obs s1 = obs s2 /\
    obs (step s1 i1) = obs (step s2 i2) /\
    flips s1 i1 = true /\
    flips s2 i2 = false.

Theorem shadow_cannot_price_exactly :
  shadow_collision ->
  forall price,
    ~ (meets_floor (shadow_cost price) /\
       never_overcharges (shadow_cost price)).
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: \texttt{flips s i} says move $i$ takes $s$ from false to true. A shadow price
is any function of what the window shows before and after a step. \code{meets\_floor} says
every flip costs at least one, \code{never\_overcharges} says every step that isn't a flip costs
nothing, and a \code{shadow\_collision} is two steps that look the same through the window,
before and after, one a flip and one not. The theorem: given a collision, no shadow price does
both. Theorem~\ref{thm:shadow-price} bundles this with three neighbours from the same file:
that a price meeting the floor charges some non-flip at least one (\code{shadow\_floor\_overcharges}),
that a window showing the reading prices exactly
(\code{window\_showing\_reading\_prices\_exactly}), and that such a window has no collision
(\code{window\_showing\_reading\_has\_no\_collision}). This statement is the second of the four
clauses, and the book says exactly what it says.

\subsection{The record is a latch}

{\raggedright \code{record\_axis\_is\_latch\_holds}, coq/kernel/foundation/StructuralRecordAxis.v; the definitions come from StructuralCoreAnyBase.v and StructuralCoreCover.v.\par}

{\scriptsize
\begin{verbatim}
Definition record_permanent (M : RCM) : Prop :=
  forall s, rc_cert M s = true -> rc_cert M (rc_next M s) = true.

Definition computation_driven (M : RCM) (B : BaseMachine) (C : BaseCover M B)
  : Prop :=
  exists f : b_state B -> bool -> bool,
    forall m, rc_cert M (rc_next M m) = f (base_state M B C m) (rc_cert M m).

Definition HonestBaseExtension (M : RCM) (B : BaseMachine) (C : BaseCover M B)
  : Prop :=
  computation_driven M B C /\ ledger_carried M /\ rc_a2 M /\
  record_permanent M /\ reachable_record_write M.

Definition latch_next (B : BaseMachine) (h : b_state B -> bool)
    (x : b_state B * bool) : b_state B * bool :=
  (b_next B (fst x), orb (snd x) (h (fst x))).

Definition latch_factorization (M : RCM) (B : BaseMachine) (C : BaseCover M B)
    (h : b_state B -> bool) : Prop :=
  forall m,
    (base_state M B C (rc_next M m), rc_cert M (rc_next M m)) =
    latch_next B h (base_state M B C m, rc_cert M m).

Definition record_axis_is_latch : Prop :=
  forall M B C, HonestBaseExtension M B C ->
    exists h, latch_factorization M B C h.

Theorem record_axis_is_latch_holds : record_axis_is_latch.
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: here a machine $M$ steps by itself (\code{rc\_next} gives the one next
state), carries a reading \code{rc\_cert} and a ledger, and sits over a base $B$ through a
cover \code{C}, a map down to the base's states that commutes with the step.
\code{computation\_driven} says the reading's next value is some function \code{f} of the base
state and the reading's current value. Honest means driven, a ledger that never falls, the
toll, a permanent reading, and some reachable step that writes it. \code{latch\_next} is the
latch of an event \code{h}: the base steps, and the record becomes ``already on, or \code{h}
holds now.'' The theorem: every honest extension evolves exactly as the latch of some event.
Theorem~\ref{thm:u11-latch} says a little more than this statement: it names the event,
$h(b) = f(b, \mathrm{off})$, where the statement only says one exists. The proof builds exactly
that event (its first move is \texttt{exists (fun b => f b false)}), so it shows the theorem's
stronger form too. And the proof uses two of the five honesty
conditions, driven and permanent; the other three are carried along and never used.

\subsection{A raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified}

{\raggedright \code{earned\_certification\_provenance}, minimal/EarnedCore.v.\par}

{\tiny
\begin{verbatim}
Theorem earned_certification_provenance : forall s0 tr,
  clean_start s0 -> cert (run tr s0) = true ->
  exists pre1 p c mid1 mid2 post,
    tr = pre1 ++ CHECK p c :: mid1 ++ COMMIT p c :: mid2 ++ CERTIFY :: post /\
    check_ok (core_of (run pre1 s0)) p c = true /\
    commit_ok (core_of (run (pre1 ++ CHECK p c :: mid1) s0)) p c = true /\
    certify_ok (core_of (run (pre1 ++ CHECK p c :: mid1 ++ COMMIT p c :: mid2) s0))
      = true /\
    ver (core_of (run pre1 s0)) c = ver (core_of (run (pre1 ++ CHECK p c :: mid1) s0)) c /\
    untouched (run (pre1 ++ [CHECK p c]) s0) mid1 c.
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: the clean-start premise on \texttt{s0} says the fact table and the channel are
empty and the flag is down, and \texttt{run tr s0} runs a list of instructions. The theorem: from a clean start,
if the flag is up at the end, the list splits as some start, CHECK \texttt{p c}, a middle, COMMIT
of the same \texttt{p c}, another middle, CERTIFY, and the rest; the CHECK, the COMMIT and the
CERTIFY each pass where they run; the counter's version at the CHECK equals its version at the
COMMIT; and nothing in the first middle touched that counter. Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned}
says exactly this.

\subsection{Checker soundness}

{\raggedright \code{checker\_soundness}, minimal/EarnedCore.v.\par}

{\scriptsize
\begin{verbatim}
Theorem checker_soundness : forall s0 tr f,
  clean_start s0 ->
  let k := core_of (run tr s0) in
  In f (facts k) -> f_ver f = ver k (f_ctr f) -> holds (f_prop f) (val k (f_ctr f)).
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: from a clean start, after any list of instructions, every fact in the table
that's about its counter's current version is true of that counter's current value, where
\code{holds} is the property's meaning written without the checker.
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-soundness} says exactly this in its first sentence; its ``in particular''
is the next corollary in the file, \code{committed\_claim\_holds}.

\subsection{No forging}

{\raggedright \code{no\_forging}, minimal/EarnedCore.v, with the two definitions it uses.\par}

{\scriptsize
\begin{verbatim}
Definition earned (s0 : state) (tr : list instr) (f : fact) : Prop :=
  exists pre mid,
    tr = pre ++ CHECK (f_prop f) (f_ctr f) :: mid /\
    check_ok (core_of (run pre s0)) (f_prop f) (f_ctr f) = true /\
    f = claim (core_of (run pre s0)) (f_prop f) (f_ctr f) /\
    (f_ver f = ver (core_of (run tr s0)) (f_ctr f) ->
     untouched (run (pre ++ [CHECK (f_prop f) (f_ctr f)]) s0) mid (f_ctr f)).

Definition no_forgery (s0 : state) (tr : list instr) : Prop :=
  forall f, In f (facts (core_of (run tr s0))) -> earned s0 tr f.

Theorem no_forging : forall s0 tr, clean_start s0 -> no_forgery s0 tr.
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: a fact is \code{earned} when a passing CHECK of exactly that property and
counter wrote it somewhere in the list, it is exactly the claim that CHECK made, and, if it's
still about the counter's current version, nothing touched the counter since. \code{no\_forgery}
says every fact in the table at the end is earned. The theorem: from every clean start, every
list of instructions leaves no forgery. That's the last clause of
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-no-forging}, with Definition~\ref{def:u34-earned} saying the same as
\code{earned}; the two one-step clauses before it are \code{facts\_step} (one instruction at a core) and \code{no\_forging\_step} (a trace with no forgery stays that way when one instruction is added).

\subsection{The minimum price of a certificate}

{\raggedright \code{certified\_run\_min\_cost}, minimal/EarnedCore.v.\par}

{\footnotesize
\begin{verbatim}
Theorem certified_run_min_cost : forall s0 tr,
  clean_start s0 -> cert (run tr s0) = true ->
  total_cost tr >= 3 /\ mu (run tr s0) >= mu s0 + 3.
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: from a clean start, a list of instructions that ends with the flag up cost at
least three in total, and the ledger rose by at least three. Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-min-price}
says exactly this in its first sentence; its form for stored programs is
\code{program\_certified\_min\_cost}.

\subsection{Three, reached by a check that could have failed}

{\raggedright \code{earned\_run\_check\_can\_fail} and \code{earned\_run\_refused\_forever}, minimal/EarnedCore.v, with the program they run.\par}

{\scriptsize
\begin{verbatim}
Definition earned_run : list instr := [CHECK PZero CA; COMMIT PZero CA; CERTIFY].

Theorem earned_run_check_can_fail : forall a b,
  (a = 0 ->
     cert (run_prog 4 earned_run (start a b)) = true /\
     mu (run_prog 4 earned_run (start a b)) = 3) /\
  (a <> 0 ->
     cert (run_prog 4 earned_run (start a b)) = false /\
     err (core_of (run_prog 4 earned_run (start a b))) = true).

Theorem earned_run_refused_forever : forall n a b,
  a <> 0 -> cert (run_prog n earned_run (start a b)) = false.
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: \code{earned\_run} is CHECK ``$A$ is 0'', COMMIT the same, CERTIFY, and
\texttt{start a b} puts $a$ in $A$ and $b$ in $B$ with an empty table. The first theorem: run it
for four program steps; if $a$ is 0 the flag is up and the ledger is exactly 3, and if $a$
isn't 0 the flag is down and the trap is up. The second: if $a$ isn't 0, the flag is down after
any number of steps. So three is reached by a check that could have failed, and when it fails
nothing ever certifies. Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-tight} says this. The older witness in the same
file, \code{min\_cost\_tight}, reaches three with ``$A$ is at least 0'', a check that can't
fail; the step doesn't police that, and Section~\ref{sec:smallest} says so.

\subsection{Thiele-complete, the four clauses}

{\raggedright \code{thiele\_complete}, minimal/ThieleComplete.v, with the clauses it is made of. \texttt{load a b} is the interface's loaded state for the start $(1, a, b)$, written inside a section that fixes \texttt{I}; \texttt{run M} runs a list of moves from a state.\par}

{\scriptsize
\begin{verbatim}
Definition universal_base_clause : Prop :=
  (forall i, ti_kind I (ub_compile (ti_base I) i) = KBase) /\
  (forall a b, ti_clean I (load a b)) /\
  (forall s m, ti_kind I m = KBase -> m_record M (m_step M s m) = m_record M s) /\
  (forall s m, m_record M s = true -> m_record M (m_step M s m) = true).

Definition earned_chain (s0 : m_state M) (tr : list (m_move M)) : Prop :=
  exists pre c chk mid1 cmt mid2 crt post,
    tr = pre ++ chk :: mid1 ++ cmt :: mid2 ++ crt :: post /\
    ti_kind I chk = KCheck c /\ ti_kind I cmt = KCommit c /\ ti_kind I crt = KCertify /\
    ti_check I (run M pre s0) c = true /\
    (forall t1 t2, mid1 = t1 ++ t2 ->
       ti_same I c (run M pre s0) (run M (pre ++ chk :: t1) s0)) /\
    m_record M (run M (pre ++ chk :: mid1 ++ cmt :: mid2) s0) = false /\
    m_record M (run M (pre ++ chk :: mid1 ++ cmt :: mid2 ++ [crt]) s0) = true.

Definition earned_record_clause : Prop :=
  (forall s, ti_clean I s -> m_record M s = false) /\
  (forall s0 tr, ti_clean I s0 -> m_record M (run M tr s0) = true -> earned_chain s0 tr) /\
  (forall s c, ti_check I s c = true -> ti_meaning I c s) /\
  (forall c s s', ti_same I c s s' -> ti_meaning I c s -> ti_meaning I c s').

Definition record_move (m : m_move M) : nat :=
  match ti_kind I m with KBase => 0 | _ => 1 end.

Definition exact_toll_clause : Prop :=
  (forall m, m_cost M m = record_move m) /\
  (forall s m, ti_ledger I (m_step M s m) = ti_ledger I s + m_cost M m).

Definition non_vacuity_clause : Prop :=
  exists c chk cmt crt,
    ti_kind I chk = KCheck c /\ ti_kind I cmt = KCommit c /\ ti_kind I crt = KCertify /\
    (forall a b, m_record M (run M [chk; cmt; crt] (load a b)) = true <->
                 ti_meaning I c (load a b)) /\
    (exists a b, ti_meaning I c (load a b)) /\
    (exists a b, ~ ti_meaning I c (load a b)).

Definition thiele_complete_with : Prop :=
  universal_base_clause /\ earned_record_clause /\ exact_toll_clause /\ non_vacuity_clause.

Definition thiele_complete (M : machine) : Prop :=
  exists I : thiele_interface M, thiele_complete_with I.

Theorem clock_not_thiele_complete : forall rd, ~ thiele_complete (clock rd).
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: \texttt{M} is a machine (states, moves, step, cost, record) and \texttt{I} an
interface for it (a universal base, claims with meanings, a checker, ``unchanged,'' clean states,
a ledger, and a kind for each move). The first clause says the compiled two-counter moves are
base moves, loaded states are clean, base moves leave the record alone, and the record never comes
down; the universal base's own fields, not printed here, say the compiled moves act on the window
exactly as the two-counter instructions act. \code{earned\_chain} is a passing check of a claim,
then a commit of the same claim with the thing it's about unchanged at every point between, then
the certify that raises the record. The earned-record clause says clean states have the record
down, every run from a clean state that raises it contains that chain, a passing check means the
claim holds, and a claim that holds keeps holding while its thing is unchanged. The exact toll:
base moves cost 0, record moves 1, and the ledger adds each move's cost. Non-vacuity: some claim's
bare chain raises the record from a loaded state exactly when the claim holds there, and the claim
holds at one loaded state and fails at another. \code{thiele\_complete} asks for one interface
meeting all four. \texttt{clock} is the two-counter machine with every move costing 1 and any
reading of its configuration as the record. Definition~\ref{def:u34-thiele-complete} says
this and adds the weaker
notion, weakly Thiele-complete (\code{weakly\_thiele\_complete}, not printed here). Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-clock} says the last line and more: the clock is weakly
Thiele-complete (\code{clock\_weakly\_thiele\_complete}), a flag that switches on at the first yes
behaves the same way (\code{latch\_clock\_weakly\_thiele\_complete} and
\code{latch\_clock\_not\_thiele\_complete}), and no machine whose every move costs at least 1 is
Thiele-complete, which comes from \code{complete\_has\_free\_move}.

\subsection{The universal program's flag and ledger}

{\raggedright \code{universal\_halting}, \code{universal\_flag\_iff}, \code{universal\_ledger\_exact} and \code{universal\_thiele\_complete}, coq/kernel/foundation/UniversalRun.v.\par}

{\scriptsize
\begin{verbatim}
Theorem universal_halting : forall P x y,
  (exists m, E.halted P (E.core_of (grun P x y m))) <->
  (exists n, M.halted U (M.core_of (hrun P x y n))).

Theorem universal_flag_iff : forall P x y,
  (exists m, E.cert (grun P x y m) = true) <-> (exists n, M.cert (hrun P x y n) = true).

Theorem universal_ledger_exact : forall P x y,
  (forall m, exists n,
     ((rel P (grun P x y m) (hrun P x y n) /\ m <= n) \/
      rel_halt P (grun P x y m) (hrun P x y n)) /\
     M.mu (hrun P x y n) = E.mu (grun P x y m)) /\
  (forall n, exists m,
     E.mu (grun P x y m) <= M.mu (hrun P x y n) <= E.mu (grun P x y (S m))).

Theorem universal_thiele_complete : TC.thiele_complete host_machine.
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: \texttt{grun P x y m} is $m$ program steps of the small machine's program
$P$ from \texttt{start x y}; \texttt{hrun P x y n} is $n$ program steps of the one fixed host
program \texttt{U} from the host loaded with $P$, $x$ and $y$. The first theorem: the
guest halts at some step exactly when \texttt{U} does. The second: the guest's flag is up at some
step exactly when the host's is. The third: for every guest step count there's a host step count
where the two are related,
with the host count at least the guest count, or both stopped, with equal ledgers; and every host point's ledger lies
between the guest's at some step and at the step after. \texttt{rel} and \texttt{rel\_halt} are the
relations Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-U-sim} spells out. The fourth: the host machine, the small machine
with a register for every whole number and the one property \code{PSlot}, read one move per
instruction, is Thiele-complete in the sense of the previous subsection.
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-U-flag} says exactly the second and the third. Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-U-halting}
says the first and more: at halting the registers, the traps, the ledgers and the flags match too
(\code{universal\_output}, not printed here). Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-U-complete} says the fourth
and more: $U$'s run is a run of the host, the floor on the cost of a run that raises the flag, and the
undecidability of $U$'s halting, each with its own Coq theorem in the table of
Section~\ref{sec:crosswalk}.

\subsection{The copy is the record, on the simpler host}

{\raggedright \code{record\_agreement}, minimal/UniversalThiele.v.\par}

{\footnotesize
\begin{verbatim}
Definition agrees (h : hstate) : Prop := mrec h = E.cert (gst h).

Theorem record_agreement : forall tr h, agrees h -> agrees (hrun tr h).
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: the host keeps a mirror bit \code{mrec} beside the guest's state \code{gst},
and \texttt{agrees h} says the mirror equals the guest's own flag. The theorem: a host state that
agrees still agrees after any list of host moves, whatever they are.
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-mirror} says this for lists of moves and adds single moves, stored programs, loading,
and the mirror after $n$ moves GSTEP 1,
which are \code{record\_agreement\_step}, \code{record\_agreement\_program}, \code{hload\_agrees} and \code{simulated\_record}.

\subsection{No free host certification, on the simpler host}

{\raggedright \code{no\_free\_host\_certification}, minimal/UniversalThiele.v, with the host's moves and their costs.\par}

{\scriptsize
\begin{verbatim}
Inductive hinstr : Type :=
| OWN (i : E.instr)
| GSTEP (b : nat).

Definition hcost (i : hinstr) : nat :=
  match i with OWN j => E.cost j | GSTEP b => b end.

Definition crossing (g g' : E.state) : bool := negb (E.cert g) && E.cert g'.

Theorem no_free_host_certification : forall tr h,
  mrec h = false -> mrec (hrun tr h) = true ->
  exists pre b post, tr = pre ++ GSTEP b :: post /\ b >= 1 /\
    crossing (gst (hrun pre h)) (gst (hexec (hrun pre h) (GSTEP b))) = true.
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: a host move is either \texttt{OWN i}, one of the small machine's own
instructions on the host's core, or \texttt{GSTEP b}, one guest step with budget \code{b}, which
costs \code{b} whatever the guest instruction cost. \texttt{crossing g g'} says the guest's flag
went from down to up. The theorem: if the mirror is down before a list of host moves and up
after it, then somewhere in the list there's a \texttt{GSTEP b} with \code{b} at least one at
which the guest's flag crossed. Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-no-free-host} prints the one-move form,
\code{no\_free\_host\_certification\_step}, which also says the host wasn't trapped and the
guest's next instruction was CERTIFY; this is the form for whole lists that it lifts to. The printed theorem says two things more, each with its own Coq theorem: a trace of OWN moves alone leaves the mirror and
the guest state where they were (\code{guestless\_runs\_leave\_mirror}), and the host's own flag rises only by an OWN CERTIFY that passes (\code{own\_record\_only\_by\_certify}). Neither the one-move form nor the list form
says what the guest did before its CERTIFY. That, after a run from a loaded host, a raised mirror means
the guest's own run
checked and committed first is the next theorem.

\subsection{A raised mirror stands on the guest's own earned chain, on the simpler host}

{\raggedright \code{host\_mirror\_earned}, minimal/UniversalThiele.v.\par}

{\tiny
\begin{verbatim}
Theorem host_mirror_earned : forall tr a b P x y,
  mrec (hrun tr (hload a b P x y)) = true ->
  exists n gtr pre1 p c mid1 mid2 post,
    gtr = E.trace_of n P (E.start x y) /\
    gst (hrun tr (hload a b P x y)) = E.run gtr (E.start x y) /\
    gtr = pre1 ++ E.CHECK p c :: mid1 ++ E.COMMIT p c :: mid2 ++ E.CERTIFY :: post /\
    E.check_ok (E.core_of (E.run pre1 (E.start x y))) p c = true /\
    E.commit_ok (E.core_of (E.run (pre1 ++ E.CHECK p c :: mid1) (E.start x y))) p c
      = true /\
    E.certify_ok (E.core_of (E.run (pre1 ++ E.CHECK p c :: mid1 ++ E.COMMIT p c :: mid2)
                               (E.start x y))) = true /\
    E.ver (E.core_of (E.run pre1 (E.start x y))) c
      = E.ver (E.core_of (E.run (pre1 ++ E.CHECK p c :: mid1) (E.start x y))) c /\
    E.untouched (E.run (pre1 ++ [E.CHECK p c]) (E.start x y)) mid1 c.
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: load the host with a guest program $P$ and a guest start \texttt{(x, y)}
(\code{hload} gives the guest a clean start), run any list of host moves, and suppose the
mirror is up at the end. Then for some number of steps \code{n}, the guest's state is its own
program's run of \code{n} steps, and the instructions that run executed split exactly the way
Theorem~\ref{thm:u34-cert-earned} splits a trace: a passing CHECK, a COMMIT of the same claim at
the same version with the counter untouched between, then a passing CERTIFY. So the host's
mirror can't be up unless the guest's own program earned it. The book's sentences citing
\code{host\_mirror\_earned} say this in words; the Coq says a little more than they need, since the chain
sits inside the instructions the guest program itself executed. Any list containing the chain
would have been enough for them.

\subsection{Structural entitlement, represented}

{\raggedright \code{ent\_representation}, minimal/EntitlementSmall.v, with the definitions it leans on.\par}

{\tiny
\begin{verbatim}
Definition ent_strict_sublist (post prior : list X) : Prop :=
  incl post prior /\ exists x, In x prior /\ ~ In x post.

Definition ent_distinguishes (obs : X -> O) (w : X) (post : list X) : Prop :=
  forall t, In t post -> obs w <> obs t.

Definition ent_member (eqb : O -> O -> bool) (obs : X -> O) (L : list X) (o : O) : bool :=
  existsb (fun t => eqb (obs t) o) L.

Definition ent_stronger (P Q : O -> bool) : Prop :=
  forall o, P o = true -> Q o = true.

Definition ent_strictly_stronger (P Q : O -> bool) : Prop :=
  ent_stronger P Q /\ exists o, P o = false /\ Q o = true.

Definition ent_reduction (r : X -> O) (T : ent_tree) (prior post : list X) : Prop :=
  exists F : X -> list X,
    (forall x, In x prior -> exists t, In t post /\ In x (F t) /\ r x = r t) /\
    length prior <= fold_right Nat.add 0 (map (fun t => length (F t)) post) /\
    (forall t, In t post -> length (F t) <= ent_leaves T).

Definition ent_certified {M : machine} (I : thiele_interface M) {O : Type}
    (s0 : m_state M) (tr : list (m_move M))
    (d : list (m_move M) -> O) (P : O -> bool) : Prop :=
  m_record M (run M tr s0) = true /\ P (d tr) = true.

Theorem ent_representation :
  forall (M : machine) (I : thiele_interface M) (X O : Type)
         (s0 : m_state M) (tr : list (m_move M))
         (d : list (m_move M) -> O) (obs r : X -> O) (eqb : O -> O -> bool)
         (prior post : list X) (T : ent_tree),
    thiele_complete_with I ->
    (forall o1 o2, eqb o1 o2 = true <-> o1 = o2) ->
    ent_strict_sublist post prior ->
    (exists w, In w prior /\ ~ In w post /\ ent_distinguishes obs w post) ->
    ti_clean I s0 ->
    ent_certified I s0 tr d (ent_member eqb obs post) ->
    ent_depth T <= record_moves I tr ->
    0 < length post ->
    ent_reduction r T prior post ->
    ent_strictly_stronger (ent_member eqb obs post) (ent_member eqb obs prior) /\
    earned_chain I s0 tr /\
    (exists pre c chk mid1 cmt rest,
       tr = pre ++ chk :: mid1 ++ cmt :: rest /\
       ti_kind I chk = KCheck c /\ ti_kind I cmt = KCommit c /\
       ti_meaning I c (run M pre s0) /\ ti_meaning I c (run M (pre ++ chk :: mid1) s0)) /\
    Nat.log2_up (length prior) - Nat.log2_up (length post) <= record_moves I tr /\
    record_moves I tr = ti_ledger I (run M tr s0) - ti_ledger I s0 /\
    ti_ledger I s0 + 3 <= ti_ledger I (run M tr s0).
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: take a machine and an interface through which it is Thiele-complete, any type of
rivals $X$ and of observations $O$ with an exact equality test, a run $t$ from a clean
state $s_0$, and a decoder $d$ that reads the run's receipts, its list of moves. Hypotheses
in order: the posterior list is inside the prior and drops at least one rival; some dropped rival
shows an observation no survivor shows; the start is clean; the run ends with the record up and the
posterior's membership test accepts the decoded run; the tree is no deeper than the number of record
moves in the run; the posterior is non-empty; and the covering is by fibres, as
\code{ent\_reduction} spells out. Conclusions in order: the posterior's test is strictly stronger; the
run contains the earned chain; some CHECK of a claim and a later COMMIT of the same claim appear in the run, with the claim holding at both; the index
bits are at most the record moves; the record moves are exactly the ledger's rise; and the rise is at
least 3. Theorem~\ref{thm:ent-machine} says this, with the hypotheses numbered (M1) to (M6)
and the conclusions numbered (1) to (5), and it says one thing more in (2): there the meanings hold at the chain's own CHECK and COMMIT. The Coq's third conclusion is a separate existential that doesn't name
the chain; the printed form follows from it with the last two parts of clause (b), a passing check means the claim holds and an unchanged thing keeps it holding.

\subsection{A raised flag stands on the CHSH check}

{\raggedright \code{small\_chsh\_flag\_implies\_tsirelson}, coq/kernel/quantum/SmallChshMachine.v, over the host machine with the one property \code{small\_chsh\_PCHSH}.\par}

{\scriptsize
\begin{verbatim}
Theorem small_chsh_flag_implies_tsirelson :
  forall (s0 : @state small_chsh_prop) (tr : list (@instr small_chsh_prop)),
  clean_start s0 ->
  cert (run small_chsh_prop_eqb small_chsh_eval tr s0) = true ->
  exists pre1 c mid1 mid2 post,
    tr = pre1 ++ CHECK small_chsh_PCHSH c :: mid1
           ++ COMMIT small_chsh_PCHSH c :: mid2 ++ CERTIFY :: post /\
    let v := vals (core_of (run small_chsh_prop_eqb small_chsh_eval pre1 s0)) c in
    let t := small_chsh_tally_of v in
    small_chsh_check t = true /\
    small_chsh_meaning t /\
    (small_chsh_score t * small_chsh_score t <= 8)%R /\
    (Rabs (small_chsh_score t) <= 2 * sqrt 2)%R /\
    vals (core_of (run small_chsh_prop_eqb small_chsh_eval
                    (pre1 ++ CHECK small_chsh_PCHSH c :: mid1) s0)) c = v.
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: start from a clean start and run any list of instructions of the host machine whose
only property is the CHSH one, and suppose the flag is up at the end. Then the list splits as some
instructions, a CHECK of the property at some counter $c$, some more, a COMMIT of the same
property at the same counter, some more, a CERTIFY, and the rest. Take the value $v$ that
counter $c$ held just before the CHECK, and read it as a tally of eight counts. That tally
passes the seven integer facts (\code{small\_chsh\_check}); it means what the check is for: every
question pair sampled and the pinned five-by-five symmetric and positive semidefinite
(\code{small\_chsh\_meaning}); its score $S$ has $S^2 \le 8$ and $|S| \le 2\sqrt 2$; and counter
$c$ still held $v$ when the COMMIT ran. Because that tally passes the check, its score is in fact
strictly below the bound, $S^2 < 8$ (\code{nec\_e\_check\_strict}), and passing tallies come as
close to 8 as you like (\code{nec\_e\_check\_sharp}), both in NecEChsh.v. Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-earned} says exactly this in
its first part. It says more in two places that have their own Coq theorems, the stored-program form
and the converse that the three instructions certify exactly when the check passes, and the real
numbers in the statement are why it carries FE and RD, three standard-library assumptions in all, as printed in
Section~\ref{sec:crosswalk}.

\subsection{The recursion theorem up to the record, and no better}

{\raggedright \code{sm2\_kleene\_obs} and \code{sm2\_no\_exact}, coq/kernel/foundation/SmFixedPoint.v and coq/kernel/foundation/SmNoExact.v, with the relation they use. Here \code{M} is the host machine's module, \code{hends P x s} says program \code{P}, started with $x$ in register 1 and everything else clean, stops (a trap counts as stopping) in state \code{s}, and \code{sm\_computes\_map T F} says that on the number of every program \code{p}, \code{T} stops with the number of \code{F p}.\par}

{\scriptsize
\begin{verbatim}
Definition sm2_obs (s t : hstate) : Prop :=
  M.vals (M.core_of s) 0 = M.vals (M.core_of t) 0 /\
  M.err (M.core_of s) = M.err (M.core_of t) /\
  M.mu s = M.mu t /\ M.cert s = M.cert t /\
  length (M.facts (M.core_of s)) = length (M.facts (M.core_of t)) /\
  (M.chan (M.core_of s) = None <-> M.chan (M.core_of t) = None).

Definition sm2_obs_equiv (P Q : list hinstr) : Prop :=
  forall x,
    (forall s, hends P x s -> exists t, hends Q x t /\ sm2_obs s t) /\
    (forall t, hends Q x t -> exists s, hends P x s /\ sm2_obs s t).

Theorem sm2_kleene_obs : forall (F : list hinstr -> list hinstr) (T : list hinstr),
  sm_computes_map T F -> exists e, sm2_obs_equiv e (F e).

Theorem sm2_no_exact :
  exists (F : list hinstr -> list hinstr) (T : list hinstr),
    sm_computes_map T F /\ forall e, ~ hequiv e (F e).
\end{verbatim}}

In plain words: \code{sm2\_obs s t} says two final states agree on register 0, the trap latch, the
ledger, the flag, the number of facts and whether the channel is empty, and nothing else.
\code{sm2\_obs\_equiv P Q} says that on every input, any state \code{P} ends in has a state \code{Q}
ends in that agrees in that sense, and the same the other way round, which includes that \code{P}
stops on an input exactly when \code{Q} does. The first theorem: for every transformation $F$
of host programs that some host program \code{T} carries out on numbers, there is a program \code{e}
that agrees with \code{F e} in that sense. \code{T} is any host program, and may itself check, commit
and certify. The second: there is a transformation $F$, carried out by a host program, such that
no program \code{e} behaves the same as \code{F e} in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:host-same}, which
compares every register, the fact table, the channel, the trap latch, the ledger and the flag.
Theorems~\ref{thm:host-kleene-record} and~\ref{thm:host-no-exact} say these two. The book's printed
version says exactly this, with the line number and versions left out of both comparisons, as the
definition does.

%===========================================================================
\section{The CHSH derivation, in full}
\label{sec:chsh-derivation}
%===========================================================================

This appendix supports Section~\ref{sec:chsh}. That section tells the story; this one does the algebra. Each
item gives the exact statement with all its hypotheses, the steps a reader needs to check
it, and the Coq name with its file; the file paths in this appendix are under coq/. Nothing here identifies any matrix with a quantum
state. Where the reading ``quantum'' appears, it is a cited result from outside the kernel.

\subsection{A. Setting and notation}
\label{sub:chsh-notation}

\begin{definition}[Settings, outcomes, correlators]\label{def:chsh-setting}
Alice receives a setting $x \in \{0,1\}$ and Bob a setting $y \in \{0,1\}$. Each answers a
bit, recoded as an outcome $a, b \in \{+1, -1\}$ (bit 0 becomes $+1$, bit 1 becomes $-1$).
The correlator $E_{xy}$ is the average of the product $ab$ over the rounds with settings
$(x, y)$. The CHSH quantity is
\[
S = E_{00} + E_{01} + E_{10} - E_{11}.
\]
I collect the four correlators into the $2 \times 2$ matrix
\[
E = \begin{pmatrix} E_{00} & E_{01} \\ E_{10} & E_{11} \end{pmatrix},
\]
whose rows are indexed by Alice's setting and whose columns by Bob's. The rows of $E$ are
$(E_{00}, E_{01})$ and $(E_{10}, E_{11})$; the columns are $(E_{00}, E_{10})$ and
$(E_{01}, E_{11})$.
\end{definition}

The same polynomial $S$ appears under three names in the source: \code{CHSH}
(kernel/quantum/TsirelsonGeneral.v), \code{CHSH\_value} (kernel/quantum/TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v)
and \code{chsh\_S} (kernel/quantum/ElliptopeCompletion.v).

\begin{definition}[Counters]\label{def:chsh-counters}
Eight counts sit in the record \code{WitnessCounts}
(kernel/quantum/CHSHColumnCheck.v): for each setting pair, $\mathrm{same}_{xy}$ counts rounds
whose two answer bits matched and $\mathrm{diff}_{xy}$ counts rounds whose bits differed. A
round adds one to exactly one of the eight. Write
\[
N_{xy} = \mathrm{same}_{xy} + \mathrm{diff}_{xy}, \qquad
D_{xy} = \mathrm{same}_{xy} - \mathrm{diff}_{xy}, \qquad
E_{xy} = \frac{D_{xy}}{N_{xy}} .
\]
\end{definition}

A matched round contributes $ab = +1$ and a differing round $ab = -1$, so $D_{xy}$ is the sum
of the products and $D_{xy}/N_{xy}$ is their average. Since $|D_{xy}| \le N_{xy}$, every
correlator from counters lies in $[-1, 1]$. In Coq the integers are \code{chsh\_n\_z} and \code{chsh\_d\_z}
(kernel/quantum/CHSHColumnCheck.v). When a bucket is empty, the real-valued correlator
\code{state\_bucket\_correlation} (kernel/quantum/CHSHColumnCheck.v) and the rational one
\code{chsh\_correlator\_q} (kernel/quantum/CHSHStatisticalBridge.v) both return 0 by
convention. The CHSH score of a tally, \code{chsh\_stat\_from\_wc} (CHSHStatisticalBridge.v),
adds the first three correlators and obtains $-E_{11}$ by swapping the two counters of the
last bucket.

\subsection{B. The classical bound}
\label{sub:chsh-classical}

\begin{lemma}[Deterministic strategies]\label{lem:chsh-deterministic}
Let $a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1 \in \{+1, -1\}$. Then
$-2 \le a_0 b_0 + a_0 b_1 + a_1 b_0 - a_1 b_1 \le 2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Factor: $a_0 b_0 + a_0 b_1 + a_1 b_0 - a_1 b_1 = a_0(b_0 + b_1) + a_1(b_0 - b_1)$. If
$b_0 = b_1$ then $b_0 + b_1 = \pm 2$ and $b_0 - b_1 = 0$; if $b_0 \ne b_1$ the other way
round. In both cases exactly one of the two brackets is $\pm 2$ and the other is $0$, so the
expression is $\pm 2$ times a sign, which is $+2$ or $-2$. There are sixteen sign choices,
and every one of them gives exactly $\pm 2$. None gives $0$ or $\pm 4$.
\end{proof}

The Coq proofs do not factor; they split into the sixteen sign cases and compute. The
rational statement is \code{local\_S\_2\_deterministic} (kernel/quantum/BoxCHSH.v): for
$f_A, f_B : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Q}$ with every value $\pm 1$, the absolute value of
$f_A(0) f_B(0) + f_A(0) f_B(1) + f_A(1) f_B(0) - f_A(1) f_B(1)$ is at most 2. The real
statement is \code{deterministic\_strategy\_chsh\_bounded} (kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v),
with conclusion $-2 \le \cdots \le 2$.

\begin{definition}[Finite factorizable model, \code{is\_factorizable}]\label{def:chsh-factorizable}
A real-valued correlation function $E(a, b, x, y)$ is factorizable
(kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v) when there exist response functions $A(x, \lambda)$,
$B(y, \lambda)$, weights $p(\lambda)$ and a natural number $\lambda_{\max}$ such that:
$0 \le p(\lambda) \le 1$ for $\lambda \le \lambda_{\max}$;
$\sum_{\lambda = 0}^{\lambda_{\max}} p(\lambda) = 1$; every $A(x, \lambda)$ and every
$B(y, \lambda)$ is $-1$ or $+1$; and for all $a, b, x, y$,
$E(a, b, x, y) = \sum_{\lambda=0}^{\lambda_{\max}} p(\lambda) A(x, \lambda) B(y, \lambda)$.
The outcome arguments $a, b$ are dummies; only correlations are modelled.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[\code{fine\_theorem}, one direction only]\label{thm:chsh-fine}
If $E$ is factorizable, then $-2 \le E(0,0,0,0) + E(0,0,0,1) + E(0,0,1,0) - E(0,0,1,1) \le 2$
(kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v; restated as \code{factorizable\_CHSH\_classical\_bound}).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Substitute the factorization: $S = \sum_\lambda p(\lambda) S_\lambda$, where $S_\lambda$ is
the deterministic expression of Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-deterministic} at the signs
$A(\cdot, \lambda), B(\cdot, \lambda)$. Each $S_\lambda \in [-2, 2]$, the weights are
nonnegative and sum to 1, so $-2 = \sum_\lambda p(\lambda)(-2) \le S \le
\sum_\lambda p(\lambda) \cdot 2 = 2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the name does and does not cover]\label{rem:chsh-fine-scope}
Fine's 1982 theorem is an equivalence between several descriptions of local models and the
Bell inequalities. \code{fine\_theorem} proves one direction: a finite factorizable model obeys
the bound. Its converse, as it's stated, is false (\code{nec\_e\_fine\_converse\_false}); the
equivalence in the form Fine meant, for correlations, with each correlator between $-1$ and $1$ and all eight inequalities, is
\code{nec\_e\_fine\_iff}. And \code{fine\_theorem} covers only finitely many hidden states
($\lambda \le \lambda_{\max}$). An arbitrary probability space is outside it. The transfer to rational
boxes is \code{local\_box\_CHSH\_bound} (kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v): if
\textnormal{\texttt{box\_correlations B}} is factorizable then the real image of $|S(B)|$ is at most 2.
\end{remark}

The finite-tally statement concerns one fixed strategy replayed on every recorded round.

\begin{definition}[\code{WCLocallyConsistent}]\label{def:chsh-wclc}
For bits $a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1 \in \{0, 1\}$ and a counter record $w$
(kernel/quantum/CHSHStatisticalBridge.v), $w$ is locally consistent with
$(a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1)$ when, for each setting pair $(x, y)$: if $a_x = b_y$ then
$\mathrm{diff}_{xy} = 0$, otherwise $\mathrm{same}_{xy} = 0$; and every bucket is sampled,
$N_{00}, N_{01}, N_{10}, N_{11} > 0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[A tally above 2 is not one replayed strategy]\label{thm:chsh-tally}
Let $w$ be a counter record whose rational score \code{chsh\_stat\_from\_wc} $w$ is greater than 2.
Then for all bits $a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1$, $w$ is not locally consistent with
$(a_0, a_1, b_0, b_1)$. This is \code{chsh\_violation\_rules\_out\_locally\_factorizable\_coupling}
(kernel/quantum/CHSHCouplingBridge.v). A stronger companion,
\code{locally\_consistent\_classical\_bound}, states that a locally consistent record has
score of absolute value at most 2; read through its contrapositive, it gives the first statement.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Under local consistency each sampled bucket is pure: if $a_x = b_y$ every round in the
bucket matched, so $E_{xy} = N_{xy}/N_{xy} = +1$; otherwise every round differed and
$E_{xy} = -1$. In signs, $E_{xy} = \alpha_x \beta_y$ with $\alpha_x = (-1)^{a_x}$ and
$\beta_y = (-1)^{b_y}$. The score is then the deterministic expression of
Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-deterministic}, which is at most 2 in absolute value. A score above 2
contradicts this.
\end{proof}

The theorem rules out one explanation, a single four-bit plan used on every round. It says
nothing about a local model that redraws its hidden state every round; Section~\ref{sec:chsh} gives a four-round
coin-flip tally with score 4.

\subsection{C. Tsirelson's bound from algebra}
\label{sub:chsh-tsirelson-algebra}

\begin{lemma}[The six-square identity, \code{chsh\_gap\_is\_sum\_of\_squares}]\label{lem:chsh-sos}
For all real $a, b, c, d$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&4(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2) - (a + b + c - d)^2 \\
&\quad = (a-b)^2 + (a-c)^2 + (a+d)^2 + (b-c)^2 + (b+d)^2 + (c+d)^2 .
\end{aligned}
\]
(kernel/quantum/TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v, closed by \code{ring}.)
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand the square on the left:
$(a+b+c-d)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 + 2ab + 2ac - 2ad + 2bc - 2bd - 2cd$. So the left side is
\[
3(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2) - 2ab - 2ac + 2ad - 2bc + 2bd + 2cd .
\]
On the right, each variable appears in exactly three of the six brackets ($a$ in
$a-b$, $a-c$, $a+d$; $b$ in $a-b$, $b-c$, $b+d$; $c$ in $a-c$, $b-c$, $c+d$; $d$ in $a+d$,
$b+d$, $c+d$), so the squared terms add to $3(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)$. The cross terms are
$-2ab$ from $(a-b)^2$, $-2ac$ from $(a-c)^2$, $+2ad$ from $(a+d)^2$, $-2bc$ from $(b-c)^2$,
$+2bd$ from $(b+d)^2$ and $+2cd$ from $(c+d)^2$. Both sides agree term by term.
\end{proof}

Since the right side is a sum of squares, $S^2 \le 4 \sum_{xy} E_{xy}^2$ for any four reals;
this is \code{cauchy\_schwarz\_chsh} (TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v).

\begin{theorem}[Row-bound form of Tsirelson's bound]\label{thm:chsh-row-tsirelson}
For all real $E_{00}, E_{01}, E_{10}, E_{11}$ with $E_{00}^2 + E_{01}^2 \le 1$ and
$E_{10}^2 + E_{11}^2 \le 1$, $S^2 \le 8$. This is \code{tsirelson\_squared}
(kernel/quantum/TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v) and \code{tsirelson\_from\_row\_bounds}
(kernel/quantum/TsirelsonGeneral.v). The absolute form $|S| \le \sqrt 8 = 2\sqrt 2$ is
\code{tsirelson\_bound\_abs} (TsirelsonGeneral.v).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Adding the two row bounds gives $\sum_{xy} E_{xy}^2 \le 2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:chsh-sos},
$S^2 \le 4 \sum_{xy} E_{xy}^2 \le 8$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tightness]\label{thm:chsh-tight}
The point $E_{00} = E_{01} = E_{10} = 1/\sqrt 2$, $E_{11} = -1/\sqrt 2$ satisfies both row
bounds and has $S = \sqrt 8$. This is \code{tsirelson\_tight} (TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v) and
\code{tsirelson\_achievable} (TsirelsonGeneral.v).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each row has squared length $1/2 + 1/2 = 1$, and $S = 4/\sqrt 2 = 2\sqrt 2 = \sqrt 8$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Where equality can happen]\label{rem:chsh-equality}
The step about where equality happens is argued here and has no Coq theorem; the conclusion about
tallies at the end is checked as \code{nec\_e\_no\_sqrt8}, \code{nec\_e\_check\_strict},
\code{nec\_e\_check\_never\_tsirelson} and \code{nec\_e\_check\_sharp} (NecEChsh.v). Equality $S^2 = 8$ under the row bounds forces
equality in both steps of the proof above: the six squares must all vanish, which gives
$a = b = c = -d$, and the rows must be tight, which gives $2a^2 = 1$. So the point of
Theorem~\ref{thm:chsh-tight} and its negative are the only places the bound is reached. A tally's correlators are
ratios of whole numbers and $2a^2 = 1$ has no such solution, so no tally reaches the bound; the integer
check's passing tallies stay strictly below it and come as near as you like.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[A rational constant above the bound, \code{rational\_tsirelson\_bound}]\label{lem:chsh-rational}
$\sqrt 8 < 5657/2000$ (kernel/quantum/TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Both numbers are positive, so it suffices to compare squares. $5657^2 = 32{,}001{,}649$ and
$8 \cdot 2000^2 = 32{,}000{,}000$, so $(5657/2000)^2 = 32{,}001{,}649/4{,}000{,}000 > 8 =
(\sqrt 8)^2$. If $\sqrt 8 \ge 5657/2000$ held, squaring both nonnegative sides would give
$8 \ge (5657/2000)^2$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

The constant is the four-decimal round-up of $2\sqrt 2 = 2.8284271\ldots$; the gap is about
$7.3 \times 10^{-5}$. It lets rational code test ``above the Tsirelson bound'' without a square
root. It plays no part in the integer check of item E.

\subsection{D. The zero-marginal 5x5 moment matrix}
\label{sub:chsh-five}

\begin{definition}[The pinned level-1 matrix]\label{def:chsh-five}
\code{zero\_marginal\_npa} (kernel/quantum/NPAMomentMatrix.v) fills the general record
\code{NPAMomentMatrix} with all four one-party entries and both within-party entries set
to zero, and \code{npa\_to\_matrix} lays it out on rows and columns
$I, A_0, A_1, B_0, B_1$:
\end{definition}

\[
M(E) \;=\;
\begin{array}{c@{\quad}c}
 & \begin{array}{ccccc} I & A_0 & A_1 & B_0 & B_1 \end{array} \\
